Le Morte d'Arthur

King Arthur and his noble knights of the Round Table, retold complete and unabridged from Caxton's 1485 printing: all twenty-one books, from the sword in the stone to the passing of Arthur

by Sir Thomas Malory

1485 2026

This is an AI modernization of Le Morte d'Arthur into contemporary English. The original is available from Standard Ebooks. Also available as an epub.

Editor's Introduction

Sir Thomas Malory finished this book in the ninth year of the reign of Edward IV, which ran from March 1469 to March 1470, and he wrote it in prison. He says so himself: at the end of several sections he asks the reader to pray for "a knight prisoner." He was most likely the Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel in Warwickshire, a landowner and former member of Parliament who spent much of the 1450s and 1460s in jail on charges that included robbery, cattle-raiding and assault. He died in 1471. England in those years was in the middle of the Wars of the Roses, and the book's last section, in which the Round Table destroys itself in a civil war, was written by a man who had lived through one.

Malory did not invent the stories. He took the long French prose romances about Arthur, Lancelot, Tristram and the Holy Grail, along with two English poems about Arthur's death, and cut, combined and retold them in English prose. When he says "as the French book says," he means a real source. Fourteen years after his death, in 1485, William Caxton printed the work at Westminster, divided it into twenty-one Books, gave every chapter a heading summarising what happens in it, added a preface, and called the whole thing Le Morte d'Arthur, the Death of Arthur, although only the last part is about Arthur's death. A manuscript that differs from Caxton in many places was found at Winchester College in 1934. This edition follows Caxton's text, because Caxton's is the book that English readers knew for four and a half centuries.

Some things will seem strange at first. Knights fight constantly, often for reasons that are hard to follow, and the jousts are told with the same moves again and again. That repetition is the form: Malory is keeping score of who is the best knight in the world, and the score matters to the plot. Many names change spelling in the original and several people share a name, including at least four women called Elaine; here each person keeps one spelling. Malory's word "worship" means honour, and his narrator often stops to say where the story is going next.

This edition retells the whole book in modern English, including the three long Books about Tristram that most selections leave out, because the ending depends on them. Caxton's preface and his chapter headings are kept, and so are Malory's own closing prayer and Caxton's colophon. The text is Alfred Pollard's 1900 edition of Caxton.

  • Chapter 19: How King Arthur and Sir Gawain made a great army ready to cross the sea and make war on Sir Lancelot
  • Chapter 20: What message Sir Gawain sent to Sir Lancelot, and how King Arthur laid siege to Benwick, and other matters
  • Chapter 21: How Sir Lancelot and Sir Gawain fought together, and how Sir Gawain was overthrown and wounded
  • Chapter 22: Of the sorrow King Arthur felt for the war, and of another battle where Sir Gawain again got the worst of it

Book Twenty-One: King Arthur's Last Departing, and How Sir Lancelot Came to Avenge His Death

  • Chapter 1: How Sir Mordred presumed to make himself King of England, and tried to marry the queen, his father's wife
  • Chapter 2: How King Arthur, when he had the news, came back to Dover, where Sir Mordred met him to stop his landing, and of the death of Sir Gawain
  • Chapter 3: How afterwards Sir Gawain's ghost appeared to King Arthur, and warned him not to fight that day
  • Chapter 4: How by the mischance of an adder the battle began, in which Mordred was slain and Arthur mortally wounded

  • Chapter 6: How Sir Bedivere found King Arthur dead the next morning in a hermitage, and how he stayed there with the hermit

William Caxton's Preface

After I had completed and finished various histories, some of devotion and some of the deeds of great conquerors and princes in this world, and also certain books of examples and teaching, many noble gentlemen of this realm of England came to me and asked me, many times over, why I had not had made and printed the noble history of the Holy Grail, and of the most renowned Christian king, first and chief of the three best and worthiest Christians, King Arthur, who ought to be remembered among us Englishmen before all other Christian kings. For it is well known through all the world that there are nine worthies, the best that ever lived: that is to say, three pagans, three Jews, and three Christian men. As for the pagans, they lived before the Incarnation of Christ, and they were these: the first Hector of Troy, whose history has come down to us both in ballad and in prose; the second Alexander the Great; and the third Julius Caesar, Emperor of Rome, whose histories are well known and easy to come by. And as for the three Jews, who also lived before the incarnation of our Lord, the first was Joshua, the leader who brought the children of Israel into the Promised Land; the second David, king of Jerusalem; and the third Judas Maccabeus; and the Bible tells all their noble histories and deeds. And since that same Incarnation there have been three noble Christian men, installed and admitted through all the world into the number of the nine best and worthiest. The first of these was the noble Arthur, whose noble deeds I intend to set down in this present book that follows. The second was Charlemagne, or Charles the Great, whose history can be had in many places, both in French and in English. And the third and last was Godfrey of Bouillon, about whose deeds and life I made a book for the excellent prince and king of noble memory, King Edward the Fourth.

These noble gentlemen urgently asked me to print the history of that noble king and conqueror King Arthur, and of his knights, with the history of the Holy Grail, and of the death and ending of Arthur himself. They argued that I ought rather to print his deeds and noble feats than those of Godfrey of Bouillon or any of the other eight, considering that he was a man born within this realm, and king and emperor of it, and that there are in French many and various noble volumes of his deeds, and of his knights' too. I answered them that various men hold the opinion that there was no such Arthur, and that all the books made about him are invented stories and fables, because some chronicles make no mention of him at all, and do not remember him or his knights. To this they answered, and one of them in particular said, that anyone who should say or think that there was never such a king called Arthur might well be charged with great folly and blindness. For he said that there was plenty of evidence to the contrary. First, you may see his tomb in the monastery of Glastonbury. And also in the Polychronicon, in the fifth book, the sixth chapter, and in the seventh book, the twenty-third chapter, you may read where his body was buried, and afterwards found, and moved into that monastery. You will see also in the history of Boccaccio, in his book De Casu Principum, "On the Fall of Princes", part of his noble deeds, and also of his fall. Also Geoffrey of Monmouth tells his life in his British book. And in various places of England there are many memorials of him still, and of his knights, and they will remain forever. First, in the abbey of Westminster, at St. Edward's shrine, there is still the print of his seal in red wax enclosed in beryl, on which is written "Patricius Arthurus Britannie, Gallie, Germanie, Dacie, Imperator", that is, "The noble Arthur, Emperor of Britain, Gaul, Germany and Denmark". Item: in the castle of Dover you may see Gawain's skull and Cradok's mantle; at Winchester, the Round Table; in other places Lancelot's sword and many other things. Then, all these things considered, no man can reasonably deny that there was a king of this land named Arthur. For in all places, Christian and heathen, he is reputed and counted one of the nine worthies, and the first of the three Christian men. And besides, he is more spoken of across the sea, and more books are made of his noble deeds there, than there are in England, in German, Italian, Spanish and Greek as well as in French. And there still remain as witnesses to him in Wales, in the town of Camelot, the great stones and the marvellous works of iron lying under the ground, and royal vaults, which various people now living have seen. So it is a marvel that he is not more renowned in his own country, except that it agrees with the Word of God, which says that no man is accepted as a prophet in his own country.

So, with all these things put to me, I could not well deny that there was such a noble king named Arthur, reputed one of the nine worthies, and first and chief of the Christian men. And many noble volumes have been made of him and of his noble knights in French, which I have seen and read across the sea, and which we do not have in our mother tongue. In Welsh there are many, and in French too, and some in English, but nowhere near all of them. Therefore, out of those that have lately been drawn out briefly into English, I have, according to the simple skill that God has sent me, and under the favour and correction of all noble lords and gentlemen, undertaken to print a book of the noble histories of this King Arthur and of certain of his knights, from a copy delivered to me, which copy Sir Thomas Malory took out of certain books in French and turned into English. And I, following my copy, have had it set in print, so that noble men may see and learn the noble deeds of chivalry, the noble and virtuous deeds that some knights did in those days, by which they came to honour, and how those who were wicked were punished and often put to shame and rebuke. And I humbly beg all noble lords and ladies, and all other people of whatever rank or degree they are, who see and read this book and work, to keep the good and honest deeds in their memory, and to follow them. In it they will find many joyful and pleasant histories, and noble and renowned deeds of humanity, nobility and chivalry. For here may be seen noble chivalry, courtesy, humanity, friendliness, hardiness, love, friendship, cowardice, murder, hate, virtue and sin. Follow the good and leave the evil, and it will bring you to good fame and renown. And to pass the time, this book will be pleasant to read in; but as for putting faith and belief in all that it contains being true, you are at your liberty. But all of it is written for our instruction, and so that we take care not to fall into vice or sin, but practise and follow virtue, by which we may come and attain to good fame and renown in this life, and after this short and passing life come to everlasting bliss in heaven: which may He grant us who reigns in heaven, the blessed Trinity. Amen.

Then, to proceed with this book, which I dedicate to all noble princes, lords and ladies, gentlemen and gentlewomen, who wish to read or hear read the noble and joyful history of the great conqueror and excellent king, King Arthur, once king of this noble realm, then called Britain: I, William Caxton, a simple person, present this book that follows, which I have undertaken to print. It treats of the noble deeds, feats of arms and of chivalry, prowess, hardiness, humanity, love, courtesy and true nobility, with many wonderful histories and adventures. And so that the contents of this volume can be understood briefly, I have divided it into twenty-one Books, and every book into chapters, as will follow hereafter, by God's grace. The First Book will tell how Uther Pendragon fathered the noble conqueror King Arthur, and contains twenty-eight chapters. The Second Book tells of Balin the noble knight, and contains nineteen chapters. The Third Book tells of the marriage of King Arthur to Queen Guinevere, with other matters, and contains fifteen chapters. The Fourth Book tells how Merlin was besotted, and of war made on King Arthur, and contains twenty-nine chapters. The Fifth Book tells of the conquest of Lucius the emperor, and contains twelve chapters. The Sixth Book tells of Sir Lancelot and Sir Lionel, and of marvellous adventures, and contains eighteen chapters. The Seventh Book tells of a noble knight called Sir Gareth, whom Sir Kay named Beaumains, and contains thirty-six chapters. The Eighth Book tells of the birth of Sir Tristram the noble knight, and of his deeds, and contains forty-one chapters. The Ninth Book tells of a knight whom Sir Kay named La Cote Male Taile, and also of Sir Tristram, and contains forty-four chapters. The Tenth Book tells of Sir Tristram and other marvellous adventures, and contains eighty-eight chapters. The Eleventh Book tells of Sir Lancelot and Sir Galahad, and contains fourteen chapters. The Twelfth Book tells of Sir Lancelot and his madness, and contains fourteen chapters. The Thirteenth Book tells how Galahad first came to King Arthur's court, and how the quest of the Holy Grail was begun, and contains twenty chapters. The Fourteenth Book tells of the quest of the Holy Grail, and contains ten chapters. The Fifteenth Book tells of Sir Lancelot, and contains six chapters. The Sixteenth Book tells of Sir Bors and Sir Lionel his brother, and contains seventeen chapters. The Seventeenth Book tells of the Holy Grail, and contains twenty-three chapters. The Eighteenth Book tells of Sir Lancelot and the queen, and contains twenty-five chapters. The Nineteenth Book tells of Queen Guinevere and Lancelot, and contains thirteen chapters. The Twentieth Book tells of the piteous death of Arthur, and contains twenty-two chapters. The Twenty-first Book tells of his last departing, and how Sir Lancelot came to avenge his death, and contains thirteen chapters. The sum is twenty-one books, which contain in all five hundred and seven chapters, as will be shown more plainly hereafter.

Book One: The Birth of King Arthur

Chapter 1: How Uther Pendragon sent for the Duke of Cornwall and his wife Igraine, and how they suddenly left

It happened in the days of Uther Pendragon, when he was king of all England and reigned there, that there was a mighty duke in Cornwall who made war on him for a long time. And the duke was called the Duke of Tintagil. And so, through go-betweens, King Uther sent for this duke, ordering him to bring his wife with him, for she was said to be a beautiful lady, and an exceedingly wise one, and her name was Igraine.

So when the duke and his wife had come to the king, the great lords worked between them and the two men were reconciled. The king liked this lady and loved her well, and he gave them a welcome beyond measure, and wanted to sleep with her. But she was an exceedingly good woman, and would not consent to the king. And then she told the duke her husband, and said, "I think we were sent for so that I should be dishonoured. So, husband, I advise you that we leave here at once, so that we can ride all night to our own castle."

And just as she said, so they left, so that neither the king nor any of his council knew they had gone. As soon as King Uther learned of their leaving so suddenly, he was furiously angry. Then he called his privy council to him and told them of the sudden departure of the duke and his wife.

Then they advised the king to send for the duke and his wife with a stern command: "And if he will not come at your summons, then you may do as you see fit; then you will have good cause to make mighty war on him." So that was done, and the messengers brought back their answers; and in short it was this, that neither he nor his wife would come to him.

Then the king was furiously angry. And then the king sent him plain word in return, and told him to make ready, and stock and arm his castles, for within forty days he would fetch him out of the strongest castle he had.

When the duke had this warning, he went at once and stocked and armed two strong castles of his, of which one was called Tintagil and the other Terrabil. So he put his wife Dame Igraine in the castle of Tintagil, and himself in the castle of Terrabil, which had many exits and back gates. Then Uther came in all haste with a great army and laid siege to the castle of Terrabil. And there he pitched many tents, and there was great fighting on both sides, and many people were killed. Then, out of sheer anger and great love for the fair Igraine, King Uther fell sick. So Sir Ulfius, a noble knight, came to King Uther and asked the king why he was sick.

"I'll tell you," said the king. "I am sick with anger and with love for the fair Igraine, so that I cannot be well."

"Well, my lord," said Sir Ulfius, "I will go and look for Merlin, and he will find you a remedy that will content your heart."

So Ulfius set off, and by chance he met Merlin dressed as a beggar, and Merlin asked Ulfius who he was looking for. And he said he had little reason to tell him.

"Well," said Merlin, "I know who you are looking for, for you are looking for Merlin. So look no further, for I am he. And if King Uther will reward me well, and swear to me to grant my wish, that will bring him more honour and profit than me; for I will see that he has all he desires."

"All this I will undertake," said Ulfius, "that there will be nothing within reason that you shall not have as you wish."

"Well," said Merlin, "he will have his purpose and his desire. And so," said Merlin, "ride on your way, for I will not be far behind."

Chapter 2: How Uther Pendragon made war on the Duke of Cornwall, and how through Merlin he lay with the duchess and fathered Arthur

Then Ulfius was glad, and rode on at better than a walking pace until he came to King Uther Pendragon, and told him he had met with Merlin.

"Where is he?" said the king.

"Sir," said Ulfius, "he will not be long."

With that Ulfius saw Merlin standing in the doorway of the tent. And then Merlin was obliged to come to the king. When King Uther saw him, he said he was welcome.

"Sir," said Merlin, "I know every bit of your heart. If you will swear to me, as you are a true anointed king, to grant my wish, you shall have your desire."

Then the king swore upon the Four Gospels.

"Sir," said Merlin, "this is my wish: the first night that you lie with Igraine you will father a child on her, and when it is born it must be handed over to me, for me to bring up wherever I choose. For it will be to your honour, and to the child's good, as much as the child is worth."

"Gladly," said the king. "Let it be as you wish."

"Now make yourself ready," said Merlin. "This very night you will lie with Igraine in the castle of Tintagil. And you will look like the duke her husband, Ulfius will look like Sir Brastias, a knight of the duke's, and I will look like a knight called Sir Jordanus, another knight of the duke's. But take care you do not make much conversation with her or her people, but say you are unwell, and so get yourself to bed, and do not get up in the morning until I come to you, for the castle of Tintagil is only ten miles from here."

So this was done as they had planned. But the Duke of Tintagil saw the king ride away from the siege of Terrabil, and so that night he sallied out of the castle by a back gate to attack the king's army. And so, by his own sally, the duke himself was killed before ever the king came to the castle of Tintagil.

So after the death of the duke, King Uther lay with Igraine, more than three hours after his death, and fathered Arthur on her that night. And at daybreak Merlin came to the king and told him to make ready, and so he kissed the lady Igraine and left in all haste. But when the lady heard the news of the duke her husband, and that by every account he was dead before ever King Uther came to her, then she wondered who it could be that had lain with her in the likeness of her lord. So she mourned in private and held her peace.

Then all the barons with one voice begged the king to make peace between the lady Igraine and himself. The king gave them leave, for he would gladly have been reconciled with her. So the king put all his trust in Ulfius to negotiate between them, and through his negotiating the king and she at last met together.

"Now we will do well," said Ulfius. "Our king is a vigorous knight and has no wife, and my lady Igraine is an exceedingly beautiful lady. It would be a great joy to us all if it pleased the king to make her his queen."

To that they all agreed, and put it to the king. And at once, like the vigorous knight he was, he agreed to it gladly, and so in all haste they were married one morning with great merriment and joy.

And King Lot of Lothian and of Orkney then married Morgause, who was Gawain's mother, and King Nentres of the land of Garlot married Elaine. All this was done at King Uther's request. And the third sister, Morgan le Fay, was sent to school in a nunnery, and there she learned so much that she became a great scholar of necromancy, the black art. And afterwards she was married to King Uriens of the land of Gore, who was the father of Sir Uwain le Blanchemains.

Chapter 3: Of the birth of King Arthur and of his upbringing

Then Queen Igraine grew bigger and bigger day by day. And so it happened, within half a year, as King Uther lay beside his queen, that he asked her, by the faith she owed him, whose child she carried. Then she was badly flustered about how to answer.

"Don't be dismayed," said the king, "but tell me the truth, and I will love you the better for it, on my life."

"Sir," she said, "I will tell you the truth. The same night that my lord died, at the hour of his death, as his knights bear witness, there came into my castle of Tintagil a man like my lord in speech and in face, and two knights with him in the likeness of his two knights Brastias and Jordanus. And so I went to bed with him, as I ought to do with my lord, and that same night, as I shall answer to God, this child was conceived in me."

"That is the truth," said the king, "as you say. For it was I myself who came in that likeness. And so do not be dismayed, for I am the father of the child."

And there he told her the whole story, how it was done on Merlin's advice. Then the queen was overjoyed when she knew who was the father of her child.

Soon Merlin came to the king, and said, "Sir, you must make provision for the bringing up of your child."

"As you wish," said the king. "Let it be so."

"Well," said Merlin, "I know a lord of yours in this land who is an exceedingly true man and a faithful one, and he shall have the bringing up of your child. His name is Sir Ector, and he is a lord with fine estates in many parts of England and Wales. Have this lord, Sir Ector, sent for to come and speak with you, and ask him yourself, as he loves you, to put his own child out to be nursed by another woman, so that his wife can nurse yours. And when the child is born, let it be handed over to me at that secret back gate over there, unchristened."

So it was done just as Merlin planned. And when Sir Ector came he gave his solemn promise to the king to bring up the child as the king wished; and there the king granted Sir Ector great rewards. Then, when the lady had given birth, the king commanded two knights and two ladies to take the child, wrapped in a cloth of gold, "and hand him over to whatever poor man you meet at the back gate of the castle." So the child was handed over to Merlin, and so he carried it away to Sir Ector, and had a holy man christen him, and named him Arthur. And so Sir Ector's wife nursed him at her own breast.

Chapter 4: Of the death of King Uther Pendragon

Then, within two years, King Uther fell sick of a great illness. And meanwhile his enemies encroached on his lands, and fought a great battle against his men, and killed many of his people.

"Sir," said Merlin, "you cannot lie here as you are doing, for you must go to the field even if you ride in a horse-litter. For you will never get the better of your enemies unless you are there in person, and then you will have the victory."

So it was done as Merlin had planned, and they carried the king out in a horse-litter with a great army against his enemies. And at St. Albans a great army from the North met the king. And that day Sir Ulfius and Sir Brastias did great deeds of arms, and King Uther's men overcame the northern army and killed many people, and put the rest to flight. And then the king returned to London, and rejoiced greatly in his victory. And then he fell desperately sick, so that for three days and three nights he could not speak. At this all the barons grieved greatly, and asked Merlin what would be the best thing to do.

"There is no other remedy," said Merlin, "but God will have His will. But see that all you barons are before King Uther tomorrow, and God and I will make him speak."

So in the morning all the barons came before the king with Merlin. Then Merlin said aloud to King Uther, "Sir, shall your son Arthur be king of this realm after your days, with all that belongs to it?"

Then Uther Pendragon turned over and said, in the hearing of them all, "I give him God's blessing and mine, and bid him pray for my soul, and claim the crown rightfully and honourably, on pain of losing my blessing."

And with that he gave up the ghost, and then he was buried as befitted a king. And the queen, the fair Igraine, grieved greatly, and so did all the barons.

Chapter 5: How Arthur was chosen king, and of the wonders and marvels of a sword drawn out of a stone by Arthur

Then the realm stood in great danger for a long while, for every lord who had many men at his command made himself strong, and many expected to be king. Then Merlin went to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and advised him to send for all the lords of the realm, and all the gentlemen of arms, to come to London by Christmas, on pain of excommunication. And this was the reason: that Jesus, who was born on that night, would of His great mercy show some miracle, as He had come to be king of mankind, to show by some miracle who should be the rightful king of this realm. So the Archbishop, on Merlin's advice, sent for all the lords and gentlemen of arms to come to London by Christmas Eve. And many of them cleansed their lives, so that their prayers might be the more acceptable to God. So in the greatest church of London (whether it was St. Paul's or not, the French book does not say) all the ranks of the realm were in the church to pray, long before daybreak. And when matins and the first mass were over, there was seen in the churchyard, facing the high altar, a great square stone, like a block of marble, and in the middle of it was something like an anvil of steel, a foot high, and in it a fine sword was stuck naked by the point, and around the sword there were letters written in gold that said this: "Whoever pulls this sword out of this stone and anvil is the true-born king of all England." Then the people marvelled, and told the Archbishop.

"I command," said the Archbishop, "that you keep yourselves within your church and go on praying to God, and that no man touch the sword until high mass is all done."

So when all the masses were done, all the lords went to look at the stone and the sword. And when they saw the inscription, some tried, those who wanted to be king. But none of them could stir the sword or move it.

"He is not here," said the Archbishop, "who will win this sword, but have no doubt God will make him known. But this is my advice," said the Archbishop, "that we provide ten knights, men of good name, to guard this sword."

So it was arranged, and then a proclamation was made that every man who wished should try to win the sword. And for New Year's Day the barons had jousts and a tournament proclaimed, so that all knights who wanted to joust or to fight in the tournament could take part; and all this was arranged to keep the lords and the common people together, for the Archbishop trusted that God would make known the one who should win the sword.

So on New Year's Day, when the service was over, the barons rode to the field, some to joust and some to fight in the tournament. And so it happened that Sir Ector, who had large estates around London, rode to the jousts, and with him rode Sir Kay his son, and young Arthur, who was his foster brother; and Sir Kay had been made a knight the All Hallows' Day before. So as they rode towards the jousts, Sir Kay found he had lost his sword, for he had left it at his father's lodging, and so he asked young Arthur to ride back for his sword.

"Gladly," said Arthur, and rode fast after the sword. And when he got home, the lady and everyone else were out to see the jousting. Then Arthur was angry, and said to himself, "I will ride to the churchyard and take the sword that is stuck in the stone, for my brother Sir Kay shall not be without a sword this day."

So when he came to the churchyard, Sir Arthur dismounted and tied his horse to the stile, and so he went to the tent, and found no knights there, for they were at the jousting. And so he took hold of the sword by the handle, and lightly and fiercely pulled it out of the stone, and took his horse and rode on his way until he came to his brother Sir Kay, and gave him the sword. And as soon as Sir Kay saw the sword, he knew very well it was the sword from the stone, and so he rode to his father Sir Ector, and said, "Sir, look, here is the sword from the stone, and so I must be king of this land."

When Sir Ector saw the sword, he turned back and came to the church, and there all three of them dismounted and went into the church. And at once he made Sir Kay swear on a holy book how he came by that sword.

"Sir," said Sir Kay, "by my brother Arthur, for he brought it to me."

"How did you get this sword?" said Sir Ector to Arthur.

"Sir, I will tell you. When I came home for my brother's sword, I found nobody at home to give me his sword. And so I thought my brother Sir Kay should not be without a sword, and so I came here in a hurry and pulled it out of the stone without any trouble."

"Did you find any knights around this sword?" said Sir Ector.

"No," said Arthur.

"Now," said Sir Ector to Arthur, "I understand that you must be king of this land."

"Why me," said Arthur, "and for what reason?"

"Sir," said Ector, "because God wills it so. For no man could ever have drawn out this sword except the one who shall be the rightful king of this land. Now let me see whether you can put the sword back where it was, and pull it out again."

"That's no great feat," said Arthur, and so he put it back in the stone. Then Sir Ector tried to pull out the sword, and failed.

Chapter 6: How King Arthur pulled out the sword several times

"Now you try," said Sir Ector to Sir Kay.

And at once he pulled at the sword with all his might, but it would not budge.

"Now you shall try," said Sir Ector to Arthur.

"Gladly," said Arthur, and pulled it out easily.

And with that Sir Ector knelt down on the ground, and Sir Kay too.

"Alas," said Arthur, "my own dear father and brother, why are you kneeling to me?"

"No, no, my lord Arthur, it is not so. I was never your father, nor of your blood, but I know well that you are of higher blood than I thought you were."

And then Sir Ector told him everything: how he had been entrusted with him to bring him up, and by whose command, and how Merlin had handed him over.

Then Arthur grieved greatly when he understood that Sir Ector was not his father.

"Sir," said Ector to Arthur, "will you be my good and gracious lord when you are king?"

"I would be much to blame otherwise," said Arthur, "for you are the man in the world I owe most to, you and my good lady and mother, your wife, who has fostered me and cared for me as well as her own. And if it is ever God's will that I am king, as you say, you shall ask of me whatever I can do, and I will not fail you. God forbid I should fail you."

"Sir," said Sir Ector, "I will ask no more of you than that you make my son, your foster brother, Sir Kay, seneschal, the steward over all your lands."

"That shall be done," said Arthur, "and more, on my life: no man shall ever have that office but him, while he and I live."

With that they went to the Archbishop, and told him how the sword had been won, and by whom. And on Twelfth Day all the barons came there to try to take the sword, whoever wanted to try. But there, in front of them all, none could take it out but Arthur. At this many lords were angry, and said it was a great shame to them all and to the realm to be ruled over by a boy not born of high blood. And so they quarrelled that time, so that it was put off until Candlemas, when all the barons were to meet there again. But all the while the ten knights were appointed to guard the sword day and night, and so they set a tent over the stone and the sword, and five were always on watch. So at Candlemas many more great lords came there to win the sword, but none could succeed. And just as Arthur had done at Christmas, he did at Candlemas, and pulled out the sword easily, at which the barons were bitterly aggrieved, and put it off again until the high feast of Easter. And as Arthur had done before, so he did at Easter. Yet there were some of the great lords who resented that Arthur should be king, and put it off again until the feast of Pentecost.

Then the Archbishop of Canterbury, by Merlin's foresight, had the best knights they could find brought together, those knights whom Uther Pendragon had loved best and trusted most in his day. And knights such as these were set about Arthur: Sir Baudwin of Britain, Sir Kay, Sir Ulfius, Sir Brastias. All these, with many others, were always about Arthur, day and night, until the feast of Pentecost.

Chapter 7: How King Arthur was crowned, and how he appointed officers

And at the feast of Pentecost all kinds of men who wished to try pulled at the sword, but none could succeed but Arthur, and he pulled it out before all the lords and common people who were there. At this all the common people cried out together, "We will have Arthur for our king! We will put him off no longer, for we all see that it is God's will that he shall be our king, and whoever holds out against it, we will kill him."

And with that they all knelt at once, both rich and poor, and begged Arthur's pardon for having put him off so long. And Arthur forgave them, and took the sword in both his hands, and offered it on the altar where the Archbishop was, and so he was made a knight by the best man who was there. And so the coronation was held at once. And there he swore to his lords and the common people to be a true king, and to stand by true justice from then on, all the days of his life. Then too he made all the lords who held land from the crown come in and do their service as they ought to do. And many complaints were made to Sir Arthur of great wrongs done since the death of King Uther, of many lands that had been taken from lords, knights, ladies and gentlemen. So King Arthur had the lands given back to those who owned them.

When this was done, and the king had settled all the country around London, then he made Sir Kay seneschal of England; and Sir Baudwin of Britain was made constable; and Sir Ulfius was made chamberlain; and Sir Brastias was made warden, to keep watch on the north from the Trent onwards, for at that time it was for the most part the king's enemies. But within a few years Arthur won all the north, Scotland, and all that were under their rule. Part of Wales also held out against Arthur, but he overcame them all, as he did the rest, through his own noble prowess and that of his knights of the Round Table.

Chapter 8: How King Arthur held a great feast in Wales at Pentecost, and what kings and lords came to his feast

Then the king moved into Wales, and had a great feast proclaimed, to be held at Pentecost after his coronation, in the city of Caerleon. To the feast came King Lot of Lothian and of Orkney, with five hundred knights. Also there came to the feast King Uriens of Gore, with four hundred knights. Also there came to that feast King Nentres of Garlot, with seven hundred knights. Also there came to the feast the King of Scotland, with six hundred knights, and he was only a young man. Also there came to the feast a king who was called the King with the Hundred Knights, and he and his men were exceedingly well equipped in every way. Also there came the King of Carados with five hundred knights. And King Arthur was glad of their coming, for he thought that all the kings and knights had come out of great love, and to do him honour at his feast. So the king rejoiced greatly, and sent the kings and knights rich presents. But the kings would accept none of them, and sent the messengers back shamefully rebuked, and said they had no wish to receive gifts from a beardless boy of low birth, and sent him word that they would have none of his gifts, but that they had come to give him gifts with hard swords between the neck and the shoulders. And that was why they had come, as they told the messengers plainly, for it was a great shame to them all to see such a boy have rule over so noble a realm as this land was. With this answer the messengers left, and told King Arthur this answer. So, on the advice of his barons, he withdrew into a strong tower with five hundred good men. And all the kings named above laid siege to him there, after a fashion; but King Arthur was well supplied with food. And within fifteen days Merlin came among them into the city of Caerleon. Then all the kings were exceedingly glad of Merlin, and asked him, "For what reason has that boy Arthur been made your king?"

"Sirs," said Merlin, "I will tell you the reason. It is because he is King Uther Pendragon's son, born in wedlock, conceived on Igraine, the wife of the Duke of Tintagil."

"Then he is a bastard," they all said.

"No," said Merlin. "Arthur was conceived more than three hours after the death of the duke, and thirteen days after that King Uther married Igraine; and so I prove to you that he is no bastard. And whoever says no to it, he shall be king and overcome all his enemies; and before he dies he shall be king of all England for a long time, and have under his rule Wales, Ireland and Scotland, and more realms than I will name now."

Some of the kings marvelled at Merlin's words, and judged that it would be as he said; and some of them laughed him to scorn, as King Lot did; and others called him a wizard. But then they came to an agreement with Merlin that King Arthur should come out and speak with the kings, and come safely and go safely: such a guarantee was given. So Merlin went to King Arthur and told him what he had done, and told him not to be afraid, but to come out boldly and speak with them, and not spare them, but answer them as their king and chieftain, "for you will overcome them all, whether they like it or not."

Chapter 9: Of the first war that King Arthur fought, and how he won the day

Then King Arthur came out of his tower, and under his gown he wore a short coat of double mail, and with him went the Archbishop of Canterbury, and Sir Baudwin of Britain, and Sir Kay, and Sir Brastias: these were the men of greatest honour that were with him. And when they met there was no meekness, but bold words on both sides; but King Arthur always answered them, and said he would make them bow if he lived. So they parted in anger, and King Arthur told them to look to themselves, and they told the king to look to himself. So the king went back to the tower again and armed himself and all his knights.

"What will you do?" said Merlin to the kings. "You had better stop, for you will not win here, even if you were ten times as many."

"Are we well advised to be afraid of a dream-reader?" said King Lot.

With that Merlin vanished, and came to King Arthur, and told him to attack them fiercely. And in the meantime three hundred good men, of the best that were with the kings, went straight over to King Arthur, and that comforted him greatly.

"Sir," said Merlin to Arthur, "do not fight with the sword that you won by miracle until you see things going against you; then draw it out and do your best."

So straight away King Arthur attacked them in their camp. And Sir Baudwin, Sir Kay and Sir Brastias killed men on the right hand and on the left so that it was a marvel to see; and all the while King Arthur on horseback laid about him with a sword, and did marvellous deeds of arms, so that many of the kings took great joy in his deeds and his boldness.

Then King Lot broke out at the rear, and the King with the Hundred Knights, and King Carados, and attacked Arthur fiercely from behind. With that Sir Arthur turned with his knights, and struck behind and before, and Sir Arthur was always in the thick of the fighting, until his horse was killed under him. And with that King Lot struck King Arthur down. Then his four knights caught him up and set him on horseback. Then he drew his sword Excalibur, and it was so bright in his enemies' eyes that it gave light like thirty torches. And with that he drove them back, and killed many people. And then the common people of Caerleon rose up with clubs and staves and killed many knights; but all the kings kept together with those of their knights who were left alive, and so fled and went away. And Merlin came to Arthur, and advised him to follow them no further.

Chapter 10: How Merlin advised King Arthur to send for King Ban and King Bors, and of the counsel they took for the war

So after the feast and the fighting, King Arthur went to London, and so, on Merlin's advice, the king called his barons to council, for Merlin had told the king that the six kings who had made war on him would in all haste take their revenge on him and on his lands. So the king asked all of them for advice. They could give no advice, but said they were strong enough.

"You speak well," said Arthur. "I thank you for your good spirit. But will all of you who love me speak with Merlin? You know well that he has done much for me, and he knows many things, and when he is before you, I would like you to ask him earnestly for his best advice."

All the barons said they would ask him and beg him. So Merlin was sent for, and courteously asked by all the barons to give them his best advice.

"I will tell you," said Merlin. "I warn you all, your enemies are far too strong for you, and they are as good men of arms as any alive. And by this time they have won over four more kings, and a mighty duke. And unless our king has more knights with him than he can raise within the bounds of his own realm, if he fights them in battle he will be overcome and killed."

"What would be best to do in this case?" said all the barons.

"I will tell you my advice," said Merlin. "There are two brothers beyond the sea, and they are both kings, and marvellously good fighting men; and one is called King Ban of Benwick, and the other is called King Bors of Gaul, that is, France. And a mighty man makes war on these two kings, King Claudas, and fights with them over a castle, and there is great war between them. But this Claudas is so rich in goods, with which he gets himself good knights, that for the most part he gets the better of these two kings. So this is my advice: that our king and sovereign lord send to the kings Ban and Bors by two trusty knights, with well-written letters, saying that if they will come and see King Arthur and his court, and so help him in his wars, he will swear to them to help them in their wars against King Claudas. Now, what do you say to this advice?" said Merlin.

"This is good advice," said the king and all the barons.

Right then, in all haste, two knights were appointed to carry the message to the two kings. So letters were written in courteous terms, according to King Arthur's wishes. Ulfius and Brastias were made the messengers, and so they rode off well horsed and well armed, as the custom was at that time, and so crossed the sea and rode toward the city of Benwick. And near there were eight knights who spotted them, and at a narrow pass they met Ulfius and Brastias, and would have taken them prisoner. So they asked them to let them pass, for they were messengers to King Ban and King Bors, sent from King Arthur.

"Then," said the eight knights, "you shall die or be prisoners, for we are knights of King Claudas."

And with that two of them lowered their spears, and Ulfius and Brastias lowered their spears, and they charged together with great force. And Claudas' knights broke their spears, and theirs held, and carried the two knights out of their saddles to the earth, and so they left them lying, and rode on their way. And the other six knights rode ahead to a pass to meet them again, and so Ulfius and Brastias struck down two more, and so went on their way. And at the fourth pass two met two, and both were laid on the earth; so there was not one of the eight knights who was not badly hurt or bruised. And when they came to Benwick, it happened that both kings were there, Ban and Bors.

And when the kings were told that messengers had come, two knights of honour were sent to them, one called Lionses, lord of the country of Payarne, and Sir Phariance, an honourable knight. At once they asked where they came from, and they said from King Arthur, king of England; so they took them in their arms and they rejoiced greatly in each other. But as soon as the two kings knew they were Arthur's messengers, there was no delay, but at once they spoke with the knights, and welcomed them in the most faithful way, and said they were more welcome to them than from any king living; and with that they kissed the letters and delivered them. And when Ban and Bors understood the letters, then the messengers were even more welcome than they were before. And after the urgency of the letters they gave them this answer: that they would fulfil the wish of King Arthur's letter, and that Ulfius and Brastias should stay there as long as they liked, and have as warm a welcome as could be given them in those border lands. Then Ulfius and Brastias told the kings of their adventure with the eight knights at the passes.

"Ha! Ah!" said Ban and Bors. "They were my good friends. I wish I had known of them; they would not have got away so lightly."

So Ulfius and Brastias had a warm welcome and great gifts, as much as they could carry away; and they had their answer by word of mouth and in writing, that those two kings would come to Arthur in all the haste they could. So the two knights rode on ahead, and crossed the sea, and came to their lord, and told him how they had fared, at which King Arthur was exceedingly glad.

"When do you suppose the two kings will be here?"

"Sir," they said, "before All Hallows."

Then the king had a great feast prepared, and had a great jousting proclaimed. And by All Hallows the two kings had come over the sea with three hundred knights, well equipped both for peace and for war. And King Arthur met them ten miles out of London, and there was as great joy as could be imagined or made. And on All Hallows, at the great feast, the three kings sat in the hall, and Sir Kay the seneschal served in the hall, and Sir Lucan the butler, who was Duke Corneus' son, and Sir Griflet, who was the son of Cardol: these three knights had charge of all the service that served the kings. And as soon as they had washed and risen from the table, all the knights who wished to joust made themselves ready; and by the time they were ready on horseback there were seven hundred knights. And Arthur, Ban and Bors, with the Archbishop of Canterbury, and Sir Ector, Kay's father, were in a place hung with cloth of gold like a hall, with ladies and gentlewomen, to watch who did best, and to give judgment on it.

Chapter 11: Of a great tournament held by King Arthur and the two kings Ban and Bors, and how they went over the sea

And King Arthur and the two kings had the seven hundred knights divided into two sides. And three hundred knights of the realm of Benwick and of Gaul were turned to the other side. Then they set their shields in place, and many good knights began to level their spears. So Griflet was the first to meet a knight, one Ladinas, and they met so eagerly that everyone wondered at it; and they fought so that their shields fell to pieces, and horse and man fell to the earth; and both the French knight and the English knight lay there so long that everyone thought they were dead. When Lucan the butler saw Griflet lying like that, he got him on his horse again at once, and the two of them did marvellous deeds of arms against many young knights. Also Sir Kay came out of an ambush with five knights with him, and the six of them struck down six others. And Sir Kay did marvellous deeds of arms that day, so that nobody did as well as he did that day. Then came Ladinas and Gracian, two knights of France, and did exceedingly well, so that everyone praised them.

Then came Sir Placidas, a good knight, and met Sir Kay, and struck him down, horse and man, at which Sir Griflet was angry, and met Sir Placidas so hard that horse and man fell to the earth. But when the five knights knew that Sir Kay had had a fall, they were angry out of their wits, and with that each of the five of them bore down a knight. When King Arthur and the two kings saw both sides beginning to grow angry, they leapt on small riding horses, and had it proclaimed that everyone should go back to their lodgings. And so they went home and took off their armour, and so to evensong and supper. And afterwards the three kings went into a garden, and gave the prize to Sir Kay, and to Lucan the butler, and to Sir Griflet. And then they went into council, and with them went Gwenbaus, the brother of King Ban and King Bors, a wise scholar, and Ulfius and Brastias went there, and Merlin. And after they had been in council, they went to bed. And in the morning they heard mass, and went to dinner, and so to their council, and argued a great deal over what was best to do. At last they agreed that Merlin should go with a token from King Ban, and that was a ring, to his men and King Bors'; and that Gracian and Placidas should go back and keep their castles and their countries, for fear of King Claudas, as King Ban of Benwick and King Bors of Gaul had ordered them. And so they crossed the sea and came to Benwick. And when the people saw King Ban's ring, and Gracian and Placidas, they were glad, and asked how the kings were, and rejoiced greatly at their good health and their alliance. And as their sovereign lords wished, the fighting men made themselves ready with all possible haste, so that there were fifteen thousand of them on horse and on foot, and they had a great plenty of food with them, by Merlin's provision. But Gracian and Placidas were left to stock and arm the castles, for fear of King Claudas. Then Merlin crossed the sea, well supplied with food both by water and by land. And when he came to the sea he sent the foot soldiers home again, and took no more with him than ten thousand men on horseback, most of them men-at-arms, and so took ship and crossed the sea into England, and landed at Dover. And through Merlin's cunning, he led the army northward, by the most secret way that could be thought of, to the forest of Bedegraine, and there in a valley he camped them in secret.

Then Merlin rode to Arthur and the two kings, and told them how he had fared; at which they marvelled greatly, that any man on earth could manage so fast, and go and come. So Merlin told them that ten thousand were in the forest of Bedegraine, well armed at all points. Then there was no more to say, but the whole army went to horse, as Arthur had arranged beforehand. So with twenty thousand he travelled by night and by day. But Merlin had made such an order beforehand, that no fighting man should ride or walk in any country on this side of the river Trent unless he had a token from King Arthur, and because of this the king's enemies did not dare ride about to spy as they had done before.

Chapter 12: How eleven kings gathered a great army against King Arthur

And so within a little while the three kings came to the castle of Bedegraine, and found there an exceedingly fine company, and well equipped, at which they rejoiced greatly, and they lacked no food. This was the reason for the northern army: it had been raised because of the insult and the rebuff the six kings had suffered at Caerleon. And those six kings, through their dealings, had won over five other kings; and so they began to gather their people.

And now they swore that, come good or ill, none of them would leave the others until they had destroyed Arthur. And then they took an oath. The first to begin the oath was the Duke of Cambenet, who swore he would bring with him five thousand men-at-arms, who were ready on horseback. Then King Brandegoris of Stranggore swore that he would bring five thousand men-at-arms on horseback. Then King Clariance of Northumberland swore he would bring three thousand men-at-arms. Then the King of the Hundred Knights, who was an exceedingly good man and a young one, swore that he would bring four thousand men-at-arms on horseback. Then King Lot swore, an exceedingly good knight, and Sir Gawain's father, that he would bring five thousand men-at-arms on horseback. Also King Uriens swore, who was Sir Uwain's father, of the land of Gore, and he would bring six thousand men-at-arms on horseback. Also King Idres of Cornwall swore that he would bring five thousand men-at-arms on horseback. Also King Cradelment swore to bring five thousand men on horseback. Also King Agwisance of Ireland swore to bring five thousand men-at-arms on horseback. Also King Nentres swore to bring five thousand men-at-arms on horseback. Also King Carados swore to bring five thousand men-at-arms on horseback. So their whole army was fifty thousand fully armed men-at-arms on horseback, and ten thousand good men on foot. Then they were soon ready, and mounted on horseback and sent out their scouts ahead of them, for these eleven kings on their way laid siege to the castle of Bedegraine. And so they set out and drew toward Arthur, and left few to stay at the siege, for the castle of Bedegraine was held for King Arthur, and the men who were in it were Arthur's.

Chapter 13: Of a dream of the King with the Hundred Knights

So on Merlin's advice scouts were sent out ahead to scour the country, and they met the scouts of the north, and made them tell which way the army was coming, and then they told it to Arthur. And on the advice of King Ban and King Bors they had all the country burned and laid waste ahead of them, wherever the enemy would ride.

The King with the Hundred Knights dreamed a marvellous dream two nights before the battle: that a great wind blew, and blew down their castles and their towns, and after that came a flood and carried it all away. All who heard of the dream said it was a sign of a great battle. Then on Merlin's advice, when they knew which way the eleven kings would ride and where they would camp that night, they attacked them at midnight, as they were in their tents. But the sentries of their army cried out, "Lords! To arms! For here are your enemies upon you!"

Chapter 14: How the eleven kings and their army fought against Arthur and his army, and of many great feats of the war

Then King Arthur and King Ban and King Bors, with their good and trusty knights, attacked them so fiercely that they brought their tents down on their heads. But the eleven kings, by manly prowess of arms, won their way to an open field; but ten thousand good men were killed there that morning. And so they had a strong pass in front of them, and still they were fifty thousand hardy men. Then it drew toward day.

"Now you shall do as I advise," said Merlin to the three kings. "I would have King Ban and King Bors, with their company of ten thousand men, put in a wood near here, in ambush, and kept secret, and they should be placed there before daylight comes, and they should not stir until you and your knights have fought with the enemy for a long time. And when it is daylight, draw up your army right in front of them and the pass, so that they can see your whole army, for then they will be the bolder, when they see you have only about twenty thousand men, and it will make them the gladder to let you and your army come over the pass."

All three kings and all the barons said that Merlin spoke exceedingly well, and it was done at once as Merlin had planned. So in the morning, when each army saw the other, the army of the north was greatly encouraged. Then three thousand men-at-arms were handed over to Ulfius and Brastias, and they attacked the enemy fiercely in the pass, and killed men on the right hand and on the left so that it was a wonder to tell.

When the eleven kings saw that so small a company did such deeds of arms, they were ashamed, and attacked them again fiercely; and there Sir Ulfius' horse was killed under him, but he did marvellously well on foot. But Duke Eustace of Cambenet and King Clariance of Northumberland kept pressing Ulfius hard. When Brastias saw how his comrade was faring, he struck the duke with a spear, so that horse and man fell down. King Clariance saw that, and turned on Brastias, and each struck the other so that horse and man went to the earth, and so they lay stunned for a long time, and their horses' knees were broken through to the hard bone. Then came Sir Kay the seneschal with six companions, and did exceedingly well. With that came the eleven kings, and there Griflet was put to the earth, horse and man, and Lucan the butler, horse and man, by King Brandegoris, and King Idres, and King Agwisance. Then the fighting grew exceedingly hard on both sides. When Sir Kay saw Griflet on foot, he rode at King Nentres and struck him down, and led his horse to Sir Griflet, and got him mounted again. Also Sir Kay with the same spear struck down King Lot, and hurt him very badly. The King with the Hundred Knights saw that, and rode at Sir Kay and struck him down, and took his horse, and gave it to King Lot, who thanked him. When Sir Griflet saw Sir Kay and Lucan the butler on foot, he took a sharp spear, great and square, and rode at Pinel, a good man of arms, and struck down horse and man, and then he took his horse and gave it to Sir Kay. Then when King Lot saw King Nentres on foot, he rode at Melot de la Roche, and struck him down, horse and man, and gave King Nentres the horse, and got him mounted again. Also the King of the Hundred Knights saw King Idres on foot; then he rode at Gwiniart de Bloi, and struck him down, horse and man, and gave King Idres the horse, and got him mounted again; and King Lot struck down Clariance de la Forest Savage, and gave the horse to Duke Eustace. And so when they had got the kings mounted again, they drew together, all eleven kings, and said they would be revenged for the damage they had taken that day. Meanwhile Sir Ector came in with an eager face, and found Ulfius and Brastias on foot, in great danger of death, badly trampled under the horses' feet.

Then Arthur, like a lion, rode at King Cradelment of North Wales, and struck him through the left side, so that horse and king fell down; and then he took the horse by the rein, and led it to Ulfius, and said, "Have this horse, my old friend, for you have great need of a horse."

"Many thanks," said Ulfius.

Then Sir Arthur did such marvels in arms that everyone wondered at it. When the King with the Hundred Knights saw King Cradelment on foot, he rode at Sir Ector, Sir Kay's father, who was well horsed, and struck down horse and man, and gave the horse to the king, and got him mounted again. And when King Arthur saw the king riding Sir Ector's horse, he was angry, and with his sword he struck the king on the helm, so that a quarter of the helm and shield fell away, and the sword carved on down to the horse's neck, and so the king and the horse fell down to the ground. Then Sir Kay came at Sir Morganore, seneschal to the King of the Hundred Knights, and struck him down, horse and man, and led the horse to his father, Sir Ector. Then Sir Ector rode at a knight called Lardans, and struck down horse and man, and led the horse to Sir Brastias, who had great need of a horse, and had been badly trampled. Then Brastias saw Lucan the butler, who lay like a dead man under the horses' feet, and all the while Sir Griflet was doing marvels to rescue him, and there were always fourteen knights on Sir Lucan. Then Brastias struck one of them on the helm, so that the blow went down to the teeth, and he rode at another and struck him, so that his arm flew into the field. Then he went to the third and struck him on the shoulder, so that shoulder and arm flew into the field. And when Griflet saw help had come, he struck a knight on the temples, so that head and helm went to the earth, and Griflet took that knight's horse, and led it to Sir Lucan, and told him to mount the horse and avenge his hurts. For Brastias had killed a knight earlier and mounted Griflet on his horse.

Chapter 15: More of the same battle

Then Lucan saw King Agwisance, who had just killed Moris de la Roche, and Lucan rode at him with a short spear that was a heavy one, and gave him such a fall that the horse went down to the earth. Also Lucan found there, on foot, Bloias de la Flandres and Sir Gwinas, two hardy knights, and in the fury that Lucan was in, he killed two young knights and got these two mounted again. Then the battle grew exceedingly hard on both sides; but Arthur was glad that his knights were mounted again, and then they fought together so that the noise and the din rang along the water and the wood. And so King Ban and King Bors made themselves ready, and set their shields and armour in order, and they were so full of spirit that many knights shook and quivered with eagerness. All this while Lucan, and Gwinas, and Briant, and Bellias of Flanders held a hard fight against six kings, that is, King Lot, King Nentres, King Brandegoris, King Idres, King Uriens and King Agwisance. So with the help of Sir Kay and Sir Griflet they pressed these six kings so hard that they scarcely had any power to defend themselves. But when Sir Arthur saw that the battle would not be ended by any means, he went wild as a lion, and steered his horse here and there, on the right hand and on the left, so that he did not stop until he had killed twenty knights. Also he wounded King Lot badly on the shoulder, and made him leave the field, for Sir Kay and Griflet did great deeds of arms there with King Arthur. Then Ulfius, and Brastias, and Sir Ector fought against Duke Eustace, and King Cradelment, and King Clariance of Northumberland, and King Carados, and against the King with the Hundred Knights. So these knights fought with these kings so that they made them give ground.

Then King Lot grieved greatly for his losses and for his companions, and said to the ten kings, "Unless you do as I advise, we shall be killed and destroyed. Let me have the King with the Hundred Knights, and King Agwisance, and King Idres, and the Duke of Cambenet, and we five kings will have fifteen thousand men-at-arms with us, and we will go to one side while you six kings keep up the fight with twelve thousand. When we see that you have fought with them for a long time, then we will come on fiercely. Otherwise we shall never match them," said King Lot, "except by this means."

So they parted as they planned here, and six kings made their side strong against Arthur, and fought hard for a long time.

In the meantime the ambush of King Ban and King Bors broke out, and Lionses and Phariance had the vanguard, and these two knights met King Idres and his company, and there began a great fight, with breaking of spears and striking of swords, and killing of men and horses, and King Idres was close to defeat.

Agwisance the king saw that, and put Lionses and Phariance in danger of death; for the Duke of Cambenet came on along with him with a great company. So these two knights were in such danger of their lives that they were forced to turn back, but all the while they defended themselves and their company marvellously. When King Bors saw those knights driven back, it grieved him badly; then he came on so fast that his company seemed as dark as indigo. When King Lot saw King Bors, he knew him well, and then he said, "O Jesus, defend us from death and horrible wounds! For I see well that we are in great danger of death. For I see over there a king, one of the most honourable men and one of the best knights in the world, who has come to join his company."

"Who is he?" said the King with the Hundred Knights.

"It is King Bors of Gaul," said King Lot. "I wonder how they came into this country without any of us knowing it."

"It was by Merlin's advice," said the knight.

"As for him," said King Carados, "I will take on King Bors, if you will rescue me when there is need."

"Go on," they all said. "We will do all we can."

Then King Carados and his army rode on at an easy pace, until they came within bowshot of King Bors; then each army let their horses run as fast as they could. And Bleoberis, who was King Bors' godson, carried his chief standard; he was an exceedingly good knight.

"Now we shall see," said King Bors, "how these northern Britons can bear arms."

And King Bors met a knight, and struck him right through with a spear, so that he fell dead on the earth; and afterwards he drew his sword and did marvellous deeds of arms, so that everyone on both sides wondered greatly at it. And his knights did not fail, but did their part, and King Carados was struck to the earth. With that came the King with the Hundred Knights and rescued King Carados mightily by force of arms, for he was an exceedingly good knight for a king, and only a young man.

Chapter 16: Still more of the same battle

By then King Ban came into the field, as fierce as a lion, with bands of green, and gold upon them.

"Ha! Ah!" said King Lot. "We must be defeated, for over there I see the most valiant knight in the world, and the man of greatest renown, for there are no two brothers living such as King Ban and King Bors. So we must either withdraw or die; and unless we withdraw manfully and wisely, there is nothing but death."

When King Ban came into the battle, he came in so fiercely that the strokes echoed back from the wood and the water; and at that King Lot wept for pity and grief, to see so many good knights meet their end. But through the great force of King Ban, the two northern armies that had separated were driven crashing together in great fear; and the three kings and their knights kept on killing, so that it was pitiful to see that multitude of people fleeing. But King Lot, and the King of the Hundred Knights, and King Morganore gathered the people together in exceedingly knightly fashion, and did great feats of arms, and held the battle all that day, hard as it was.

When the King of the Hundred Knights saw the great damage that King Ban did, he drove at him with his horse, and struck him high upon the helm, a great stroke, and stunned him badly. Then King Ban was angry with him, and went after him fiercely. The other saw that, and threw up his shield, and spurred his horse forward; but King Ban's stroke fell and cut a piece out of the shield, and the sword slid down the hauberk, his mail shirt, behind his back, and cut through the horse's steel armour and through the horse itself, clean in two, so that the sword struck the earth. Then the King of the Hundred Knights got clear of the horse nimbly, and with his sword he ran King Ban's horse through and through. With that King Ban sprang nimbly clear of the dead horse, and then King Ban struck at the other so eagerly, and hit him on the helm, so that he fell to the earth. Also in that fury he felled King Morganore, and there was great slaughter of good knights and of many people. By then King Arthur came into the thick of the fighting, and found King Ban standing among dead men and dead horses, fighting on foot like a raging lion, so that nobody came near him, as far as he could reach with his sword, without catching a grievous blow; and King Arthur felt great pity for him. And Arthur was so bloody that no man could know him by his shield, for it was all blood and brains on his sword. And as Arthur looked beside him he saw a knight who was exceedingly well horsed, and with that Sir Arthur rode at him, and struck him on the helm, so that his sword went down to his teeth, and the knight sank down to the earth dead. And at once Arthur took the horse by the rein, and led it to King Ban, and said, "Fair brother, have this horse, for you have great need of it, and I am deeply sorry for your great losses."

"It shall soon be avenged," said King Ban, "for I trust in God that my hand has not lost its habit so far that some of them will not sorely regret this."

"I can well believe it," said Arthur, "for I see your deeds are full of action. Even so, I could not get to you at that time."

But when King Ban was mounted on horseback, then a new battle began, which was fierce and hard, with exceedingly great slaughter. And so through great force King Arthur, King Ban and King Bors made their knights draw back a little. But all the while the eleven kings with their knights never turned back; and so they withdrew to a little wood, and so over a little river, and there they rested, for at night they could have no rest on the field. And then the eleven kings and knights drew into a close mass, all together, like men afraid and past all comfort. But no man could break through them, they held so hard together both behind and before, so that King Arthur marvelled at their deeds of arms, and was exceedingly angry.

"Ah, Sir Arthur," said King Ban and King Bors, "don't blame them, for they are doing as good men ought to do. For by my faith," said King Ban, "they are the best fighting men, and the knights of greatest prowess, that I ever saw or heard tell of, and those eleven kings are men of great honour; and if they belonged to you, there would be no king under heaven who had eleven such knights, and of such honour."

"I cannot love them," said Arthur. "They would destroy me."

"We know that well," said King Ban and King Bors, "for they are your mortal enemies, and that has been proved already; and this day they have done their part, and it is a great pity they are so wilful."

Then all the eleven kings drew together, and then King Lot said, "Lords, you must act otherwise than you are doing, or else the great loss is still to come. You can see what people we have lost, and what good men we are losing, because we keep waiting for these foot soldiers; and every time we save one of the foot soldiers we lose ten horsemen for him. So this is my advice: let us send our foot soldiers away from us, for it is near night, and the noble Arthur will not stop for the foot soldiers, and they can save themselves, for the wood is close at hand. And when we horsemen are together, see that each one of you kings gives such orders that no man breaks ranks, on pain of death. And whoever sees any man turn to run, let him be killed at once, for it is better that we kill a coward than that all of us be killed through a coward. What do you say?" said King Lot. "Answer me, all you kings."

"It is well said," said King Nentres; so said the King of the Hundred Knights; the same said King Carados, and King Uriens; so did King Idres and King Brandegoris; and so did King Cradelment, and the Duke of Cambenet; the same said King Clariance and King Agwisance. And they swore they would never fail one another, neither for life nor for death. And whoever fled, and did not do as they did, should be killed. Then they repaired their armour, and set their shields straight, and took new spears and rested them on their thighs, and stood as still as if they had been a clump of trees.

Chapter 17: Still more of the same battle, and how Merlin ended it

When Sir Arthur and King Ban and King Bors saw them and all their knights, they praised them highly for their noble knightly bearing, as the hardiest fighters they had ever heard of or seen. With that some forty noble knights made themselves ready, and told the three kings that they would break the enemy's line. These were their names: Lionses, Phariance, Ulfius, Brastias, Ector, Kay, Lucan the butler, Griflet le Fise de Dieu, Mariet de la Roche, Guinas de Bloi, Briant de la Forest Savage, Bellaus, Morians of the Castle of Maidens, Flannedrius of the Castle of Ladies, Annecians, who was King Bors' godson, a noble knight, Ladinas de la Rouse, Emerause, Caulas, Graciens le Castlein, one Blois de la Case, and Sir Colgrevaunce de Gorre. All these knights rode on ahead with their spears resting on their thighs, and spurred their horses as hard as the horses could run. And the eleven kings with part of their knights charged with their horses as fast as they could with their spears, and there on both sides they did marvellous deeds of arms. So Arthur, Ban and Bors came into the thick of the fighting, and cut men down right and left, so that their horses went in blood up to the fetlocks. But all the while the eleven kings and their army kept their faces turned to Arthur. And at this Ban and Bors marvelled greatly, considering the great slaughter there was; but at last the enemy were driven back over a little river.

With that Merlin came on a great black horse, and said to Arthur, "Will you never be done? Haven't you done enough? Of sixty thousand men you have left only fifteen thousand alive this day, and it is time to call a halt! For God is angry with you, that you will never be done. For those eleven kings over there will not be overthrown this time, and if you keep on at them any longer, your fortune will turn and theirs will grow. And so withdraw to your lodging, and rest as soon as you can, and reward your good knights with gold and with silver, for they have well deserved it. No riches can be too costly for them, for out of so few men as you have, there were never men who did more feats of prowess than they have done today, for you have been matched this day with the best fighters in the world."

"That is the truth," said King Ban and King Bors.

"Also," said Merlin, "withdraw wherever you wish, for I dare promise that for these three years they will not harm you; and by then you will hear new tidings."

And then Merlin said to Arthur, "These eleven kings have more on their hands than they know, for the Saracens have landed in their countries, more than forty thousand of them, who burn and kill, and have laid siege to the castle of Wandesborow, and are doing great destruction. So do not be afraid for these three years. Also, sir, have all the goods that were taken in this battle searched out, and when you have them in your hands, have them given freely to these two kings, Ban and Bors, so that they may reward their knights with them; and that will make strangers more willing to serve you in time of need. And you are able to reward your own knights out of your own goods whenever you please."

"It is well said," said Arthur, "and as you have planned, so it shall be done."

When it was handed over to Ban and Bors, they gave the goods to their knights as freely as it had been given to them. Then Merlin took his leave of Arthur and of the two kings, to go and see his master Bleise, who lived in Northumberland. And so he left and came to his master, who was exceedingly glad of his coming; and there he told how Arthur and the two kings had fared at the great battle, and how it had ended, and told the names of every king and knight of honour who was there. And so Bleise wrote down the battle word for word, as Merlin told it to him, how it began, and by whom, and likewise how it ended, and who had the worst of it. All the battles that were fought in Arthur's days, Merlin had his master Bleise write down; and he also had written down all the battles that every worthy knight of Arthur's court fought.

After this Merlin left his master and came to King Arthur, who was in the castle of Bedegraine, which was one of the castles that stand in the forest of Sherwood. And Merlin was so disguised that King Arthur did not know him, for he was all wrapped in black sheepskins, with a great pair of boots, and a bow and arrows, in a russet gown, and he had wild geese in his hand; and it was the morning after Candlemas Day. But King Arthur did not know him.

"Sir," said Merlin to the king, "will you give me a gift?"

"And why should I give you a gift, peasant?" said King Arthur.

"Sir," said Merlin, "you would do better to give me a gift that is not in your hand than to lose great riches, for here, in the same place where the great battle was, there is great treasure hidden in the earth."

"Who told you so, peasant?" said Arthur.

"Merlin told me so," said he.

Then Ulfius and Brastias knew him well enough, and smiled.

"Sir," said these two knights, "it is Merlin who is speaking to you."

Then King Arthur was greatly taken aback, and marvelled at Merlin, and so did King Ban and King Bors, and so they had great fun at his expense.

Meanwhile there came a damsel who was an earl's daughter: his name was Sanam, and her name was Lionors, an exceedingly beautiful damsel; and so she came there to do homage, as other lords did after the great battle. And King Arthur set his love greatly on her, and so did she on him, and the king lay with her, and fathered a child on her: his name was Borre, who was afterwards a good knight, and of the Round Table. Then word came that King Rience of North Wales was making great war on King Leodegrance of Cameliard, at which Arthur was angry, for he loved him well, and hated King Rience, for he was always against him. So, by arrangement of the three kings, those who were sent home to Benwick were all to leave, for fear of King Claudas: Phariance, and Antemes, and Gracian, and Lionses of Payarne, with the leaders of those who were to keep the kings' lands.

Chapter 18: How King Arthur, King Ban, and King Bors rescued King Leodegrance, and other events

And then King Arthur, and King Ban, and King Bors set out with their company, some twenty thousand, and within six days came into the country of Cameliard, and there rescued King Leodegrance, and killed many of King Rience's people there, to the number of ten thousand men, and put him to flight. And then these three kings had a great welcome from King Leodegrance, who thanked them for their great goodness in avenging him on his enemies. And there Arthur had his first sight of Guinevere, the daughter of the King of Cameliard, and ever after he loved her. Afterwards they were married, as the book tells. So, to make an end briefly, the kings took their leave to go to their own countries, for King Claudas was doing great destruction on their lands.

Then Arthur said, "I will go with you."

"No," said the kings, "you shall not at this time, for you still have much to do in these lands. So we will go, and with the great riches we have won in these lands by your gifts, we will hire good knights and stand against King Claudas' malice. For by the grace of God, if we have need we will send to you for your help; and if you have need, send for us, and we will not delay, on our lives."
