"There will be no need," said Merlin, "for these two kings to come back by way of war. But I know well that King Arthur will not be long away from you, for within a year or two you will have great need, and then he will avenge you on your enemies, as you have done on his. For these eleven kings shall all die in one day, by the great might and prowess of arms of two valiant knights (as is told later); their names are Balin le Savage and Balan his brother, and they are as marvellously good knights as any living."

Now we turn to the eleven kings, who went back to a city called Sorhaute, which was in King Uriens' land, and there they refreshed themselves as well as they could, and had doctors look to their wounds, and grieved greatly for the death of their people. With that a messenger came and told how people had come into their lands who were lawless men as well as Saracens, some forty thousand, and had burned and killed all the people they could reach, without mercy, and had laid siege to the castle of Wandesborow.

"Alas," said the eleven kings, "here is sorrow upon sorrow. If we had not made war on Arthur as we have done, he would soon avenge us. As for King Leodegrance, he loves Arthur better than us; and as for King Rience, he has enough to do with Leodegrance, for he has laid siege to him."

So they agreed together to guard all the borders of Cornwall, of Wales and of the North. So first they put King Idres in the city of Nauntes in Brittany, with four thousand men-at-arms, to watch both the water and the land. Also they put King Nentres of Garlot in the city of Windesan, with four thousand knights, to watch both on water and on land. Also they had more than eight thousand other fighting men, to fortify all the fortresses on the borders of Cornwall. Also they put more knights all along the borders of Wales and Scotland, with many good men-at-arms; and so they held together for the space of three years, and all the while made alliances with mighty kings and dukes and lords. And King Rience of North Wales joined them, and with him Nero, who was a mighty man of men. And all this while they stocked and armed themselves with good men-at-arms, and food, and every kind of equipment that belongs to war, to avenge themselves for the battle of Bedegraine, as is told in the book of adventures that follows.

Chapter 19: How King Arthur rode to Caerleon, and of his dream, and how he saw the Questing Beast

Then, after King Ban and King Bors had gone, King Arthur rode into Caerleon. And there came to him King Lot's wife, of Orkney, as if bearing a message, but in fact she had been sent there to spy on King Arthur's court. And she came richly dressed, with her four sons, Gawain, Gaheris, Agravain and Gareth, and with many other knights and ladies. For she was an exceedingly beautiful lady, and so the king fell deeply in love with her, and wanted to sleep with her. So they agreed, and he fathered Mordred on her, and she was his sister, on his mother's side, Igraine's. So she stayed there a month, and at last she left. Then the king dreamed a marvellous dream, which badly frightened him. But all this time King Arthur did not know that King Lot's wife was his sister. This was Arthur's dream: he dreamed that griffins and serpents had come into this land, and he dreamed that they burned and killed all the people in the land, and then he dreamed that he fought with them, and they did him exceedingly great harm, and wounded him very badly, but at last he killed them. When the king woke, he was exceedingly heavy-hearted over his dream, and so, to put it out of his thoughts, he made ready with many knights to ride hunting. As soon as he was in the forest the king saw a great hart in front of him.

"This hart I will chase," said King Arthur.

And so he spurred his horse, and rode after it a long way, and by sheer force he was often on the point of striking the hart. But the king had chased the hart so long that his horse lost its wind and fell down dead. Then a yeoman fetched the king another horse.

So when the king saw the hart had gone to cover, and his horse was dead, he sat down by a spring, and there he fell deep into thought. And as he sat like this, he thought he heard a noise of hounds, as many as thirty. And with that the king saw coming towards him the strangest beast that he had ever seen or heard of. So the beast went to the spring and drank, and the noise in the beast's belly was like the baying of thirty couple of hounds on the scent; but all the while the beast drank there was no noise in its belly. And with that the beast went off with a great noise, at which the king marvelled greatly. And so he was deep in thought, and with that he fell asleep. Just then a knight came on foot to Arthur and said, "Knight, sitting there sleepy and lost in thought, tell me if you saw a strange beast pass this way."

"I saw one like that," said King Arthur, "and by now it is two miles off. What do you want with the beast?" said Arthur.

"Sir, I have followed that beast a long time, and killed my horse doing it. So I wish to God I had another, to follow my quest."

Just then someone came with the king's horse, and when the knight saw the horse, he begged the king to give it to him: "For I have followed this quest this past twelvemonth, and either I shall take the beast, or I will shed the best blood of my body."

Pellinore, a king at that time, followed the Questing Beast, and after his death Sir Palomides followed it.

Chapter 20: How King Pellinore took Arthur's horse and followed the Questing Beast, and how Merlin met Arthur

"Sir knight," said the king, "give up that quest, and let me have it, and I will follow it for another twelvemonth."

"You fool," said the knight to Arthur, "you want it for nothing. It shall never be achieved except by me, or by my next of kin."

With that he leapt to the king's horse and mounted into the saddle, and said, "Many thanks. This horse is mine now."

"Well," said the king, "you may take my horse by force, but I would like to find out whether you are better on horseback than I am."

"Well," said the knight, "look for me here whenever you like, and here near this spring you will find me." And so he went on his way.

Then the king sat deep in thought, and told his men to fetch his horse as fast as ever they could. Just then Merlin came by him, looking like a child of fourteen, and greeted the king, and asked him why he was so thoughtful.

"I may well be thoughtful," said the king, "for I have seen the most marvellous sight that I ever saw."

"I know that well," said Merlin, "as well as you do yourself, and all your thoughts besides. But you are a fool to brood, for it will not help you. I also know who you are, and who your father was, and who you were born to. King Uther Pendragon was your father, and fathered you on Igraine."

"That is false," said King Arthur. "How could you know it? You are not old enough to have known my father."

"Yes," said Merlin, "I know it better than you or any man alive."

"I will not believe you," said Arthur, and he was angry with the child.

So Merlin went away, and came back in the likeness of an old man of eighty, at which the king was very glad, for he seemed to be very wise.

Then said the old man, "Why are you so sad?"

"I may well be heavy-hearted," said Arthur, "for many reasons. Besides, there was a child here, and he told me many things that I think he had no business knowing, for he was not old enough to have known my father."

"Yes," said the old man, "the child told you the truth, and he would have told you more if you had let him. But you have lately done a thing for which God is displeased with you, for you have lain with your sister, and on her you have fathered a child who will destroy you and all the knights of your realm."

"Who are you," said Arthur, "to tell me this news?"

"I am Merlin, and it was I who was in the child's likeness."

"Ah," said King Arthur, "you are a marvellous man. But I marvel greatly at your words, that I must die in battle."

"Do not marvel," said Merlin, "for it is God's will that your body be punished for your foul deeds. But I may well be sorry," said Merlin, "for I shall die a shameful death, to be put into the earth alive, and you shall die an honourable death."

And as they were talking of this, someone came with the king's horse, and so the king mounted his horse, and Merlin another, and so they rode to Caerleon. And at once the king asked Ector and Ulfius how he had been fathered, and they told him that Uther Pendragon was his father and Queen Igraine his mother.

Then he said to Merlin, "I want my mother sent for, so that I may speak with her; and if she says so herself, then I will believe it."

In all haste the queen was sent for, and she came, and brought with her Morgan le Fay, her daughter, who was as beautiful a lady as any could be. And the king welcomed Igraine in the best way he could.

Chapter 21: How Ulfius accused Queen Igraine, Arthur's mother, of treason; and how a knight came and asked for vengeance for his master's death

Just then Ulfius came, and said openly, so that the king and everyone feasting there that day could hear, "You are the falsest lady in the world, and the greatest traitor to the king's person."

"Be careful what you say," said Arthur. "That is a heavy charge."

"I know very well what I am saying," said Ulfius, "and here is my glove, to prove it on the body of any man who says otherwise: that this Queen Igraine is the cause of your great harm, and of your great war. For if she had spoken out in the lifetime of King Uther Pendragon about your birth, and how you were fathered, you would never have had the deadly wars you have had. For most of the barons of your realm never knew whose son you were, nor who fathered you. And she who bore you in her body should have made it known openly, to clear her own honour and yours, and likewise to the whole realm. And so I prove her false to God and to you and to all your realm, and whoever says otherwise, I will prove it on his body."

Then Igraine spoke and said, "I am a woman and I cannot fight, but rather than be dishonoured, some good man would take up my quarrel. What is more," she said, "Merlin knows well, and so do you, Sir Ulfius, how King Uther came to me in the castle of Tintagil in the likeness of my lord, who had been dead three hours before, and so fathered a child on me that night. And thirteen days after, King Uther married me, and by his command, when the child was born, it was handed over to Merlin and brought up by him. And so I never saw the child again, nor do I know what his name is, for I have never known him yet."

And there Ulfius said to the queen, "Merlin is more to blame than you."

"I know well," said the queen, "that I bore a child by my lord King Uther, but I do not know what has become of him."

Then Merlin took the king by the hand, saying, "This is your mother."

And with that Sir Ector bore witness how he had brought him up by Uther's command. And with that King Arthur took his mother, Queen Igraine, in his arms and kissed her, and they wept over each other. And then the king had a feast made that lasted eight days.

Then one day there came into the court a squire on horseback, leading before him a knight wounded to the death, and told him how there was a knight in the forest who had put up a tent by a spring, "and he has killed my master, a good knight; his name was Miles. And so I beg you that my master may be buried, and that some knight may avenge my master's death."

Then there was great talk in the court of that knight's death, and every man gave his opinion. Then Griflet came, who was only a squire, and he was young, the same age as King Arthur; and he begged the king, for all the service he had done him, to give him the order of knighthood.

Chapter 22: How Griflet was made a knight, and jousted with a knight

"You are very young and tender in years," said Arthur, "to take so high an order on yourself."

"Sir," said Griflet, "I beg you, make me a knight."

"Sir," said Merlin, "it would be a great pity to lose Griflet, for he will be an exceedingly good man when he comes of age, and will stay with you all his life. And if he risks his body against that knight at the spring, he is in great danger of never coming back, for that is one of the best knights in the world, and the strongest man at arms."

"Well," said Arthur.

So at Griflet's wish the king made him a knight.

"Now," said Arthur to Sir Griflet, "since I have made you a knight, you must grant me a gift."

"Whatever you wish," said Griflet.

"You shall promise me on your life that when you have jousted with the knight at the spring, whether you end up on foot or on horseback, you will come straight back to me without any further fighting."

"I promise you," said Griflet, "as you wish."

Then Griflet took his horse in great haste, and set his shield and took a spear in his hand, and so he rode at a great gallop until he came to the spring. And beside it he saw a rich tent, and beside that, under a cloth, stood a fine horse, well saddled and bridled, and on a tree hung a shield of several colours and a great spear. Then Griflet struck the shield with the butt of his spear, so that the shield fell down to the ground. With that the knight came out of the tent, and said, "Fair knight, why did you strike down my shield?"

"Because I will joust with you," said Griflet.

"It is better you don't," said the knight, "for you are only young, and newly made a knight, and your strength is nothing to mine."

"Be that as it may," said Griflet, "I will joust with you."

"I am loath to," said the knight, "but since I must, I will make ready for it. Where are you from?" said the knight.

"Sir, I am from Arthur's court."

So the two knights charged together, and Griflet's spear shattered to pieces; and with that the knight struck Griflet through the shield and the left side, and broke his spear, so that the stump stuck in his body, and horse and knight fell down.

Chapter 23: How twelve knights came from Rome and demanded tribute from Arthur for this land, and how Arthur fought with a knight

When the knight saw him lying on the ground like that, he dismounted, and was exceedingly heavy-hearted, for he thought he had killed him. And then he unlaced his helmet and gave him air, and so, with the spear-stump still in him, he set him on his horse, and so commended him to God, and said he had a mighty heart, and if he lived he would prove an exceedingly good knight. And so Sir Griflet rode to the court, where there was great grieving over him. But through good doctors he was healed and saved.

Just then twelve knights came into the court, and they were old men, and they came from the Emperor of Rome. And they demanded tribute from Arthur for this realm, or else the emperor would destroy him and his land.

"Well," said King Arthur, "you are messengers, and so you may say what you like, or else you would die for it. But this is my answer: I owe the emperor no tribute, and I will pay him none. But on a fair field I will give him his tribute, and it shall be with a sharp spear, or else with a sharp sword, and that shall not be long in coming, by my father's soul, Uther Pendragon."

And with that the messengers left, exceedingly angry, and King Arthur just as angry, for they had come at a bad time; for the king was exceedingly angry over the wounding of Sir Griflet. And so he commanded a trusted man of his chamber that before daybreak his best horse and armour, with everything that belonged to his person, should be outside the city before the next morning. So before the next morning he met his man and his horse, and so he mounted and set his shield and took his spear, and told his chamberlain to wait there until he came back. And so Arthur rode at an easy pace until it was day, and then he saw three peasants chasing Merlin, and they would have killed him. Then the king rode up to them, and ordered them, "Run, you churls!" Then they were afraid when they saw a knight, and ran.

"O Merlin," said Arthur, "you would have been killed here, for all your arts, if it had not been for me."

"No," said Merlin, "not so, for I could save myself if I wanted to. And you are nearer your death than I am, for you are riding to your death, unless God is your friend."

So as they went along talking like this, they came to the spring, and the rich tent beside it. Then King Arthur saw a knight sitting in a chair, in armour.

"Sir knight," said Arthur, "for what reason do you wait here, so that no knight may ride this way unless he jousts with you?" said the king. "My advice to you is to give up that custom," said Arthur.

"This custom," said the knight, "I have kept and I will keep, in spite of anyone who says no; and whoever is aggrieved by my custom, let him change it, whoever wants to."

"I will change it," said Arthur.

"And I will defend it against you," said the knight.

At once he took his horse and set his shield and took a spear, and they met so hard, each on the other's shield, that both their spears shattered to pieces. With that Arthur at once pulled out his sword.

"No, not so," said the knight. "It is better," said the knight, "for the two of us to run at each other again with sharp spears."

"Gladly," said Arthur, "if I had any more spears."

"I have plenty," said the knight.

So a squire came and brought two good spears, and Arthur chose one and the knight the other. So they spurred their horses and came together with all their might, so that each broke his spear off in his hand. Then Arthur put his hand to his sword.

"No," said the knight, "you shall do better. You are as good a jouster as any I ever met, and for the love of the high order of knighthood, let us joust just once more."

"I agree," said Arthur.

At once two great spears were brought, and each knight took a spear, and with that they charged together, so that Arthur's spear shattered to pieces. But the other knight hit him so hard in the middle of the shield that horse and man fell to the earth. And with that Arthur was fierce, and pulled out his sword, and said, "I will try you on foot, sir knight, for I have lost the honour on horseback."

"I will stay on horseback," said the knight.

Then Arthur was angry, and set his shield towards him with his sword drawn. When the knight saw that, he dismounted, for he thought there was no honour in having a knight at such a disadvantage, himself on horseback and the other on foot. And so he dismounted and set his shield towards Arthur. And there began a hard battle with many great strokes, and they hewed so with their swords that the pieces of their armour flew across the fields, and they both bled so much that the whole place where they fought was soaked with blood. And so they fought a long time, and rested, and then they went back to the battle, and so crashed together like two rams that both fell to the earth. So at last they struck together so that both their swords met squarely. But the knight's sword struck King Arthur's sword into two pieces, and at that he was heavy-hearted.

Then said the knight to Arthur, "You are in my power, to save or to kill as I please. And unless you yield yourself beaten and a recreant, a knight who begs for his life, you shall die."

"As for death," said King Arthur, "it is welcome whenever it comes. But as for yielding to you as a recreant, I would rather die than be so shamed."

And with that the king leapt at Pellinore, and took him by the middle and threw him down, and tore off his helmet. When the knight felt that, he was afraid, for he was an exceedingly big man and a strong one. And at once he brought Arthur under him, and tore off his helmet, and would have struck off his head.

Chapter 24: How Merlin saved Arthur's life, and cast an enchantment on King Pellinore and put him to sleep

With that Merlin came and said, "Knight, hold your hand! For if you kill that knight you will do this realm the greatest harm that any realm ever suffered. For this knight is a man of more honour than you know."

"Why, who is he?" said the knight.

"It is King Arthur."

Then he would have killed him, for fear of his anger, and raised his sword. And with that Merlin cast an enchantment on the knight, so that he fell to the earth in a deep sleep. Then Merlin took up King Arthur, and rode off on the knight's horse.

"Alas!" said Arthur. "What have you done, Merlin? Have you killed this good knight with your arts? There is no knight alive as honourable as he was. I would give a year's revenue from my land to have him alive again."

"Don't worry," said Merlin, "for he is in better health than you; he is only asleep, and will wake within three hours. I told you," said Merlin, "what a knight he was. You would have been killed here if it had not been for me. Besides, there is no bigger knight alive than he is, and from now on he will do you very good service. And his name is Pellinore, and he will have two sons who will be exceedingly good men; except for one, they will have no equal in prowess and in good living. And their names will be Percival of Wales and Lamorak of Wales. And he will tell you the name of your own son, fathered on your sister, who will be the destruction of all this realm."

Chapter 25: How Arthur, through Merlin, got his sword Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake

Then the king and Merlin left, and went to a hermit who was a good man and a great healer. So the hermit searched all his wounds and gave him good salves. So the king was there three days, and by then his wounds had mended well enough that he could ride and walk, and so they left. And as they rode, Arthur said, "I have no sword."

"No matter," said Merlin. "Near here is a sword that shall be yours, if I can manage it."

So they rode until they came to a lake, which was a fair, broad water, and in the middle of the lake Arthur saw an arm clothed in white samite, a rich silk, that held a fair sword in that hand.

"Look!" said Merlin. "There is the sword I spoke of."

With that they saw a damsel going upon the lake.

"What damsel is that?" said Arthur.

"That is the Lady of the Lake," said Merlin. "And within that lake is a rock, and in it is as fair a place as any on earth, and richly furnished. And this damsel will come to you soon, and then speak courteously to her, so that she will give you that sword."

At once the damsel came to Arthur, and greeted him, and he greeted her in return.

"Damsel," said Arthur, "what sword is that, which the arm over there holds above the water? I wish it were mine, for I have no sword."

"Sir Arthur, king," said the damsel, "that sword is mine, and if you will give me a gift when I ask it of you, you shall have it."

"On my faith," said Arthur, "I will give you whatever gift you ask."

"Well!" said the damsel. "Get into that barge over there, and row yourself to the sword, and take it and the scabbard with you, and I will ask for my gift when I see my time."

So Sir Arthur and Merlin dismounted and tied their horses to two trees, and so they went into the boat. And when they came to the sword that the hand held, Sir Arthur took it up by the handle, and took it with him, and the arm and the hand went under the water. And so they came to land and rode on, and then Sir Arthur saw a rich tent.

"What is that tent over there?"

"It is the tent of the knight you fought with last," said Merlin, "Sir Pellinore. But he is out; he is not there. He has had a fight with a knight of yours called Egglame, and they have fought together, but in the end Egglame fled, or else he would have been dead, and Pellinore has chased him all the way to Caerleon. And we shall meet him soon on the highway."

"That is well said," said Arthur. "Now I have a sword, now I will do battle with him, and be avenged on him."

"Sir, you shall not," said Merlin, "for the knight is weary of fighting and chasing, so that there would be no honour for you in fighting him. Also, he will not easily be matched by any one knight alive. And so it is my advice: let him pass, for he will do you good service before long, and his sons after his days. Also, you will see the day, before long, when you will be very glad to give him your sister in marriage."

"When I see him, I will do as you advise," said Arthur.

Then Sir Arthur looked at the sword, and liked it exceedingly well.

"Which do you like better," said Merlin, "the sword or the scabbard?"

"I like the sword better," said Arthur.

"Then you are the less wise," said Merlin, "for the scabbard is worth ten of the sword. For while you have the scabbard on you, you will never lose any blood, however badly you are wounded. So always keep the scabbard safe with you."

So they rode to Caerleon, and on the way they met Sir Pellinore. But Merlin had worked such a craft that Pellinore did not see Arthur, and he passed by without a word.

"I wonder," said Arthur, "that the knight would not speak."

"Sir," said Merlin, "he did not see you, for if he had seen you, you would not have got away so easily."

So they came to Caerleon, and his knights were exceedingly glad of it. And when they heard of his adventures, they marvelled that he would risk his person like that, alone. But all men of honour said it was a fine thing to serve under such a chieftain, who would put his person at risk in adventures as other poor knights did.

Chapter 26: How news came to Arthur that King Rience had overcome eleven kings, and how he wanted Arthur's beard to trim his cloak

Meanwhile a messenger came from King Rience of North Wales, and he was king of all Ireland too, and of many islands. And this was his message, greeting King Arthur in this way: saying that King Rience had defeated and overcome eleven kings, and every one of them did him homage, and this was how: they gave him their beards, flayed clean off, as much as there was of them. And so the messenger had come for King Arthur's beard. For King Rience had trimmed a cloak with kings' beards, and there was one place lacking on the cloak; and so he sent for his beard, or else he would invade his lands, and burn and kill, and never stop until he had the head and the beard.

"Well," said Arthur, "you have delivered your message, which is the most insulting and ignorant message that any man ever heard sent to a king. Also, you can see that my beard is still very young to make a trimming out of. But tell your king this: I owe him no homage, and none of my forefathers did; but before long he shall do me homage on both his knees, or else he shall lose his head, on my life. For this is the most shameful message that I ever heard of. I can see your king has never yet met a man of honour. But tell him I will have his head unless he does me homage."

Then the messenger left.

"Now, is there anyone here," said Arthur, "who knows King Rience?"

Then a knight called Naram answered, "Sir, I know the king well. He is an exceedingly good fighting man, as few alive are, and an exceedingly proud man. And sir, have no doubt he will make war on you with a mighty army."

"Well," said Arthur, "I will deal with him before long."

Chapter 27: How all the children born on May Day were sent for, and how Mordred was saved

Then King Arthur had all the children born on May Day sent for, fathered by lords and born of ladies; for Merlin had told King Arthur that the one who would destroy him would be born on May Day. And so he sent for them all, on pain of death. And so many lords' sons were found, and all were sent to the king, and so Mordred was sent by King Lot's wife. And all were put in a ship and sent out to sea, and some were four weeks old, and some less. And so by chance the ship was driven against a castle, and was broken all to pieces, and most of them were lost, except that Mordred was cast up, and a good man found him, and brought him up until he was fourteen years old, and then he brought him to the court, as it is told afterwards, towards the end of the Death of Arthur. So many lords and barons of this realm were displeased, because their children were lost like this, and many put the blame on Merlin more than on Arthur; so, what with fear and what with love, they held their peace. But when the messenger came back to King Rience, he was mad with rage beyond measure, and gathered a great army, as it is told later in the book of Balin le Savage, which follows next, and how by chance Balin got the sword.

Here ends the first book.

Book Two: Balin, the Noble Knight

Chapter 1: Of a damsel who came with a sword belted at her side, looking for a man good enough to draw it out of the scabbard

After the death of Uther Pendragon, Arthur his son reigned, and he had great wars in his day to bring all England into his hand. For there were many kings within the realm of England, and in Wales, Scotland and Cornwall. So it happened one time, when King Arthur was at London, that a knight came and told the king the news that King Rience of North Wales had raised a great number of men, and they had entered the land, and were burning and killing the king's loyal subjects.

"If this is true," said Arthur, "it would be a great shame to my rank unless he were mightily resisted."

"It is the truth," said the knight, "for I saw the army myself."

"Well," said the king, "have a proclamation made, that all the lords, knights and gentlemen of arms should gather at a castle called Camelot in those days, and there the king will hold a general council and a great joust."

So when the king had come there with all his barons, and they were lodged as seemed best to them, a damsel had come there who was sent with a message from the great lady Lile of Avalon. And when she came before King Arthur, she told him whom she came from, and how she had been sent to him with a message, for these reasons. Then she let her richly furred cloak fall, and then she was seen to be wearing a noble sword belted at her side. The king marvelled at it, and said, "Damsel, why are you wearing that sword? It does not become you."

"Now I will tell you," said the damsel. "This sword that I am wearing gives me great sorrow and trouble, for I cannot be freed of this sword except by a knight, and he must be an exceedingly good man of his hands and of his deeds, and without baseness or treachery, and without treason. And if I can find such a knight who has all these virtues, he can draw this sword out of the sheath. For I have been at King Rience's court, where I was told there were exceedingly good knights, and he and all his knights have tried it and none can succeed."

"This is a great marvel," said Arthur, "if it is true. I will try to draw out the sword myself, not presuming that I am the best knight, but so that I will start drawing at your sword as an example to all the barons, so that they will try, every one after another, when I have tried it."

Then Arthur took the sword by the sheath and by the belt and pulled at it hard, but the sword would not come out.

"Sir," said the damsel, "you need not pull half so hard, for the man who is to pull it out will do it with little strength."

"You speak well," said Arthur. "Now try, all my barons; but take care that you are not stained with shame, treachery or guile."

"Then it will be no use," said the damsel, "for he must be a clean knight without baseness, and of gentle blood on his father's side and his mother's side."

Most of the barons of the Round Table who were there at that time all tried in turn, but none could succeed. And so the damsel grieved beyond measure, and said, "Alas! I thought the best knights without treachery or treason were in this court."

"On my faith," said Arthur, "there are good knights here, I believe, as good as any in the world, but it is not their fortune to help you, and that displeases me."

Chapter 2: How Balin, dressed like a poor knight, pulled out the sword, which afterwards was the cause of his death

Then it so happened at that time that there was a poor knight at King Arthur's court who had been his prisoner for half a year and more for killing a knight who was a cousin of King Arthur's. This knight's name was Balin, and through the good offices of the barons he had been released from prison, for he was known as a good man of his body, and he was born in Northumberland. And so he went quietly into the court, and saw this adventure, and it lifted his heart, and he wanted to try it as the other knights did. But because he was poor and poorly dressed, he did not push himself far forward into the crowd. Yet in his heart he was fully confident that he would do as well as any knight there, if fortune favoured him.

And as the damsel took her leave of Arthur and of all the barons, and was leaving, this knight Balin called to her, and said, "Damsel, I beg you, of your courtesy, allow me to try as these lords have. Though I am so poorly dressed, in my heart I feel as confident as some of these others, and in my heart I feel I shall succeed very well."

The damsel looked at the poor knight, and saw that he was a likely man; but because of his poor clothes she thought he could not be a man of honour, free of baseness or treachery. And then she said to the knight, "Sir, there is no need to put me to more pain or trouble, for it does not seem likely that you will succeed where others have failed."

"Ah, fair damsel," said Balin, "worthiness, and good qualities, and good deeds, are not only in a man's clothes; manhood and honour are hidden within a man's person, and many an honourable knight is not known to all people. And therefore honour and boldness are not in clothes."

"By God," said the damsel, "you speak the truth. Therefore you shall try to do what you can."

Then Balin took the sword by the belt and sheath, and drew it out easily; and when he looked at the sword it pleased him greatly. Then the king and all the barons marvelled greatly that Balin had achieved that adventure, and many knights felt great spite against Balin.

"Certainly," said the damsel, "this is an exceedingly good knight, and the best I ever found, and the most honourable, without treason, treachery or baseness, and he will do many marvels. Now, noble and courteous knight, give me the sword back."

"No," said Balin, "for I will keep this sword, unless it is taken from me by force."

"Well," said the damsel, "you are not wise to keep the sword from me, for with that sword you will kill the best friend you have, and the man you love most in the world, and the sword will be your destruction."

"I will take whatever adventure God sends me," said Balin, "but you shall not have the sword at this time, on my life."

"You will regret it before long," said the damsel, "for I would have the sword more for your good than for mine, for I am exceedingly sad for your sake. For you will not believe that the sword will be your destruction, and that is a great pity."

With that the damsel left, grieving greatly.

Immediately afterwards Balin sent for his horse and armour, and meant to leave the court, and took his leave of King Arthur.

"No," said the king, "I hope you will not leave this fellowship so lightly. I suppose you are displeased that I have treated you unkindly. Blame me the less for it, for I was misinformed about you; I did not think you were such a knight as you are, of honour and prowess. And if you will stay at this court among my fellowship, I will advance you so that you shall be pleased."

"God thank your highness," said Balin. "No man could praise your generosity and highness half as much as they are worth. But at this time I must leave, begging you always for your good grace."

"Truly," said the king, "I am very sorry and angry at your leaving. I beg you, fair knight, not to stay away long, and you shall be most welcome to me and to my barons, and I will make amends for every wrong I have done you."

"God thank your great lordship," said Balin, and with that he made ready to leave.

Then most of the knights of the Round Table said that Balin had not achieved this adventure by strength alone, but by witchcraft.

Chapter 3: How the Lady of the Lake demanded the head of the knight who had won the sword, or else the damsel's head

Meanwhile, while this knight was making ready to leave, there came into the court a lady who was called the Lady of the Lake. And she came on horseback, richly dressed, and greeted King Arthur, and there she asked him for the gift he had promised her when she gave him the sword.

"That is true," said Arthur. "I promised you a gift, but I have forgotten the name of the sword you gave me."

"The name of it," said the lady, "is Excalibur, which is as much as to say Cut-steel."

"You speak well," said the king. "Ask what you will and you shall have it, if it lies in my power to give it."

"Well," said the lady, "I ask for the head of the knight who has won the sword, or else the head of the damsel who brought it. I would not care if I had both their heads, for he killed my brother, a good knight and a true one, and that gentlewoman was the cause of my father's death."

"Truly," said King Arthur, "I cannot grant either of their heads with my honour. So ask for anything else you will, and I will fulfil your desire."

"I will ask for nothing else," said the lady.

When Balin was ready to leave, he saw the Lady of the Lake, who by her doing had killed Balin's mother, and he had been looking for her for three years. And when he was told that she had asked King Arthur for his head, he went straight to her and said, "Ill met! You want my head, and so you shall lose yours." And with his sword he swiftly struck off her head in front of King Arthur.

"Alas, for shame!" said Arthur. "Why have you done this? You have shamed me and all my court, for this was a lady I was indebted to, and she came here under my safe-conduct. I will never forgive you that offence."

"Sir," said Balin, "I am sorry for your displeasure, but this same lady was the falsest lady living, and by enchantment and sorcery she has been the destroyer of many good knights, and she was the cause of my mother being burned, through her falsehood and treachery."

"Whatever cause you had," said Arthur, "you should have spared her in my presence. So make no mistake, you will regret it, for I never had such an insult in my court. Therefore leave my court as fast as you can."

Then Balin took up the lady's head, and carried it with him to his lodging, and there he met his squire, who was sorry that he had displeased King Arthur; and so they rode out of the town.

"Now," said Balin, "we must part. Take this head and carry it to my friends, and tell them how I have fared, and tell my friends in Northumberland that my greatest enemy is dead. Also tell them how I am out of prison, and what adventure happened to me in winning this sword."

"Alas!" said the squire. "You are greatly to blame for displeasing King Arthur."

"As for that," said Balin, "I will hurry, as fast as I can, to meet King Rience and destroy him, or else die in the attempt. And if I have the luck to defeat him, then King Arthur will be my good and gracious lord."

"Where shall I meet you?" said the squire.

"At King Arthur's court," said Balin.

So he and his squire parted at that time. Then King Arthur and all the court grieved greatly, and were ashamed at the death of the Lady of the Lake. Then the king buried her richly.

Chapter 4: How Merlin told the story of this damsel

At that time there was a knight who was the son of the king of Ireland, and his name was Lanceor. He was a proud knight, and counted himself one of the best of the court; and he felt great spite against Balin for achieving the sword, that anyone should be counted bolder, or of more prowess. And he asked King Arthur if he would give him leave to ride after Balin and avenge the insult he had done.

"Do your best," said Arthur. "I am very angry with Balin. I wish he were paid back for the insult he has done to me and to my court."

Then this Lanceor went to his lodging to make himself ready. In the meantime Merlin came to King Arthur's court, and there he was told the adventure of the sword, and of the death of the Lady of the Lake.

"Now I will tell you," said Merlin. "This same damsel who stands here, who brought the sword to your court, I will tell you the reason for her coming: she is the falsest damsel alive."

"Do not say so," they said.

"She has a brother, an exceedingly good knight of prowess and a thoroughly true man. And this damsel loved another knight, who kept her as his lover; and this good knight her brother met the knight who kept her as his lover, and killed him by force of his hands. When this false damsel learned of this, she went to the Lady Lile of Avalon, and begged her for help, to be avenged on her own brother."

Chapter 5: How Balin was pursued by Sir Lanceor, a knight of Ireland, and how he jousted with him and slew him

"And so," said Merlin, "this Lady Lile of Avalon gave her this sword that she brought with her, and said that no man would pull it out of the sheath unless he was one of the best knights of this realm, and he would be hardy and full of prowess, and with that sword he would kill her brother. This was the reason the damsel came to this court. I know it as well as you do. Would to God she had never come to this court! But she never came into honourable company to do good, but always great harm. And the knight who has achieved the sword will be destroyed by that sword, and that will be a great loss, for there is no knight alive of more prowess than he is. And he will do you, my lord Arthur, great honour and kindness; and it is a great pity that he will not last but a little while, for I know of no man living to match his strength and boldness."

So the knight of Ireland armed himself at all points, and set his shield on his shoulder, and mounted his horse, and took his spear in his hand, and rode after him at a great pace, as fast as his horse could go. And within a little while, on a mountain, he caught sight of Balin, and with a loud voice he cried, "Stop, knight! For you will stop whether you like it or not, and the shield in front of you will not help you."

When Balin heard the shout, he turned his horse fiercely, and said, "Fair knight, what do you want with me? Do you want to joust with me?"

"Yes," said the Irish knight, "that is why I have come after you."

"Perhaps," said Balin, "it would have been better for you to have stayed at home. For many a man expects to put his enemy to shame, and often it falls on himself. From what court have you been sent?" said Balin.

"I have come from the court of King Arthur," said the knight of Ireland, "and I have come here to avenge the insult you did today to King Arthur and to his court."

"Well," said Balin, "I see well I must fight you, and I am sorry for it, to grieve King Arthur or any of his court. And your quarrel with me is a very weak one," said Balin, "for the lady who is dead did me great harm, and otherwise I would have been as unwilling as any knight living to kill a lady."

"Make ready," said the knight Lanceor, "and square up to me, for only one of us will stay alive on this field."

Then they took their spears, and came together as fast as their horses could drive, and the Irish knight struck Balin on the shield, so that his spear all went to splinters. And Balin hit him through the shield, and the hauberk gave way, and so the spear pierced through his body and the horse's rump. And at once Balin turned his horse fiercely, and drew out his sword, and did not know that he had killed him; and then he saw him lying like a dead corpse.

Chapter 6: How a damsel who loved Lanceor killed herself for love, and how Balin met his brother Balan

Then he looked around him, and saw a damsel who came riding as fast as the horse could go, on a fine palfrey. And when she saw that Lanceor was dead, she grieved beyond measure, and said, "O Balin, you have killed two bodies and one heart, and two hearts in one body, and you have lost two souls."

And with that she took the sword from her love who lay dead, and fell to the ground in a faint. And when she got up she grieved beyond measure, and her sorrow grieved Balin exceedingly. And he went to her to take the sword out of her hand, but she held it so tight that he could not take it out of her hand without hurting her. And suddenly she set the pommel to the ground, and ran herself through the body.

When Balin saw what she had done, he was exceedingly heavy at heart, and ashamed that so fair a damsel had destroyed herself for love of the man he had killed.

"Alas," said Balin, "I bitterly regret the death of this knight, for the love of this damsel, for there was much true love between them both."

And for sorrow he could not look at him any longer, but turned his horse and looked towards a great forest, and there, by his coat of arms, he recognised his brother Balan. And when they met they took off their helmets and kissed each other, and wept for joy and pity.

Then Balan said, "I little expected to meet you by this sudden chance. I am very glad of your release from your grievous imprisonment, for a man in the castle of Four Stones told me that you had been released, and that man had seen you at the court of King Arthur. And so I came here into this country, for here I expected to find you."

At once the knight Balin told his brother of his adventure of the sword, and of the death of the Lady of the Lake, and how King Arthur was displeased with him. "And so he sent this knight after me, who lies here dead, and the death of this damsel grieves me deeply."

"So it does me," said Balan, "but you must take whatever adventure God sends you."

"Truly," said Balin, "I am very heavy-hearted that my lord Arthur is displeased with me, for he is the most honourable knight who reigns on earth now, and I will win his love or else risk my life. For King Rience is laying siege to the Castle Terrabil, and we will go there in all haste, to prove our honour and prowess on him."

"Gladly," said Balan, "let us do that, and we will help each other as brothers should."

Chapter 7: How a dwarf reproached Balin for the death of Lanceor, and how King Mark of Cornwall found the dead lovers and made a tomb over them

"Now let us go from here," said Balin, "and well met are we."

Meanwhile, as they talked, a dwarf came from the city of Camelot on horseback, as fast as he could, and found the dead bodies. At this he grieved greatly, and pulled out his hair for sorrow, and said, "Which of you knights has done this deed?"

"Why do you ask?" said Balan.

"Because I want to know," said the dwarf.

"It was I," said Balin, "who killed this knight in my own defence, for he came here to chase me, and either I had to kill him or he me. And this damsel killed herself for love of him, and I regret it, and for her sake I will love all women the better."

"Alas," said the dwarf, "you have done yourself great harm, for this knight who lies here dead was one of the most valiant men alive. And be sure of this, Balin: this knight's kin will hunt you through the world until they have killed you."

"As for that," said Balin, "I am not greatly afraid; but I am very heavy-hearted that I have displeased my lord King Arthur by the death of this knight."

So as they talked together, a king of Cornwall came riding up, who was called King Mark. And when he saw these two bodies lying dead, and learned from the two knights mentioned above how they had died, then the king grieved greatly for the true love that had been between them, and said, "I will not leave until I have made a tomb here on this earth."

And there he pitched his tents and searched through all the country to find a tomb, and in a church they found one that was fair and rich. And then the king had them both laid in the earth, and put the tomb over them, and wrote the names of them both on the tomb: how here lies Lanceor, the son of the king of Ireland, who at his own request was killed by the hands of Balin; and how his lady and lover, Colombe, killed herself with her love's sword for grief and sorrow.

Chapter 8: How Merlin prophesied that the two best knights in the world would fight there, and that they would be Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram

Meanwhile, as this was being done, Merlin came in to King Mark, and seeing all that he was doing, said, "Here in this same place there will be the greatest battle between two knights that ever was or ever will be, and they will be the truest lovers, and yet neither of them will kill the other."

And there Merlin wrote on the tomb, in letters of gold, the names of the two who would fight in that place, and their names were Lancelot du Lake and Tristram.

"You are a strange man," said King Mark to Merlin, "to speak of such marvels. You are a rough fellow, and an unlikely one to tell of such deeds. What is your name?" said King Mark.

"At this time," said Merlin, "I will not tell it. But at the time when Sir Tristram is caught with his sovereign lady, then you shall hear and know my name, and at that time you shall hear news that will not please you."

Then Merlin said to Balin, "You have done yourself great harm, because you did not save this lady who killed herself, when you might have saved her if you had wanted to."

"On my life," said Balin, "I could not save her, for she killed herself suddenly."

"I am sorry for it," said Merlin. "Because of the death of that lady you will strike the most dolorous stroke that ever man struck, except the stroke of our Lord. For you will wound the truest knight and the man of most honour who is alive now, and through that stroke three kingdoms will be in great poverty, misery and wretchedness for twelve years, and the knight will not be healed of that wound for many years."

Then Merlin took his leave of Balin.

And Balin said, "If I knew that what you say were true, that I should do such a terrible deed as that, I would kill myself to make you a liar."

With that Merlin suddenly vanished. And then Balan and his brother took their leave of King Mark.

"First," said the king, "tell me your name."

"Sir," said Balan, "you can see he carries two swords; so you may call him the Knight with the Two Swords."

And so King Mark went off to Camelot to King Arthur, and Balin took the road towards King Rience. And as the brothers rode together they met Merlin in disguise, but they did not recognise him.

"Where are you riding?" said Merlin.

"We have little reason to tell you that," said the two knights.

"But what is your name?" said Balin.

"At this time," said Merlin, "I will not tell it to you."

"It looks bad," said the knights. "A man who will not tell his name is no honest man."

"As for that," said Merlin, "be that as it may, I can tell you why you are riding this way: to meet King Rience. But it will do you no good unless you have my advice."

"Ah!" said Balin. "You are Merlin. We will be guided by your advice."

"Come on," said Merlin. "You will win great honour; and see that you act like knights, for you will have great need to."

"As for that," said Balin, "do not be afraid. We will do what we can."

Chapter 9: How Balin and his brother, on Merlin's advice, captured King Rience and brought him to King Arthur

Then Merlin lodged them in a wood among the leaves beside the highway, and took the bridles off their horses and put them out to grass, and they lay down to rest until it was near midnight. Then Merlin told them to get up and make ready, for the king was near them. He had stolen away from his army with some sixty horsemen of his best knights, and twenty of them rode on ahead to warn the Lady de Vance that the king was coming; for that night King Rience was to have slept with her.

"Which is the king?" said Balin.

"Wait," said Merlin. "Here, in a narrow way, you will meet him." And with that he showed Balin and his brother where he was riding.

At once Balin and his brother met the king, and struck him down, and wounded him fiercely, and laid him on the ground. And there they killed men on the right hand and the left, and killed more than forty of his men, and the rest fled. Then they went back to King Rience and would have killed him if he had not surrendered himself to their mercy.

Then he spoke like this: "Knights full of prowess, do not kill me, for you may gain by my life, and by my death you will gain nothing."

Then these two knights said, "You speak truly and well." And so they laid him on a horse-litter.

With that Merlin vanished, and came to King Arthur ahead of them, and told him how his greatest enemy had been captured and defeated.

"By whom?" said King Arthur.

"By two knights," said Merlin, "who would like to please your lordship, and tomorrow you shall know what knights they are."

Soon afterwards the Knight with the Two Swords and Balan his brother came, and brought King Rience of North Wales with them, and there they handed him over to the porters, and gave him into their charge. And so the two of them went back again at the dawning of the day.

King Arthur then came to King Rience, and said, "Sir king, you are welcome. By what chance have you come here?"

"Sir," said King Rience, "I came here by a hard chance."

"Who captured you?" said King Arthur.

"Sir," said the king, "the Knight with the Two Swords and his brother, who are two marvellous knights of prowess."

"I do not know them," said Arthur, "but I am much indebted to them."

"Ah," said Merlin, "I will tell you. It is Balin, who achieved the sword, and his brother Balan, a good knight; there is no better knight living for prowess and worthiness. And it will be the greatest sorrow over him that I ever knew over any knight, for he will not last long."

"Alas," said King Arthur, "that is a great pity; for I am much indebted to him, and I have repaid him badly for his kindness."

"No," said Merlin, "he will do much more for you, and you will know that soon. But, sir, are you prepared?" said Merlin. "For tomorrow, before noon, Nero, King Rience's brother, will attack you with a great army. So make ready, for I will leave you."

Chapter 10: How King Arthur fought a battle against Nero and King Lot of Orkney, and how King Lot was deceived by Merlin, and how twelve kings were slain

Then King Arthur made his army ready in ten divisions, and Nero was ready in the field before the Castle Terrabil with a great army, and he had ten divisions, with many more men than Arthur had. Then Nero had the vanguard with most of his men, and Merlin came to King Lot of the Isle of Orkney, and kept him there with a tale of prophecy until Nero and his men were destroyed. And there Sir Kay the seneschal did exceedingly well, so that for all the days of his life the honour of it never left him. And Sir Hervis de Revel did marvellous deeds with King Arthur, and King Arthur killed twenty knights that day and maimed forty. At that time the Knight with the Two Swords and his brother Balan came in, and the two of them did so marvellously that the king and all the knights marvelled at them. And all who saw them said they were sent from heaven as angels, or as devils from hell; and King Arthur himself said they were the best knights he ever saw, for they struck such blows that all men wondered at them.

Meanwhile someone came to King Lot, and told him that while he lingered there Nero had been destroyed and killed with all his men.

"Alas," said King Lot, "I am ashamed, for through my fault many an honourable man has been killed. For if we had been together, there would have been no army under heaven able to match us. This vagabond with his prophecy has made a fool of me."

Merlin did all that, for he knew well that if King Lot had been there in person at the first battle, King Arthur would have been killed, and all his people destroyed. And Merlin knew well that one of the two kings would be dead that day, and Merlin was unwilling that either of them should be killed; but of the two, he would rather King Lot were killed than King Arthur.

"Now what is best to do?" said King Lot of Orkney. "Is it better for me to make terms with King Arthur or to fight, since the greater part of our people are killed and destroyed?"

"Sir," said a knight, "attack Arthur, for they are weary and worn out with fighting, and we are fresh."

"As for me," said King Lot, "I wish every knight would do his part as I will do mine."

And then they advanced their banners and clashed together and shattered all their spears to pieces; and Arthur's knights, with the help of the Knight with the Two Swords and his brother Balan, got the better of King Lot and his army. But King Lot kept himself always in the very front, and did marvellous deeds of arms, for his whole army was held up by his hands, for he stood against every knight. Alas, he could not last, and that was a great pity, that so worthy a knight as he was should be overmatched, who not long before had been one of King Arthur's knights, and had married King Arthur's sister. And because King Arthur had lain with King Lot's wife, who was Arthur's sister, and fathered Mordred on her, King Lot held out against Arthur.

So there was a knight who was called the Knight with the Strange Beast, and at that time his right name was Pellinore, and he was a good man of prowess. And he struck a mighty blow at King Lot as he fought against all his enemies, and he missed his stroke and struck the horse's neck, so that it fell to the ground with King Lot. And with that, at once, Pellinore struck him a great blow through the helmet and the head, down to the brows. And then all the army of Orkney fled because of the death of King Lot, and many mothers' sons were killed there. But King Pellinore bore the blame for the death of King Lot, and for that reason Sir Gawain avenged the death of his father in the tenth year after he was made a knight, and killed King Pellinore with his own hands. Also there were killed at that battle twelve kings on the side of King Lot and Nero, and all were buried in the Church of Saint Stephen's in Camelot, and the rest of the knights and of the others were buried in a great rock.

Chapter 11: Of the burial of twelve kings, and of Merlin's prophecy, and how Balin would strike the Dolorous Stroke

So to the burial came King Lot's wife Morgause with her four sons, Gawain, Agravain, Gaheris and Gareth. Also there came King Uriens, Sir Uwain's father, and Morgan le Fay his wife, who was King Arthur's sister. All these came to the burial. But of all these twelve kings, King Arthur had the tomb of King Lot made exceedingly rich, and had his tomb made by itself; and then Arthur had twelve images made of brass and copper, and gilded over with gold, to stand for the twelve kings, and each one of them held a wax taper that burned day and night. And King Arthur was made as a figure standing above them with a drawn sword in his hand, and all the twelve figures had faces like men who had been overcome. All this Merlin made by his subtle craft, and there he told the king, "When I am dead these tapers will burn no longer, and soon after that the adventures of the Holy Grail will come among you and be achieved." Also he told Arthur how Balin, the honourable knight, would strike the Dolorous Stroke, from which great vengeance would fall.

"Oh, where are Balin and Balan and Pellinore?" said King Arthur.

"As for Pellinore," said Merlin, "he will meet you soon. And as for Balin, he will not be long away from you. But the other brother will go away, and you will see him no more."

"On my faith," said Arthur, "they are two marvellous knights, and above all Balin surpasses in prowess any knight I ever found, for I owe him a great deal. I wish to God he would stay with me."

"Sir," said Merlin, "see that you keep the scabbard of Excalibur well, for you will lose no blood while you have the scabbard on you, though you have as many wounds on you as you can have."

So afterwards, out of great trust, Arthur gave the scabbard into the keeping of Morgan le Fay his sister. And she loved another knight better than her husband King Uriens or King Arthur, and she wanted to have Arthur her brother killed. And so she had another scabbard made like it by enchantment, and gave the scabbard of Excalibur to her lover; and the knight's name was Accolon, who afterwards nearly killed King Arthur. After this Merlin told King Arthur of the prophecy that there would be a great battle near Salisbury, and that Mordred his own son would be against him. Also he told him that Bagdemagus was his cousin, and closely related to King Uriens.

Chapter 12: How a sorrowful knight came before Arthur, and how Balin fetched him, and how that knight was slain by an invisible knight

Within a day or two King Arthur was somewhat sick, and he had his tent pitched in a meadow, and there he lay down on a straw bed to sleep, but he could get no rest. Just then he heard a great noise of a horse, and with that the king looked out at the entrance of the tent, and saw a knight coming right past him, grieving greatly.

"Wait, fair sir," said Arthur, "and tell me why you are grieving like this."

"You can do little to help me," said the knight, and so rode on to the castle of Meliot.

Soon afterwards Balin came by, and when he saw King Arthur he got down from his horse, and came to the king on foot, and greeted him.

"By my head," said Arthur, "you are welcome. Sir, just now a knight came riding this way grieving greatly, for what reason I cannot tell. So I would ask you, out of your courtesy and your noble nature, to bring that knight back, either by force or else of his own free will."

"I will do more than that for you, my lord," said Balin. And so he rode at better than a walking pace, and found the knight with a damsel in a forest, and said, "Sir knight, you must come with me to King Arthur, to tell him of your sorrow."

"That I will not do," said the knight, "for it will do me great harm, and you no good."

"Sir," said Balin, "I beg you, make ready, for you must go with me, or else I must fight you and bring you by force, and I would be very unwilling to do that."

"Will you be my safeguard," said the knight, "if I go with you?"

"Yes," said Balin, "or else I will die for it."

And so he made ready to go with Balin, and left the damsel where she was. And just as they were in front of King Arthur's tent, someone invisible came and struck the knight who was riding with Balin right through the body with a spear.

"Alas," said the knight, "I have been killed while under your protection, by a knight called Garlon. So take my horse, which is better than yours, and ride to the damsel, and follow the quest I was on as she leads you, and avenge my death when you can."

"That I will do," said Balin, "and I make a vow of it on my knighthood." And so he left this knight with great sorrow.

So King Arthur had this knight buried richly, and had an inscription made on his tomb telling how Herlews le Berbeus was killed there, and by whom the treachery was done, the knight Garlon. But the damsel always carried with her the broken shaft of the spear that Sir Herlews was killed with.

Chapter 13: How Balin and the damsel met a knight who was slain in the same way, and how the damsel gave her blood for the custom of a castle

So Balin and the damsel rode into a forest, and there they met a knight who had been out hunting, and that knight asked Balin why he was grieving so greatly.

"I don't care to tell you," said Balin.

"Now," said the knight, "if I were armed as you are, I would fight you."

"There would be little need of that," said Balin. "I am not afraid to tell you." And he told him the whole reason, how it had happened.

"Ah," said the knight, "is that all? Here I promise you, on my life, never to leave you as long as I live."

And so they went to the inn, and the knight armed himself, and so rode on with Balin. And as they came by a hermitage right beside a churchyard, the knight Garlon came invisible, and struck this knight, Perin de Mountbeliard, through the body with a spear.

"Alas," said the knight, "I am killed by this traitor knight who rides invisible."

"Alas," said Balin, "this is not the first insult he has done me."

And there the hermit and Balin buried the knight under a rich stone, in a royal tomb. And in the morning they found letters of gold written there, saying that Sir Gawain would avenge his father King Lot's death on King Pellinore.

Soon after this Balin and the damsel rode until they came to a castle, and there Balin dismounted, and he and the damsel started to go into the castle. And as soon as Balin came inside the castle gate, the portcullis fell down behind him, and a crowd of men fell upon the damsel, and would have killed her. When Balin saw that, he was badly upset, for he could not help the damsel. Then he went up into the tower, and leapt over the walls into the moat, and did not hurt himself; and at once he pulled out his sword and would have fought them. And they all said no, they would not fight him, for they were only keeping the old custom of the castle. And they told him how their lady was sick, and had been bedridden for many years, and she could not be cured unless she had a silver dish full of the blood of a pure maiden who was a king's daughter. "And so the custom of this castle is that no damsel shall pass this way unless she bleeds a silver dish full of her blood."

"Well," said Balin, "she shall bleed as much as she can bleed, but I will not let her lose her life while my life lasts."

And so Balin had her bleed, with her consent, but her blood did not help the lady. And so he and she rested there all night, and were given a very good welcome there, and in the morning they went on their way. And as it is told later in the story of the Holy Grail, Sir Percival's sister helped that lady with her blood, and died of it.

Chapter 14: How Balin met the knight named Garlon at a feast and slew him there, to have his blood to heal his host's son

Then they rode for three or four days and never met with any adventure, and by chance they were lodged with a gentleman who was a rich man and lived in comfort. And as they sat at their supper, Balin heard someone near him, in a chair, groaning grievously.

"What is this noise?" said Balin.

"Truly," said his host, "I will tell you. I was at a joust not long ago, and there I jousted with a knight who is brother to King Pellam, and twice I struck him down. And then he promised to pay me back through my best friend; and so he wounded my son, who cannot be healed until I have some of that knight's blood. And he always rides invisible, but I do not know his name."

"Ah!" said Balin. "I know that knight. His name is Garlon. He has killed two knights of mine in the same way, and so I would rather meet that knight than have all the gold in this realm, for the insults he has done me."

"Well," said his host, "I will tell you. King Pellam of Listeneise has had a great feast proclaimed throughout this country, to be held within these twenty days, and no knight may come to it unless he brings his wife with him, or his lady-love. And that knight, your enemy and mine, you will see there that day."

"Then I promise you," said Balin, "some of his blood to heal your son with."

"We will set out tomorrow morning," said his host.

So in the morning all three of them rode toward Pellam's country, and they had fifteen days' journey before they got there; and that same day the great feast began. And so they dismounted and stabled their horses, and went into the castle; but Balin's host could not be let in, because he had no lady. Then Balin was well received and brought to a chamber, and took off his armour; and robes were brought to him, as he pleased, and they wanted Balin to leave his sword behind him.

"No," said Balin, "that I will not do, for it is the custom of my country that a knight always keeps his weapon with him, and I will keep that custom, or else I will leave as I came."

Then they gave him leave to wear his sword, and so he went into the castle hall, and was seated among knights of honour, and his lady in front of him.

Soon Balin asked a knight, "Is there not a knight in this court whose name is Garlon?"

"There he goes, over there," said a knight, "the one with the dark face. He is the most extraordinary knight now living, for he destroys many good knights, for he goes invisible."

"Ah, well," said Balin, "is that him?"

Then Balin thought it over for a long time: "If I kill him here I will not escape, and if I leave him now, perhaps I will never meet him again at such a chance, and he will do much harm if he lives."

With that this Garlon noticed that Balin was looking at him, and then he came and struck Balin in the face with the back of his hand, and said, "Knight, what are you staring at me for? Shame on you. Eat your food and do what you came for."

"That's true enough," said Balin. "This is not the first insult you have done me, and so I will do what I came for." And he rose up fiercely and split Garlon's head to the shoulders.

"Give me the broken spear shaft," said Balin to his lady, "that he killed your knight with."

At once she gave it to him, for she always carried the shaft with her. And with that Balin struck him through the body with it, and said for all to hear, "With that shaft you killed a good knight, and now it sticks in your own body."

And then Balin called his host to him, saying, "Now you can fetch blood enough to heal your son with."

Chapter 15: How Balin fought King Pellam, and how his sword broke, and how he got a spear with which he struck the Dolorous Stroke

At once all the knights rose from the table to set upon Balin, and King Pellam himself rose up fiercely, and said, "Knight, have you killed my brother? You will die for it before you leave."

"Well," said Balin, "do it yourself, then."

"Yes," said King Pellam, "no man shall fight you but me myself, for the love of my brother."

Then King Pellam caught up a grim weapon in his hand and struck fiercely at Balin. But Balin put his sword between his head and the stroke, and with that his sword burst in pieces. And when Balin was weaponless he ran into a chamber to look for some weapon, and so from chamber to chamber, and he could find no weapon, and King Pellam was always after him. And at last he came into a chamber that was marvellously and richly furnished, with a bed hung with cloth of gold, the richest that could be imagined, and someone lying in it. And beside it stood a table of pure gold, with four pillars of silver holding up the table, and on the table stood a marvellous spear, strangely made. And when Balin saw that spear, he took it in his hand and turned to King Pellam, and struck him exceedingly hard with that spear, so that King Pellam fell down in a faint. And with that the castle's roof and walls broke and fell to the ground, and Balin fell down so that he could not stir hand or foot. And so the greater part of the castle, which had fallen down through that Dolorous Stroke, lay on top of Pellam and Balin for three days.

Chapter 16: How Balin was freed by Merlin, and saved a knight who would have killed himself for love

Then Merlin came there and lifted Balin up, and got him a good horse, for his own was dead, and told him to ride out of that country.

"I want my damsel," said Balin.

"Look," said Merlin, "there she lies dead."

And King Pellam lay like that for many years, badly wounded, and could never be healed until Galahad, the high prince, healed him in the quest of the Holy Grail. For in that place was part of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which Joseph of Arimathea brought into this land, and it was Joseph himself who lay in that rich bed. And that was the same spear with which Longius struck our Lord to the heart. And King Pellam was close kin to Joseph, and he was the most honourable man who lived in those days, and his hurt was a great pity, for through that stroke all turned to great grief, sorrow and suffering.

Then Balin left Merlin, and said, "In this world we will never meet again."

So he rode on through the fair countries and cities, and found the people dead, killed on every side. And all who were still alive cried out, "O Balin, you have caused great damage in these countries! Because of the Dolorous Stroke you gave King Pellam, three countries are destroyed, and have no doubt the vengeance will fall on you in the end."

When Balin was past those countries he was exceedingly glad.

So he rode for eight days before he met with any adventure. And at last he came into a fair forest in a valley, and noticed a tower, and close by it he saw a great warhorse tied to a tree, and beside it a fine knight sat on the ground grieving greatly; and he was a handsome man, and well built.

Balin said, "God save you, why are you so sad? Tell me, and I will put it right, if it is in my power."

"Sir knight," he answered, "you are doing me great harm, for I was lost in happy thoughts, and now you are putting me in more pain."

Balin went a little way off from him, and looked at his horse. Then Balin heard him say this: "Ah, fair lady, why have you broken your promise to me? For you promised to meet me here by noon. And I may curse you for ever giving me this sword, for with this sword I will kill myself." And he pulled it out.

And with that Balin leapt to him and took him by the hand.

"Let go of my hand," said the knight, "or else I will kill you."

"There will be no need of that," said Balin, "for I promise you my help to win your lady, if you will tell me where she is."

"What is your name?" said the knight.

"My name is Balin le Savage."

"Ah, sir, I know you well enough. You are the Knight with the Two Swords, and the man of greatest prowess with his hands now living."

"What is your name?" said Balin.

"My name is Garnish of the Mount, a poor man's son, but for my prowess and boldness a duke made me a knight, and gave me lands. His name is Duke Hermel, and his daughter is the one I love, and she loves me, as I believed."

"How far from here is she?" said Balin.

"Only six miles," said the knight.

"Now let us ride from here," said these two knights.

So they rode at better than a walking pace, until they came to a fair castle, well walled and moated.

"I will go into the castle," said Balin, "and see if she is there."

So he went in and searched from chamber to chamber, and found her bed, but she was not in it. Then Balin looked into a fair little garden, and under a laurel tree he saw her lying on a quilt of green samite, and a knight in her arms, the two of them holding each other close, and grass and herbs under their heads. When Balin saw her lying like that with the ugliest knight he had ever seen, and she a fair lady, then Balin went back through all the chambers again, and told the knight how he had found her as if she were fast asleep, and so brought him to the place where she lay sound asleep.

Chapter 17: How that knight killed his love and a knight lying beside her, and afterwards killed himself with his own sword, and how Balin rode toward a castle where he lost his life

And when Garnish saw her lying like that, out of pure sorrow his mouth and nose burst out bleeding, and with his sword he struck off both their heads. And then he grieved beyond measure, and said, "O Balin, you have brought great sorrow on me, for if you had not shown me that sight I would have got over my sorrow."

"Truly," said Balin, "I did it so that it would raise your spirits, and so that you could see and know her falseness, and to make you give up loving such a lady. God knows I did nothing but what I would want you to do for me."

"Alas," said Garnish, "now my sorrow is doubled, so that I cannot bear it. Now I have killed what I loved most in all my life." And with that he suddenly ran himself through on his own sword up to the hilt.

When Balin saw that, he made off from there, in case people would say he had killed them. And so he rode on, and within three days he came by a cross, and on it were letters of gold written, which said, "It is not for any knight to ride alone toward this castle."

Then he saw an old white-haired gentleman coming toward him, who said, "Balin le Savage, you are going beyond your bounds to come this way. So turn back, and it will be to your good." And at once he vanished away.

And then he heard a horn blow as if for the death of a hunted beast.

"That blast," said Balin, "is blown for me, for I am the prey, and yet I am not dead."

At once with that he saw a hundred ladies and many knights, who welcomed him with friendly faces, and gave him an exceedingly good welcome to all appearances, and led him into the castle, and there was dancing and music and every kind of joy.

Then the chief lady of the castle said, "Knight with the Two Swords, you must fight and joust with a knight near here who guards an island, for no man may pass this way unless he jousts before he passes."

"That is an unlucky custom," said Balin, "that a knight may not pass this way unless he jousts."

"You will only have to fight one knight," said the lady.

"Well," said Balin, "since I must, I am ready. But travelling men are often weary, and their horses too. But though my horse is weary, my heart is not weary. I would gladly be where my death is to be."

"Sir," said a knight to Balin, "I think your shield is not good. I will lend you a bigger one."

"I beg you, do."

And so he took the shield that was unknown and left his own, and so rode to the island, and put himself and his horse in a great boat. And when he came to the other side he met a damsel, and she said, "O Knight Balin, why have you left your own shield? Alas, you have put yourself in great danger, for by your shield you would have been known. It is as great a pity about you as ever there was about any knight, for in prowess and boldness you have no equal living."

"I regret," said Balin, "that I ever came into this country. But I cannot turn back now for shame, and whatever adventure befalls me, be it life or death, I will take the adventure that comes to me."

And then he looked over his armour, and saw that he was well armed, and with that he crossed himself and mounted his horse.

Chapter 18: How Balin met his brother Balan, and how each of them slew the other without knowing him, until both were mortally wounded

Then in front of him he saw a knight come riding out of a castle, with his horse trapped all in red, and himself in the same colour. When this knight in red saw Balin, he thought it must be his brother Balin, because of his two swords, but because he did not know his shield he decided it was not him. And so they set their spears in rest and came together marvellously fast, and they struck each other on the shields; but their spears and their charge were so mighty that it bore down horse and man, so that they both lay in a faint. But Balin was badly bruised by the fall of his horse, for he was weary from travelling. And Balan was the first to get to his feet, and he drew his sword and went toward Balin, and Balin rose and went against him. But Balan struck Balin first, and Balin put up his shield, and Balan struck him through the shield and cut into his helm. Then Balin struck him back with that ill-fated sword, and very nearly felled his brother Balan, and so they fought there together until their breath failed. Then Balin looked up to the castle and saw the towers full of ladies. So they went into battle again, and wounded each other grievously, and then they stopped for breath many times, and so went into battle again, until all the place where they fought was blood red.
