And by that time each of them had given the other seven great wounds, so that the least of them might have been the death of the mightiest giant in this world.

Then they went into battle again so marvellously that it was dreadful to hear of that battle, for the great bloodshed; and their hauberks had burst their rivets, so that they were bare on every side. At last Balan, the younger brother, drew back a little and lay down.

Then Balin le Savage said, "What knight are you? For before now I never found a knight who matched me."

"My name," he said, "is Balan, brother to the good knight Balin."

"Alas," said Balin, "that I should ever see this day." And with that he fell backward in a faint.

Then Balan crawled on his hands and feet, and took the helm off his brother, and could not recognise him by his face, it was so hacked and bloody. But when Balin came to, he said, "O Balan, my brother, you have killed me and I you, and so all the wide world will speak of us both."

"Alas," said Balan, "that I ever saw this day, that by ill luck I could not recognise you. For I saw your two swords well enough, but because you had another shield I thought you were another knight."

"Alas," said Balin, "an ill-fated knight in the castle did all this, for he made me leave my own shield, to the destruction of us both. And if I could live, I would destroy that castle for its evil customs."

"That would be well done," said Balan, "for I have never been allowed to leave them since I came here. For here it happened that I killed a knight who guarded this island, and since then I could never leave; and no more could you, brother, if you had managed to kill me, as you have, and escaped with your own life."

Just then the lady of the tower came to them with four knights and six ladies and six yeomen, and there she heard how they made their lament to each other, and said, "We both came out of one tomb, that is to say one mother's womb, and so we shall both lie in one grave."

So Balan begged the lady, out of her kindness, in return for his true service, to bury them both in the same place where the battle was fought. And she granted them, weeping, that it would be done richly, in the best way.

"Now, will you send for a priest, so that we may receive our sacrament, and receive the blessed body of our Lord Jesus Christ?"

"Yes," said the lady, "it shall be done." And so she sent for a priest and gave them their last rites.

"Now," said Balin, "when we are buried in one tomb, and the inscription made over us telling how two brothers killed each other, no good knight or good man will ever see our tomb without praying for our souls."

And so all the ladies and gentlewomen wept for pity. Then soon Balan died, but Balin did not die until the midnight after; and so they were both buried, and the lady had an inscription made for Balan, telling how he was killed there by his brother's hands, but she did not know Balin's name.

Chapter 19: How Merlin buried them both in one tomb, and of Balin's sword

In the morning Merlin came and had Balin's name written on the tomb in letters of gold: "Here lies Balin le Savage, who was the Knight with the Two Swords, and he who struck the Dolorous Stroke."

Also Merlin had a bed made there, such that no man should ever lie in it without going out of his mind; yet Lancelot du Lake undid that bed through his nobility.

And soon after Balin was dead, Merlin took his sword, and took off the pommel and put on another pommel. Then Merlin told a knight who stood in front of him to handle that sword, and he tried, and he could not handle it. Then Merlin laughed.

"Why are you laughing?" said the knight.

"This is the reason," said Merlin. "No man shall ever handle this sword but the best knight in the world, and that will be Sir Lancelot or else Galahad his son. And with this sword Lancelot will kill the man he loved best in the world, and that will be Sir Gawain."

All this he had written on the pommel of the sword.

Then Merlin had a bridge of iron and of steel made out to that island, and it was only half a foot wide, and no man shall ever cross that bridge, or have the courage to go over it, unless he is an exceedingly good man and a good knight, without treachery or baseness. Also Merlin left the scabbard of Balin's sword on this side of the island, so that Galahad would find it. Also Merlin by his subtle craft had Balin's sword set in a marble stone standing upright, as big as a millstone, and the stone floated always above the water, and did so for many years. And so by chance it floated down the stream to the City of Camelot, which in English is Winchester. And that same day Galahad, the high prince, came with King Arthur, and so Galahad brought the scabbard with him and won the sword that was there in the marble stone floating on the water. And on Whitsunday he won the sword, as it is told in the book of the Holy Grail.

Soon after this was done, Merlin came to King Arthur and told him of the Dolorous Stroke that Balin gave King Pellam, and how Balin and Balan fought together the most marvellous battle that was ever heard of, and how they were both buried in one tomb.

"Alas," said King Arthur, "this is the greatest pity I ever heard tell of two knights, for I know of no two such knights in the world."

So ends the tale of Balin and of Balan, two brothers born in Northumberland, good knights.

Here follows the third book.

Book Three: The Marriage of King Arthur

Chapter 1: How King Arthur took a wife and married Guinevere, daughter of Leodegrance, King of the Land of Cameliard, from whom he received the Round Table

In the beginning of Arthur's reign, after he was chosen king by chance and by grace, most of the barons did not know that he was Uther Pendragon's son, except as Merlin made it openly known. And yet many kings and lords made great war against him for that reason. But Arthur overcame them all well, for for most of the days of his life he was guided much by the counsel of Merlin. So it happened one time that King Arthur said to Merlin, "My barons will give me no rest, but I must take a wife, and I will take none except by your counsel and by your advice."

"It is well done," said Merlin, "that you take a wife, for a man of your goodness and nobility should not be without a wife. Now, is there any woman you love more than another?"

"Yes," said King Arthur. "I love Guinevere, the daughter of King Leodegrance of the land of Cameliard, who keeps in his house the Round Table that you told me he had from my father Uther. And this damsel is the most worthy and the fairest lady that I know living, or that I could ever find."

"Sir," said Merlin, "as for her beauty and fairness, she is one of the fairest alive. But if you did not love her as well as you do, I could find you a damsel of beauty and of goodness who would suit you and please you, if your heart were not set. But where a man's heart is set, he will be unwilling to turn back."

"That is true," said King Arthur.

But Merlin warned the king in veiled words that Guinevere was not good for him to take as his wife, for he warned him that Lancelot would love her, and she him in return. And so he turned his talk to the adventures of the Holy Grail.

Then Merlin asked the king for men to go with him to make enquiries about Guinevere, and the king granted it him. And Merlin went off to King Leodegrance of Cameliard, and told him of the king's wish to have his daughter Guinevere as his wife.

"That is the best news I ever heard," said King Leodegrance, "that so worthy a king, of such prowess and nobility, will marry my daughter. And as for my lands, I would give them to him if I knew it would please him, but he has lands enough; he needs none. But I will send him a gift that will please him much more, for I will give him the Round Table, which Uther Pendragon gave me. And when it is fully complete, there are a hundred and fifty knights at it. As for a hundred good knights, I have them myself, but I lack fifty, for so many have been killed in my days."

And so Leodegrance handed over his daughter Guinevere to Merlin, and the Round Table with the hundred knights, and so they rode briskly, with great royal splendour, partly by water and partly by land, until they came near to London.

Chapter 2: How the Knights of the Round Table were established and their seats blessed by the Bishop of Canterbury

When King Arthur heard of the coming of Guinevere and the hundred knights with the Round Table, then King Arthur rejoiced greatly at her coming and at that rich present, and said openly, "This fair lady is exceedingly welcome to me, for I have loved her long, and so there is nothing so dear to me. And these knights with the Round Table please me more than very great riches."

And in all haste the king had the marriage and the coronation arranged in the most honourable way that could be devised.

"Now, Merlin," said King Arthur, "go and find me fifty knights in all this land who are of the most prowess and honour."

Within a short time Merlin had found knights enough to fill twenty-eight places, but he could find no more. Then the Bishop of Canterbury was fetched, and he blessed the seats with great royal splendour and devotion, and there seated the twenty-eight knights in their places. And when this was done Merlin said, "Fair sirs, you must all rise and come to King Arthur to do him homage; he will be the more willing to support you."

And so they rose and did their homage. And when they had gone, Merlin found on every seat letters of gold that told the names of the knights who had sat there. But two seats were empty.

And so at once young Gawain came and asked the king for a gift.

"Ask," said the king, "and I will grant it you."

"Sir, I ask that you will make me a knight on the same day that you marry fair Guinevere."

"I will do it gladly," said King Arthur, "and do you all the honour I can, for I must by right: you are my nephew, my sister's son."

Chapter 3: How a poor man riding a thin mare asked King Arthur to make his son a knight

Straight away a poor man came into the court, and brought with him a handsome young man of eighteen years of age riding on a thin mare. And the poor man asked everyone he met, "Where will I find King Arthur?"

"There he is," said the knights. "Do you want something with him?"

"Yes," said the poor man, "that is why I came here."

As soon as he came before the king, he greeted him and said, "O King Arthur, the flower of all knights and kings, I pray Jesus save you. Sir, I was told that at this time of your marriage you would give any man the gift he asked for, except one that was unreasonable."

"That is true," said the king. "I had such proclamations made, and I will keep to it, so long as it does not weaken my realm or my estate."

"You speak well and graciously," said the poor man. "Sir, I ask nothing else but that you will make my son here a knight."

"It is a great thing you ask of me," said the king. "What is your name?" said the king to the poor man.

"Sir, my name is Aries the cowherd."

"Does this come from you or from your son?" said the king.

"No, sir," said Aries, "this wish comes from my son and not from me. For I tell you, I have thirteen sons, and they will all turn to whatever work I set them to, and are very glad to work. But this boy will not work for me, whatever my wife or I may do, but he is always shooting or throwing darts, and glad to see battles and to watch knights, and always, day and night, he begs me to have him made a knight."

"What is your name?" said the king to the young man.

"Sir, my name is Tor."

The king looked at him hard, and saw that he was exceedingly good-looking and exceedingly well built for his years.

"Well," said King Arthur to Aries the cowherd, "bring all your sons before me so that I can see them."

And so the poor man did, and they were all shaped much like the poor man. But Tor was not like any of them, in build or in face, for he was much bigger than any of them.

"Now," said King Arthur to the cowherd, "where is the sword he will be made a knight with?"

"It is here," said Tor.

"Take it out of the sheath," said the king, "and ask me to make you a knight."

Then Tor got down off his mare and drew his sword, kneeling, and asked the king to make him a knight, and that he might be a knight of the Round Table.

"As for a knight, I will make you one." And with that he struck him on the neck with the sword, saying, "Be a good knight, and I pray to God that you may be so; and if you prove to be of prowess and worth, you shall be a knight of the Round Table. Now, Merlin," said Arthur, "say whether this Tor will be a good knight or not."

"Yes, sir, he ought to be a good knight, for he comes from as good a man as any alive, and of kings' blood."

"How so, sir?" said the king.

"I will tell you," said Merlin. "This poor man, Aries the cowherd, is not his father; he is no kin to him at all, for King Pellinore is his father."

"I don't believe it," said the cowherd.

"Bring your wife before me," said Merlin, "and she will not deny it."

At once the wife was fetched, and she was a handsome housewife. And there she answered Merlin very modestly, and there she told the king and Merlin that when she was a girl and went out to milk the cows, a stern knight met her, "and half by force he took my virginity, and at that time he fathered my son Tor, and he took away from me my greyhound that I had with me at that time, and said that he would keep the greyhound for love of me."

"Ah," said the cowherd, "I never suspected this, but I can well believe it, for he never had any of my ways about him."

"Sir," said Tor to Merlin, "do not dishonour my mother."

"Sir," said Merlin, "it brings you more honour than harm, for your father is a good man and a king, and he may very well advance you and your mother, for you were conceived before ever she was married."

"That is true," said the wife.

"It is the less grief to me," said the cowherd.

Chapter 4: How Sir Tor was recognised as the son of King Pellinore, and how Gawain was made a knight

So in the morning King Pellinore came to the court of King Arthur, who was overjoyed to see him, and told him about Tor, how he was his son, and how he had made him a knight at the request of the cowherd. When Pellinore looked at Tor, he was very pleased with him. So the king made Gawain a knight, but Tor was the first he made at the feast.

"What is the reason," said King Arthur, "that there are two places empty among the seats?"

"Sir," said Merlin, "no man shall sit in those places but those who are of the most honour. But in the Siege Perilous, the Perilous Seat, no man shall sit but one, and if anyone is bold enough to try it he will be destroyed; and he who sits there shall have no equal."

And with that Merlin took King Pellinore by the hand, and at the place next to the two seats and the Siege Perilous he said, in the hearing of all, "This is your place, and of anyone here you are the most worthy to sit in it."

At that Sir Gawain sat in great envy, and told his brother Gaheris, "That knight over there is given great honour, which grieves me badly, for he killed our father King Lot. So I will kill him," said Gawain, "with a sword that was sent to me that is exceedingly sharp."

"You shall not do that," said Gaheris, "not now. For at this time I am only a squire, and when I am made a knight I will be avenged on him. And so, brother, it is best that you wait until another time, when we can get him out of the court; for if we did it now we would disturb this high feast."

"Gladly," said Gawain, "as you wish."

Chapter 5: How at the feast of King Arthur's wedding to Guinevere a white hart came into the hall with thirty couple of hounds, and how a little hound bit the hart and was carried off

Then the high feast was made ready, and the king was married to Dame Guinevere at Camelot, in the church of Saint Stephen's, with great solemnity. And when every man was seated according to his rank, Merlin went to all the knights of the Round Table and told them to sit still, and that none of them should leave his place. "For you shall see a strange and a marvellous adventure."

Just as they sat there, a white hart came running into the hall, and a little white hound right behind him, and thirty couple of black running hounds came after with a great baying. And the hart went round the Round Table, and past the other tables. The little white hound bit him in the haunch and pulled out a piece, and at that the hart leapt a great leap and knocked over a knight who sat at the side of a table. And with that the knight got up and picked up the hound, and so went out of the hall, and took his horse and rode away with the hound.

At once a lady came in on a white palfrey, a lady's riding horse, and cried aloud to King Arthur, "Sir, do not let me suffer this insult, for the hound that the knight led away was mine."

"I can do nothing about it," said the king.

With this a knight came riding in, fully armed, on a great horse, and took the lady away with him by force, and all the while she cried out and made great lament. When she had gone the king was glad, for she made such a noise.

"No," said Merlin, "you cannot let these adventures go so lightly; for these adventures must be brought back, or else it would be a dishonour to you and to your feast."

"I wish," said the king, "that everything be done by your advice."

"Then," said Merlin, "have Sir Gawain called, for he must bring back the white hart. Also, sir, you must have Sir Tor called, for he must bring back the hound and the knight, or else kill him. Also have King Pellinore called, for he must bring back the lady and the knight, or else kill him. And these three knights will do marvellous deeds before they come back."

Then all three were called, as was told before, and each of them took on his charge, and armed himself securely. But Sir Gawain had the first request, and so we will begin with him.

Chapter 6: How Sir Gawain rode to bring back the hart, and how two brothers fought each other over the hart

Sir Gawain rode at better than a walking pace, and his brother Gaheris rode with him in place of a squire, to serve him. So as they rode they saw two knights fighting on horseback exceedingly hard, so Sir Gawain and his brother rode between them, and asked them why they were fighting like that.

One knight answered and said, "We are fighting over a trivial matter, for we two are brothers, born and fathered of one man and one woman."

"Alas," said Sir Gawain, "why are you doing this?"

"Sir," said the elder, "a white hart came this way today, and many hounds chased him, and a little white hound was always right behind him. And we understood it was an adventure sent for the high feast of King Arthur, and so I would have gone after it to win myself honour. And here my younger brother said he would go after the hart, because he was a better knight than I. And for this reason we fell to quarrelling, and so we thought to prove which of us was the better knight."

"This is a trivial cause," said Sir Gawain. "You should quarrel with strangers, and not brother with brother. So unless you will follow my advice I will fight you; that is, you shall surrender to me, and go to King Arthur and surrender to his mercy."

"Sir knight," said the two brothers, "we are worn out with fighting, and we have lost much blood through our own wilfulness, and so we would be unwilling to fight you."

"Then do as I tell you," said Sir Gawain.

"We agree to do your will. But by whom shall we say we were sent there?"

"You may say: by the knight who follows the quest of the white hart. Now what is your name?" said Gawain.

"Sorlouse of the Forest," said the elder.

"And my name," said the younger, "is Brian of the Forest."

And so they left and went to the king's court, and Sir Gawain went on his quest.

And as Gawain followed the hart by the baying of the hounds, there was a great river right in front of him, and the hart swam across. And as Sir Gawain was about to follow after, there stood a knight on the other side, and said, "Sir knight, do not come across after this hart unless you will joust with me."

"I will not fail on that account," said Sir Gawain, "to follow the quest I am on." And so he made his horse swim across the water.

And at once they took their spears and ran together very hard; but Sir Gawain struck him off his horse, and then he turned his horse and ordered him to surrender.

"No," said the knight, "not so, even though you have the better of me on horseback. I ask you, valiant knight, get down on foot, and let us match ourselves with swords."

"What is your name?" said Sir Gawain.

"Allardin of the Isles," said the other.

Then each of them set his shield and they struck at each other, but Sir Gawain struck him so hard through the helmet that it went into the brain, and the knight fell down dead.

"Ah!" said Gaheris. "That was a mighty stroke for a young knight."

Chapter 7: How the hart was chased into a castle and slain there, and how Sir Gawain killed a lady

Then Gawain and Gaheris rode at better than a walking pace after the white hart, and let slip three couple of greyhounds at the hart. And so they chased the hart into a castle, and in the main courtyard of the castle they killed the hart; Sir Gawain and Gaheris followed after. Just then a knight came out of a chamber with a drawn sword in his hand and killed two of the greyhounds, right in front of Sir Gawain, and the rest he chased out of the castle with his sword.

And when he came back, he said, "O my white hart, I grieve that you are dead, for my sovereign lady gave you to me, and I have kept you badly, and your death will be dearly paid for if I live."

And at once he went into his chamber and armed himself, and came out fiercely, and there he met Sir Gawain.

"Why have you killed my hounds?" said Sir Gawain. "For they only did what is in their nature, and I would rather you had taken out your anger on me than on a dumb beast."

"You speak the truth," said the knight. "I have taken my revenge on your hounds, and I will on you too, before you go."

Then Sir Gawain got down on foot and set his shield, and they struck at each other mightily, and split their shields, and battered their helmets, and broke their hauberks so that the blood ran down to their feet.

At last Sir Gawain struck the knight so hard that he fell to the ground, and then he begged for mercy, and surrendered, and begged him, as he was a knight and a gentleman, to spare his life.

"You die," said Sir Gawain, "for killing my hounds."

"I will make amends," said the knight, "as far as I am able."

Sir Gawain would have no mercy, but unlaced his helmet to strike off his head. Just then his lady came out of a chamber and fell over him, and so he struck off her head by mischance.

"Alas," said Gaheris, "that is foully and shamefully done; that shame will never leave you. Also, you should give mercy to those who ask for mercy, for a knight without mercy is without honour."

Sir Gawain was so stunned by the death of this fair lady that he did not know what he was doing, and said to the knight, "Get up, I will give you mercy."

"No, no," said the knight, "I care nothing for mercy now, for you have killed my love and my lady, whom I loved best of all earthly things."

"I bitterly regret it," said Sir Gawain, "for I meant to strike at you. But now you shall go to King Arthur and tell him of your adventures, and how you were overcome by the knight who went on the quest of the white hart."

"I don't care," said the knight, "whether I live or die."

But for fear of death he swore to go to King Arthur, and Gawain made him carry one greyhound in front of him on his horse, and another behind him.

"What is your name?" said Sir Gawain, "before we part."

"My name," said the knight, "is Ablamar of the Marsh."

So he left for Camelot.

Chapter 8: How four knights fought against Gawain and Gaheris, and how they were overcome, and their lives spared at the request of four ladies

And Sir Gawain went into the castle, and made ready to stay there all night, and was about to take off his armour.

"What are you doing?" said Gaheris. "Will you take off your armour in this country? You can be sure you have many enemies here."

No sooner had he said that than four knights came, well armed, and attacked Sir Gawain hard, and said to him, "You new-made knight, you have shamed your knighthood, for a knight without mercy is dishonoured. You have also killed a fair lady, to your great shame to the world's end. And make no mistake, you will have great need of mercy before you leave us."

And with that one of them struck Sir Gawain such a great blow that he nearly fell to the ground, and Gaheris struck him back hard. And so they fought, on the one side and on the other, until Sir Gawain and Gaheris were in danger of their lives. And one with a bow, an archer, shot Sir Gawain through the arm, so that it pained him terribly. And as they were about to be killed, four fair ladies came and begged the knights to show grace to Sir Gawain. And courteously, at the ladies' request, they gave Sir Gawain and Gaheris their lives, and made them surrender as prisoners. Then Gawain and Gaheris grieved greatly.

"Alas!" said Sir Gawain. "My arm pains me badly; I am likely to be maimed." And so he lamented pitifully.

Early the next morning one of the four ladies, who had heard all his lament, came to Sir Gawain and said, "Sir knight, how are you?"

"Not well," he said.

"It is your own fault," said the lady, "for you have done an exceedingly foul deed in killing the lady, which will be a great disgrace to you. But are you not of King Arthur's kin?" said the lady.

"Yes, truly," said Sir Gawain.

"What is your name?" said the lady. "You must tell me before you go."

"My name is Gawain, son of King Lot of Orkney, and my mother is King Arthur's sister."

"Ah! Then you are King Arthur's nephew," said the lady, "and I will speak for you so that you will have safe conduct to go to King Arthur, for love of him."

And so she left and told the four knights that their prisoner was King Arthur's nephew, and that his name was Sir Gawain, King Lot of Orkney's son. And they gave him the hart's head, because it was his quest. Then at once they released Sir Gawain on this condition: that he should carry the dead lady with him in this way. Her head was hung around his neck, and the whole of her body lay in front of him on his horse's mane. And so he rode off to Camelot.

And as soon as he arrived, Merlin asked King Arthur to have Sir Gawain sworn to tell of all his adventures, and how he killed the lady, and how he would give no mercy to the knight, which was how the lady came to be killed. Then the king and the queen were greatly displeased with Sir Gawain for the killing of the lady. And there, by order of the queen, a jury of ladies was set to judge Sir Gawain. And they sentenced him, for ever, as long as he lived, to be on the side of all ladies, and to fight for their causes; and that he should always be courteous, and never refuse mercy to anyone who asks for mercy. So Gawain was sworn on the Four Gospels that he would never fight against a lady or a gentlewoman, unless he was fighting for one lady and his opponent was fighting for another. And so ends the adventure that Sir Gawain had at the marriage of King Arthur. Amen.

Chapter 9: How Sir Tor rode after the knight with the little hound, and of his adventures along the way

When Sir Tor was ready, he mounted his horse and rode after the knight with the little hound. And as he rode, he suddenly met a dwarf, who struck his horse on the head with a staff, so that it went backward a spear's length.

"Why did you do that?" said Sir Tor.

"Because you shall not pass this way," said the dwarf, "unless you joust with those knights in the tents over there."

Then Tor saw that there were two tents there, with great spears standing outside them, and two shields hanging on trees by the tents.

"I cannot stay," said Sir Tor, "for I am on a quest that I must follow."

"You shall not pass," said the dwarf, and with that he blew his horn.

Then there came a man armed on horseback, and he set his shield in place and came fast toward Tor, and Tor squared up to him, and they ran together so that Tor bore him off his horse. And at once the knight yielded himself to Tor's mercy.

"But, sir," he said, "I have a companion in that tent over there who will fight with you at once."

"He will be welcome," said Sir Tor.

Then he saw another knight coming at a great charge, and they set themselves at each other so that it was a marvel to see. But the knight struck Sir Tor a great stroke in the middle of the shield, so that his spear shattered to pieces. And Sir Tor struck him through the shield, low down, so that the spear went into the knight's side, but the stroke did not kill him. And with that Sir Tor dismounted and struck him a great stroke on the helm, and with that the knight yielded himself and begged him for mercy.

"Gladly," said Sir Tor, "but you and your companion must go to King Arthur, and give yourselves up to him as prisoners."

"By whom shall we say we were sent there?"

"You shall say by the knight who went on the quest of the knight who went with the little hound. Now, what are your two names?" said Sir Tor.

"My name," said the one, "is Sir Felot of Langduk."

"And my name," said the other, "is Sir Petipase of Winchelsea."

"Now go your way," said Sir Tor, "and God speed you and me."

Then the dwarf came and said to Sir Tor, "I beg you to grant me a gift."

"Gladly," said Sir Tor. "Ask."

"I ask no more," said the dwarf, "than that you will allow me to serve you, for I will serve no more cowardly knights who beg for their lives."

"Take a horse," said Sir Tor, "and ride on with me."

"I know you are riding after the knight with the white hound, and I will bring you to where he is," said the dwarf.

And so they rode through a forest, and at last they saw two tents, close by a priory, with two shields, and the one shield was painted white, and the other shield was red.

Chapter 10: How Sir Tor found the little hound with a lady, and how a knight attacked him over the hound

With that Sir Tor dismounted and gave the dwarf his sword, and so he came to the white tent, and saw three damsels lying in it, on one pallet, asleep. And so he went to the other tent, and found a lady lying asleep in it, but the white hound was there, and it bayed at her hard. And with that the lady went out of the tent, and all her damsels too. But as soon as Sir Tor saw the white hound, he took her by force and handed her to the dwarf.

"What, will you do that," said the lady, "take my hound from me?"

"Yes," said Sir Tor. "I have searched for this hound all the way here from King Arthur's court."

"Well, knight," said the lady, "you will not get far with her before you are met and made to suffer for it."

"I will face whatever adventure comes, by the grace of God," he said, and so he mounted his horse and went on his way toward Camelot. But it was so near night that he could go only a little further.

"Do you know of any lodging?" said Tor.

"I know of none," said the dwarf, "but there is a hermitage close by here, and there you must take lodging as you find it."

And within a while they came to the hermitage and took lodging there. And there was grass, oats and bread for their horses. That was soon seen to, and their own supper was very poor; but there they rested all night until the morning, and heard a mass devoutly, and took their leave of the hermit, and Sir Tor asked the hermit to pray for him. He said he would, and commended him to God. And so they mounted and rode towards Camelot a long while.

With that they heard a knight who was coming after them call out loud, and he said, "Knight, stop and give back my hound that you took from my lady!"

Sir Tor turned back and looked at him, and saw that he was a handsome knight, well mounted, and well armed at every point. Then Sir Tor set his shield in place, and took his spear in his hands, and the other came fiercely at him, and they struck each other down, both horse and man, to the earth. At once they got nimbly to their feet and drew their swords as fiercely as lions, and put their shields in front of them, and struck through the shields so that pieces fell off on both sides. They battered each other's helms too, so that the hot blood ran out, and they hacked and tore apart the thick mail of their hauberks, so that the hot blood ran to the earth, and both had many wounds and were exceedingly weary. But Sir Tor saw that the other knight was weakening, and then he pressed hard upon him, and doubled his strokes, and forced him to the earth on one side. Then Sir Tor told him to yield.

"That I will not," said Abelleus, "while my life lasts and the soul is in my body, unless you give me the hound."

"That I will not do," said Sir Tor, "for it was my quest to bring back your hound, or you, or both."

Chapter 11: How Sir Tor overcame the knight, and how that knight lost his head at the request of a lady

With that a damsel came riding on a palfrey as fast as she could drive it, and called out to Sir Tor in a loud voice.

"What do you want with me?" said Sir Tor.

"I beg you," said the damsel, "for King Arthur's love, grant me a gift. I ask it of you, good knight, as you are a man of noble birth."

"Now," said Tor, "ask a gift and I will give it to you."

"Thank you," said the damsel. "Now I ask for the head of the false knight Abelleus, for he is the most violent knight alive, and the greatest murderer."

"I regret the gift I have granted you," said Sir Tor. "Let him make amends for the wrong he has done you."

"Now," said the damsel, "he cannot, for he killed my own brother before my own eyes, and my brother was a better knight than he, if he had had the luck. And I knelt half an hour in the mud in front of him to save my brother's life, though my brother had done him no harm, but had fought him by the chance of arms. And for all that I could do, he struck off his head. And so I ask you, as you are a true knight, to give me my gift, or else I will shame you before all the court of King Arthur; for he is the falsest knight living, and a great destroyer of good knights."

Then when Abelleus heard this, he was more afraid, and yielded himself and asked for mercy.

"I cannot now," said Sir Tor, "unless I am to be found false to my promise. For when I would have granted you mercy, you would ask for none, unless you had the hound back, and that was my quest."

And with that he took off his helm, and Abelleus got up and ran, and Sir Tor went after him, and struck his head clean off.

"Now, sir," said the damsel, "it is near night. I beg you to come and lodge with me here at my house; it is close by here."

"Gladly," said Sir Tor, for his horse and he had fared badly since they left Camelot. And so he rode with her, and had an exceedingly good welcome from her. And she had for her husband an old knight, a very fine one, who gave him an exceedingly good welcome, and made both his horse and him thoroughly comfortable. And in the morning he heard mass, and had breakfast, and took his leave of the knight and the lady, who begged him to tell them his name.

"Truly," he said, "my name is Sir Tor, who was lately made a knight, and this was the first quest of arms that I ever undertook: to bring back what this knight Abelleus took away from King Arthur's court."

"O fair knight," said the lady and her husband, "if you come into our country here, come and see our poor house, and it will always be at your command."

So Sir Tor left, and came to Camelot on the third day by noon. And the king and the queen and all the court were exceedingly glad of his coming, and rejoiced greatly that he had come back; for he went from the court with little help, except that King Pellinore his father gave him an old warhorse, and King Arthur gave him armour and a sword, and besides that he had no other help, but rode out like that, alone. And then the king and the queen, on Merlin's advice, made him swear to tell of his adventures, and so he told them and gave proof of his deeds, as has been told before, at which the king and the queen rejoiced greatly.

"No, no," said Merlin, "these are only trifles to what he will do. For he will prove a noble knight of prowess, as good as any living, and well-bred and courteous, and of good qualities, and exceedingly true to his promise, and he will never do a violent wrong."

Because of Merlin's words, King Arthur gave him an earldom of lands that had fallen to the crown. And here ends the quest of Sir Tor, King Pellinore's son.

Chapter 12: How King Pellinore rode after the lady and the knight who had carried her off, and how a lady asked him for help, and how he fought two knights for that lady, killing one of them with the first stroke

Then King Pellinore armed himself and mounted his horse, and rode at better than a walking pace after the lady whom the knight had led away. And as he rode in a forest, he saw in a valley a damsel sitting by a spring, with a wounded knight in her arms, and Pellinore greeted her. And when she saw him, she cried out very loud, "Help me, knight, for Christ's sake, King Pellinore!"

And he would not stop, he was so eager in his quest, and she cried after him for help a hundred times. When she saw he would not stay, she prayed to God to send him as much need of help as she had, and that he might feel it before he died. So, as the book tells, the knight who lay wounded there died, and because of that the lady killed herself with his sword out of pure sorrow. As King Pellinore rode through that valley he met a poor man, a labourer.

"Did you see," said Pellinore, "a knight riding by and leading away a lady?"

"Yes," said the man, "I saw that knight, and the lady, who was grieving greatly. And down there in a valley you will see two tents, and one of the knights from the tents claimed that lady from that knight, and said she was his near cousin, and so he should lead her no further. And so they agreed to fight over that quarrel. The one said he would have her by force, and the other said he would have charge of her, because he was her kinsman, and would take her to her family. I left them fighting over this quarrel. And if you ride hard you will find them fighting, and the lady was left behind with the two squires in the tents."

"God thank you," said King Pellinore.

Then he rode at a gallop until he came in sight of the two tents and the two knights fighting. At once he rode to the tents, and saw the lady who was his quest, and said, "Fair lady, you must come with me to the court of King Arthur."

"Sir knight," said the two squires who were with her, "over there are two knights fighting for this lady. Go there and part them, and come to terms with them, and then you can have her as you please."

"You speak well," said King Pellinore.

And at once he rode between them, and parted them, and asked them why they were fighting.

"Sir knight," said the one, "I will tell you. This lady is my near kinswoman, my aunt's daughter, and when I heard her complain that she was with him against her will, I took up the fight with him."

"Sir knight," said the other, whose name was Hontzlake of Wentland, "I won this lady by my prowess in arms this very day at Arthur's court."

"That is untruly said," said King Pellinore, "for you came in suddenly where we were at the high feast, and took this lady away before any man could make himself ready. And so it was my quest to bring her back, and both of you, or else for one of us to remain on the field. So the lady will go with me, or I will die for it, for I have promised it to King Arthur. And so fight no more, for neither of you shall have any part of her this time. And if you wish to fight for her, fight with me, and I will defend her."

"Well," said the knights, "make yourself ready, and we will attack you with all our strength."

And as King Pellinore was turning his horse away from them, Sir Hontzlake ran his horse through with a sword, and said, "Now you're on foot, the same as us!"

When King Pellinore saw that his horse was killed, he leapt nimbly from his horse and pulled out his sword, and put his shield in front of him, and said, "Knight, look to your head, for you'll take a blow for killing my horse."

So King Pellinore gave him such a stroke on the helm that he split his head down to the chin, so that he fell to the earth dead.

Chapter 13: How King Pellinore won the lady and brought her to Camelot, to the court of King Arthur

And then he turned to the other knight, who was badly wounded. But when that knight saw the blow the other had taken, he would not fight, but knelt down and said, "Take my cousin the lady with you, as you ask, and I beg you, as you are a true knight, to put her to no shame or dishonour."

"What," said King Pellinore, "will you not fight for her?"

"No, sir," said the knight, "I will not fight with a knight of such prowess as you are."

"Well," said Pellinore, "you speak well. I promise you she shall suffer no dishonour from me, as I am a true knight. But now I need a horse," said Pellinore, "and I will take Hontzlake's horse."

"You will not need to," said the knight, "for I will give you a horse that will please you, provided you will lodge with me, for it is near night."

"Gladly," said King Pellinore. "I will stay with you all night."

And there he had a very good welcome with him, and fared on the best, with exceedingly good wine, and had a merry rest that night. And in the morning he heard a mass and dined; and then a fine bay warhorse was brought to him, with King Pellinore's saddle set on it.

"Now, what shall I call you?" said the knight. "For you have my cousin as you desired, by your quest."

"Sir, I will tell you. My name is King Pellinore of the Isles, and I am a knight of the Round Table."

"Now I am glad," said the knight, "that such a noble man will have charge of my cousin."

"Now, what is your name?" said Pellinore. "I beg you to tell me."

"Sir, my name is Sir Meliot de Logres, and this lady my cousin is called Nimue. And the knight who was in the other tent is my sworn brother, an exceedingly good knight, and his name is Brian of the Isles. And he is very unwilling to do wrong, and very unwilling to fight with any man, unless he is hard pressed, so that for shame he cannot refuse."

"It is a wonder," said Pellinore, "that he will not fight with me."

"Sir, he will fight with no man unless it is at his own request."

"Bring him to the court one of these days," said Pellinore.

"Sir, we will come together."

"And you will be welcome," said Pellinore, "to the court of King Arthur, and greatly praised for your coming."

And so he left with the lady, and brought her to Camelot.

So as they rode in a valley, it was full of stones, and there the lady's horse stumbled and threw her down, so that her arm was badly bruised, and she nearly fainted with the pain.

"Alas, sir," said the lady, "my arm is out of joint, and because of it I must rest."

"So you shall," said King Pellinore.

And so he dismounted under a fine tree where there was good grass, and he put his horse to it, and so lay down under the tree and slept until it was nearly night. And when he woke he wanted to ride on.

"Sir," said the lady, "it is so dark that you might as well ride backward as forward."

So they stayed where they were and made their lodging there. Then Sir Pellinore took off his armour. Then a little before midnight they heard the trotting of a horse.

"Be still," said King Pellinore, "for we shall hear of some adventure."

Chapter 14: How on the way, as he lay at night in a valley, King Pellinore overheard two knights, and of their adventures

And with that he armed himself. So right in front of him two knights met, the one coming from Camelot and the other from the north, and each greeted the other.

"What news at Camelot?" said the one.

"By my head," said the other, "I have been there and spied on the court of King Arthur, and there is such a fellowship there that it can never be broken, and nearly all the world holds with Arthur, for there is the flower of chivalry. Now for this reason I am riding into the north, to tell our chieftains about the fellowship of knights that Arthur keeps about him."

"As for that," said the other knight, "I have brought a remedy with me, the greatest poison you ever heard of, and I am taking it to Camelot. For we have a friend very close to King Arthur, and well loved by him, who will poison King Arthur; for he has promised our chieftains to do it, and received great gifts for doing it."

"Beware of Merlin," said the other knight, "for he knows all things by the devil's craft."

"I will not hold back for that," said the knight.

And so they parted. Soon after, Pellinore made himself ready, and his lady too, and rode toward Camelot. And as they came by the spring where the wounded knight and the lady had been, there he found the knight, and the lady eaten by lions or wild beasts, all except the head. And at that he grieved greatly, and wept exceedingly hard, and said, "Alas, I might have saved her life; but I was so fierce in my quest that I would not stop."

"Why do you grieve so?" said the lady.

"I do not know," said Pellinore, "but my heart mourns hard for her death, for she was an exceedingly beautiful lady, and a young one."

"Now, will you take my advice?" said the lady. "Take this knight and have him buried at a hermitage, and then take the lady's head and carry it with you to Arthur."

So King Pellinore took this dead knight on his shoulders, and brought him to the hermitage, and gave the hermit charge of the body, so that a service should be said for his soul, "and take his armour for your trouble."

"It shall be done," said the hermit, "as I will answer to God."

Chapter 15: How when King Pellinore came to Camelot he was sworn on a book to tell the truth about his quest

And with that they left, and came to where the head of the lady lay, with its fair yellow hair, and it grieved King Pellinore exceedingly when he looked at it, for his heart was much drawn to that face. And so by noon they came to Camelot; and the king and the queen were exceedingly glad of his coming to the court. And there he was made to swear upon the Four Gospels to tell the truth of his quest from beginning to end.

"Ah, Sir Pellinore," said Queen Guinevere, "you were greatly to blame that you did not save this lady's life."

"Madam," said Pellinore, "you would be greatly to blame if you would not save your own life when you could. But, saving your pleasure, I was so fierce in my quest that I would not stop, and I am sorry for it, and shall be all the days of my life."

"Truly," said Merlin, "you ought to be bitterly sorry for it, for that lady was your own daughter, fathered on the lady of the Rule. And the knight who was dead was her love, and was to have married her, and he was a very good knight for a young man, and would have proved a good man. And he was on his way to this court, and his name was Sir Miles of the Launds. And a knight came up behind him and killed him with a spear, and his name is Loraine le Savage, a false knight and a coward. And she, for great sorrow and grief, killed herself with his sword, and her name was Elaine. And because you would not stop and help her, you will see your best friend fail you when you are in the greatest distress that you ever were or ever will be. And that is the penance God has ordained for you for that deed: that the man you trust most of any man alive will leave you where you will be killed."

"I am sorry," said King Pellinore, "that this will befall me, but God can well undo destiny."

Thus, when the quest of the white hart was done, which Sir Gawain followed; and the quest of the little hound, followed by Sir Tor, Pellinore's son; and the quest of the lady whom the knight took away, which King Pellinore followed at that time; then the king established all his knights, and to those who were not rich in lands he gave lands. And he charged them never to commit outrage or murder, and always to flee treason; and by no means to be cruel, but to give mercy to anyone who asks for mercy, on pain of forfeiting their honour and their lordship from King Arthur for evermore; and always to give help to ladies, damsels and gentlewomen, on pain of death. Also, that no man should take up a fight in a wrongful quarrel, not for any law, nor for any worldly goods. To this all the knights of the Round Table were sworn, both old and young. And every year they were sworn again at the high feast of Pentecost.

Here ends the Wedding of King Arthur.

Here follows the fourth book.

Book Four: How Merlin Was Besotted, and of the Wars Against King Arthur

Chapter 1: How Merlin was besotted with one of the ladies of the lake and doted on her, and how he was shut in a rock under a stone and died there

So after these quests of Sir Gawain, Sir Tor and King Pellinore, it happened that Merlin fell into a foolish passion for the damsel whom King Pellinore had brought to court; and she was one of the damsels of the lake, and her name was Nimue. But Merlin would give her no rest, but always wanted to be with her. And she always gave him a good welcome until she had learned from him everything she wanted to know; and he was so besotted with her that he could not keep away from her. So one time he told King Arthur that he would not last long, but that for all his crafts he would be put into the earth alive. And so he told the king many things that would come to pass, but always he warned the king to guard his sword and the scabbard well, for he told him how the sword and the scabbard would be stolen from him by a woman, one he trusted most. He also told King Arthur that he would miss him: "And yet you would rather have me back than have all your lands."

"Ah," said the king, "since you know what is going to happen to you, provide against it, and put away that misfortune with your crafts."

"No," said Merlin, "it will not be." And so he left the king.

And within a while the Damsel of the Lake left, and Merlin went with her always, wherever she went. And many times Merlin would have liked to have his way with her in secret by his subtle crafts; then she made him swear that he would never work any enchantment on her, if he wanted to have his will. And so he swore. So she and Merlin went over the sea to the land of Benwick, where King Ban was king, who was fighting a great war against King Claudas. And there Merlin spoke with King Ban's wife, a fair lady and a good one, and her name was Elaine; and there he saw young Lancelot. There the queen grieved greatly for the deadly war that King Claudas was making on her lord and on her lands.

"Do not be so sad," said Merlin, "for this same child, within twenty years from now, will take revenge for you on King Claudas, so that all Christendom will speak of it. And this same child will be the man of greatest honour in the world; and his first name is Galahad, that I know well," said Merlin, "and since then you have had him confirmed as Lancelot."

"That is true," said the queen. "His first name was Galahad. Oh, Merlin," said the queen, "shall I live to see my son such a man of prowess?"

"Yes, lady, on my life you shall see it, and live many winters after."

And so, soon after, the lady and Merlin left, and on the way Merlin showed her many wonders, and they came into Cornwall. And all the time Merlin was pressing the lady to take her maidenhood, and she was exceedingly weary of him, and would gladly have been rid of him, for she was afraid of him because he was a devil's son; and she could not shake him off by any means. And so one time it happened that Merlin showed her a great wonder in a rock, made by enchantment, that went in under a great stone. So by her subtle working she got Merlin to go in under that stone to let her know of the marvels there; but she worked her craft on him there so that he never came out again, for all the craft he could do. And so she left, and left Merlin there.

Chapter 2: How five kings came into this land to make war on King Arthur, and what counsel Arthur took against them

And King Arthur rode to Camelot, and held a great feast there with mirth and joy, and soon after he returned to Cardoile. And there new tidings came to Arthur that the King of Denmark, and the King of Ireland who was his brother, and the King of the Vale, and the King of Soleise, and the King of the Isle of Longtains, all these five kings with a great army, had entered King Arthur's land, and were burning and killing everything before them, both cities and castles, so that it was pitiful to hear.

"Alas," said Arthur, "I have never yet had one month's rest since I was crowned king of this land. Now I shall never rest until I meet those kings in a fair field, and I make my vow on that. For my true and loyal people shall not be destroyed through my failing. Come with me who will, and stay behind who will."

Then the king had a letter written to King Pellinore, and begged him to make ready in all haste, with as many men as he could most quickly raise, and to hurry after him in all haste. All the barons were secretly angry that the king would leave so suddenly; but the king would by no means wait, but sent letters to those who were not there, and told them to hurry after him, those who were not at the court at that time. Then the king came to Queen Guinevere, and said, "Lady, make yourself ready, for you shall go with me, for I cannot be without you for long. You will make me all the bolder, whatever chance befalls me. I will not have my lady be in any danger."

"Sir," she said, "I am at your command, and I shall be ready whenever you are ready."

So in the morning the king and the queen left with such company as they had, and came into the north, into a forest beside the Humber, and camped there. When the word and the tidings came to the five kings named above that Arthur was in a forest beside the Humber, there was a knight, brother to one of the five kings, who gave them this advice: "You know well that Sir Arthur has the flower of the chivalry of the world with him, as was proved by the great battle he fought with the eleven kings. And therefore hurry to him night and day until we are near him, for the longer he waits the bigger he grows, and we always the weaker. And he is so bold in himself that he has come to the field with few men, and therefore let us set upon him before daybreak, and we shall cut them down. Of his knights not one shall escape."

Chapter 3: How King Arthur fought them and defeated them, killed the five kings, and put the rest to flight

These five kings agreed to this advice, and so they went on with their army through North Wales, and came upon Arthur by night, and fell on his army while the king and his knights were in their tents. King Arthur was unarmed, and had lain down to rest with his Queen Guinevere.

"Sir," said Sir Kay, "it is not good for us to be unarmed."

"We shall have no need," said Sir Gawain and Sir Griflet, who lay in a little tent beside the king.

With that they heard a great noise, and many cried, "Treason, treason!"

"Alas," said King Arthur, "we are betrayed! To arms, my fellows!" he cried then.

So they were armed at once, from head to foot. Then a wounded knight came to the king, and said, "Sir, save yourself and my lady the queen, for our army is destroyed, and many of our men are killed."

So at once the king and the queen and the three knights took their horses, and rode towards the Humber to cross it; and the water was so rough that they were afraid to cross.

"Now you may choose," said King Arthur, "whether you will stay and take your chance on this side; for if you are taken, they will kill you."

"I would rather," said the queen, "die in the water than fall into your enemies' hands and be killed there."

And as they stood there talking, Sir Kay saw the five kings coming on horseback by themselves, alone, with their spears in their hands, straight towards them.

"Look," said Sir Kay, "there are the five kings. Let us go at them and take them on."

"That would be folly," said Sir Gawain, "for we are only three and they are five."

"That is true," said Sir Griflet.

"No matter," said Sir Kay. "I will take on two of them, and then you three can take on the other three."

And with that Sir Kay let his horse run as fast as it could, and struck one of them through the shield and the body a fathom deep, so that the king fell to the earth stone dead. Sir Gawain saw that, and charged another king so hard that he struck him through the body. And with that King Arthur charged another, and struck him through the body with a spear, so that he fell to the earth dead. Then Sir Griflet charged the fourth king, and gave him such a fall that his neck broke. At once Sir Kay charged the fifth king, and struck him so hard on the helm that the stroke split the helm and the head down to the earth.

"That was a fine stroke," said King Arthur, "and you have kept your promise honourably, and so I shall honour you as long as I live."

And with that they put the queen in a barge on the Humber. But all the while Queen Guinevere praised Sir Kay for his deeds, and said, "Whatever lady you love, if she does not love you back, she would be greatly to blame. And among ladies," said the queen, "I shall spread your noble fame, for you spoke a great word, and you fulfilled it honourably." And with that the queen left.

Then the king and the three knights rode into the forest, for they expected to hear there of those who had escaped; and there he found most of his people, and told them all how the five kings were dead. "And therefore let us hold together until it is day, and when their army sees that their chieftains are killed, they will grieve so wildly that they will be no more able to help themselves."

And just as the king said, so it was; for when they found the five kings dead, they grieved so wildly that they fell from their horses. With that King Arthur came on them with only a few men, and killed them on the left hand and on the right, so that very nearly not a man escaped, but all were killed, to the number of thirty thousand. And when the battle was all over, the king knelt down and humbly thanked God. And then he sent for the queen, and soon she came, and she rejoiced greatly at the winning of that battle.

Chapter 4: How the battle was over before King Pellinore came, and how King Arthur founded an abbey where the battle had been

With that someone came to King Arthur and told him that King Pellinore was within three miles with a great army.

And he said, "Go to him, and let him know how we have fared."

So within a while King Pellinore came with a great army, and greeted the people and the king, and there was great rejoicing on every side. Then the king had a search made to find how many of his side had been killed; and there were found to be only a little over two hundred men killed, and eight knights of the Round Table in their tents. Then the king had a fair abbey raised and planned on the same spot where the battle was fought, and endowed it with a great income, and had it called the Abbey of La Beale Adventure. But when some of them came into the countries where the five kings had been kings, and told them how they had been killed, there was great grief. And all King Arthur's enemies, such as the King of North Wales and the kings of the North, when they knew of the battle, were exceedingly downcast. And so the king returned to Camelot in haste.

And when he had come to Camelot he called King Pellinore to him, and said, "You understand well that we have lost eight of the best knights of the Round Table, and on your advice we will choose eight more, the best we can find in this court."

"Sir," said Pellinore, "I shall advise you the best I can as I see it. There are very noble knights in your court, both old and young; and therefore my advice is that you choose half from the old and half from the young."

"Which are the old?" said King Arthur.

"Sir," said King Pellinore, "it seems to me King Uriens, who has married your sister Morgan le Fay, and the King of the Lake, and Sir Hervise de Revel, a noble knight, and Sir Galagars as the fourth."

"This is well planned," said King Arthur, "and so it shall be. Now, which are the four young knights?" said Arthur.

"Sir," said Pellinore, "the first is Sir Gawain, your nephew, who is as good a knight for his age as any in this land. And the second, as it seems best to me, is Sir Griflet le Fise de Dieu, who is a good knight and very eager in arms, and whoever lives to see him will see him prove a good knight. And the third, as it seems to me, well fit to be one of the knights of the Round Table, is Sir Kay the Seneschal, for many times he has done very honourably, and now at your last battle he did most honourably in taking it on himself to kill two kings."

"By my head," said Arthur, "he is the most worthy to be a knight of the Round Table of any you have named, even if he had done no other deed of prowess in all his life."

Chapter 5: How Sir Tor was made a knight of the Round Table, and how Bagdemagus was offended

"Now," said King Pellinore, "I shall put two knights before you, and you shall choose which is the more worthy: that is, Sir Bagdemagus, and Sir Tor, my son. But because Sir Tor is my son I may not praise him; but otherwise, if he were not my son, I would dare to say that for his age there is no better knight in this land than he is, nor one of better character, and loath to do any wrong, and loath to take any wrong."

"By my head," said Arthur, "he is as exceedingly good a knight as any you have spoken of today, that I know well," said the king. "For I have seen him proved; but he says little and he does much more. For I know no one in all this court, if he were as well born on his mother's side as he is on yours, who is his equal in prowess and in might. And therefore I will have him this time, and leave Sir Bagdemagus until another time."

So when they had been chosen in this way with the consent of all the barons, the names of every one of the knights named here were found written on their seats; and so they were set in their seats. At this Sir Bagdemagus was furiously angry, that Sir Tor had been advanced before him, and so he left the court suddenly, and took his squire with him, and rode a long way in a forest until they came to a cross; and there they dismounted, and he said his prayers devoutly. Meanwhile his squire found written on the cross that Bagdemagus should never return to the court again until he had won the body of a knight of the Round Table, body for body.

"So, sir," said the squire, "here I find writing about you, and therefore I advise you to go back to the court."

"That I will never do," said Bagdemagus, "until men speak of my great honour, and I am worthy to be a knight of the Round Table."

And so he rode on, and there on the way he found a branch of a holy herb that was the sign of the Holy Grail; and no knight found such tokens unless he lived a good life.

So, as Sir Bagdemagus rode on to seek out many adventures, he happened to come to the rock where the Lady of the Lake had put Merlin under the stone, and there he heard him lamenting greatly. And at that Sir Bagdemagus would have helped him, and went to the great stone; and it was so heavy that a hundred men could not have lifted it. When Merlin knew he was there, he told him to give up his labour, for it was all in vain, for he could never be helped except by her who put him there. And so Bagdemagus left, and achieved many adventures, and proved afterwards a very good knight, and came back to the court and was made a knight of the Round Table. So in the morning new tidings came, and other adventures.

Chapter 6: How King Arthur, King Uriens, and Sir Accolon of Gaul chased a hart, and of their marvellous adventures

Then it happened that Arthur and many of his knights rode hunting into a great forest; and King Arthur, King Uriens and Sir Accolon of Gaul happened to follow a great hart, for the three of them were well mounted. And so they chased so fast that within a while the three of them were ten miles from their company. And at last they chased so hard that they killed their horses under them. Then all three of them were on foot, and all the time they saw the hart ahead of them, exceedingly weary and making for cover.

"What shall we do?" said King Arthur. "We are in a hard spot."

"Let us go on foot," said King Uriens, "until we can find some lodging."

Then they saw the hart lying on the bank of a great river, and a hound biting at his throat, and more hounds coming after. Then King Arthur blew the horn call for the kill, and dressed the hart.

Then the king looked all about him, and saw before him on a great river a little ship, all hung with silk down to the water; and the ship came straight to them and landed on the sands. Then Arthur went to the bank and looked in, and saw no earthly creature in it.

"Sirs," said the king, "come over here, and let us see what is in this ship."

So all three of them went in, and found it richly hung with silk cloth. By then it was dark night, and suddenly there were a hundred torches all about them, set on every side of the ship's planking, and they gave a great light. And with that twelve fair damsels came out and greeted King Arthur on their knees, and called him by his name, and said he was most welcome, and that he should have the best of such hospitality as they had. The king thanked them courteously. With that they led the king and his two companions into a fair room, and there a cloth was laid, richly furnished with everything that belonged to a table; and there they were served with every wine and every dish they could think of. At this the king marvelled greatly, for he had never fared better in his life at a single supper. And so when they had dined at their leisure, King Arthur was led into a room, and he never saw a more richly furnished room; and King Uriens was served the same, and led into another room like it; and Sir Accolon was led into the third room, exceedingly rich and well furnished. And so they were laid comfortably in their beds. And at once they fell asleep, and slept wonderfully deeply all night. And in the morning King Uriens was in Camelot, in bed in the arms of his wife, Morgan le Fay. And when he awoke he marvelled greatly how he had come there, for on the evening before he had been two days' journey from Camelot. And when King Arthur awoke he found himself in a dark prison, hearing all around him the many laments of wretched knights.

Chapter 7: How Arthur undertook to fight to win his own release from prison, and also to free twenty knights who were in prison

"Who are you that lament like this?" said King Arthur.

"We are twenty knights here, prisoners," they said, "and some of us have lain here seven years, and some more and some less."

"For what reason?" said Arthur.

"We will tell you," said the knights. "The lord of this castle is called Sir Damas, and he is the falsest knight alive, and full of treason, and as complete a coward as any alive. And he has a younger brother, a good knight of prowess, whose name is Sir Ontzlake. And this traitor Damas, the elder brother, will give him no share of his inheritance, except what Sir Ontzlake holds by the prowess of his own hands. And so he holds from him a very fair manor, and a rich one, and Sir Ontzlake lives there honourably, and is well loved by all the people. And this Sir Damas, our master, is as much hated, for he is without mercy, and he is a coward. And there has been great war between the two of them, but Ontzlake always has the better of it; and he keeps offering to fight Sir Damas for the inheritance, body for body, but he will not do it, or else to find a knight to fight for him. Sir Damas agreed to find a knight, but he is so disliked and hated that there is not one knight who will fight for him. And when Damas saw this, that there was not one knight who would fight for him, he has lain in wait every day with many knights, and taken all the knights in this country who come to see and look for adventures; he has taken them by force and brought them to his prison. And so he took us one by one as we rode on our adventures; and many good knights have died of hunger in this prison, eighteen knights in number. And if any of us all who are here, or have been here, had been willing to fight his brother Ontzlake, he would have set us free; but because this Damas is so false and so full of treason, we would never fight for him, even if we die for it. And we are so thin with hunger that we can scarcely stand on our feet."

"God deliver you, of His mercy," said Arthur.

At once, with that, a damsel came to Arthur, and asked him, "How are you?"

"I cannot say," he said.

"Sir," she said, "if you will fight for my lord, you shall be released from prison; and otherwise you will never escape with your life."

"Now," said Arthur, "that is hard. Yet I would rather fight with a knight than die in prison. If by this," said Arthur, "I can be freed, and all these prisoners, I will fight the battle."

"Yes," said the damsel.

"I am ready," said Arthur, "if I had a horse and armour."

"You shall lack nothing," said the damsel.

"It seems to me, damsel, that I have seen you in the court of Arthur."

"No," said the damsel, "I have never been there. I am the daughter of the lord of this castle."

Yet she was false, for she was one of the damsels of Morgan le Fay.

At once she went to Sir Damas, and told him how he would fight the battle for him, and so he sent for Arthur. And when he came he had a good colour and was well made in his limbs, so that all the knights who saw him said it would be a pity for such a knight to die in prison. So Sir Damas and he agreed that he should fight for him on this condition, that all the other knights should be set free; and Sir Damas swore that to Arthur, and Arthur also swore to fight the battle to the uttermost. And with that all twenty knights were brought out of the dark prison into the hall and set free, and so they all stayed to see the battle.

Chapter 8: How Accolon found himself beside a well, and undertook to do battle against Arthur

Now we leave Arthur and turn to Accolon of Gaul. When he awoke, he found himself beside a deep well, within half a foot of its edge, in great danger of death. And out of that spring there came a silver pipe, and out of that pipe water ran up high into a basin of marble. When Sir Accolon saw this, he crossed himself and said, "Jesus save my lord King Arthur and King Uriens, for these damsels in this ship have betrayed us. They were devils and not women. And if I can escape this mischance, I shall destroy these false damsels who use enchantments, wherever I can find them."

Just then there came a dwarf with a great mouth and a flat nose, and greeted Sir Accolon, and said that he came from Queen Morgan le Fay, "and she greets you well, and bids you be strong of heart, for you will fight tomorrow with a knight at the hour of prime, at six in the morning. And therefore she has sent you Excalibur, Arthur's sword, and the scabbard. And she bids you, as you love her, to fight the battle to the uttermost, without any mercy, just as you promised her when you spoke together in private. And whatever damsel brings her the head of the knight you will fight with, she will make her a queen."

"Now I understand you well," said Accolon. "I shall keep what I have promised her, now that I have the sword. When did you see my lady Queen Morgan le Fay?"

"Very lately," said the dwarf.

Then Accolon took him in his arms and said, "Commend me to my lady the queen, and tell her that everything I have promised her shall be done, or else I will die for it. Now I suppose," said Accolon, "she has made all these crafts and enchantments for this battle."

"You may well believe it," said the dwarf.

Just then there came a knight and a lady with six squires, and greeted Accolon, and begged him to get up and come and rest at their manor. And so Accolon mounted a spare horse, and went with the knight to a fair manor beside a priory, and there he was given an exceedingly good welcome.

Then Sir Damas sent word to his brother Sir Ontzlake, and told him to make ready by the next morning at the hour of prime, and to be in the field to fight with a good knight, for he had found a good knight who was ready to do battle in every way. When this word came to Sir Ontzlake he was exceedingly downcast, for a little before he had been wounded through both thighs with a spear, and he grieved greatly; but wounded as he was, he would have taken on the battle. So it happened at that time, through Morgan le Fay's contriving, that Accolon was lodged with Sir Ontzlake; and when he heard of that battle, and how Ontzlake was wounded, he said that he would fight for him. Because Morgan le Fay had sent him Excalibur and the sheath to fight the knight in the morning: that was the reason Sir Accolon took the battle on himself. Then Sir Ontzlake was exceedingly glad, and thanked Sir Accolon with all his heart for doing so much for him. And with that Sir Ontzlake sent word to his brother Sir Damas that he had a knight who would be ready in the field for him by the hour of prime.

So in the morning Sir Arthur was armed and well mounted, and asked Sir Damas, "When do we go to the field?"

"Sir," said Sir Damas, "you shall hear mass first."

And so Arthur heard a mass, and when mass was done a squire came on a great horse, and asked Sir Damas if his knight was ready, "for our knight is ready in the field." Then Sir Arthur mounted his horse, and all the knights and common people of that country were there; and so by common counsel twelve good men of the country were chosen to attend on the two knights. And just as Arthur was on horseback, a damsel came from Morgan le Fay, and brought Sir Arthur a sword like Excalibur, and the scabbard, and said to Arthur, "Morgan le Fay sends you your sword here, out of great love."

And he thanked her, and thought it was so; but she was false, for the sword and the scabbard were counterfeit, and brittle, and false.

Chapter 9: Of the battle between King Arthur and Accolon

And then they took up their places at either end of the field, and let their horses run so fast that each struck the other in the middle of the shield with their spearheads, so that both horse and man went to the earth. And then they both leapt up, and drew their swords. While they were fighting like this, the Damsel of the Lake, who put Merlin under the stone, came into the field; and she came there out of love for King Arthur, for she knew how Morgan le Fay had arranged things so that King Arthur would be killed that day, and so she came to save his life. And so they went eagerly at the battle, and gave many great strokes; but all the time Arthur's sword did not bite like Accolon's sword. But for the most part, every stroke that Accolon gave wounded Arthur badly, so that it was a marvel he stood, and all the time his blood ran from him fast.

When Arthur saw the ground so soaked with his blood he was dismayed, and then he suspected treason, that his sword had been changed; for his sword did not bite into steel as it used to, and so he was sorely afraid he would die. For it always seemed to him that the sword in Accolon's hand was Excalibur, for at every stroke Accolon struck he drew blood from Arthur.

"Now, knight," said Accolon to Arthur, "look out for yourself."

But Arthur gave no answer, and gave him such a blow on the helm that it made him stoop, nearly falling to the earth. Then Sir Accolon drew back a little, and came on with Excalibur raised high, and struck Sir Arthur such a blow that he nearly fell to the earth. Then they were both angry, and gave each other many heavy strokes; but all the time Sir Arthur lost so much blood that it was a marvel he stood on his feet. But he was so full of knighthood that he endured the pain like a knight. And Sir Accolon lost not a drop of blood, and so he grew exceedingly lively, and Sir Arthur was exceedingly weak, and truly expected to die. But for all that he kept a face as though he could hold out, and kept Accolon as close as he could. But Accolon was so bold because of Excalibur that he grew exceedingly daring. But all the men who watched said they had never seen a knight fight as well as Arthur did, considering the blood he had lost. So all the people were sorry for him; but the two brothers would not come to terms. Then they went on fighting together like fierce knights, and Sir Arthur drew back a little to rest, and Sir Accolon called him back to the fight and said, "This is no time for me to let you rest."

And with that he came at Arthur fiercely; and Sir Arthur was angry for the blood he had lost, and struck Accolon high on the helm, so mightily that he made him nearly fall to the earth. And with that Arthur's sword burst at the crossguard, and fell in the grass among the blood, and he was left holding the pommel and the grip in his hands. When Sir Arthur saw that, he was in great fear of dying; but all the time he held up his shield, and gave no ground, and did not let his face fall.

Chapter 10: How the sword King Arthur fought with broke, and how he won back his own sword Excalibur from Accolon and overcame his enemy

Then Sir Accolon began with treacherous words, and said, "Knight, you are beaten, and you can't hold out. You have no weapon, too, and you have lost a great deal of blood, and I am very unwilling to kill you. So yield to me and admit yourself beaten."

"No," said Sir Arthur, "I cannot do that, for I have promised on my life to fight this battle to the very end, while life lasts in me. And so I would rather die with honour than live with shame. And if it were possible for me to die a hundred times, I would rather die that many times than yield to you. For though I lack a weapon, I shall lack no honour, and if you kill me weaponless, the shame will be yours."

"Well," said Accolon, "as for the shame, I won't hold back for that. Now defend yourself, for you are as good as dead."

And with that Accolon gave him such a stroke that he nearly fell to the ground, and he would have had Arthur beg him for mercy. But Sir Arthur pressed in on Accolon with his shield, and struck him such a blow with the pommel in his hand that he went three strides backwards.

When the Damsel of the Lake saw Arthur, how full of prowess his body was, and the false treason that had been worked to have him killed, she had great pity that so good a knight and so honourable a man should be destroyed in that way. And at the next stroke Sir Accolon struck him such a blow that, by the damsel's enchantment, the sword Excalibur fell out of Accolon's hand to the ground. And with that Sir Arthur leapt swiftly to it, and got it in his hand, and at once he knew that it was his sword Excalibur, and said, "You have been away from me far too long, and you have done me great harm." And with that he saw the scabbard hanging by Accolon's side, and suddenly he leapt at him and pulled the scabbard off him, and threw it as far away as he could throw it.

"Now, knight," said Arthur, "this day you have done me great harm with this sword. Now you have come to your death, for I promise you that before we part you shall be paid back with this sword just as you have paid me. For you have made me endure much pain, and I have lost much blood."
