And with that Sir Arthur rushed at him with all his might and pulled him to the ground, and then tore off his helmet, and struck him such a blow on the head that the blood came out of his ears, his nose and his mouth.

"Now I will kill you," said Arthur.

"You may well kill me," said Accolon, "if it pleases you, for you are the best knight I ever met, and I see well that God is with you. But because I promised to fight this battle to the very end," said Accolon, "and never to yield and beg for my life while I lived, I will never yield with my own mouth, and God do with my body what He will."

Then Sir Arthur stopped to think, and it seemed to him that he had seen this knight before.

"Now tell me," said Arthur, "or I will kill you: what country are you from, and what court?"

"Sir Knight," said Sir Accolon, "I am of the court of King Arthur, and my name is Accolon of Gaul."

Then Arthur was more dismayed than he had been before, for then he remembered his sister Morgan le Fay, and the enchantment of the ship.

"O sir knight," he said, "I beg you, tell me who gave you this sword, and from whom you had it."

Chapter 11: How Accolon confessed the treason of Morgan le Fay, King Arthur's sister, and how she would have had Arthur killed

Then Sir Accolon thought it over, and said, "Cursed be this sword, for through it I have got my death."

"That may well be," said the king.

"Now, sir," said Accolon, "I will tell you. This sword has been in my keeping for most of this past year. And Morgan le Fay, King Uriens' wife, sent it to me yesterday by a dwarf, for this purpose: that I should kill King Arthur, her brother. For you must understand that King Arthur is the man in the world she hates most, because he has the most honour and prowess of anyone of her blood. Also she loves me beyond measure as her lover, and I love her in return. And if she could bring about Arthur's death by her arts, she would easily kill her husband King Uriens, and then she had planned for me to be king in this land, and so to reign, and she to be my queen. But that is all over now," said Accolon, "for I am sure of my death."

"Well," said Sir Arthur, "I can tell from what you say that you would have been king in this land. It would have been a great wrong to have destroyed your lord," said Arthur.

"That is the truth," said Accolon. "But now I have told you the truth, so I beg you, tell me where you are from, and of what court."

"O Accolon," said King Arthur, "now I tell you that I am King Arthur, to whom you have done great harm."

When Accolon heard that, he cried aloud, "Fair, sweet lord, have mercy on me, for I did not know you."

"O Sir Accolon," said King Arthur, "you shall have mercy, because I can tell from your words this time that you did not know who I was. But I understand well from your words that you agreed to my death, and so you are a traitor. But I blame you the less, for my sister Morgan le Fay, by her false arts, made you agree and consent to her false desires. But I shall be avenged on her so hard, if I live, that all Christendom will speak of it. God knows I have honoured her and esteemed her above all my kin, and I have trusted her more than my own wife and all my kin besides."

Then Sir Arthur called the keepers of the field, and said, "Sirs, come here, for here are two knights who have fought each other to the great harm of us both, and each of us was likely to have killed the other, if it had so happened. And if either of us had known the other, there would have been no battle here, and no stroke struck."

Then Accolon cried aloud to all the knights and men who were gathered there, and spoke to them in this way: "O lords, this noble knight I have fought with, which I bitterly regret, is the greatest man of prowess, of manhood and of honour in the world, for he is King Arthur himself, the liege lord of us all. And by mischance and misfortune I have fought this battle with the king and lord to whom I am bound."

Chapter 12: How Arthur reconciled the two brothers and freed the twenty knights, and how Sir Accolon died

Then all the people fell down on their knees and begged King Arthur's pardon.

"You shall have mercy," said Arthur. "Here you can see what adventures often befall knights errant, how I have fought with a knight of my own, to my great harm and to his too. But, sirs, because I am badly hurt, and he is too, and I have great need of a little rest, you shall hear my judgement between you two brothers. As for you, Sir Damas, for whom I have been champion and won the field against this knight: even so I will judge that, because you, Sir Damas, are called a proud knight, and full of villainy, and your deeds have no prowess in them, you shall give your brother the whole manor with everything that belongs to it, on these terms: that Sir Ontzlake hold the manor from you, and give you a palfrey every year to ride on, for that will suit you better to ride on than a warhorse. Also I charge you, Sir Damas, on pain of death, that you never harass any knights errant who ride on their adventures. And also that you give back to these twenty knights, whom you have kept prisoner so long, all their armour, so that they are satisfied. And if any of them comes to my court and complains of you, by my head, you shall die for it. Also, Sir Ontzlake, as for you, because you are called a good knight, and full of prowess, and true and noble in all your deeds, this is the charge I give you: that with all good speed you come to me and my court, and you shall be a knight of mine. And if your deeds match your name, I shall so advance you, by the grace of God, that in a short time you will have the means to live as honourably as your brother Sir Damas."

"God thank you for your generosity, your goodness and your bounty. From now on I shall be at your command at all times. For, sir," said Sir Ontzlake, "as God willed it, I was lately wounded through both thighs by a knight seeking adventures, which hurt me badly, or else I would have fought this battle with you."

"Would to God," said Arthur, "it had been so, for then I would not have been hurt as I am. I will tell you the reason why: I would not have been hurt as I am, if it had not been for my own sword, which was stolen from me by treason. And this battle was arranged beforehand to have me killed, and so it was brought about by false treason and by false enchantment."

"Alas," said Sir Ontzlake, "it is a great pity that any man or woman could find it in their hearts to work treason against so noble a man as you are, in your deeds and your prowess."

"I shall reward them," said Arthur, "in a short time, by the grace of God. Now tell me," said Arthur, "how far am I from Camelot?"

"Sir, you are two days' journey from there."

"I would gladly be at some honourable place," said Sir Arthur, "where I might rest."

"Sir," said Sir Ontzlake, "near here there is a rich abbey of nuns, founded by your forefathers, only three miles away."

So the king took his leave of all the people, and mounted on horseback, and Sir Accolon with him. And when they had come to the abbey, he had doctors fetched to examine his wounds and Accolon's both. But Sir Accolon died within four days, for he had lost so much blood that he could not live; but King Arthur recovered well. So when Accolon was dead, he had him sent on a horse-bier with six knights to Camelot, and said, "Carry him to my sister Morgan le Fay, and say that I send him to her as a present, and tell her I have my sword Excalibur and the scabbard."

So they set off with the body.

Chapter 13: How Morgan tried to kill Sir Uriens her husband, and how Sir Uwain her son saved him

Meanwhile Morgan le Fay believed King Arthur was dead. So one day she saw King Uriens lying asleep in his bed. Then she called to her a maiden who was in her confidence, and said, "Go and fetch me my lord's sword, for I never saw a better time to kill him than now."

"O madam," said the damsel, "if you kill my lord you can never escape."

"Never you mind," said Morgan le Fay, "for now I see that this is the best time to do it. So hurry, quickly, and fetch me the sword."

Then the damsel left, and found Sir Uwain sleeping on a bed in another room. So she went to Sir Uwain, and woke him, and told him, "Get up, and keep watch on my lady your mother, for she means to kill the king your father as he sleeps in his bed, and I am going to fetch his sword."

"Well," said Sir Uwain, "go on your way, and leave this to me."

At once the damsel brought Morgan the sword with trembling hands, and she took the sword swiftly, and drew it, and went boldly to the bedside, and watched for how and where she could best kill him. And as she lifted up the sword to strike, Sir Uwain leapt at his mother, and caught her by the hand, and said, "Ah, fiend, what are you doing? If you were not my mother, I would strike off your head with this sword. Ah," said Sir Uwain, "men say that Merlin was fathered by a devil, but I can say an earthly devil bore me."

"O fair son, Uwain, have mercy on me. I was tempted by a devil, and so I beg your pardon. I will never do such a thing again. Save my honour and do not give me away."

"On this condition," said Sir Uwain, "I will forgive you: that you will never set about such deeds again."

"No, son," she said, "and I give you my word on it."

Chapter 14: How Queen Morgan le Fay grieved bitterly for the death of Accolon, and how she stole the scabbard from Arthur

Then news came to Morgan le Fay that Accolon was dead, and his body brought to the church, and that King Arthur had his sword again. But when Queen Morgan knew that Accolon was dead, she was so sorrowful that her heart nearly burst. But because she did not want it known, outwardly she kept her composure, and showed no sign of sorrow. But she knew well that if she stayed until her brother Arthur came there, no amount of gold would buy her life.

Then she went to Queen Guinevere, and asked her leave to ride into the country.

"You might wait," said Queen Guinevere, "until your brother the king comes home."

"I cannot," said Morgan le Fay, "for I have such urgent news that I cannot delay."

"Well," said Guinevere, "you may leave when you like."

So early in the morning, before it was day, she took her horse and rode all that day and most of the night, and the next morning by noon she came to the same abbey of nuns where King Arthur lay. And knowing he was there, she asked where he was. And they answered that he had gone to bed to sleep, for he had had very little rest these three nights.

"Well," she said, "I order that none of you wake him until I do."

And then she got down from her horse, meaning to steal his sword Excalibur, and so she went straight to his room, and no one dared disobey her command. And there she found Arthur asleep in his bed, with Excalibur naked in his right hand. When she saw that, she was exceedingly unhappy that she could not get at the sword without waking him, and then she knew well she would have been dead. Then she took the scabbard and went her way on horseback.

When the king woke and missed his scabbard, he was angry, and he asked who had been there. And they said his sister Queen Morgan had been there, and had put the scabbard under her cloak and was gone.

"Alas," said Arthur, "you have kept a false watch over me."

"Sir," they all said, "we did not dare disobey your sister's command."

"Ah," said the king, "have the best horse fetched that can be found, and tell Sir Ontzlake to arm himself in all haste, and take another good horse and ride with me."

So at once the king and Ontzlake were well armed, and rode after this lady. And so they came by a cross and found a cowherd, and they asked the poor man whether any lady had come riding that way.

"Sir," said this poor man, "just now a lady came riding with some forty horses, and she rode to that forest over there."

Then they spurred their horses, and followed fast, and after a while Arthur caught sight of Morgan le Fay. Then he chased as fast as he could. When she saw him following her, she rode at a greater pace through the forest until she came to a plain. And when she saw she could not escape, she rode to a lake nearby, and said, "Whatever becomes of me, my brother shall not have this scabbard." And then she threw the scabbard into the deepest part of the water, so that it sank, for it was heavy with gold and precious stones.

Then she rode into a valley where there were many great stones, and when she saw she must be overtaken, she turned herself, horse and man, by enchantment into a great marble stone. Right after that Sir Arthur and Sir Ontzlake came to where the king could recognise his sister and her men, and one knight from another.

"Ah," said the king, "here you can see the vengeance of God, and now I am sorry that this misfortune has happened."

And then he looked for the scabbard, but it could not be found, so he returned to the abbey he had come from. So when Arthur had gone, she turned them all back into the likeness they had had before, and said, "Sirs, now we can go wherever we like."

Chapter 15: How Morgan le Fay saved a knight who was about to be drowned, and how King Arthur returned home again

Then Morgan said, "Did you see Arthur, my brother?"

"Yes," said her knights, "very well, and you would have found that out if we could have stirred from the spot, for by his warlike face he would have made us run."

"I believe you," said Morgan.

Soon after, as she rode, she met a knight leading another knight on his horse in front of him, bound hand and foot and blindfolded, to drown him in a spring. When she saw this knight bound like that, she asked him, "What are you going to do with that knight?"

"Lady," he said, "I am going to drown him."

"For what reason?" she asked.

"Because I found him with my wife, and she shall have the same death soon."

"That would be a pity," said Morgan le Fay. "Now, what do you say, knight? Is it true, what he says of you?" she said to the knight who was to be drowned.

"No, truly, madam, he does not speak rightly of me."

"Where are you from," said Morgan le Fay, "and of what country?"

"I am of the court of King Arthur, and my name is Manassen, cousin to Accolon of Gaul."

"You speak well," she said, "and for love of him you shall be set free, and you shall have your enemy in the same plight you are in."

So Manassen was untied and the other knight bound. And at once Manassen took off the other knight's armour, and armed himself in it, and so mounted on horseback, with the knight in front of him, and so threw him into the spring and drowned him. And then he rode back to Morgan, and asked if she had any message for King Arthur.

"Tell him that I rescued you, not for love of him but for love of Accolon. And tell him I do not fear him while I can turn myself and those who are with me into the likeness of stones. And let him know I can do much more when I see my time."

And so she went away into the country of Gore, and there she was richly received, and she made her castles and towns exceedingly strong, for she always greatly feared King Arthur.

When the king had rested well at the abbey, he rode to Camelot, and found his queen and his barons very glad of his coming. And when they heard of his strange adventures, as told above, they all marvelled at the falseness of Morgan le Fay; many knights wished her burnt. Then Manassen came to court and told the king of his adventure.

"Well," said the king, "she is a kind sister! I shall be so avenged on her, if I live, that all Christendom will speak of it."

So in the morning a damsel came from Morgan to the king, and she brought with her the richest cloak that was ever seen in that court, for it was set as full of precious stones as they could stand one beside another, and they were the richest stones the king ever saw. And the damsel said, "Your sister sends you this cloak, and asks that you accept this gift from her. And in whatever way she has offended you, she will make amends entirely as you please."

When the king looked at this cloak it pleased him greatly, but he said very little.

Chapter 16: How the Damsel of the Lake saved King Arthur from a cloak that would have burnt him

With that the Damsel of the Lake came to the king, and said, "Sir, I must speak with you in private."

"Say what you like," said the king.

"Sir," said the damsel, "do not put on this cloak until you have seen more, and on no account let it come on you, or on any knight of yours, until you command the one who brought it to put it on herself."

"Well," said King Arthur, "it shall be done as you advise me."

And then he said to the damsel who had come from his sister, "Damsel, this cloak you have brought me, I want to see it on you."

"Sir," she said, "it would not be fitting for me to wear a king's garment."

"By my head," said Arthur, "you shall wear it before it comes on my back, or on the back of any man here."

And so the king had it put on her, and at once she fell down dead, and never spoke a word again, and was burnt to cinders. Then the king was furiously angry, more than he had been before, and said to King Uriens, "My sister, your wife, is always plotting to betray me, and I know well that either you or my nephew, your son, is in league with her to have me destroyed. But as for you," said the king to King Uriens, "I do not much believe that you are in league with her, for Accolon confessed to me with his own mouth that she would have destroyed you as well as me, so I hold you excused. But as for your son, Sir Uwain, I hold him under suspicion, so I charge you to send him away from my court."

So Sir Uwain was dismissed. And when Sir Gawain knew of it, he made ready to go with him, and said, "Whoever banishes my first cousin banishes me."

So the two of them left, and rode into a great forest, and so they came to an abbey of monks, and there they were well lodged. But when the king learned that Sir Gawain had left the court, there was great sorrow among all the ranks.

"Now," said Gaheris, Gawain's brother, "we have lost two good knights for the love of one."

So in the morning they heard mass in the abbey, and so they rode on until they came to a great forest. Then Sir Gawain saw in a valley, by a tower, twelve fair damsels, and two knights armed on great horses, and the damsels were walking to and fro by a tree. And then Sir Gawain saw that a white shield hung on that tree, and every time the damsels came by it they spat on it, and some threw mud on the shield.

Chapter 17: How Sir Gawain and Sir Uwain met twelve fair damsels, and how they complained of Sir Marhaus

Then Sir Gawain and Sir Uwain went and greeted them, and asked why they were insulting the shield like that.

"Sir," said the damsels, "we will tell you. There is a knight in this country who owns this white shield, and he is an exceedingly good fighter, but he hates all ladies and gentlewomen, and so we heap all this insult on the shield."

"I will tell you," said Sir Gawain, "it ill becomes a good knight to despise all ladies and gentlewomen. And perhaps, though he hates you, he has some particular reason, and perhaps somewhere else he loves ladies and gentlewomen, and is loved in return, if he is such a man of prowess as you say. Now, what is his name?"

"Sir," they said, "his name is Marhaus, the son of the king of Ireland."

"I know him well," said Sir Uwain. "He is as fine a knight as any alive, for I saw him tested once at a joust where many knights were gathered, and that time no man could stand against him."

"Ah, damsels!" said Sir Gawain. "I think you are to blame. For it is to be supposed that whoever hung that shield there will not be long away from it, and then those knights may match him on horseback, and that would be more to your honour than this. For I will not stay any longer to see a knight's shield dishonoured."

And with that Sir Uwain and Gawain moved off a little way from them, and then they saw Sir Marhaus come riding on a great horse straight toward them. And when the twelve damsels saw Sir Marhaus, they fled into the tower as if they were wild, so that some of them fell on the way. Then one of the knights of the tower set his shield, and called out loudly, "Sir Marhaus, defend yourself!"

And so they charged together, so that the knight broke his spear on Marhaus, and Marhaus struck him so hard that he broke his neck and the horse's back. The other knight of the tower saw that, and squared up to Marhaus, and they met so fiercely that the knight of the tower was soon struck down, horse and man, stone dead.

Chapter 18: How Sir Marhaus jousted with Sir Gawain and Sir Uwain, and unhorsed them both

And then Sir Marhaus rode to his shield, and saw how it had been fouled, and said, "For this insult I am partly avenged. But for love of her who gave me this white shield, I will wear you, and hang mine where you were." And so he hung it around his neck.

Then he rode straight to Sir Gawain and Sir Uwain, and asked them what they were doing there. They answered him that they had come from King Arthur's court to look for adventures.

"Well," said Sir Marhaus, "here I am, ready: a knight in search of adventure who will carry out any adventure you wish." And so he rode away from them, to take his distance for the charge.

"Let him go," said Sir Uwain to Sir Gawain, "for he is as fine a knight as any living. I would not, if I had my way, have either of us matched against him."

"No," said Sir Gawain, "not so. It would be a shame to us if he were not tried, however good a knight he may be."

"Well," said Sir Uwain, "I will try him before you, for I am weaker than you, and if he strikes me down, then you can avenge me."

So these two knights came together with a great charge, so that Sir Uwain struck Sir Marhaus and his spear burst in pieces on the shield, and Sir Marhaus struck him so hard that he bore him to the ground, horse and man, and wounded Sir Uwain on the left side.

Then Sir Marhaus turned his horse and rode toward Gawain with his spear. And when Sir Gawain saw that, he set his shield, and they set their spears in rest, and they came together with all the might of their horses, so that each knight struck the other very hard in the middle of the shield. But Sir Gawain's spear broke, and Sir Marhaus' spear held, and with that Sir Gawain and his horse went crashing down to the ground. And Sir Gawain rose swiftly to his feet, and drew his sword, and squared up to Sir Marhaus on foot. And Sir Marhaus saw that, and drew his sword, and began to come at Sir Gawain on horseback.

"Sir knight," said Sir Gawain, "get down on foot, or else I will kill your horse."

"Many thanks," said Sir Marhaus. "Out of your courtesy you teach me good manners, for it is not right for one knight to be on foot and the other on horseback."

And with that Sir Marhaus set his spear against a tree and dismounted, and tied his horse to a tree, and set his shield, and each came at the other fiercely, and they struck at each other with their swords so that their shields flew in pieces, and they battered their helmets and their hauberks, and wounded each other. But from past nine o'clock in the morning Sir Gawain grew ever stronger and stronger, for then it was coming on to the hour of noon, and his strength was increased threefold. Sir Marhaus saw all this, and wondered greatly how his strength increased, and so they wounded each other exceedingly badly. And then, when it was past noon, and when it drew toward evening, Sir Gawain's strength weakened, and he grew exceedingly faint, so that he could scarcely hold out any longer, and Sir Marhaus was then stronger and stronger.

"Sir knight," said Sir Marhaus, "I have felt well that you are an exceedingly good knight, and as marvellous a man of strength as I ever felt, while it lasts. And our quarrel is not great, and so it would be a pity to do you harm, for I can feel that you are exceedingly weak."

"Ah," said Sir Gawain, "noble knight, you say the very word that I should say."

And with that they took off their helmets, and kissed each other, and there they swore together to love each other as brothers. And Sir Marhaus begged Sir Gawain to lodge with him that night. And so they took their horses, and rode toward Sir Marhaus' house. And as they rode along the way, Sir Gawain said, "Sir knight, I wonder that so valiant a man as you are loves no ladies or damsels."

"Sir," said Sir Marhaus, "those who give me that name call me so wrongly. But I know well it is the damsels of the tower who call me so, and others like them. Now I will tell you why I hate them: for many of them are sorceresses and enchantresses, and however good a knight may be in body, and as full of prowess as a man can be, they will make him an utter coward to get the better of him. And this is the chief reason I hate them. And to all good ladies and gentlewomen I owe my service, as a knight ought to."

As the book tells in French, there were many knights who outmatched Sir Gawain, for all the threefold strength that he had: Sir Lancelot du Lake, Sir Tristram, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Percival, Sir Pelleas and Sir Marhaus; these six knights had the better of Sir Gawain. Then within a little while they came to Sir Marhaus' place, which was in a little priory, and there they dismounted, and ladies and damsels unarmed them, and quickly saw to their wounds, for all three of them were hurt. And so all three had good lodging with Sir Marhaus, and a warm welcome. For when he knew that they were the sons of King Arthur's sisters, he made them all the welcome that lay in his power. And so they stayed there a week, and were well healed of their wounds, and at last they left.

"Now," said Sir Marhaus, "we will not part so easily, for I will bring you through the forest." And they rode day after day for a good seven days before they found any adventure.

At last they came into a great forest that was called the country and forest of Arroy, and the country of strange adventures.

"In this country," said Sir Marhaus, "no knight ever came since it was christened but he found strange adventures."

And so they rode, and came into a deep valley full of stones, and nearby they saw a fair stream of water. Above it, at the head of the stream, was a fair spring, and three damsels sitting beside it. And then they rode up to them, and greeted each other. And the eldest had a garland of gold about her head, and she was sixty winters old or more, and her hair was white under the garland. The second damsel was thirty winters old, with a circlet of gold about her head. The third damsel was only fifteen years old, with a garland of flowers about her head. When these knights had looked at them, they asked them why they sat at that spring.

"We are here," said the damsels, "for this reason: in case we see any knights errant, to lead them to strange adventures. And you are three knights who seek adventures, and we are three damsels, and so each one of you must choose one of us. And when you have done so, we will lead you to where three roads part, and there each of you shall choose a road, and his damsel with him. And this day twelve months from now you must meet here again, if God spares your lives, and to this you must pledge your word."

"This is well said," said Sir Marhaus.

Chapter 19: How Sir Marhaus, Sir Gawain, and Sir Uwain met three damsels, and each of them took one

"Now each of us shall choose a damsel."

"I will tell you," said Sir Uwain, "I am the youngest and the weakest of us, so I will have the eldest damsel, for she has seen much, and can best help me when I am in need, for I have more need of help than either of you."

"Now," said Sir Marhaus, "I will have the damsel of thirty winters, for she suits me best."

"Well," said Sir Gawain, "I thank you, for you have left me the youngest and the fairest, and she is the one I like best."

Then each damsel took her knight by the reins of his bridle, and brought him to where the three roads parted, and there they swore their oath to meet at the spring that day twelve months, if they were alive. And so they kissed and parted, and each knight set his lady up behind him. And Sir Uwain took the road that lay west, and Sir Marhaus took the road that lay south, and Sir Gawain took the road that lay north.

Now we will begin with Sir Gawain, who kept to that road until he came to a fair manor where there lived an old knight and a good householder. And there Sir Gawain asked the knight if he knew of any adventures in that country.

"I will show you some tomorrow," said the old knight, "and marvellous ones."

So in the morning they rode into the forest of adventures, to a clearing, and there they found a cross. And as they stood and waited there, there came by them the fairest knight and the handsomest man they ever saw, grieving more than any man ever grieved. And then he saw Sir Gawain, and greeted him, and prayed God to send him much honour.

"As for that," said Sir Gawain, "many thanks. And I also pray God to send you honour and renown."

"Ah," said the knight, "I may set that aside, for sorrow and shame come to me after honour."

Chapter 20: How a knight and a dwarf quarrelled over a lady

And with that he rode over to one side of the clearing; and on the other side Sir Gawain saw ten knights who waited there without moving, and made themselves ready with their shields and spears against the one knight who had passed by Sir Gawain.

Then this one knight set a great spear in rest, and one of the ten knights rode against him, but this woeful knight struck him so hard that he fell back over his horse's tail. So this same sorrowful knight served them all, so that at the very least he struck down horse and man, and he did all of it with one spear. And so when all ten were on foot, they went to that one knight, and he stood stock still, and let them pull him down off his horse, and bind him hand and foot, and tie him under the horse's belly, and so they led him away with them.

"O Jesus!" said Sir Gawain. "This is a sorry sight, to see that knight treated like that. And by the look of the knight it seems he lets them bind him so, for he puts up no resistance."

"No," said his host, "that is the truth, for if he wanted to, they would all be too weak to do that to him."

"Sir," said the damsel to Sir Gawain, "I think it would be to your honour to help that sorrowful knight, for I think he is one of the best knights I ever saw."

"I would do it for him," said Sir Gawain, "but it seems he will have no help."

"Then," said the damsel, "I think you have no wish to help him."

As they were talking they saw a knight on the other side of the clearing, all armed except for his head. And on the other side there came a dwarf on horseback, all armed except for his head, with a great mouth and a short nose. And when the dwarf came near he said, "Where is the lady who was to meet us here?" And with that she came out of the wood. And then they began to quarrel over the lady; for the knight said he would have her, and the dwarf said he would have her.

"Shall we do the sensible thing?" said the dwarf. "There is a knight over there at the cross. Let us leave it to him, both of us, and as he judges, so it shall be."

"Gladly," said the knight. And so all three went to Sir Gawain and told him why they were quarrelling.

"Well, sirs," he said, "will you put the matter in my hands?"

"Yes," they both said.

"Now, damsel," said Sir Gawain, "you shall stand between the two of them, and whichever of them you would rather go to, he shall have you."

And when she was set between the two of them, she left the knight and went to the dwarf, and the dwarf took her and went on his way singing, and the knight went on his way grieving greatly.

Then two knights came, fully armed, and called out loudly, "Sir Gawain! Knight of King Arthur's, make ready in all haste and joust with me!"

So they ran together, so that each fell down, and then on foot they drew their swords and fought very vigorously. Meanwhile the other knight went to the damsel, and asked her why she stayed with that knight. "And if you would stay with me, I will be your faithful knight."

"And with you I will be," said the damsel, "for I cannot find it in my heart to be with Sir Gawain. For just now here was a knight who beat ten knights, and in the end he was led away like a coward; and so let us two go while they are fighting."

And Sir Gawain fought with that other knight a long time, but in the end the two of them made peace. And then the knight begged Sir Gawain to lodge with him that night. So as Sir Gawain went along with this knight he asked him, "Who is that knight in this country who struck down the ten knights? For when he had done so manfully, he let them bind him hand and foot, and so they led him away."

"Ah," said the knight, "that is the best knight in the world, I believe, and the man of greatest prowess, and he has been treated the way he was more than ten times. His name is Sir Pelleas, and he loves a great lady in this country, and her name is Ettard. And so, when he fell in love with her, a great three-day joust was proclaimed in this country, and all the knights of this country were there, and gentlewomen too. And whoever proved himself the best knight was to have an exceedingly good sword and a circlet of gold, and the knight was to give the circlet to the fairest lady who was at the jousts. And this knight Sir Pelleas was the best knight there, and there were five hundred knights; but there was never a man that Sir Pelleas met whom he did not strike down, or else knock from his horse. And on every one of the three days he struck down twenty knights, and so they gave him the prize. And at once he went to where the Lady Ettard was, and gave her the circlet, and said openly that she was the fairest lady there, and that he would prove it on any knight who said otherwise."

Chapter 21: How Sir Pelleas let himself be taken prisoner so that he could catch sight of his lady, and how Sir Gawain promised to win him his lady's love

"And so he chose her for his sovereign lady, and vowed never to love any other but her. But she was so proud that she scorned him, and said that she would never love him even if he died for her. Because of this all the ladies and gentlewomen scorned her for being so proud, for there were fairer ladies there than she was, and there was not one of them there who would not have loved him for his noble prowess, if Sir Pelleas had offered them his love. And so this knight promised the Lady Ettard to follow her into this country, and never to leave her until she loved him. And so he is here, close to her, most of the time, and lodges by a priory, and every week she sends knights to fight with him. And when he has beaten them, then he lets them take him prisoner of his own free will, because he wants a sight of this lady. And she always treats him with great contempt, for sometimes she has her knights tie him to his horse's tail, and sometimes bind him under the horse's belly; and so he is brought to her in the most shameful ways she can think of. And she does all this to make him leave this country, and give up his love; but none of it can make him leave. For if he had chosen to fight on foot, he could have beaten the ten knights on foot as well as on horseback."

"Alas," said Sir Gawain, "it is a great pity for him. And after tonight I will look for him tomorrow in this forest, to give him all the help I can."

So in the morning Sir Gawain took his leave of his host Sir Carados, and rode into the forest; and at last he met Sir Pelleas, grieving beyond measure. So they greeted each other, and Sir Gawain asked him why he was in such sorrow. And Sir Pelleas told Sir Gawain all that has been told above. "But I always let her knights treat me the way you saw yesterday, trusting to win her love in the end, for she knows well that all her knights could not easily win against me, if I chose to fight them to the utmost. So, if I did not love her so much, I would rather die a hundred times, if I could die so often, than put up with that insult. But I trust she will have pity on me at last, for love makes many a good knight suffer to have his desire. But alas, I am unlucky." And with that he grieved and sorrowed so greatly that he could scarcely keep his seat on his horse.

"Now," said Sir Gawain, "leave off your mourning, and I promise you on my life to do all in my power to win you the love of your lady, and I will give you my solemn word on it."

"Ah," said Sir Pelleas, "what court are you from? Tell me, please, my good friend."

And then Sir Gawain said, "I am of the court of King Arthur, and his sister's son, and King Lot of Orkney was my father, and my name is Sir Gawain."

And then he said, "My name is Sir Pelleas, born in the Isles, and I am lord of many isles, and I have never loved lady or damsel until now, in an ill-fated hour. And, sir knight, since you are so close a kinsman to King Arthur, and a king's son, do not betray me, but help me. For I can never come at her except by means of some good knight, for she is in a strong castle close by here, within four miles, and she is lady of all this country. And so I can never come into her presence except by letting her knights take me; and if I did not do that, so that I could have a sight of her, I would have been dead long before now. And yet I never had a kind word from her, but when I am brought before her she rebukes me in the foulest way. And then they take my horse and armour and put me out of the gates, and she will not allow me to eat or drink. And I always offer myself to be her prisoner, but she will not allow that, for I would ask for nothing more, whatever pains I had, if only I could have a sight of her every day."

"Well," said Sir Gawain, "I will put all this right, if you will do as I plan. I will have your horse and your armour, and so I will ride to her castle and tell her that I have killed you. And so I will get inside with her and make her treat me kindly, and then I will play my part faithfully, so that you shall not fail to have her love."

Chapter 22: How Sir Gawain came to the Lady Ettard, and how Sir Pelleas found them sleeping

And with that Sir Gawain gave his solemn word to Sir Pelleas to be true and faithful to him; so each gave his word to the other, and so they exchanged horses and armour, and Sir Gawain left, and came to the castle where the lady's tents stood outside the gate. And as soon as Ettard saw Sir Gawain she fled towards the castle. Sir Gawain called out loudly, and told her to wait, for he was not Sir Pelleas. "I am another knight, who has killed Sir Pelleas."

"Take off your helmet," said the Lady Ettard, "so that I can see your face."

And so when she saw that it was not Sir Pelleas, she told him to dismount, and led him into her castle, and asked him in good faith whether he had killed Sir Pelleas. And he told her yes, and told her his name was Sir Gawain, of the court of King Arthur, and his sister's son.

"Truly," she said, "that is a great pity, for he was an exceedingly good knight in his own person. But of all men alive I hated him most, for I could never be rid of him. And since you have killed him, I will be your woman, and do anything that might please you."

So she gave Sir Gawain a warm welcome. Then Sir Gawain said that he loved a lady, and that she would on no account love him.

"She is to blame," said Ettard, "if she will not love you. For you are so well-born a man, and such a man of prowess, that there is no lady in the world too good for you."

"Will you," said Sir Gawain, "promise me on your faith to do all you can to win me the love of my lady?"

"Yes, sir," she said, "and I promise you that on my faith."

"Now," said Sir Gawain, "it is you yourself that I love so well; so I beg you, keep your promise."

"I have no choice," said the Lady Ettard, "unless I am to break my oath." And so she granted him all his desire.

So it was then in the month of May that she and Sir Gawain went out of the castle and had supper in a tent, and a bed was made there, and there Sir Gawain and the Lady Ettard went to bed together. And in another tent she put her damsels to sleep, and in the third tent she put some of her knights to sleep, for by then she had no fear of Sir Pelleas. And there Sir Gawain lay with her in that tent for two days and two nights. And on the third day, early in the morning, Sir Pelleas armed himself, for he had never slept since Sir Gawain left him; for Sir Gawain had promised him on his life to come back to him at his tent by that priory within the space of a day and a night.

Then Sir Pelleas mounted his horse and came to the tents that stood outside the castle, and in the first tent he found three knights in three beds, and three squires lying at their feet. Then he went to the second tent and found four gentlewomen lying in four beds. And then he went to the third tent and found Sir Gawain lying in bed with his Lady Ettard, each with their arms around the other. And when he saw that, his heart nearly burst for sorrow, and he said, "Alas, that ever a knight should be found so false!" And then he took his horse, and could stay no longer for pure sorrow. And when he had ridden nearly half a mile he turned back, and meant to kill them both. And when he saw the two of them lying there so fast asleep, he could scarcely keep his seat on his horse for sorrow, and he said to himself, "However false this knight may be, I will never kill him sleeping, for I will never destroy the high order of knighthood." And with that he left again. And before he had ridden half a mile he turned back again, and this time meant to kill them both, grieving more than any man ever grieved. And when he came to the tents, he tied his horse to a tree, and drew his sword and went with it naked in his hand to where they lay. And still he thought it would be shameful to kill them sleeping, and he laid the naked sword across both their throats, and so took his horse and rode away.

And when Sir Pelleas came back to his tents he told his knights and his squires how he had fared, and said to them, "For the true and good service you have done me I will give you all my goods, for I am going to my bed and will never get up until I am dead. And when I am dead, I order you to take the heart out of my body and carry it to her between two silver dishes, and tell her how I saw her lying with the false knight Sir Gawain."

Then and there Sir Pelleas took off his armour and went to his bed, grieving and sorrowing marvellously.

When Sir Gawain and Ettard woke from their sleep and found the naked sword across their throats, she knew well that it was Sir Pelleas' sword.

"Alas!" she said to Sir Gawain. "You have betrayed me and Sir Pelleas both, for you told me you had killed him, and now I know well it is not so: he is alive. And if Sir Pelleas had been as discourteous to you as you have been to him, you would be a dead knight. But you have deceived me and betrayed me falsely, so that all ladies and damsels may take warning from you and me."

And with that Sir Gawain made himself ready and went into the forest. So it happened then that the Damsel of the Lake, Nimue, met a knight of Sir Pelleas' who was going on foot in the forest, grieving greatly, and she asked him the cause. And so the woeful knight told her how his master and lord had been betrayed through a knight and a lady, and how he would never get up out of his bed until he was dead.

"Bring me to him," she said at once, "and I will guarantee his life: he shall not die for love. And she who has made him love like this shall be in as bad a plight as he is before long, for there is no joy in such a proud lady, who will have no mercy on such a valiant knight."

At once that knight brought her to him, and when she saw him lying in his bed, she thought she had never seen so handsome a knight. And with that she cast an enchantment on him, and he fell asleep. And meanwhile she rode to the Lady Ettard, and ordered that no man should wake him until she came back. So within two hours she brought the Lady Ettard there, and both ladies found him asleep.

"Look," said the Damsel of the Lake, "you ought to be ashamed to murder such a knight."

And with that she cast such an enchantment on her that she loved him so desperately she was nearly out of her mind.

"O Lord Jesus," said the Lady Ettard, "how has it come about that I now love the man I have hated most of any man alive?"

"That is the righteous judgement of God," said the damsel.

And then at once Sir Pelleas woke and looked at Ettard; and when he saw her he knew her, and then he hated her more than any woman alive, and said, "Away, traitress! Never come into my sight again."

And when she heard him say that, she wept and grieved beyond measure.

Chapter 23: How Sir Pelleas stopped loving Ettard through the Damsel of the Lake, whom he loved ever after

"Sir Pelleas, sir knight," said the Damsel of the Lake, "take your horse and come away with me out of this country, and you shall love a lady who will love you."

"Gladly," said Sir Pelleas, "for this Lady Ettard has done me great insult and shame." And there he told her the whole story from beginning to end, and how he had meant never to get up again until he was dead. "And now God has sent me such grace that I hate her as much as ever I loved her, thanks be to our Lord Jesus!"

"Thank me," said the Damsel of the Lake.

At once Sir Pelleas armed himself, and took his horse, and ordered his men to bring his tents and his belongings after him to wherever the Damsel of the Lake should direct. So the Lady Ettard died of sorrow, and the Damsel of the Lake gave Sir Pelleas joy, and they loved each other all the days of their lives.

Chapter 24: How Sir Marhaus rode with the damsel, and how he came to the Duke of the South Marches

Now we turn to Sir Marhaus, who rode southward with the damsel who was thirty years old. And so they came into a deep forest, and as luck would have it night overtook them, and they rode a long way along a deep track, and at last they came to a farmyard, and there they asked for shelter. But the man of the farmyard would not lodge them, however they tried to bargain with him. But this much the good man did say: "If you will take your chances on your lodging, I will bring you to where you shall be lodged."

"What chance is it that I shall have to take for my lodging?" said Sir Marhaus.

"You will find out when you get there," said the good man.

"Sir, whatever chance it is, bring me there, please," said Sir Marhaus, "for I am weary, and so are my damsel and my horse."

So the good man went and opened the gate, and within an hour he brought him to a fine castle. And then the poor man called the porter, and at once he was let into the castle, and so he told the lord that he had brought him a knight errant and a damsel who wanted lodging with him.

"Let him in," said the lord. "It may be he will regret that they took their lodging here."

So Sir Marhaus was let in by torchlight, and there was a fine company of young men who welcomed him. And then his horse was led into the stable, and he and the damsel were brought into the hall, and there stood a mighty duke with many fine men about him. Then this lord asked him what his name was, and where he came from, and whose household he belonged to.

"Sir," he said, "I am a knight of King Arthur's and a knight of the Round Table, and my name is Sir Marhaus, and I was born in Ireland."

And then the duke said to him, "I am very sorry to hear it, and this is why: I have no love for your lord, nor for any of your fellows of the Round Table. So rest yourself tonight as best you can, for tomorrow I and my six sons will take you on."

"Is there no help for it but that I must fight you and your six sons at once?" said Sir Marhaus.

"No," said the duke, "for I made my vow for this reason: Sir Gawain killed my seven sons in an encounter. So I made my vow that no knight of King Arthur's court should ever lodge with me, or come anywhere I could fight him, without my taking revenge for my sons' death."

"What is your name?" said Sir Marhaus. "I ask you to tell me, if you please."

"Know this: I am the Duke of the South Marches."

"Ah," said Sir Marhaus, "I have heard it said that you have long been a great enemy of my lord Arthur and of his knights."

"You will feel that tomorrow," said the duke.

"Shall I have to fight you?" said Sir Marhaus.

"Yes," said the duke. "You have no choice about it. And so go to your room, and you shall have everything that is fitting for you."

So Sir Marhaus left and was led to a room, and his damsel was led to her room. And in the morning the duke sent to Sir Marhaus and told him to make ready. And so Sir Marhaus got up and armed himself, and then a mass was sung before him, and he had breakfast, and so he mounted his horse in the courtyard of the castle where they were to fight. So there was the duke, all ready on horseback, fully armed, and his six sons beside him, and each of them had a spear in his hand. And so they charged, and the duke and two of his sons broke their spears on him, but Sir Marhaus held up his spear and touched none of them.

Chapter 25: How Sir Marhaus fought the duke and his four sons and made them surrender

Then the four sons came two by two, and two of them broke their spears, and so did the other two. And all this while Sir Marhaus did not touch them. Then Sir Marhaus ran at the duke, and struck him with his spear so that horse and man fell to the ground, and he served his sons the same way. And then Sir Marhaus dismounted and told the duke to yield or else he would kill him. And then some of his sons got up again and would have set on Sir Marhaus. Then Sir Marhaus said to the duke, "Call off your sons, or I'll do my worst to all of you."

Then, when the duke saw he could not escape death, he called out to his sons and ordered them to yield to Sir Marhaus; and they all knelt down and held out the pommels of their swords to the knight, and so he accepted their surrender. And then they helped their father up, and so by common consent they promised Sir Marhaus never to be enemies of King Arthur, and to come at the next Pentecost, the duke and his sons, and put themselves at the king's mercy.

Then Sir Marhaus left, and within two days his damsel brought him to where there was a great tournament that the Lady de Vawse had proclaimed. And whoever did best was to have a rich circlet of gold worth a thousand gold coins. And there Sir Marhaus did so nobly that he was renowned, and at one time had forty knights down, and so the circlet of gold was awarded to him. Then he left them with great honour. And so within seven nights his damsel brought him to an earl's place; his name was Earl Fergus, who was later Sir Tristram's knight. And this earl was only a young man, and had lately come into his lands, and there was a giant close by him called Taulurd, who had another brother in Cornwall called Taulas, whom Sir Tristram killed when he was out of his mind. So this earl complained to Sir Marhaus that there was a giant near him who was destroying all his lands, and that because of him he dared not ride or walk anywhere.

"Sir," said the knight, "does he usually fight on horseback or on foot?"

"No," said the earl, "no horse can carry him."

"Well," said Sir Marhaus, "then I will fight him on foot."

So in the morning Sir Marhaus asked the earl for one of his men to bring him to where the giant was; and so he was brought, for he saw him sitting under a holly tree with many iron clubs and battle-axes around him. So this knight squared up to the giant, holding his shield before him, and the giant took an iron club in his hand, and with the first stroke he split Sir Marhaus' shield in two. And there he was in great danger, for the giant was a crafty fighter; but at last Sir Marhaus struck off his right arm above the elbow.

Then the giant fled, and the knight after him, and so he drove him into the water; but the giant was so tall that he could not wade in after him. And then Sir Marhaus made Earl Fergus' man fetch him stones, and with those stones the knight gave the giant many hard knocks, until at last he made him fall down into the water, and so he died there. Then Sir Marhaus went to the giant's castle, and there he freed twenty-four ladies and twelve knights from the giant's prison, and there he found great riches beyond counting, so that he was never a poor man all the days of his life. Then he went back to Earl Fergus, who thanked him greatly, and would have given him half his lands, but he would take none. So Sir Marhaus stayed with the earl nearly half a year, for he was badly bruised by the giant, and at last he took his leave. And as he rode along the way, he met Sir Gawain and Sir Uwain; and so by chance he met four knights of Arthur's court: the first was Sir Sagramore le Desirous, then Sir Osanna, Sir Dodinas le Savage, and Sir Felot of Listinoise. And there Sir Marhaus struck down these four knights with one spear, and badly hurt them. So he went on his way, to keep the meeting on the appointed day.

Chapter 26: How Sir Uwain rode with the damsel of sixty years, and how he won the prize at a tournament

Now we turn to Sir Uwain, who rode westward with his damsel of sixty years of age, and she brought him to where there was a tournament near the border of Wales. And at that tournament Sir Uwain struck down thirty knights, and so the prize was given to him, and that was a gerfalcon, and a white horse trapped with cloth of gold. So then Sir Uwain had many strange adventures through the old damsel, and so she brought him to a lady who was called the Lady of the Rock, who was very courteous. Now there were two knights in that country who were brothers, and they were called the two perilous knights: the one knight was called Sir Edward of the Red Castle, and the other Sir Hue of the Red Castle. And these two brothers had robbed the Lady of the Rock of a barony of lands by their extortion. And while this knight was lodging with this lady, she made her complaint to him about these two knights.

"Madam," said Sir Uwain, "they are to blame, for they act against the high order of knighthood, and the oath that they made. And if you please, I will speak with them, because I am a knight of King Arthur's, and I will try to persuade them fairly; and if they will not be persuaded, I will do battle with them, in defence of your right."

"Many thanks," said the lady, "and where I cannot repay you, God will."

So in the morning the two knights were sent for, to come there to speak with the Lady of the Rock; and you may be sure they did not fail to come, for they came with a hundred horsemen. But when this lady saw them come in such strength, she would not let Sir Uwain go out to them on any guarantee or for any fair words, but she made him speak with them from a tower. But in the end these two brothers would not be persuaded, and answered that they would keep what they had.

"Well," said Sir Uwain, "then I will fight one of you, and prove that you are doing this lady wrong."

"We will not do that," they said, "for if we do battle, we two will fight one knight together. And so if you will fight that way, we will be ready at whatever hour you choose. And if you beat us in battle, the lady shall have her lands back."

"Well said," said Sir Uwain. "So make yourselves ready, and be here tomorrow, in defence of the lady's right."

Chapter 27: How Sir Uwain fought two knights and overcame them

So assurances were given on both sides that no treachery should be done by either side. So then the knights left and made themselves ready, and that night Sir Uwain was given a warm welcome. And in the morning he got up early and heard mass, and had breakfast, and so he rode to the plain outside the gates, where the two brothers waited for him on their horses. So they rode at each other exceedingly hard, so that Sir Edward and Sir Hue broke their spears on Sir Uwain. And Sir Uwain struck Sir Edward so that he fell over his horse, and still his spear did not break. And then he spurred his horse and came at Sir Hue and overthrew him. But they soon got up again, and set their shields and drew their swords, and told Sir Uwain to dismount and fight his battle to the utmost. Then Sir Uwain quickly got clear of his horse, and put his shield before him and drew his sword, and so they squared up to each other, and each gave the other such strokes. And there these two brothers wounded Sir Uwain so grievously that the Lady of the Rock thought he would die. And so they fought together for five hours, like men gone out of their minds with rage. And at last Sir Uwain struck Sir Edward such a stroke on the helmet that his sword cut down to his collarbone; and then Sir Hue lost heart, but Sir Uwain pressed hard on him to kill him. Sir Hue saw that: he knelt down and yielded to Sir Uwain. And Sir Uwain, out of his nobility, accepted his sword, and took him by the hand, and they went into the castle together. Then the Lady of the Rock was exceedingly glad, and the other brother grieved greatly for his brother's death. Then all the lady's lands were restored to her, and Sir Hue was ordered to be at the court of King Arthur at the next feast of Pentecost. So Sir Uwain stayed with the lady nearly half a year, for it was a long time before he could be healed of his great wounds. And so when it drew near the appointed day when Sir Gawain, Sir Marhaus and Sir Uwain were to meet at the crossroads, each knight made his way there to keep the promise they had made. And Sir Marhaus and Sir Uwain brought their damsels with them, but Sir Gawain had lost his damsel, as has been told before.

Chapter 28: How at the year's end all three knights met with their three damsels at the spring

Then and there, at the twelvemonth's end, all three knights met at the spring, and their damsels with them. But the damsel Sir Gawain had had could say little to his honour. So they parted from the damsels and rode through a great forest, and there they met a messenger who had come from King Arthur, who had been looking for them for nearly a year throughout all England, Wales and Scotland, and had orders, if ever he could find Sir Gawain and Sir Uwain, to bring them back to the court. And then they were all glad, and so they begged Sir Marhaus to ride with them to the king's court. And so within twelve days they came to Camelot, and the king was exceedingly glad of their coming, and so was all the court. Then the king made them swear on a book to tell him all the adventures that had happened to them that year, and so they did. And there Sir Marhaus was well known, for there were knights there he had fought before, and he was named as one of the best knights living.

Before the feast of Pentecost the Damsel of the Lake came and brought Sir Pelleas with her; and at that high feast there was great jousting of knights, and of all the knights who were at those jousts Sir Pelleas won the prize, and Sir Marhaus was named next. But Sir Pelleas was so strong that very few knights could stand a blow of his spear. And at that next feast Sir Pelleas and Sir Marhaus were made knights of the Round Table, for there were two empty seats, because two knights had been killed that year; and King Arthur had great joy of Sir Pelleas and of Sir Marhaus. But Pelleas never loved Sir Gawain afterwards, though he spared him for the love of King Arthur; but many times at jousts and tournaments Sir Pelleas paid Sir Gawain back, for so it is told in the French book. So, many days after, Sir Tristram fought with Sir Marhaus on an island, and there they fought a great battle, but in the end Sir Tristram killed him. And Sir Tristram was so badly wounded that he could scarcely recover, and lay at a nunnery for half a year. And Sir Pelleas was an honourable knight, and was one of the four who achieved the Holy Grail. And the Damsel of the Lake saw to it, by her arts, that he never fought Sir Lancelot du Lake; for wherever Sir Lancelot was at any jousts or any tournament, she would not let him be there that day, unless it was on Sir Lancelot's side.

Here ends the fourth book.

Here follows the fifth book.

Book Five: The Conquest of Lucius the Emperor

Chapter 1: How twelve aged ambassadors from Rome came to King Arthur to demand tribute for Britain

When King Arthur had rested after long war, and was holding a royal feast and a Round Table with his allies, the kings, princes and noble knights, all of the Round Table, there came into his hall, as he sat on his royal throne, twelve old men, each of them carrying a branch of olive, as a sign that they came as ambassadors and messengers from the Emperor Lucius, who was called at that time Dictator, or Procurator of the Commonwealth of Rome. These messengers, after they had entered and come into the presence of King Arthur, made their obeisance to him and bowed to him with reverence, and spoke to him in this way: "The high and mighty Emperor Lucius sends greeting to the King of Britain, and commands you to acknowledge him as your lord, and to send him the tribute that this realm owes to the Empire, which your father and others of your predecessors have paid, as is on record. And you, as a rebel who does not acknowledge him as your sovereign, withhold it and keep it back, against the statutes and decrees made by the noble and worthy Julius Caesar, conqueror of this realm and first Emperor of Rome. And if you refuse his demand and his command, know for certain that he will make strong war against you, your realms and your lands, and will punish you and your subjects, so that it will be an example forever to all kings and princes who would deny their tribute to that noble Empire which rules over the whole world."

Then when they had delivered the substance of their message, the king commanded them to withdraw, and said he would take counsel and give them an answer. Then some of the young knights, hearing their message, would have rushed at them and killed them, saying that it was an insult to all the knights who were present to allow them to speak so to the king. And at once the king commanded that none of them, on pain of death, should speak ill of them or do them any harm, and he commanded a knight to bring them to their lodging, "and see that they have all that is necessary and fitting for them, with the best welcome, and that no delicacy is spared, for the Romans are great lords. And though their message does not please me or my court, still I must remember my honour."

After this the king had all his lords and knights of the Round Table called to take counsel on this matter, and asked them to give their advice. Then Sir Cador of Cornwall spoke first, and said, "Sir, this message pleases me well, for we have rested many days and been idle, and now I hope you will make sharp war on the Romans, where I have no doubt we shall win honour."

"I can well believe," said Arthur, "that this matter pleases you well, but this message cannot be answered so lightly, for the demand grieves me badly. For truly I will never pay tribute to Rome, and so I ask you to advise me. I have learned that Belinus and Brenius, kings of Britain, held the Empire in their hands for many days, and also Constantine the son of Helena, which is plain evidence that we owe no tribute to Rome, but that by right we who are descended from them have the right to claim the title of the Empire."

Chapter 2: How the kings and lords promised King Arthur aid and help against the Romans

Then King Anguish of Scotland answered, "Sir, by right you ought to be above all other kings, for there is none like you or equal to you in Christendom, in knighthood or in dignity. And I advise you never to obey the Romans, for when they reigned over us they oppressed our forefathers, and burdened this land with great extortions and taxes. And so I make my vow here to avenge myself on them; and to strengthen your cause I will supply twenty thousand good fighting men, and pay their wages at my own cost, and they shall attend on you, with me, whenever it pleases you."

And the king of Little Britain, that is, Brittany, promised him thirty thousand for the same purpose, and King Arthur thanked them for it. And then every man agreed to make war, and to help as far as he was able. That is to say, the lord of West Wales promised to bring thirty thousand men, and Sir Uwain and Sir Ider his son, with their cousins, promised to bring thirty thousand. Then Sir Lancelot and all the others in the same way each promised a great host of men.

And when King Arthur understood their spirit and their good will, he thanked them heartily, and afterwards had the ambassadors called to hear their answer. And in the presence of all his lords and knights he spoke to them in this way: "It is my will that you go back to your lord, the Procurator of the Commonwealth of the Romans, and say this to him: that I set no value on his demand and his command, and that I know of no tribute or payment that I owe to him, or to any earthly prince, Christian or heathen. Rather, I claim to have and hold the sovereignty of the Empire, to which I am entitled by the right of my predecessors, who were once kings of this land. And tell him that I am determined and fully resolved to go with my army, in strength and in power, to Rome, by the grace of God, to take possession of the Empire and to subdue those who are rebels. And so I command him and all the people of Rome that they do homage to me forthwith, and acknowledge me as their Emperor and Governor, on pain of what will follow."

And then he commanded his treasurer to give them great and generous gifts, and to pay all their expenses, and he appointed Sir Cador to escort them out of the land. And so they took their leave and departed, and took ship at Sandwich, and travelled on through Flanders, Germany, the mountains, and all Italy, until they came to Lucius. And after they had made their bow, they reported their answer, just as you have heard it already.

When the Emperor Lucius had fully understood their report, he was badly shaken, as if he were in a rage, and said, "I had supposed that Arthur would have obeyed my command, and come to serve you himself, as was fitting for him or for any other king to do."

"O sir," said one of the senators, "leave off such empty words, for I tell you that my fellows and I were sorely afraid to look upon his face. I'm afraid you have made a rod for your own back, for he means to be lord of this Empire, which is greatly to be feared if he comes. For he is a different man altogether from what you think, and he keeps the noblest court in the world; no other kings or princes can compare with his noble state. On New Year's Day we saw him in his royal state, which was the most royal we ever saw, for he was served at his table by nine kings, and by the noblest fellowship of other princes, lords and knights that there is in the world, and every knight proven, and like a lord, and he keeps the Round Table. And in his own person he is the most manly man alive, and is likely to conquer all the world, for the world is too small for his spirit. And so I advise you to guard your borders well, and the passes in the mountains, for certainly he is a lord to be feared."

"Well," said Lucius, "before Easter I mean to cross the mountains, and so on into France, and there strip him of his lands, with the Genoese and other mighty warriors of Tuscany and Lombardy. And I will send for all those who are subjects and allies of the Empire of Rome to come to my aid."

And at once he sent old, wise knights to the countries that follow: first to Ambage and Arrage, to Alexandria, to India, to Armenia, where the river Euphrates runs into Asia, to Africa, and to Europe the Large, to Ertayne and Elamye, to Arabia, to Egypt, and to Damascus, to Damietta and Cayer, to Cappadocia, to Tarsus, Turkey, Pontus and Pamphylia, to Syria and Galatia. And all these were subject to Rome, and many more, such as Greece, Cyprus, Macedonia, Calabria, Cateland and Portugal, with many thousands of Spaniards. So all these kings, dukes and emirs assembled around Rome, sixteen kings at once, with a great multitude of people. When the emperor learned of their coming, he made ready his Romans and all the people between him and Flanders.

He had also brought with him fifty giants who had been fathered by fiends, and they were appointed to guard his person, and to break the front line of King Arthur's army. And so he set out from Rome, and came down over the mountains to destroy the lands that Arthur had conquered, and came to Cologne, and besieged a castle near it, and soon won it, and garrisoned it with two hundred Saracens, or infidels. And afterwards he destroyed many fair countries which Arthur had won from King Claudas. And so Lucius came with all his army, which was spread out sixty miles wide, and commanded them to meet him in Burgundy, for he meant to destroy the realm of Brittany.

Chapter 3: How King Arthur held a parliament at York, and how he arranged for the realm to be governed in his absence

Now we leave Lucius the Emperor and speak of King Arthur, who commanded all the men of his household to be ready at the octave of St. Hilary, a week after the saint's day, to hold a parliament at York. And at that parliament it was decided to seize all the ships of the land, and to be ready within fifteen days at Sandwich. And there he explained to his army how he meant to conquer the Empire, which he ought to have by right. And there he appointed two governors of this realm, that is to say, Sir Baudwin of Britain, to give the best counsel, and Sir Constantine, son of Sir Cador of Cornwall, who after the death of Arthur was king of this realm. And in the presence of all his lords he handed over to them the rule of the realm, and Guinevere his queen. At this Sir Lancelot was angry, for he left Sir Tristram with King Mark for the love of Isolde the Fair. Then Queen Guinevere grieved greatly at the departure of her lord and the others, and fainted so that the ladies carried her into her room. So the king departed with his great army, leaving the queen and the realm in the keeping of Sir Baudwin and Constantine. And when he was on his horse he said in a loud voice, "If I die on this expedition, it is my will that Sir Constantine shall be my heir, and crowned king of this realm, as the next of my blood."

And afterwards he departed and put to sea at Sandwich with all his army, with a great multitude of ships, galleys, small boats and great warships, sailing on the sea.

Chapter 4: How King Arthur, on board ship and lying in his cabin, had a marvellous dream, and of its interpretation

And as the king lay in his cabin in the ship, he fell into a doze and dreamed a marvellous dream. It seemed to him that a dreadful dragon drowned many of his people, and he came flying out of the west, and his head was enamelled with azure, and his shoulders shone like gold, his belly was like mail of a marvellous hue, his tail was all in tatters, his feet were covered in fine sable fur, and his claws were like fine gold. And a hideous flame of fire flew out of his mouth, as if the land and the water were all ablaze. After that, it seemed to him, there came out of the east a grim boar, all black, in a cloud, and his paws were as big as a post. He was shaggy and rough-looking, he was the foulest beast that ever man saw, and he roared and bellowed so hideously that it was a marvel to hear. Then the dreadful dragon came on and swooped down on the wind like a falcon, giving great strokes on the boar, and the boar struck back at him with his grisly tusks so that the dragon's breast was all bloody, and the hot blood made all the sea red. Then the dragon flew away high up, and came down with such a rush of wind, and struck the boar on the spine, which was ten feet long from the head to the tail, and struck the boar all to powder, both flesh and bones, so that it fluttered all over the sea.

And with that the king woke at once, and was badly shaken by this dream, and sent at once for a wise philosopher, commanding him to tell him the meaning of his dream.

"Sir," said the philosopher, "the dragon that you dreamed of stands for your own person, sailing here, and the colours of his wings are your realms that you have won, and his tail, which is all in tatters, means the noble knights of the Round Table. And the boar that the dragon killed, coming from the clouds, stands for some tyrant who torments the people; or else you are likely to fight with some giant yourself, horrible and abominable, whose equal you never saw in all your days. And so do not be afraid at all of this dreadful dream, but go forward yourself as a conqueror."

Then soon after this they sighted land, and sailed until they arrived at Barflete in Flanders, and when they were there he found many of his great lords ready, as they had been commanded, to wait on him.

Chapter 5: How a local man told him of a monstrous giant, and how he fought and conquered him

Then a farmer of that country came to him, and told him how there was, in the country of Constantine near Brittany, a great giant who had slain, murdered and devoured many people of the country, and had fed himself for seven years on the children of the common people of that land, so that the children were all slain and destroyed. "And just lately he has taken the Duchess of Brittany as she rode with her household, and has carried her off to his lair, which is on a mountain, to rape her and lie with her for the rest of her life. And many people followed her, more than five hundred, but for all that they could not rescue her, and they left her shrieking and crying pitifully. And so I suppose that he has killed her in satisfying his foul lust. She was the wife of your cousin Sir Howell, whom we count very near of your blood. Now, as you are a rightful king, have pity on this lady, and avenge us all, as you are a noble conqueror."

"Alas," said King Arthur, "this is a great misfortune. I would rather have given the best realm I have than not have been a furlong ahead of him, to have rescued that lady. Now, fellow," said King Arthur, "can you take me to where this giant has his haunt?"

"Yes, sir," said the good man. "Look over there, where you see those two great fires. There you will find him, and more treasure than I suppose there is in all France."

When the king had understood this pitiful matter, he went back into his tent. Then he called Sir Kay and Sir Bedivere to him, and commanded them secretly to make ready horses and armour for himself and the two of them, for after evensong he would ride on pilgrimage, with the two of them only, to Saint Michael's Mount. And then at once he made himself ready, and armed himself at all points, and took his horse and his shield. And so the three of them set off from there and rode on as fast as ever they could, until they came to the foreshore below that mount. And there they dismounted, and the king commanded them to wait there, for he would go up that mount himself. And so he climbed up that hill until he came to a great fire, and there he found a sorrowful widow wringing her hands and grieving greatly, sitting by a newly made grave. And then King Arthur greeted her, and asked her why she was lamenting so.

And she answered him and said, "Sir knight, speak softly, for over there is a devil. If he hears you speak he will come and destroy you. I count you an unlucky man. What are you doing here on this mountain? For if there were fifty of you, such as you are, you could not hold out against this devil. Here lies a duchess dead, who was the fairest woman in all the world, wife of Sir Howell, Duke of Brittany. He has murdered her in forcing himself on her, and has split her open to the navel."

"Lady," said the king, "I come from the noble conqueror King Arthur, to negotiate with that tyrant on behalf of his liege people."

"A curse on such negotiations," she said. "He cares nothing for the king, or for any man else. But if you had brought Arthur's wife, Dame Guinevere, he would be gladder than if you had given him half France. Take care, do not go too near him, for he has vanquished fifteen kings, and has had a coat made for himself, full of precious stones, and embroidered with their beards, which they sent him to win his favour, for the safety of their people, this last Christmas. And if you want to, speak with him at that great fire over there, at his supper."

"Well," said Arthur, "I will carry out my message, for all your fearful words."

And he went on along the crest of that hill, and saw where the giant sat at his supper, gnawing on a man's limb, warming his huge limbs by the fire, with no breeches on; and three fair damsels were turning three spits, and on the spits were skewered twelve young children, newly born, like young birds.

When King Arthur saw that pitiful sight, he had great compassion on them, so that his heart bled for sorrow, and he hailed the giant, saying this: "May He who rules all the world give you a short life and a shameful death, and the devil have your soul! Why have you murdered these young innocent children, and murdered this duchess? So get up and arm yourself, you glutton, for this day you shall die by my hand."

Then the glutton at once jumped up, and took a great club in his hand, and struck at the king so that the circlet on his helm fell to the ground. And the king struck him back so that he slashed open his belly and cut off his genitals, so that his guts and his entrails fell down to the ground. Then the giant threw away his club, and caught the king in his arms so that he crushed his ribs. Then the three maidens knelt down and called on Christ for help and comfort for Arthur. And then Arthur writhed and twisted, so that one moment he was underneath and the next on top. And so, writhing and wrestling, they rolled down the hill until they came to the high-water mark, and all the while as they rolled Arthur stabbed him with his dagger.

And it so happened that they came to the place where the two knights were, keeping Arthur's horse. Then, when they saw the king held fast in the giant's arms, they came and freed him. And then the king commanded Sir Kay to strike off the giant's head, and to set it on the broken shaft of a spear, and carry it to Sir Howell, and tell him that his enemy was slain. "And after that, have this head fixed on a gate-tower, so that all the people can see it and look at it. And you two, go up to the mountain and fetch me my shield, my sword and the club of iron. And as for the treasure, take it yourselves, for you will find riches there beyond counting. As long as I have the coat and the club, I want nothing more. This was the fiercest giant I ever met, except one on the mountain of Araby, whom I overcame; but this one was bigger and fiercer."

Then the knights fetched the club and the coat, and some of the treasure they took for themselves, and went back to the army. And at once this became known through all the country, and so the people came and thanked the king.

And he answered them, "Give the thanks to God, and share out the goods among yourselves."

And after that King Arthur told and commanded his cousin Howell that he should arrange for a church to be built on the same hill, in honour of Saint Michael. And in the morning the king moved on with his great army, and came into Champagne, into a valley, and there they pitched their tents.
