And as the king sat at his dinner, two messengers came in, one of whom was the Marshal of France, and told the king that the emperor had entered France, and had destroyed a great part of it, and was in Burgundy, and had destroyed and made great slaughter of the people, and burnt towns and boroughs, "and so, if you do not come quickly, they will have to surrender their bodies and their goods."

Chapter 6: How King Arthur sent Sir Gawain and others to Lucius, and how they were attacked and escaped with honour

Then the king had Sir Gawain, Sir Bors, Sir Lionel and Sir Bedivere called, and commanded them to go straight to Sir Lucius, "and tell him that he is to get out of my land at once; and if he will not, tell him to make ready for battle, and not to harass the poor people."

Then at once these noble knights mounted their horses, and when they came to the green wood, they saw many tents of silk of various colours set up in a meadow beside a river, and the emperor's tent was in the middle, with an eagle displayed above it. Our knights rode toward that tent, and arranged that Sir Gawain and Sir Bors should deliver the message, and left Sir Lionel and Sir Bedivere in ambush. And then Sir Gawain and Sir Bors delivered their message, and commanded Lucius, in Arthur's name, to leave his land, or else to make ready for battle without delay.

Lucius answered them and said, "You shall go back to your lord, and tell him that I will subdue him and all his lands."

Then Sir Gawain was angry, and said, "I would rather fight against you than have all France."

"And so would I," said Sir Bors, "rather than have all Brittany or Burgundy."

Then a knight named Sir Gainus, a near cousin of the emperor, said, "Look how full of pride and boasting these Britons are, and they brag as if they held up the whole world."

Then Sir Gawain was badly stung by these words, and pulled out his sword and struck off his head. And with that they turned their horses and rode over rivers and through woods until they came to their ambush, where Sir Lionel and Sir Bedivere were waiting. The Romans followed hard after them, on horseback and on foot, across an open field to a wood. Then Sir Bors turned his horse and saw a knight coming on fast, and he struck him through the body with a spear so that he fell down dead to the earth. Then came Caliburn, one of the strongest men of Pavia, and struck down many of Arthur's knights. And when Sir Bors saw him do so much harm, he made for him, and struck him through the breast, so that he fell down dead to the earth. Then Sir Feldenak thought to avenge the death of Gainus on Sir Gawain, but Sir Gawain saw it coming, and struck him on the head, and the stroke did not stop until it came to his breast. And then he turned back and came to his fellows in the ambush. And there was a clash, for the ambush broke out on the Romans, and slew and hewed down the Romans, and forced the Romans to flee and turn back, and the noble knights chased them to their tents.

Then the Romans gathered more men, and foot soldiers came on as well, and there was a new battle, and so many men that Sir Bors and Sir Berel were taken. But when Sir Gawain saw that, he took with him Sir Idrus, the good knight, and said he would never see King Arthur again unless he rescued them, and he pulled out Galatine, his good sword, and went after the men who were leading those two knights away. And he struck down the man who was leading Sir Bors, and took Sir Bors from him and handed him over to his fellows. And Sir Idrus in the same way rescued Sir Berel. Then the battle began to be great, so that our knights were in great danger, and so Sir Gawain sent to King Arthur for help, asking him to hurry, "for I am badly wounded, and our prisoners can pay ransoms beyond counting."

And the messenger came to the king and told him his message. And at once the king had his army assembled; but straight away, before he set out, the prisoners arrived, and Sir Gawain and his fellows had won the field and put the Romans to flight, and afterwards returned and came back with their company in such a way that no man of honour among them was lost, except that Sir Gawain was badly hurt. Then the king had his wounds probed, and comforted him. And so this was the beginning of the first engagement between the Britons and the Romans, and more than ten thousand of the Romans were slain, and there was great joy and merriment that night in King Arthur's army. And in the morning he sent all the prisoners to Paris under the guard of Sir Lancelot, with many knights, and of Sir Cador.

Chapter 7: How Lucius sent spies to lie in ambush to recapture his knights who had been taken prisoner, and how they were stopped

Now we turn to the Emperor of Rome, who learned that these prisoners were to be sent to Paris, and at once he sent certain knights and princes with sixty thousand men to lie in ambush, to rescue his knights and lords who were prisoners. And so the next morning, as Lancelot and Sir Cador, the chieftains and commanders of all those who were escorting the prisoners, were about to pass through a wood, Sir Lancelot sent certain knights ahead to scout whether anyone was in the woods to stop them. And when these knights came into the wood, at once they spotted the great ambush, and went back and told Sir Lancelot that sixty thousand Romans lay in wait for them. And then Sir Lancelot, with such knights as he had, and fighting men to the number of ten thousand, put them in battle order, and met them and fought them bravely, and killed and cut to pieces many of the Romans, and killed many knights and emirs on the side of the Romans and Saracens. There the king of Lyly was killed, and three great lords, Aladuke, Herawd and Heringdale. But Sir Lancelot fought so nobly that no man could withstand a stroke of his hand, and wherever he went he showed his prowess and his might, for he cut men down on every side; and the Romans and Saracens fled from him like sheep from the wolf or from the lion, and he put all of them who were left alive to flight.

And they fought so long that word came to King Arthur, and at once he made himself ready and came to the battle. And when he saw how his knights had won the battle, he embraced them in his arms, knight by knight, and said, "You are worthy to hold all your honour and renown. There was never a king, except myself, who had such noble knights."

"Sir," said Cador, "not one of us failed another. But the prowess and manhood of Sir Lancelot were more than a wonder to tell of, and so too were those of his cousins, who did many noble feats of war that day."

And Sir Cador also told which of his knights had been killed, such as Sir Berel, and others, Sir Moris and Sir Maurel, two good knights. Then the king wept, and dried his eyes with a handkerchief, and said, "Your courage very nearly destroyed you. For even if you had turned back, you would have lost no honour; for I call it folly for knights to stand their ground when they are outmatched."

"No," said Lancelot and the others, "for shame once taken can never be won back."

Chapter 8: How a senator told Lucius of their defeat, and also of the great battle between Arthur and Lucius

Now we leave King Arthur and his noble knights, who had won the field and had brought their prisoners to Paris, and speak of a senator who escaped from the battle, and came to Lucius the emperor, and said to him, "Sir emperor, I advise you to withdraw. What are you doing here? You will win nothing in these borderlands but great blows beyond all measure, for today one of Arthur's knights was worth a hundred of ours in the battle."

"Shame on you," said Lucius. "You talk like a coward. Your words grieve me more than all the loss I had today."

And at once he sent out a king called Sir Leomie, with a great army, and ordered him to hurry on ahead, and he would follow close behind. King Arthur was warned in secret, and sent his people to Sessoine, and took the towns and castles there from the Romans. Then the king commanded Sir Cador to take the rearguard, and to take with him certain knights of the Round Table, "and Sir Lancelot, Sir Bors, Sir Kay, Sir Marrok, with Sir Marhaus, shall wait upon our own person." So King Arthur divided his army into several parts, so that his enemies should not escape.

When the emperor had entered the vale of Sessoine, he could see where King Arthur was drawn up for battle with his banner displayed; and he was surrounded on every side by his enemies, so that he had no choice but to fight or surrender, for he could not flee. But he said openly to the Romans, "Sirs, I urge you to fight today and acquit yourselves like men, and remember how Rome rules and is chief and head over all the earth and the whole world, and do not let these Britons stand against us today."

And with that he had his trumpets blow the bloody calls to battle, so that the ground trembled and shook.

Then the armies drew near, and shoved and shouted on both sides, and great blows were struck on both sides, and many men were overthrown, wounded and killed; and great deeds of valour, prowess and feats of war were shown that day, too many to recount, the noble feats of every man, for they would fill a whole volume. But above all, King Arthur rode through the battle urging his knights to do well, and he himself did as nobly with his own hands as any man could do. He drew out Excalibur his sword, and watched always for where the Romans were thickest and were hurting his people most, and at once he turned to that place, and hewed and cut men down on every side, and rescued his people. And he killed a great giant named Galapas, who was a man of huge size and height. He cut him shorter, and struck off both his legs at the knees, saying, "Now you're a better size to deal with than you were!" And afterwards he struck off his head. There Sir Gawain fought nobly and killed three emirs in that battle. And so did all the knights of the Round Table. So the battle between King Arthur and Lucius the Emperor went on a long time. Lucius had many Saracens on his side, and they were killed. And so the battle was great, and often one side had the advantage and then at once the disadvantage, and it went on so long that at last King Arthur saw where Lucius the Emperor was fighting, and doing wonders with his own hands. And at once he rode at him. And each struck the other fiercely, and at last Lucius struck Arthur across the face, and gave him a broad wound. And when King Arthur felt himself hurt, at once he struck him back with Excalibur, so that it split his head from the crown, and did not stop until it came to his breast. And then the emperor fell down dead, and there his life ended.

And when it was known that the emperor was killed, at once all the Romans with all their army took to flight, and King Arthur with all his knights followed the chase, and cut down all those they could overtake. And so the victory was given to King Arthur, and the triumph; and more than a hundred thousand were killed on the side of Lucius. And afterwards King Arthur had the dead bodies searched, and had those of his own following who were killed buried, every man according to his estate and rank. And for those who were wounded, he had the surgeons examine their hurts and wounds, and commanded them to spare no salves or medicines until they were healed.

Then the king rode straight to the place where the Emperor Lucius lay dead, and with him he found killed the Sultan of Syria, and the King of Egypt and the King of Ethiopia, who were two noble kings, with seventeen other kings of various countries, and also sixty senators of Rome, all noble men. All of these the king had embalmed with many good aromatic gums, and afterwards had them wrapped in sixty folds of waxed cloth of sendal, a fine silk, and laid in chests of lead, so that they would not rot or smell; and on all these bodies their shields with their arms and banners were set, so that it would be known what country they were from. And afterwards he found three senators who were alive, and he said to them, "To save your lives, I want you to take these dead bodies and carry them with you to great Rome, and present them to the Potestate, Rome's governor, on my behalf, showing him my letters, and tell them that I in my own person will soon be at Rome. And I expect the Romans will think twice before they demand any tribute of me. And I command you to say, when you come to Rome, to the Potestate and all the Council and Senate, that I send them these dead bodies for the tribute they have demanded. And if they are not content with these, I will pay more when I come, for I owe no other tribute, and no other will I pay. And I think this is enough for Britain, Ireland and all the German lands. And furthermore, I charge you to tell them that I command them, on pain of their heads, never to demand tribute or tax from me or from my lands."

Then with this charge and command, the three senators already named departed with all the dead bodies, laying the body of Lucius all alone in a cart covered with the arms of the Empire; and after it always two bodies of kings in a chariot, and then the bodies of the senators after them. And so they went toward Rome, and delivered their embassy and message to the Potestate and the Senate, recounting the battle fought in France, and how the field was lost and a great many people killed, beyond counting. And so they advised them by no means to make any more war against that noble conqueror Arthur, for his might and prowess were greatly to be feared, seeing the noble kings and the great multitude of knights of the Round Table, with whom no earthly prince can compare.

Chapter 9: How Arthur, after he had won the battle against the Romans, entered Germany, and then Italy

Now we turn to King Arthur and his noble knights, who, after the great battle won against the Romans, entered Lorraine, Brabant and Flanders, and then went back into Upper Germany, and so over the mountains into Lombardy, and after that into Tuscany. And there was a city there that would by no means surrender or obey, so King Arthur besieged it, and lay a long time around it, and made many assaults on the city; and those inside defended themselves bravely. Then one day the king called Sir Florence, a knight, and said to him that they were short of food, "and not far from here are great forests and woods, where many of my enemies are, with a great deal of cattle. I want you to make ready and go there foraging, and take with you Sir Gawain my nephew, Sir Wisshard, Sir Clegis, Sir Cleremond, and the Captain of Cardiff, with others, and bring back with you all the beasts you can get there."

And at once these knights made ready, and rode over woods and hills, through forests and woods, until they came into a fair meadow full of fair flowers and grass; and there they rested themselves and their horses all that night. And at the break of day the next morning, Sir Gawain took his horse and stole away from his companions, to look for some adventures. And at once he caught sight of an armed man walking his horse at an easy pace along the side of a wood, with his shield laced to his shoulder, sitting on a strong warhorse, with no man with him except a page carrying a mighty spear. The knight bore on his shield three griffins of gold on black, with a carbuncle, and the top band of the shield in silver. When Sir Gawain saw this splendid knight, he set his spear in its rest, and rode straight at him, and asked him where he came from. The other answered and said he was from Tuscany, and he asked Sir Gawain, "What, proud knight, are you challenging me so boldly? You'll get no plunder here. Try what you like: you'll be my prisoner before you leave."

Then Gawain said, "You boast a great deal and speak proud words. I advise you, for all your boasting, to make yourself ready and take up your weapons, before worse harm comes to you."

Chapter 10: Of a fight between Sir Gawain and a Saracen, who afterwards surrendered and became a Christian

Then they took their spears and charged at each other with all the might they had, and struck each other through their shields into their shoulders. So at once they pulled out their swords, and struck such great blows that the sparks flew from their helmets. Then Sir Gawain was thoroughly shaken, and with Galatine his good sword he struck through the shield and the thick hauberk made of thick rings of mail, and smashed the precious stones on it all to pieces, and gave him a broad wound, so that men could see both liver and lung. Then that knight groaned, and turned on Sir Gawain, and with a backhand stroke gave him a great wound and cut a vein, which hurt Gawain badly, and he bled heavily.

Then the knight said to Sir Gawain, "Bind up your wound before the bleeding drains your colour, for you are bloodying all your horse and your fine armour. And all the barber-surgeons of Brittany will not be able to stop your blood, for whoever is hurt with this blade will never stop bleeding."

Then Gawain answered, "It troubles me very little. Your big words will not frighten me or lessen my courage; but you will suffer pain and sorrow before we part. But tell me quickly who can stop my bleeding."

"I can do that," said the knight, "if I want to, and so I will, if you will help and support me so that I may be christened and believe in God. And I ask this of you by your manhood, and it will be a great merit for your soul."

"I grant it," said Gawain, "so help me God, to fulfil all your wish. But first tell me what you were looking for here like this, alone, and what land you are from, and whose allegiance you owe."

"Sir," he said, "my name is Priamus, and my father is a great prince, and he has rebelled against Rome and overrun many of their lands. My father is descended in the direct line from Alexander and from Hector. And Duke Joshua and Maccabaeus were of our lineage. I am the rightful heir of Alexandria and Africa, and all the outer islands; yet I will believe in the Lord you believe in, and for your trouble I will give you treasure enough. I was so proud and haughty in my heart that I thought no man was my equal, or like me. I was sent into this war with seven score knights, and now I have met with you, who have given me my fill of fighting. So, sir knight, I beg you to tell me who you are."

"I am no knight," said Gawain. "I have been brought up for many years in the wardrobe of the noble King Arthur, the department that keeps his gear, to look after his armour and his other clothing, and to lace up the short coats that belong to him. Last Christmas he made me a yeoman, and gave me a horse and armour, and a hundred pounds in money; and if fortune is my friend, I have no doubt I will be well advanced and helped by my liege lord."

"Ah," said Priamus, "if his servants are so keen and fierce, his knights must be exceedingly good. Now for the love of the King of Heaven, whether you are a servant or a knight, tell me your name."

"By God," said Sir Gawain, "now I will tell you the truth. My name is Sir Gawain, and I am known in his court and in his chamber, and I am one of the knights of the Round Table. He dubbed me a duke with his own hand. So do not resent it if this grace has fallen to me; it is the goodness of God that lent me my strength."

"Now I am better pleased," said Priamus, "than if you had given me all Provence and rich Paris. I would rather have been torn apart by wild horses than that any servant should have won such renown, or that any page or hard rider should have had the prize over me. But now, sir knight, I warn you that near here is a Duke of Lorraine with his army, and the noblest men of Dauphiny, and lords of Lombardy, with the garrison of Godard, and Saracens of Southland, numbering sixty thousand good men-at-arms. So unless we hurry away from here, it will go hard with us both, for we are badly hurt and not likely ever to recover. But keep an eye on my page, so that he does not blow his horn; for if he does, there are a hundred knights waiting close by here to attend on me, and if they take you, no ransom of gold or silver will set you free."

Then Sir Gawain rode across a river to save himself, and the knight followed him, and so they rode on until they came to his companions, who were in the meadow where they had been all night. As soon as Sir Wisshard caught sight of Sir Gawain and saw that he was hurt, he ran to him weeping with sorrow, and asked him who had hurt him like this. And Gawain told how he had fought with that man, and each of them had wounded the other, and how he had salves to heal them, "but I can tell you other news: soon we will have to fight many enemies."

Then Sir Priamus and Sir Gawain dismounted, and let their horses graze in the meadow, and took off their armour, and then the blood ran fresh from their wounds. And Priamus took from his page a flask full of the four waters that came out of Paradise, and anointed their wounds with a certain balm, and washed them with that water, and within an hour they were both as sound as they had ever been. And then they were all called together to council with a trumpet, and there Priamus told them what lords and knights had sworn to rescue him, and that without fail they would be attacked by many thousands; so he advised them to withdraw.

Then Sir Gawain said it would be a great shame to them to leave without striking a blow. "So I advise that we take up our arms and make ready to meet these Saracens and unbelievers, and with the help of God we shall overthrow them and have a fine day of it against them. And Sir Florence shall stay here in this field to hold the position, as a noble knight, and we shall not abandon those fellows over there."

"Now," said Priamus, "stop talking, for I warn you, you will find many dangerous knights in those woods over there. They will drive out beasts to lure you on. They are past counting, and you are not more than seven hundred, which is far too few to fight with so many."

"Nevertheless," said Sir Gawain, "we will meet them once, and see what they can do, and the best shall have the victory."

Chapter 11: How the Saracens came out of a wood to rescue their cattle, and of a great battle

Then Sir Florence called Sir Floridas to him, with a hundred knights, and drove off the herd of beasts. Then seven hundred men-at-arms followed him; and Sir Ferant of Spain came galloping out of the woods on a fine steed, and came to Sir Florence and asked him why he was running away. Then Sir Florence took his spear and rode against him, and struck him in the forehead and broke his neck. Then all the others were stirred up, and meant to avenge the death of Sir Ferant, and charged in among them; and there was a great fight, and many were killed and laid on the ground. And Sir Florence with his hundred knights held the position the whole time, and fought bravely.

Then, when Priamus the good knight saw how great the fight was, he went to Sir Gawain and told him to go and help his companions, who were hard pressed by their enemies.

"Sir, don't worry," said Sir Gawain, "for the prize will be theirs. I will not move my horse one step toward them unless I see more of the enemy than there are now; for they are strong enough to match them."

And with that he saw an earl called Sir Ethelwold, and the duke of the Germans, come charging out of a wood with many thousands, and Priamus' knights with them, and they came straight into the battle. Then Sir Gawain encouraged his knights, and told them not to be dismayed, for it would all be theirs. Then they began to gallop, and met their enemies, and men were killed and overthrown on every side. Then the knights of the Round Table thrust in among them, and struck to the earth all those who stood against them, so that they forced them to fall back and flee.

"By God," said Sir Gawain, "this gladdens my heart, for now they are fewer by twenty thousand."

Then Jubance, a giant, entered the battle, and fought and cut men down on every side, and harmed many of our knights, among whom Sir Gherard, a knight of Wales, was killed. Then our knights took heart, and killed many Saracens. And then Sir Priamus came in with his pennon, and rode with the knights of the Round Table, and fought so bravely that many of their enemies lost their lives. And there Sir Priamus killed the Marquis of Moises land, and Sir Gawain and his companions acquitted themselves so well that they won the field. But in that fight Sir Chestelaine was killed, a young squire who was Sir Gawain's ward, and there was great grief for it, and his death was soon avenged. So the battle ended, and many lords of Lombardy and many Saracens were left dead on the field.

Then Sir Florence and Sir Gawain lodged their people safely, and took a great quantity of cattle, and of gold and silver, and great treasure and riches, and went back to King Arthur, who was still at the siege. And when they came to the king, they presented their prisoners and told of their adventures, and how they had defeated their enemies.

Chapter 12: How Sir Gawain returned to King Arthur with his prisoners, and how the King won a city, and how he was crowned Emperor

"Now God be thanked," said the noble King Arthur. "But what sort of man is that standing by himself? He doesn't look like a prisoner."

"Sir," said Gawain, "this is a good man-at-arms. He matched me, but he has yielded himself to God, and to me, to become a Christian. If it had not been for him, we would never have come back. So I beg you to let him be baptised, for there lives no nobler man, nor a better knight with his hands."

Then the king had him christened at once, and had him called by his first name, Priamus, and made him a duke and a knight of the Round Table. And then at once the king had the assault on the city proclaimed, and there was raising of ladders and breaking of walls, and the ditch was filled, so that men could enter the city with little trouble. Then a duchess came out, and Clarisin the countess, with many ladies and damsels, and knelt before King Arthur, and begged him for the love of God to accept the city's surrender and not to take it by storm, for then many innocent people would be killed. Then the king lowered his visor, with a meek and noble face, and said, "Madam, none of my subjects shall do any wrong to you or your maidens, or to anyone who belongs to you; but the duke shall abide my judgement."

Then at once the king commanded the assault to stop, and at once the duke's eldest son brought out the keys, and kneeling handed them to the king, and begged him for mercy; and the king took possession of the town with the consent of his lords, and took the duke and sent him to Dover, to stay there a prisoner for the rest of his life, and set aside certain rents for the duchess's dower and for her children.

Then he appointed lords to rule those lands, and made laws, as a lord ought to do in his own country; and afterwards he set out on his journey toward Rome, and sent Sir Floris and Sir Floridas ahead with five hundred men-at-arms. And they came to the city of Urbino and laid an ambush there, where it seemed best to them, and rode up before the town, where at once a great many people sallied out and skirmished with the scouts. Then the ambush broke out and won the bridge, and afterwards the town, and set the king's banner on the walls. Then the king came up on a hill, and saw the city and his banner on the walls, by which he knew that the city was won. And at once he sent word and commanded that none of his liegemen should dishonour or lie with any lady, wife or maiden; and when he came into the city, he went to the castle, and comforted those who were in sorrow, and appointed a captain there, a knight of his own country.

And when the people of Milan heard that this same city was won, they sent great sums of money to King Arthur, and begged him as their lord to have pity on them, promising to be his subjects for ever, and to do him homage and fealty for the lands of Piacenza and Pavia, Petersaint, and the Port of Tremble, and to give him a million in gold every year for all his lifetime. Then he rode into Tuscany, and won towns and castles, and laid waste everything in his way that would not obey him, and so on to Spoleto and Viterbo, and from there he rode into the Vale of Vicecount among the vines. And from there he sent to the senators, to learn whether they would acknowledge him as their lord. But soon afterwards, on a Saturday, all the senators who were left alive came to King Arthur, and the noblest cardinals who lived in Rome at that time, and begged him for peace, and offered him a great deal, and asked him as their ruler to give them leave for six weeks to assemble all the Romans, and then to crown him emperor with chrism, the holy anointing oil, as befits so high a rank.

"I agree," said the king, "just as you have proposed, and I will be crowned there at Christmas, and hold my Round Table with my knights as it pleases me."

And then the senators made ready for his enthronement. And on the appointed day, as the romance tells, he came into Rome, and was crowned emperor by the Pope's hand, with all the royal splendour that could be made, and stayed there for a time, and settled all his lands from Rome to France, and gave lands and realms to his servants and knights, to each according to what he deserved, in such a way that no one complained, rich or poor. And he gave Sir Priamus the duchy of Lorraine; and Priamus thanked him, and said he would serve him all the days of his life. And afterwards he made dukes and earls, and made every man rich.

Then after this all his knights and lords gathered before him, and said, "Blessed be God, your war is finished and your conquest achieved, so much so that we know of no one so great or mighty who dares make war against you. So we beg you to return home, and give us leave to go home to our wives, from whom we have been away a long time, and to rest, for your expedition is finished with honour and renown."

Then the king said, "You speak the truth, and it is no wisdom to tempt God. So make yourselves ready, and let us return to England."

Then there was packing of armour and baggage, and a great train of carts. And when leave had been given, he turned back, and commanded that no man, on pain of death, should rob or take food or anything else along the way unless he paid for it. And so he came over the sea and landed at Sandwich, where Queen Guinevere his wife came to meet him; and he was nobly received by all his common people in every city and town, and great gifts were presented to him to welcome him at his homecoming.

Here ends the fifth book, of the conquest that King Arthur won against Lucius the Emperor of Rome.

Here follows the sixth book, which is of Sir Lancelot du Lake.

Book Six: Sir Lancelot and Sir Lionel

Chapter 1: How Sir Lancelot and Sir Lionel left the court, and how Sir Lionel left him sleeping and was captured

Soon after King Arthur had come back from Rome to England, all the knights of the Round Table gathered to the king, and held many jousts and tournaments. And some there were who were only plain knights, who grew so much in arms and in honour that they surpassed all their fellows in prowess and noble deeds, and that was well proved on many; but above all it was proved on Sir Lancelot du Lake. For in all tournaments and jousts and deeds of arms, both in sport and in earnest, he surpassed all other knights, and at no time was he ever overcome, unless it was by treason or enchantment. So Sir Lancelot grew so marvellously in renown and in honour that he is the first knight the French book makes mention of after King Arthur came back from Rome. And so Queen Guinevere held him in great favour above all other knights, and certainly he loved the queen in return above all other ladies and damsels all his life, and for her he did many deeds of arms, and saved her from the fire through his noble chivalry.

So Sir Lancelot rested a long while with play and games. And then he thought he would prove himself in strange adventures, and he told his nephew, Sir Lionel, to make himself ready, "for we two will go and look for adventures." So they mounted their horses, armed in every point, and rode into a deep forest and so out onto a wide plain. And then the weather was hot about noon, and Sir Lancelot had a great wish to sleep. Then Sir Lionel noticed a great apple tree that stood by a hedge, and said, "Brother, there is a fine shade over there. We can rest ourselves and our horses there."

"Well said, fair brother," said Sir Lancelot, "for these eight years I have not been as sleepy as I am now."

And so they dismounted there and tied their horses to separate trees, and so Sir Lancelot lay down under an apple tree, with his helmet under his head. And Sir Lionel kept watch while he slept. So Sir Lancelot was sound asleep.

And meanwhile three knights came riding, fleeing as fast as ever they could ride. And there followed them only one knight. And when Sir Lionel saw him, he thought he had never seen so big a knight, nor so fine-looking a man, nor one so well equipped in every point. So within a little while this strong knight had overtaken one of these knights, and there he struck him to the cold earth, so that he lay still. And then he rode at the second knight, and struck him so that man and horse fell down. And then he rode straight at the third knight, and struck him a spear's length out over his horse's rump. And then he dismounted and took his horse by the bridle, and tied all three knights fast with the reins of their own bridles. When Sir Lionel saw him do this, he thought he would try him, and made himself ready, and quietly and secretly he took his horse, and took care not to wake Sir Lancelot. And when he was mounted on his horse, he overtook this strong knight, and told him to turn. And the other struck Sir Lionel so hard that he bore horse and man to the earth, and so he dismounted and tied him fast, and threw him across his own horse. And so he served all four of them, and rode away with them to his own castle. And when he came there he had them stripped of their armour, and had them beaten naked with thorns, and afterwards put them in a deep prison where there were many more knights, who were grieving bitterly.

Chapter 2: How Sir Ector followed to look for Sir Lancelot, and how he was captured by Sir Turquine

When Sir Ector de Maris learned that Sir Lancelot had left the court to look for adventures, he was angry with himself, and made himself ready to look for Sir Lancelot. And when he had ridden a long way in a great forest, he met a man who looked like a forester.

"Good fellow," said Sir Ector, "do you know of any adventures near here in this country?"

"Sir," said the forester, "I know this country well. And near here, within this mile, there is a strong manor, well moated, and by that manor, on the left hand, there is a good ford for horses to drink at, and over that ford there grows a fine tree, and on it hang many fine shields that once belonged to good knights. And on the trunk of the tree hangs a basin of copper and brass. Strike that basin three times with the butt of your spear, and soon after you will hear news, or else you will have the best luck that any knight has had for many a year who passed through this forest."

"Many thanks," said Sir Ector, and left, and came to the tree, and saw many fine shields. And among them he saw his brother Sir Lionel's shield, and many more that he knew, belonging to his fellows of the Round Table, which grieved his heart, and he vowed to avenge his brother.

Then at once Sir Ector beat on the basin like a madman, and then he gave his horse a drink at the ford. And a knight came up behind him and told him to come out of the water and make himself ready. And at once Sir Ector turned sharply, and set his spear in rest, and struck the other knight such a great blow that his horse spun round twice.

"That was well done," said the strong knight, "and you have struck me like a true knight."

And with that he drove his horse at Sir Ector, and seized him under his right arm, and carried him clean out of the saddle, and rode away with him into his own hall, and threw him down in the middle of the floor. The name of this knight was Sir Turquine. Then he said to Sir Ector, "Because you have done more to me today than any knight has done these twelve years, now I will grant you your life, as long as you will swear to be my prisoner all the days of your life."

"No," said Sir Ector, "I will never promise you that, but I will do the best I can for myself."

"I am sorry for that," said Sir Turquine.

And then he had him stripped of his armour, and had him beaten naked with thorns, and then put him down in a deep dungeon, where he found many of his fellows that he knew. But when Sir Ector saw Sir Lionel, he grieved greatly.

"Alas, brother," said Sir Ector, "where is my brother Sir Lancelot?"

"Fair brother, I left him asleep under an apple tree when I went away from him, and what has become of him I cannot tell you."

"Alas," said the knights, "unless Sir Lancelot helps us we can never be set free, for we know of no knight now who is able to match our master Turquine."

Chapter 3: How four queens found Lancelot sleeping, and how he was captured by enchantment and taken to a castle

Now we leave these knights in prison, and speak of Sir Lancelot du Lake, who lies sleeping under the apple tree. Right about noon four queens of high rank came by him. And so that the heat should not trouble them, four knights rode around them, and carried a cloth of green silk on four spears, between them and the sun, and the queens rode on four white mules. And as they rode they heard a great horse neigh fiercely nearby, and then they noticed a sleeping knight who lay in full armour under an apple tree. As soon as these queens looked at his face, they knew it was Sir Lancelot. Then they began to quarrel over that knight, and each one said she would have him for her lover.

"We shall not quarrel," said Morgan le Fay, who was King Arthur's sister. "I will put an enchantment on him so that he will not wake for six hours, and then I will take him away to my castle. And when he is safely in my keeping, I will take the enchantment off him, and then let him choose which of us he will have for his lover."

So this enchantment was cast on Sir Lancelot, and then they laid him on his shield, and carried him that way on horseback between two knights, and brought him to the Castle Chariot. And there they laid him in a cold room, and at night they sent a fair damsel to him with his supper ready prepared. By then the enchantment had passed, and when she came she greeted him, and asked him how he was.

"I cannot say, fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "for I don't know how I came into this castle, unless it was by an enchantment."

"Sir," she said, "you must keep your spirits up. And if you are the kind of knight people say you are, I will tell you more tomorrow at first light."

"Many thanks, fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot. "I ask for your good will."

And so she left. And there he lay all that night without comfort from anyone. And early in the morning these four queens came, exceedingly richly dressed, all of them bidding him good morning, and he them in return.

"Sir knight," the four queens said, "you must understand you are our prisoner. And we know you well here, that you are Sir Lancelot du Lake, King Ban's son. And because we know your worth, that you are the noblest knight living, and as we well know, no lady can have your love but one, and that is Queen Guinevere: now you will lose her for ever, and she you. And so you must now choose one of us four. I am Queen Morgan le Fay, queen of the land of Gore, and here is the Queen of North Wales, and the Queen of Eastland, and the Queen of the Out Isles. Now choose one of us, whichever you will have for your lover, for if you do not choose, you will die in this prison."

"This is a hard case," said Sir Lancelot, "that either I must die or else choose one of you. Yet I would rather die in this prison with honour than have one of you for my lover against my will. And so you have your answer: I will have none of you, for you are false enchantresses. And as for my lady, Dame Guinevere, if I were at liberty as I was, I would prove it on you or on your champions that she is the truest lady to her lord alive."

"Well," said the queens, "is this your answer, that you will refuse us?"

"Yes, on my life," said Sir Lancelot, "I refuse you."

So they left and left him there alone, grieving greatly.

Chapter 4: How Sir Lancelot was freed with the help of a damsel

Just then, at noon, the damsel came to him with his dinner, and asked him how he was.

"Truly, fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "never so badly in all the days of my life."

"Sir," she said, "I am sorry for that. But if you will be guided by me, I will help you out of this distress, and you will suffer no shame or dishonour, provided you keep a promise to me."

"Fair damsel, I will grant it you, for I am badly afraid of these sorceress queens, since they have destroyed many a good knight."

"Sir," said she, "that is true. And because of the renown and goodness they hear of in you, they want your love. And sir, they say your name is Sir Lancelot du Lake, the flower of knights, and they are exceedingly angry with you because you have refused them. But sir, if you would promise me to help my father next Tuesday, who has arranged a tournament between himself and the King of North Wales (for last Tuesday my father lost the field through three knights of Arthur's court), if you will be there next Tuesday and help my father, then tomorrow before first light, by the grace of God, I will set you completely free."

"Fair maiden," said Sir Lancelot, "tell me your father's name, and then I will give you an answer."

"Sir knight," she said, "my father is King Bagdemagus, who was shamefully beaten at the last tournament."

"I know your father well," said Sir Lancelot, "for a noble king and a good knight. And on my life, you shall have me ready to serve your father and you on that day."

"Sir," she said, "many thanks. And tomorrow see that you are ready early, and I will be the one who sets you free and brings you your armour and your horse, shield and spear. And near here, within ten miles, there is an abbey of white monks. There I beg you to wait for me, and I will bring my father to you there."

"All this shall be done," said Sir Lancelot, "as I am a true knight."

And so she left, and came early in the morning, and found him ready. Then she brought him out through twelve locks, and brought him to his armour. And when he was fully armed, she brought him to his own horse, and quickly he saddled him and took a great spear in his hand and so rode off, and said, "Fair damsel, I will not fail you, by the grace of God."

And so he rode into a great forest all that day, and could never find any highway, and so night fell on him. And then he noticed, in a little glen, a tent of red silk.

"By my faith," said Sir Lancelot, "I will lodge in that tent all this night."

And so he dismounted there, and tied his horse to the tent, and there he took off his armour, and there he found a bed, and lay down in it and fell sound asleep.

Chapter 5: How a knight found Sir Lancelot lying in his lover's bed, and how Sir Lancelot fought the knight

Then within an hour the knight who owned the tent came, and he thought his lady-love was lying in that bed, and so he lay down beside Sir Lancelot, and took him in his arms and began to kiss him. And when Sir Lancelot felt a rough beard kissing him, he leapt nimbly out of the bed, and the other knight after him, and each of them got his sword in his hand. And out of the tent door went the knight of the tent, and Sir Lancelot followed him, and there in a little glen Sir Lancelot wounded him badly, close to death. And then he yielded to Sir Lancelot, and so Lancelot spared him, on condition that he would tell him why he came into the bed.

"Sir," said the knight, "the tent is my own, and I had arranged for my lady to sleep with me here tonight, and now I am likely to die of this wound."

"I am sorry for your hurt," said Lancelot, "but I was afraid of treason, for I was tricked not long ago. And so come along into your tent and take your rest, and I think I can stop your bleeding."

And so they both went into the tent, and at once Sir Lancelot stopped his bleeding.

With that the knight's lady came, who was an exceedingly beautiful lady, and when she saw that her lord Belleus was badly wounded, she cried out against Sir Lancelot, and grieved beyond measure.

"Peace, my lady and my love," said Belleus, "for this knight is a good man, and a knight-errant."

And there he told her the whole reason how he was wounded. "And when I yielded to him, he spared me courteously and has stopped my bleeding."

"Sir," said the lady, "I beg you to tell me what knight you are, and what is your name?"

"Fair lady," he said, "my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"I always thought so from your speech," said the lady, "for I have often seen you before this, and I know you better than you think. But now, if you would promise me of your courtesy, for the harm you have done to me and my lord Belleus, that when he comes to Arthur's court you will have him made a knight of the Round Table; for he is an exceedingly good man of arms, and a mighty lord of lands in many outlying isles."

"Fair lady," said Sir Lancelot, "let him come to the court at the next high feast, and see that you come with him, and I will do all I can, if he proves himself valiant with his hands, so that you shall have your desire."

So in a little while, as they talked like this, the night passed, and the day shone, and then Sir Lancelot armed himself, and took his horse, and they showed him the way to the abbey, and he rode there within the space of two hours.

Chapter 6: How Sir Lancelot was welcomed by King Bagdemagus' daughter, and how he made his complaint to her father

And as soon as Sir Lancelot came into the abbey yard, King Bagdemagus' daughter heard a great horse on the paving. And then she got up and went to a window, and there she saw Sir Lancelot. And at once she had men quickly take his horse from him and lead it into a stable, and he himself was led into a fine room, and his armour taken off, and the lady sent him a long gown, and soon she came herself. And then she gave Lancelot an exceedingly warm welcome, and she said he was the knight in the world who was most welcome to her. Then in all haste she sent for her father Bagdemagus, who was within twelve miles of that abbey, and before evening he came, with a fine company of knights with him. And when the king had dismounted from his horse, he went straight to Sir Lancelot's room, and there he found his daughter. And then the king embraced Sir Lancelot in his arms, and each greeted the other warmly.

At once Sir Lancelot made his complaint to the king of how he had been betrayed, and how his brother Sir Lionel had gone from him he did not know where, and how his daughter had freed him from prison. "So as long as I live I will serve her and all her kindred."

"Then I am sure of your help," said the king, "next Tuesday."

"Yes, sir," said Sir Lancelot, "I will not fail you, for I have promised so to my lady your daughter. But, sir, which knights of my lord Arthur's were they who were with the King of North Wales?"

And the king said it was Sir Mador de la Porte, and Sir Mordred, and Sir Gahalantine who had worsted all his knights, for against those three neither he nor his knights could hold out.

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "since I hear that the tournament is to be here, within three miles of this abbey, send me three knights of yours, such as you trust, and see that the three knights all have white shields, and I too, with no painting on the shields. And we four will come out of a little wood between the two sides, and we will fall on the front of our enemies and do them all the harm we can; and that way no one will know what knight I am."

So they took their rest that night, and this was on the Sunday. And so the king left, and sent Sir Lancelot three knights with the four white shields. And on the Tuesday they lodged themselves in a little leafy wood beside the place where the tournament was to be. And there were stands and viewing places so that lords and ladies might watch and award the prize. Then the King of North Wales came into the field with a hundred and sixty helmed knights. And the three knights of Arthur's stood by themselves. Then King Bagdemagus came into the field with eighty helmed knights. And then they set their spears in rest, and came together with a great crash, and at the first encounter twelve knights of King Bagdemagus' side were killed, and six of the King of North Wales' side, and King Bagdemagus' side was driven far back.

Chapter 7: How Sir Lancelot bore himself in a tournament, and how he met Sir Turquine leading Sir Gaheris

With that came Sir Lancelot du Lake, and he thrust in with his spear into the thick of the crowd, and there he struck down five knights with one spear, and he broke the backs of four of them. And in that throng he struck down the King of North Wales, and broke his thigh in that fall. The three knights of Arthur's saw all this that Sir Lancelot did.

"There's a dangerous guest over there," said Sir Mador de la Porte, "so here goes, I'll have a go at him."

So they met, and Sir Lancelot bore him down, horse and man, so that his shoulder came out of joint.

"Now it falls to me to joust," said Mordred, "for Sir Mador has had a bad fall."

Sir Lancelot saw him, and got a great spear in his hand, and met him. And Sir Mordred broke a spear on him, and Sir Lancelot gave him such a blow that the saddlebow broke, and so he flew over his horse's tail, so that his helmet drove into the earth a foot and more, and his neck was nearly broken, and there he lay a long while in a faint.

Then Sir Gahalantine came in with a great spear, and Lancelot against him, with all the strength they could drive, so that both their spears burst right up to their hands. And then they flung out their swords and gave many a grim stroke. Then Sir Lancelot was angry beyond measure, and then he struck Sir Gahalantine on the helmet so that his nose burst out bleeding, and his ears and mouth both, and with that his head hung low. And with that his horse ran away with him, and he fell down to the earth. At once Sir Lancelot got a great spear in his hand, and before that great spear broke, he bore sixteen knights to the earth, some horse and man, and some the man and not the horse. And there was none he hit squarely who bore arms again that day. And then he got another great spear, and struck down twelve knights, and most of them never prospered afterwards. And then the knights of the King of North Wales would joust no more. And there the prize was given to King Bagdemagus.

So each side went off to its own place, and Sir Lancelot rode off with King Bagdemagus to his castle, and there he had an exceedingly warm welcome both from the king and from his daughter, and they offered him great gifts. And in the morning he took his leave, and told the king that he would go and look for his brother Sir Lionel, who had gone from him while he slept. So he took his horse, and commended them all to God. And there he said to the king's daughter, "If you ever have need of my service, I beg you let me know, and I will not fail you, as I am a true knight."

And so Sir Lancelot left, and by chance he came into the same forest where he had been captured sleeping. And in the middle of a highway he met a damsel riding on a white palfrey, and they greeted each other.

"Fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "do you know of any adventures in this country?"

"Sir knight," said the damsel, "there are adventures close by, if you dare try them."

"Why should I not try adventures?" said Sir Lancelot. "That is why I came here."

"Well," said she, "you certainly look like a good knight. And if you dare meet a good knight, I will bring you to where the best knight is, and the mightiest you ever met, as long as you will tell me your name, and what knight you are."

"Damsel, I care nothing about telling you my name. Truly my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"Sir, you look the part well. There are adventures near here that are fit for you. For near here lives a knight who will not be overmatched by any man I know, unless you overmatch him, and his name is Sir Turquine. And as I understand, he has in his prison sixty-four good knights of Arthur's court, whom he has won with his own hands. But when you have done that day's work, you must promise me, as you are a true knight, to go with me, and to help me and other damsels who are wronged every day by a false knight."

"All your purpose and desire, damsel, I will fulfil, as long as you will bring me to this knight."

"Now, fair knight, come along."

And so she brought him to the ford and the tree where the basin hung.

So Sir Lancelot let his horse drink, and then he beat on the basin with the butt of his spear, so hard, with all his might, that the bottom fell out. And he went on a long while, but he saw nothing. Then he rode up and down along the gates of that manor for nearly half an hour. And then he caught sight of a great knight driving a horse in front of him, and across the horse there lay an armed knight, tied up. And as they came nearer and nearer, Sir Lancelot thought he ought to know him. Then Sir Lancelot saw that it was Sir Gaheris, Gawain's brother, a knight of the Round Table.

"Now, fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "I see a knight coming over there, tied fast, who is a fellow of mine, and he is Sir Gawain's brother. And from the very start I promise you, God willing, to rescue that knight; and unless his master sits better in the saddle, I will free all the prisoners he has from their peril, for I am sure he has two brothers of mine prisoner with him."

By the time each had seen the other, they gripped their spears.

"Now, fair knight," said Sir Lancelot, "put that wounded knight off the horse, and let him rest a while, and let us two try our strength. For as I am told, you do and have done great insult and shame to knights of the Round Table, and so now defend yourself."

"If you're of the Round Table," said Turquine, "I defy you and your whole fellowship."

"That is saying too much," said Sir Lancelot.

Chapter 8: How Sir Lancelot and Sir Turquine fought each other

And then they set their spears in rest, and came together with their horses as fast as they could run, and each struck the other in the middle of his shield, so that both their horses' backs broke under them, and the knights were both stunned. And as soon as they could get clear of their horses, they took their shields in front of them, and drew their swords, and came together eagerly, and each gave the other many strong strokes, for neither shields nor armour could hold out against their strokes. And so within a little while they both had grim wounds, and bled exceedingly badly. So they went on for two hours or more, pressing and slashing at each other, wherever they could hit any bare place.

Then at last they were both out of breath, and stood leaning on their swords.

"Now, fellow," said Sir Turquine, "hold your hand a while, and answer what I ask you."

"Say on."

Then Turquine said, "You are the biggest man I ever met, and the one with the best wind, and like one knight I hate above all other knights. So as long as you are not he, I will gladly make peace with you, and for your sake I will free all the prisoners I have, which is sixty-four, as long as you will tell me your name. And you and I will be companions together, and I will never fail you as long as I live."

"Well said," said Sir Lancelot. "But since I may have your friendship on those terms, what knight is it that you hate so much above all others?"

"In good faith," said Sir Turquine, "his name is Sir Lancelot du Lake, for he killed my brother, Sir Carados, at the Dolorous Tower, who was one of the best knights alive. And so I except him out of all knights; for if I can once meet him, one of us will make an end of the other, I swear it. And for Sir Lancelot's sake I have killed a hundred good knights, and maimed as many so utterly that they could never help themselves afterwards, and many have died in prison. And I still have sixty-four, and all shall be freed, as long as you will tell me your name, provided you are not Sir Lancelot."

"Now I see well," said Sir Lancelot, "that if I were one kind of man I might have peace, and if I were another, there would be war to the death between us. And now, sir knight, at your request I want you to know for certain that I am Lancelot du Lake, King Ban's son of Benwick, and a true knight of the Round Table. And now I defy you, and do your worst."

"Ah," said Turquine, "Lancelot, you are the most welcome to me of any knight there ever was, for we shall never part until one of us is dead."

Then they crashed together like two wild bulls, rushing and lashing with their shields and swords, so that sometimes they both fell flat on their faces. So they fought on for two hours and more, and would never rest, and Sir Turquine gave Sir Lancelot many wounds, so that all the ground where they fought was spattered with blood.

Chapter 9: How Sir Turquine was slain, and how Sir Lancelot told Sir Gaheris to free all the prisoners

Then at last Sir Turquine grew faint, and gave back somewhat, and held his shield low out of weariness. Sir Lancelot saw that, and leapt on him fiercely and got him by the visor of his helmet, and pulled him down on his knees, and at once he tore off his helmet, and struck his neck in two. And when Sir Lancelot had done this, he went to the damsel and said, "Damsel, I am ready to go with you wherever you want me, but I have no horse."

"Fair sir," said she, "take this wounded knight's horse, and send him into this manor, and command him to free all the prisoners."

So Sir Lancelot went to Gaheris, and begged him not to take it badly if he borrowed his horse.

"No, fair lord," said Gaheris, "I want you to take my horse to do with as you please, for you have saved both me and my horse. And this day I say you are the best knight in the world, for today, before my eyes, you have killed the mightiest man and the best knight, except you, that I ever saw. And, fair sir," said Gaheris, "I beg you, tell me your name."

"Sir, my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake, who ought by rights to help you for King Arthur's sake, and above all for the sake of my lord Sir Gawain, your own dear brother. And when you go into that manor over there, I am sure you will find many knights of the Round Table there, for I have seen many of their shields that I know on that tree over there. There is Kay's shield, and Sir Brandel's shield, and Sir Marhaus' shield, and Sir Galind's shield, and Sir Brian de Listnois' shield, and Sir Aliduke's shield, with many more that I can't call to mind now, and also my two brothers' shields, Sir Ector de Maris and Sir Lionel. So I beg you, greet them all from me, and say that I tell them to take whatever goods they find there, and that by all means my brothers are to go to the court and wait for me there until I come; for I mean to be there by the feast of Pentecost. For at this time I must ride with this damsel, to keep my promise."

And so he left Gaheris, and Gaheris went into the manor, and there he found a yeoman porter keeping many keys there. At once Sir Gaheris threw the porter to the ground and took the keys from him, and quickly he opened the prison door, and there he let out all the prisoners, and every man loosed the others from their bonds. And when they saw Sir Gaheris, they all thanked him, for they thought, since he was wounded, that it was he who had done it.

"Not so," said Gaheris. "It was Lancelot who killed him, honourably, with his own hands. I saw it with my own eyes. And he sends you all his greetings, and begs you to hurry to the court; and as for Sir Lionel and Ector de Maris, he begs you to wait for him at the court."

"That we will not do," say his brothers. "We will find him, if we live."

"So will I," said Sir Kay. "I will find him before I come to the court, as I am a true knight."

Then all those knights looked for the house where the armour was, and then they armed themselves, and every knight found his own horse, and everything that belonged to him. And when this was done, a forester came with four horses loaded with fat venison.

At once Sir Kay said, "Here is good food for us for one meal, for we haven't had a good meal for many a day."

And so that venison was roasted, baked and boiled. And so after supper some stayed there all night, but Sir Lionel and Ector de Maris and Sir Kay rode after Sir Lancelot, to find him if they could.

Chapter 10: How Sir Lancelot rode with a damsel and slew a knight who preyed on all ladies, and also a low-born man who guarded a bridge

Now we turn to Sir Lancelot, who rode with the damsel along a fine highway.

"Sir," said the damsel, "along this road there haunts a knight who preys on all ladies and gentlewomen, and at the very least he robs them or lies with them."

"What?" said Sir Lancelot. "Is he a thief and a knight and a ravisher of women? He brings shame on the order of knighthood, and goes against his oath; it is a pity that he is alive. But, fair damsel, you ride on ahead by yourself, and I will keep myself under cover, and if he troubles you or harms you I will come to your rescue and teach him to behave like a knight."

So the maiden rode on along the road at a soft ambling pace, and after a while that knight came out of the wood on horseback, with his page beside him, and there he pulled the damsel from her horse, and then she cried out. With that Lancelot came as fast as he could until he reached that knight, saying, "You false knight, you traitor to knighthood, who taught you to prey on ladies and gentlewomen?"

When the knight saw Sir Lancelot rebuking him like this he did not answer, but drew his sword and rode at Sir Lancelot. And Sir Lancelot threw his spear away from him, and drew out his sword, and struck him such a blow on the helmet that he split his head and neck down to the throat.

"Now you have the payment you have long deserved!"

"That is true," said the damsel. "For just as Sir Turquine lay in wait to destroy knights, so this knight lay in wait to destroy and harm ladies, damsels and gentlewomen, and his name was Sir Peris de Forest Savage."

"Now, damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "do you want any more service from me?"

"No, sir," she said, "not at this time. But may almighty Jesus keep you wherever you ride or walk, for you are the most courteous knight, and the gentlest to all ladies and gentlewomen, of any now alive. But one thing, sir knight, I think you lack, you who are a knight without a wife: that you will not love some maiden or gentlewoman. For I never heard it said that you loved anyone at all, of any rank, and that is a great pity. But it is rumoured that you love Queen Guinevere, and that she has arranged by enchantment that you shall never love anyone but her, and that no other damsel or lady shall ever make you glad; and for that reason many in this land, of high rank and low, grieve greatly."

"Fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "I cannot stop people saying whatever they please about me. But as for being a married man, I do not intend it; for then I would have to lie with her, and give up arms and tournaments, battles and adventures. And as for taking my pleasure with lovers, that I refuse above all for fear of God. For knights who are adulterous or lecherous will not be lucky or fortunate in war: either they will be overcome by a lesser knight than themselves, or else, through ill luck and their own wickedness, they will kill better men than themselves. And so whoever keeps lovers will be unlucky, and everything around them is unlucky."

And so Sir Lancelot and she parted. And then he rode in a deep forest for two days and more, and had poor lodging. So on the third day he rode over a long bridge, and there a very ugly peasant leapt out at him suddenly, and struck his horse on the nose so that it turned around, and asked him why he was riding over that bridge without his permission.

"Why shouldn't I ride this way?" said Sir Lancelot. "I cannot ride round it."

"You don't get to choose," said the peasant, and swung at him with a great club shod with iron.

Then Sir Lancelot drew his sword and beat the blow aside, and split his head down to the chest. At the end of the bridge was a fine village, and all the people, men and women, cried out at Sir Lancelot, and said, "You never did a worse deed for yourself, for you have killed the chief porter of our castle."

Sir Lancelot let them say what they liked, and he went straight into the castle. And when he came into the castle he dismounted, and tied his horse to a ring on the wall, and there he saw a fine green courtyard, and he made his way there, for he thought it was a good place to fight in. So he looked about, and saw many people in doorways and windows, who said, "Fair knight, you are out of luck."

Chapter 11: How Sir Lancelot slew two giants, and set a castle free

At that very moment two great giants came at him, well armed all except their heads, with two horrible clubs in their hands. Sir Lancelot put his shield in front of him and turned aside the blow of one giant, and with his sword he split his head in two. When his fellow saw that, he ran away as if he were mad, for fear of those horrible strokes, and Lancelot went after him with all his might, and struck him on the shoulder, and split him down to the navel. Then Sir Lancelot went into the hall, and there came before him sixty ladies and damsels, and they all knelt to him, and thanked God and him for their deliverance.

"For, sir," they said, "most of us have been their prisoners here these seven years, and we have worked all kinds of silk work for our food, and we are all gentlewomen of high birth. And blessed be the time, knight, that ever you were born, for you have done the most honourable deed that ever a knight did in this world, and we will bear witness to that. And we all beg you to tell us your name, so that we can tell our friends who freed us from prison."

"Fair damsels," he said, "my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"Ah, sir," they all said, "you may well be he, for we judged that no knight but you could ever get the better of these two giants. For many good knights have tried it, and ended here, and many times we have wished for you, and these two giants feared no knight but you."

"Now you may tell your friends," said Sir Lancelot, "how you were freed and who freed you, and greet them all from me. And if I come into any of your lands, give me such welcome as you have cause to. And whatever treasure there is in this castle I give it to you as a reward for your suffering. And as for the lord who owns this castle, I would have him receive it, as is right."

"Fair sir," they said, "the name of this castle is Tintagil, and a duke once owned it who had married the fair Igraine, and after him Uther Pendragon married her, and fathered Arthur on her."

"Well," said Sir Lancelot, "I understand who this castle belongs to." And so he left them, and commended them to God.

And then he mounted his horse, and rode into many strange and wild countries, and through many rivers and valleys, and he was badly lodged. And at last, as luck would have it, towards nightfall he came to a fine house with a courtyard, and there he found an old gentlewoman who lodged him gladly, and there he was well looked after, he and his horse. And when it was time, his host brought him to a fine room in the garret, over the gate, to his bed. There Sir Lancelot took off his armour, and set it beside him, and went to bed, and he fell asleep at once. So soon afterwards someone came on horseback and knocked at the gate in great haste. And when Sir Lancelot heard this, he got up and looked out of the window, and saw by the moonlight three knights come riding after that one man, and all three laid into him at once with swords, and that one knight turned on them again like a true knight, and defended himself.

"Truly," said Sir Lancelot, "I will help that one knight, for it would be a shame for me to watch three knights on one, and if he is killed I am a partner in his death."

And with that he took his armour, and went out of the window, down a sheet, to the four knights. And then Sir Lancelot said loudly, "Turn to me, knights, and leave off fighting that knight."

And then all three of them left Sir Kay, and turned on Sir Lancelot, and there a great battle began, for all three dismounted, and struck many great blows at Sir Lancelot, and attacked him on every side. Then Sir Kay got ready to help Sir Lancelot.

"No, sir," he said, "I want none of your help. So if you want my help, leave me alone with them."

Sir Kay, to please the knight, let him have his way, and so stood aside. And then, within six strokes, Sir Lancelot had struck them to the ground.

And then all three of them cried, "Sir knight, we yield to you, as a man of might without equal."

"As to that," said Sir Lancelot, "I will not accept your surrender to me. But if you will yield to Sir Kay the Seneschal, on that condition I will spare your lives, and not otherwise."

"Fair knight," they said, "we would be loath to do that. For as for Sir Kay, we chased him here, and would have overcome him if it had not been for you; so to yield to him would make no sense."

"Well, as to that," said Lancelot, "think it over carefully, for you may choose whether you will die or live. For if you yield, it shall be to Sir Kay."

"Fair knight," they said then, "to save our lives we will do as you command us."

"Then," said Sir Lancelot, "on Whitsunday next you shall go to the court of King Arthur, and there you shall yield to Queen Guinevere, and put all three of you at her grace and mercy, and say that Sir Kay sent you there to be her prisoners."

"Sir," they said, "it shall be done, on our lives, if we are still living." And there every knight swore it upon his sword.

And so Sir Lancelot let them go. And then Sir Lancelot knocked at the gate with the pommel of his sword, and with that his host came, and Sir Kay and he went in.

"Sir," said his host, "I thought you were in your bed."

"So I was," said Sir Lancelot, "but I got up and leapt out of my window to help an old comrade of mine."

And so when they came near the light, Sir Kay saw clearly that it was Sir Lancelot, and with that he knelt down and thanked him for all his kindness, for he had saved him from death twice.

"Sir," he said, "I have done nothing but what I ought to do, and you are welcome, and here you shall rest and take your ease."

So when Sir Kay had taken off his armour, he asked for food; so food was fetched for him, and he ate heartily. And when he had had supper they went to bed, and were lodged together in one bed. In the morning Sir Lancelot got up early, and left Sir Kay sleeping, and Sir Lancelot took Sir Kay's armour and his shield, and armed himself, and so he went to the stable, and took his horse, and took his leave of his host, and so he left. Then soon afterwards Sir Kay got up and missed Sir Lancelot. And then he saw that he had his armour and his horse.

"Now, on my faith, I know well that he will trouble some of King Arthur's court; for knights will be bold with him, and think that it is me, and that will deceive them. And because of his armour and shield I am sure I shall ride in peace."

And then soon afterwards Sir Kay left, and thanked his host.

Chapter 12: How Sir Lancelot rode disguised in Sir Kay's armour, and how he struck down a knight

Now we turn to Sir Lancelot, who had ridden a long way through a great forest, and at last he came into low country, full of fine rivers and meadows. And ahead of him he saw a long bridge, and three tents stood on it, of silks of various kinds and colours. And outside the tents hung three white shields on the shafts of spears, and great long spears stood upright by the tents, and at the door of every tent stood three lively squires. And so Sir Lancelot passed by them and said not a word. When he had passed, the three knights said to each other that it was the proud Kay.

"He thinks no knight is as good as he is, and the opposite is often proved."

"On my faith," said one of the knights (his name was Sir Gaunter), "I will ride after him and test him for all his pride, and you can watch how I get on."

So this knight, Sir Gaunter, armed himself, and hung his shield on his shoulder, and mounted a great horse, and took his spear in his hand, and galloped after Sir Lancelot. And when he came near him, he cried, "Stop, you proud knight Sir Kay, for you shall not get away free."

So Sir Lancelot turned, and each of them set his spear in rest, and they came together with all their might. And Sir Gaunter's spear broke, but Sir Lancelot struck him down, horse and man. And when Sir Gaunter was on the ground his brothers said to each other, "That knight is not Sir Kay, for he is bigger than he is."

"I'll bet my head," said Sir Gilmere, "that knight has killed Sir Kay and taken his horse and his armour."

"Whether it is so or not," said Sir Raynold, the third brother, "let us mount our horses now and rescue our brother Sir Gaunter, on pain of death. We shall all have work enough to match that knight, for by the look of him I think it is Sir Lancelot, or Sir Tristram, or Sir Pelleas, the good knight."

Then at once they took their horses and overtook Sir Lancelot. And Sir Gilmere put out his spear and ran at Sir Lancelot, and Sir Lancelot struck him down so that he lay in a faint.

"Sir knight," said Sir Raynold, "you are a strong man, and as I suppose you have killed my two brothers, and for that my heart rises hard against you. And if I could do it with honour I would not fight you, but I must take my part as they did. And so, knight," he said, "defend yourself."

And so they crashed together with all their might, and both their spears shattered to pieces. And then they drew their swords and laid into each other fiercely. Then at once Sir Gaunter got up, and came to his brother Sir Gilmere, and said to him, "Get up, and let us help our brother Sir Raynold, who is fighting that good knight over there with marvellous skill."

With that they leapt on their horses and charged at Sir Lancelot. And when he saw them coming he struck a hard blow at Sir Raynold, so that he fell off his horse to the ground, and then he struck at the other two brothers, and with two strokes he struck them down to the ground. With that Sir Raynold began to get up, with his head all bloody, and came straight at Sir Lancelot.

"Now let it be," said Sir Lancelot. "I was not far from you when you were made a knight, Sir Raynold, and I also know you are a good knight, and I would be loath to kill you."

"Many thanks," said Sir Raynold, "for your kindness. And I dare say, for me and my brothers, that we would not be loath to yield to you, provided we knew your name, for we know well you are not Sir Kay."

"As for that, let it be as it may, for you shall yield yourselves to Dame Guinevere. And see that you are with her on Whitsunday, and yield to her as prisoners, and say that Sir Kay sent you to her."

Then they swore it would be done, and so Sir Lancelot went on his way, and each of the brothers helped the others as well as he could.

Chapter 13: How Sir Lancelot jousted against four knights of the Round Table and unhorsed them

So Sir Lancelot rode into a deep forest, and there in a little valley he saw four knights waiting on their horses under an oak, and they were of Arthur's court: one was Sir Sagramour le Desirous, and Ector de Maris, and Sir Gawain, and Sir Uwain. As soon as these four knights saw Sir Lancelot, they thought from his arms that it was Sir Kay.

"Now, on my faith," said Sir Sagramour, "I will test Sir Kay's strength." And he took his spear in his hand, and came towards Sir Lancelot.

Sir Lancelot saw him coming and knew him well, and set his spear in rest against him, and struck Sir Sagramour so hard that horse and man both fell to the ground.

"Look, my fellows," said he, "you can see what a blow he has there; that knight is much bigger than Sir Kay ever was. Now you shall see what I can do to him."

So Sir Ector took his spear in his hand and galloped towards Sir Lancelot, and Sir Lancelot struck him through the shield and shoulder, so that man and horse went to the ground, and still his spear held.

"On my faith," said Sir Uwain, "that is a strong knight, and I am sure he has killed Sir Kay; and I can see by his great strength that he will be hard to match."

And with that Sir Uwain took his spear in his hand and rode towards Sir Lancelot. And Sir Lancelot knew him well, and so he met him on the open ground, and gave him such a blow that he was stunned, so that for a long while he did not know where he was.

"Now I see clearly," said Sir Gawain, "that I must take on that knight."

Then he set his shield and took a good spear in his hand, and Sir Lancelot knew him well. And then they let their horses run with all their might, and each knight struck the other in the middle of the shield. But Sir Gawain's spear burst apart, and Sir Lancelot came down on him so hard that his horse went over upside down. And Sir Gawain had great trouble getting clear of his horse. And so Sir Lancelot rode on at a walk and smiled, and said, "God give joy to the man who made this spear, for there never came a better one into my hand."

Then the four knights went to each other and comforted each other.

"What do you make of this deed?" said Sir Gawain. "One spear has felled all four of us."

"We commend him to the devil," they all said, "for he is a man of great might."

"You may well say that he is a man of might," said Sir Gawain, "for I'll bet my head it is Sir Lancelot; I know him by his riding. Let him go," said Sir Gawain, "for when we come to the court then we shall know."

And then they had great trouble catching their horses again.

Chapter 14: How Sir Lancelot followed a hound into a castle, where he found a dead knight, and how afterwards a damsel asked him to heal her brother

Now we leave that and speak of Sir Lancelot, who rode a long while in a deep forest, where he saw a black hound, casting about as if she were on the track of a wounded deer. And with that he rode after the hound, and he saw a large trail of blood lying on the ground. And then Sir Lancelot rode after her. And all the while the hound looked behind her, and so she went through a great marsh, and all the while Sir Lancelot followed. And then he caught sight of an old manor house, and the hound ran there, and so over the bridge. So Sir Lancelot rode over that bridge, which was old and weak; and when he came into the middle of a great hall, there he saw a dead knight lying, who was a handsome man, and the hound was licking his wounds. And with that a lady came out weeping and wringing her hands, and then she said, "O knight, you have brought me too much sorrow."

"Why do you say so?" said Sir Lancelot. "I never did this knight any harm, for this hound brought me here by the trail of blood. And so, fair lady, do not be displeased with me, for I am deeply grieved at your grief."
