"Truly, sir," she said, "I believe it is not you who killed my husband, for the man who did that deed is badly wounded, and he is never likely to recover, I can promise him that."

"What was your husband's name?" said Sir Lancelot.

"Sir," she said, "his name was Sir Gilbert the Bastard, one of the best knights in the world, and I do not know the name of the man who killed him."

"Now God send you better comfort," said Sir Lancelot.

And so he left and went into the forest again, and there he met a damsel who knew him well, and she said aloud, "Well met, my lord! And now I beg you, on your knighthood, help my brother, who is badly wounded and never stops bleeding. For today he fought with Sir Gilbert the Bastard and killed him in fair fight, and there my brother was badly wounded. And there is a lady, a sorceress, who lives in a castle near here, and today she told me my brother's wounds would never be healed until I could find a knight who would go into the Chapel Perilous. And there he would find a sword, and a bloody cloth that the wounded knight was wrapped in, and a piece of that cloth and the sword would heal my brother's wounds, provided his wounds were touched with the sword and the cloth."

"This is a marvellous thing," said Sir Lancelot, "but what is your brother's name?"

"Sir," she said, "his name is Sir Meliot de Logres."

"I am sorry to hear it," said Sir Lancelot, "for he is a fellow of the Round Table, and I will do all in my power to help him."

"Then, sir," she said, "follow this highway straight on, and it will bring you to the Chapel Perilous. And I will wait here until God sends you back here again. And unless you succeed, I know no knight alive who can achieve that adventure."

Chapter 15: How Sir Lancelot came into the Chapel Perilous and took from a dead body there a piece of its cloth and a sword

Right away Sir Lancelot left, and when he came to the Chapel Perilous he dismounted, and tied his horse to a little gate. And as soon as he was inside the churchyard he saw on the front of the chapel many fine rich shields turned upside down, and many of those shields Sir Lancelot had seen knights carry before. With that he saw standing near him some thirty great knights, taller by a yard than any man he had ever seen, and all of them grinned and gnashed their teeth at Sir Lancelot. And when he saw their faces he was badly afraid, and so he put his shield in front of him, and took his sword in his hand, ready for battle. And they were all armed in black armour, ready, with their shields and their swords drawn. And when Sir Lancelot went to pass through them, they scattered on every side of him, and gave him the way. And with that he grew bold, and went into the chapel, and then he saw no light but a dim lamp burning, and then he caught sight of a corpse covered with a silk cloth. Then Sir Lancelot stooped down, and cut away a piece of that cloth, and then the ground under him shook as if the earth had quaked a little, and at that he was afraid. And then he saw a fine sword lying by the dead knight, and he took it in his hand and hurried out of the chapel.

As soon as he was in the chapel yard all the knights spoke to him in a grim voice, and said, "Knight, Sir Lancelot, put that sword down or else you will die."

"Whether I live or die," said Sir Lancelot, "you won't get it back with big words. So fight for it, if you want it."

Then right away he passed through them, and beyond the chapel yard a fair damsel met him, and said, "Sir Lancelot, leave that sword behind you, or you will die for it."

"I will not leave it," said Sir Lancelot, "for any pleading."

"No," she said. "If you left that sword, you would never see Queen Guinevere again."

"Then I would be a fool if I left this sword," said Lancelot.

"Now, noble knight," said the damsel, "I beg you to kiss me, just once."

"No," said Sir Lancelot, "God forbid."

"Well, sir," she said, "if you had kissed me, the days of your life would have been over. But now, alas," she said, "I have lost all my labour, for I made this chapel for your sake, and for Sir Gawain's. And once I had Sir Gawain in here, and at that time he fought with that knight who lies dead there in the chapel, Sir Gilbert the Bastard; and at that time he struck the left hand off Sir Gilbert the Bastard. And, Sir Lancelot, now I tell you, I have loved you these seven years, but no woman may have your love except Queen Guinevere. But since I could not have the joy of your body alive, I had no other joy left in this world but to have your body dead. Then I would have embalmed it and tended it, and so kept it all the days of my life, and every day I would have embraced you and kissed you, in spite of Queen Guinevere."

"You speak plainly," said Sir Lancelot. "Jesus keep me from your cunning arts."

And with that he took his horse and so left her. And as the book says, when Sir Lancelot had gone she took such grief that she died within a fortnight, and her name was Hellawes the sorceress, Lady of the Castle Nigramous.

At once Sir Lancelot met the damsel, Sir Meliot's sister. And when she saw him she clapped her hands, and wept for joy. And then they rode to a castle near by where Sir Meliot lay. And as soon as Sir Lancelot saw him he knew him, but he was exceedingly pale, the colour of earth, from bleeding. When Sir Meliot saw Sir Lancelot he went down on his knees and cried aloud, "O lord Sir Lancelot, help me!"

At once Sir Lancelot leapt to him and touched his wounds with Sir Gilbert's sword. And then he wiped his wounds with a piece of the bloody cloth that Sir Gilbert was wrapped in, and at once he was a more whole man than he had ever been in his life. And then there was great joy between them, and they gave Sir Lancelot all the welcome they could. And so in the morning Sir Lancelot took his leave, and told Sir Meliot to hurry to the court of my lord Arthur, "for it is getting near the Feast of Pentecost, and there, by the grace of God, you shall find me."

And with that they parted.

Chapter 16: How Sir Lancelot, at a lady's request, recovered a falcon, and how he was tricked by it

And so Sir Lancelot rode through many strange countries, over marshes and valleys, until by chance he came to a fine castle. And as he passed beyond the castle he thought he heard two bells ring. And then he caught sight of a falcon flying over his head towards a high elm, with long leashes about her feet. And as she flew to the elm to take her perch, the leashes wound themselves around a bough. And when she tried to take flight she hung fast by the legs. And Sir Lancelot saw how she hung, and looked at the beautiful peregrine falcon, and he was sorry for her.

Meanwhile a lady came out of the castle and cried aloud, "O Lancelot, Lancelot, as you are the flower of all knights, help me get my hawk back! For if my hawk is lost my lord will destroy me. For I had charge of the hawk and she slipped away from me, and if my lord my husband learns of it, he is so hot-tempered that he will kill me."

"What is your lord's name?" said Sir Lancelot.

"Sir," she said, "his name is Sir Phelot, a knight who serves the King of North Wales."

"Well, fair lady, since you know my name, and ask me on my knighthood to help you, I will do what I can to get your hawk. And yet God knows I am a poor climber, and the tree is exceedingly high, and there are few boughs to help me."

And with that Sir Lancelot dismounted, and tied his horse to the same tree, and asked the lady to take off his armour. And so when his armour was off, he took off all his clothes down to his shirt and breeches, and with might and main he climbed up to the falcon, and tied the leashes to a big rotten branch, and threw the hawk down, and the branch with her.

At once the lady caught the hawk in her hand. And with that Sir Phelot, her husband, suddenly came out of the trees, fully armed and with his naked sword in his hand, and said, "Well, knight Lancelot, now I have found you just as I wanted you." And he stood at the trunk of the tree to kill him.

"Ah, lady," said Sir Lancelot, "why have you betrayed me?"

"She has done only what I ordered her to," said Sir Phelot, "and so there's no help for it: your hour has come, and you must die."

"That would be a shame to you," said Sir Lancelot, "you, an armed knight, killing a naked man by treachery."

"You'll get no other mercy," said Sir Phelot, "so save yourself if you can."

"Truly," said Sir Lancelot, "this will be your shame. But since you will do nothing else, take my armour with you, and hang my sword on a bough where I can get it, and then do your best to kill me if you can."

"No, no," said Sir Phelot, "for I know you better than you think. So you get no weapon, if I can keep you from it."

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "that ever a knight should die without a weapon!"

And with that he looked above him and below him, and over his head he saw a big leafless bough, and with that he broke it off at the trunk. And then he came lower and watched where his own horse stood, and suddenly he leapt down on the far side of the horse, away from the knight. And then Sir Phelot swung at him fiercely, meaning to kill him. But Sir Lancelot turned the stroke aside with the bough, and with it he struck him on the side of the head, so that he fell down to the ground in a faint. So then Sir Lancelot took his sword out of his hand, and struck his head from his body.

Then the lady cried, "Alas! Why have you killed my husband?"

"I am not the cause of it," said Sir Lancelot, "for you would have killed me by treachery and falsehood, and now it has fallen on you both."

And then she fainted as if she would die. And with that Sir Lancelot got all his armour together as well as he could, and put it on, for fear more men would come, since he was afraid because the knight's castle was so near. And so, as soon as he could, he took his horse and left, and thanked God that he had come safely through that adventure.

Chapter 17: How Sir Lancelot overtook a knight who was chasing his wife to kill her, and what he said to him

So Sir Lancelot rode many wild ways, through borderlands and many wild ways. And as he rode in a valley he saw a knight chasing a lady with a naked sword, to kill her. And by chance, just as this knight was about to kill this lady, she called on Sir Lancelot and begged him to rescue her. When Sir Lancelot saw that wickedness, he took his horse and rode between them, saying, "Knight, shame on you, why would you kill this lady? You bring shame on yourself and on all knights."

"What business have you between me and my wife?" said the knight. "I'll kill her, whether you like it or not."

"That you shall not," said Sir Lancelot, "for sooner than that, we two will fight."

"Sir Lancelot," said the knight, "you are not doing right, for this lady has betrayed me."

"It is not so," said the lady. "Truly he wrongs me. Because I love and cherish my first cousin, he is jealous of him and me; and as I shall answer to God, there was never any sin between us. But, sir," said the lady, "as you are called the most honourable knight in the world, I beg you by true knighthood, keep me and save me. For whatever you say, he will kill me, for he has no mercy."

"Have no fear," said Lancelot. "It shall not be in his power."

"Sir," said the knight, "in your sight I will be ruled as you wish."

And so Sir Lancelot rode on one side and she on the other. He had only ridden a little while when the knight told Sir Lancelot to turn and look behind him, and said, "Sir, there are men-at-arms riding after us over there."

And so Sir Lancelot turned, suspecting no treachery, and with that the knight was on the same side as the lady, and suddenly he struck off his lady's head.

And when Sir Lancelot saw what he had done, he cried out and called him, "Traitor, you have shamed me for ever!"

And at once Sir Lancelot dismounted from his horse, and pulled out his sword to kill him. And with that the knight threw himself flat on the ground, and gripped Sir Lancelot by the thighs, and begged for mercy.

"Shame on you," said Sir Lancelot. "You shameful knight, you can have no mercy. So get up and fight me."

"No," said the knight, "I will never get up until you grant me mercy."

"Now I'll make you a fair offer," said Lancelot. "I will take off my armour down to my shirt, and I will have nothing on me but my shirt, and my sword in my hand. And if you can kill me, you go free for ever."

"No, sir," said Pedivere, "that I will never do."

"Well," said Sir Lancelot, "take this lady and the head, and carry it on you; and here you shall swear on my sword to carry it always on your back, and never to rest until you come to Queen Guinevere."

"Sir," he said, "I will do that, on my life."

"Now," said Lancelot, "tell me, what is your name?"

"Sir, my name is Pedivere."

"In a shameful hour you were born," said Lancelot.

So Pedivere left with the dead lady and the head, and found the queen with King Arthur at Winchester, and there he told the whole truth.

"Sir knight," said the queen, "this is a horrible deed and a shameful one, and a great reproach to Sir Lancelot; and yet his honour is known in many different lands. But this I will give you as penance; make whatever shift you can: you shall carry this lady with you on horseback to the Pope of Rome, and receive your penance from him for your foul deeds. And you shall never rest two nights in the same place; and if you go to any bed, the dead body shall lie with you."

There he swore this oath, and so left. And as the French book tells it, when he came to Rome the Pope told him to go back to Queen Guinevere, and his lady was buried in Rome by the Pope's command. And after this Sir Pedivere turned to great goodness, and was a holy man and a hermit.

Chapter 18: How Sir Lancelot came to King Arthur's court, and how all his noble feats and deeds were recounted there

Now we turn to Sir Lancelot du Lake, who came home two days before the Feast of Pentecost; and the king and all the court were exceedingly glad of his coming. And when Sir Gawain, Sir Uwain, Sir Sagramour and Sir Ector de Maris saw Sir Lancelot in Kay's armour, then they knew for certain it was he who had struck them all down with one spear. Then there was laughing and smiling among them. And every now and then all the knights whom Sir Turquine had held prisoner came home, and they all honoured Sir Lancelot and praised him.

When Sir Gaheris heard them speak, he said, "I saw the whole battle from beginning to end." And there he told King Arthur exactly how it had gone, and how Sir Turquine was the strongest knight he had ever seen except Sir Lancelot; and there were many knights to bear him witness, nearly sixty. Then Sir Kay told the king how Sir Lancelot had rescued him when he would have been killed, "and how he made the knights yield to me, and not to him." And there they were, all three, and bore witness to it.

"And by Jesus," said Sir Kay, "because Sir Lancelot took my armour and left me his, I rode in perfect peace, and no man would fight me."

Then at once the three knights who had fought with Sir Lancelot at the long bridge came in. And there they yielded themselves to Sir Kay, and Sir Kay refused them, and said he had never fought with them.

"But I will set your hearts at ease," said Sir Kay. "That is Sir Lancelot over there, who overcame you."

When they knew that, they were glad. And then Sir Meliot de Logres came home, and told the king how Sir Lancelot had saved him from death. And all his deeds were made known: how four queens, sorceresses, had held him in prison, and how he was freed by King Bagdemagus's daughter. Also all the great deeds of arms that Sir Lancelot did between the two kings were told, that is to say the King of North Wales and King Bagdemagus. Sir Gahalantine told the whole truth of it, and Sir Mador de la Porte and Sir Mordred, for they were at that same tournament. Then the lady came in who had known Sir Lancelot when he wounded Sir Belleus at the tent. And there, at Sir Lancelot's request, Sir Belleus was made a knight of the Round Table. And so at that time Sir Lancelot had the greatest name of any knight in the world, and he was the most honoured by high and low.

Here ends the noble tale of Sir Lancelot du Lake, which is the sixth book.

Here follows the tale of Sir Gareth of Orkney, who was called Beaumains by Sir Kay, and is the seventh book.

Book Seven: Sir Gareth, Whom Sir Kay Called Beaumains

Chapter 1: How Beaumains came to King Arthur's court and asked three favours of King Arthur

When Arthur held his Round Table at its fullest, it happened that he commanded the high feast of Pentecost to be held at a city and a castle which in those days was called Kynke Kenadonne, on the sands that bordered on Wales. Now the king always had a custom that at the feast of Pentecost especially, above all the other feasts in the year, he would not go to his meal that day until he had heard of or seen some great marvel. And because of that custom all kinds of strange adventures came before Arthur at that feast more than at any other. And so Sir Gawain, a little before noon on the day of Pentecost, saw from a window three men on horseback, and a dwarf on foot. And the three men dismounted, and the dwarf held their horses, and one of the three men was taller than the other two by a foot and a half. Then Sir Gawain went to the king and said, "Sir, go to your meal, for strange adventures are close at hand."

So Arthur went to his meal with many other kings. And all the knights of the Round Table were there, except only those who were prisoners or had been killed in some encounter. For at the high feast they were always to make up the whole number of a hundred and fifty, for then the Round Table was complete.

Just then there came into the hall two men, well equipped and richly dressed, and on their shoulders there leaned the handsomest and the finest young man they had ever seen. He was big and tall, and broad in the shoulders, and fine of face, and he had the fairest and the largest hands that anyone ever saw; but he behaved as though he could not walk or hold himself up unless he leaned on their shoulders. As soon as Arthur saw him there was silence, and room was made, and so they went with him up to the high dais without saying a word. Then this tall young man drew himself back, and easily stood up straight, and said, "King Arthur, God bless you and all your fair fellowship, and especially the fellowship of the Round Table. And this is why I have come here: to beg you and ask you to give me three gifts. And they shall not be unreasonably asked, but such as you may grant me honourably and with dignity, and at no great hurt or loss to you. The first gift I will ask now, and the other two I will ask a year from today, wherever you hold your high feast."

"Now ask," said Arthur, "and you shall have what you ask."

"Now, sir, this is my request for this feast: that you will give me food and drink enough for this twelvemonth, and on that day I will ask my other two gifts."

"My fair son," said Arthur, "ask for something better, I advise you, for this is only a simple request. For my heart goes out to you greatly, and tells me you come of honourable men; and my judgement is badly wrong if you do not prove a man of very great honour."

"Sir," he said, "be that as it may, I have asked what I will ask."

"Well," said the king, "you shall have food and drink enough. I never refused that to anyone, neither my friend nor my foe. But what is your name? I would like to know."

"I cannot tell you," he said.

"That is a marvel," said the king, "that you do not know your own name, and you the handsomest young man I ever saw."

Then the king handed him over to Sir Kay the steward, and ordered him to give him every kind of food and drink of the best, and to see that he had every kind of provision, as though he were a lord's son.

"There will be little need," said Sir Kay, "to go to such expense on him. For I dare swear he is a peasant born, and will never amount to anything; for if he had come of gentlefolk he would have asked you for a horse and armour, but he asks for what suits what he is. And since he has no name, I will give him one, and it shall be Beaumains, that is to say Fair-hands. And I will take him into the kitchen, and there he shall have fat broth every day, so that by the end of the twelvemonth he will be as fat as a pig fattened for pork."

With that the two men left, and left him to Sir Kay, who scorned him and mocked him.

Chapter 2: How Sir Lancelot and Sir Gawain were angry because Sir Kay mocked Beaumains, and of a damsel who asked for a knight to fight for a lady

At this Sir Gawain was angry, and Sir Lancelot especially told Sir Kay to stop his mocking, "for I dare bet my head he will prove a man of great honour."

"Let it be," said Sir Kay. "It cannot be, by any reasoning, for he has asked for what suits what he is."

"Beware," said Sir Lancelot. "You gave the good knight Bruin le Noire, Sir Dinadan's brother, a name in the same way, and called him La Cote Male Taile, the Badly Cut Coat, and that turned to your annoyance afterwards."

"As for that," said Sir Kay, "this one will never prove anything of the kind. For Sir Bruin always wanted honour, and this one wants bread and drink and broth. On my life, he was brought up in some abbey, and however it was, they ran short of food and drink, and so he has come here for his keep."

And so Sir Kay told them to find him a place and sit him down to eat. So Beaumains went to the hall door, and sat down among the boys and lads, and there he ate steadily. And then after the meal Sir Lancelot told him to come to his room, and there he would have food and drink enough. And Sir Gawain did the same. But he refused them all; he would do nothing but what Sir Kay commanded him, whatever was offered. But as for Sir Gawain, he had reason to offer him lodging, food and drink, for that offer came from his blood, for he was closer kin to him than he knew. But what Sir Lancelot did was out of his great nobility and courtesy.

So he was put into the kitchen, and slept at night as the kitchen boys did. And so he endured all that twelvemonth, and never displeased man or child, but was always meek and mild. But whenever there was any jousting of knights, he would watch it if he could. And Sir Lancelot would always give him gold to spend, and clothes, and so would Sir Gawain. And wherever there were any contests of strength, he would be there, and no one could throw the bar or the stone within two yards of him. Then Sir Kay would say, "How do you like my kitchen boy?"

So time went on until the feast of Whitsun. And that year the king held it at Caerleon, in the most royal manner that could be, as he did every year. But the king would eat nothing on Whitsunday until he had heard of some adventure. Then a squire came to the king and said, "Sir, you may go to your meal, for here comes a damsel with some strange adventure."

Then the king was glad, and sat down. At that very moment a damsel came into the hall and greeted the king, and begged him for help.

"For whom?" said the king. "What is the adventure?"

"Sir," she said, "I serve a lady of great honour and renown, and she is besieged by a tyrant, so that she cannot get out of her castle. And because the noblest knights in the world are said to be here, I have come to you to beg you for help."

"What is your lady called, and where does she live, and who is she, and what is the name of the man who has besieged her?"

"Sir king," she said, "as for my lady's name, you shall not learn it from me at this time. But I tell you she is a lady of great honour and of great lands. And as for the tyrant who besieges her and lays waste her lands, he is called the Red Knight of the Red Launds."

"I don't know him," said the king.

"Sir," said Sir Gawain, "I know him well, for he is one of the most dangerous knights in the world. Men say he has the strength of seven men, and I once escaped from him with my life, and only barely."

"Fair damsel," said the king, "there are knights here who would do all in their power to rescue your lady. But because you will not tell her name, or where she lives, none of my knights who are here now shall go with you with my consent."

"Then I must say more," said the damsel.

Chapter 3: How Beaumains asked for the battle, and how it was granted him, and how he asked to be knighted by Sir Lancelot

At these words Beaumains came before the king, while the damsel was still there, and said, "Sir king, God thank you, I have been in your kitchen this twelvemonth, and have had my full keep, and now I will ask the two gifts that are still owing."

"Ask, and I will stand by it," said the king.

"Sir, these shall be my two gifts. First, that you will grant me this damsel's adventure, for it belongs to me."

"You shall have it," said the king. "I grant it to you."

"Then, sir, this is the other gift: that you will order Lancelot du Lake to make me a knight, for I will be made a knight by him and by no one else. And when I have gone, I beg you to let him ride after me, and make me a knight when I ask him."

"All this shall be done," said the king.

"Shame on you!" said the damsel. "Am I to have no one but your kitchen page?"

Then she was angry, and took her horse and left. And with that someone came to Beaumains and told him his horse and armour had come for him. And there was the dwarf, come with everything he needed, of the richest kind; and the whole court marvelled greatly where all that gear had come from. So when he was armed, there were only a few men as handsome as he was. And so he came into the hall and took his leave of King Arthur, and Sir Gawain, and Sir Lancelot, and begged Lancelot to hurry after him; and so he left, and rode after the damsel.

Chapter 4: How Beaumains set out, and how he won a spear and a shield from Sir Kay, and how he jousted with Sir Lancelot

But many went after him to see how well he was mounted, and his horse decked in cloth of gold; but he had neither shield nor spear. Then Sir Kay said openly in the hall, "I will ride after my kitchen boy, to find out whether he will recognise me as his better."

"Stay at home all the same," said Sir Lancelot and Sir Gawain.

So Sir Kay made himself ready and took his horse and his spear, and rode after him. And just as Beaumains caught up with the damsel, along came Sir Kay and said, "Beaumains! What, sir, don't you know me?"

Then he turned his horse, and saw it was Sir Kay, who had done him all the insults you have heard about before.

"Yes," said Beaumains, "I know you for an ill-bred knight of the court, and so beware of me."

With that Sir Kay put his spear in the rest and charged straight at him. And Beaumains came at him just as fast with his sword in his hand, and so he knocked aside his spear with his sword, and with a thrust ran him through the side, so that Sir Kay fell down as if he were dead. And Beaumains dismounted and took Sir Kay's shield and his spear, and leapt onto his own horse and rode on his way.

Sir Lancelot saw all of this, and so did the damsel. And then Beaumains told his dwarf to jump up on Sir Kay's horse, and so he did. By then Sir Lancelot had come up, and Beaumains offered to joust with him. And each of them made ready, and they came together so fiercely that each bore the other down to the earth, and they were badly bruised. Then Sir Lancelot got up and helped him clear of his horse. And then Beaumains threw his shield away from him, and offered to fight with Sir Lancelot on foot. And so they rushed together like boars, pressing and slashing and thrusting, for the space of an hour. And Sir Lancelot found him so strong that he marvelled at his strength, for he fought more like a giant than a knight, and his fighting was tireless and exceedingly dangerous. For Sir Lancelot had so much to do with him that he was afraid he would be shamed, and said, "Beaumains, don't fight so hard. Your quarrel and mine is not so great that we cannot leave off."

"Truly, that is true," said Beaumains. "But it does me good to feel your strength. And yet, my lord, I have not shown you my utmost."

Chapter 5: How Beaumains told Sir Lancelot his name, and how he was knighted by Sir Lancelot, and afterwards caught up with the damsel

"In God's name," said Sir Lancelot, "I promise you, on my life, I had all I could do to save myself from you without shame. And so you need have no fear of any knight on earth."

"Do you really think that I could hold my own for any length of time as a proven knight?" said Beaumains.

"Yes," said Lancelot. "Do as you have done, and I will vouch for you."

"Then I beg you," said Beaumains, "give me the order of knighthood."

"Then you must tell me your name," said Lancelot, "and what family you were born of."

"Sir, I will, as long as you will not give me away," said Beaumains.

"No," said Sir Lancelot, "and I promise you that on my life, until it is openly known."

"Then, sir," he said, "my name is Gareth, and I am brother to Sir Gawain, by father and by mother."

"Ah, sir," said Sir Lancelot, "I am all the gladder of you. For I always thought you must be of great blood, and that you had not come to the court for food or for drink."

And then Sir Lancelot gave him the order of knighthood. And then Sir Gareth begged him to leave and let him go on alone.

So Sir Lancelot left him and came to Sir Kay, and had him carried home on his shield; and so he was healed, though he barely escaped with his life. And everyone scorned Sir Kay, and Sir Gawain and Sir Lancelot especially said it was not his place to rebuke any young man, for he knew very little what birth he came of, or why he had come to this court. And so we leave Sir Kay and turn to Beaumains.

When he had caught up with the damsel, at once she said, "What are you doing here? You stink of the kitchen. Your clothes are filthy with the grease and tallow you get in King Arthur's kitchen. Do you think," she said, "that I think any better of you for that knight you killed back there? No, truly, for you killed him by a fluke, and like a coward. So turn back, you filthy kitchen page. I know you well, for Sir Kay named you Beaumains. What are you but a lout, and a turner of spits, and a washer of ladles?"

"Damsel," said Beaumains, "say what you like to me, I will not leave you, whatever you say. For I have undertaken to King Arthur to achieve your adventure, and so I will finish it to the end, or die in the attempt."

"Shame on you, kitchen boy! Will you finish my adventure? You'll soon meet someone you wouldn't look in the face once for all the broth you ever swallowed."

"I will try," said Beaumains.

So as they rode in the wood, there came a man running away as fast as ever he could.

"Where are you going?" said Beaumains.

"O lord," he said, "help me! For close by here, in a little valley, there are six thieves who have taken my lord and tied him up, and I am afraid they will kill him."

"Take me there," said Beaumains.

And so they rode together until they came to where the knight lay bound. And then he rode at them, and struck one dead, and then another, and at the third stroke he killed the third thief; and then the other three fled. And he rode after them and caught them up. And then those three thieves turned round and attacked Beaumains hard, but at last he killed them, and came back and untied the knight. And the knight thanked him, and begged him to ride with him to his castle, a little way off, and he would reward him honourably for his good deeds.

"Sir," said Beaumains, "I will have no reward. I was made a knight this day by the noble Sir Lancelot, and so I will have no reward but God's. And besides, I must follow this damsel."

And when he came near her she told him to ride further off from her, "for you stink of the kitchen. Do you think I am pleased with you? For all this deed you have done was just luck. But you will see a sight that will make you turn back, and quickly too."

Then the same knight who had been rescued from the thieves rode after the damsel, and begged her to lodge with him that night. And because it was nearly night, the damsel rode with him to his castle, and there they had a warm welcome. And at supper the knight sat Sir Beaumains facing the damsel.

"Shame, shame," she said. "Sir knight, it is discourteous of you to seat a kitchen page in front of me. It would suit him better to be sticking a pig than to sit in front of a damsel of high birth."

Then the knight was ashamed at her words, and took Beaumains up and sat him at a side table, and sat himself facing him. And so all that night they had good cheer and a pleasant rest.

Chapter 6: How Beaumains fought and slew two knights at a river crossing

And in the morning the damsel and he took their leave and thanked the knight, and so they left, and rode on their way until they came to a great forest. And there was a great river there, with only one crossing, and two knights were waiting on the far side to stop them crossing.

"What do you say?" said the damsel. "Will you take on those knights over there, or turn back?"

"No," said Sir Beaumains, "I will not turn back if there were six more of them."

And with that he rushed into the water, and in the middle of the water each of them broke his spear on the other right down to the hand. And then they drew their swords and struck fiercely at each other. And at last Sir Beaumains struck the other knight on the helmet so that his head was stunned, and with that he fell down into the water, and there he was drowned. And then Beaumains spurred his horse up onto the land, where the other knight fell upon him and broke his spear; and so they drew their swords and fought together a long time. At last Sir Beaumains split his helmet and his head down to the shoulders. And so he rode to the damsel and told her to ride on her way.

"Alas," she said, "that a kitchen page should ever have the luck to destroy two such brave knights! You think you have done bravely. That is not so. For as for the first knight, his horse stumbled, and he was drowned there in the water, and it was never by your strength or by your might. And as for the last knight, you came up behind him by bad luck, and by bad luck you killed him."

"Damsel," said Beaumains, "you may say what you like. But whoever I have to fight with, I trust to God to deal with him before he leaves. And so I care nothing for what you say, as long as I can win your lady."

"Shame, shame, you foul kitchen boy! You will see knights who will put a stop to your boasting."

"Fair damsel, speak kindly to me, and then I have no other care. For whatever knights they are, I don't care, and I am not afraid of them."

"Besides," she said, "I am saying it for your own good. You can still turn back with your honour. For if you follow me you are as good as dead, for I can see that all you do is done by chance, and not by the strength of your hands."

"Well, damsel, you may say what you like, but wherever you go I will follow you."

So this Beaumains rode with that lady until evensong time, and all the while she scolded him, and would not stop. And they came to a black clearing; and there was a black hawthorn, and on it hung a black banner, and on the other side there hung a black shield, and beside it stood a black spear, great and long, and a great black horse covered with silk, and a black stone close by.

Chapter 7: How Beaumains fought with the Knight of the Black Launds, and fought on until the knight fell down and died

There sat a knight all armed in black armour, and his name was the Knight of the Black Launds. Then the damsel, when she saw that knight, told Beaumains to flee down the valley, for the knight's horse was not saddled.

"Many thanks," said Beaumains, "for you always want me to be a coward."

With that the Black Knight, when she came near him, spoke and said, "Damsel, have you brought this knight of King Arthur's to be your champion?"

"No, fair knight," she said, "this is only a kitchen boy who was fed in King Arthur's kitchen out of charity."

"Why does he come," said the knight, "dressed like that? It is a shame that he keeps you company."

"Sir, I cannot get rid of him," she said, "for he rides with me against my will. I wish to God you would rid me of him, or kill him if you can, for he is an ill-starred lout, and he has done ill-starred things today. By mere luck I saw him kill two knights at the river crossing; and other deeds he did before that, quite marvellous, and all by luck."

"It amazes me," said the Black Knight, "that any man of honour will fight with him."

"They don't know him," said the damsel, "and because he rides with me, they think he is some man of honourable birth."

"That may be," said the Black Knight. "Even so, though you say he is no man of honour, he is a very likely-looking fellow, and very like to be a strong man. But this much I will grant you," said the Black Knight. "I will put him down on his own two feet, and he will leave his horse and his armour with me, for it would be a shame to me to do him any more harm."

When Sir Beaumains heard him say this, he said, "Sir knight, you are very free with my horse and my armour. I tell you they cost you nothing. And whether you like it or not, I will cross this clearing in spite of you. And you'll get neither horse nor armour of mine, unless you win them with your hands. So let's see what you can do."

"Is that what you say?" said the Black Knight. "Now give up your lady, for it never suits a kitchen page to ride with such a lady."

"You lie," said Beaumains. "I am a gentleman born, and of higher lineage than you, and I will prove it on your body."

Then in great anger they drew apart on their horses, and came together like thunder. And the Black Knight's spear broke, and Beaumains thrust him through both his sides, and with that his own spear broke, and the broken shaft was left in his side. But nevertheless the Black Knight drew his sword, and struck many fierce strokes of great might, and hurt Beaumains very badly. But at last, within an hour and a half, the Black Knight fell down off his horse in a faint, and there he died. And when Beaumains saw how well he was horsed and armed, he dismounted and armed himself in his armour, and so took his horse and rode after the damsel.

When she saw him come near, she said, "Away, kitchen boy, out of the wind, for the smell of your filthy clothes sickens me. Alas," she said, "that such a lout should ever by mischance kill so good a knight as you have done! But all this is your blind luck. But close by here is one who will pay you everything you have coming. And so I still advise you: flee."

"It may happen to me," said Beaumains, "to be beaten or killed. But I warn you, fair damsel, I will not flee away, nor leave your company, for all that you can say. For you keep saying that they will kill me or beat me, but however it happens, I escape, and they lie on the ground. And so you might as well hold your tongue, rather than spend all day rebuking me like this. For I will not go away until I see the very end of this journey, or else I will be killed or soundly beaten. So ride on your way, for follow you I will, whatever happens."

Chapter 8: How the brother of the knight who was slain met Beaumains, and fought with Beaumains until he surrendered

As they rode on together, they saw a knight come riding hard past them, all in green, both his horse and his armour. And when he came near the damsel, he asked her, "Is that my brother the Black Knight you have brought with you?"

"No, no," she said, "this ill-starred kitchen boy has killed your brother by mischance."

"Alas," said the Green Knight, "that is a great pity, that so noble a knight as he was should be killed so unluckily, and above all by a lout's hand, as you say he is. Ah, traitor!" said the Green Knight. "You will die for killing my brother. He was a very noble knight, and his name was Sir Perard."

"I defy you," said Beaumains, "for I tell you I killed him like a knight, and not shamefully."

With that the Green Knight rode to a horn that was green, and it hung on a thorn tree, and there he blew three deadly notes. And two damsels came and armed him quickly. And then he took a great horse, and a green shield, and a green spear. And then they ran together with all their might, and broke their spears right down to their hands. And then they drew their swords, and dealt many heavy strokes, and each of them wounded the other very badly. And at last, as they crossed, Beaumains drove his horse into the side of the Green Knight's horse, so that it fell to the earth. And then the Green Knight got quickly clear of his horse, and squared up on foot. Beaumains saw that, and with that he dismounted, and they rushed together like two mighty champions for a long while, and they both bled badly. With that the damsel came up and said, "My lord the Green Knight, for shame, why do you stand fighting so long with the kitchen boy? Alas, it is a shame that you were ever made a knight, to see such a lad match such a knight, as if the weed should overgrow the corn."

At that the Green Knight was ashamed, and with that he struck a great stroke with all his might, and split his shield right through. When Beaumains saw his shield split in two, he was somewhat ashamed of that stroke and of her words; and then he gave him such a blow on the helmet that he fell on his knees. And then all at once Beaumains pulled him face down on the ground. And then the Green Knight begged him for mercy, and yielded himself to Sir Beaumains, and begged him not to kill him.

"It's all in vain," said Beaumains, "for you shall die, unless this damsel who came with me asks me to save your life."

And with that he unlaced his helmet as if he meant to kill him.

"Shame on you, false kitchen page! I will never ask you to save his life, for I will never put myself so far in your power."

"Then he shall die," said Beaumains.

"Don't you dare kill him, you filthy knave," said the damsel.

"Alas," said the Green Knight, "do not let me die, when a fair word may save me. Fair knight," said the Green Knight, "save my life, and I will forgive you the death of my brother, and become your man for ever, and thirty knights who hold their lands from me shall do you service for ever."

"In the devil's name," said the damsel, "that such a filthy kitchen boy should have you and thirty knights' service!"

"Sir knight," said Beaumains, "none of this does you any good, unless my damsel speaks to me for your life."

And with that he made as if to kill him.

"Leave him be, you filthy knave," said the damsel. "Don't kill him, for if you do you'll be sorry for it."

"Damsel," said Beaumains, "your command is a pleasure to me, and at your command his life shall be saved, and not otherwise." Then he said, "Sir knight with the green arms, I set you free at this damsel's request, for I will not anger her. I will do everything she commands me."

And then the Green Knight knelt down, and did him homage with his sword.

Then the damsel said, "I am sorry, Green Knight, for your hurt, and for your brother's death, the Black Knight. For I had great need of your help, for I am badly afraid to pass through this forest."

"No, don't be afraid," said the Green Knight, "for you shall lodge with me tonight, and tomorrow I will help you through this forest."

So they took their horses and rode to his manor, which was close by.

Chapter 9: How the damsel rebuked Beaumains again, and would not let him sit at her table, but called him kitchen boy

And all the while she rebuked Beaumains, and would not let him sit at her table; but the Green Knight took him and sat him at a side table.

"It seems a marvel to me," said the Green Knight to the damsel, "why you rebuke this noble knight as you do. For I warn you, damsel, he is a very noble knight, and I know of no knight able to match him. And so you do great wrong to rebuke him, for he will do you very good service. For whatever he makes himself out to be, you will find in the end that he comes of noble blood and of a king's lineage."

"Shame, shame," said the damsel. "It is shameful of you to speak such honour of him."

"Truly," said the Green Knight, "it would be shameful of me to speak any dishonour of him, for he has proved himself a better knight than I am. And yet I have met many knights in my day, and never before now have I found any knight his match."

And so that night they went to rest. And all that night the Green Knight had thirty knights secretly keep watch over Beaumains, to guard him against any treachery.

And so in the morning they all got up, and heard their mass and broke their fast. And then they took their horses and rode on their way, and the Green Knight escorted them through the forest. And there the Green Knight said, "My lord Beaumains, I and these thirty knights will always be at your summons, both early and late, at your call, and wherever you wish to send us."

"That is well said," said Beaumains. "When I call on you, you must yield yourself to King Arthur, and all your knights."

"If you so command us, we shall be ready at all times," said the Green Knight.

"Shame, shame on you, in the devil's name," said the damsel, "that any good knights should be obedient to a kitchen boy!"

So then the Green Knight and the damsel parted. And then she said to Beaumains, "Why are you following me, you kitchen boy? Throw away your shield and your spear, and run away. I advise you while there is still time, or very soon you'll be saying 'alas'. For if you were as strong as ever Wade was, the hero of the old songs, or Lancelot, or Tristram, or the good knight Sir Lamorak, you will not get through a pass here that is called the Pass Perilous."

"Damsel," said Beaumains, "whoever is afraid, let him run away. For it would be a shame to turn back, since I have ridden so far with you."

"Well," said the damsel, "you'll soon turn back, whether you want to or not."

Chapter 10: How the third brother, called the Red Knight, jousted and fought against Beaumains, and how Beaumains overcame him

So within a while they saw a tower as white as any snow, with defensive openings all along its battlements, and with a double moat. And over the tower gate there hung some fifty shields of various colours, and below that tower there was a fair meadow. And in it were many knights and squires to be seen, and stands and tents; for there was to be a great tournament there the next morning. And the lord of the tower was in his castle and looked out of a window, and saw a damsel, a dwarf, and a knight armed at all points.

"So help me God," said the lord, "I will joust with that knight, for I see that he is a knight-errant."

And so he armed himself and mounted in haste. And when he was on horseback with his shield and his spear, it was all red, both his horse and his armour, and everything that belonged to him. And when he came near him he thought it was his brother the Black Knight; and then he cried aloud, "Brother, what are you doing in these borders?"

"No, no," said the damsel, "it is not he. This is only a kitchen boy who was brought up on charity in King Arthur's court."

"Nevertheless," said the Red Knight, "I will have words with him before he leaves."

"Ah," said the damsel, "this lout has killed your brother, and Sir Kay named him Beaumains, and this horse and this armour were your brother's, the Black Knight's. I also saw your brother the Green Knight beaten at his hands. Now you can be revenged on him, for I can never be rid of him."

With this the two knights drew apart, and they came together with all their might, and both their horses fell to the ground. And they got clear of their horses, and put their shields before them and drew their swords, and each gave the other steadfast strokes, now here, now there, slashing, circling, thrusting and charging like two boars, for the space of two hours. And then she cried out loud to the Red Knight, "Alas, you noble Red Knight, think what honour has followed you! Never let a kitchen boy hold out against you so long as he is doing."

Then the Red Knight grew angry and doubled his strokes, and wounded Beaumains wonderfully badly, so that the blood ran down to the ground, and it was a wonder to see that hard battle. Yet at last Sir Beaumains struck him to the ground, and as he was about to kill the Red Knight, he begged for mercy, saying, "Noble knight, do not kill me, and I will yield myself to you with fifty knights who are at my command. And I forgive you all the insult you have done me, and the death of my brother the Black Knight."

"All this is no use," said Beaumains, "unless my damsel asks me to save your life."

And with that he made as if to strike off his head.

"Stop, you Beaumains, don't kill him," said the damsel, "for he is a noble knight; and on peril of your head, don't you dare do anything but save him."

Then Beaumains told the Red Knight, "Stand up, and thank the damsel for your life now."

Then the Red Knight begged him to see his castle, and to stay there all night. So the damsel agreed to it, and there they had a merry welcome. But all the while the damsel spoke many foul words to Beaumains, at which the Red Knight marvelled greatly; and all that night the Red Knight had sixty knights watch over Beaumains, so that he should suffer no shame or dishonour. And in the morning they heard mass and dined, and the Red Knight came before Beaumains with his sixty knights, and there he offered him his homage and fealty for all time, he and his knights to do him service.

"I thank you," said Beaumains, "but this you must grant me: when I call on you, you will come before my lord King Arthur, and yield yourselves to him to be his knights."

"Sir," said the Red Knight, "I will be ready, and my company too, at your summons."

So Sir Beaumains left with the damsel, and the whole way she rode beside him scolding him in the foulest manner.

Chapter 11: How Sir Beaumains endured great scorn from the damsel, and bore it patiently

"Damsel," said Beaumains, "you are discourteous to scold me as you do, for it seems to me I have done you good service. And all the time you threaten me that I will be beaten by the knights we meet, but for all your boasting they always end up lying in the dust or in the mud. And so I beg you, scold me no more; and when you see me beaten, or yielding and begging for my life, then you may bid me leave you in disgrace. But first I tell you this: I will not leave you, for I would be worse than a fool if I left you while I am winning honour."

"Well," she said, "very soon you'll meet a knight who will pay you all your wages, for he is the most honoured man in the world, except King Arthur."

"So much the better," said Beaumains. "The more honour he has, the more honour it will be to me to fight him."

Then at once they became aware of a city ahead of them, rich and fair. And between them and the city, a mile and a half off, there was a fair meadow that looked newly mown, and in it were many tents, fair to see.

"Look," said the damsel, "over there is a lord who owns that city, and his custom is, when the weather is fine, to camp in this meadow to joust and fight in tournaments. And there are always five hundred knights and gentlemen of arms around him, and there are all the kinds of games that any gentleman could devise."

"I would gladly see that fine lord," said Beaumains.

"You'll see him soon enough," said the damsel. And as she rode nearer she spotted the tent where he was. "Look," she said, "do you see that tent over there, that is all of the colour of Inde, a deep blue? And everything there is around it, men and women, and the horses in their trappings, the shields and spears, are all of the colour of Inde. And his name is Sir Persant of Inde, the lordliest knight you ever laid eyes on."

"That may well be," said Beaumains, "but however bold a knight he is, I will stay in this field until I see him under his shield."

"Ah, fool," she said, "you had better run while you can."

"Why?" said Beaumains. "If he is the kind of knight you make him out to be, he will not set on me with all his men, or with his five hundred knights. For if no more than one comes at a time, I will not fail him as long as my life lasts."

"Fie, fie," said the damsel, "that a stinking lout should ever make such a boast!"

"Damsel," he said, "you are to blame for scolding me so, for I would rather fight five battles than be scolded like this. Let him come, and then let him do his worst."

"Sir," she said, "I wonder what you are, and what family you come from. You speak boldly, and you have acted boldly, that I have seen. So I beg you, save yourself if you can, for your horse and you have had great hardship, and I am afraid we are staying too long away from the siege. For it is only seven miles from here, and we have passed all the perilous passages except this one only; and here I am badly afraid that you will come to some harm. So I wish you were away from here, so that you would not be bruised or hurt by this strong knight. But I tell you this: Sir Persant of Inde is nothing in might or strength compared to the knight who laid the siege around my lady."

"As for that," said Sir Beaumains, "let it be as it may. For since I have come so near this knight, I will test his might before I leave him, or else I will be shamed if I withdraw from him now. And so, damsel, have no doubt: by the grace of God I will deal with this knight in such a way that within two hours after noon I will be done with him. And then we will come to the siege by daylight."

"Oh Jesus," said the damsel, "I marvel what kind of man you are, for it can only be that you are of noble blood. For no woman ever treated a knight as foully and shamefully as I have treated you, and you have always borne it courteously, and that never came from anything but noble blood."

"Damsel," said Beaumains, "a knight is worth little who cannot bear with a damsel. For whatever you said to me, I took no notice of your words; the more you said, the more you angered me, and I took out my anger on the men I fought. And so all the abuse you heaped on me helped me in my battles, and made me think to show and prove at the end what I was. For perhaps, though I took my food in King Arthur's kitchen, I might have had food enough in other places; but I did all that to prove and test my friends, and that will be known another day. And whether I am a gentleman born or not, I tell you, fair damsel, I have done you a gentleman's service, and perhaps I will do you better service yet before I leave you."

"Alas," she said, "fair Beaumains, forgive me all that I have said or done against you."

"With all my heart," he said, "I forgive you, for you did nothing but what you should have done, for all your evil words pleased me. And damsel," said Beaumains, "since it pleases you to speak so kindly to me, believe me, it gladdens my heart greatly, and now it seems to me there is no knight living whom I am not able enough for."

Chapter 12: How Beaumains fought Sir Persant of Inde, and made him surrender

With this Sir Persant of Inde had spotted them as they waited in the field, and in knightly fashion he sent to ask whether he came in war or in peace.

"Tell your lord," said Beaumains, "I don't care which, but let it be as he pleases himself."

So the messenger went back to Sir Persant and gave him the whole answer.

"Well then, I will fight him to the uttermost," he said. And so he made himself ready and rode against him. And Beaumains saw him and made himself ready, and there they met with all the speed their horses could run, and each broke his spear in three pieces, and their horses crashed together so hard that both horses fell dead on the ground. And swiftly they got clear of their horses and put their shields before them, and drew their swords, and gave many great strokes, so that sometimes they crashed together and fell flat on the ground. So they fought for two hours and more, until their shields and their hauberks were all hacked to pieces, and they were wounded in many places. So at last Sir Beaumains struck him through the side of the body, and then he drew back here and there, and kept up his fight in knightly fashion for a long time. And at last, loath as he was to do it, Beaumains struck Sir Persant on the top of the helm, so that he fell flat on the ground; and then he leapt on him across his body and unlaced his helm to kill him.

Then Sir Persant yielded and begged him for mercy. With that the damsel came and begged him to save his life.

"Gladly," he said, "for it would be a pity for this noble knight to die."

"Many thanks," said Persant, "noble knight and damsel. For now I know for certain it was you who killed my brother the Black Knight at the black thorn. He was a very noble knight; his name was Sir Percard. I am also sure that you are the one who beat my other brother the Green Knight; his name was Sir Pertolepe. You also beat my brother the Red Knight, Sir Perimones. And now, since you have beaten these, I will do this to please you: you shall have homage and fealty from me, and a hundred knights always at your command, to go and ride wherever you command us."

And so they went to Sir Persant's tent and drank wine and ate spiced sweets, and afterwards Sir Persant had him rest on a bed until supper time, and after supper to bed again. When Beaumains was in bed, Sir Persant had a lady, a fair daughter eighteen years old, and he called her to him and charged and commanded her, on his blessing, to go to the knight's bed and lie down by his side. "And don't be cold to him, but be warm with him, and take him in your arms and kiss him, and see that this is done, I charge you, as you want to keep my love and my good will."

So Sir Persant's daughter did as her father told her, and so she went to Sir Beaumains' bed, and undressed in secret, and lay down by him. And then he woke and saw her, and asked her who she was.

"Sir," she said, "I am Sir Persant's daughter, and I have come here by my father's command."

"Are you a maiden or a wife?" he said.

"Sir," she said, "I am a pure maiden."

"God forbid," he said, "that I should dishonour you and do Sir Persant such a shame. So, fair damsel, get out of this bed, or else I will."

"Sir," she said, "I did not come to you of my own will, but as I was commanded."

"Alas," said Sir Beaumains, "I would be a shameful knight if I did your father any dishonour." And so he kissed her, and so she left and came to Sir Persant her father, and told him everything of how she had fared.

"Truly," said Sir Persant, "whoever he is, he is of noble blood."

And so we leave them there till the morning.

Chapter 13: Of the friendly talk between Sir Persant and Beaumains, and how he told him that his name was Sir Gareth

And so in the morning the damsel and Sir Beaumains heard mass and had breakfast, and so took their leave.

"Fair damsel," said Persant, "where are you leading this knight?"

"Sir," she said, "this knight is going to the siege that is besieging my sister in the Castle Dangerous."

"Ah, ah," said Persant, "that is the Knight of the Red Launds, the most dangerous knight I know of now living, and a man without mercy, and men say that he has the strength of seven men. God save you from that knight," he said to Beaumains, "for he does that lady a great wrong, and that is a great pity, for she is one of the fairest ladies in the world. And it seems to me that your damsel is her sister. Isn't your name Linet?" he said.

"Yes, sir," she said, "and my lady my sister's name is Dame Lionesse."

"Now I will tell you," said Sir Persant. "This Red Knight of the Red Launds has lain at the siege a long time, almost two years now, and many times he could have had her if he had wanted to. But he draws out the time for this purpose: to have Sir Lancelot du Lake fight him, or Sir Tristram, or Sir Lamorak de Galis, or Sir Gawain. And that is the reason he stays so long at the siege."

"Now, my lord Sir Persant of Inde," said the damsel Linet, "I ask you to make this gentleman a knight before ever he fights the Red Knight."

"I will with all my heart," said Sir Persant, "if it pleases him to take the order of knighthood from so simple a man as I am."

"Sir," said Beaumains, "I thank you for your good will, but I am better provided for, for the noble knight Sir Lancelot certainly made me a knight."

"Ah," said Sir Persant, "you could not have been made a knight by a more renowned knight. For of all knights he may be called the chief of knighthood. And all the world says that knighthood is clearly divided among three knights, that is, Lancelot du Lake, Sir Tristram de Liones, and Sir Lamorak de Galis: these are the ones who hold the renown now. There are many other knights, such as Sir Palomides the Saracen and Sir Safere his brother; also Sir Bleoberis and Sir Blamore de Ganis his brother; also Sir Bors de Ganis and Sir Ector de Maris and Sir Percival de Galis. These and many more are noble knights, but there are none who surpass the three I named. And so God speed you well," said Sir Persant, "for if you can match the Red Knight you will be called the fourth knight of the world."

"Sir," said Beaumains, "I would gladly be of good fame and good knighthood. And I tell you that I come of good men, for I dare say my father was a noble man. And on condition that you keep it secret, you and this damsel, I will tell you what family I come from."

"We will not give you away," they both said, "until you command us to, by the faith we owe to God."

"Truly then," he said, "my name is Gareth of Orkney, and King Lot was my father, and my mother is King Arthur's sister; her name is Dame Morgause. And Sir Gawain is my brother, and Sir Agravain and Sir Gaheris, and I am the youngest of them all. And still neither King Arthur nor Sir Gawain knows who I am."

Chapter 14: How the besieged lady had word from her sister that she was bringing a knight to fight for her, and of the battles he had won

So the book says that the lady who was besieged had word from the dwarf that her sister was coming, and a knight with her, and how he had passed all the perilous passages.

"What kind of man is he?" said the lady.

"He is a noble knight, truly, madam," said the dwarf, "and only a young man, but he is as promising a man as you ever saw."

"Who is he?" said the lady. "And what family does he come from, and who made him a knight?"

"Madam," said the dwarf, "he is the son of the King of Orkney, but I will not tell you his name at this time. But you may be sure that he was made a knight by Sir Lancelot, for he would be made a knight by no one else; and Sir Kay named him Beaumains."

"How did he escape," said the lady, "from the brothers of Persant?"

"Madam," he said, "as a noble knight should. First he killed two brothers at a crossing of a river."

"Ah!" she said. "They were good knights, but they were murderers. One was called Gherard le Breuse, and the other knight was called Sir Arnold le Breuse."

"Then, madam, he encountered the Black Knight, and killed him in open battle, and so he took his horse and his armour and fought the Green Knight and beat him in open battle. And he served the Red Knight in the same way, and after that he served the Blue Knight in the same way and beat him in open battle."

"Then," said the lady, "he has overcome Sir Persant of Inde, one of the noblest knights in the world."

And the dwarf said, "He has beaten all four brothers and killed the Black Knight, and he did more before that: he overthrew Sir Kay and left him half dead on the ground. He also fought a great battle with Sir Lancelot, and there they parted even; and then Sir Lancelot made him a knight."

"Dwarf," said the lady, "I am glad of this news. So go to a hermitage of mine near here, and take with you some of my wine in two silver flagons, each holding two gallons, and also two batches of loaves, with fat venison baked in pastry, and dainty birds. And here I give you a cup of gold, which is rich and precious; and take all this to my hermitage, and put it in the hermit's hands. And after that go to my sister and greet her well, and commend me to that noble knight, and beg him to eat and drink and build up his strength. And tell him I thank him for his courtesy and goodness, that he would take on such labour for me, who never did him any kindness or courtesy. Also beg him to be of good heart and courage, for he will meet a very noble knight, but one who has neither goodness, courtesy, nor gentleness; for he cares for nothing but murder, and that is the reason I cannot praise him or love him."

So this dwarf left, and came to Sir Persant's, where he found the damsel Linet and Sir Beaumains, and there he told them everything as you have heard. And then they took their leave, but Sir Persant took a small ambling horse and escorted them on their way, and then commended them to God. And so within a little while they came to that hermitage, and there they drank the wine, and ate the venison and the baked birds. And so when they had eaten well, the dwarf went back again with his vessels to the castle; and there the Red Knight of the Red Launds met him, and asked him where he came from, and where he had been.

"Sir," said the dwarf, "I have been with the sister of my lady of this castle, and she has been at King Arthur's court, and has brought a knight back with her."

"Then I count her labour as wasted," said the Red Knight, "for even if she had brought Sir Lancelot with her, or Sir Tristram, Sir Lamorak, or Sir Gawain, I would think myself good enough for them all."

"That may well be," said the dwarf, "but this knight has passed all the perilous passages, and killed the Black Knight and two others besides, and beaten the Green Knight, the Red Knight, and the Blue Knight."

"Then he is one of those four I named just now."

"He is none of those," said the dwarf, "but he is a king's son."

"What is his name?" said the Red Knight of the Red Launds.

"That I will not tell you," said the dwarf, "but Sir Kay named him Beaumains in scorn."

"I don't care," said the knight, "what knight he is, for I will soon be done with him. And if I ever get the better of him, he will die a shameful death, as many others have."

"That would be a pity," said the dwarf, "and it is a marvel that you make such shameful war on noble knights."

Chapter 15: How the damsel and Beaumains came to the siege, and came to a sycamore tree, where Beaumains blew a horn, and then the Knight of the Red Launds came to fight him

Now we leave the knight and the dwarf, and speak of Beaumains, who lay all night in the hermitage; and in the morning he and the damsel Linet heard their mass and had breakfast. And then they took their horses and rode right through a fair forest; and then they came to a plain, and saw many pavilions and tents there, and a fair castle, and there was much smoke and a great noise. And when they came near the siege, Sir Beaumains saw, as he rode, very finely armed knights hanging by the neck from great trees, with their shields about their necks and their swords, and gilt spurs on their heels; and so there hung some forty knights there, shamefully, in very rich armour.

Then Sir Beaumains' face fell, and he said, "What does this mean?"

"Fair sir," said the damsel, "don't let your face fall at this sight, for you must take courage, or else you are utterly lost. For all these knights came here to this siege to rescue my sister Dame Lionesse, and when the Red Knight of the Red Launds had overcome them, he put them to this shameful death without mercy or pity. And he will serve you the same way unless you acquit yourself better."

"Now Jesus defend me," said Beaumains, "from such a vile death and such disgrace in arms. For rather than be dealt with like that, I would rather be killed like a man in open battle."

"You would be better so," said the damsel. "For don't trust him; there is no courtesy in him, but everything goes to death or shameful murder. And that is a pity, for he is a very handsome man, well built, and a very noble knight in prowess, and a lord of great lands and possessions."

"Truly," said Beaumains, "he may well be a good knight, but he keeps shameful customs, and it is a marvel that he has lasted so long without any of the noble knights of my lord Arthur's court having dealt with him."

And then they rode to the moats, and saw that the castle was double moated, with very warlike walls; and many great lords were lodged near the walls, and there was a great noise of minstrels. And the sea beat against the walls on one side, where there were many ships, and the noise of the sailors crying "heave-ho". And also, close by, there was a sycamore tree, and on it hung a horn, the biggest they had ever seen, made of an elephant's tusk. And this Knight of the Red Launds had hung it there so that if any knight-errant came, he must blow that horn, and then he would make himself ready and come to him to do battle.

"But, sir, I beg you," said the damsel Linet, "do not blow the horn until it is high noon, for now it is about prime, and his might is growing now, so that, as men say, he has the strength of seven men."

"Ah, fie for shame, fair damsel, never say such a thing to me again. For if he were as good a knight as ever lived, I will never fail him at his greatest might. For either I will win honour honourably, or die like a knight in the field."

And with that he spurred his horse straight to the sycamore tree, and blew the horn so eagerly that the whole siege and the castle rang with it. And then knights leapt out of their tents and pavilions, and those inside the castle looked over the walls and out of the windows.

Then the Red Knight of the Red Launds armed himself in haste, and two barons fastened his spurs on his heels, and everything was blood red, his armour, spear and shield. And an earl buckled his helm on his head, and then they brought him a red spear and a red warhorse, and so he rode into a little valley below the castle, so that everyone in the castle and at the siege could watch the battle.

Chapter 16: How the two knights met, and of their talk, and how they began their battle

"Sir," said the damsel Linet to Sir Beaumains, "see that you are glad and light of heart, for over there is your deadly enemy, and at that window over there is my lady, my sister, Dame Lionesse."

"Where?" said Beaumains.

"Over there," said the damsel, and pointed with her finger.

"That is true," said Beaumains. "From far off she seems the fairest lady I ever looked on. And truly," he said, "I ask for no better cause to fight in than this one now, for truly she shall be my lady, and for her I will fight."

And all the while he looked up at the window with a glad face, and the Lady Lionesse curtsied to him down to the ground, holding up both her hands.

With that the Red Knight of the Red Launds called to Sir Beaumains, "Stop your looking, sir knight, and look at me, I advise you. For I warn you plainly, she is my lady, and for her I have fought many hard battles."

"If you have done so," said Beaumains, "it seems to me it was only wasted labour, for she loves no one of your company, and for you to love one who does not love you is nothing but great folly. For if I understood that she was not glad of my coming, I would think twice before I fought for her. But I understand from your besieging of this castle that she could well do without your company. And so know this, you Red Knight of the Red Launds: I love her, and will rescue her, or else die."

"Is that what you say?" said the Red Knight. "It seems to me you ought in reason to take warning from those knights you saw hanging on those trees over there."

"Fie for shame," said Beaumains, "that you should ever say or do such evil, for in that you shame yourself and knighthood. And you can be sure that no lady who knows your wicked customs will love you. And now you think the sight of these hanged knights should frighten me. No, truly, not so: that shameful sight gives me more courage and boldness against you than I would have had against you if you were a well-conducted knight."

"Get ready," said the Red Knight of the Red Launds, "and talk to me no longer."

Then Sir Beaumains told the damsel to move away from him; and then they put their spears in their rests, and came together with all the might they both had, and each struck the other in the middle of the shield, so that the breast straps, girths and cruppers of their horses burst, and both of them fell to the ground with the reins of their bridles in their hands. And so they lay a long while, badly stunned, so that everyone in the castle and at the siege thought their necks were broken. And then many a stranger and others said the strange knight was a big man and a noble jouster, "for before now we never saw any knight match the Red Knight of the Red Launds." So they said, both inside the castle and outside. Then swiftly they got clear of their horses and put their shields before them, and drew their swords and ran together like two fierce lions, and each gave the other such blows on the helm that they both reeled back two strides. And then they both recovered, and hewed great pieces off each other's armour and shields, so that a great part fell into the fields.

Chapter 17: How after long fighting Beaumains overcame the knight and would have slain him, but at the lords' request spared his life and made him surrender to the lady

And so they fought until it was past noon, and they would never stop, until at last they were both out of breath. And then they stood swaying and staggering, panting, blowing and bleeding, so that most of those who watched them wept for pity. So when they had rested a while they went into battle again, circling, rushing and thrusting like two boars. And at times they took a run at each other like two rams, and crashed together so that sometimes they fell flat on the ground; and at times they were so dazed that each took the other's sword instead of his own.

So they held out until the hour of evensong, so that none of those who watched them could tell which of them was likely to win the battle. And their armour was so hacked to pieces that men could see their naked sides; and in other places they were naked too, but they always defended the naked places. And the Red Knight was a cunning knight in war, and his cunning fighting taught Sir Beaumains to be wise; but he paid for it very dearly before he saw through his way of fighting.

And so by agreement between them they granted each other a rest; and so they sat down on two molehills there beside the place of the fight, and each of them unlaced his helm and took the cool wind. For each of them had his page close by him, to come when they called to unlace their armour and to put it on again at their command. And then, when Sir Beaumains' helm was off, he looked up at the window, and there he saw the fair lady Dame Lionesse, and she gave him such a look that his heart grew light and merry. And with that he told the Red Knight of the Red Launds to make ready, "and let us fight the battle to the uttermost."

"Gladly," said the knight. And then they laced up their helms, and their pages withdrew, and they stepped together and fought vigorously. But the Red Knight of the Red Launds watched his chance, and with a stroke across struck him on the hand, so that his sword fell out of his hand; and then he gave him another blow on the helm, so that he fell flat on the ground, and the Red Knight fell on top of him, to hold him down.

Then the maiden Linet cried aloud, "Oh, Sir Beaumains, where has your courage gone? Alas, my lady my sister is watching you, and she sobs and weeps, and that makes my heart heavy."

When Sir Beaumains heard her say this, he started up with great might and got to his feet, and swiftly he leapt to his sword and gripped it in his hand, and quickened his pace towards the Red Knight, and there they fought a new battle together. But Sir Beaumains then doubled his strokes, and struck so thick and fast that he struck the sword out of his hand, and then he struck him on the helm so that he fell to the ground. And Sir Beaumains fell on him, and unlaced his helm to kill him; and then he yielded and begged for mercy, and said in a loud voice, "Oh noble knight, I yield myself to your mercy."

Then Sir Beaumains thought of the knights he had had hanged so shamefully, and then he said, "I cannot save your life with honour, because of the shameful deaths you have made so many very good knights die."

"Sir," said the Red Knight of the Red Launds, "hold your hand and you will know the reasons why I put them to so shameful a death."

"Speak on," said Sir Beaumains.

"Sir, I once loved a lady, a fair damsel, and she had her brother killed; and she said it was Sir Lancelot du Lake, or else Sir Gawain. And she begged me, as I loved her with all my heart, to make her a promise on the faith of my knighthood to labour in arms every day until I met one of them; and that all whom I could overcome I should put to a vile death. And this is the reason I have put all these knights to death, and so I gave her my word to do every kind of shame to King Arthur's knights, and to take vengeance on all these knights. And, sir, now I will tell you that every day my strength increases until noon, and all that time I have the strength of seven men."

Chapter 18: How the knight surrendered, and how Beaumains made him go to King Arthur's court and beg Sir Lancelot's mercy

Then many earls and barons and noble knights came and begged that knight to save his life, "and take him as your prisoner." And they all fell on their knees, and begged him for mercy, and that he would save his life.

"And, sir," they all said, "it would be more honourable of you to take his homage and fealty, and let him hold his lands from you, than to kill him. You will gain no advantage by his death, and his misdeeds that are done cannot be undone; and so he will make amends to everyone concerned, and we will all become your men and do you homage and fealty."

"Fair lords," said Beaumains, "you may be sure I am very loath to kill this knight; nevertheless he has done exceedingly evil and shameful things. But since all he did was at a lady's request, I blame him the less. And so for your sake I will release him, so that he will have his life on this condition: that he goes into the castle and yields himself there to the lady, and if she will forgive him and let him go, I am content, provided that he makes her amends for all the wrong he has done against her and her lands. And also, when that is done, that you go to the court of King Arthur, and there ask Sir Lancelot's pardon, and Sir Gawain's, for the ill will you have had against them."

"Sir," said the Red Knight of the Red Launds, "I will do all this as you command, and you shall have sure guarantees and pledges."

And so then, when the guarantee was given, he did his homage and fealty, and all those earls and barons with him.

And then the maiden Linet came to Sir Beaumains, and took off his armour and examined his wounds, and stopped his bleeding, and she did the same for the Red Knight of the Red Launds. And there they stayed ten days in their tents; and the Red Knight had his lords and servants do everything they could to please Sir Beaumains. And so within a while the Red Knight of the Red Launds went to the castle and put himself at her mercy. And so she received him on sufficient security, so that all her injuries were fully made good, everything she could complain of.
