And then he left for the court of King Arthur, and there, before everyone, the Red Knight of the Red Launds put himself at the mercy of Sir Lancelot and Sir Gawain, and there he told openly how he had been overcome and by whom, and he also told of all the battles from the beginning to the end.

"Jesus have mercy," said King Arthur and Sir Gawain, "we wonder greatly what blood he comes of, for he is a noble knight."

"Don't wonder at it," said Sir Lancelot, "for you may be quite sure that he comes of very noble blood. And as for his might and boldness, there are only a few now living who are as mighty as he is, and as noble in prowess."

"It seems from what you say," said King Arthur, "that you know his name, and where he comes from, and what blood he is of."

"I believe I do," said Lancelot, "or else I would not have given him the order of knighthood. But he gave me such a charge at that time that I should never give him away until he asked me to, or else until it was made known openly by someone else."

Chapter 19: How Beaumains came to the lady, and when he reached the castle the gates were shut against him, and of what the lady said to him

Now we turn to Sir Beaumains, who asked Linet that he might see her sister, his lady.

"Sir," she said, "I would gladly have you see her."

Then Sir Beaumains armed himself completely, and took his horse and his spear, and rode straight to the castle. And when he came to the gate he found many armed men there, who pulled up the drawbridge and shut the gate tight.

Then he wondered why they would not let him in. And then he looked up at the window; and there he saw the fair Lionesse, who called down from above, "Go on your way, Sir Beaumains, for you shall not have my love wholly yet, not until you are counted one of the number of the worthy knights. And so go and labour to win honour for these twelve months, and then you will hear news."

"Alas, fair lady," said Beaumains, "I have not deserved that you should show me this coldness. I had expected that I would have a warm welcome from you, and as far as I was able I have earned your thanks, and I am quite sure I have bought your love with part of the best blood in my body."

"Fair courteous knight," said Dame Lionesse, "do not be displeased or over-hasty. For believe me, your great toil and your true love shall not be lost, for I take account of your great toil and labour, your worth and your goodness, as I ought to do. And so go on your way, and see that you keep up your heart, for everything will be for your honour and for the best. And by God, a twelvemonth will soon be over. And trust me, fair knight, I shall be true to you, and never betray you, but until my death I shall love you and no one else."

And with that she turned away from the window, and Sir Beaumains rode off away from the castle, grieving greatly. And so he rode here and there and did not know where he was riding, until it was dark night. And then he happened to come to a poor man's house, and there he was given lodging all that night.

But Sir Beaumains had no rest, but tossed and writhed for love of the lady of the castle. And so the next morning he took his horse and rode until the middle of the morning, and then he came to a broad river, and beside it was a great lodge, and there he dismounted to sleep, and laid his head on his shield, and handed his horse over to the dwarf, and ordered him to keep watch all night.

Now we turn to the lady of that same castle, who thought much about Beaumains. And then she called to her Sir Gringamore, her brother, and begged him in every way, as he loved her with all his heart, to ride after Sir Beaumains. "And keep watching him all the time until you find him sleeping, for I am sure that in his low spirits he will dismount somewhere and lie down to sleep. And so keep your watch on him, and as secretly as you can, take his dwarf, and go off with him as fast as you possibly can before Sir Beaumains wakes. For my sister Linet tells me that the dwarf can tell what family he comes from, and what his real name is. And meanwhile my sister and I will ride to your castle to wait for you to bring the dwarf with you. And then, when you have brought him to your castle, I will question him myself. Until I know what his real name is, and what family he comes from, I shall never be merry at heart."

"Sister," said Sir Gringamore, "all this shall be done as you wish."

And so he rode all the next day and the night until he found Sir Beaumains lying by a river, with his head on his shield, to sleep. And then, when he saw Sir Beaumains fast asleep, he came creeping quietly up behind the dwarf, and snatched him up tight under his arm, and so he rode away with him as fast as ever he could to his own castle. And this Sir Gringamore's arms were all black, as was his right. But all the time, as he rode with the dwarf toward his castle, the dwarf cried out to his lord and begged him for help. And with that Sir Beaumains woke, and leapt up quickly, and saw Sir Gringamore riding off with the dwarf, and so Sir Gringamore rode out of his sight.

Chapter 20: How Sir Beaumains rode after his dwarf to rescue him, and came into the castle where he was held

Then Sir Beaumains put on his helm at once, and buckled on his shield, and took his horse, and rode after him as hard as ever he could ride, through marshes and fields and great valleys, so that many times he and his horse plunged in over their heads in deep bogs. For he did not know the way, but took the shortest way in that frenzy, so that many times he was close to dying. And at last he happened to come to a fine green road, and there he met a poor man of the country, whom he greeted, and asked him whether he had not met a knight on a black horse and in all-black armour, with a little dwarf sitting behind him looking downcast.

"Sir," said the poor man, "Sir Gringamore the knight came by me here, with just such a dwarf as you describe, grieving. And so I advise you not to follow him, for he is one of the most dangerous knights in the world, and his castle is close by here, only two miles off. So we advise you not to ride after Sir Gringamore, unless you bear him good will."

So we leave Sir Beaumains riding toward the castle, and speak of Sir Gringamore and the dwarf. As soon as the dwarf had come to the castle, Dame Lionesse and Dame Linet her sister asked the dwarf where his master was born, and what lineage he came from.

"And unless you tell me," said Dame Lionesse, "you shall never get out of this castle, but stay here a prisoner forever."

"As for that," said the dwarf, "I am not much afraid to tell his name and what family he comes from. Believe me, he is a king's son, and his mother is sister to King Arthur, and he is brother to the good knight Sir Gawain, and his name is Sir Gareth of Orkney. And now that I have told you his real name, I beg you, fair lady, let me go back to my lord, for he will never leave this country until he has me back. And if he is angry he will do a great deal of harm before he is stopped, and bring ruin on you in this country."

"As for that threat," said Sir Gringamore, "be that as it may, we will go to dinner."

And so they washed and went to their meal, and made merry and were at their ease, and because the Lady Lionesse of the castle was there, they rejoiced greatly.

"Truly, madam," said Linet to her sister, "he may well be a king's son, for he has many good qualities. For he is courteous and mild, and the most patient man I ever met. For I dare say there was never a gentlewoman who reviled a man in so foul a way as I have abused him; and every time he gave me gracious and gentle answers back."

And as they sat talking like this, Sir Gareth came in at the gate with an angry face and his sword drawn in his hand, and shouted so that the whole castle could hear it, "You traitor, Sir Gringamore, give me back my dwarf, or by the faith I owe to the order of knighthood, I'll do you all the harm I can!"

Then Sir Gringamore looked out of a window and said, "Sir Gareth of Orkney, stop your boasting. You're not getting your dwarf back."

"You coward knight," said Sir Gareth, "bring him with you, and come and fight me, and win him and keep him."

"So I will," said Sir Gringamore, "if I feel like it. But for all your big words, you're not getting him."

"Ah, fair brother," said Dame Lionesse, "I wish he had his dwarf back, for I would not want him angry. For now that the dwarf has told me all I wanted, I care no more about him. And also, brother, Sir Gareth has done a great deal for me, and freed me from the Red Knight of the Red Launds, and so, brother, I owe him my service before all knights living. And believe me, I love him above all others, and I would very gladly speak with him. But on no account would I want him to know who I am, but to think I was some other lady, a stranger."

"Well," said Sir Gringamore, "since I know your wishes now, I will do as he wants."

And right then he went down to Sir Gareth, and said, "Sir, I beg your pardon, and all the wrong I have done I will make good as you wish. And so I beg you to dismount, and accept such hospitality as I can give you in this castle."

"Shall I have my dwarf?" said Sir Gareth.

"Yes, sir, and all the pleasure I can give you. For as soon as your dwarf told me who you were, and what blood you come from, and what noble deeds you have done in these borderlands, I repented of what I had done."

And then Sir Gareth dismounted, and his dwarf came and took his horse.

"Oh, my good fellow," said Sir Gareth, "I've been through many adventures for your sake."

And so Sir Gringamore took him by the hand and led him into the hall where his own wife was.

Chapter 21: How Sir Gareth, also called Beaumains, came into his lady's presence, and how they became acquainted, and of their love

And then Dame Lionesse came out dressed like a princess, and she gave him an exceedingly warm welcome, and he her in return; and they talked graciously together and looked lovingly at each other. And many times Sir Gareth thought, "Jesus, if only the lady of the Castle Perilous were as beautiful as she is!" There were all kinds of games and entertainments, dancing and singing. And the more Sir Gareth looked at that lady, the more he loved her; and he so burned with love that he was beside himself and lost his reason. And as night came on they went in to supper, and Sir Gareth could not eat, for his love was so hot that he did not know where he was.

Sir Gringamore noticed all these looks, and then after supper he called his sister Dame Lionesse into a room, and said, "Fair sister, I have watched well the looks between you and this knight. And sister, I want you to know that he is a very noble knight, and if you can make him stay here I will give him every pleasure I can. For even if you were better than you are, you would be well bestowed on him."

"Fair brother," said Dame Lionesse, "I understand well that the knight is good, and that he comes from a noble house. Even so, I will test him further, though I am more beholden to him than to any man on earth. For he has gone through great labour for my love, and passed through many a dangerous passage."

Just then Sir Gringamore went to Sir Gareth, and said, "Sir, be of good cheer, for you shall have no reason to be otherwise. For this lady, my sister, is yours at all times, saving her honour. For believe me, she loves you as well as you love her, and better, if better may be."

"If I knew that," said Sir Gareth, "there would not be a happier man alive than I."

"Upon my honour," said Sir Gringamore, "trust my promise. And as long as it pleases you, you shall stay with me, and this lady shall be with us day and night to give you all the pleasure she can."

"Gladly," said Sir Gareth, "for I have promised to stay near this country for this twelvemonth. And I am quite sure King Arthur and other noble knights will find me wherever I am within this twelvemonth. For I shall be looked for and found, if I am alive."

And then the noble knight Sir Gareth went to Dame Lionesse, whom he now loved very much, and kissed her many times, and each of them rejoiced greatly in the other. And there she promised him her love for certain, to love him and no one else all the days of her life. Then this lady, Dame Lionesse, with her brother's consent, told Sir Gareth the whole truth of who she was, and how she was the same lady he had fought for, and how she was lady of the Castle Perilous. And there she told him how she had had her brother take away his dwarf, for this reason: "to know for certain what your name was, and what family you came from."

Chapter 22: How at night an armed knight came and fought Sir Gareth, and how Gareth, badly wounded in the thigh, struck off the knight's head

And then she had Linet brought before him, the damsel who had ridden with him along so many desolate ways. Then Sir Gareth was gladder than he had been before. And then they plighted their troth to each other, to love, and never to fail while their lives lasted. And they both so burned with love that they agreed to satisfy their desire in secret. And there Dame Lionesse advised Sir Gareth to sleep nowhere else but in the hall. And there she promised him to come to his bed a little before midnight.

This plan was not kept so secret that it was not found out; for they were both young, and tender in years, and had never practised such arts before. And so the damsel Linet was a little displeased, and she thought her sister Dame Lionesse was a little over-hasty, that she could not wait for the time of her marriage; and to save their honour, she meant to cool their hot desire. And so by her subtle arts she arranged that neither of them should have their will of the other, as for their pleasures, until they were married. And so it went on. After supper the hall was cleared, so that every lord and lady should go to their rest. But Sir Gareth said plainly he would go no farther than the hall, for such places, he said, were fitting for a knight-errant to take his rest in. And so great couches were set out, and feather beds on them, and there he lay down to sleep. And within a while Dame Lionesse came, wrapped in a cloak furred with ermine, and lay down beside Sir Gareth. And with that he began to kiss her. And then he looked in front of him, and there he noticed and saw an armed knight coming, with many lights about him; and this knight had a long battle-axe in his hand, and looked grimly as if to strike him. When Sir Gareth saw him coming in that way, he leapt out of his bed, and got his sword in his hand, and leapt straight at that knight. And when the knight saw Sir Gareth coming at him so fiercely, he struck him with a thrust through the thick of the thigh, so that the wound was a hand's breadth wide and had cut through many veins and sinews. And with that Sir Gareth struck him on the helm such a blow that he fell flat on his face; and then he leapt on him and unlaced his helm, and struck his head off his body. And then he bled so fast that he could not stand, but laid himself down on his bed, and there he fainted and lay as if he were dead.

Then Dame Lionesse cried out, so that her brother Sir Gringamore heard, and came down. And when he saw Sir Gareth so shamefully wounded he was very much displeased, and said, "I am ashamed that this noble knight is honoured like this. Sister," said Sir Gringamore, "how can this be, that you are here, and this noble knight wounded?"

"Brother," she said, "I cannot tell you, for it was not done by me, nor with my consent. For he is my lord and I am his, and he is to be my husband. And so, my brother, I want you to know that I am not ashamed to be with him, nor to give him all the pleasure I can."

"Sister," said Sir Gringamore, "and I want you to know it, and Sir Gareth too, that this ill-fated deed was never done by me, nor with my consent."

And there they staunched his bleeding as well as they could, and Sir Gringamore and Dame Lionesse grieved greatly.

And right away Dame Linet came, and picked up the head in the sight of them all, and anointed it with an ointment where it had been struck off; and in the same way she did the other part, where the head had been attached, and then she set them together, and it stuck as fast as it ever had. And the knight got up quickly, and the damsel Linet put him in her room. Sir Gringamore and Dame Lionesse saw all this, and so did Sir Gareth; and he saw well that it was the damsel Linet, who had ridden with him through the perilous passages.

"Ah, damsel," said Sir Gareth, "I never thought you would have done what you have done."

"My lord Gareth," said Linet, "everything I have done I will stand by, and everything I have done shall be for your honour and good name, and for all of us."

And so within a while Sir Gareth was nearly healed, and grew lively and cheerful, and sang, danced and played games; and he and Dame Lionesse burned so hot with love that they made an agreement that on the tenth night after, she should come to his bed. And because he had been wounded before, he laid his armour and his sword close beside his bed.

Chapter 23: How the same knight came back the next night and was beheaded again, and how at the feast of Pentecost all the knights Sir Gareth had overcome came and surrendered to King Arthur

Just as she had promised, she came; and she was no sooner in his bed than she saw an armed knight coming toward the bed. With that she warned Sir Gareth, and quickly, through the good help of Dame Lionesse, he was armed; and they crashed together with great anger and malice all about the hall. And there was a great light, as if there were twenty torches both in front and behind, so that Sir Gareth strained himself until his old wound burst open bleeding again. But he was hot and full of courage and paid no attention, but with his great strength he struck down that knight, and pulled off his helm, and struck off his head. Then he hacked the head into a hundred pieces. And when he had done that he picked up all those pieces, and threw them out of a window into the ditches of the castle. And by the time this was done he was so faint from bleeding that he could scarcely stand. And when he was almost out of his armour he fell in a deathly faint on the floor; and then Dame Lionesse cried out so that Sir Gringamore heard. And when he came and found Sir Gareth in that state he grieved greatly; and there he brought Sir Gareth round, and gave him a drink that revived him wonderfully well. But the grief that Dame Lionesse showed there no tongue can tell, for she carried on as if she would have died.

Just then this damsel Linet came before them all, and she had fetched all the lumps of the head that Sir Gareth had thrown out of the window, and there she anointed them as she had done before, and set them together again.

"Well, damsel Linet," said Sir Gareth, "I have not deserved all this insult you are doing me."

"Sir knight," she said, "I have done nothing that I will not stand by, and everything I have done shall be to your honour, and for all of us."

And then Sir Gareth's bleeding was staunched. But the doctors said that no man alive could heal him completely of his wound unless the one who had caused that stroke by enchantment healed him.

So we leave Sir Gareth there with Sir Gringamore and his sisters, and turn to King Arthur, who held his feast at the next feast of Pentecost. And there came the Green Knight with fifty knights, and they all surrendered to King Arthur. And so there came the Red Knight, his brother, and surrendered to King Arthur, and sixty knights with him. Also there came the Blue Knight, their brother, with a hundred knights, and they surrendered to King Arthur. And the Green Knight's name was Pertolepe, and the Red Knight's name was Perimones, and the Blue Knight's name was Sir Persant of Inde. These three brothers told King Arthur how they had been overcome by a knight that a damsel had with her, whom she called Beaumains.

"Jesus," said the king, "I wonder what knight he is, and what lineage he comes from. He was with me a twelvemonth, and he was kept poorly and shamefully, and Sir Kay named him Beaumains in scorn."

So, just as the king stood talking like this with these three brothers, Sir Lancelot du Lake came and told the king that a fine lord had come, with six hundred knights with him.

Then the king went out of Caerleon, for the feast was there, and this lord came to him, and greeted the king courteously.

"What do you want," said King Arthur, "and what is your errand?"

"Sir," he said, "I am called the Red Knight of the Red Launds, but my name is Sir Ironside. And sir, believe me, I am sent here to you by a knight who is called Beaumains, for he won me in open battle, hand to hand, and no knight but he has ever had the better of me these thirty years. And he commanded me to surrender myself to you, to do with as you will."

"You are welcome," said the king, "for you have long been a great enemy to me and my court, and now I trust to God I shall treat you so that you will be my friend."

"Sir, both I and these five hundred knights shall always be at your summons to do you service, as far as lies in our power."

"Jesus have mercy," said King Arthur, "I am much beholden to that knight who has exerted himself so to do honour to me and my court. And as for you, Ironside, who are called the Red Knight of the Red Launds, you are said to be a dangerous knight. And if you will hold your lands from me, I will honour you and make you a knight of the Round Table; but then you must be a murderer no longer."

"Sir, as for that, I have promised Sir Beaumains never again to keep such customs. For all the shameful customs I kept, I kept at the request of a lady I loved. And so I must go to Sir Lancelot and to Sir Gawain, and ask their forgiveness for the ill will I had toward them; for all those I put to death were put to death only for the love of Sir Lancelot and of Sir Gawain."

"They are here now," said the king, "in front of you. Now you may say to them what you will."

And then he knelt down to Sir Lancelot and to Sir Gawain, and begged them to forgive him for the enmity he had ever had against them.

Chapter 24: How King Arthur pardoned them, and asked them where Sir Gareth was

Then they all said graciously at once, "God forgive you, and so do we. And we beg you to tell us where we may find Sir Beaumains."

"Fair lords," said Sir Ironside, "I cannot tell you, for he is very hard to find. For young knights such as he is, when they are on their adventures, never stay in any one place."

But as for the praise that the Red Knight of the Red Launds, and Sir Persant and his brother, gave Beaumains, it was a marvel to hear.

"Well, my fair lords," said King Arthur, "you may be sure I shall do you honour for the love of Sir Beaumains, and as soon as ever I meet him I shall make you all knights of the Round Table on one day. And as for you, Sir Persant of Inde, you have always been called a very noble knight, and so your three brothers have always been called. But I wonder," said the king, "that I hear nothing of the Black Knight, your brother. He was a very noble knight."

"Sir," said Pertolepe, the Green Knight, "Sir Beaumains killed him in an encounter with his spear. His name was Sir Percard."

"That was a great pity," said the king, and so said many knights. For these four brothers were very well known in King Arthur's court as noble knights, for they had long made war on the knights of the Round Table.

Then Pertolepe, the Green Knight, said to the king, "At a crossing of the water of Mortaise Sir Beaumains met two brothers who for the most part always kept that crossing, and they were two deadly knights. And there he killed the eldest brother in the water: he struck him on the head such a blow that he fell down in the water, and there he was drowned, and his name was Sir Gherard le Breusse. And afterwards he killed the other brother on the land, and his name was Sir Arnold le Breusse."

Chapter 25: How the Queen of Orkney came to this feast of Pentecost, and Sir Gawain and his brothers came to ask her blessing

So then the king and they went to their meal, and were served in the best way. And as they sat at the meal, the Queen of Orkney came in, with a great number of ladies and knights. And then Sir Gawain, Sir Agravain and Gaheris got up, and went to her and greeted her on their knees, and asked her blessing; for they had not seen her in fifteen years. Then she spoke out loud to her brother King Arthur: "What have you done with my young son Sir Gareth? He was here among you a twelvemonth, and you made a kitchen boy of him, which is a shame to you all. Alas, what have you done with my dear son, who was my joy and delight?"

"Oh, dear mother," said Sir Gawain, "I didn't know him."

"Nor I," said the king, "and I regret it now. But thanks be to God, he has proved as honourable a knight as any now living of his years, and I shall never be glad until I can find him."

"Ah, brother," said the queen to King Arthur, and to Sir Gawain, and to all her sons, "you brought great shame on yourselves when you kept my son among you in the kitchen and fed him like a poor hog."

"Fair sister," said King Arthur, "you may be quite sure I didn't know him, and no more did Sir Gawain, nor his brothers. But since it is so," said the king, "that he has gone away from us all like this, we must work out a way to find him. Also, sister, it seems to me you might have let me know of his coming, and then, if I had not treated him well, you might have blamed me. For when he came to this court he came leaning on two men's shoulders, as though he could not walk. And then he asked me for three gifts; and one he asked that same day, which was that I would give him enough food for that twelvemonth. And the other two gifts he asked that day a twelvemonth later, and those were that he might have the adventure of the damsel Linet, and the third, that Sir Lancelot should make him a knight when he asked him. And so I granted him all he wanted, and many in this court wondered that he asked for his keep for a twelvemonth. And from that, many of us judged that he did not come of a noble house."

"Sir," said the Queen of Orkney to King Arthur her brother, "believe me, I sent him to you very well armed and horsed, and handsomely turned out, and with plenty of gold and silver to spend."

"That may be," said the king, "but we saw none of it, except that on the same day he left us, knights told me that a dwarf suddenly came here, and brought him armour and a good horse, very well and richly equipped. And we all wondered where those riches came from, so that we all judged he came of honourable people."

"Brother," said the queen, "I believe all you say, for ever since he was grown he has been wonderfully clever, and he was always faithful and true to his promise. But I wonder," she said, "that Sir Kay mocked him and scorned him, and gave him that name Beaumains. Yet Sir Kay," said the queen, "named him more truly than he thought, for I dare say, if he is alive, he is as fair-handed a man, and as well made, as any man living."

"Sister," said Arthur, "let this talk be. By the grace of God he shall be found, if he is within these seven kingdoms. And let all this pass, and be merry, for he has proved himself a man of honour, and that is my joy."

Chapter 26: How King Arthur sent for the Lady Lionesse, and how she had a tournament proclaimed at her castle, where many knights came

Then Sir Gawain and his brothers said to Arthur, "Sir, if you will give us leave, we will go and look for our brother."

"No," said Sir Lancelot, "you won't need to do that." And so said Sir Baudwin of Britain. "For on our advice the king shall send a messenger to Dame Lionesse, and ask her to come to the court in all the haste she can, and have no doubt, she will come. And then she can give you the best advice on where you will find him."

"That is well said," said the king.

So then courteous letters were written, and the messenger sent off, and he travelled night and day until he came to the Castle Perilous. And then the lady, Dame Lionesse, was sent for where she was, with Sir Gringamore her brother and Sir Gareth. And when she understood this message, she told him to ride on his way to King Arthur, and she would come after in all fitting haste. Then, when she came to Sir Gringamore and to Sir Gareth, she told them all how King Arthur had sent for her.

"That is because of me," said Sir Gareth.

"Now advise me," said Dame Lionesse, "what I shall say, and how I shall conduct myself."

"My lady and my love," said Sir Gareth, "I beg you, on no account let it be known where I am. But I know well my mother is there, and all my brothers, and they will take it on themselves to look for me; I know very well they will. But this, madam, is what I would have you say, and advise the king, when he questions you about me. Then you may say that this is your advice: that, if it pleases his good grace, you will have it proclaimed, for the feast of the Assumption of our Lady, that whatever knight proves himself best there shall have you and all your land. And if it so happens that he is a married man, then his wife shall have the prize, and a circlet of gold set with stones of magic power, to the value of a thousand pounds, and a white gyrfalcon."

So Dame Lionesse set off and came to King Arthur, where she was nobly received, and there she was closely questioned by the king and by the Queen of Orkney. And she answered that she could not tell where Sir Gareth was. But this much she said to Arthur: "Sir, I will have a tournament proclaimed, to be held before my castle at the Assumption of our Lady, and the proclamation shall be this: that you, my lord Arthur, shall be there, and your knights, and I will see to it that my knights shall be against yours. And then I am sure you will hear of Sir Gareth."

"That is well thought out," said King Arthur; and so she left. And the king and she made great preparations for that tournament.

When Dame Lionesse had come to the Isle of Avalon, which was the same isle where her brother Sir Gringamore lived, then she told them all what she had done, and what promise she had made to King Arthur.

"Alas," said Sir Gareth, "I have been so unluckily wounded since I came into this castle, that I won't be able to perform like a knight at that tournament; for I have never been fully healed since I was hurt."

"Cheer up," said the damsel Linet, "for I undertake to make you whole within these fifteen days, and as vigorous as you ever were."

And then she laid an ointment and a salve on him, as she saw fit, so that he was never so fresh nor so vigorous. Then the damsel Linet said, "Send to Sir Persant of Inde, and summon him and his knights to be here with you, as they have promised. Also, send to Sir Ironside, who is the Red Knight of the Red Launds, and order him to be ready with you with his whole company of knights, and then you will be able to match King Arthur and his knights."

So this was done, and all the knights were sent for to the Castle Perilous. And then the Red Knight answered, and said to Dame Lionesse and to Sir Gareth, "Madam, and my lord Sir Gareth, you should know that I have been at King Arthur's court, and Sir Persant of Inde and his brothers too, and there we have done our homage as you commanded us."

Also Sir Ironside said, "I have undertaken, with Sir Persant of Inde and his brothers, to take sides against my lord Sir Lancelot and the knights of that court. And this I have done for the love of my lady Dame Lionesse, and of you, my lord Sir Gareth."

"You have done well," said Sir Gareth. "But believe me, you will be very hard matched against the noblest knights in the world. And so we must provide ourselves with good knights, wherever we can get them."

"That is well said," said Sir Persant, "and honourably."

And so the proclamation was made in England, Wales and Scotland, Ireland, Cornwall, and in all the Out Isles, and in Brittany and in many countries: that at the feast of the Assumption of our Lady next coming, men should come to the Castle Perilous beside the Isle of Avalon; and there all the knights who came should have the choice whether they wished to be on the one side, with the knights of the castle, or on the other side, with King Arthur. And it was two months to the day before the tournament was to be. And so many good knights came who were free of any lord, and for the most part they held against King Arthur and his knights of the Round Table, and came in on the side of those of the castle. For Sir Epinogrus was the first, and he was the son of the King of Northumberland; and Sir Palomides the Saracen was another, and Sir Safere his brother, and Sir Segwarides his brother, but they were christened; and Sir Malegrine another; and Sir Brian de les Isles, a noble knight; and Sir Grummore Grummursum, a good knight of Scotland; and Sir Carados of the Dolorous Tower, a noble knight; and Sir Turquine his brother; and Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, two brothers, good knights of Cornwall. There came Sir Tristram de Liones, and with him Sir Dinas the Seneschal, and Sir Sadok; but this Sir Tristram was not a knight of the Round Table at that time, but he was one of the best knights in the world. And so all these noble knights joined the lady of the castle, and the Red Knight of the Red Launds; but as for Sir Gareth, he would take on himself no more than any other ordinary knight.

Chapter 27: How King Arthur went to the tournament with his knights, and how the lady received him with honour, and how the knights met in combat

And then there came with King Arthur Sir Gawain, Agravain and Gaheris, his brothers. And then his nephews Sir Uwain le Blanchemains, and Sir Aglovale, Sir Tor, Sir Percival de Galis, and Sir Lamorak de Galis. Then came Sir Lancelot du Lake with his brothers, nephews and cousins, such as Sir Lionel, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Bors de Ganis, and Sir Galihodin, Sir Galihud, and many more of Sir Lancelot's blood; and Sir Dinadan, Sir La Cote Male Taile, his brother, a good knight, and Sir Sagramore, a good knight; and the greater part of the Round Table. Also there came with King Arthur these knights: the King of Ireland, King Agwisance, and the King of Scotland, King Carados, and King Uriens of the land of Gore, and King Bagdemagus and his son Sir Meliagaunce, and Sir Galahalt the noble prince. All these kings, princes and earls, barons and other noble knights, such as Sir Brandiles, Sir Uwain les Avoutres, and Sir Kay, Sir Bedivere, Sir Meliot de Logres, Sir Petipase of Winchelsea, Sir Godelake: all these came with King Arthur, and more than can be listed.

Now we leave these kings and knights, and let us speak of the great preparations that were made inside the castle and around the castle for both sides. The Lady Dame Lionesse made great preparations on her side for her noble knights, with every kind of lodging and food, coming by land and by water, so that nothing was lacking for her side, nor for the other; but there was plenty to be had for gold and silver for King Arthur and his knights. And then King Arthur's harbingers came, the officers sent ahead to find lodging for him and his kings, dukes, earls, barons and knights. And then Sir Gareth begged Dame Lionesse and the Red Knight of the Red Launds, and Sir Persant and his brother, and Sir Gringamore, that on no account should any of them tell his name, and that they should make no more of him than of the least knight there. "For," he said, "I will not be known by anyone, great or small, neither at the beginning nor at the end."

Then Dame Lionesse said to Sir Gareth, "Sir, I will lend you a ring, but I would beg you, as you love me with all your heart, to let me have it back when the tournament is over, for that ring makes me much more beautiful than I am by nature. And the power of my ring is this: what is green it will turn to red, and what is red it will turn in likeness to green, and what is blue it will turn to the likeness of white, and what is white it will turn in likeness to blue, and so it will do with every kind of colour. Also, whoever wears my ring shall lose no blood. And for great love I will give you this ring."

"Many thanks, my own lady," said Sir Gareth, "for this ring suits me exceedingly well, for it will change every likeness I am in, and that will make sure I am not known."

Then Sir Gringamore gave Sir Gareth a bay warhorse that was an exceedingly good horse; and he also gave him good, sound armour, and a noble sword that Sir Gringamore's father had once won from a heathen tyrant. And so every knight made himself ready for that tournament. And King Arthur had come two days before the Assumption of our Lady. And there was every kind of royal show, with all the minstrelsy that could be found. Also Queen Guinevere came, and the Queen of Orkney, Sir Gareth's mother.

And on the day of the Assumption, when mass and matins were done, the heralds with trumpets were commanded to sound to the field. And so Sir Epinogrus, the son of the King of Northumberland, came out from the castle, and Sir Sagramore le Desirous met him, and each of them broke his spear right to his hand. And then Sir Palomides came in out of the castle, and Gawain met him, and each of them struck the other so hard that both the good knights and their horses fell to the earth. And then knights of each side rescued their knights. And then Sir Safere and Sir Segwarides came in, brothers to Sir Palomides; and there Sir Agravain met Sir Safere, and Sir Gaheris met Sir Segwarides. So Sir Safere struck down Agravain, Sir Gawain's brother; and so did Sir Segwarides, Sir Safere's brother. And Sir Malegrine, a knight of the castle, met Sir Uwain le Blanchemains, and there Sir Uwain gave Sir Malegrine such a fall that he almost broke his neck.

Chapter 28: How the knights bore themselves in the battle

Then Sir Brian de les Isles and Grummore Grummursum, knights of the castle, met Sir Aglovale and Sir Tor, and Sir Tor struck Sir Grummore Grummursum down to the ground. Then Sir Carados of the Dolorous Tower and Sir Turquine, knights of the castle, came in; and against them came Sir Percival de Galis and Sir Lamorak de Galis, who were two brothers. And there Sir Percival met Sir Carados, and each of them broke his spear right up to his hand; and then Sir Turquine met Sir Lamorak, and each of them struck the other down to the ground, horse and all, and each side rescued its man and got them on horseback again. And Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights of the castle, met Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay, and these four knights came together mightily, and broke their spears right up to their hands. Then Sir Tristram, Sir Sadok and Sir Dinas, knights of the castle, came in, and there Sir Tristram met Sir Bedivere, and there Sir Bedivere was struck to the ground, both horse and man. And Sir Sadok met Sir Petipase, and there Sir Sadok was unhorsed. And there Uwain les Avoutres struck down Sir Dinas, the Seneschal. Then Sir Persant of Inde, a knight of the castle, came in, and against him came Sir Lancelot du Lake, and there he struck Sir Persant to the ground, horse and man. Then Sir Pertolepe came from the castle, and against him came Sir Lionel, and there Sir Pertolepe, the Green Knight, struck down Sir Lionel, Sir Lancelot's brother. All this was noted by noble heralds, who bore himself best, and their names.

And then Sir Perimones, the Red Knight, Sir Persant's brother, who was a knight of the castle, came into the field, and he met Sir Ector de Maris, and each struck the other so hard that both their horses and they themselves fell to the ground. And then the Red Knight of the Red Launds and Sir Gareth came in from the castle, and against them came Sir Bors de Ganis and Sir Bleoberis; and there the Red Knight and Sir Bors struck each other so hard that their spears burst, and their horses fell grovelling to the ground. Then Sir Bleoberis broke his spear on Sir Gareth, but from that stroke Sir Bleoberis fell to the ground. When Sir Galihodin saw that, he told Sir Gareth to defend himself, and Sir Gareth struck him to the ground. Then Sir Galihud got a spear to avenge his brother, and Sir Gareth served him the same way, and Sir Dinadan and his brother La Cote Male Taile, and Sir Sagramore le Desirous, and Sir Dodinas le Savage. All these he bore down with one spear.

When King Agwisance of Ireland saw Sir Gareth go on like this, he wondered who he could be, who one time seemed green, and another time, when he came back again, seemed blue. And so at every course that he rode to and fro he changed his colour, so that neither king nor knight could readily recognise him. Then Sir Agwisance, the King of Ireland, met Sir Gareth, and there Sir Gareth struck him from his horse, saddle and all. And then King Carados of Scotland came, and Sir Gareth struck him down, horse and man. And he served King Uriens of the land of Gore the same way. And then Sir Bagdemagus came in, and Sir Gareth struck him to the ground, horse and man. And Bagdemagus's son, Meliagaunce, broke a spear on Sir Gareth mightily and like a true knight. And then Sir Galahalt, the noble prince, called out loud, "Knight with the many colours, you have jousted well! Now make yourself ready, so that I can joust with you."

Sir Gareth heard him, and he got a great spear, and so they met, and there the prince broke his spear; but Sir Gareth struck him on the left side of the helm, so that he reeled this way and that, and he would have fallen if his men had not caught him.

"God help me," said King Arthur, "that same knight with the many colours is a good knight."

So the king called Sir Lancelot to him, and asked him to joust with that knight.

"Sir," said Lancelot, "I can well find it in my heart to leave him alone this time, for he has had labour enough today. And when a good knight does so well on a given day, it is no good knight's part to rob him of his honour, especially when he sees a knight has done such great labour. For perhaps," said Sir Lancelot, "his quarrel lies here today, and perhaps he is the best loved by this lady of all who are here; for I can see well that he strains and drives himself to do great deeds. And therefore," said Sir Lancelot, "as far as I am concerned, he shall have the honour today. Even if it lay in my power to take it from him, I would not."

Chapter 29: More of the same tournament

Then, when this was done, swords were drawn, and then a hard tournament began. And there Sir Lamorak did marvellous deeds of arms; and between Sir Lamorak and Sir Ironside, who was the Red Knight of the Red Launds, there was a strong fight; and between Sir Palomides and Bleoberis there was a strong fight; and Sir Gawain and Sir Tristram met, and there Sir Gawain had the worst of it, for Sir Tristram pulled Sir Gawain from his horse, and there he was a long while on foot, and trampled. Then Sir Lancelot came in, and he struck Sir Turquine, and Sir Turquine him; and then his brother Sir Carados came, and both at once they attacked him, and he, as the noblest knight in the world, fought both of them honourably, so that all men wondered at the nobility of Sir Lancelot. And then Sir Gareth came in, and saw that it was Sir Lancelot who was fighting the two dangerous knights. And then Sir Gareth came up on his good horse and drove them apart, and he would not strike a single stroke at Sir Lancelot. Sir Lancelot noticed that, and judged that it must be the good knight Sir Gareth. And then Sir Gareth rode here and there, and struck on the right hand and on the left, and all the people could easily see where he rode. And by chance he met his brother Sir Gawain, and there he got the better of Sir Gawain, for he knocked off his helm; and he served five or six knights of the Round Table the same way, so that all men said he took the most pains, and did his duty best.

For when Sir Tristram watched how he first jousted and afterwards fought so well with a sword, he rode to Sir Ironside and to Sir Persant of Inde, and asked them, by their faith, "What sort of knight is that knight over there, who appears in so many different colours? Truly, it seems to me," said Tristram, "that he puts himself to great pains, for he never stops."

"Don't you know who he is?" said Sir Ironside.

"No," said Sir Tristram.

"Then you shall know that this is the one who loves the lady of the castle, and she loves him in return; and this is the one who beat me when I besieged the lady of this castle, and this is the one who beat Sir Persant of Inde and his three brothers."

"What is his name," said Sir Tristram, "and what blood does he come of?"

"At King Arthur's court he was called Beaumains, but his true name is Sir Gareth of Orkney, Sir Gawain's brother."

"On my life," said Sir Tristram, "he is a good knight, and a great man of arms, and if he is young he will prove a very noble knight."

"He is only a boy," they all said, "and he was made a knight by Sir Lancelot."

"Then he is all the better for it," said Tristram.

And then Sir Tristram, Sir Ironside, Sir Persant and his brother rode together to help Sir Gareth; and then many strong strokes were given.

And then Sir Gareth rode out to one side to mend his helm; and then his dwarf said, "Give me your ring, so that you don't lose it while you drink."

And so, when he had drunk, he put on his helm, and eagerly took his horse and rode into the field, and left his ring with his dwarf; and the dwarf was glad the ring was off him, for then he knew very well that he would be recognised. And then, when Sir Gareth was in the field, all the people saw him well and plainly, that he was in yellow colours; and there he tore off helms and pulled down knights, so that King Arthur wondered what knight he was, for the king saw by his hair that it was the same knight.

Chapter 30: How Sir Gareth was spotted by the heralds, and how he slipped away from the field

But before, he had been in so many colours, and now he was in only one colour, and that was yellow.

"Now go," said King Arthur to several heralds, "and ride around him, and find out what sort of knight he is, for I have asked many knights today who are on his side, and they all say they don't know him."

And so a herald rode as near Gareth as he could, and there he saw written around his helm in gold: "This helm is Sir Gareth of Orkney's."

Then the herald shouted like a madman, and many heralds with him, "This is Sir Gareth of Orkney in the yellow arms!" At this all of Arthur's kings and knights looked at him and watched him; and then they all pressed forward to see him, and all the while the heralds shouted, "This is Sir Gareth of Orkney, King Lot's son!"

And when Sir Gareth saw that he had been found out, he doubled his strokes, and struck down Sir Sagramore, and his brother Sir Gawain.

"Oh, brother," said Sir Gawain, "I thought you would not have struck me."

So when he heard him say that, he pushed his way here and there, and so with great difficulty he got out of the thick of the crowd, and there he met his dwarf.

"Oh, boy," said Sir Gareth, "you've played me a foul trick today, keeping my ring. Give it back to me at once, so that I can hide myself with it."

And so he gave it to him. And then none of them knew what had become of him; but Sir Gawain had more or less seen where Sir Gareth rode, and he rode after him with all his might. Sir Gareth noticed that, and rode swiftly into the forest, so that Sir Gawain did not know what had become of him. And when Sir Gareth knew that Sir Gawain had gone by, he asked the dwarf for his best advice.

"Sir," said the dwarf, "it seems to me it would be best, now that you have escaped from being spied on, that you send my lady Dame Lionesse her ring."

"That's good advice," said Sir Gareth. "Now take it here and carry it to her, and say that I commend myself to her good grace, and tell her I will come when I can, and I beg her to be true and faithful to me as I will be to her."

"Sir," said the dwarf, "it shall be done as you command."

And so he rode on his way, and did his errand to the lady. Then she said, "Where is my knight, Sir Gareth?"

"Madam," said the dwarf, "he told me to say that he would not be long away from you."

And so the dwarf came back swiftly to Sir Gareth, who would very gladly have had a lodging, for he needed rest. And then there came thunder and rain, as if heaven and earth were coming together. And Sir Gareth was more than a little weary, for all that day he had had very little rest, neither his horse nor he. So this Sir Gareth rode on in that forest until night came. And all the while it lightened and thundered, as if it had gone mad. At last by chance he came to a castle, and there he heard the watchmen on the walls.

Chapter 31: How Sir Gareth came to a castle where he was well lodged, and jousted with a knight and slew him

Then Sir Gareth rode up to the gate-tower of the castle, and asked the porter politely to let him into the castle. The porter answered him rudely, and said, "You'll get no lodging here."

"Fair sir, don't say that, for I am a knight of King Arthur's; and I beg the lord or the lady of this castle to give me shelter for the love of King Arthur."

Then the porter went to the duchess, and told her that there was a knight of King Arthur's who wanted shelter.

"Let him in," said the duchess, "for I want to see that knight, and for King Arthur's sake he shall not be without shelter."

Then she went up into a tower over the gate, with a great blaze of torches. When Sir Gareth saw that torchlight he called out loud, "Whether you are lord or lady, giant or champion, I care nothing for that, so long as I may have shelter tonight. And if it happens that I must fight, don't spare me tomorrow morning when I have rested, for both I and my horse are weary."

"Sir knight," said the lady, "you speak like a knight, and boldly. But you may be sure that the lord of this castle does not love King Arthur, nor anyone of his court, for my lord has always been against him. And therefore you would do better not to come into this castle; for if you come in tonight, you must come in on these terms: that wherever you meet my lord, by path or by road, you must yield yourself to him as his prisoner."

"Madam," said Sir Gareth, "who is your lord, and what is his name?"

"Sir, my lord's name is the Duke de la Rowse."

"Well, madam," said Sir Gareth, "I promise you that wherever I meet your lord I will yield myself to him and to his good grace, on the understanding that he will do me no harm. And if I find that he means to, I will free myself if I can, with my spear and my sword."

"You speak well," said the duchess.

And then she had the drawbridge let down, and so he rode into the hall, and there he dismounted, and his horse was led into a stable. And in the hall he took off his armour, and said, "Madam, I will not stir out of this hall tonight; and when it is daylight, whoever wants to fight me will find me ready."

Then he was seated at supper, and had many good dishes. Then Sir Gareth had a fine appetite, and he ate his food like a knight, and eagerly. There were many fair ladies near him, and some said they had never seen a finer-looking man, nor one who ate so well. Then they gave him an exceedingly warm welcome, and soon, when he had had his supper, his bed was made up there; so he rested all night.

And in the morning he heard mass, and broke his fast, and took his leave of the duchess and of them all, and thanked her graciously for his lodging and for his good welcome. And then she asked him his name.

"Madam," he said, "truly my name is Gareth of Orkney, and some men call me Beaumains."

Then she knew well that it was the same knight who had fought for Dame Lionesse. So Sir Gareth left, and rode up onto a mountain, and there a knight met him, whose name was Sir Bendelaine, and he said to Sir Gareth, "You won't pass this way. Either you joust with me, or you're my prisoner."

"Then I will joust," said Sir Gareth.

And so they let their horses run, and there Sir Gareth struck him clean through the body; and Sir Bendelaine rode on to his castle near by, and there he died. So Sir Gareth, wanting to rest, came riding up to Bendelaine's castle. Then his knights and servants saw that it was he who had killed their lord. Then they armed twenty good men, and came out and attacked Sir Gareth; and he had no spear, only his sword, and he set his shield in front of him; and there they broke their spears on him, and they attacked him exceedingly hard. But all the while Sir Gareth defended himself like a knight.

Chapter 32: How Sir Gareth fought a knight who held thirty ladies in his castle, and how he slew him

So when they saw that they could not overcome him, they rode away from him, and decided among themselves to kill his horse; and so they came in on Sir Gareth, and with spears they killed his horse, and then they attacked him hard. But when he was on foot, there was not one he fought whom he did not give such a blow that he never recovered. So he killed them one by one until there were only four, and then they fled; and Sir Gareth took a good horse that was one of theirs, and rode on his way.

Then he rode at a great pace until he came to a castle, and there he heard a great mourning of ladies and gentlewomen. So a page came by him.

"What is this noise," said Sir Gareth, "that I hear inside this castle?"

"Sir knight," said the page, "there are thirty ladies inside this castle, and all of them are widows; for there is a knight who lies in wait every day outside this castle, and his name is the Brown Knight without Pity, and he is the most dangerous knight alive now. And therefore, sir," said the page, "I advise you to flee."

"No," said Sir Gareth, "I will not flee, though you are afraid of him."

And then the page saw the Brown Knight coming. "Look," said the page, "there he comes."

"Let me deal with him," said Sir Gareth.

And when each caught sight of the other they let their horses run, and the Brown Knight broke his spear, and Sir Gareth struck him clean through the body, so that he threw him to the ground stone dead. So Sir Gareth rode into the castle, and asked the ladies if he might rest there.

"Alas," said the ladies, "you cannot be lodged here."

"Give him a good welcome," said the page, "for this knight has killed your enemy."

Then they all gave him as good a welcome as lay in their power. But you may be sure they gave him a good welcome only as they could, for they could do no better, for they were poor.

And so in the morning he went to mass, and there he saw the thirty ladies kneeling, and lying grovelling on various tombs, grieving greatly and sorrowing. Then Sir Gareth knew well that their lords lay in the tombs.

"Fair ladies," said Sir Gareth, "you must be at King Arthur's court at the next feast of Pentecost, and say that I, Sir Gareth, sent you there."

"We shall do this," said the ladies.

So he left, and by chance he came to a mountain, and there he found a fine-looking knight who called to him, "Stop, sir knight, and joust with me."

"Who are you?" said Sir Gareth.

"My name," he said, "is the Duke de la Rowse."

"Ah, sir, you are the same knight in whose castle I once lodged; and there I promised your lady that I would yield myself to you."

"Ah," said the duke, "so you're that proud knight who offers to fight my knights? Then make yourself ready, for I will fight you."

So they let their horses run, and there Sir Gareth struck the duke down from his horse. But the duke swiftly got clear of his horse, and set his shield and drew his sword, and told Sir Gareth to dismount and fight with him. So he did dismount, and they fought a great fight together for more than an hour, and each wounded the other very badly. At last Sir Gareth got the duke to the ground, and would have killed him, and then he yielded to him.

"Then you must go," said Sir Gareth, "to Sir Arthur my lord at the next feast, and say that I, Sir Gareth of Orkney, sent you to him."

"It shall be done," said the duke, "and I will do homage and fealty to you, with a hundred knights with me; and all the days of my life I will do you service wherever you command me."

Chapter 33: How Sir Gareth and Sir Gawain fought each other, and how they recognised each other through the damsel Linet

So the duke left, and Sir Gareth stood there alone; and there he saw an armed knight coming towards him. Then Sir Gareth took the duke's shield, and mounted his horse, and so without waiting they ran together as if it had been thunder. And there that knight wounded Sir Gareth in the side with his spear. And then they dismounted and drew their swords, and gave such great strokes that the blood ran trailing to the ground. And so they fought for two hours.

At last the damsel Linet came, whom some men called the Damsel Savage, and she came riding on an ambling mule; and there she cried out loud, "Sir Gawain, Sir Gawain, stop fighting your brother Sir Gareth!"

And when he heard her say so, he threw away his shield and his sword, and ran to Sir Gareth, and took him in his arms, and then knelt down and begged his pardon.

"Who are you," said Sir Gareth, "who just now were so strong and so mighty, and now so suddenly yield to me?"

"Oh, Gareth, I am your brother Sir Gawain, who has had great sorrow and labour for your sake."

Then Sir Gareth unlaced his helm, and knelt down to him, and begged his pardon. Then they both rose, and embraced each other in their arms, and wept a long while before they could speak, and each of them gave the other the prize of the fight. And there were many kind words between them.

"Alas, my fair brother," said Sir Gawain, "by God, I ought by rights to honour you even if you were not my brother, for you have done honour to King Arthur and all his court, for in this twelvemonth you have sent him more honourable knights than six of the best of the Round Table have done, except Sir Lancelot."

Then the Damsel Savage came up, who was the Lady Linet, who had ridden with Sir Gareth so long, and there she staunched Sir Gareth's wounds and Sir Gawain's.

"Now what will you do?" said the Damsel Savage. "It seems to me it would be well if Arthur knew about you both, for your horses are so bruised that they cannot carry you."

"Now, fair damsel," said Sir Gawain, "I beg you to ride to my lord my uncle, King Arthur, and tell him what has happened to me here, and I expect he will not be long in coming."

Then she took her mule, and swiftly she came to King Arthur, who was only two miles from there. And when she had told him the news, the king had a palfrey brought for him. And when he was on its back he told the lords and ladies to come after, whoever wished; and there was saddling and bridling of queens' horses and princes' horses, and lucky was the one who could be ready soonest.

So when the king came to where they were, he saw Sir Gawain and Sir Gareth sitting on a little hillside, and then the king got down from his horse. And when he came near Sir Gareth he tried to speak but could not; and with that he sank down in a faint for gladness. And so they leapt up and went to their uncle, and begged him of his good grace to take comfort. Believe me, the king rejoiced greatly, and many a pitiful lament he made to Sir Gareth, and all the while he wept like a child. With that his mother came, the Queen of Orkney, Dame Morgause, and when she saw Sir Gareth plainly face to face she could not weep, but suddenly fell down in a faint, and lay there a long while as if she were dead. And then Sir Gareth comforted his mother in such a way that she recovered and grew cheerful. Then the king commanded that all the knights who were under his rule should make their lodging right there, for the love of his nephews. And so it was done, and every kind of provision was supplied, so that nothing was lacking that could be got, tame or wild, for gold or silver. And then, through the care of the Damsel Savage, Sir Gawain and Sir Gareth were healed of their wounds; and there they stayed eight days.

Then King Arthur said to the Damsel Savage, "I wonder that your sister, Dame Lionesse, does not come here to me, and especially that she does not come to visit her knight, my nephew Sir Gareth, who has had so much labour for her love."

"My lord," said the damsel Linet, "of your good grace you must hold her excused, for she does not know that my lord, Sir Gareth, is here."

"Go for her, then," said King Arthur, "so that we can settle what is best to be done, according to the wishes of my nephew."

"Sir," said the damsel, "that shall be done."

And so she rode to her sister. And as swiftly as she could, Dame Lionesse made herself ready; and she came in the morning with her brother Sir Gringamore, and with her forty knights. And so when she had come she had all the welcome that could be given, both from the king and from many other kings and queens.

Chapter 34: How Sir Gareth acknowledged to King Arthur that he and Dame Lionesse loved each other, and of the arrangements for their wedding

And among all these ladies she was named the fairest, and without equal. Then, when Sir Gareth saw her, there were many fond looks and fond words, so that all men of honour were glad to see them. Then King Arthur came, and many other kings, and Dame Guinevere, and the Queen of Orkney. And there the king asked his nephew, Sir Gareth, whether he would have that lady as his lover, or have her as his wife.

"My lord, you may be sure that I love her above all ladies living."

"Now, fair lady," said King Arthur, "what do you say?"

"Most noble king," said Dame Lionesse, "you may be sure that I would rather have and hold my lord Sir Gareth as my husband than any king or prince who is christened; and if I cannot have him, I promise you I will never have anyone. For, my lord Arthur," said Dame Lionesse, "believe me, he is my first love, and he shall be the last; and if you will allow him his will and free choice, I dare say he will have me."

"That is the truth," said Sir Gareth. "If I do not have you, and hold you as my wife, no lady or gentlewoman will ever gladden me."

"What, nephew," said the king, "is that the way the wind blows? Believe me, I would not for the loss of my crown be the cause of parting your hearts; and you may be sure you cannot love so well that I will not rather increase it than hinder it. And you shall also have my love and my lordship in the fullest way that lies in my power."

And Sir Gareth's mother said the same.

Then provision was made for the day of the marriage; and on the king's advice it was arranged that it should be at the following Michaelmas, at Kink Kenadon by the seaside, for that is a plentiful country. And so it was proclaimed in every place throughout the realm. And then Sir Gareth sent his summons to all those knights and ladies whom he had won in battle before, that they should be at his wedding day at Kink Kenadon by the sands.

And then Dame Lionesse, and the damsel Linet, with Sir Gringamore, rode to their castle; and she gave Sir Gareth a fine and rich ring, and he gave her another. And King Arthur gave her a rich rosary of gold beads; and so she left.

And King Arthur and his fellowship rode towards Kink Kenadon, and Sir Gareth escorted his lady on her way, and so came back to the king again and rode with him.

Lord, what a welcome Sir Lancelot gave Sir Gareth, and he him! For there was never any knight Sir Gareth loved so well as he did Sir Lancelot, and he would nearly always be in Sir Lancelot's company. For after Sir Gareth had seen what Sir Gawain's character was, he withdrew himself from his brother Sir Gawain's fellowship, for he was vengeful, and where he hated he would be avenged by murder; and Sir Gareth hated that.

Chapter 35: Of the great splendour, and what officers were appointed at the wedding feast, and of the jousts at the feast

So Michaelmas drew near; and Dame Lionesse, the lady of the Castle Perilous, came there, and her sister, Dame Linet, with Sir Gringamore, her brother, with them, for he had the escorting of these ladies. And there they were lodged as King Arthur arranged. And on Michaelmas Day the Bishop of Canterbury performed the wedding between Sir Gareth and the Lady Lionesse with great solemnity. And King Arthur had Gaheris marry the Damsel Savage, who was Dame Linet; and King Arthur had Sir Agravain marry Dame Lionesse's niece, a fair lady, whose name was Dame Laurel.

And so, when this ceremony was done, the Green Knight, Sir Pertolepe, came in with thirty knights, and there he did homage and fealty to Sir Gareth, and these knights were to hold their lands of him for evermore. Sir Pertolepe also said, "I beg you that at this feast I may be your chamberlain."

"Willingly," said Sir Gareth, "since it pleases you to take so humble an office."

Then the Red Knight came in, with sixty knights with him, and did homage and fealty to Sir Gareth, and all those knights were to hold their lands of him for evermore. And then this Sir Perimones asked Sir Gareth to grant that he might be his chief butler at that high feast.

"Gladly," said Sir Gareth, "you shall have this office, and a better one if it were mine to give."

Then Sir Persant of Inde came in, with a hundred knights with him, and there he did homage and fealty, and all his knights were to do him service, and hold their lands of him for ever; and there he asked Sir Gareth to make him his chief sewer at the feast, the officer who sets the dishes on the table and tastes them.

"Gladly," said Sir Gareth, "you shall have it, and a better one if it were mine to give."

Then the Duke de la Rowse came, with a hundred knights with him, and there he did homage and fealty to Sir Gareth, and so they were to hold their lands of him for ever. And he asked Sir Gareth that he might serve him the wine on that day of the feast.

"Gladly," said Sir Gareth, "and a better office if it were mine to give."

Then the Red Knight of the Red Launds came in, who was Sir Ironside, and he brought three hundred knights with him, and there he did homage and fealty, and all these knights were to hold their lands of him for ever. And then he asked Sir Gareth to be his carver.

"Gladly," said Sir Gareth, "if it pleases you."

Then thirty ladies came into the court, and all of them looked like widows, and those thirty ladies brought many fair gentlewomen with them. And all of them knelt down at once before King Arthur and Sir Gareth, and there all those ladies told the king how Sir Gareth had freed them from the Dolorous Tower, and killed the Brown Knight without Pity: "And therefore we, and our heirs for evermore, will do homage to Sir Gareth of Orkney."

So then the kings and queens, princes and earls, barons and many bold knights, went to their meal; and you may well believe there was every kind of food in plenty, every kind of revel and game, with every kind of minstrelsy that was used in those days. There were also great jousts for three days. But the king would not allow Sir Gareth to joust, because of his new bride; for, as the French book says, Dame Lionesse asked the king that no one who was married should joust at that feast.

So on the first day Sir Lamorak de Galis jousted, for he unhorsed thirty knights, and did exceedingly marvellous deeds of arms; and then King Arthur made Sir Persant and his two brothers Knights of the Round Table to their lives' end, and gave them great lands. On the second day Tristram jousted best, and he unhorsed forty knights, and did marvellous deeds of arms there. And there King Arthur made Ironside, who was the Red Knight of the Red Launds, a Knight of the Round Table to his life's end, and gave him great lands. On the third day Sir Lancelot du Lake jousted, and he unhorsed fifty knights, and did many marvellous deeds of arms, so that all men wondered at him. And there King Arthur made the Duke de la Rowse a Knight of the Round Table to his life's end, and gave him great lands to live on. But when these jousts were done, Sir Lamorak and Sir Tristram left suddenly, and would not make themselves known, at which King Arthur and all the court were greatly displeased. And so they held the court forty days with great solemnity. And this Sir Gareth was a noble knight, and a well-governed one, and well-spoken.

Thus ends this tale of Sir Gareth of Orkney, who married Dame Lionesse of the Castle Perilous. And Sir Gaheris also married her sister, Dame Linet, who was called the Damsel Savage. And Sir Agravain married Dame Laurel, a fair lady and a great one; and King Arthur gave great riches and mighty lands with them, so that they might live royally to their lives' end.

Here follows the eighth book, which is the first book of Sir Tristram de Liones, and tells who his father and his mother were, and how he was born and brought up, and how he was made a knight.

Book Eight: The Birth and Deeds of Sir Tristram

Chapter 1: How Sir Tristram de Liones was born, and how his mother died when he was born, and why she named him Tristram

There was a king called Meliodas, and he was lord and king of the country of Liones, and this Meliodas was as fine a knight as any living at that time. And as fortune had it he married King Mark of Cornwall's sister, and she was called Elizabeth, and she was said to be both good and beautiful. And at that time King Arthur reigned, and he was king of all England, Wales and Scotland, and of many other realms. Yet there were many kings who were lords of many countries, but they all held their lands from King Arthur; for in Wales there were two kings, and in the north there were many kings, and in Cornwall and in the west there were two kings; also in Ireland there were two or three kings, and all of them were under the rule of King Arthur. So was the King of France, and the King of Brittany, and all the lordships as far as Rome.

So when this King Meliodas had been with his wife, within a while she was big with child, and she was a very gentle lady, and she loved her lord well, and he loved her in return, so there was great joy between them. Now there was a lady in that country who had long loved King Meliodas, and by no means could she ever win his love. So one day, as King Meliodas rode hunting, for he was a great huntsman, she had it arranged that by an enchantment she made him chase a hart by himself alone, until he came to an old castle, and there at once he was taken prisoner by the lady who loved him. When Elizabeth, King Meliodas' wife, missed her lord, she was nearly out of her mind, and big with child as she was, she took a gentlewoman with her and ran into the forest to look for her lord. And when she was far into the forest she could go no farther, for her labour came on her fast. And she had many terrible pains; her gentlewoman helped her all she could, and so by a miracle of Our Lady of Heaven she was delivered, with great pain. But she had taken such a chill for lack of help that the deep pull of death took her, so that she must die and leave this world; there was no help for it.

And when this Queen Elizabeth saw that there was no help for it, she grieved greatly, and said to her gentlewoman, "When you see my lord, King Meliodas, commend me to him, and tell him what pains I suffer here for his love, and how I must die here for his sake for lack of good help; and let him know that I am very sorry to leave this world and him, and so beg him to be a friend to my soul. Now let me see my little child, for whom I have had all this sorrow."

And when she saw him she said this: "Ah, my little son, you have murdered your mother, and so I think that you, who are a murderer so young, are very likely to be a valiant man when you are grown. And because I shall die of giving birth to you, I charge you, gentlewoman, to beg my lord, King Meliodas, that when he is christened he have him named Tristram, which is as much as to say a sorrowful birth."

And with that the queen gave up the ghost and died. Then the gentlewoman laid her in the shade of a great tree, and then she wrapped the child as well as she could against the cold. Just then the barons came, following after the queen, and when they saw that she was dead, and took it for certain that the king was dead too, then some of them would have killed the child, because they wanted to be lords of the country of Liones.

Chapter 2: How Sir Tristram's stepmother prepared poison to poison Sir Tristram

But then, through the fair speech of the gentlewoman and the efforts she made, most of the barons would not agree to it. And then they had the dead queen carried home, and there was much grieving for her.

Then in the meantime Merlin freed King Meliodas from prison, on the morning after his queen died. And so when the king came home most of the barons rejoiced greatly. But the sorrow the king felt for his queen, no tongue could tell. So then the king had her buried richly, and afterwards he had his child christened as his wife had commanded before her death. And then he had him named Tristram, the sorrowful-born child. Then King Meliodas lived seven years without a wife, and all this time Tristram was well brought up. Then it happened that King Meliodas married King Howell of Brittany's daughter, and soon she had children by King Meliodas. Then she was downcast and angry that her children would not inherit the country of Liones, and so this queen planned to poison young Tristram. So she had poison put in a silver cup in the room where Tristram and her children were together, intending that when Tristram was thirsty he should drink that drink. And so it happened one day that the queen's son, while he was in that room, saw the cup with the poison, and he thought it was good drink, and because the child was thirsty he took the cup with the poison and drank deeply; and with that the child suddenly burst and was dead.

When the queen of Meliodas learned of her son's death, you may be sure she was downcast. But still the king knew nothing of her treason. All the same the queen would not give this up, but she had more poison prepared again, and put it in a cup. And as fortune had it King Meliodas, her husband, found the cup with the wine where the poison was, and since he was very thirsty he took the cup to drink from it. And as he was about to drink from it the queen saw him, and then she ran to him and snatched the cup from him. The king wondered why she did so, and remembered how her son had been suddenly killed with poison. And then he took her by the hand and said, "You lying traitress, you will tell me what kind of drink this is, or I will kill you."

And with that he drew his sword, and swore a great oath that he would kill her unless she told him the truth.

"Ah, mercy, my lord," she said, "and I will tell you everything."

And then she told him why she had wanted to kill Tristram: so that her children would inherit his land.

"Well," said King Meliodas, "then you shall have the law."

And so she was condemned to be burned, with the agreement of the barons. And then a great fire was made, and just as she was at the fire to be executed, young Tristram knelt before King Meliodas and begged him to grant him a favour.

"Gladly," said the king.

Then young Tristram said, "Give me the life of your queen, my stepmother."

"That is wrongly asked," said King Meliodas, "for by rights you ought to hate her, since she would have killed you with that poison if she could have had her way; and it is mostly for your sake that I want her to die."

"Sir," said Tristram, "as for that, I beg you of your mercy to forgive her for it. And as for my part, may God forgive her, and I do. And since it pleased your highness to grant me my favour, for the love of God I ask you to keep your promise."

"Since that is how it is," said the king, "I will that you have her life." Then the king said, "I give her to you; go to the fire and take her, and do with her what you will."

So Sir Tristram went to the fire, and by the king's command saved her from death. But after that King Meliodas would never have anything to do with her, at bed or at table. But through young Tristram's good offices he made the king and her reconciled. But then the king would not allow young Tristram to stay any longer at his court.

Chapter 3: How Sir Tristram was sent to France with a tutor named Gouvernail, and how he learned to play the harp, to hawk, and to hunt

And then he appointed a gentleman who was well learned and well taught, and his name was Gouvernail; and then he sent young Tristram with Gouvernail into France, to learn the language, and good manners, and deeds of arms. And Tristram was there more than seven years. And then, when he could speak the language well, and had learned all that he could learn in that country, he came home again to his father, King Meliodas. And so Tristram learned to be a harper beyond all others, so that there was none like him in any country, and so in his youth he set himself to learn the harp and instruments of music.

And afterwards, as he grew in might and strength, he worked always at hunting and hawking, more than any gentleman we ever heard read of. And as the book says, he devised the proper horn calls for the beasts of the hunt (the great game of venery, the lesser beasts of the chase, and every kind of vermin), and all these terms of hawking and hunting we still have. And that is why the book of hunting and hawking is called the book of Sir Tristram. So, it seems to me, all gentlemen who bear ancient coats of arms ought by rights to honour Sir Tristram for the fine terms that gentlemen have and use, and will use until the Day of Judgement, so that by them, in a way, all men of honour can tell a gentleman from a yeoman, and a yeoman from a peasant. For the man who is well-born will be drawn to well-born ways, and will follow the customs of noble gentlemen.

So Sir Tristram lived in Cornwall until he was big and strong, eighteen years old. And then King Meliodas had great joy of Sir Tristram, and so did the queen, his wife. For ever after, all her life, because Sir Tristram had saved her from the fire, she never hated him again, but loved him always, and gave Tristram many great gifts; for people of every rank loved him, wherever he went.

Chapter 4: How Sir Marhaus came over from Ireland to demand tribute from Cornwall, or else to fight for it

Then it happened that King Anguish of Ireland sent to King Mark of Cornwall for his tribute, which Cornwall had paid for many years. And all that time King Mark had been seven years behind with the tribute. And King Mark and his barons gave the messenger from Ireland this answer: that they would pay none. And they told the messenger to go to his King Anguish and tell him, "We will pay him no tribute. But tell your lord, if he insists on having tribute from us of Cornwall, to send a trusty knight of his land who will fight for his right, and we will find another to defend our right."

With this answer the messengers left for Ireland. And when King Anguish heard the messengers' answer he was furiously angry. And then he called to him Sir Marhaus, the good knight, who was nobly proven, and a knight of the Round Table. And this Marhaus was the brother of the queen of Ireland. Then the king said this: "Fair brother, Sir Marhaus, I beg you to go into Cornwall for my sake, and fight for our tribute, which by right we ought to have; and whatever you spend, you shall have plenty, more than you will need."
