"Sir," said Marhaus, "you may be sure I will not be unwilling to fight for the right of you and your land against the best knight of the Round Table; for I know them, most of them, and what their deeds are. And to advance my deeds and to increase my honour I will very gladly go on this venture for our right."

So in all haste provision was made for Sir Marhaus, and he had everything he needed; and so he left Ireland, and landed in Cornwall right beside the Castle of Tintagil. And when King Mark understood that he had landed there to fight for Ireland, then King Mark was in great sorrow, when he understood that the good and noble knight Sir Marhaus had come. For they knew of no knight who dared fight him. For at that time Sir Marhaus was called one of the most famous and renowned knights in the world. And so Sir Marhaus stayed on the sea, and every day he sent to King Mark to pay the tribute that was seven years behind, or else to find a knight to fight him for the tribute. This kind of message Sir Marhaus sent to King Mark every day.

Then the men of Cornwall had proclamations made everywhere that whatever knight would fight to save Cornwall from the tribute would be rewarded so that he would be the better for it all his life. Then some of the barons spoke to King Mark and advised him to send to King Arthur's court to look for Sir Lancelot du Lake, who was at that time named the most marvellous knight in all the world. Then there were some other barons who advised the king not to do so, and said that it was labour in vain, because Sir Marhaus was a knight of the Round Table, and so any of them would be unwilling to fight another, unless it were some knight who chose of his own accord to fight disguised and unknown. So the king and all his barons agreed that there was no point in looking for any knight of the Round Table. Meanwhile word and rumour came to King Meliodas of how Sir Marhaus was waiting for a fight close by Tintagil, and how King Mark could find no knight at all to fight for him. When young Tristram heard of this he was angry, and deeply ashamed that no knight in Cornwall dared fight Sir Marhaus of Ireland.

Chapter 5: How Tristram took on the fight for the tribute of Cornwall, and how he was made a knight

With that Tristram went to his father, King Meliodas, and asked his advice on what was best to do to free Cornwall from the tribute. "For it seems to me," said Sir Tristram, "it would be a shame if Sir Marhaus, the Irish queen's brother, went away without someone having fought him."

"As for that," said King Meliodas, "believe me, son Tristram, Sir Marhaus is called one of the best knights in the world, and a knight of the Round Table; and so I know of no knight in this country who is able to match him."

"Alas," said Sir Tristram, "that I am not made a knight! If Sir Marhaus should leave for Ireland like this, may God never let me have honour: if I were made a knight I would match him. And sir," said Tristram, "I beg you to give me leave to ride to King Mark; and, if you are not displeased, I will be made a knight by King Mark."

"I am content," said King Meliodas, "that you be ruled as your heart rules you."

Then Sir Tristram thanked his father warmly. And then he made himself ready to ride into Cornwall.

In the meanwhile there came a messenger with love letters to Sir Tristram from the daughter of King Faramon of France, and they were very pitiful letters, and in them were written many laments of love; but Sir Tristram took no joy in her letters, and paid them no regard. She also sent him a little hound that was exceedingly beautiful. But when the king's daughter understood that Sir Tristram would not love her, as the book says, she died of sorrow. And then the same squire who brought the letter and the hound came back to Sir Tristram, as you will hear later in the tale.

So this young Sir Tristram rode to his uncle, King Mark of Cornwall. And when he came there he heard it said that no knight would fight Sir Marhaus. Then Sir Tristram went to his uncle and said, "Sir, if you will give me the order of knighthood, I will fight Sir Marhaus."

"Who are you," said the king, "and where have you come from?"

"Sir," said Tristram, "I come from King Meliodas, who married your sister, and I am a gentleman, you may be sure."

King Mark looked at Sir Tristram and saw that he was only a young man in years, but he was exceedingly well made and big.

"Fair sir," said the king, "what is your name, and where were you born?"

"Sir," he answered, "my name is Tristram, and I was born in the country of Liones."

"Well spoken," said the king. "And if you will do this battle I will make you a knight."

"That is why I come to you," said Sir Tristram, "and for no other reason."

So then King Mark made him a knight. And with that, as soon as he had made him a knight, he sent a messenger to Sir Marhaus with letters saying that he had found a young knight ready to take on the battle to the uttermost.

"That may well be," said Sir Marhaus, "but tell King Mark I will not fight any knight unless he is of royal blood, that is to say, either a king's son or a queen's son, born of a prince or a princess."

When King Mark heard that, he sent for Sir Tristram de Liones and told him what Sir Marhaus had answered. Then Sir Tristram said, "Since he says so, let him know that on my father's side and my mother's side I come of blood as noble as his. For, sir, now you shall know that I am King Meliodas' son, born of your own sister, Dame Elizabeth, who died in the forest giving birth to me."

"Oh, Jesus," said King Mark, "you are welcome, fair nephew, to me."

Then in all haste the king had Sir Tristram horsed, and armed him in the best way that could be had or got for gold or silver. And then King Mark sent to Sir Marhaus, and let him know that a better-born man than he was himself would fight him, "and his name is Sir Tristram de Liones, fathered by King Meliodas, and born of King Mark's sister." Then Sir Marhaus was glad and happy that he would fight such a gentleman. And so, by the agreement of King Mark and of Sir Marhaus, they arranged that they would fight on an island near Sir Marhaus' ships; and so Sir Tristram was put into a boat, both his horse and he, and everything that belonged to him, both for himself and for his horse. Sir Tristram lacked nothing. And when King Mark and his barons of Cornwall saw young Sir Tristram set off in such style to fight for the right of Cornwall, there was no man or woman of rank who did not weep to see and understand that so young a knight would put himself in danger for their right.

Chapter 6: How Sir Tristram landed on the island to fight his battle with Sir Marhaus

So, to cut this tale short, when Sir Tristram had landed on the island he looked to the far side, and there he saw six ships at anchor near the shore; and in the shadow of the ships, on the land, the noble knight Sir Marhaus of Ireland was waiting. Then Sir Tristram commanded his servant Gouvernail to bring his horse ashore and set his armour in order in every respect. And then, when he had done so, he mounted his horse; and when he was in his saddle, well equipped, and his shield set on his shoulder, Tristram asked Gouvernail, "Where is this knight I am to fight?"

"Sir," said Gouvernail, "don't you see him? I thought you had seen him. He is waiting over there in the shadow of his ships, on horseback, with his spear in his hand and his shield on his shoulder."

"That's true," said the noble knight Sir Tristram. "Now I see him well enough."

Then he commanded his servant Gouvernail to go back to his boat: "And commend me to my uncle King Mark, and ask him, if I am killed in this battle, to bury my body as he thinks best. And as for me, let him know that I will never yield out of cowardice; and if I am killed and do not flee, then they have lost no tribute because of me. And if it happens that I flee, or yield and beg for my life, tell my uncle never to bury me in Christian ground. And on your life," said Sir Tristram to Gouvernail, "do not come near this island until you see me beaten or killed, or else see me win against that knight over there."

So they parted from each other, weeping bitterly.

Chapter 7: How Sir Tristram fought against Sir Marhaus and won his battle, and how Sir Marhaus fled to his ship

And then Sir Marhaus looked Sir Tristram over, and said this: "Young knight, Sir Tristram, what are you doing here? I am very sorry for your boldness. For believe me, I have been tested, and the best knights of this land have been tested by my hand; and I have also matched myself with the best knights of the world. And so take my advice and go back to your boat."

"Fair knight, and well-proven knight," said Sir Tristram, "you may be sure I cannot abandon you in this quarrel, for it is for your sake I was made a knight. And you may be sure that I am a king's son by birth, fathered on a queen; and I have made such a promise, at my uncle's request and at my own seeking, that I will fight you to the uttermost, and free Cornwall from the old tribute. And believe me also, Sir Marhaus, this is the chief reason you give me the heart to fight you: because you are called one of the most renowned knights in the world, and because of that report and fame you have, you give me the courage to fight you, for I have never yet been tested against a good knight. And since I took the order of knighthood this very day, I am well pleased that I can fight so good a knight as you are. And now believe me, Sir Marhaus, I mean to win honour on your body; and if I am not yet proven, I trust to God that I shall be honourably proven on your body, and free the country of Cornwall for ever from every kind of tribute to Ireland, for ever."

When Sir Marhaus had heard him say what he would, he answered him like this: "Fair knight, since you mean to win honour from me, I tell you that you can lose no honour by me if you can stand three blows from me. For I tell you that for my noble deeds, proven and seen, King Arthur made me a knight of the Round Table."

Then they set their spears in rest, and they met so fiercely that they struck each other down, horse and all. But Sir Marhaus gave Sir Tristram a great wound in the side with his spear. And then they got clear of their horses, and drew their swords, and threw their shields in front of them. And then they laid into each other like men who were wild and full of fight. And when they had struck at each other like this for a long time, then they left off their blows and thrust at each other's breathing holes and visors; and when they saw that this could not help them, then they crashed together like rams, each trying to bear the other down. So they fought on for more than half a day, and each of them was badly wounded, so that the blood ran down fresh from them onto the ground. By then Sir Tristram was fresher than Sir Marhaus, and had better wind, and was bigger. And with a mighty stroke he hit Sir Marhaus on the helmet with such a blow that it went through his helmet, and through the steel cap under it, and through the skull; and the sword stuck so fast in the helmet and in his skull that Sir Tristram pulled three times at his sword before he could pull it out of his head. And there Marhaus fell down on his knees, with the edge of Tristram's sword left in his skull. And suddenly Sir Marhaus got up, stumbling, and threw his sword and his shield away from him, and so ran to his ships and fled; and Sir Tristram kept his shield and his sword.

And when Sir Tristram saw Sir Marhaus pull back, he said, "Ah, Sir Knight of the Round Table, why are you pulling back? You bring great shame on yourself and your kin. I am only a young knight, and was never tested before now, and rather than pull back from you I would sooner be hacked into a hundred pieces."

Sir Marhaus answered not a word, but went his way, groaning badly.

"Well, Sir Knight," said Sir Tristram, "I promise you your sword and your shield shall be mine; and I will wear your shield in every place I ride on my adventures, and in the sight of King Arthur and all the Round Table."

Chapter 8: How Sir Marhaus, after he reached Ireland, died of the blow Sir Tristram had given him, and how Tristram was wounded

At once Sir Marhaus and his company left for Ireland. And as soon as he came to the king, his brother-in-law, he had his wounds probed. And when his head was probed a piece of Sir Tristram's sword was found in it, and no surgeons could ever get it out of his head, and so he died of Sir Tristram's sword. And that piece of the sword the queen, his sister, kept with her always, for she meant to be avenged if she could.

Now we turn back to Sir Tristram, who was badly wounded, and bled so heavily that, after a little while, when he had taken a chill, he could scarcely move his limbs. And then he sat himself down gently on a little hill, and bled fast. Then Gouvernail, his man, came at once with his boat; and the king and his barons came in procession to meet him. And when he had come to land, King Mark took him in his arms, and the king and Sir Dinas the Seneschal led Sir Tristram into the castle of Tintagil. And then his wounds were probed in the best way, and he was laid in his bed. And when King Mark saw his wounds he wept from his heart, and so did all his lords.

"So help me God," said King Mark, "I would not have my nephew die for all my lands."

So Sir Tristram lay there a month and more, and all the time he was likely to die of the blow that Sir Marhaus first gave him with the spear. For, as the French book says, the spearhead was poisoned, so that Sir Tristram could not be healed. Then King Mark and all his barons were exceedingly downcast, for they thought nothing else but that Sir Tristram would not recover. Then the king had all kinds of doctors and surgeons sent for, both men and women, and there was none who would promise him his life. Then there came a lady who was a very wise lady, and she said plainly to King Mark, and to Sir Tristram, and to all his barons, that he would never be healed unless Sir Tristram went into the same country the poison came from, and in that country he would be healed, or else never. That is what the lady said to the king.

When King Mark understood that, he had a fine ship made ready for Sir Tristram, well stocked with food, and Sir Tristram was put into it, and Gouvernail with him, and Sir Tristram took his harp with him; and so he was put out to sea to sail to Ireland. And so by good fortune he landed in Ireland right beside a castle where the king and the queen were; and as he arrived he sat up in his bed and played a merry song on his harp, such a one as they had never heard in Ireland before that time.

And when the king and the queen were told of such a knight who was such a harper, the king at once sent for him, and had his wounds probed, and then asked him his name. Then he answered, "I am from the country of Liones, and my name is Tramtrist, and I was wounded like this in a battle when I fought for a lady's right."

"So help me God," said King Anguish, "you shall have all the help in this land that you can have here. But I tell you, in Cornwall I had as great a loss as ever a king had, for there I lost the best knight in the world. His name was Marhaus, a very noble knight, and a knight of the Round Table."

And there he told Sir Tristram why Sir Marhaus had been killed. Sir Tristram put on a face as if he were sorry, and he knew better than the king how it had happened.

Chapter 9: How Sir Tristram was first put in the care of Isolde the Fair to be healed of his wound

Then the king, out of great favour, had Tramtrist put in his daughter's charge and keeping, because she was a fine surgeon. And when she had probed him she found poison at the bottom of his wound, and so she healed him in a while. And because of that Tramtrist fell deeply in love with Isolde the Fair, for she was at that time the most beautiful maiden and lady in the world. And there Tramtrist taught her to play the harp, and she began to take a great fancy to him. And at that time Sir Palomides, the Saracen, was in that country, and much made of by the king and the queen. And every day Sir Palomides came close to Isolde the Fair and offered her many gifts, for he loved her exceedingly. Tramtrist saw all this, and he knew very well that Sir Palomides was a noble knight and a mighty man. And believe me, Sir Tramtrist bore Sir Palomides a great grudge, for Isolde the Fair told Tramtrist that Palomides was willing to be christened for her sake. So there was great rivalry between Tramtrist and Sir Palomides.

Then it happened that King Anguish had great jousts and a great tournament proclaimed for a lady who was called the Lady of the Launds, and she was a close cousin of the king. And whatever man won her should marry her three days later and have all her lands. This proclamation was made in England, Wales and Scotland, and also in France and in Brittany. One day Isolde the Fair came to Sir Tramtrist and told him about this tournament. He answered and said, "Fair lady, I am only a weak knight, and not long ago I would have been dead had it not been for your good ladyship. Now, fair lady, what would you have me do in this matter? You know well, my lady, that I cannot joust."

"Ah, Tramtrist," said Isolde the Fair, "why won't you fight at that tournament? I know well Sir Palomides will be there, and will do all he can; and so, Tramtrist, I beg you to be there, for otherwise Sir Palomides is likely to win the prize."

"Madam," said Tramtrist, "as for that, it may be so, for he is a proven knight, and I am only a young knight and lately made; and in the first battle I fought I had the bad luck to be badly wounded, as you see. But if I knew you would be my good lady, I will be at that tournament, provided you keep my secret and let no creature know that I am going to joust except yourself and those you trust to keep your secret. I will risk my poor person there for your sake, so that perhaps Sir Palomides will know when I come."

"As to that," said Isolde the Fair, "do your best. And as far as I can," said Isolde the Fair, "I will provide you with a horse and armour of my own choosing."

"As you wish, so be it," said Sir Tramtrist. "I will be at your command."

So on the day of the jousts Sir Palomides came with a black shield, and he overthrew many knights, so that all the people marvelled at him. For he got the better of Sir Gawain, Gaheris, Agravain, Bagdemagus, Kay, Dodinas le Savage, Sagramore le Desirous, Gumret le Petit, and Griflet le Fise de Dieu. All these Sir Palomides struck down to the earth on the first day. And then knights of every kind were afraid of Sir Palomides, and many called him the Knight with the Black Shield. So that day Sir Palomides won great honour.

Then King Anguish came to Tramtrist and asked him why he would not joust.

"Sir," he said, "I was hurt only lately, and I don't yet dare to risk myself."

Then there came the same squire who had been sent to Sir Tristram from the King of France's daughter. And when he saw Sir Tristram he fell flat at his feet. Isolde the Fair saw all this, and what courtesy the squire showed to Sir Tristram. And with that Sir Tristram suddenly ran to his squire, whose name was Hebes le Renoumes, and begged him earnestly not to tell his name on any account.

"Sir," said Hebes, "I will not reveal your name unless you command me to."

Chapter 10: How Sir Tristram won the prize at a tournament in Ireland, and there made Palomides give up wearing armour for a year

Then Sir Tristram asked him what he was doing in those parts.

"Sir," he said, "I came here with Sir Gawain to be made a knight, and, if it pleases you, to be made a knight by your hands."

"Wait for me secretly tomorrow morning, and in the field I will make you a knight."

Then Isolde the Fair had a strong suspicion about Tramtrist, that he was some proven man of honour, and with that she took comfort, and loved him more than she had before. And so in the morning Sir Palomides made himself ready to come into the field, as he had the first day. And there he struck down the King with the Hundred Knights, and the King of Scots. Then Isolde the Fair had fitted out Sir Tristram well, with a white horse and white armour. And just then she had him let out at a secret back gate, and so he came into the field as if he had been a bright angel. And at once Sir Palomides saw him, and with that he set a spear in rest against Sir Tramtrist, and he did the same against him. And there Sir Tristram struck Sir Palomides down to the earth. And then there was a great uproar among the people: some said Sir Palomides had had a fall, some said the Knight with the Black Shield had had a fall. And you may be sure Isolde the Fair was exceedingly glad. And then Sir Gawain and his nine companions marvelled at what knight it could be who had struck down Sir Palomides. Then no one would joust with Tramtrist, but everyone there refused him, great and small. Then Sir Tristram made Hebes a knight, and made him put himself forward, and he did very well that day. So afterwards Sir Hebes stayed with Sir Tristram.

And when Sir Palomides had taken this fall, you may be sure he was deeply ashamed, and as secretly as he could he slipped away out of the field. Sir Tristram saw all this, and he rode swiftly after Sir Palomides and overtook him, and told him to turn, for he wanted to test him better before he left. Then Sir Palomides turned, and each of them slashed at the other with their swords. But at the first stroke Sir Tristram struck Palomides down, and gave him such a blow on the head that he fell to the earth. So then Tristram told him to yield and do as he commanded, or else he would kill him. When Sir Palomides saw the look on his face, he feared his blows so much that he granted everything he asked.

"Well said," said Sir Tristram. "This shall be your charge. First, on pain of your life, that you give up my lady Isolde the Fair, and in no way whatever come near her. Also, that for this twelvemonth and a day you wear no armour and no gear of war. Now promise me this, or you die here."

"Alas," said Palomides, "I am shamed for ever."

Then he swore as Sir Tristram had commanded him. Then, out of resentment and anger, Sir Palomides cut off his armour and threw it away.

And so Sir Tristram turned back to the castle where Isolde the Fair was. And on the way he met a damsel who was asking after Sir Lancelot, who had honourably won the Dolorous Gard; and this damsel asked Sir Tristram who he was. For she had been told that it was he who had struck down Sir Palomides, by whom the ten knights of King Arthur's had been struck down. Then the damsel begged Sir Tristram to tell her who he was, and whether he was Sir Lancelot du Lake, for she thought there was no knight in the world who could do such deeds of arms unless it were Lancelot.

"Fair damsel," said Sir Tristram, "believe me, I am not Sir Lancelot, for I was never of such prowess. But it is all in God's hands, and He may make me as good a knight as the good knight Sir Lancelot."

"Now, noble knight," she said, "put up your visor."

And when she saw his face she thought she had never seen a better man's face, nor a finer-looking knight. And then, when the damsel knew for certain that he was not Sir Lancelot, she took her leave and went away from him. And then Sir Tristram rode secretly to the back gate, where Isolde the Fair was waiting for him, and there she gave him a warm welcome, and thanked God for his good success. So soon after, within a little while, the king and the queen learned that it was Tramtrist who had struck down Sir Palomides; then he was made much more of than he had been before.

Chapter 11: How the queen discovered by his sword that Sir Tristram had slain her brother Sir Marhaus, and what danger he was in

So Sir Tramtrist stayed there a long time, well cared for by the king and the queen, and above all by Isolde the Fair. Then one day the queen and Isolde the Fair prepared a bath for Sir Tramtrist. And while he was in his bath the queen and Isolde, her daughter, wandered up and down the room; and meanwhile Gouvernail and Hebes waited on Tramtrist, and the queen looked at his sword where it lay on his bed. And then, by ill luck, the queen drew out his sword and looked at it a long while, and both of them thought it an exceedingly fine sword; but a foot and a half from the point a great piece had been broken out of the edge. And when the queen saw that gap in the sword, she remembered a piece of a sword that had been found in the skull of Sir Marhaus, the good knight who was her brother.

"Alas," she said then to her daughter, Isolde the Fair, "this is the same traitor knight who killed my brother, your uncle."

When Isolde heard her say so she was badly shaken, for she loved Tramtrist exceedingly well, and she knew full well how cruel her mother the queen could be.

At once the queen went to her own room, and searched her chest, and there she took out the piece of the sword that had been pulled out of Sir Marhaus' head after he was dead. And then she ran with that piece of iron to the sword that lay on the bed. And when she put that piece of steel and iron to the sword, it fitted as exactly as it could have done when it was newly broken. And then the queen gripped that sword fiercely in her hand, and with all her might she ran straight at Tramtrist where he sat in his bath, and there she would have run him through if Sir Hebes had not caught her in his arms and pulled the sword from her; otherwise she would have thrust him through.

Then, when she was stopped from her evil intent, she ran to King Anguish, her husband, and said on her knees, "O my lord, here in your house you have the traitor knight who killed my brother and your servant, that noble knight, Sir Marhaus."

"Who is that," said King Anguish, "and where is he?"

"Sir," she said, "it is Sir Tramtrist, the same knight my daughter healed."

"Alas," said the king, "that makes me very sorry, for he is as noble a knight as I ever saw in the field. But I charge you," said the king to the queen, "not to meddle with that knight; leave him to me."

Then the king went into the room to Sir Tramtrist, but by then he had gone to his own room, and the king found him fully armed and ready to mount his horse. When the king saw him all armed and ready to ride, the king said, "No, Tramtrist, it will do you no good to match yourself against me. But this much I will do, for my honour and for the love I bear you: since you are within my court, it would be no honour to me to kill you. So on this condition I will give you leave to depart from this court in safety: that you tell me who your father was, and what your name is, and whether you killed Sir Marhaus, my brother."

Chapter 12: How Sir Tristram took leave of the king and Isolde the Fair and left Ireland to come to Cornwall

"Sir," said Tristram, "now I will tell you the whole truth. My father's name is Sir Meliodas, King of Liones, and my mother was called Elizabeth, who was sister to King Mark of Cornwall; and my mother died giving birth to me in the forest, and because of that she commanded, before she died, that when I was christened they should christen me Tristram. And because I did not want to be known in this country I turned my name around and had myself called Tramtrist. And I fought over the tribute of Cornwall for my uncle's sake, and for the right of Cornwall, which you had held for many years. And believe me," said Tristram to the king, "I fought that battle for the love of my uncle, King Mark, and for the love of the country of Cornwall, and to increase my honour; for on the same day that I fought with Sir Marhaus I was made a knight, and never before then had I fought with any knight; and he went away from me alive, and left his shield and his sword behind."

"God help me," said the king, "I cannot deny that you did as a knight should, and it was your part to do it for your cause, and to increase your honour as a knight should. Even so, I cannot keep you in this country and keep my honour, unless I am willing to displease my barons, and my wife and her kin."

"Sir," said Tristram, "I thank you for the good lordship I have had from you here, and for the great kindness my lady, your daughter, has shown me. And so," said Sir Tristram, "it may happen that you will gain more by my life than by my death, for in the lands of England I may be able to do you a service some day, so that you will be glad you ever showed me your good lordship. What is more, I promise you, as I am a true knight, that in every place I will be my lady your daughter's servant and knight, in right and in wrong, and I will never fail her, but do as much as a knight may do. Also I beg your good grace that I may take my leave of my lady, your daughter, and of all the barons and knights."

"Gladly," said the king.

Then Sir Tristram went to Isolde the Fair and took his leave of her. And then he told her everything: who he was, and how he had changed his name because he did not want to be known, and how a lady had told him that he would never be healed until he came into this country where the poison was made, "which brought me close to my death, if your ladyship had not been there."

"O gentle knight," said Isolde the Fair, "I am full of sorrow at your going, for I never saw a man I wished so well." And with that she wept from the heart.

"Madam," said Sir Tristram, "you must understand that my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, begotten by King Meliodas, and born of his queen. And I promise you faithfully that I will be your knight all the days of my life."

"Many thanks," said Isolde the Fair, "and I promise you in return that I will not be married for these seven years except with your consent; and whomever you wish me to marry, him I will have, if he will have me and you consent."

And then Sir Tristram gave her a ring, and she gave him another; and with that he left her, grieving and lamenting greatly. And he went straight to the court among all the barons, and there he took his leave of great and small, and openly he said among them all, "Fair lords, it is so now that I must depart. If there is any man here whom I have offended, or who has any grievance against me, let him make his complaint here before me, before I go, and I will make it right as far as I can. And if there is anyone who wants to do me wrong, or speak wrong or shame of me behind my back, let him say it now or never, and here is my body to prove it on his, body against body."

And they all stood still; there was not one who would say a word. Yet there were some knights there who were of the queen's blood, and of Sir Marhaus' blood, but they would not meddle with him.

Chapter 13: How Sir Tristram and King Mark wounded each other for the love of a knight's wife

So Sir Tristram departed, and took to the sea, and with a good wind he landed at Tintagil in Cornwall. And when King Mark was well and prospering, news came that Sir Tristram had arrived, healed of his wounds. King Mark was exceedingly glad of it, and so were all the barons. And when he saw his time Sir Tristram rode to his father, King Meliodas, and there he had all the welcome that the king and the queen could give him. And then King Meliodas and his queen generously shared out lands and goods to Sir Tristram.

Then, with the leave of King Meliodas, his father, he went back to the court of King Mark, and there he lived in great joy for a long time, until at last there arose a jealousy and an ill will between King Mark and Sir Tristram, for they both loved one lady. And she was the wife of an earl called Sir Segwarides. And this lady loved Sir Tristram exceedingly well. And he loved her in return, for she was an exceedingly beautiful lady, and Sir Tristram saw that plainly. Then King Mark understood it and was jealous, for King Mark loved her exceedingly well.

So it happened one day that this lady sent a dwarf to Sir Tristram, and bade him, as he loved her, to be with her the following night. "Also she charges you," said the dwarf, "not to come to her unless you are well armed, for her husband is called a good knight."

Sir Tristram answered the dwarf, "Commend me to my lady, and tell her I will not fail, but I will be with her at the time she has set me."

And with this answer the dwarf left. And King Mark saw that the dwarf had been with Sir Tristram on a message from Segwarides' wife. Then King Mark sent for the dwarf, and when he came he made the dwarf by force tell him everything, why and for what reason he had come on a message to Sir Tristram.

"Now," said King Mark, "go where you like, and on pain of death say not a word about what you said to me."

So the dwarf left the king.

And that same night that the meeting was set between Segwarides' wife and Sir Tristram, King Mark armed himself and made himself ready, and took two knights who were in his confidence with him; and so he rode ahead to lie in wait by the road for Sir Tristram. And as Sir Tristram came riding on his way with his spear in his hand, King Mark came charging at him suddenly with his two knights. And all three struck at him with their spears, and King Mark wounded Sir Tristram in the chest very badly. And then Sir Tristram set his spear in rest, and struck his uncle, King Mark, so hard that he hurled him to the earth, and bruised him so that he lay still in a swoon, and it was a long time before he could move himself. And then he ran at the one knight, and then at the other, and struck them to the cold earth, so that they lay still. And with that Sir Tristram rode on, badly wounded, to the lady, and found her waiting for him at a back gate.

Chapter 14: How Sir Tristram slept with the lady, and how her husband fought with Sir Tristram

And there she welcomed him warmly, and they embraced each other in their arms, and she had his horse stabled in the best way, and then she unarmed him. And so they ate a light supper, and went to bed with great joy and pleasure; and in his passion he paid no heed to the fresh wound that King Mark had given him. And so Sir Tristram bled all over both the upper sheet and the lower, and the pillows, and the head sheet. And after a while someone came ahead who warned her that her husband was close by, within a bowshot. So she made Sir Tristram get up, and he armed himself, and took his horse, and so left. By then Segwarides, her husband, had come, and when he found her bed disordered and torn, and went near and looked at it by candlelight, he saw that a wounded knight had lain there.

"Ah, false traitress," he said then, "why have you betrayed me?" And with that he swung out a sword, and said, "Unless you tell me who has been here, here you die."

"Ah, my lord, mercy," said the lady, and held up her hands, saying, "Do not kill me, and I will tell you everything about who has been here."

"Tell me the whole truth at once," said Segwarides.

At once, out of fear, she said, "Sir Tristram was here with me, and on the way, as he came toward me, he was badly wounded."

"Ah, false traitress," said Segwarides, "where has he gone?"

"Sir," she said, "he has armed and gone on horseback, not half a mile from here yet."

"That's well said," said Segwarides.

Then he armed himself quickly, and got his horse, and rode after Sir Tristram, who was riding straight to Tintagil. And after a while he overtook Sir Tristram, and then he called on him, "Turn, false traitor knight!"

And Sir Tristram at once turned to face him. And with that Segwarides struck Sir Tristram with a spear so that it burst all to pieces; and then he swung out his sword and struck hard at Sir Tristram.

"Sir knight," said Sir Tristram, "I advise you to strike no more. Even so, for the wrongs I have done you, I will hold back from you as long as I can."

"No," said Segwarides, "that shall not be, for either you die or I do."

Then Sir Tristram drew his sword, and drove his horse at him fiercely, and he struck Sir Segwarides through the waist of the body so that he fell to the earth in a swoon. And so Sir Tristram rode away and left him there. And so he rode to Tintagil and took his lodging secretly, for he did not want it known that he was hurt. Sir Segwarides' men rode after their master too, and found him lying in the field badly wounded, and brought him home on his shield, and there he lay a long time before he was healed; but at last he recovered. King Mark, too, would not let it be known that he and Sir Tristram had met that night. And as for Sir Tristram, he did not know that it was King Mark who had met him. And so the king came casually to Sir Tristram, to comfort him as he lay sick in his bed. But as long as King Mark lived he never loved Sir Tristram after that; though there was fair speech, there was no love. And so many weeks and days passed, and all was forgiven and forgotten; for Sir Segwarides did not dare fight with Sir Tristram, because of his noble prowess, and also because he was King Mark's nephew. So he let it pass: for a man with a private hurt is loath to have a public shame.

Chapter 15: How Sir Bleoberis asked for the fairest lady in King Mark's court and carried her off, and how he was fought

Then it happened one day that the good knight Bleoberis de Ganis, brother to Blamore de Ganis, and a close cousin of the good knight Sir Lancelot du Lake, this Bleoberis came to the court of King Mark, and there he asked King Mark for a favour: to give him whatever gift he would ask for in his court. When the king heard him ask this, he wondered at the request; but because he was a knight of the Round Table, and of great renown, King Mark granted him all he asked.

"Then," said Sir Bleoberis, "I will have the fairest lady in your court that I care to choose."

"I cannot say no," said King Mark. "Now choose as you like."

And so Sir Bleoberis chose Sir Segwarides' wife, and took her by the hand, and so went his way with her; and so he took his horse and had her set up behind his squire, and rode on his way.

When Sir Segwarides heard that his lady had gone with a knight of King Arthur's court, he armed himself and rode after that knight to rescue his lady. So when Bleoberis had gone with this lady, King Mark and all the court were angry that she was taken away. Then there were certain ladies who knew that there was great love between Sir Tristram and her, and also that that lady loved Sir Tristram above all other knights. Then there was one lady who rebuked Sir Tristram in the most horrible way, and called him a coward knight, that he could, to the shame of his knighthood, see a lady so shamefully carried off from his uncle's court. But what she meant was that the two of them had loved each other with all their hearts.

But Sir Tristram answered her like this: "Fair lady, it is not my part to meddle in such matters while her lord and husband is here. And if it had been that her lord was not here in this court, then for the honour of this court perhaps I would have been her champion. And if it turns out that Sir Segwarides does not fare well, it may happen that I will have words with that good knight before he leaves this country."

Then within a while one of Sir Segwarides' squires came, and told the court that Sir Segwarides was badly beaten and wounded almost to death: as he tried to rescue his lady, Sir Bleoberis had overthrown him and badly wounded him. Then King Mark was downcast at this, and all the court. When Sir Tristram heard of it he was ashamed and badly grieved; and then he was soon armed and on horseback, and Gouvernail, his servant, carried his shield and spear. And as Sir Tristram rode hard he met Sir Andred, his cousin, who by King Mark's command had been sent to bring in, if it lay in his power, two knights of Arthur's court who were riding through the country looking for adventures. When Sir Tristram saw Sir Andred he asked him what news.

"God help me," said Sir Andred, "it was never worse with me. For here, by King Mark's command, I was sent to fetch two knights of King Arthur's court, and one of them beat me and wounded me, and cared nothing for my message."

"Fair cousin," said Sir Tristram, "ride on your way, and if I can meet them it may happen that I will avenge you."

So Sir Andred rode into Cornwall, and Sir Tristram rode after the two knights, one of whom was called Sagramore le Desirous, and the other Dodinas le Savage.

Chapter 16: How Sir Tristram fought with two knights of the Round Table

Then within a while Sir Tristram saw them ahead of him, two fine-looking knights.

"Sir," said Gouvernail to his master, "sir, I would advise you not to fight with them, for they are two proven knights of Arthur's court."

"As for that," said Sir Tristram, "have no fear: I will fight with them, to increase my honour, for it is many a day since I did any deeds of arms."

"Do as you like," said Gouvernail.

And with that Sir Tristram at once asked them where they came from, and where they were going, and what they were doing in those borders. Sir Sagramore looked at Sir Tristram, and scorned his words, and asked him in return, "Fair knight, are you a knight of Cornwall?"

"Why do you ask?" said Sir Tristram.

"Because it is seldom seen," said Sir Sagramore, "that you Cornish knights are valiant men-at-arms. For within these two hours one of your Cornish knights met us, and he talked big, and at once, with little strength, he was laid on the ground. And I believe," said Sir Sagramore, "you will get the same welcome he got."

"Fair lords," said Sir Tristram, "it may happen that I can hold out better than he did. And whether you like it or not, I will fight with you, because it was my cousin you beat. So do your best here, and believe me, unless you acquit yourselves better here on this ground, one knight of Cornwall will beat you both."

When Sir Dodinas le Savage heard him say so he took a spear in his hand, and said, "Sir knight, look out for yourself!"

And then they drew apart and came together as if it had been thunder. And Sir Dodinas' spear burst in pieces, but Sir Tristram struck him with greater force, so that he knocked him clean over his horse's rump, and very nearly broke his neck. When Sir Sagramore saw his companion take such a fall he wondered what knight this might be. And he lowered his spear with all his might, and Sir Tristram did the same against him, and they came together like thunder, and there Sir Tristram struck Sir Sagramore so strong a blow that he bore him and his horse to the earth, and in the fall he broke his thigh.

When this was done Sir Tristram asked them, "Fair knights, will you have any more? Are there no bigger knights in the court of King Arthur? It is a shame on you to speak dishonour of us knights of Cornwall, for it may happen that a Cornish knight can match you."

"That is the truth," said Sir Sagramore, "we have proved that well. But I beg you," said Sir Sagramore, "tell us your real name, by the faith and loyalty you owe to the high order of knighthood."

"You charge me with a great thing," said Sir Tristram, "and since you want to know it, you shall know and understand that my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, King Meliodas' son, and nephew to King Mark."

Then those two knights were glad that they had met Tristram, and so they begged him to stay in their company.

"No," said Sir Tristram, "for I must fight with one of your companions; his name is Sir Bleoberis de Ganis."

"God speed you well," said Sir Sagramore and Dodinas.

Sir Tristram left and rode on his way. And then he saw ahead of him, in a valley, Sir Bleoberis riding with Sir Segwarides' lady, who rode behind his squire on a palfrey.

Chapter 17: How Sir Tristram fought with Sir Bleoberis for a lady, and how the lady was given the choice of which of them she would go with

Then Sir Tristram rode at more than a walk until he had overtaken him. Then Sir Tristram spoke. "Stop," he said, "knight of Arthur's court! Bring that lady back, or hand her over to me."

"I will do neither," said Bleoberis, "for I fear no Cornish knight so badly that I would care to hand her over."

"Why," said Sir Tristram, "can't a Cornish knight do as well as any other knight? This same day, within these three miles, two knights of your court met me, and before we parted they found one Cornish knight good enough for them both."

"What were their names?" said Bleoberis.

"They told me," said Sir Tristram, "that one of them was called Sir Sagramore le Desirous, and the other Dodinas le Savage."

"Ah," said Sir Bleoberis, "have you met them? God help me, they were two good knights and men of great honour, and if you have beaten them both you must be a good knight indeed. But even if you have beaten them both, you will not frighten me: you will have to beat me before you have this lady."

"Then defend yourself," said Sir Tristram.

So they drew apart and came together like thunder, and each bore the other down, horse and all, to the earth.

Then they got clear of their horses, and laid into each other eagerly and mightily with swords, now circling and sidestepping to the right and to the left for more than two hours. And sometimes they rushed together with such force that they both lay sprawling on the ground. Then Sir Bleoberis de Ganis leapt back, and said, "Now, good and gentle knight, hold your hands a while, and let us talk together."

"Say what you like," said Tristram, "and I will answer you."

"Sir," said Bleoberis, "I would like to know where you are from, and whose son you are, and what your name is."

"God help me," said Sir Tristram, "I am not afraid to tell you my name. Believe me, I am King Meliodas' son, and my mother is King Mark's sister, and my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, and King Mark is my uncle."

"Truly," said Bleoberis, "I am very glad of you, for you are the one who killed Marhaus the knight, hand to hand on an island, over the tribute of Cornwall. You also overcame Sir Palomides, the good knight, at a tournament on an island, where you beat Sir Gawain and his nine companions."

"God help me," said Sir Tristram, "believe me, I am the same knight. Now I have told you my name; tell me yours, and gladly."

"Believe me, my name is Sir Bleoberis de Ganis, and my brother is called Sir Blamore de Ganis, who is reckoned a good knight; and we are the sons of a sister of my lord Sir Lancelot du Lake, whom we count one of the best knights in the world."

"That is the truth," said Sir Tristram. "Sir Lancelot is called peerless in courtesy and in knighthood; and for his sake," said Sir Tristram, "I will not, if I can help it, fight with you any more, for the great love I have for Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"In good faith," said Bleoberis, "as for me, I would be loath to fight with you. But since you have followed me here to have this lady, I will offer you kindness, courtesy and gentleness right here on this ground. This lady shall stand between us both, and whichever of us she wants to go to, let him have her in peace."

"Gladly," said Tristram, "for, as I judge it, she will leave you and come to me."

"You will soon find out," said Bleoberis.

Chapter 18: How the lady rejected Sir Tristram and stayed with Sir Bleoberis, and how she asked to go back to her husband

So when she was set between the two of them she said these words to Sir Tristram: "Believe me, Sir Tristram de Liones, until lately you were the man in the world I most loved and trusted, and I thought you loved me in return above all ladies. But when you saw this knight lead me away you made no move to rescue me, but let my lord Segwarides ride after me. Until that time I thought you loved me; and so now I will leave you, and never love you again."

And with that she went over to Sir Bleoberis.

When Sir Tristram saw her do so he was furiously angry with that lady, and ashamed to go back to the court.

"Sir Tristram," said Sir Bleoberis, "you are at fault, for I hear from this lady's words that before this day she trusted you above all earthly knights, and, as she says, you have deceived her. So believe me, no man can hold one who wants to go. And rather than have you heartily displeased with me, I would wish you had her, if she would stay with you."

"No," said the lady, "God help me, I will never go with him; for the one I loved most, I thought he loved me. And so, Sir Tristram," she said, "ride back the way you came, for even if you had beaten this knight, as you were likely to, I would never have gone with you. And I will beg this knight, as fairly as I can by his knighthood, that before he leaves this country he will take me to the abbey where my lord Sir Segwarides lies."

"God help me," said Bleoberis, "I'll have you know, good knight Sir Tristram, that because King Mark gave me the choice of a gift in his court, this lady pleased me best. Nevertheless, she is wedded and has a husband, and I have fulfilled my quest; she shall be sent back to her husband, and most especially for your sake, Sir Tristram. And if she would go with you, I would wish you had her."

"I thank you," said Sir Tristram, "but because of her love I shall be careful what kind of lady I love or trust. For if her husband, Sir Segwarides, had been away from the court, I would have been the first to follow you. But since you have refused me," he said to the lady, "as I am a true knight, I shall know her exceedingly well before I love or trust her."

And so they took their leave of one another and parted.

And so Sir Tristram rode to Tintagil, and Sir Bleoberis rode to the abbey where Sir Segwarides lay badly wounded, and there he handed over his lady, and departed as a noble knight. And when Sir Segwarides saw his lady, he was greatly comforted; and then she told him that Sir Tristram had fought a great battle with Sir Bleoberis, and made him bring her back. These words pleased Sir Segwarides very well, that Sir Tristram would do so much; and so that lady told King Mark all about the battle between Sir Tristram and Sir Bleoberis.

Chapter 19: How King Mark sent Sir Tristram to Ireland for Isolde the Fair, and how by chance he landed in England

Then, when this was done, King Mark was always scheming in his heart how he might destroy Sir Tristram. And then he devised a plan to send Sir Tristram to Ireland for Isolde the Fair. For Sir Tristram had praised her beauty and her goodness so highly that King Mark said he would marry her, and so he asked Sir Tristram to make the journey to Ireland as his messenger. And all this was done with the aim of getting Sir Tristram killed. Nevertheless, Sir Tristram would not refuse the errand for any danger or peril that might befall, for the sake of pleasing his uncle; instead he made himself ready to go in the finest style that could be devised. For Sir Tristram took with him the finest knights he could find at the court; and they were dressed, in the fashion of that time, in the finest manner. So Sir Tristram departed and took to the sea with all his company. And soon, when he was out on the open sea, a storm caught him and his company, and drove them back to the coast of England; and there they came ashore close by Camelot, and were very glad to reach land.

And when they had landed Sir Tristram pitched his tent on the land of Camelot, and there he had his shield hung on the tent. And that same day two of King Arthur's knights came by, one of them Sir Ector de Maris, and the other Sir Morganor. And they touched the shield, and called on him to come out of the tent to joust, if he would joust.

"You shall have your answer," said Sir Tristram, "if you will wait a little while."

So he made himself ready, and first he struck down Sir Ector de Maris, and then he struck down Sir Morganor, all with one spear, and badly bruised them. And as they lay on the ground they asked Sir Tristram who he was, and of what country he was a knight.

"Fair lords," said Sir Tristram, "believe me, I am from Cornwall."

"Alas," said Sir Ector, "now I am ashamed that any Cornish knight should ever overcome me."

And then, out of vexation, Sir Ector took off his armour, and went on foot, and would not ride.

Chapter 20: How King Anguish of Ireland was summoned to King Arthur's court on a charge of treason

Then it happened that Sir Bleoberis and Sir Blamore de Ganis, who were brothers, had summoned King Anguish of Ireland to come to Arthur's court on pain of losing King Arthur's good grace. And if the King of Ireland did not come in on the day assigned and set, the king would lose his lands. So it happened that on the day assigned, neither King Arthur nor Sir Lancelot could be there to give the judgment, for King Arthur was with Sir Lancelot at the castle of Joyous Gard. And so King Arthur appointed King Carados and the King of Scots to be judges there that day. So when the kings were at Camelot, King Anguish of Ireland had come to learn who his accusers were. Then Sir Blamore de Ganis was there, and accused the King of Ireland of treason, saying that he had killed a cousin of his in his court in Ireland by treason. The king was badly shaken by the accusation, because he had come at King Arthur's summons, and before he came to Camelot he did not know why he had been sent for. And when the king heard Sir Blamore say what he had to say, he understood well that there was no other remedy but to answer him as a knight; for the custom in those days was that if any man was accused of any treason or murder he had to fight body for body, or else find another knight to fight for him. And all kinds of murder in those days were called treason.

So when King Anguish understood the charge against him he was exceedingly downcast, for he knew Sir Blamore de Ganis for a noble knight, and one born of noble knights. Then the King of Ireland was poorly provided with an answer; so the judges gave him until the third day to give his answer. So the king went to his lodging.

Meanwhile a lady came by Sir Tristram's tent, grieving greatly.

"What is the matter with you," said Sir Tristram, "that you grieve so?"

"Ah, fair knight," said the lady, "I am disgraced unless some good knight helps me. For a great lady of high honour sent by me a fair child, and a rich one, to Sir Lancelot du Lake, and near here a knight met me, and threw me down from my palfrey, and took the child away from me."

"Well, my lady," said Sir Tristram, "for the sake of my lord Sir Lancelot I will get that child back for you, or else I will be beaten for it."

And so Sir Tristram took his horse, and asked the lady which way the knight had ridden; and she told him. And he rode after him, and within a while he overtook that knight. And then Sir Tristram called on him to turn and give back the child.

Chapter 21: How Sir Tristram rescued a child from a knight, and how Gouvernail told him about King Anguish

The knight turned his horse and made ready to fight. And then Sir Tristram struck him such a blow with his sword that he tumbled to the ground. And then he yielded to Sir Tristram.

"Then come along," said Sir Tristram, "and take the child back to the lady."

So he took his horse meekly and rode with Sir Tristram; and on the way Sir Tristram asked him his name.

Then he said, "My name is Breuse Saunce Pité."

So when he had handed the child back to the lady, he said, "Sir, as for this, the child is put right."

Then Sir Tristram let him go again, which he bitterly regretted afterwards, for he was a great enemy to many good knights of King Arthur's court.

Then, when Sir Tristram was in his tent, Gouvernail his man came and told him that King Anguish of Ireland had come there, and was in great distress; and there Gouvernail told Sir Tristram how King Anguish had been summoned and accused of murder.

"God help me," said Sir Tristram, "this is the best news that has come to me these seven years, for now the King of Ireland will need my help. For I dare say there is no knight in this country who is not of Arthur's court who dares do battle with Sir Blamore de Ganis; and to win the love of the King of Ireland I will take the battle on myself. And so, Gouvernail, I charge you, take me to the king."

Then Gouvernail went to King Anguish of Ireland, and greeted him courteously. The king welcomed him and asked him what he wanted.

"Sir," said Gouvernail, "there is a knight close by who wishes to speak with you. He told me to say he would do you service."

"What knight is he?" said the king.

"Sir," he said, "it is Sir Tristram de Liones, who wants to repay you in this country for the good grace you showed him in your lands."

"Come on, fellow," said the king, "come with me at once and take me to Sir Tristram."

So the king took a small riding horse and only a few companions with him, and rode until he came to Sir Tristram's tent. And when Sir Tristram saw the king he ran to him and would have held his stirrup. But the king leapt nimbly from his horse, and each of them embraced the other in his arms.

"My gracious lord," said Sir Tristram, "many thanks for the great kindnesses you showed me in your borders and lands. And at that time I promised to do you service, if ever it lay in my power."

"And, noble knight," said the king to Sir Tristram, "now I have great need of you. I never had such great need of any knight's help."

"How so, my good lord?" said Sir Tristram.

"I will tell you," said the king. "I am summoned and accused, far from my own country, of the death of a knight who was kin to the good knight Sir Lancelot. And for this Sir Blamore de Ganis, brother to Sir Bleoberis, has called on me to fight with him, or else to find a knight to fight in my place. And I know well," said the king, "that those who come of King Ban's blood, such as Sir Lancelot and these others, are exceedingly good knights, and as hard to beat in battle as any men I know of now alive."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "for the good lordship you showed me in Ireland, and for the sake of my lady your daughter, Isolde the Fair, I will take the battle on myself for you, on this condition, that you grant me two things. The first is that you swear to me that you are in the right, and that you never consented to the knight's death."

"Sir," then said Sir Tristram, "the second is that when I have fought this battle, if God gives me the grace to succeed, you will give me a reward, whatever reasonable thing I ask of you."

"God help me," said the king, "you shall have whatever you ask."

"That is well said," said Sir Tristram.

Chapter 22: How Sir Tristram fought for King Anguish and overcame his opponent, and how his opponent would never surrender

"Now give your answer that your champion is ready, for I would rather die in your cause than be shamed as a recreant."

"I have no doubts about you," said the king, "though if you had to fight with Sir Lancelot du Lake..."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "as for Sir Lancelot, he is called the noblest knight in the world, and you may be sure that the knights of his blood are noble men, and fear shame. And as for Bleoberis, brother to Sir Blamore, I have done battle with him, so on my life it is no shame to call him a good knight."

"It is rumoured," said the king, "that Blamore is the bolder knight."

"Sir, as for that, let it be. He shall never be refused, even if he were the best knight who now carries shield or spear."

So King Anguish went to King Carados and the kings who were acting as judges at that time, and told them that he had found his champion ready. Then, by the command of the kings, Sir Blamore de Ganis and Sir Tristram were sent for to hear the charge. And when they had come before the judges there were many kings and knights who looked at Sir Tristram, and much talk they had of him, because he had killed Sir Marhaus, the good knight, and because he had outjousted Sir Palomides, the good knight. So when they had taken their charge they withdrew to make ready to do battle.

Then Sir Bleoberis said to his brother, Sir Blamore, "Dear brother, remember what kin we come of, and what a man Sir Lancelot du Lake is, neither further nor nearer to us than brothers' children; and there was never any of our kin who was shamed in battle. Brother, suffer death rather than be shamed."

"Brother," said Blamore, "have no doubts of me, for I shall never shame any of my blood. Though I am sure that the knight over there is called as good a knight as any in the world in his day, yet I shall never yield, nor say the shameful word. He may well happen to strike me down with his great might of chivalry, but he shall kill me before I yield as a recreant."

"God speed you," said Sir Bleoberis, "for you will find him the mightiest knight you ever fought with, for I know him, since I have fought with him."

"God speed me," said Sir Blamore de Ganis.

And with that he took his horse at one end of the lists, and Sir Tristram at the other end of the lists, and so they set their spears in rest and came together as if it had been thunder; and there Sir Tristram, through his great might, struck Sir Blamore and his horse to the ground. Then at once Sir Blamore got clear of his horse and pulled out his sword and threw his shield in front of him, and told Sir Tristram to dismount: "For though a horse has failed me, I trust to God the earth will not fail me."

And then Sir Tristram dismounted, and squared up to fight; and there they laid into each other hard, pressing and circling, thrusting and dashing, with many heavy blows, so that the kings and knights wondered greatly that they could stand. For all the while they fought like madmen, so that knights were never seen to fight more fiercely than they did; for Sir Blamore was so hasty that he would take no rest, so that all men wondered that they had breath to stand on their feet; and all the place they fought in was bloody. And at last Sir Tristram struck Sir Blamore such a blow on the helm that he fell down there on his side, and Sir Tristram stood and looked at him.

Chapter 23: How Sir Blamore begged Tristram to kill him, and how Sir Tristram spared him, and how they came to terms

Then, when Sir Blamore could speak, he said this: "Sir Tristram de Liones, I beg you, as you are a noble knight, and the best knight I ever met, that you kill me outright. For I would not live to be made lord of all the earth, for I would rather die with honour than live with shame. And you must kill me, Sir Tristram, or else you will never win the field, for I will never say the shameful word. And so, if you dare kill me, kill me, I beg you."

When Sir Tristram heard him speak so knightly, he did not know what to do with him. He thought of both sides: of what blood he came, and that for Sir Lancelot's sake he would be loath to kill him; and on the other side, that he had no choice at all but to make him say the shameful word, or else kill him.

Then Sir Tristram leapt back, and went to the kings who were the judges, and there he knelt down before them, and begged them, for their honour, and for King Arthur's and Sir Lancelot's sake, to take this matter into their own hands.

"For, my fair lords," said Sir Tristram, "it would be a shame and a pity for this noble knight who lies over there to be killed. For you hear well that he will not be shamed, and I pray to God that he is never killed nor shamed because of me. And as for the king I am fighting for, I will ask him, as I am his true champion and true knight in this field, to have mercy on this good knight."

"God help me," said King Anguish, "I will, for your sake. Sir Tristram, I will be ruled as you wish, for I know you for my true knight; and so I will heartily pray the kings who are here as judges to take it into their hands."

And the kings who were judges called Sir Bleoberis to them, and asked his advice.

"My lords," said Bleoberis, "though my brother is beaten, and has had the worse of it through might of arms, I dare say that though Sir Tristram has beaten his body he has not beaten his heart, and I thank God he is not shamed this day. And rather than have him shamed, I beg you," said Bleoberis, "let Sir Tristram kill him outright."

"It shall not be so," said the kings, "for the other party, both the king and the champion, have pity on Sir Blamore's knighthood."

"My lords," said Bleoberis, "I am well content to do as you will."

Then the kings called the King of Ireland, and found him gracious and ready to come to terms. And then, by all their advice, Sir Tristram and Sir Bleoberis lifted up Sir Blamore, and the two brothers were reconciled with King Anguish, and kissed and made friends for ever. And then Sir Blamore and Sir Tristram kissed each other, and there they swore their oaths that neither of the two brothers would ever fight with Sir Tristram, and Sir Tristram swore the same oath. And for that noble battle all the blood of Sir Lancelot loved Sir Tristram for ever.

Then King Anguish and Sir Tristram took their leave, and sailed to Ireland with great pomp and joy. So when they were in Ireland the king had it made known throughout the land how, and in what way, Sir Tristram had acted for him. Then the queen and everyone there made as much of him as they could. But no tongue could tell the joy that Isolde the Fair had of Sir Tristram, for of all earthly men she loved him most.

Chapter 24: How Sir Tristram asked for Isolde the Fair on King Mark's behalf, and how Sir Tristram and Isolde drank the love potion

Then one day King Anguish asked Sir Tristram why he did not ask for his reward, for whatever he had promised him he should have without fail.

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "now it is time. This is all I will ask: that you give me Isolde the Fair, your daughter, not for myself, but for my uncle, King Mark, who shall have her for his wife, for I have promised him so."

"Alas," said the king, "I would rather than all the land I have that you would marry her yourself."

"Sir, if I did, then I would be shamed for ever in this world, and false to my promise. And so," said Sir Tristram, "I pray you keep the promise you made me. For this is my wish, that you give me Isolde the Fair to go with me into Cornwall to be married to King Mark, my uncle."

"As for that," said King Anguish, "you shall have her with you, to do with her as you please. That is to say, if you care to marry her yourself, that is what I would like best; and if you will give her to King Mark, your uncle, that is your choice."

So, to cut a long story short, Isolde the Fair was made ready to go with Sir Tristram, and Dame Bragwaine went with her as her chief lady-in-waiting, with many others.

Then the queen, Isolde's mother, gave a drink to her and to Dame Bragwaine, her daughter's lady-in-waiting, and to Gouvernail, and charged them that on the day King Mark was married, that same day they should give him that drink, so that King Mark should drink to Isolde the Fair, "and then," said the queen, "I promise you each will love the other all the days of their lives."

So this drink was given to Dame Bragwaine and to Gouvernail. And then at once Sir Tristram put to sea, and Isolde the Fair with him. And when they were in their cabin, it so happened that they were thirsty, and they saw a little flask of gold standing beside them, and it seemed by the colour and the taste that it was noble wine. Then Sir Tristram took the flask in his hand, and said, "Madam Isolde, here is the best drink you ever drank, which Dame Bragwaine, your maid, and Gouvernail, my servant, have kept for themselves."

Then they laughed and were merry, and each drank freely to the other, and they thought that no drink they ever drank to each other was so sweet or so good. But by the time that drink was in their bodies, they loved each other so well that their love never parted, for good or for ill. And so it happened, the first love between Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair, which love never parted all the days of their lives.

So then they sailed on until by chance they came near a castle that was called Pluere, and landed there to rest, expecting to find good lodging. But as soon as Sir Tristram was inside the castle they were taken prisoner; for the custom of the castle was this: whoever rode by that castle and brought any lady with him had to fight with the lord, who was called Breunor. And if Breunor won the field, then the stranger knight and his lady were to be put to death, whoever they were; and if the strange knight won the field against Sir Breunor, then he was to die, and his lady too. This custom had been kept for many winters, and so it was called the Castle Pluere, that is to say the Weeping Castle.

Chapter 25: How Sir Tristram and Isolde were taken prisoner, and how he fought over her beauty and cut off another lady's head

So while Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair were in prison, it happened that a knight and a lady came to them where they were, to cheer them up.

"I wonder," said Tristram to the knight and the lady, "why the lord of this castle keeps us in prison. It was never the custom of any place of honour that I ever came to, when a knight and a lady asked for lodging and were taken in, to destroy them afterwards, being his guests."

"Sir," said the knight, "this is the old custom of this castle: that when a knight comes here he must fight with our lord, and the one who is weaker must lose his head. And when that is done, if the lady he brings is uglier than our lord's wife, she must lose her head; and if she is proved fairer than our lady, then the lady of this castle shall lose her head."

"God help me," said Sir Tristram, "this is a foul custom and a shameful one. But I have one advantage," said Sir Tristram. "I have a lady who is fair enough; I never saw a fairer in all the days of my life, and I have no fear that she will lose her head for lack of beauty. And rather than lose my own head I will fight for it on a fair field. So, sir knight, I pray you tell your lord that I will be ready tomorrow morning, with my lady, and myself ready to do battle, if I may have my horse and my armour."

"Sir," said that knight, "I promise you your wish shall be well granted." And then he said, "Take your rest, and see that you are up early and make yourself and your lady ready, for you shall lack nothing that you need."

And with that he left. And early the next morning that same knight came to Sir Tristram, and fetched him and his lady out, and brought him his own horse and armour, and told him to make ready for the field, for all the ranks and the common people of that lordship were there ready to watch that battle and that judgement.

Then Sir Breunor, the lord of that castle, came with his lady by the hand, veiled, and asked Sir Tristram where his lady was. "For if your lady is fairer than mine, then with your sword strike off my lady's head; and if my lady is fairer than yours, with my sword I must strike off her head. And if I can beat you, your lady shall still be mine, and you shall lose your head."

"Sir," said Tristram, "this is a foul custom and a horrible one; and rather than have my lady lose her head, I would sooner lose my own."

"No, no," said Sir Breunor, "the ladies shall first be shown side by side, and one of them shall have her judgement."

"No, I will not have it so," said Sir Tristram, "for there is no one here who will give a just judgement. But I have no doubt," said Sir Tristram, "that my lady is fairer than yours, and that I will prove and make good with my hand. And whoever says the contrary, I will prove it on his head."

And with that Sir Tristram showed Isolde the Fair, and turned her three times round, with his naked sword in his hand. And when Sir Breunor saw that, he turned his lady round the same way. But when Sir Breunor looked at Isolde the Fair, he thought he had never seen a fairer lady, and then he feared his lady's head would be off. And so all the people who were there gave judgement that Isolde the Fair was the fairer lady and the better made.

"How now," said Sir Tristram, "it seems to me it would have been a pity for my lady to lose her head. But because you and she have kept this wicked custom for a long time, and many good knights and ladies have been destroyed by the two of you, for that reason it would be no loss to destroy you both."

"God help me," said Sir Breunor, "to tell the truth, your lady is fairer than mine, and I am bitterly sorry for it. And so I hear the people saying quietly, for of all women I never saw one so fair. And so, if you kill my lady, I have no doubt I will kill you and have your lady."

"You shall win her," said Sir Tristram, "as dearly as ever knight won lady. And because of your own judgement, which you would have carried out on my lady if she had been the uglier, and because of the evil custom, give me your lady," said Sir Tristram.

And with that Sir Tristram strode up to him and took his lady from him, and with a backhand stroke he struck off her head clean.

"Well, knight," said Sir Breunor, "now you have done me an insult. Now take your horse. Since I am without a lady, I will win your lady if I can."

Chapter 26: How Sir Tristram fought with Sir Breunor and at last cut off his head

Then they took their horses and came together as if it had been thunder; and Sir Tristram struck Sir Breunor clean off his horse, and he quickly got up. And as Sir Tristram came past him again, he ran his horse through both the shoulders, so that the horse plunged here and there and fell dead to the ground. And all the while Sir Breunor ran after him to kill Sir Tristram, but Sir Tristram was quick and nimble, and got clear of his horse swiftly. And before Sir Tristram could set his shield and his sword, the other gave him three or four heavy blows. Then they rushed together like two boars, circling and sidestepping mightily and skilfully, like two noble knights. For this Sir Breunor was a proven knight, and before that had been the death of many good knights, so that it was a pity he had lasted so long.

So they fought, crashing here and there, for nearly two hours, and both were badly wounded. Then at last Sir Breunor rushed at Sir Tristram and took him in his arms, for he trusted greatly in his strength. At that time Sir Tristram was called the strongest and the tallest knight in the world; for he was said to be bigger than Sir Lancelot, but Sir Lancelot had the better wind. So at once Sir Tristram threw Sir Breunor down flat on his face, and then he unlaced his helm and struck off his head. And then all those who belonged to the castle came to him, and did him homage and swore him fealty, begging him to stay there a little while longer to undo that foul custom. Sir Tristram agreed to it. Meanwhile one of the knights of the castle rode to Sir Galahalt, the high prince, who was Sir Breunor's son, and who was a noble knight, and told him what misfortune had befallen his father and his mother.

Chapter 27: How Sir Galahalt fought with Sir Tristram, and how Sir Tristram surrendered to him and promised to join Lancelot's fellowship

Then Sir Galahalt came, and the King with the Hundred Knights with him; and this Sir Galahalt offered to fight with Sir Tristram hand to hand. And so they made ready to go into battle on horseback with great spirit. Then Sir Galahalt and Sir Tristram met so hard that each bore the other down, horse and all, to the ground. And then they got clear of their horses like noble knights, and set their shields, and drew their swords in anger and rancour, and they laid into each other with many heavy blows, now striking, now thrusting, circling and sidestepping like noble knights. So they fought for a long time, nearly half a day, and both were badly wounded. At last Sir Tristram grew quick and strong, and doubled his strokes, and drove Sir Galahalt back on the one side and on the other, so that he was likely to have been killed.

With that the King with the Hundred Knights came, and all that company went fiercely at Sir Tristram. When Sir Tristram saw them coming at him, he knew well he could not hold out. Then, as a knight wise in war, he said to Sir Galahalt, the high prince, "Sir, you show me no knighthood in letting all your men fight with me at once; and since you seem to me a noble knight with your own hands, it is a great shame to you."

"God help me," said Sir Galahalt, "there is no other way but that you must yield to me, or else die," said Sir Galahalt to Sir Tristram.

"I will rather yield to you than die, for this is more by the might of your men than of your hands."

And with that Sir Tristram took his own sword by the point, and put the pommel into the hand of Sir Galahalt.

With that the King with the Hundred Knights came up, and began to attack Sir Tristram hard.

"Leave him be," said Sir Galahalt. "Don't you dare touch him, for I have given this knight his life."

"That is your shame," said the King with the Hundred Knights. "Has he not killed your father and your mother?"

"As for that," said Sir Galahalt, "I can hardly blame him much, for my father held him in prison, and forced him to do battle with him. And my father had a custom, and a shameful custom it was, that whatever knight came there to ask for lodging, his lady had to die unless she was fairer than my mother; and if my father overcame that knight, he had to die. This was a shameful custom and practice, that a knight who asked for lodging should have such lodging as that. And because of this custom I would never have anything to do with him."

"God help me," said the king, "this was a shameful custom."

"Truly," said Sir Galahalt, "so it seemed to me; and it seemed to me it would have been a great pity for this knight to have been killed, for I dare say he is the noblest man alive, unless it is Sir Lancelot du Lake. Now, fair knight," said Sir Galahalt, "I ask you to tell me your name, and where you are from, and where you are going."

"Sir," he said, "my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, and I was sent on an errand from King Mark of Cornwall to King Anguish of Ireland, to fetch his daughter to be his wife; and here she is, ready to go with me into Cornwall, and her name is Isolde the Fair."

"And, Sir Tristram," said Sir Galahalt, the high prince, "you are well met in these borders. And if you will promise me to go to Sir Lancelot du Lake, and keep company with him, you shall go where you will, and your fair lady with you; and I promise you that never in all my days shall such customs be kept in this castle as have been kept here."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "now let me tell you, God help me, that I thought you were Sir Lancelot du Lake when I first saw you, and so I feared you the more. And, sir, I promise you," said Sir Tristram, "as soon as I can I will see Sir Lancelot and join his fellowship; for of all the knights in the world, his fellowship is what I most desire."

Chapter 28: How Sir Lancelot met Sir Carados carrying off Sir Gawain, and of the rescue of Sir Gawain

And then Sir Tristram took his leave when he saw his time, and put to sea. And in the meantime word came to Sir Lancelot and to Sir Tristram that Sir Carados, the mighty king, who was built like a giant, had fought with Sir Gawain, and given him such blows that he fainted in his saddle; and after that he took him by the collar and pulled him out of his saddle, and bound him fast to his saddlebow, and so rode on his way with him towards his castle. And as he rode, by chance Sir Lancelot met with Sir Carados, and at once he recognised Sir Gawain, who lay bound behind him.

"Ah," said Sir Lancelot to Sir Gawain, "how goes it with you?"

"Never so hard," said Sir Gawain, "unless you help me. For, God help me, unless you rescue me I know of no knight who can, except either you or Sir Tristram."
