At this Sir Lancelot was grieved by Sir Gawain's words. And then Sir Lancelot said to Sir Carados, "Put down that knight and fight with me."

"You're nothing but a fool," said Sir Carados, "for I'll serve you the same way."

"As for that," said Sir Lancelot, "don't spare me, for I warn you I will not spare you."

And then he bound Sir Gawain hand and foot, and so threw him to the ground. And then he took his spear from his squire, and rode away from Sir Lancelot to take his distance for the charge. And so each met the other, and they broke their spears right down to their hands; and then they pulled out their swords, and crashed together on horseback for more than an hour. And at last Sir Lancelot struck Sir Carados such a blow on the helm that it pierced his skull. So then Sir Lancelot took Sir Carados by the collar and pulled him down under his horse's feet, and then he dismounted and pulled off his helm and struck off his head. And then Sir Lancelot unbound Sir Gawain.

So this same tale was told to Sir Galahalt and to Sir Tristram (here you may hear of the nobleness that follows Sir Lancelot).

"Alas," said Sir Tristram, "if I did not have this errand in hand with this fair lady, truly I would never stop until I had found Sir Lancelot."

Then Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair went to sea and came into Cornwall, and there all the barons met them.

Chapter 29: Of the wedding of King Mark and Isolde the Fair, and of Bragwaine her maid, and of Palomides

And at once they were richly married with great pomp. But always, as the French book says, Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair loved each other still. Then there were great jousts and great tourneying, and many lords and ladies were at that feast, and Sir Tristram was praised most of all. So the feast lasted a long time. And after the feast was done, within a little while after, two ladies who were with Queen Isolde plotted together, out of hatred and envy, to destroy Dame Bragwaine, who was maid and lady-in-waiting to Isolde the Fair. And she was sent into the forest to fetch herbs, and there she was waylaid, and bound feet and hands to a tree, and so she was kept bound for three days. And by chance Sir Palomides found Dame Bragwaine, and there he saved her from death, and brought her to a nunnery close by, to recover.

When Isolde the queen missed her maid, you may be sure she was as downcast as ever any queen was, for of all earthly women she loved her best; the reason was that she had come with her out of her own country. And so one day Queen Isolde walked into the forest to put her thoughts aside, and there she went by herself to a spring and lamented bitterly. And suddenly Palomides came to her, who had heard all her lament, and said, "Madam Isolde, if you will grant me my wish, I will bring Dame Bragwaine to you safe and sound."

And the queen was so glad of his offer that, on the spur of the moment and without thinking, she granted all he asked.

"Well, madam," said Palomides, "I trust to your promise, and if you will wait here half an hour I will bring her to you."

"I will wait for you," said Isolde the Fair.

And Sir Palomides rode off on his way to that nunnery, and quickly came back with Dame Bragwaine. But by her own will she would not have come back, because for love of the queen she had put her life in danger. Nevertheless, half against her will, she went with Sir Palomides to the queen. And when the queen saw her she was exceedingly glad.

"Now, madam," said Palomides, "remember your promise, for I have kept mine."

"Sir Palomides," said the queen, "I do not know what your wish is, but I want you to know that though I promised you freely, I meant no harm, and I warn you I will do no harm."

"Madam," said Sir Palomides, "for now you shall not know my wish. But before my lord your husband you shall know that I will have the wish you have promised me."

And with that the queen left, and rode home to the king, and Sir Palomides rode after her. And when Sir Palomides came before the king, he said, "Sir King, I ask you, as you are a just king, to judge my case rightly."

"Tell me your case," said the king, "and you shall have justice."

Chapter 30: How Palomides claimed Queen Isolde, and how Lambegus rode after her to rescue her, and of Isolde's escape

"Sir," said Palomides, "I promised your Queen Isolde to bring back Dame Bragwaine, whom she had lost, on this agreement: that she would grant me a wish that I would ask, and she granted it to me without grudging or thinking it over."

"What do you say, my lady?" said the king.

"It is as he says, God help me," said the queen. "To tell you the truth, I promised him what he asked out of the love and joy I had in seeing her."

"Well, madam," said the king, "even if you were hasty in granting him whatever wish he asked, I will have you keep your promise."

"Then," said Palomides, "I want you to know that I will have your queen, to lead her away and keep her wherever I please."

At that the king stood still, and thought of Sir Tristram, and judged that he would rescue her. And then the king answered hastily, "Take her, with whatever adventures may come of it, for I expect you won't enjoy her for long."

"As for that," said Palomides, "I dare well risk the adventure."

And so, to cut a long story short, Sir Palomides took her by the hand and said, "Madam, do not be unwilling to go with me, for I want nothing but your own promise."

"As for that," said the queen, "I am not much afraid to go with you, though you have the advantage of me through my promise; for I have no doubt I shall be honourably rescued from you."

"As for that," said Sir Palomides, "let it be as it may."

So Queen Isolde was set behind Palomides on his horse, and he rode on his way.

At once the king sent for Sir Tristram, but he could not be found anywhere, for he was in the forest hunting; for that was always his custom, when he was not bearing arms, to chase and to hunt in the forests.

"Alas," said the king, "now I am shamed for ever, since by my own consent my lady and my queen will be destroyed."

Then a knight came forward. His name was Lambegus, and he was one of Sir Tristram's knights.

"My lord," said this knight, "since you have trust in my lord, Sir Tristram, you may be sure that for his sake I will ride after your queen and rescue her, or else I shall be beaten."

"Many thanks," said the king. "As I live, Sir Lambegus, I will repay you for it."

And then Sir Lambegus armed himself, and rode after them as fast as he could. And then within a while he overtook Sir Palomides. And then Sir Palomides left the queen.

"Who are you?" said Palomides. "Are you Tristram?"

"No," he said, "I am his servant, and my name is Sir Lambegus."

"I'm sorry for that," said Palomides. "I'd rather you had been Sir Tristram."

"I well believe you," said Lambegus, "but when you meet Sir Tristram you'll have your hands full."

And then they crashed together and burst their spears to pieces, and then they pulled out their swords, and hewed at helms and hauberks. At last Sir Palomides gave Sir Lambegus such a wound that he fell to the ground like a dead knight.

Then he looked round for Isolde the Fair, and by then she was gone, he did not know where. You may be sure Sir Palomides was never so downcast. For the queen had run into the forest, and there she found a spring, and she had thought to drown herself in it. And as good fortune would have it, a knight came to her who had a castle near by; his name was Sir Adtherp. And when he found the queen in that distress he rescued her, and brought her to his castle. And when he knew who she was he armed himself, and took his horse, and said he would be avenged on Palomides. And so he rode on until he met with him, and there Sir Palomides wounded him badly, and by force made him tell him why he had done battle with him, and how he had taken the queen to his castle.

"Now take me there," said Palomides, "or you'll die at my hands."

"Sir," said Sir Adtherp, "I am so wounded I cannot follow, but ride this way and it will bring you to my castle, and the queen is inside it."

Then Sir Palomides rode on until he came to the castle. And at a window Isolde the Fair saw Sir Palomides; then she had the gates shut fast. And when he saw he could not get into the castle, he took off his horse's bridle and saddle, and turned his horse out to graze, and sat himself down at the gate like a man out of his wits, who cared nothing for himself.

Chapter 31: How Sir Tristram rode after Palomides, found him and fought with him, and how through Isolde the fight was stopped

Now we turn to Sir Tristram. When he came home and learned that Isolde the Fair had gone off with Sir Palomides, believe me, he was angry beyond measure.

"Alas," said Sir Tristram, "this day I am shamed."

Then he called to Gouvernail his man, "Hurry and get me armed and on horseback, for I know well that Lambegus has neither the might nor the strength to stand against Sir Palomides. Alas that I was not there in his place!"

So as soon as he was armed and mounted, Sir Tristram and Gouvernail rode after them into the forest, and within a while he found his knight Lambegus wounded almost to the death. And Sir Tristram carried him to a forester, and charged him to look after him well. And then he rode on, and there he found Sir Adtherp badly wounded, and he told him how the queen would have drowned herself if it had not been for him, and how for her sake and her love he had taken it upon himself to fight Sir Palomides.

"Where is my lady?" said Sir Tristram.

"Sir," said the knight, "she is safe enough inside my castle, if she can keep herself within it."

"Many thanks," said Sir Tristram, "for your great goodness."

And so he rode until he came near that castle. And then Sir Tristram saw Sir Palomides sitting asleep at the gate, with his horse grazing close in front of him.

"Now you go, Gouvernail," said Sir Tristram, "and tell him to wake up and make himself ready."

So Gouvernail rode up to him and said, "Sir Palomides, get up, and put on your armour."

But he was so lost in thought that he did not hear what Gouvernail said. So Gouvernail came back and told Sir Tristram that he was asleep, or else he was mad.

"Go back again," said Sir Tristram, "and tell him to get up, and tell him that I am here, his mortal enemy."

So Gouvernail rode back again and prodded him with the butt of his spear, and said, "Sir Palomides, make yourself ready, for believe me, Sir Tristram is waiting over there, and sends you word that he is your mortal enemy."

And with that Sir Palomides got up quietly, without a word, and went to his horse, and saddled him and bridled him, and lightly he leapt up, and took his spear in his hand. And each of them set his spear in rest and they crashed together fast; and there Tristram struck Sir Palomides down over his horse's tail. Then Sir Palomides quickly put his shield in front of him and drew his sword. And there a hard fight began on both sides, for they both fought for the love of one lady, and all the while she lay on the walls and watched them fight beyond measure. And each of them was wounded exceedingly badly, but Palomides was much the worse wounded. So they fought, circling and sidestepping, for more than two hours, until Isolde the Fair nearly fainted from grief and sorrow.

"Alas," she said, "the one I loved and love still, and the other I do not love; and yet it would be a great pity for me to see Sir Palomides killed. For I know well that by the time this is over Sir Palomides is as good as a dead knight. And because he is not christened I would be loath for him to die a Saracen."

And with that she came down and begged Sir Tristram to fight no more.

"Ah, madam," he said, "what do you mean? Do you want me shamed? You know well that I will be ruled by you."

"I do not want your dishonour," said Isolde the Fair, "but I wish that for my sake you would spare this ill-fated Saracen Palomides."

"Madam," said Sir Tristram, "I will stop fighting for now, for your sake."

Then she said to Sir Palomides, "This shall be your charge: you are to leave this country for as long as I am in it."

"I will obey your command," said Sir Palomides, "though it is sorely against my will."

"Then take your way," said Isolde the Fair, "to the court of King Arthur, and there commend me to Queen Guinevere, and tell her I send her word that there are only four lovers in this land, that is, Sir Lancelot du Lake and Queen Guinevere, and Sir Tristram de Liones and Queen Isolde."

Chapter 32: How Sir Tristram brought Queen Isolde home, and of the quarrel between King Mark and Sir Tristram

And so Sir Palomides went away, very heavy-hearted. And Sir Tristram took the queen and brought her back to King Mark, and then there was great rejoicing at her homecoming. And who was made much of but Sir Tristram! Then Sir Tristram had his knight Sir Lambegus fetched from the forester's house, and it was a long time before he was healed, but at last he made a good recovery.

So they lived a long while in joy and pleasure. But all the while Sir Andred, who was Sir Tristram's close cousin, lay in wait to watch Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair, so as to catch them and bring scandal on them. So one day Sir Tristram was talking with Isolde the Fair in a window, and Sir Andred saw it, and told the king. Then King Mark took a sword in his hand and came at Sir Tristram, and called him a false traitor, and would have struck him. But Sir Tristram was close to him, and ran in under his sword, and took it out of his hand.

And then the king cried, "Where are my knights and my men? I order you to kill this traitor!"

But at that time there was not one who would stir at his words. When Sir Tristram saw that there was not one who would stand against him, he shook the sword at the king, and made as though he would have struck him. And then King Mark ran, and Sir Tristram went after him, and struck him five or six blows on the neck with the flat of the sword, so that he made him fall flat on his face. And then Sir Tristram went his way and armed himself, and took his horse and his man, and so he rode into that forest.

And there one day Sir Tristram met two brothers who were knights of King Mark's, and there he struck off the head of the one, and wounded the other to the death; and he made him carry his brother's head in his helmet to the king. And thirty more he wounded there. And when that knight came before the king to give his message, he died there in front of the king and the queen. Then King Mark called his council to him, and asked his barons' advice about what was best to do with Sir Tristram.

"Sir," said the barons, and Sir Dinas the Seneschal in particular, "sir, our advice to you is to send for Sir Tristram, for we want you to know that many men would side with Sir Tristram if he were in a hard spot. And sir," said Sir Dinas, "you must understand that Sir Tristram is called peerless and without equal among Christian knights, and for might and boldness we know of no knight as good, unless it is Sir Lancelot du Lake. And if he leaves your court and goes to King Arthur's court, you may be sure he will win himself such friends there that he will care nothing for your malice. And so, sir, I advise you to take him back into your favour."

"I am content," said the king, "that he be sent for, so that we may be friends."

Then the barons sent for Sir Tristram under a safe-conduct. And so when Sir Tristram came to the king he was made welcome, and nothing was said of what had passed, and there was sport and pleasure. And then the king and the queen went hunting, and Sir Tristram with them.

Chapter 33: How Sir Lamorak jousted with thirty knights, and how Sir Tristram, at King Mark's request, struck his horse down

The king and the queen pitched their pavilions and their tents in that forest beside a river, and there was hunting and jousting every day, for there were always thirty knights ready to joust against all who came by at that time. And there by chance came Sir Lamorak de Galis and Sir Driant; and there Sir Driant jousted very well, but at last he had a fall. Then Sir Lamorak offered to joust. And when he began, he dealt so with the thirty knights that there was not one of them he did not give a fall, and some of them were badly hurt.

"I wonder," said King Mark, "what knight he is who does such deeds of arms."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I know him well for as noble a knight as few now living are, and his name is Sir Lamorak de Galis."

"It would be a great shame," said the king, "for him to go away like this, unless some of you can meet him better."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "it seems to me there would be no honour for a noble man in fighting him. Because at this time he has done more than enough for any ordinary knight alive, it seems to me it would be a great shame and a low thing to put him to the test any more at this time, since he and his horse are both weary. For the deeds of arms he has done today, if they are well considered, would be enough for Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"As for that," said King Mark, "I ask you, as you love me and my lady the queen, Isolde the Fair, take your arms and joust with Sir Lamorak de Galis."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "you are telling me to do a thing that is against knighthood. And I can well judge that I shall give him a fall, for it is no great feat, since my horse and I are both fresh, and his horse and he are not. And believe me, he will take it as a great unkindness, for one good knight is always loath to take another at a disadvantage. But because I do not wish to displease you, as you ask me, so I will do, and obey your command."

And so Sir Tristram armed himself and took his horse, and rode out, and there Sir Lamorak met him mightily. And what with the force of his own spear and of Sir Tristram's spear, Sir Lamorak's horse fell to the earth, with him sitting in the saddle. Then as nimbly as he could he got clear of the saddle and his horse, and put his shield in front of him and drew his sword.

And then he called to Sir Tristram, "Get down, knight, if you dare!"

"No," said Sir Tristram, "I will have no more to do with you, for I have done too much to you already, to my dishonour and to your credit."

"As for that," said Sir Lamorak, "I owe you no thanks. Since you have outjousted me on horseback, I demand of you, and I beg you, if you are Sir Tristram, fight with me on foot."

"I will not," said Sir Tristram. "And believe me, my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, and I know well that you are Sir Lamorak de Galis. And what I have done to you was against my will, but I was asked to do it. But as for doing what you ask at this time, I will have no more to do with you, for I am ashamed of what I have done."

"As for the shame," said Sir Lamorak, "on your side or on mine, carry it yourself if you like. For though a mare's son has failed me, a queen's son shall not fail you. And so, if you are the knight men call you, I demand of you, get down and fight with me."

"Sir Lamorak," said Sir Tristram, "I understand that your heart is high, and you have cause for it, to tell you the truth. For it would grieve me if any knight kept himself fresh and then struck down a weary knight; for there was never knight or horse made that could always stand firm or hold out. And so," said Sir Tristram, "I will not fight you, for I am sorry for what I have done."

"As for that," said Sir Lamorak, "I shall pay you back, if ever I see my chance."

Chapter 34: How Sir Lamorak sent a horn to King Mark to spite Sir Tristram, and how Sir Tristram was driven into a chapel

So he rode away from him with Sir Driant, and on the way they met a knight who had been sent from Morgan le Fay to King Arthur. And this knight had a fine horn mounted with gold, and the horn had this power: that no lady or gentlewoman could drink from that horn unless she was true to her husband; and if she was false she would spill all the drink, and if she was true to her lord she could drink in peace. And it was because of Queen Guinevere, and to spite Sir Lancelot, that this horn was being sent to King Arthur. And Sir Lamorak forced that knight to tell the whole reason why he carried that horn.

"Now you shall carry this horn," said Lamorak, "to King Mark, or else choose to die for it. For I tell you plainly, to spite and shame Sir Tristram you shall carry that horn to King Mark, his uncle, and tell him that I sent it to him to test his lady, and if she is true to him he will find it out."

So the knight went on his way to King Mark, and brought him that rich horn, and said that Sir Lamorak had sent it to him, and told him besides what power the horn had. Then the king made Queen Isolde drink from it, and a hundred ladies, and of all those who drank there were only four ladies who drank clean.

"Alas," said King Mark, "this is a great insult." And he swore a great oath that she should be burned, and the other ladies too.

Then the barons gathered together, and said plainly that they would not have those ladies burned for a horn made by sorcery, which came from as false a sorceress and witch as was then alive. For that horn never did any good, but caused strife and quarrelling, and all her days she had been an enemy to all true lovers. So there were many knights who swore that if ever they met Morgan le Fay, they would show her short courtesy. Sir Tristram too was exceedingly angry that Sir Lamorak had sent that horn to King Mark, for he knew well that it was done to spite him. And so he meant to pay Sir Lamorak back.

Then Sir Tristram took to going to Queen Isolde by day and by night whenever he could, and all the while Sir Andred his cousin watched him night and day so as to catch him with Isolde the Fair. And so one night Sir Andred spied out the hour and the time when Sir Tristram went to his lady. Then Sir Andred got together twelve knights, and at midnight he fell on Sir Tristram secretly and suddenly, and there Sir Tristram was taken naked in bed with Isolde the Fair. And then he was bound hand and foot, and so he was kept until day.

And then, with the consent of King Mark, and of Sir Andred, and of some of the barons, Sir Tristram was led to a chapel that stood on the rocks above the sea, to receive his sentence there; and so he was led there bound, with forty knights. And when Sir Tristram saw that there was no other help for it, but he must die, then he said, "Fair lords, remember what I have done for the country of Cornwall, and what danger I have been in for the good of you all. For when I fought for the tribute of Cornwall with Sir Marhaus, the good knight, I was promised a better reward, when all of you refused to take on the fight. And so, as you are good, well-born knights, do not see me die so shamefully, for it is a shame to all knighthood to see me die like this. For I dare say," said Sir Tristram, "that I never met a knight but I was as good as he, or better."

"Shame on you," said Sir Andred, "you false traitor, with your boasting! For all your bragging you shall die this day."

"O Andred, Andred," said Sir Tristram, "you ought to be my kinsman, and now you are utterly unfriendly to me. But if there were no one here but you and me, you would not put me to death."

"No?" said Sir Andred, and with that he drew his sword, and would have killed him.

When Sir Tristram saw him make such a show, he looked at both his hands, which were bound fast to two knights; and suddenly he pulled them both to him, and wrenched his hands free. And then he leapt at his cousin, Sir Andred, and wrested his sword out of his hands; then he struck Sir Andred so that he fell to the earth. And so Sir Tristram fought until he had killed ten knights. So then Sir Tristram took the chapel and held it mightily. Then there was a great outcry, and the people flocked to Sir Andred, more than a hundred of them. When Sir Tristram saw the people coming at him, he remembered that he was naked, and bolted the chapel door fast, and broke the bars of a window, and so he leapt out and fell on the crags in the sea. And so at that time neither Sir Andred nor any of his companions could get to him, at that time.

Chapter 35: How Sir Tristram was rescued by his men, and of Queen Isolde, who was put in a lepers' hut, and how Tristram was wounded

So when they had gone, Gouvernail, and Sir Lambegus, and Sir Sentraille de Lushon, who were Sir Tristram's men, went looking for their master. When they heard he had escaped, they were exceedingly glad; and they found him on the rocks, and pulled him up with towels. And then Sir Tristram asked them where Isolde the Fair was, for he thought she had been carried off by Andred's people.

"Sir," said Gouvernail, "she has been put in a lepers' hut."

"Alas," said Sir Tristram, "that is a most unfitting place for such a fair lady, and if I can help it she shall not be there long."

And so he took his men and went to where Isolde the Fair was, and fetched her away, and brought her into a forest to a fine manor house, and Sir Tristram stayed there with her. So the good knight told his men to leave him: "For at this time I cannot help you." So they all went away except Gouvernail.

And so one day Sir Tristram went into the forest to amuse himself, and then it happened that he fell asleep there. And there came a man whose brother Sir Tristram had killed some time before, and when this man found him he shot him through the shoulder with an arrow; and Sir Tristram leapt up and killed that man. And in the meantime King Mark was told how Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair were in that same manor, and as soon as ever he could he came there with many knights to kill Sir Tristram. And when he got there he found him gone; and there he took Isolde the Fair home with him, and kept her so closely guarded that by no means could she ever get word of Tristram or send to him, nor he to her. And then, when Sir Tristram came back towards the old manor, he found the tracks of many horses, and from that he knew his lady was gone. And then Sir Tristram grieved greatly, and suffered great pain for a long time, for the arrow he had been wounded with was poisoned.

Then Isolde the Fair found a way to tell a lady who was a cousin of Dame Bragwaine, and she came to Sir Tristram, and told him that he could not be healed by any means: "For your lady, Isolde the Fair, cannot help you, and so she bids you hurry to Brittany, to King Howell, and there you will find his daughter, Isolde of the White Hands, and she will help you."

Then Sir Tristram and Gouvernail found themselves a ship, and so they sailed to Brittany. And when King Howell knew that it was Sir Tristram, he was very glad of him.

"Sir," he said, "I have come to this country to have help from your daughter, for I am told that there is no one else who can heal me but she."

And so within a while she healed him.

Chapter 36: How Sir Tristram served King Howell of Brittany in his war, and killed his enemy on the field

There was an earl called Grip, and this earl made great war on the king, and got the better of the king, and besieged him. And one time Sir Kehydius, who was King Howell's son, was badly wounded, near to death, as he sallied out.

Then Gouvernail went to the king and said, "Sir, I advise you to ask my lord, Sir Tristram, to help you in your need."

"I will do as you advise," said the king.

And so he went to Sir Tristram, and begged him to help him in his wars: "For my son, Sir Kehydius, cannot go into the field."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I will go to the field and do what I can."

Then Sir Tristram sallied out of the town with such a company as he could get together, and did such deeds that all Brittany talked of him. And then at last, by great might and force, he killed the Earl Grip with his own hands, and he killed more than a hundred knights that day. And then Sir Tristram was received with honour, with a procession.

Then King Howell took him in his arms, and said, "Sir Tristram, I will give up all my kingdom to you."

"God forbid," said Sir Tristram, "for I am bound to serve you for your daughter's sake."

Then, through the great efforts of King Howell and his son Kehydius, and by great offers, great love grew up between Isolde and Sir Tristram, for that lady was both good and beautiful, and a woman of noble blood and good name. And because Sir Tristram had such welcome and riches and every other pleasure he had there, he had almost forsaken Isolde the Fair. And so at one time Sir Tristram agreed to marry Isolde of the White Hands. And at last they were married, and solemnly held their wedding. And so, when they were both in bed, Sir Tristram remembered his old lady, Isolde the Fair. And then such a sudden grief took hold of him that he was utterly dismayed, and he gave her no other welcome than embracing and kissing. As for any other bodily desire, Sir Tristram never thought of it, nor lay with her: so the French book says. It says too that the lady thought there was no pleasure but kissing and embracing.

And in the meantime there was a knight in Brittany whose name was Suppinabiles, and he came over the sea to England, and then he came to the court of King Arthur, and there he met Sir Lancelot du Lake, and told him of Sir Tristram's marriage.

Then Sir Lancelot said, "Shame on him, a knight untrue to his lady, that so noble a knight as Sir Tristram should be found false to his first lady, Isolde the Fair, Queen of Cornwall! But tell him this," said Sir Lancelot, "that of all knights in the world I loved him most, and took most joy in him, and all for his noble deeds. And let him know that the love between him and me is over for ever, and that from this day on I give him warning as his mortal enemy."

Chapter 37: How Sir Suppinabiles told Sir Tristram how he was slandered at King Arthur's court, and of Sir Lamorak

Then Sir Suppinabiles went back to Brittany, and there he found Sir Tristram, and told him that he had been at King Arthur's court.

Then Sir Tristram said, "Did you hear anything of me?"

"God help me," said Sir Suppinabiles, "I heard Sir Lancelot speak great shame of you there, saying that you are a false knight to your lady; and he told me to let you know that he will be your mortal enemy wherever he may meet you."

"I am sorry for that," said Tristram, "for of all knights, his was the company I loved to be in."

So Sir Tristram lamented greatly, and was ashamed that noble knights should speak ill of him for the sake of his lady. And meanwhile Isolde the Fair wrote a letter to Queen Guinevere, complaining of Sir Tristram's faithlessness, and of how he had married the King of Brittany's daughter. Queen Guinevere sent her another letter, and told her to take heart, for she would have joy after sorrow; for Sir Tristram was known as so noble a knight that ladies would use sorcery to make such noble men marry them. "But in the end," Queen Guinevere said, "it shall be this way: that he will hate her, and love you better than ever he did before."

So we leave Sir Tristram in Brittany, and speak of Sir Lamorak de Galis. As he was sailing, his ship struck a rock and was lost with all aboard, except Sir Lamorak and his squire. And there he swam mightily, and fishermen of the Isle of Servage picked him up; and his squire was drowned. And the seamen had great labour to save Sir Lamorak's life, for all the comfort they could give him.

And the lord of that isle was called Sir Nabon le Noire, a great mighty giant. And this Sir Nabon hated all King Arthur's knights, and would do them no favour of any kind. And these fishermen told Sir Lamorak all Sir Nabon's ways: how no knight of King Arthur's ever came there but he destroyed him. And at the last fight he had, Sir Nanowne le Petite was killed, whom he put to a shameful death to spite King Arthur, for he was torn limb from limb.

"I am sorry for that knight's death," said Sir Lamorak, "for he was my cousin; and if I were as well as ever I was, I would avenge his death."

"Hush," said the fishermen, "and say nothing of that here, for before ever you leave this place Sir Nabon must know that you have been here, or else we would die for your sake."

"So long as I am healed," said Lamorak, "of the sickness I have taken in the sea, I want you to tell him that I am a knight of King Arthur's, for I was never afraid to own my lord."

Chapter 38: How Sir Tristram and his wife landed in Wales, and how he met Sir Lamorak there

Now we turn to Sir Tristram. One day he took a little boat, with his wife Isolde of the White Hands and Sir Kehydius her brother, to amuse themselves along the coast. And when they were out from the land, a wind drove them in to the coast of Wales, onto this Isle of Servage, where Sir Lamorak was, and there the boat broke up; and there Dame Isolde was hurt. And as best they could they got into the forest, and there by a spring he saw Segwarides and a damsel. And then they greeted each other.

"Sir," said Segwarides, "I know you for Sir Tristram de Liones, the man in the world I have most cause to hate, because you came between me and my wife. But as for that," said Sir Segwarides, "I will never hate a noble knight for the sake of a faithless woman. And so I beg you, be my friend, and I will be yours as far as I can. For believe me, you are in a hard spot in this valley, and we shall each have enough to do to help the other."

And then Sir Segwarides brought Sir Tristram to a lady nearby who had been born in Cornwall, and she told him all the dangers of that valley, and how no knight ever came there but he was taken prisoner or killed.

"Believe me, fair lady," said Sir Tristram, "I killed Sir Marhaus and freed Cornwall from the tribute to Ireland, and I am the one who freed the King of Ireland from Sir Blamore de Ganis, and I am the one who beat Sir Palomides. And you may be sure I am Sir Tristram de Liones, who by the grace of God shall free this woeful Isle of Servage."

So Sir Tristram was well looked after. Then someone told him there was a knight of King Arthur's who had been wrecked on the rocks.

"What is his name?" said Sir Tristram.

"We do not know," said the fishermen, "but he makes no secret that he is a knight of King Arthur's, and he cares nothing for the mighty lord of this isle."

"I beg you," said Sir Tristram, "if you can, bring him here so that I may see him, and if he is any of Arthur's knights I shall know him."

Then the lady asked the fishermen to bring him to her house. So the next day they brought him there in a fisherman's clothes; and as soon as Sir Tristram saw him he smiled at him and knew him well, but he did not know Sir Tristram.

"Fair sir," said Sir Tristram, "it seems to me from your face that you have been ill not long ago, and I also think I ought to know you from before."

"I can well believe," said Sir Lamorak, "that you have seen me and met me."

"Fair sir," said Sir Tristram, "tell me your name."

"I will tell you on one condition," said Sir Lamorak, "that is, that you tell me whether or not you are the lord of this island, the one called Nabon le Noire."

"Truly," said Sir Tristram, "I am not he, nor do I hold land from him. I am his enemy as much as you are, and so I shall be found before I leave this isle."

"Well," said Sir Lamorak, "since you have spoken so freely to me, my name is Sir Lamorak de Galis, son of King Pellinore."

"Truly, I well believe it," said Sir Tristram, "for if you said otherwise I know the contrary."

"Who are you," said Sir Lamorak, "who know me?"

"I am Sir Tristram de Liones."

"Ah, sir, do you not remember the fall you gave me once, and afterwards refused to fight me on foot?"

"That was not for any fear I had of you," said Sir Tristram, "but I was ashamed at that time to have any more to do with you, for it seemed to me you had had enough. But, Sir Lamorak, in return for my kindness you brought shame on many ladies when you sent the horn from Morgan le Fay to King Mark, for you did it to spite me."

"Well," he said, "if it were to do again, I would do it, for I would rather strife and quarrelling fell out in King Mark's court than in Arthur's court, for the honour of the two courts is not alike."

"As to that," said Sir Tristram, "I know it well. But what was done was done to spite me; but all your malice, I thank God, did no great harm. And so," said Sir Tristram, "you shall put aside all your malice, and so will I, and let us try how we may win honour between us on this giant Sir Nabon le Noire, who is lord of this island, and destroy him."

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "now I understand your knighthood. What all men say cannot be false: for goodness, nobility and honour you are peerless among all knights, and for your courtesy and your gentleness I showed you discourtesy, and now I am sorry for it."

Chapter 39: How Sir Tristram fought with Sir Nabon and overcame him, and made Sir Segwarides lord of the island

In the meantime word came that Sir Nabon had had it proclaimed that all the people of that isle were to be at his castle on the fifth day after. And that same day Nabon's son was to be made a knight, and all the knights of that valley and round about were to be there to joust, and all those of the realm of Logres were to be there to joust against those of North Wales. And five hundred knights came there, and the people of the country brought Sir Lamorak there, and Sir Tristram, and Sir Kehydius, and Sir Segwarides, for they dared not do otherwise. And then Sir Nabon lent Sir Lamorak a horse and armour, at Sir Lamorak's request. And Sir Lamorak jousted and did such deeds of arms that Nabon and all the people said there was never a knight they had ever seen do such deeds of arms. For, as the French book says, he outjousted everyone who was there, most of the five hundred knights, so that not one of them kept his saddle against him.

Then Sir Nabon offered to play his own game with him: "For I never saw any knight do so much in one day."

"Gladly," said Sir Lamorak, "I will play as well as I can, but I am weary and badly bruised."

And there each of them took a spear, but Nabon would not meet Sir Lamorak in the joust, but struck his horse in the forehead, and so killed it. And then Sir Lamorak went on foot, and turned his shield and drew his sword, and there a hard fight began on foot. But Sir Lamorak was so badly bruised and so short of breath that he circled and sidestepped somewhat backwards.

"Fair fellow," said Sir Nabon, "hold your hand, and I will show you more courtesy than ever I showed a knight, because I have seen your noble knighthood today. And so stand aside, and I will find out whether any of your companions will fight me."

Then, when Sir Tristram heard that, he stepped forward and said, "Nabon, lend me a horse and sound armour, and I will fight you."

"Well, fellow," said Sir Nabon, "go to that pavilion over there, and arm yourself in the best you find there, and I will play a marvellous game with you."

Then Sir Tristram said, "Mind you play well, or else perhaps I shall teach you a new game."

"That is well said, fellow," said Sir Nabon.

So when Sir Tristram was armed as he liked best, and well shielded and sworded, he squared up to him on foot; for he knew well that Sir Nabon would not wait for a stroke of the spear, and so he would kill all the knights' horses.

"Now, fair fellow, Sir Nabon, let us play."

So then they fought on foot for a long time, circling and sidestepping, striking and thrusting, for a long while without any rest. At last Sir Nabon begged him to tell him his name.

"Sir Nabon, I tell you my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, a knight of Cornwall under King Mark."

"You are welcome," said Sir Nabon, "for of all knights I have most wanted to fight with you or with Sir Lancelot."

So then they went at each other fiercely, and Sir Tristram killed Sir Nabon. And straight away he leapt at his son, and struck off his head; and then all the country said they would hold their lands from Sir Tristram.

"No," said Sir Tristram, "I will not have it so. Here is an honourable knight, Sir Lamorak de Galis, and for my part he shall be lord of this country, for he has done great deeds of arms here."

"No," said Sir Lamorak, "I will not be lord of this country, for I have not deserved it as well as you. And so give it to whoever you like, for I will have none of it."

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "since neither you nor I will have it, let us give it to someone who has not deserved it so well."

"Do as you please," said Segwarides, "for the gift is yours; for I would have none of it, even if I had deserved it."

So it was given to Segwarides, and he thanked them for it; and so he was lord, and governed it honourably. And then Sir Segwarides set all the prisoners free, and put that valley under good government. And so he went back to Cornwall, and told King Mark and Isolde the Fair how Sir Tristram had made him lord of the Isle of Servage, and there he proclaimed through all Cornwall all the adventures of these two knights, so that they were known openly. But Isolde the Fair was full of sorrow when she heard that Sir Tristram was married to Isolde of the White Hands.

Chapter 40: How Sir Lamorak parted from Sir Tristram, and how he met Sir Frol, and afterwards Sir Lancelot

So we turn to Sir Lamorak, who rode towards Arthur's court; and Sir Tristram's wife and Kehydius took a ship and sailed to Brittany, to King Howell, where he was welcome. And when he heard of these adventures they marvelled at his noble deeds.

Now we turn to Sir Lamorak. When he had parted from Sir Tristram he rode out of the forest until he came to a hermitage. When the hermit saw him, he asked him where he had come from.

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "I come from this valley."

"Sir," said the hermit, "that amazes me. For these twenty years I never saw any knight pass through this country but he was either killed or shamefully wounded, or passed as a poor prisoner."

"Those evil customs," said Sir Lamorak, "are done away with, for Sir Tristram has killed your lord, Sir Nabon, and his son."

Then the hermit was glad, and all his brothers, for he said there was never such a tyrant among Christian men. "And so," said the hermit, "we will hold this valley and its liberties from Sir Tristram."

So the next day Sir Lamorak left; and as he rode he saw four knights fighting against one, and that one knight defended himself well, but at last the four knights had him down. And then Sir Lamorak went between them, and asked them why they wanted to kill that one knight, and said it was a shame, four against one.

"You may be sure," said the four knights, "that he is false."

"That is your story," said Sir Lamorak, "and when I have heard him speak as well, I will say as you say." Then Lamorak said, "Ah, knight, can you not clear yourself of being a false knight?"

"Sir," he said, "I can clear myself, both with my word and with my hands, and I will prove it on any one of the best of them, my body against his body."

Then they all spoke at once: "We will not risk our bodies for you. But you may be sure," they said, "that if King Arthur himself were here, it would not be in his power to save this man's life."

"That is too much said," said Sir Lamorak, "but many men say more behind a man's back than they will say to his face. And because of your words, you shall understand that I am one of the least of King Arthur's court. For the honour of my lord, now do your worst, and in spite of you I shall rescue him."

And then all of them rushed at Sir Lamorak at once, but with two strokes Sir Lamorak quickly killed two of them, and then the other two fled. So then Sir Lamorak turned back to that knight, and asked him his name.

"Sir," he said, "my name is Sir Frol of the Out Isles."

Then he rode with Sir Lamorak and kept him company. And as they rode along the way they saw a handsome knight riding towards them, all in white.

"Ah," said Frol, "that knight over there jousted with me not long ago and struck me down, and so I will joust with him."

"You shall not do so," said Sir Lamorak, "if you take my advice, unless you tell me your quarrel, whether you jousted at his request or he at yours."

"No," said Sir Frol, "I jousted with him at my own request."

"Sir," said Lamorak, "then I advise you to have no more to do with him, for it seems to me by his bearing that he must be a noble knight, and no joker; for I think he must be of the Round Table."

"I will not hold back for that," said Sir Frol. And then he shouted, "Sir knight, get ready to joust!"

"There is no need for that," said the White Knight, "for I have no wish to joust with you."

But still they set their spears in rest, and the White Knight overthrew Sir Frol, and then he rode on his way at an easy pace. Then Sir Lamorak rode after him, and begged him to tell him his name: "For it seems to me you must be of the fellowship of the Round Table."

"On one condition," he said, "I will tell you my name: that you will not give my name away, and also that you will tell me yours."

"Then," he said, "my name is Sir Lamorak de Galis."

"And my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake."

Then they put up their swords, and kissed each other warmly, and each rejoiced greatly in the other.

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "if it please you, I will do you service."

"God forbid," said Lancelot, "that anyone of such noble blood as you should do me service." Then he said, "Besides, I am on a quest that I must do by myself alone."

"Now God speed you," said Sir Lamorak, and so they parted.

Then Sir Lamorak came to Sir Frol and got him on his horse again.

"What knight is that?" said Sir Frol.

"Sir," he said, "it is not for you to know, and it is no part of my business to tell you."

"Then you are all the more discourteous," said Sir Frol, "and so I will leave you."

"You may do as you please," said Sir Lamorak, "and yet by keeping my company you have saved the fairest flower of your garland." And so they parted.

Chapter 41: How Sir Lamorak slew Sir Frol, and of the courteous fight with his brother Sir Belliance

Then within two or three days Sir Lamorak found a knight asleep by a spring, and his lady sat beside him and kept watch. Just then Sir Gawain came and took the knight's lady, and set her up behind his squire. So Sir Lamorak rode after Sir Gawain, and said, "Sir Gawain, turn back."

And then Sir Gawain said, "What do you want with me? For I am King Arthur's nephew."

"Sir," he said, "for that reason I will spare you; otherwise that lady would stay with me, or else you would have to joust with me."

Then Sir Gawain turned and rode at the knight the lady belonged to, with his spear; but the knight, by sheer strength, struck Sir Gawain down, and took his lady with him. Sir Lamorak saw all this, and said to himself, "Unless I avenge my companion, he will speak dishonour of me in King Arthur's court."

Then Sir Lamorak turned back and offered to joust with that knight.

"Sir," he said, "I am ready."

And there they came together with all their might, and there Sir Lamorak struck the knight through both sides, so that he fell to the earth dead.

Then that lady rode to that knight's brother, who was called Belliance le Orgulous, who lived close by, and she told him how his brother had been killed.

"Alas," he said, "I will be avenged."

And so he got on his horse, and armed himself, and within a while he overtook Sir Lamorak, and called to him, "Turn and leave that lady, for you and I must play a new game. For you have killed my brother Sir Frol, who was a better knight than ever you were."

"That may well be," said Sir Lamorak, "but today in the field I was found the better."

So they rode at each other, and each unhorsed the other, and they turned their shields and drew their swords, and fought mightily, like proven noble knights, for the space of two hours. So then Sir Belliance begged him to tell him his name.

"Sir," he said, "my name is Sir Lamorak de Galis."

"Ah," said Sir Belliance, "you are the man in the world I hate most, for I killed my sons for your sake, when I saved your life, and now you have killed my brother Sir Frol. Alas, how could I ever be reconciled with you? So defend yourself, for you shall die; there is no other remedy."

"Alas," said Sir Lamorak, "I ought to have known you full well, for you are the man who has done most for me."

And with that Sir Lamorak knelt down, and begged him for mercy.

"Get up," said Sir Belliance, "or else I shall kill you where you kneel."

"There will be no need for that," said Sir Lamorak, "for I will yield to you, not for fear of you, nor for your strength, but your goodness makes me utterly loath to fight you. And so I beg you, for God's sake, and for the honour of knighthood, forgive me all the wrong I have done you."

"Alas," said Belliance, "stop your kneeling, or else I shall kill you without mercy."

Then they went back to the fight, and each wounded the other, so that all the ground where they fought was bloody. And at last Belliance drew back and sat himself down gently on a little hill, for he was so faint from bleeding that he could not stand. Then Sir Lamorak threw his shield onto his back, and asked him how he was.

"Well," said Sir Belliance.

"Ah, sir, yet I shall show you favour in your distress."

"Ah, Sir Belliance, good knight," said Sir Lamorak, "you are a fool, for if I had had you at such an advantage as you had me, I would have killed you. But your gentleness is so good and so generous that I must forgive you my ill will."

And then Sir Lamorak knelt down, and first unlaced the other's visor, and then his own, and then they kissed each other with weeping tears. Then Sir Lamorak led Sir Belliance to an abbey close by, and there Sir Lamorak would not leave Belliance until he was healed. And then they swore together that neither of them would ever fight against the other. So Sir Lamorak left and went to the court of King Arthur.

Here we leave Sir Lamorak and Sir Tristram. And here begins the history of La Cote Male Taile.

Book Nine: La Cote Male Taile, and Sir Tristram

Chapter 1: How a young man came to King Arthur's court, and how Sir Kay mockingly called him La Cote Male Taile

To King Arthur's court there came a young man, big and strongly built, and he was richly dressed; and he asked the king to make him a knight. But his outer coat sat crooked on him, even though it was rich cloth of gold.

"What is your name?" said King Arthur.

"Sir," he said, "my name is Bruin le Noire, and in a short while you shall know that I am of good family."

"That may well be," said Sir Kay the Seneschal, "but in mockery you shall be called La Cote Male Taile, which is to say, the badly cut coat."

"It is a great thing that you ask," said the king. "And why do you wear that rich coat? Tell me, for I can well believe there is some reason for it."

"Sir," he answered, "I had a father, a noble knight, and as he rode hunting one day it happened that he lay down to sleep. And there came a knight who had long been his enemy, and when he saw that he was fast asleep he hacked him all to pieces. And my father was wearing this same coat at the time, and that is what makes this coat sit so badly on me, for the sword strokes are on it just as I found it, and it will never be mended by me. So I wear this coat to keep my father's death in mind until I am avenged. And because you are called the noblest king in the world, I have come to you so that you should make me a knight."

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak and Sir Gaheris, "it would be well done to make him a knight, for he looks well in body and in face, so that he will prove a good man, and a good knight, and a mighty one. For, sir, if you remember, just such a one was Sir Lancelot du Lake when he first came to this court, and very few of us knew where he came from; and now he has proved himself the man of greatest honour in the world, and all your court and all your Round Table is honoured and bettered by Sir Lancelot more than by any knight now living."

"That is true," said the king, "and tomorrow, at your request, I shall make him a knight."

So the next morning a hart was found, and King Arthur rode out there with a company of his knights to kill the hart. And this young man whom Sir Kay had named La Cote Male Taile was left behind with Queen Guinevere. And by sudden chance there was a fearsome lion kept in a strong tower of stone, and it happened that at that very time he broke loose, and came charging at the queen and her knights. And when the queen saw the lion she cried out and fled, and begged her knights to rescue her. And of them all only twelve stood their ground, and all the others fled.

Then La Cote Male Taile said, "Now I see well that not all the coward knights are dead."

And with that he drew his sword and squared up to the lion. And that lion gaped wide and came at him, rearing up, to kill him. And then he struck him in the middle of the head such a mighty stroke that it split his head apart, and he crashed to the ground. Then the queen was told how the young man whom Sir Kay in scorn had named La Cote Male Taile had killed the lion. With that the king came home. And when the queen told him of that adventure, he was well pleased, and said, "I'll stake my head on it, he will prove a noble man and a faithful knight, and true to his word."

Then the king made him a knight on the spot.

"Now, sir," said this young knight, "I ask you and all the knights of your court to call me by no other name but La Cote Male Taile. Since Sir Kay has named me so, so I will be called."

"I agree to that gladly," said the king.

Chapter 2: How a damsel came to the court and asked for a knight to take on a quest, which La Cote Male Taile undertook

Then that same day a damsel came into the court, and she brought with her a great black shield, with a white hand in the middle of it holding a sword. There was no other device on that shield. When King Arthur saw her he asked her where she came from and what she wanted.

"Sir," she said, "I have ridden long, and many a day, with this shield, by many roads, and this is why I have come to your court. There was a good knight who owned this shield, and this knight had undertaken a great deed of arms, to carry it through to the end. And so it was his misfortune that another strong knight met him by sudden chance, and there they fought a long time, and each wounded the other exceedingly badly; and they were so weary that they left that battle even. So this knight who owned this shield saw no other way but that he must die. And then he commanded me to carry this shield to the court of King Arthur, asking and praying some good knight to take this shield, and to fulfil the quest that he was on."

"Now what do you say to this quest?" said King Arthur. "Is there any of you here who will undertake to bear this shield?"

Then there was not one who would speak a single word. Then Sir Kay took the shield in his hands.

"Sir knight," said the damsel, "what is your name?"

"Believe me," he said, "my name is Sir Kay the Seneschal, known far and wide."

"Sir," said that damsel, "put down that shield, for believe me, it is not for you. The knight who bears this shield must be a better knight than you."

"Damsel," said Sir Kay, "believe me, I took this shield in my hands with your leave, to look at it, not with that intent. But go wherever you like, for I'm not going with you."

Then the damsel stood still for a long while and looked at many of those knights. Then the knight La Cote Male Taile spoke up.

"Fair damsel," he said, "I will take the shield and that adventure upon me, if only I knew which way my journey would lead; for since I was made a knight this day, I would take this adventure upon me."

"What is your name, fair young man?" said the damsel.

"My name," he said, "is La Cote Male Taile."

"Well may you be called that," said the damsel, "the knight with the badly cut coat. But if you are bold enough to take it on yourself to bear that shield and to follow me, believe me, your skin will be as well hacked as your coat."

"As for that," said La Cote Male Taile, "when I am so hacked, I will ask you for no salve to heal me with."

And just then two squires came into the court and brought him great horses, and his armour, and his spears, and at once he was armed and took his leave.

"It is not by my will," said the king, "that you take that hard adventure upon you."

"Sir," he said, "this adventure is mine, and the first that ever I took upon me, and I will follow it, whatever becomes of me."

Then that damsel left, and La Cote Male Taile followed close after her. And within a while he overtook the damsel, and at once she abused him in the foulest way.

Chapter 3: How La Cote Male Taile overthrew Sir Dagonet, the king's fool, and of the scolding he got from the damsel

Then Sir Kay arranged for Sir Dagonet, King Arthur's fool, to follow after La Cote Male Taile. And there Sir Kay had Sir Dagonet horsed and armed, and told him to follow La Cote Male Taile and offer to joust with him; and so he did. And when he saw La Cote Male Taile, he shouted and told him to make ready to joust. So Sir La Cote Male Taile struck Sir Dagonet over his horse's rump. Then the damsel mocked La Cote Male Taile.

"Shame on you!" she said. "Now you're disgraced in Arthur's court, when they send a fool to fight you, and at your very first joust too."

So she rode on a long way, and scolded. And within a while there came Sir Bleoberis, the good knight, and there he jousted with La Cote Male Taile, and there Sir Bleoberis struck him so hard that horse and all fell to the ground. Then La Cote Male Taile got up quickly, and set his shield, and drew his sword, and would have fought to the uttermost, for he was mad with rage.

"Not so," said Sir Bleoberis de Ganis. "At this time I will not fight on foot."

Then the damsel Maledisant rebuked him in the foulest way, and told him, "Turn back, coward!"

"Ah, damsel," he said, "I beg you for mercy, abuse me no more. My grief is enough without your adding to it. I never count myself the worse knight when a mare's son lets me down, and I don't count myself the worse knight for a fall from Sir Bleoberis either."

So he rode with her like this for two days. And by chance there came Sir Palomides and met him, and he served him in the same way as Bleoberis had done before.

"What are you doing here in my company?" said the damsel Maledisant. "You can't keep your seat against any knight, or stand up to a single blow from him, unless it's Sir Dagonet."

"Ah, fair damsel, I am none the worse for taking a fall from Sir Palomides, and yet I have no great dishonour from it, for neither Bleoberis nor Palomides would fight with me on foot."

"As for that," said the damsel, "believe me, they think it beneath them, and scorn to get off their horses to fight such an ignorant knight as you are."

So in the meantime there came Sir Mordred, Sir Gawain's brother, and so he fell into company with the damsel Maledisant. And then they came before the Castle Orgulous, and there was a custom there that no knight could pass that castle without either jousting or being taken prisoner, or at the least losing his horse and his armour. And two knights came out against them, and Sir Mordred jousted with the first, and that knight of the castle struck Sir Mordred down off his horse. And then La Cote Male Taile jousted with the other, and each of them struck the other down, horse and all, to the ground. And when they got clear of their horses, each of them took the other's horse. And then La Cote Male Taile rode at the knight who had struck down Sir Mordred, and jousted with him. And there Sir La Cote Male Taile hurt and wounded him exceedingly badly, and put him off his horse as if he were dead. So he turned to the one he had met before, and that knight took flight towards the castle, and Sir La Cote Male Taile rode after him into the Castle Orgulous, and there La Cote Male Taile killed him.

Chapter 4: How La Cote Male Taile fought against a hundred knights, and how he escaped with a lady's help

And at once a hundred knights came around him and attacked him. And when he saw that his horse would be killed, he dismounted and got clear of his horse, and put the bridle under its feet, and so put it out of the gate. And when he had done that, he charged in among them, and set his back against the wall of a lady's chamber, thinking to himself that he would rather die there with honour than put up with the abuse of the damsel Maledisant. And in the meantime, as he stood and fought, the lady whose chamber it was went out quietly by her back gate, and outside the gates she found La Cote Male Taile's horse, and quickly she took him by the bridle and tied him to the back gate. And then she went quietly back to her chamber to watch how that one knight fought against a hundred knights. And when she had watched him a long time, she went to a window behind his back.

"Knight," she said, "you fight marvellously well, but for all that you must die in the end, unless through your mighty prowess you can make your way to that back gate over there, for I have tied your horse there to wait for you. But believe me, you must think of your honour and not think of dying, for you cannot make your way to that back gate unless you act nobly and mightily."

When La Cote Male Taile heard her say this, he gripped his sword in his hands, and put his shield well in front of him, and pushed his way through the thickest of the crowd. And when he came to the back gate he found four knights there ready for him, and with the first two strokes he killed two of the knights, and the others fled. And so he won his horse and rode away from them. And all of it, just as it happened, was told in King Arthur's court, how he killed twelve knights within the Castle Orgulous; and so he rode on his way.

And in the meanwhile the damsel said to Sir Mordred, "I expect my fool of a knight is either killed or taken prisoner."

Then they saw him come riding. And when he had come up to them, he told them all how he had fared, and how he had escaped in spite of them all. "And some of the best of them will tell no tales."

"You're lying," said the damsel, "and I dare prove it. They let you pass as a fool and a disgrace to all knighthood."

"You may prove that," said La Cote Male Taile.

With that she sent a courier of hers, who always rode with her, to learn the truth of this deed. And so he rode there quickly, and asked how, and in what manner, La Cote Male Taile had escaped out of the castle. Then all the knights cursed him, and said that he was a fiend and no man: "For he has killed twelve of our best knights here, and until today we thought that would have been too much for Sir Lancelot du Lake or for Sir Tristram de Liones. And in spite of us all he has gone from us, against our will."

With this answer the courier left, and came to Maledisant his lady, and told her everything, how Sir La Cote Male Taile had fared at the Castle Orgulous. Then she hung her head, and said little.

"By my head," said Sir Mordred to the damsel, "you are much to blame for rebuking him so, for I warn you plainly, he is a good knight, and I have no doubt that he will prove a noble knight. But as yet he cannot sit firm on horseback, for being a good horseman must come from practice and exercise. But when it comes to the strokes of his sword, then he is noble and mighty, and Sir Bleoberis and Sir Palomides saw that. For believe me, they are wily men of arms, and they know at once, when they see a young knight, by his riding, how sure they are to give him a fall from his horse or a great blow. But for the most part they will not get down on foot with young knights, for they are strong and well armed. For in the same way Sir Lancelot du Lake, when he was first made knight, was often worsted on horseback, but on foot he always won back his renown, and killed and trampled many knights of the Round Table. And so the shame Sir Lancelot dealt to many knights makes men of prowess wary. For I have often seen old, proven knights shamed and killed by men who were only young beginners."

So they rode on, talking earnestly together along the way.

Chapter 5: How Sir Lancelot came to the court and heard of La Cote Male Taile, and how he followed after him, and how La Cote Male Taile was taken prisoner

Here we leave this tale for a while, and speak of Sir Lancelot du Lake: how, when he had come to the court of King Arthur, he heard tell of the young knight La Cote Male Taile, how he killed the lion, and how he took upon himself the adventure of the black shield, which was called at that time the hardiest adventure in the world.

"God save me," said Sir Lancelot to many of his companions, "it was a shame to all the noble knights to let such a young knight take such an adventure upon him, to his destruction. For I want you to know," said Sir Lancelot, "that that damsel Maledisant has carried that shield many a day to seek out the most proven knights. And she was the one from whom Breuse Saunce Pité took that shield, and afterwards Tristram de Liones rescued that shield from him and gave it back to the damsel, a little before the time that Sir Tristram fought with my nephew Sir Blamore de Ganis, over a quarrel between the King of Ireland and him."

Then many knights were sorry that Sir La Cote Male Taile had gone out on that adventure.

"Truly," said Sir Lancelot, "I mean to ride after him."

And within seven days Sir Lancelot overtook La Cote Male Taile, and then he greeted him and the damsel Maledisant. And when Sir Mordred saw Sir Lancelot, he left their company. And so Sir Lancelot rode with them for a whole day, and all the while that damsel rebuked La Cote Male Taile. And then Sir Lancelot answered for him, and then she left off, and rebuked Sir Lancelot.

So in the meantime Sir Tristram sent a letter by a damsel to Sir Lancelot, excusing himself for his marriage to Isolde of the White Hands; and he said in the letter that, as he was a true knight, he had never lain with Isolde of the White Hands. And Sir Tristram wrote to Sir Lancelot exceedingly courteously and like a gentleman, all the while begging him to be his good friend, and a good friend to Isolde the Fair of Cornwall, and that Sir Lancelot would speak for him if ever he saw her. And within a short time, by the grace of God, said Sir Tristram, he would speak with Isolde the Fair, and with him too, very soon. Then Sir Lancelot left the damsel and Sir La Cote Male Taile, to read that letter over and to write another letter to Sir Tristram de Liones.

And in the meanwhile La Cote Male Taile rode with the damsel until they came to a castle called Pendragon. And there were six knights standing in front of him, and one of them offered to joust with La Cote Male Taile. And there La Cote Male Taile struck him over his horse's rump. And then the other five knights set on him all at once with their spears, and there they struck La Cote Male Taile down, horse and man. And then they dismounted quickly, and all laid hands on him at once, and took him prisoner, and so led him into the castle and kept him there as a prisoner.

And in the morning Sir Lancelot got up, and sent the damsel off with letters to Sir Tristram, and then he took his way after La Cote Male Taile. And on the way, on a bridge, there was a knight who offered to joust with Sir Lancelot, and Sir Lancelot struck him down. And then they fought a noble battle together on foot, and a mighty one, and at last Sir Lancelot struck him down grovelling on his hands and his knees. And then that knight yielded, and Sir Lancelot received him kindly.

"Sir," said the knight, "I ask you to tell me your name, for my heart warms to you greatly."

"No," said Sir Lancelot, "at this time I will not tell you my name, unless you first tell me yours."

"Certainly," said the knight. "My name is Sir Nerovens, and I was made a knight by my lord Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"Ah, Nerovens de Lile," said Sir Lancelot, "I am very glad that you have proved a good knight; for now, believe me, my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"Alas," said Sir Nerovens de Lile, "what have I done!"

And with that he fell flat at his feet, and would have kissed them, but Sir Lancelot would not let him; and then each of them rejoiced greatly in the other. And then Sir Nerovens told Sir Lancelot that he should not go by the Castle of Pendragon. "For there is a lord there, a mighty knight, and many knights with him, and tonight I heard it said that yesterday they took a knight prisoner who was riding with a damsel, and they say he is a knight of the Round Table."

Chapter 6: How Sir Lancelot fought with six knights, and afterwards with Sir Brian, and how he freed the prisoners

"Ah," said Sir Lancelot, "that knight is my companion, and I shall rescue him or else lose my life for it."

And with that he rode hard until he came before the Castle of Pendragon. And at once six knights came out, and all made ready to set on Sir Lancelot at once. Then Sir Lancelot set his spear in rest, and struck the foremost so that he broke his back in two; and three of them hit him and three missed. And then Sir Lancelot passed through them, and swiftly he turned back in again, and struck another knight through the breast and out through the back more than a yard, and with that his spear broke. So then all the four knights who remained drew their swords and slashed at Sir Lancelot. And Sir Lancelot placed his strokes so well that with four separate strokes they were out of their saddles, exceedingly badly wounded. And straight away he rode charging into that castle.

And at once the lord of the castle, who at that time was called Sir Brian de les Isles, who was a noble man and a great enemy to King Arthur, was armed within a short while and on horseback. And then they set their spears in rest and crashed together so hard that both their horses went down to the ground. And then they got clear of their saddles, and set their shields, and drew their swords, and rushed at each other like madmen, and many strokes were given in a short while. At last Sir Lancelot gave Sir Brian such a blow that he went down on his knees, and then Sir Lancelot rushed on him, and with great force pulled off his helm. And when Sir Brian saw that he would be killed, he yielded, and put himself at his mercy and in his grace. Then Sir Lancelot made him free all the prisoners he had in his castle, and in it Sir Lancelot found thirty of Arthur's knights and forty ladies, and so he freed them, and then he rode on his way. And as soon as La Cote Male Taile was freed, he got his horse, and his armour, and his damsel Maledisant.

Meanwhile Sir Nerovens, whom Sir Lancelot had fought with before at the bridge, sent a damsel after Sir Lancelot to learn how he fared at the Castle of Pendragon. And then those within the castle wondered what knight he was, when Sir Brian and his knights freed all those prisoners.

"Don't wonder at it," said the damsel, "for the best knight in this world was here and did this day's work. And believe me," she said, "it was Sir Lancelot."

Then Sir Brian was very glad, and so was his lady, and all his knights, that such a man should have beaten them. And when the damsel and La Cote Male Taile understood that it was Sir Lancelot du Lake who had ridden with them in their company, and she remembered how she had rebuked him and called him a coward, then she was exceedingly downcast.

Chapter 7: How Sir Lancelot met the damsel called Maledisant, and renamed her the Damsel Bienpensant

So then they took their horses and rode off at a good pace after Sir Lancelot. And within two miles they overtook him, and greeted him, and thanked him, and the damsel begged Sir Lancelot's pardon for her ill conduct, saying, "For now I know that the flower of all knighthood is divided evenly between Sir Tristram and you. For God knows," said the damsel, "that I have long been looking for you, my lord Sir Lancelot, and for Sir Tristram, and now I thank God I have met you. And once at Camelot I met Sir Tristram, and there he won back for me this black shield, with the white hand holding a naked sword, which Sir Breuse Saunce Pité had taken from me."

"Now, fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "who told you my name?"

"Sir," she said, "there came a damsel from a knight you fought with at the bridge, and she told me your name was Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"Blame on her, then," said Sir Lancelot, "but her lord, Sir Nerovens, must have told her. But, damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "I will ride with you on this condition: that you do not rebuke this knight Sir La Cote Male Taile any more. For he is a good knight, and I have no doubt he will prove a noble knight; and it was for his sake, and for pity that he should not be destroyed, that I followed him, to help him in this great need."

"Ah, Jesus thank you," said the damsel. "For now I will tell you and him both: I never rebuked him out of any hate I had for him, but for the great love I had for him. For all along I thought that he was too young and too tender to take these adventures upon him. And so, if I had had my way, I would have driven him off, out of the fear I had for his life; for it can be no young knight's deed to carry this adventure through to the end."

"By God," said Sir Lancelot, "that is well said. And where you are called the Damsel Maledisant, the evil-speaking, I will call you the Damsel Bienpensant, the kind-thinking."

And so they rode on a long while until they came to the border of the country of Surluse, and there they found a fine village with a strong bridge like a fortress. And when Sir Lancelot and the others were at the bridge, a crowd of gentlemen and yeomen leapt out in front of them.

"Fair lords," they said, "you may not pass this bridge and this fortress because of that black shield that I see one of you carrying; and so only one of you shall pass at a time. So choose which of you shall go onto this bridge first."

Then Sir Lancelot offered himself to go onto this bridge first.

"Sir," said La Cote Male Taile, "I beg you, let me go into this fortress, and if I fare well I will send for you; and if it happens that I am killed, so be it. And if it turns out that I am taken prisoner, then you can rescue me."

"I am unwilling," said Sir Lancelot, "to let you take this passage."

"Sir," said La Cote Male Taile, "I beg you, let me put my body to this adventure."

"Now go your way," said Sir Lancelot, "and Jesus speed you."

So he went in, and at once two brothers met him; the one was called Sir Plaine de Force, and the other was called Sir Plaine de Amours. And at once they came at Sir La Cote Male Taile; and first La Cote Male Taile struck down Plaine de Force, and after that he struck down Plaine de Amours. And then they took up their shields and swords, and told La Cote Male Taile to dismount, and so he did. And there was slashing and thrusting with swords, and so they began to press La Cote Male Taile very hard, and they gave him many great wounds on his head, and on his breast, and on his shoulders. And every now and then he gave heavy blows back. And then the two brothers circled and sidestepped to get on both sides of Sir La Cote Male Taile, but by sheer force and knightly prowess he got them in front of him. And then, when he felt himself so wounded, he doubled his strokes, and gave them so many wounds that he felled them to the ground, and would have killed them if they had not yielded.

And straight away Sir La Cote Male Taile took the best horse of the three of them, and so rode on his way to the next fortress and bridge. And there he met the third brother, whose name was Sir Plenorius, a very noble knight, and there they jousted together, and each struck the other down, horse and man, to the ground. And then they got clear of their horses, and set their shields, and drew their swords, and gave many heavy blows; and one while the one knight was forward on the bridge, and another while the other. And so they fought for two hours and more, and never rested. And all the while Sir Lancelot and the damsel watched them.

"Alas," said the damsel, "my knight is fighting exceedingly hard and too long."

"Now you can see," said Sir Lancelot, "that he is a noble knight; for, considering this is his first battle, and his grievous wounds, and wounded as he is, it is a marvel that he can endure this long battle with that good knight."

Chapter 8: How La Cote Male Taile was taken prisoner and then rescued by Sir Lancelot, and how Sir Lancelot overcame four brothers

Meanwhile Sir La Cote Male Taile sank right down on the ground; what with his wounds and what with the loss of blood, he could not stand. Then the other knight took pity on him.

"Fair young knight," he said, "don't be dismayed, for if you had been fresh when you met me, as I was, I know well that I would not have lasted as long as you have done. And so, for your noble deeds of arms, I will show you kindness and courtesy in every way I can."

And at once this noble knight, Sir Plenorius, took him up in his arms and led him into his tower. And then he had wine brought for him, and had him examined, and his bleeding wounds stopped.

"Sir," said La Cote Male Taile, "leave me, and hurry to that bridge again, for there you will meet a very different kind of knight from me."

"Why," said Plenorius, "is there another kind of knight behind you, of your company?"

"Yes," said La Cote Male Taile, "there is a much better knight than I am."

"What is his name?" said Plenorius.

"You won't learn it from me," said La Cote Male Taile.

"Well," said the knight, "he shall be met, whoever he is."

Then Sir Plenorius heard a knight calling, who said, "Sir Plenorius, where are you? Either you hand over to me the prisoner you have led into your tower, or else come out and fight me."

Then Plenorius got his horse, and came galloping with a spear in his hand towards Sir Lancelot. And then they set their spears in rest, and came together like thunder, and each struck the other so mightily that their horses fell down under them. And then they got clear of their horses, and pulled out their swords, and like two bulls they laid into each other with great strokes and thrusts. But all the while Sir Lancelot gained ground on him, and Sir Plenorius circled to try to get round him. But Sir Lancelot would not allow that, but drove him back and back, until he came near his tower gate.

And then Sir Lancelot said, "I know you well for a good knight, but believe me, your life and death are in my hand; and so yield to me, and hand over your prisoner."

The other answered not a word, but struck mightily on Sir Lancelot's helm, so that the fire sprang out of his eyes. Then Sir Lancelot doubled his strokes, so thick, and struck at him so mightily, that he made him kneel on his knees. And with that Sir Lancelot leapt on him, and pulled him down grovelling. Then Sir Plenorius yielded himself, and his tower, and all his prisoners, to do with as he wished.

Then Sir Lancelot received him and accepted his pledge. And then he rode to the other bridge, and there Sir Lancelot jousted with three more of his brothers: one was called Pillounes, and the second was called Pellogris, and the third Sir Pellandris. And first, on horseback, Sir Lancelot struck them down, and afterwards he beat them on foot, and made them yield to him. And then he returned to Sir Plenorius, and there in his prison he found King Carados of Scotland, and many other knights, and they were all freed. And then Sir La Cote Male Taile came to Sir Lancelot, and then Sir Lancelot would have given him all these fortresses and these bridges.
