"No," said La Cote Male Taile, "I will not take Sir Plenorius' lands. Provided that he will promise you, my lord Sir Lancelot, to come to King Arthur's court and be his knight, he and all his brothers, I will beg you, my lord, to let him keep his lands."

"I am content," said Sir Lancelot, "on condition that he will come to the court of King Arthur and become his man, and his five brothers too. And as for you, Sir Plenorius," said Sir Lancelot, "I will undertake that at the next feast, if a seat falls vacant, you shall be a knight of the Round Table."

"Sir," said Plenorius, "at the next feast of Pentecost I will be at Arthur's court, and at that time I will be guided and ruled as King Arthur and you wish."

Then Sir Lancelot and Sir La Cote Male Taile rested there until Sir La Cote Male Taile was healed of his wounds, and there they had merry times and good rest, and many good games, and there were many fair ladies.

Chapter 9: How Sir Lancelot made La Cote Male Taile lord of the Castle of Pendragon, and how he was afterwards made a knight of the Round Table

And in the meanwhile Sir Kay the Seneschal and Sir Brandiles came, and at once they joined their company. And then, within ten days, those knights of Arthur's court left these fortresses. And as Sir Lancelot came by the Castle of Pendragon, he put Sir Brian de les Isles out of his lands, because he would never take service with King Arthur; and all that Castle of Pendragon and all its lands he gave to Sir La Cote Male Taile. And then Sir Lancelot sent for Nerovens, whom he had once made a knight, and he gave him the whole rule of that castle and of that country, under La Cote Male Taile. And so they all rode together to Arthur's court. And at the next Pentecost, Sir Plenorius and Sir La Cote Male Taile, whose right name was Sir Bruin le Noire, were both made knights of the Round Table; and King Arthur gave them great lands. And there Bruin le Noire married that damsel Maledisant. And afterwards she was called Beauvivante, the fair-living, but ever after, for the most part, he was called La Cote Male Taile. And he proved an exceedingly noble knight, and a mighty one, and he did many honourable deeds afterwards in his life. And Sir Plenorius proved a noble knight and full of prowess, and all the days of their lives, for the most part, they waited on Sir Lancelot; and Sir Plenorius' brothers were always knights of King Arthur. And also, as the French book mentions, Sir La Cote Male Taile avenged his father's death.

Chapter 10: How Isolde the Fair sent letters to Sir Tristram by her maid Bragwaine, and of several adventures of Sir Tristram

Now we leave Sir La Cote Male Taile here, and turn to Sir Tristram de Liones, who was in Brittany. When Isolde the Fair learned that he was married, she sent him, by her maid Bragwaine, letters as piteous as could be thought of and written, and her conclusion was that, if it pleased Sir Tristram, he should come to her court, and bring Isolde of the White Hands with him, and they would be looked after as well as she was herself. Then Sir Tristram called Sir Kehydius to him, and asked him whether he would go with him into Cornwall secretly. He answered him that he was ready at all times. And then he had a little ship made ready in secret, and in it they went, Sir Tristram, Kehydius, Dame Bragwaine, and Gouvernail, Sir Tristram's squire. So when they were at sea a contrary wind blew them onto the coast of North Wales, near the Castle Perilous. Then Sir Tristram said, "You will wait for me here for these ten days, and Gouvernail, my squire, with you. And if it happens that I have not come back by that day, take the shortest way into Cornwall; for in this forest there are many strange adventures, as I have heard tell, and I mean to try some of them before I leave. And when I can, I will hurry after you."

Then Sir Tristram and Kehydius took their horses and left their company. And so they rode a mile and more into that forest; and at last Sir Tristram saw ahead of him a fine-looking knight, armed, sitting by a spring, and a strong, mighty horse tied to an oak very near him, and a man waiting on horseback beside him, leading a horse loaded with spears. And this knight who sat at the spring seemed by his face to be exceedingly downcast. Then Sir Tristram rode up to him and said, "Fair knight, why do you sit there drooping so? You look like a knight-errant by your arms and armour, and so square up to joust with one of us, or with both."

At that the knight said nothing, but took his shield and buckled it about his neck, and nimbly he took his horse and leapt onto him. And then he took a great spear from his squire, and rode off a furlong. Sir Kehydius asked Sir Tristram's leave to joust first.

"Do your best," said Sir Tristram.

So they met, and there Sir Kehydius had a fall, and was badly wounded high up above the breast. Then Sir Tristram said, "Knight, that was well jousted. Now make yourself ready for me."

"I am ready," said the knight.

And then that knight took a bigger spear in his hand, and charged against Sir Tristram, and there by great force that knight struck Sir Tristram down from his horse, and he had a great fall. Then Sir Tristram was deeply ashamed, and nimbly he got clear of his horse, and put his shield before his shoulder, and drew his sword. And then Sir Tristram asked that knight, by his knighthood, to dismount and fight with him on foot.

"Gladly," said the knight; and so he dismounted, and got clear of his horse, and threw his shield onto his shoulder, and drew his sword, and there they fought a long battle together, very nearly two hours. Then Sir Tristram said, "Fair knight, hold your hand, and tell me where you come from, and what your name is."

"As for that," said the knight, "I will think about it; but if you will tell me your name, perhaps I will tell you mine."

Chapter 11: How Sir Tristram met Sir Lamorak de Galis, and how they fought, and afterwards agreed never to fight each other again

"Now, fair knight," he said, "my name is Sir Tristram de Liones."

"Sir," said the other knight, "and my name is Sir Lamorak de Galis."

"Ah, Sir Lamorak," said Sir Tristram, "well met! Now remember the insult you did me by sending the horn to King Mark's court, meaning to have my lady the queen, Isolde the Fair, killed or dishonoured. And so know this," said Sir Tristram, "one of us will die before we part."

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "remember that we were together on the Isle of Servage, and at that time you promised me great friendship."

Then Sir Tristram would make no more delay, but laid into Sir Lamorak; and so they fought a long time, until each was weary of the other. Then Sir Tristram said to Sir Lamorak, "In all my life I never met a knight so strong and with such staying power as you. And so," said Sir Tristram, "it would be a pity if either of us should come to harm here."

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "for your renown and your name, I want you to have the honour of this battle, and so I will yield to you."

And with that he took his sword by the point to yield himself.

"No," said Sir Tristram, "you shall not do that, for I know very well that you make this offer out of your courtesy, more than from any fear or dread you have of me."

And with that Sir Tristram offered him his sword and said, "Sir Lamorak, as an overcome knight I yield to you, as to a man of the noblest prowess I ever met."

"No," said Sir Lamorak, "I will do you a courtesy. I ask that we swear together that neither of us shall ever fight the other after this day."

And with that Sir Tristram and Sir Lamorak swore that neither of them would ever fight against the other, not for good fortune nor for bad.

Chapter 12: How Sir Palomides followed the Questing Beast, and struck down Sir Tristram and Sir Lamorak with one spear

And meanwhile there came Sir Palomides, the good knight, following the Questing Beast, which had a head shaped like a serpent's head, and a body like a leopard, haunches like a lion, and feet like a hart; and in its body there was a noise as if it were the noise of thirty couple of hounds on the scent, and that beast made such a noise wherever it went; and Sir Palomides followed this beast forever, for it was called his quest. And just as he was following this beast, it came past Sir Tristram, and soon after came Palomides. And to cut a long story short, he struck down Sir Tristram and Sir Lamorak both with one spear; and so he went on after the beast Glatisant, which was called the Questing Beast; and so these two knights were exceedingly angry that Sir Palomides would not fight with them on foot. Here men of honour may understand that no man was ever made who could stand at all times, but sometimes he was put to the worse by ill luck; and at times the worse knight put the better knight to shame.

Then Sir Tristram and Sir Lamorak got Sir Kehydius onto a shield between the two of them, and took him to a forester's lodge, and there they gave him into the forester's charge to look after him well, and they stayed with him three days. Then the two knights took their horses, and at the crossroads they parted. And then Sir Tristram said to Sir Lamorak, "I ask you, if you happen to meet Sir Palomides, tell him that he will find me at the same spring where I met him, and there I, Sir Tristram, will prove whether he is a better knight than I am."

And so each went his separate way from the other, and Sir Tristram rode close to where Sir Kehydius was; and Sir Lamorak rode until he came to a chapel, and there he put his horse out to pasture. And at once there came Sir Meliagaunce, who was King Bagdemagus' son, and he put his horse out to pasture there, and was not aware of Sir Lamorak; and then this knight Sir Meliagaunce made his lament over the love he had for Queen Guinevere, and there he made a woeful complaint. Sir Lamorak heard all this, and in the morning Sir Lamorak took his horse and rode into the forest, and there he met two knights waiting under the cover of the wood.

"Fair knights," said Sir Lamorak, "what are you doing, waiting and watching here? And if you are knights-errant who want to joust, look, I am ready."

"No, sir knight," they said, "not so. We are not waiting here to joust with you, but we are lying in wait here for a knight who killed our brother."

"What knight was that," said Sir Lamorak, "whom you would so gladly meet?"

"Sir," they said, "it is Sir Lancelot who killed our brother, and if we can ever meet him he will not escape, but we will kill him."

"You are taking a great deal on yourselves," said Sir Lamorak, "for Sir Lancelot is a noble, proven knight."

"As for that, we have no doubt, for there is not one of us who is not good enough for him."

"I will not believe that," said Sir Lamorak, "for never in all the days of my life have I heard of any knight that Sir Lancelot was not too strong for."

Chapter 13: How Sir Lamorak met Sir Meliagaunce, and how they fought over the beauty of Queen Guinevere

Just as they stood talking like this, Sir Lamorak saw Sir Lancelot come riding straight towards them; then Sir Lamorak greeted him, and he greeted him in return. And then Sir Lamorak asked Sir Lancelot if there was anything he could do for him in these borders.

"No," said Sir Lancelot, "not at this time, thank you."

Then each went his way from the other, and Sir Lamorak rode back to where he had left the two knights, and then he found them hidden in the leafy wood.

"Shame on you," said Sir Lamorak, "you false cowards! It is a pity and a shame that any of you should take the high order of knighthood."

So Sir Lamorak left them, and within a while he met Sir Meliagaunce. And then Sir Lamorak asked him why he loved Queen Guinevere as he did: "For I was not far from you when you made your complaint by the chapel."

"Were you?" said Sir Meliagaunce. "Then I will stand by it: I love Queen Guinevere. What do you want to do about it? I will prove and make good that she is the fairest lady and the most beautiful in the world."

"As to that," said Sir Lamorak, "I say no to it, for Queen Morgause of Orkney, Sir Gawain's mother, is the fairest queen and lady alive."

"That is not so," said Sir Meliagaunce, "and I will prove it with my hands on your body."

"Will you indeed?" said Sir Lamorak. "I could not ask for a better quarrel to fight in."

Then they parted from each other in great anger. And then they came riding together as if it were thunder, and each struck the other so hard that their horses fell backwards to the earth. And then they got clear of their horses, and set their shields, and drew their swords. And then they crashed together like wild boars, and so they fought a long while. For Meliagaunce was a good man and of great strength, but Sir Lamorak was far too strong for him, and kept driving him back, though each had wounded the other badly.

And as they stood fighting like this, by chance Sir Lancelot and Sir Bleoberis came riding by. And then Sir Lancelot rode between them, and asked them why they were fighting each other like this: "And you are both knights of King Arthur's!"

Chapter 14: How Sir Meliagaunce told why they were fighting, and how Sir Lamorak jousted with King Arthur

"Sir," said Meliagaunce, "I will tell you why we are fighting this battle. I praised my lady, Queen Guinevere, and said she was the fairest lady in the world, and Sir Lamorak said no to it, for he said Queen Morgause of Orkney was fairer than she and more beautiful."

"Ah, Sir Lamorak, why do you say that?" said Sir Lancelot. "It is not your place to run down your princess, when you are under her rule, as we all are."

And with that he dismounted and said, "For this quarrel, get ready, for I will prove on your body that Queen Guinevere is the fairest lady and the most gracious in the world."

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "I am loath to fight you in this quarrel, for every man thinks his own lady the fairest; and though I praise the lady I love most, you should not be angry; for though my lady Queen Guinevere is fairest in your eyes, you may be sure that Queen Morgause of Orkney is fairest in mine, and so every knight thinks his own lady the fairest. And believe me, sir, you are the man in the world, except Sir Tristram, whom I am most loath of all to fight. But if you insist on fighting me, I will hold out against you as long as I can."

Then Sir Bleoberis spoke up and said, "My lord Sir Lancelot, I never knew you so ill-advised as you are now, for Sir Lamorak is speaking to you only reasonably and knightly. For I tell you, I have a lady, and I think she is the fairest lady in the world. Would that be good reason for you to be angry with me for such words? And you know well that Sir Lamorak is as noble a knight as any I know, and he has always borne you and us good will, and so I beg you, be good friends."

Then Sir Lancelot said to Sir Lamorak, "I beg you, forgive me my ill will, and if I was ill-advised I will make amends."

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "amends are soon made between you and me."

And so Sir Lancelot and Sir Bleoberis went on their way, and Sir Meliagaunce and Sir Lamorak took their horses, and each went his way from the other.

And within a while King Arthur came, and met Sir Lamorak, and jousted with him; and there he struck Sir Lamorak down, and wounded him badly with a spear, and so he rode away from him; and so Sir Lamorak was angry that he would not fight with him on foot, although Sir Lamorak did not know it was King Arthur.

Chapter 15: How Sir Kay met Sir Tristram, and of the insults afterwards spoken about the knights of Cornwall, and how they jousted

Now we leave this tale, and speak of Sir Tristram, who as he rode met Sir Kay the Seneschal; and there Sir Kay asked Sir Tristram what country he was from. He answered that he was from the country of Cornwall.

"That may well be," said Sir Kay, "for I never yet heard of any good knight who came out of Cornwall."

"That is ill said," said Sir Tristram, "but if it pleases you to tell me your name, I ask you to."

"Sir, you may be sure," said Sir Kay, "that my name is Sir Kay the Seneschal."

"Is that your name?" said Sir Tristram. "Now believe me, you are called the most shameful-tongued knight now living. All the same, you are called a good knight, but you are called unlucky, and exceedingly perverse with your tongue."

And so they rode together until they came to a bridge. And there was a knight who would not let them pass until one of them jousted with him; and so that knight jousted with Sir Kay, and there that knight gave Sir Kay a fall. His name was Sir Tor, Sir Lamorak's half-brother. And then the two of them rode to their lodging, and there they found Sir Brandiles, and Sir Tor came there soon after. And as these four knights sat at supper, three of them said every shameful thing about Cornish knights. Sir Tristram heard all that they said, and he said little, but he thought the more; but at that time he did not reveal his name.

In the morning Sir Tristram took his horse and waited for them on their way. And there Sir Brandiles offered to joust with Sir Tristram, and Sir Tristram struck him down, horse and all, to the earth. Then Sir Tor le Fise de Vayshoure rode against Sir Tristram, and there Sir Tristram struck him down, and then he rode on his way; and Sir Kay followed him, but he wanted none of his company. Then Sir Brandiles came to Sir Kay and said, "I would gladly know what that knight's name is."

"Come on with me," said Sir Kay, "and we will ask him to tell us his name."

So they rode together until they came near him, and then they saw where he sat by a spring, and had taken off his helmet to drink at the spring. And when he saw them coming he laced on his helmet quickly, and took his horse, and offered to joust with them.

"No," said Sir Brandiles, "we jousted with you lately enough; we have not come for that. But we have come for this: to ask you, by your knighthood, to tell us your name."

"My fair knights, since that is your wish, and to please you, you shall know that my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, nephew to King Mark of Cornwall."

"Well and good," said Sir Brandiles, "and well met! And believe me, we are very glad that we have found you, and we belong to a fellowship that would be very glad of your company. For you are the knight in the world whose company the noble fellowship of the Round Table most desires to have."

"God thank them," said Sir Tristram, "for their great goodness. But as yet I feel well that I am not fit to be of their fellowship, for I have never yet done such worthy deeds as would make me fit for the company of such a fellowship."

"Ah," said Sir Kay, "if you are Sir Tristram de Liones, you are the man now said to have the most prowess, except Sir Lancelot du Lake; for there is no one alive, Christian or heathen, who can find another knight like him, to speak of his prowess, and of his hands, and his truth as well. For no creature has ever yet been able to say dishonour of him and make it good."

So they talked a long while, and then they parted from each other, each going whatever way seemed best to them.

Chapter 16: How King Arthur was lured into the Forest Perilous, and how Sir Tristram saved his life

Now you shall hear what the cause was that King Arthur came into the Forest Perilous, which was in North Wales, through the doing of a lady. Her name was Annowre, and this lady came to King Arthur at Cardiff; and by fair promises and fair pledges she made King Arthur ride with her into that Forest Perilous; and she was a great sorceress; and she had loved King Arthur for many days, and because she wanted him to lie with her she came into that country. So when the king had gone with her, many of his knights followed after King Arthur when they missed him, such as Sir Lancelot, Brandiles, and many others; and when she had brought him to her tower she wanted him to lie with her; and then the king remembered his lady, and would not lie with her for any craft she could work. Then every day she would make him ride into that forest to fight with his own knights, meaning to have King Arthur killed. For when this Lady Annowre saw that she could not have him at her will, then she worked by false means to have King Arthur destroyed, and killed.

Then the Lady of the Lake, who was always friendly to King Arthur, understood by her subtle crafts that King Arthur was likely to be destroyed. And so this Lady of the Lake, who was called Nimue, came into that forest to look for Sir Lancelot du Lake or Sir Tristram to help King Arthur; for this Lady of the Lake knew well that on that same day King Arthur would be killed, unless he had help from one of these two knights. And so she rode up and down until she met Sir Tristram, and as soon as she saw him she knew him.

"Oh my lord Sir Tristram," she said, "well met, and blessed be the time that I have met you! For this same day, and within these two hours, the foulest deed that was ever done in this land will be done."

"Oh fair damsel," said Sir Tristram, "can I set it right?"

"Come with me," she said, "and as fast as you can, for you will see the most honourable knight in the world in a hard spot."

Then Sir Tristram said, "I am ready to help such a noble man."

"He is neither better nor worse," said the Lady of the Lake, "than the noble King Arthur himself."

"God forbid," said Sir Tristram, "that he should ever be in such distress."

Then they rode together at a great pace, until they came to a little tower or castle; and below that castle they saw a knight standing on foot fighting with two knights; and so Sir Tristram watched them, and at last the two knights struck down the one knight, and one of them unlaced his helmet to kill him. And the Lady Annowre got King Arthur's sword into her hand to strike off his head. And with that Sir Tristram came with all his might, crying, "Traitress, traitress, leave that!"

And at once Sir Tristram struck one of the knights through the body so that he fell dead; and then he rushed at the other and struck his back in two; and meanwhile the Lady of the Lake cried to King Arthur, "Don't let that false lady escape!"

Then King Arthur overtook her, and with the same sword he struck off her head, and the Lady of the Lake took up her head and hung it by the hair from her saddlebow. And then Sir Tristram got King Arthur onto a horse and rode on with him, but he charged the Lady of the Lake not to reveal his name for the time being.

When the king was on horseback he thanked Sir Tristram heartily, and wanted to know his name; but he would not tell him, except that he was a poor knight-errant; and so he kept King Arthur company until he met some of his knights. And within a while he met Sir Ector de Maris, and he did not know King Arthur or Sir Tristram, and he wanted to joust with one of them. Then Sir Tristram rode at Sir Ector, and struck him from his horse. And when he had done so he came back to the king and said, "My lord, there is one of your knights; he can keep you company. And another day, I trust to God, you will understand from that deed I have done for you that I would do you service."

"Alas," said King Arthur, "let me know who you are."

"Not at this time," said Sir Tristram.

So he left, and left King Arthur and Sir Ector together.

Chapter 17: How Sir Tristram came to Isolde the Fair, and how Kehydius fell in love with her, and of a letter that Tristram found

And then on the day appointed Sir Tristram and Sir Lamorak met at the spring; and then they took Kehydius from the forester's house, and so they rode with him to the ship where they had left Dame Bragwaine and Gouvernail, and so they all sailed into Cornwall together. And by the agreement and the advice of Dame Bragwaine, when they had landed they rode to Sir Dinas the Seneschal, a trusty friend of Sir Tristram's. And so Dame Bragwaine and Sir Dinas rode to King Mark's court, and told the queen, Isolde the Fair, that Sir Tristram was near her in that country. Then for very pure joy Isolde the Fair fainted; and when she could speak she said, "Noble knight Seneschal, help me to speak with him, or my heart will burst."

Then Sir Dinas and Dame Bragwaine brought Sir Tristram and Kehydius secretly into the court, to a chamber that Isolde the Fair had appointed for it; and as for the joy there was between Isolde the Fair and Sir Tristram, there is no tongue that can tell it, nor heart think it, nor pen write it. And as the French book tells, the very first time that Sir Kehydius ever saw Isolde the Fair he was so in love with her that for very pure love he could never draw back from it. And in the end, as you shall hear before the book is ended, Sir Kehydius died for the love of Isolde the Fair. And then he secretly wrote her letters and ballads, of the finest that were in fashion in those days. And when Isolde the Fair understood his letters she took pity on his lament, and without thinking she wrote another letter to comfort him with.

And all this while Sir Tristram was in a tower at the command of Isolde the Fair, and whenever she could she came to Sir Tristram. So one day King Mark was playing chess below a chamber window; and at that time Sir Tristram and Sir Kehydius were inside the chamber above King Mark, and as ill luck would have it Sir Tristram found the letter that Kehydius had sent to Isolde the Fair, and he had also found the letter that she wrote to Kehydius, and at that same time Isolde the Fair was in the same chamber. Then Sir Tristram came to Isolde the Fair and said, "Madam, here is a letter that was sent to you, and here is the letter that you sent to the man who sent you that letter. Alas, madam, for the good love I have loved you with! And I have forsaken many lands and riches for your love, and now you are a traitress to me, which gives me great pain. But as for you, Sir Kehydius, I brought you out of Brittany into this country, and I won back the lands of your father, King Howell, and on top of that I married your sister Isolde of the White Hands for the goodness she did me. And yet, as I am a true knight, she is still a virgin as far as I am concerned. But know this, Sir Kehydius: for this falsehood and treason you have done me, I will take my revenge on you."

And with that Sir Tristram drew out his sword and said, "Sir Kehydius, defend yourself!"

And then Isolde the Fair fell to the ground in a faint. And when Sir Kehydius saw Sir Tristram coming at him he saw no other remedy, but leapt out of a bay window, right over the head of King Mark where he sat playing chess. And when the king saw someone come hurtling over his head he said, "Fellow, who are you, and why are you leaping out of that window?"

"My lord the king," said Kehydius, "it happened that I was asleep in the window above your head, and as I slept I dozed off, and so I fell down."

And so Sir Kehydius excused himself.

Chapter 18: How Sir Tristram left Tintagil, and how he grieved and stayed so long in a forest that he went out of his mind

Then Sir Tristram was badly afraid that the king would find out he was there; and so he withdrew into the stronghold of the Tower, and armed himself in such armour as he had, to fight with anyone who would stand against him. And so when Sir Tristram saw there was no resistance against him, he sent Gouvernail for his horse and his spear, and like a knight he rode out of the castle openly, which was called the Castle of Tintagil. And right at the gate he met Gingalin, Sir Gawain's son. And at once Sir Gingalin put his spear in its rest, and charged at Sir Tristram and broke his spear; and Sir Tristram at that time had only a sword, and gave him such a blow on the helmet that he fell down from his saddle, and his sword slid down and cut clean through his horse's neck. And so Sir Tristram rode his way into the forest, and King Mark saw all this happen. And then he sent a squire to the hurt knight, and commanded him to come to him, and so he did. And when King Mark learned that it was Sir Gingalin, he welcomed him and gave him a horse, and asked him what knight it was who had fought with him.

"Sir," said Gingalin, "I do not know what knight he was, but I know very well that he sighs and grieves greatly."

Then within a while Sir Tristram met a knight of his own who was called Sir Fergus. And when he had met him he grieved so greatly that he fell down off his horse in a faint, and he was in such sorrow for three days and three nights. Then at last Sir Tristram sent Sir Fergus to the court, to ask what news there was. And as he rode along the way he met a damsel who came from Sir Palomides, to find out and learn how Sir Tristram was doing. Then Sir Fergus told her how he was almost out of his mind.

"Alas," said the damsel, "where shall I find him?"

"In such and such a place," said Sir Fergus.

Then Sir Fergus found Queen Isolde sick in her bed, grieving more than any earthly woman ever grieved. And when the damsel found Sir Tristram she grieved greatly because she could not help him, for the more she made of him, the greater was his pain. And at last Sir Tristram took his horse and rode away from her. And then it was three days before she could find him, and then she brought him food and drink, but he would have none of it; and then another time Sir Tristram escaped from the damsel, and it happened that he rode by the same castle where Sir Palomides and Sir Tristram fought when Isolde the Fair parted them. And there by chance the damsel met Sir Tristram again, grieving more than any earthly creature ever grieved; and she went to the lady of that castle and told her of Sir Tristram's misfortune.

"Alas," said the lady of that castle, "where is my lord, Sir Tristram?"

"Right here by your castle," said the damsel.

"It is a happy chance," said the lady, "that he is so near me. He shall have the best food and drink; and I have a harp of his, on which he taught me, for in fine harping he takes the prize of the world."

So this lady and the damsel brought him food and drink, but he ate little of it. Then one night he sent his horse away from him, and then he unlaced his armour, and then Sir Tristram would go into the wilderness, and break down the trees and boughs; and at other times, when he found the harp that the lady had sent him, then he would harp, and play on it and weep at the same time. And sometimes, when Sir Tristram was in the wood and the lady did not know where he was, then she would sit down and play on that harp: then Sir Tristram would come to that harp, and listen to it, and sometimes he would harp himself. So he lived there for a quarter of a year. Then at last he ran away, and she did not know what had become of him. And then he was naked, and grew lean and wasted; and so he fell in with herdsmen and shepherds, and every day they would give him some of their food and drink. And when he did any mischief they would beat him with rods, and so they clipped his hair with shears and made him look like a fool.

Chapter 19: How Sir Tristram dunked Dagonet in a well, and how Palomides sent a damsel to look for Tristram, and how Palomides met King Mark

And one day Dagonet, King Arthur's fool, came into Cornwall with two squires; and as they rode through that forest they came to a fair well where Sir Tristram used to stay. And the weather was hot, and they dismounted to drink from that well, and meanwhile their horses broke loose. Just then Sir Tristram came up to them, and first he dunked Sir Dagonet in that well, and then his squires, and the shepherds laughed at it. And straight away he ran after their horses and brought them back one by one, and then, wet as they were, he made them jump up and ride on their way. So Sir Tristram lived there half a year naked, and would never come into town or village.

Meanwhile the damsel that Sir Palomides had sent to look for Sir Tristram went back to Sir Palomides and told him all the misery that Sir Tristram was suffering.

"Alas," said Sir Palomides, "it is a great pity that so noble a knight should ever be brought so low for the love of a lady. But all the same, I will go and look for him, and comfort him if I can."

Now a little before that time Isolde the Fair had ordered Sir Kehydius out of the country of Cornwall. So Sir Kehydius left with a sorrowful heart, and by chance he met Sir Palomides, and they joined company. And each of them complained to the other of the burning love they had for Isolde the Fair.

"Now let us," said Sir Palomides, "look for Sir Tristram, who loved her as well as we do, and let us see whether we can bring him back to himself."

So they rode into that forest, and for three days and three nights they never once took lodging, but went on looking for Sir Tristram.

And once, by chance, they met King Mark, who had ridden away from his men all alone. When they saw him Sir Palomides knew him, but Sir Kehydius did not.

"Ah, false king," said Sir Palomides, "it is a pity you are alive, for you are a destroyer of all honourable knights, and by your malice and your vengeance you have destroyed that most noble knight, Sir Tristram de Liones. And so defend yourself," said Sir Palomides, "for you shall die this day."

"That would be a shameful thing," said King Mark, "for you two are armed and I am unarmed."

"As for that," said Sir Palomides, "I shall find a remedy. Here is a knight with me, and you shall have his armour."

"No," said King Mark, "I will not fight with you, for you have no quarrel with me. All the trouble that Sir Tristram has came from a letter that he found. As for me, I did him no wrong, and God knows I am very sorry for his distress and his sickness."

So when the king had excused himself in this way they were friends, and King Mark would have taken them to Tintagil; but Sir Palomides would not go, and turned towards the realm of Logres, and Sir Kehydius said that he would go into Brittany.

Now we turn back to Sir Dagonet. When he and his squires were on horseback again, he decided that the shepherds had set that fool on to treat them so, because they had laughed at them. And so they rode up to the herdsmen and beat them soundly. Sir Tristram saw them beating the men who used to give him food and drink, and he ran over there and got Sir Dagonet by the head, and threw him to the ground so hard that he was badly bruised and lay still. And then he wrenched his sword out of his hand, and with it he ran at one of his squires and struck off his head, and the other fled. And so Sir Tristram went on his way with that sword in his hand, running as if he were raving mad.

Then Sir Dagonet rode to King Mark and told him how he had fared in that forest. "And so," said Sir Dagonet, "beware, King Mark, and do not come near that well in the forest, for there is a naked fool there, and that fool and I, fool, met together, and he nearly killed me."

"Ah," said King Mark, "that is Sir Matto le Breune, who went out of his wits because he lost his lady. For when Sir Gaheris struck down Sir Matto and won his lady from him, he was never in his right mind again, and that was a pity, for he was a good knight."

Chapter 20: How a rumour spread that Sir Tristram was dead, and how Isolde the Fair tried to kill herself

Then Sir Andred, who was Sir Tristram's cousin, had a lady who was his lover say and spread it about that she had been with Sir Tristram before he died. And she brought this tale to King Mark's court: that she had buried him by a spring, and that before he died he had begged King Mark to make his cousin, Sir Andred, king of the country of Liones, of which Sir Tristram was lord. Sir Andred did all this because he wanted to have Sir Tristram's lands. And when King Mark heard that Sir Tristram was dead he wept and grieved greatly.

But when Queen Isolde heard this news she was in such sorrow that she was nearly out of her mind; and so one day she resolved to kill herself and not to live on after Sir Tristram's death. And so one day Isolde the Fair got hold of a sword secretly and carried it into her garden, and there she drove the sword through a plum tree up to the hilt, so that it stuck fast, and it stood breast-high. And as she was about to run upon the sword and kill herself, King Mark saw it all: how she knelt down and said, "Sweet Lord Jesus, have mercy on me, for I cannot live after the death of Sir Tristram de Liones, for he was my first love and he shall be the last."

And with these words King Mark came up and took her in his arms, and then he took up the sword, and carried her away with him into a tower; and there he had her guarded, and kept a close watch on her, and after that she lay sick a long while, near to the point of death.

Meanwhile Sir Tristram ran naked in the forest with the sword in his hand, and so he came to a hermitage, and there he lay down and slept. And while he slept the hermit stole his sword away, and laid food down beside him. So he was kept there ten days, and at last he left and came back to the herdsmen.

And there was a giant in that country called Taulas, and for fear of Sir Tristram he had not dared to go about freely for more than seven years, but mostly kept himself in a strong castle of his own. And so this Taulas heard that Sir Tristram was dead, from the rumour at King Mark's court. Then this Taulas went about freely every day. And so it happened one day that he came to the herdsmen, wandering and sauntering, and there he sat down to rest among them.

Meanwhile there came a knight of Cornwall who had a lady with him, and his name was Sir Dinant. And when the giant saw him he left the herdsmen and hid under a tree, and so the knight came to that spring, and there he dismounted to rest. And as soon as he was off his horse this giant Taulas came between the knight and his horse, and took the horse and leapt on it. Then at once he rode at Sir Dinant and took him by the collar, and pulled him up in front of him on the horse, and was about to strike off his head.

Then the herdsmen said to Sir Tristram, "Help that knight over there."

"You help him," said Sir Tristram.

"We don't dare," said the herdsmen.

Then Sir Tristram noticed the knight's sword where it lay; and so he ran over there and took up the sword and struck off Sir Taulas's head, and so he went his way back to the herdsmen.

Chapter 21: How King Mark found Sir Tristram naked and had him carried home to Tintagil, and how he was recognised there by a little hound

Then the knight took up the giant's head and carried it with him to King Mark, and told him what adventure had happened to him in the forest, and how a naked man had rescued him from the grim giant, Taulas.

"Where did you have this adventure?" said King Mark.

"Truly," said Sir Dinant, "at the fair spring in your forest where many knights-errant meet, and that is where the madman is."

"Well," said King Mark, "I will see that wild man."

So within a day or two King Mark commanded his knights and his huntsmen to be ready in the morning to hunt, and so in the morning he went into that forest. And when the king came to that well he found lying beside it a fine naked man, and a sword by him. Then King Mark blew his horn and sounded the strake, the call that gathers in the hunt, and with that his knights came to him. And then the king commanded his knights: "Take that naked man gently, and bring him to my castle."

So they did, softly and gently, and threw cloaks over Sir Tristram, and so led him to Tintagil; and there they bathed him, and washed him, and gave him hot broths until they had brought him well back to his memory. But all this while there was no one who knew Sir Tristram, or what man he was.

So it happened one day that the queen, Isolde the Fair, heard of such a man, who had run naked in the forest, and how the king had brought him home to the court. Then Isolde the Fair called Dame Bragwaine to her and said, "Come with me, for we will go and see this man that my lord brought from the forest the other day."

So they went out, and asked where the sick man was. And then a squire told the queen that he was in the garden taking his rest, and resting himself in the sun. So when the queen looked at Sir Tristram she did not remember him. But all the while she kept saying to Dame Bragwaine, "It seems to me I must have seen him before in many places."

But as soon as Sir Tristram saw her he knew her well enough. And then he turned his face away and wept.

Now the queen always had with her a little hound that Sir Tristram had given her the first time she ever came into Cornwall, and that hound would never leave her unless Sir Tristram was near where Isolde the Fair was; and this hound had been sent from the King of France's daughter to Sir Tristram for great love. And as soon as this little hound caught the scent of Sir Tristram, she leapt up on him and licked his cheeks and his ears, and then she whined and gave tongue, and she sniffed at his feet and at his hands, and at every part of his body she could get to.

"Ah, my lady," said Dame Bragwaine to Isolde the Fair, "alas, alas," she said, "I see it is my own lord, Sir Tristram."

And with that Isolde fell down in a swoon, and lay so a long while. And when she could speak she said, "My lord Sir Tristram, blessed be God that you are alive! And now I am sure you will be discovered by this little hound, for she will never leave you. And I am sure too that as soon as my lord, King Mark, knows who you are he will banish you out of the country of Cornwall, or else he will destroy you. For God's sake, my own lord, give way to King Mark, and then make your way to the court of King Arthur, for there you are loved; and whenever I can I shall send to you; and when you wish you may come to me, and at all times, early and late, I will be at your command, to live as poor a life as ever queen or lady did."

"Oh, madam," said Sir Tristram, "go away from me, for I have escaped great anger and danger for your love."

Chapter 22: How King Mark, on the advice of his council, banished Sir Tristram from Cornwall for ten years

Then the queen left, but the hound would not leave him; and with that King Mark came up, and the hound went for him, and bayed at them all. With that Sir Andred spoke and said, "Sir, this is Sir Tristram, I can tell by the hound."

"No," said the king, "I cannot believe that."

Then the king asked him on his faith who he was, and what his name was.

"So help me God," said he, "my name is Sir Tristram de Liones. Now do with me what you will."

"Ah," said King Mark, "I am sorry you have recovered."

And then he had his barons called to sentence Sir Tristram to death. But many of his barons would not agree to it, and especially Sir Dinas the Seneschal, and Sir Fergus. And so, on the advice of them all, Sir Tristram was banished out of the country for ten years, and he swore his oath to it on a book before the king and his barons. And so he was made to leave the country of Cornwall; and many barons brought him to his ship, some of whom were his friends and some his enemies.

And in the meantime there came a knight of King Arthur's, whose name was Dinadan, and he had come to look for Sir Tristram. Then they showed him where he was, armed at all points, going to the ship.

"Now, fair knight," said Sir Dinadan, "before you leave this court, I ask you to joust with me."

"With a good will," said Sir Tristram, "if these lords will give me leave."

Then the barons granted it, and so they ran together, and there Sir Tristram gave Sir Dinadan a fall. And then he begged Sir Tristram to give him leave to go in his company.

"You shall be very welcome," said Sir Tristram then.

And so they took their horses and rode to their ships together. And when Sir Tristram was out at sea he said, "Give my greetings to King Mark and all my enemies, and tell them I will come back when I can. And I am well rewarded for fighting Sir Marhaus, and freeing all this country from bondage; and I am well rewarded for the fetching of Queen Isolde out of Ireland, and the cost of it, and the danger I was in first and last, and on the way home what danger I had to bring Queen Isolde back from the Castle Pluere; and I am well rewarded for when I fought with Sir Bleoberis for Sir Segwarides' wife; and I am well rewarded for when I fought with Sir Blamore de Ganis for King Anguish, father of Isolde the Fair; and I am well rewarded for when I struck down the good knight Sir Lamorak de Galis at King Mark's request; and I am well rewarded for when I fought with the King with the Hundred Knights and the King of North Wales, who would both have put his land in bondage, and by me they were put to shame; and I am well rewarded for the killing of Taulas, the mighty giant, and many other deeds I have done for him, and now I have my reward. And tell King Mark that many noble knights of the Round Table have spared the barons of this country for my sake. And am I not well rewarded for when I fought with the good knight Sir Palomides and rescued Queen Isolde from him? And at that time King Mark said before all his barons that I should have been better rewarded."

And with that he put to sea.

Chapter 23: How a damsel looked for someone to help Sir Lancelot against thirty knights, and how Sir Tristram fought with them

And at the next landing place, close by the sea, Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan were met by Sir Ector de Maris and Sir Bors de Ganis; and there Sir Ector jousted with Sir Dinadan, and struck him and his horse down. And then Sir Tristram wanted to joust with Sir Bors, and Sir Bors said that he would not joust with any Cornish knights, for they are not counted men of honour; and all this happened on a bridge. And with that Sir Bleoberis and Sir Driant came up, and Sir Bleoberis offered to joust with Sir Tristram, and there Sir Tristram struck down Sir Bleoberis.

Then Sir Bors de Ganis said, "I never knew a Cornish knight of such great valour, or so brave, as that knight who wears the trappings embroidered with crowns."

And then Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan left them and rode into a forest, and there a damsel met them who had come, for the love of Sir Lancelot, to look for some noble knights of King Arthur's court to rescue Sir Lancelot. For it had been arranged, through the treachery of Queen Morgan le Fay, that Sir Lancelot should be killed, and for that purpose she had set thirty knights to lie in wait for Sir Lancelot, and this damsel knew of this treachery. And for this reason the damsel had come to look for noble knights to help Sir Lancelot. For that night, or the day after, Sir Lancelot was to come to where these thirty knights were. And so this damsel had met Sir Bors and Sir Ector and Sir Driant, and there she told all four of them of the treachery of Morgan le Fay; and then they promised her that they would be close by where Sir Lancelot was to meet the thirty knights: "And if it turns out they set upon him, we will come to his rescue as best we can."

So the damsel left, and by chance the damsel met Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan, and there the damsel told them all the treachery that had been planned against Sir Lancelot.

"Fair damsel," said Sir Tristram, "take me to the place where they are to meet Sir Lancelot."

Then Sir Dinadan said, "What are you going to do? It is not for us to fight thirty knights, and believe me, I will have none of it. To take on one knight, two or three of us is quite enough, if they are real men; but to take on fifteen knights apiece, that I will never undertake."

"For shame," said Sir Tristram, "just do your part."

"No," said Sir Dinadan, "I will have none of it, unless you will lend me your shield, for you carry a shield of Cornwall; and the knights of Cornwall have such a name for cowardice that nobody ever bothers a man behind one of your shields."

"No," said Sir Tristram, "I will not part with my shield, for the sake of the lady who gave it to me. But one thing," said Sir Tristram, "I promise you, Sir Dinadan: unless you promise me to stand by me, I will kill you here and now. For I ask nothing more of you than to take on one knight. And if your heart fails you, stand by and watch me and them."

"Sir," said Sir Dinadan, "I promise you to watch, and to do what I can to save myself; but I wish I had never met you."

So then at once these thirty knights came close by the other four knights, and the four saw them, and each party saw the other. And so the thirty knights let them pass, for this reason: that they did not want to anger them, in case they had to fight Sir Lancelot; and the four knights let them pass with this intent, that they wanted to see and watch what they would do with Sir Lancelot. And so the thirty knights passed on and came by Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan, and then Sir Tristram shouted out, "Look, here is a knight against you, for the love of Sir Lancelot!"

And there he killed two with one spear and ten with his sword. And then Sir Dinadan came in, and he did exceedingly well, and so of the thirty knights only ten got away, and they fled. Sir Bors de Ganis and his three companions saw this whole battle, and then they saw plainly that it was the same knight who had jousted with them at the bridge. Then they took their horses and rode up to Sir Tristram, and praised him and thanked him for his good deeds, and they all asked Sir Tristram to go with them to their lodging; and he said no, he would not go to any lodging. Then all four knights begged him to tell them his name.

"Fair lords," said Sir Tristram, "for the present I will not tell you my name."

Chapter 24: How Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan came to a lodging where they had to joust with two knights

Then Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan rode on their way until they came to the shepherds and the herdsmen, and there they asked them if they knew of any lodging or shelter near at hand.

"Truly, sirs," said the herdsmen, "there is good lodging close by in a castle; but there is a custom there that no knight shall be lodged unless he jousts with two knights, and if he is only one knight he must joust with two. And as soon as you are inside you will be matched."

"That's a nasty sort of lodging," said Sir Dinadan. "Lodge where you like, for I will not lodge there."

"For shame," said Sir Tristram, "are you not a knight of the Round Table? So you cannot refuse your lodging and keep your honour."

"Not so," said the herdsmen, "for if you are beaten and get the worst of it you will not be lodged there, and if you beat them you will be well lodged."

"Ah," said Sir Dinadan, "they are two solid knights."

Then Sir Dinadan would not lodge there on any account, except that Sir Tristram charged him by his knighthood; and so they rode there. And to cut a long story short, Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan struck them both down, and so they went into the castle and had as good a welcome as they could think of or wish for.

And when they had taken off their armour, and meant to be merry and well rested, there came in at the gates Sir Palomides and Sir Gaheris, demanding the custom of the castle.

"What's all this?" said Sir Dinadan. "I want my rest."

"That cannot be," said Sir Tristram. "Now we must defend the custom of this castle, since we have got the better of the lords of this castle; and so," said Sir Tristram, "you must make yourself ready."

"It was in the devil's name," said Sir Dinadan, "that I ever came into your company."

And so they made themselves ready; and Sir Gaheris met Sir Tristram, and Sir Gaheris had a fall; and Sir Palomides met Sir Dinadan, and Sir Dinadan had a fall: so it was fall for fall. So then they had to fight on foot. Sir Dinadan would not do that, for he was so badly bruised from the fall that Sir Palomides had given him. Then Sir Tristram unlaced Sir Dinadan's helmet, and begged him to help him.

"I will not," said Sir Dinadan, "for I am badly wounded from the thirty knights we had to deal with only a little while ago. But you behave," said Sir Dinadan to Sir Tristram, "like a madman, like a man out of his mind who wants to throw his life away, and I may curse the hour I ever set eyes on you. For in all the world there are no two knights so mad as Sir Lancelot and you, Sir Tristram. Once I fell into Sir Lancelot's company, as I have now with you, and he set me such a job of work that I kept to my bed for a quarter of a year. Jesus defend me," said Sir Dinadan, "from two such knights, and especially from your company!"

"Then," said Sir Tristram, "I will fight them both." Then Sir Tristram told them both to come on: "For I will fight with you."

Then Sir Palomides and Sir Gaheris made ready, and struck at them both. Then Dinadan struck at Sir Gaheris a stroke or two, and turned away from him.

"No," said Sir Palomides, "it is too great a shame for two of us knights to fight one."

And then he told Sir Gaheris to stand aside with that knight who had no appetite for fighting. Then they rushed together and fought a long time, and at last Sir Tristram doubled his strokes, and drove Sir Palomides back more than three strides. And then by common consent Sir Gaheris and Sir Dinadan went between them, and parted them. And then, with Sir Tristram's agreement, they would have lodged together. But Sir Dinadan would not lodge in that castle. And then he cursed the hour he ever came into their company, and so he took his horse and his armour and left.

Then Sir Tristram asked the lords of that castle to lend him a man to bring him to a lodging, and so they did, and they overtook Sir Dinadan, and rode to their lodging two miles from there with a good man in a priory, and there they were very comfortable. And that same night Sir Bors and Sir Bleoberis, and Sir Ector and Sir Driant, stayed on in the same place where Sir Tristram had fought with the thirty knights; and there they met Sir Lancelot that same night, and they had promised to lodge with Sir Colgrevance that same night.

Chapter 25: How Sir Tristram jousted with Sir Kay and Sir Sagramore le Desirous, and how Sir Gawain turned Sir Tristram away from Morgan le Fay

But as soon as the noble knight Sir Lancelot heard of the shield of Cornwall, he knew well that it was Sir Tristram who had fought with his enemies. And then Sir Lancelot praised Sir Tristram, and called him the man of most honour in the world.

Now there was a knight in that priory called Pellinore, and he wanted to know Sir Tristram's name, but he could not get it by any means; and so Sir Tristram left, and left Sir Dinadan in the priory, for he was so weary and so badly bruised that he could not ride.

Then this knight, Sir Pellinore, said to Sir Dinadan, "Since you will not tell me that knight's name, I will ride after him and make him tell me his name, or he shall die for it."

"Beware, sir knight," said Sir Dinadan, "for if you follow him you will regret it."

So that knight, Sir Pellinore, rode after Sir Tristram and challenged him to joust. Then Sir Tristram struck him down and wounded him through the shoulder, and so he went on his way.

And on the next day Sir Tristram met some pursuivants, the heralds' messengers, and they told him that a great tournament had been proclaimed between King Carados of Scotland and the King of North Wales, and that each side was to joust against the other at the Castle of Maidens. And these pursuivants were searching all the country for the good knights, and in particular King Carados had a search made for Sir Lancelot du Lake, and the King of North Wales had a search made for Sir Tristram de Liones. And at that time Sir Tristram meant to be at those jousts.

And so by chance they met Sir Kay the Seneschal and Sir Sagramore le Desirous; and Sir Kay asked Sir Tristram to joust, and Sir Tristram more or less refused him, because he did not want to be hurt or bruised before the great jousts that were to be held at the Castle of Maidens, and so he meant to take his ease and rest. And all the while Sir Kay kept shouting, "Sir knight of Cornwall, joust with me, or else yield to me as a recreant!"

When Sir Tristram heard him say so he turned towards him, and then Sir Kay refused him and turned his back.

Then Sir Tristram said, "As I find you, so I'll take you."

Then Sir Kay turned, against his will, and Sir Tristram struck Sir Kay down, and so he rode on.

Then Sir Sagramore le Desirous rode after Sir Tristram, and made him joust with him, and there Sir Tristram struck Sir Sagramore le Desirous down from his horse, and rode on his way. And the same day he met a damsel who told him that he could win great honour from a knight-errant who was doing much harm all over that country. When Sir Tristram heard her say so, he was glad to go with her to win honour. So Sir Tristram rode with that damsel about six miles, and then Sir Gawain met him, and at once Sir Gawain recognised the damsel, that she was a damsel of Queen Morgan le Fay's. Then Sir Gawain understood that she was leading that knight into some harm.

"Fair knight," said Sir Gawain, "where are you riding now with that damsel?"

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I do not know where I am riding, except as the damsel leads me."

"Sir," said Sir Gawain, "you shall not ride with her, for she and her lady never did good, but only ill."

And then Sir Gawain drew his sword and said, "Damsel, unless you tell me this minute why you are leading this knight with you, you will die for it on the spot. I know all your lady's treachery, and yours."

"Mercy, Sir Gawain," she said, "and if you will spare my life I will tell you."

"Speak," said Sir Gawain, "and you shall have your life."

"Sir," she said, "Queen Morgan le Fay, my lady, has set some thirty ladies to search and watch for Sir Lancelot or Sir Tristram. And by the wiles of these ladies, whichever of them first met either of these two knights was to lead him to Morgan le Fay's castle, saying that he would do deeds of honour there; and if either of the two knights came there, there are thirty knights lying in wait in a tower, watching for Sir Lancelot or for Sir Tristram."

"Shame on it," said Sir Gawain, "that such false treachery should ever be worked or used by a queen, and a king's sister, and the daughter of a king and queen!"

Chapter 26: How Sir Tristram and Sir Gawain rode out to fight the thirty knights, but they did not dare to come out

"Sir," said Sir Gawain, "will you stand with me, and we will see what the malice of these thirty knights amounts to?"

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "go to them, if you please, and you will see that I will not fail you. For it is not long since I and a companion met with thirty knights of that queen's company; and God speed us, so that we may win honour."

So then Sir Gawain and Sir Tristram rode towards the castle where Morgan le Fay was, and all the while Sir Gawain judged that he must be Sir Tristram de Liones, because he had heard that two knights had killed and beaten thirty knights. And when they came before the castle Sir Gawain spoke out loud and said, "Queen Morgan le Fay, send out your knights that you have set lying in wait for Sir Lancelot and for Sir Tristram. Now," said Sir Gawain, "I know your false treachery, and everywhere I ride men shall know of your false treachery. And now let us see," said Sir Gawain, "whether you dare come out of your castle, you thirty knights."

Then the queen spoke, and all the thirty knights together, and said, "Sir Gawain, you know very well what you are doing and saying; for by God we know you exceedingly well, but all that you say and do, you say it trusting in the pride of that good knight who is there with you. For there are some of us who know the hands of that knight very well indeed. And believe this, Sir Gawain: it is more for his sake than for yours that we will not come out of this castle. For you may be sure, Sir Gawain, that we know the knight who carries the arms of Cornwall, and who he is."

Then Sir Gawain and Sir Tristram left and rode on their way together for a day or two; and there by chance they met Sir Kay and Sir Sagramore le Desirous. And they were glad of Sir Gawain, and he of them, but they did not know who the knight with the shield of Cornwall was, except by guessing. And so they rode together for a day or two. And then they caught sight of Sir Breuse Saunce Pité chasing a lady to kill her, for he had already killed her lover.

"Keep still, all of you," said Sir Gawain, "and none of you show yourselves, and you will see me pay back that false knight over there; for if he spots you he is so well horsed that he will get away."

And then Sir Gawain rode between Sir Breuse and the lady, and said, "False knight, leave her, and fight with me."

When Sir Breuse saw no one but Sir Gawain he set his spear in rest, and Sir Gawain did the same against him; and there Sir Breuse overthrew Sir Gawain, and then he rode over him, and across him twenty times, to destroy him. And when Sir Tristram saw him do so base a deed, he charged out against him. And when Sir Breuse saw him with the shield of Cornwall he knew well that it was Sir Tristram, and then he fled, and Sir Tristram went after him; and Sir Breuse Saunce Pité was so well horsed that he got clean away, and Sir Tristram followed him a long way, for he would gladly have been avenged on him. And so when he had chased him a long time, he saw a fair well, and he rode over to it to rest, and tied his horse to a tree.

Chapter 27: How the damsel Bragwaine found Tristram sleeping by a spring, and how she gave him letters from Isolde the Fair

And then he pulled off his helmet and washed his face and his hands, and so he fell asleep. Meanwhile there came a damsel who had looked for Sir Tristram by many ways and on many days within this land. And when she came to the spring she looked at him, and had forgotten what Sir Tristram looked like, but she knew him by his horse, called Passe-Brewel, which had been Sir Tristram's horse for many years. For when he was mad in the forest Sir Fergus had kept the horse. So this lady, Dame Bragwaine, waited there until he was awake. So when she saw him wake she greeted him, and he her in return, for each knew the other from long acquaintance. Then she told him how she had looked for him far and wide, and there she told him that she had letters from Queen Isolde the Fair. Then at once Sir Tristram read them, and you may be sure he was glad, for there were many piteous laments in them.

Then Sir Tristram said, "Lady Bragwaine, you shall ride with me until that tournament at the Castle of Maidens is over, and then you shall carry letters and news back with you."

And then Sir Tristram took his horse and looked for lodging, and there he met a good old knight and asked him to lodge him. Just then Gouvernail came to Sir Tristram, and he was glad of that lady. Now this old knight's name was Sir Pellounes, and he told of the great tournament that was to be at the Castle of Maidens. And there Sir Lancelot and thirty-two knights of his blood had had shields of Cornwall made. And just then someone came to Sir Pellounes and told him that Sir Persides de Bloise had come home; then that knight held up his hands and thanked God for his homecoming. And there Sir Pellounes told Sir Tristram that he had not seen his son, Sir Persides, in two years.

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I know your son well enough for a good knight."

So once Sir Tristram and Sir Persides came to their lodging both at the same time, and so they took off their armour and put on their clothes. And then these two knights welcomed each other. And when Sir Persides understood that Sir Tristram was from Cornwall, he said he had once been in Cornwall: "And there I jousted before King Mark; and it so happened that at that time I overthrew ten knights, and then Sir Tristram de Liones came at me and overthrew me, and took my lady away from me, and that I shall never forget, but I shall remember it if ever I see my chance."

"Ah," said Sir Tristram, "now I understand that you hate Sir Tristram. What do you think, do you suppose that Sir Tristram is not able to withstand your malice?"

"Yes," said Sir Persides, "I know well that Sir Tristram is a noble knight and a much better knight than I am; yet I shall not owe him my good will."

Just as they stood talking like this at a bay window of that castle, they saw many knights riding to and fro towards the tournament. And then Sir Tristram noticed a fine-looking knight riding on a great black horse, with a black-covered shield.

"What knight is that," said Sir Tristram, "with the black horse and the black shield? He looks a good knight."

"I know him well," said Sir Persides. "He is one of the best knights in the world."

"Then it is Sir Lancelot," said Tristram.

"No," said Sir Persides, "it is Sir Palomides, who is still unchristened."

Chapter 28: How Sir Tristram was unhorsed by Sir Palomides, and how Lancelot overthrew two knights

Then they saw many people of the country greet Sir Palomides. And a little while after there came a squire of the castle, who told Sir Pellounes, the lord of that castle, that a knight with a black shield had struck down thirteen knights.

"Fair brother," said Sir Tristram to Sir Persides, "let us throw cloaks over ourselves and go and watch the sport."

"Not so," said Sir Persides. "We will not go there like servants. We will ride like men and good knights, ready to stand up to our enemies."

So they armed themselves, and took their horses and great spears, and went to where many knights were trying themselves out before the tournament. And at once Sir Palomides saw Sir Persides, and then he sent a squire to him, and said, "Go to that knight over there with the green shield with a gold lion on it, and tell him I request him to joust with me, and tell him that my name is Sir Palomides."

When Sir Persides understood Sir Palomides' request, he made himself ready, and at once they met together, but Sir Persides took a fall. Then Sir Tristram squared up to be revenged on Sir Palomides, and Sir Palomides saw it, and he was ready and Sir Tristram was not, and so he took him at a disadvantage and struck him over his horse's tail when he had no spear in his rest. Then Sir Tristram leapt up and quickly took his horse, and he was angry beyond measure and badly ashamed of that fall. Then Sir Tristram sent Gouvernail to Sir Palomides, and asked him to joust with him at his request.

"No," said Sir Palomides, "I will not joust with that knight at this time, for I know him better than he thinks. And if he is angry he may put it right tomorrow at the Castle of Maidens, where he can see me and many other knights."

With that came Sir Dinadan, and when he saw Sir Tristram angry he did not care to joke.

"Look," said Sir Dinadan, "here's the proof of it: however good a man is, he can still take a fall; and no man was ever so wise that he couldn't be caught out; and the only man who rides well is the one who never fell."

So Sir Tristram was exceedingly angry, and said to Sir Persides and to Sir Dinadan, "I will have my revenge."

Just as they stood there talking, there came past Sir Tristram a fine-looking knight with a black shield, riding very soberly and heavily.

"What knight is that?" said Sir Tristram to Sir Persides.

"I know him well," said Sir Persides, "for his name is Sir Briant of North Wales."

So he passed on among the other knights of North Wales. And then Sir Lancelot du Lake came in with a shield bearing the arms of Cornwall, and he sent a squire to Sir Briant, and requested him to joust with him.

"Well," said Sir Briant, "since I am asked to joust, I will do what I can."

And there Sir Lancelot struck Sir Briant down from his horse with a great fall. And then Sir Tristram wondered what knight he was who bore the shield of Cornwall.

"Whoever he is," said Sir Dinadan, "I promise you he is of King Ban's blood, and they are the knights of the most noble prowess in the world, if you count them man for man."

Then there came two knights of North Wales, one called Hew de la Montaine and the other Sir Madok de la Montaine, and they challenged Sir Lancelot on the spot. Sir Lancelot did not refuse them but made himself ready, and with one spear he struck them both down over their horses' rumps. And so Sir Lancelot rode his way.

"By the good Lord," said Sir Tristram, "he is a good knight who bears the shield of Cornwall, and it seems to me he rides in the best manner that I ever saw a knight ride."

Then the King of North Wales rode to Sir Palomides and begged him earnestly, for his sake, to joust with that knight "who has done us of North Wales this insult."

"Sir," said Sir Palomides, "I am very unwilling to fight that knight, and the reason is that the great tournament is tomorrow, and so, by my own choice, I will keep myself fresh."

"No," said the King of North Wales, "I beg you, ask him to joust."

"Sir," said Sir Palomides, "I will joust at your request, and ask that knight to joust with me; and I have often seen a man take a fall that he asked for himself."

Chapter 29: How Sir Lancelot jousted with Palomides and overthrew him, and how afterwards he was attacked by twelve knights

Then Sir Palomides sent a squire to Sir Lancelot, and requested him to joust.

"Good fellow," said Sir Lancelot, "tell me your lord's name."

"Sir," said the squire, "my lord's name is Sir Palomides, the good knight."

"Well and good," said Sir Lancelot, "for there is no knight I have seen these seven years whom I would rather fight than him."

And so each knight made himself ready with two great spears.

"Now," said Sir Dinadan, "you'll see that Sir Palomides will acquit himself very well."

"That may be so," said Sir Tristram, "but I promise you that knight with the shield of Cornwall will give him a fall."

"I don't believe it," said Sir Dinadan.

Just then they spurred their horses and set their spears in rest, and each hit the other. And Sir Palomides broke a spear on Sir Lancelot, and he sat firm and did not move; but Sir Lancelot struck him so swiftly that he made him leave his horse's saddle, and the stroke broke his shield and his hauberk, and if he had not fallen he would have been killed.

"How about that?" said Sir Tristram. "I knew well, by the way they both rode, that Sir Palomides would have a fall."

Then Sir Lancelot rode his way, and rode to a spring to drink and to rest himself, and the men of North Wales watched where he rode. And then twelve knights followed him to do him harm, for this reason: so that he should not win the victory the next day at the tournament of the Castle of Maidens. So they came upon Sir Lancelot suddenly, and he scarcely had time to put on his helmet and take his horse before they were at him. And then Sir Lancelot got his spear, and rode through them, and there he killed a knight and broke a spear in his body. Then he drew his sword and struck to the right and to the left, so that within a few strokes he had killed three more knights, and the rest who stayed, he wounded them badly, every one who stayed. So Sir Lancelot escaped from his enemies of North Wales, and then Sir Lancelot rode his way to a friend's, and lodged there until the next morning; for he would not fight in the tournament on the first day, because of his great exertion. And on the first day he was with King Arthur, where he was set up high on a stand to judge who was most worthy for his deeds. So Sir Lancelot was with King Arthur, and did not joust on the first day.

Chapter 30: How Sir Tristram bore himself on the first day of the tournament, and how he won the prize there

Now we turn to Sir Tristram de Liones, who commanded Gouvernail, his servant, to get him a black shield with no other device on it. And so Sir Persides and Sir Tristram left their host Sir Pellounes, and rode early towards the tournament, and then they joined King Carados' side, the King of Scotland's. And at once knights opened the field, some of the King of North Wales' side and some of King Carados' side, and there the fighting began in earnest. Then there was crashing and rushing. Just then Sir Persides and Sir Tristram came in, and they fared so well that they drove the King of North Wales back. Then Sir Bleoberis de Ganis and Sir Gaheris came in with the men of North Wales, and then Sir Persides was struck down and nearly killed, for more than forty horsemen rode over him. For Sir Bleoberis did great deeds of arms, and Sir Gaheris did not fail him. When Sir Tristram saw them, and saw them do such deeds of arms, he wondered who they were. Sir Tristram also thought it a shame that Sir Persides was so treated; and then he took a great spear in his hand, and rode at Sir Gaheris and struck him down from his horse. And then Sir Bleoberis was angry, and took a spear and rode against Sir Tristram in great fury; and there Sir Tristram met him, and struck Sir Bleoberis from his horse. So then the King with the Hundred Knights was angry, and he put Sir Bleoberis and Sir Gaheris back on their horses, and there a great fight began. And all the while Sir Tristram held them very hard, and all the while Sir Bleoberis was exceedingly busy against Sir Tristram. And there Sir Dinadan came against Sir Tristram, and Sir Tristram gave him such a blow that he swooned in his saddle. Then Sir Dinadan came straight to Sir Tristram and said, "Sir, I know you better than you think. But here I give you my solemn word: I will never come against you again, because I promise you that sword of yours is never landing on my helmet again."

With that Sir Bleoberis came, and Sir Tristram gave him such a blow that down went his head; and then he caught him so hard by the helmet that he pulled him under his horse's feet. And then King Arthur had the horn blown to end the day. Then Sir Tristram went off to his tent, and Sir Dinadan rode with him; and Sir Persides and King Arthur, and the kings on both sides, wondered what knight that was with the black shield. Many gave their opinion, and some recognised him as Sir Tristram, and held their peace and would say nothing. So on that first day King Arthur, and all the kings and lords who were judges, gave Sir Tristram the prize; and yet they did not know him, but named him the Knight with the Black Shield.

Chapter 31: How Sir Tristram went over to the side against King Arthur's because he saw Sir Palomides on that side

Then the next morning Sir Palomides left the King of North Wales and rode over to King Arthur's side, where King Carados was, and the King of Ireland, and Sir Lancelot's kin, and Sir Gawain's kin. So Sir Palomides sent the damsel to Sir Tristram, the same damsel he had sent to look for him when he was out of his mind in the forest, and this damsel asked Sir Tristram who he was and what his name was.

"As for that," said Sir Tristram, "tell Sir Palomides that he shall not know at this time, not until I have broken two spears on him. But let him know this much," said Sir Tristram, "that I am the same knight he struck down the evening before the tournament; and tell him plainly that whichever side Sir Palomides is on, I will be on the opposite side."

"Sir," said the damsel, "you must understand that Sir Palomides will be on King Arthur's side, where the noblest knights in the world are."

"In the name of God," said Sir Tristram, "then I will be with the King of North Wales, because Sir Palomides will be on King Arthur's side; and I would not do it otherwise, except for his sake."

So when King Arthur had come they sounded for the field; and then the fighting began in earnest, and King Carados jousted with the King of the Hundred Knights, and there King Carados had a fall. Then there was crashing and rushing, and just then knights of King Arthur's came in, and they drove back the King of North Wales' knights.

Then Sir Tristram came in, and began so roughly and so mightily that no one could stand against him, and so Sir Tristram kept it up a long time. And at last Sir Tristram fell in among the company of King Ban's kin, and there Sir Bors de Ganis fell on him, and Sir Ector de Maris, and Sir Blamore de Ganis, and many other knights. And then Sir Tristram struck to the right and to the left, so that all the lords and ladies spoke of his noble deeds. But at last Sir Tristram would have had the worst of it, had it not been for the King with the Hundred Knights. And then he came with his company and rescued Sir Tristram, and brought him away from those knights who bore the shields of Cornwall. And then Sir Tristram saw another company keeping to themselves, some forty knights together, and Sir Kay the Seneschal was their commander. Then Sir Tristram rode in among them, and there he struck Sir Kay down from his horse; and there he went through those knights like a greyhound among rabbits.

Then Sir Lancelot found a knight who was badly wounded in the head.

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "who wounded you so badly?"

"Sir," he said, "a knight who bears a black shield, and I may curse the hour I ever met him, for he is a devil and no man."

So Sir Lancelot left him and meant to meet Sir Tristram, and so he rode with his sword drawn in his hand to look for Sir Tristram; and then he saw him, how he charged here and there, and at every stroke Sir Tristram all but struck down a knight.

"Jesus have mercy!" said the king. "Since the time I first bore arms I never saw any knight do such marvellous deeds of arms."

"And if I were to attack this knight," said Sir Lancelot to himself, "I would shame myself."

And with that Sir Lancelot put up his sword. And then the King with the Hundred Knights, and a hundred more of North Wales, attacked the twenty of Sir Lancelot's kin; and those twenty knights held together all the time like wild boars, and none would fail another. And so when Sir Tristram saw the nobility of these twenty knights he marvelled at their good deeds, for he saw by their bearing and by their discipline that they would rather die than leave the field.

"Now, Jesus," said Sir Tristram, "well may he be valiant and full of prowess who has such a company of noble knights among his kin, and very likely he is a noble man who is their leader and commander."

He meant Sir Lancelot du Lake. So when Sir Tristram had watched them a long time, he thought it a shame to see two hundred knights battering at twenty knights. Then Sir Tristram rode to the King with the Hundred Knights and said, "Sir, leave off your fighting with those twenty knights, for you win no honour from them, you being so many and they so few; and believe me, they will not leave the field, I can see it by their faces and their bearing; and you will get no honour if you kill them. So leave off fighting them, for, to increase my own honour, I will ride to the twenty knights and help them with all my might and power."

"No," said the King with the Hundred Knights, "you shall not do so. Now that I see your spirit and courtesy, I will withdraw my knights for your pleasure; for a good knight will always favour another, and like will draw to like."

Chapter 32: How Sir Tristram found Palomides by a spring, and brought him back with him to his lodging

Then the King with the Hundred Knights withdrew his knights. And all this while, and long before, Sir Lancelot had been watching Sir Tristram, fully intending to join company with him. And then suddenly Sir Tristram, Sir Dinadan, and Gouvernail, his man, rode their way into the forest, so that no one noticed where they went. So then King Arthur sounded the end of the day, and gave the King of North Wales the prize, because Sir Tristram had been on his side. Then Sir Lancelot rode here and there, as mad as a lion that has missed its kill, because he had lost Sir Tristram, and so he went back to King Arthur.
