And then over the whole field there was such a noise that it could be heard on the wind two miles away, as the lords and ladies cried, "The Knight with the Black Shield has won the field!"

"Alas," said King Arthur, "what has become of that knight? It is a shame to all of you in the field to let him get away from you like that; with gentleness and courtesy you might have brought him to me at the Castle of Maidens."

Then the noble King Arthur went to his knights and comforted them as best he could, and said, "My good companions, don't be dismayed, even though you have lost the field today."

And many were hurt and badly wounded, and many were unharmed.

"My companions," said King Arthur, "see that you keep your spirits up, for tomorrow I will be in the field with you and avenge you on your enemies."

So that night King Arthur and his knights rested.

The damsel who came from Isolde the Fair to Sir Tristram had been with Queen Guinevere all the while the tournament was going on, and the queen kept asking her for what reason she had come into that country.

"Madam," she answered, "I have come for no other reason than from my lady Isolde the Fair, to learn how you are."

For on no account would she tell the queen that she came for Sir Tristram's sake. So this lady, Dame Bragwaine, took her leave of Queen Guinevere, and she rode after Sir Tristram. And as she rode through the forest she heard a great cry; then she commanded her squire to go into the forest to find out what that noise was. And so he came to a spring, and there he found a knight tied to a tree, crying out as if he were mad, with his horse and his armour standing by him. And when he saw the squire, he started up and broke himself loose, and took his sword in his hand, and ran to kill the squire. Then the squire took his horse and fled as fast as ever he could to Dame Bragwaine, and told her what had happened to him. Then she rode to Sir Tristram's tent, and told Sir Tristram what she had come upon in the forest.

"Alas," said Sir Tristram, "on my life, there is some good knight in trouble."

Then Sir Tristram took his horse and his sword and rode there, and there he heard how the knight lamented to himself and said, "I, woeful knight, Sir Palomides, what misfortune has fallen on me, that I am trampled down like this by falsehood and treason, through Sir Bors and Sir Ector! Alas," he said, "why do I live so long!"

And then he took his sword in his hands, and made many strange signs and gestures; and so in his raging he threw his sword into that spring. Then Sir Palomides wailed and wrung his hands. And at last, out of pure sorrow, he ran into that spring, up to his belly, and searched for his sword. Then Sir Tristram saw that, and ran at Sir Palomides, and held him fast in his arms.

"Who are you," said Palomides, "holding me like this?"

"I am a man of this forest, who means you no harm."

"Alas," said Sir Palomides, "I can never win honour where Sir Tristram is; for wherever he is, if I am there too, then I get no honour; and if he is away, then for the most part I win the prize, unless Sir Lancelot is there, or Sir Lamorak."

Then Sir Palomides said, "Once in Ireland Sir Tristram got the better of me, and another time in Cornwall, and in other places in this land."

"What would you do," said Sir Tristram, "if you had Sir Tristram?"

"I would fight with him," said Sir Palomides, "and ease my heart on him. And yet, to tell you the truth, Sir Tristram is the noblest knight living in this world."

"What will you do?" said Sir Tristram. "Will you come with me to your lodging?"

"No," he said, "I will go to the King with the Hundred Knights, for he rescued me from Sir Bors de Ganis and Sir Ector, or else I would have been treacherously killed."

Sir Tristram spoke such kind words to him that Sir Palomides went with him to his lodging. Then Gouvernail went on ahead, and told Dame Bragwaine to go out of the way to her own lodging, "and tell Sir Persides not to pick any quarrel with him." And so they rode together until they came to Sir Tristram's tent, and there Sir Palomides had all the welcome that could be had, all that night. But on no account could Sir Palomides find out who Sir Tristram was; and so after supper they went to rest, and Sir Tristram, from his great exertion, slept until it was day. And Sir Palomides could not sleep for anguish; and at dawn he took his horse secretly, and rode his way to Sir Gaheris and to Sir Sagramore le Desirous, where they were in their tents; for the three of them had been companions at the beginning of the tournament. And then in the morning the king sounded for the tournament on the third day.

Chapter 33: How Sir Tristram struck down Sir Palomides, and how he jousted with King Arthur, and other feats

So the King of North Wales and the King with the Hundred Knights, the two of them, met King Carados and the King of Ireland; and there the King with the Hundred Knights struck down King Carados, and the King of North Wales struck down the King of Ireland. With that Sir Palomides came in, and when he came he did great work, for he was well known by his indented shield, its colours cut in a zigzag. Then King Arthur came in, and they did great deeds of arms together, and put the King of North Wales and the King with the Hundred Knights to the worse. Then Sir Tristram came in with his black shield, and at once he jousted with Sir Palomides, and there by sheer force Sir Tristram struck Sir Palomides over his horse's rump.

Then King Arthur cried, "Knight with the Black Shield, get ready for me!"

And in the same way Sir Tristram struck King Arthur down. And then, by the strength of King Arthur's knights, the king and Sir Palomides were put back on their horses. Then King Arthur, with a great eager heart, took a spear in his hand, and there from the one side he struck Sir Tristram over his horse. Then at once Sir Palomides came at Sir Tristram, while he was on foot, to ride him down. Then Sir Tristram saw him coming, and there he stepped aside, and in great fury he caught him by the arm and pulled him down from his horse. Then Sir Palomides quickly got up, and then they laid into each other mightily with their swords; and many kings, queens, and lords stood and watched them. And at last Sir Tristram struck Sir Palomides on the helmet three mighty strokes, and at every stroke he gave him he said, "This one is for Sir Tristram's sake!"

With that Sir Palomides fell face down on the ground.

Then the King with the Hundred Knights came, and brought Sir Tristram a horse, and so he was mounted again. By then Sir Palomides was mounted, and in great fury he rode at Sir Tristram with his spear in the rest, and gave him a great blow with his sword. Then Sir Tristram dodged his spear, and caught him by the neck with both his hands, and pulled him clean out of his saddle, and so he carried him in front of him the length of ten spears, and then in front of them all he let him fall wherever he might. Then Sir Tristram saw King Arthur with a naked sword in his hand, and Sir Tristram rode at King Arthur with his spear; and King Arthur boldly stood his ground and with his sword he cut his spear in two, and with that Sir Tristram was stunned; and so King Arthur gave him three or four strokes before he could get out his sword. And at last Sir Tristram drew his sword, and each attacked the other very hard. With that the great crush of the fighting parted them. Then Sir Tristram rode here and there and did his utmost, so that that day Sir Tristram struck down eleven of the good knights of King Ban's blood, who were of Sir Lancelot's kin; so that all the great lords marvelled at his great deeds, and all cried out for the Knight with the Black Shield.

Chapter 34: How Sir Lancelot wounded Sir Tristram, and how afterwards Sir Tristram struck down Sir Palomides

Then this cry was so loud that Sir Lancelot heard it. And then he took a great spear in his hand and came towards the cry.

Then Sir Lancelot cried, "Knight with the Black Shield, get ready to joust with me!"

When Sir Tristram heard him say so, he took his spear in his hand, and both of them lowered their heads, and they came together like thunder. And Sir Tristram's spear broke in pieces, and Sir Lancelot, by ill luck, struck Sir Tristram in the side, a deep wound, near to death; but still Sir Tristram did not leave his saddle, and so the spear broke. With that Sir Tristram, wounded as he was, got out his sword, and he rushed at Sir Lancelot, and gave him three great strokes on the helmet so that the fire sprang out of it, and Sir Lancelot bowed his head low toward his saddlebow. And with that Sir Tristram left the field, for he felt himself so wounded that he thought he would die; and Sir Dinadan saw him and followed him into the forest. Then Sir Lancelot stayed and did many marvellous deeds.

So when Sir Tristram had got away to the edge of the forest he dismounted, and unlaced his armour and bathed his wound. Then Sir Dinadan thought he was going to die.

"No, no," said Sir Tristram, "Dinadan, never fear, for my heart is whole, and I shall soon be whole of this wound, by the mercy of God."

By then Sir Dinadan noticed Palomides coming, riding straight at them. And then Sir Tristram saw that Sir Palomides was coming to destroy him.

And so Sir Dinadan gave him warning, and said, "Sir Tristram, my lord, you are so badly wounded that you can't fight him, so I will ride against him and do to him what I can; and if I am killed, you can pray for my soul. And meanwhile you can slip away and go into the castle, or into the forest, so that he won't meet you."

Sir Tristram smiled and said, "I thank you, Sir Dinadan, for your good will, but you shall know that I am able to handle him."

And then he quickly armed himself, and took his horse, and a great spear in his hand, and said to Sir Dinadan, "Goodbye."

And he rode toward Sir Palomides at a gentle pace. Then when Sir Palomides saw that, he made as if to see to his horse, but he did it for this reason: he was waiting for Sir Gaheris, who was coming after him. And when he had come, he rode toward Sir Tristram. Then Sir Tristram sent to Sir Palomides and asked him to joust with him; and if he struck down Sir Palomides, he would do nothing more to him; and if it so happened that Sir Palomides struck down Sir Tristram, he told him to do his worst. So they were agreed. Then they met together, and Sir Tristram struck down Sir Palomides so that he had a grievous fall, and lay as still as if he were dead. And then Sir Tristram rode at Sir Gaheris, and he did not want to joust; but whether he wanted to or not, Sir Tristram struck him over his horse's rump, so that he lay as still as if he were dead. And then Sir Tristram rode his way and left Sir Persides' squire in the tents, and Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan rode to an old knight's house to lodge. And that old knight had five sons at the tournament, and he prayed God earnestly for their coming home. And so, as the French book says, they came home, all five of them, well beaten.

And when Sir Tristram had gone off into the forest, Sir Lancelot kept up the fight just as hard, like a man in a frenzy who took no care for himself, and you may be sure there were many noble knights against him. And when King Arthur saw Sir Lancelot do such marvellous deeds of arms, he armed himself, and took his horse and his armour, and rode into the field to help Sir Lancelot; and many knights came in with King Arthur. And to cut a long story short, in the end the King of North Wales and the King of the Hundred Knights were put to the worse; and because Sir Lancelot stayed and was the last in the field, the prize was given to him. But Sir Lancelot would not have the prize, not for king, queen, or knight; and where the cry was cried through the field, "Sir Lancelot, Sir Lancelot has won the field today!", Sir Lancelot had another cry made against it: "Sir Tristram has won the field, for he began first, and he has held out to the last, and so he has done on the first day, the second, and the third!"

Chapter 35: How the prize of the third day was given to Sir Lancelot, and Sir Lancelot gave it to Sir Tristram

Then all ranks and degrees, high and low, spoke of Sir Lancelot with great honour, for the honour he had done to Sir Tristram; and for doing that honour to Sir Tristram he was more praised and renowned at that time than if he had overthrown five hundred knights. And all the people, every one, for this nobility, first the great lords both high and low, and after them the common people, cried out at once, "Sir Lancelot has won the field, whoever says no!"

Then Sir Lancelot was angry and ashamed, and so with that he rode to King Arthur.

"Alas," said the king, "we are all dismayed that Sir Tristram has left us like this. By God," said King Arthur, "he is one of the noblest knights I ever saw hold spear or sword in hand, and the most courteous knight in his fighting; for I saw him hard at it," said King Arthur, "when he struck Sir Palomides on the helmet three times, so that he battered his helmet down with his strokes, and he also said, 'Here is a stroke for Sir Tristram,' and he said it three times."

Then King Arthur, Sir Lancelot, and Sir Dodinas le Savage took their horses to look for Sir Tristram, for through Sir Persides the king had been told where Sir Tristram was in his tent. But when they came there, Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan were gone.

Then King Arthur and Sir Lancelot were downcast, and went back again to the Castle of Maidens, grieving greatly for Sir Tristram's wound and his sudden departure.

"So help me God," said King Arthur, "I am sadder that I cannot meet him than for all the hurts all my knights have had at the tournament."

Just then Sir Gaheris came and told King Arthur how Sir Tristram had struck down Sir Palomides, and that it was at Sir Palomides' own request.

"Alas," said King Arthur, "that was a great dishonour to Sir Palomides, seeing that Sir Tristram was badly wounded. And now all of us, kings and knights and men of honour, may say that Sir Tristram may be called a noble knight, and one of the best knights I ever saw in all the days of my life. For I want you all to know, kings and knights," said King Arthur, "that I never saw a knight do so marvellously as he has done these three days; for he was the first to begin and the one who held out longest, except for this last day. And though he was hurt, it was a manly chance between two noble knights; and when two noble men meet, one of them must needs have the worse, as God allows at the time."

"As for me," said Sir Lancelot, "I would not have hurt Sir Tristram, not for all the lands my father ever left me, if I had known him at the time. I hurt him because I did not see his shield. For if I had seen his black shield, I would not have meddled with him, for many reasons; for not long ago he did as much for me as any knight ever did, and it is well known that he fought thirty knights, with no help except Sir Dinadan. And I promise you one thing," said Sir Lancelot, "Sir Palomides shall regret his ungracious dealing in going after that noble knight whom I hurt like that by mischance."

Sir Lancelot said all the honour of Sir Tristram that could be said. Then King Arthur held a great feast for all who would come. And so we let King Arthur pass, and turn a little to Sir Palomides, who, after his fall from Sir Tristram, was nearly driven out of his wits for spite against Sir Tristram. And so he followed him, trusting to chance. And as he came by a river, in his frenzy he would have made his horse leap over it; and the horse lost its footing and fell into the river, so that Sir Palomides was afraid he would be drowned. And then he got clear of his horse, and swam to the land, and let his horse go down the river wherever it might.

Chapter 36: How Palomides came to the castle where Sir Tristram was, and of the quest that Sir Lancelot and ten knights made for Sir Tristram

And when he came to the land he took off his armour, and sat roaring and crying like a man out of his mind. Just then a damsel came right past Sir Palomides, who had been sent from Sir Gawain and his brother to Sir Mordred, who lay sick in the same place, with that old knight where Sir Tristram was. For, as the French book says, Sir Persides had wounded Sir Mordred badly some ten days before; and if it had not been for love of Sir Gawain and his brother, Sir Persides would have killed Sir Mordred. And so this damsel came past Sir Palomides, and she and he had words together, which pleased neither of them. And so the damsel rode on her way until she came to the old knight's place, and there she told that old knight how she had met by chance the maddest knight she had ever met.

"What did he bear on his shield?" said Sir Tristram.

"It was indented with white and black," said the damsel.

"Ah," said Sir Tristram, "that was Sir Palomides, the good knight. For I know him well," said Sir Tristram, "as one of the best knights living in this realm."

Then that old knight took a little riding horse, and rode for Sir Palomides, and brought him to his own manor. And Sir Tristram knew Sir Palomides very well, but he said very little, for at that time Sir Tristram was up and walking on his feet, and well recovered from his wounds. And always when Sir Palomides saw Sir Tristram he would stare at him in great wonder, and it always seemed to him that he had seen him before.

Then he would say to Sir Dinadan, "If I ever meet Sir Tristram, he won't escape my hands."

"I'm amazed," said Sir Dinadan, "that you boast like this behind Sir Tristram's back, when it is not long since he was in your hands, and you in his. Why didn't you hold on to him when you had him? For I saw myself, two or three times, that you got precious little honour out of Sir Tristram."

Then Sir Palomides was ashamed. So we leave them for a little while in the old castle with the old knight, Sir Darras.

Now we shall speak of King Arthur, who said to Sir Lancelot, "If it had not been for you, we would not have lost Sir Tristram, for he was here every day until the time you met him; and it was in an evil hour," said Arthur, "that you fought him."

"My lord Arthur," said Lancelot, "you lay it on me that I was the cause of his going; God knows it was against my will. But when men are hot in deeds of arms they often hurt their friends as well as their foes. And my lord," said Sir Lancelot, "you must understand that Sir Tristram is a man I am loath to offend, for he has done more for me than I have ever yet done for him."

But then Sir Lancelot had a book brought out, and then Sir Lancelot said, "Here we are, ten knights who will swear on a book never to rest one night where we rested the night before, for this twelvemonth, until we find Sir Tristram. And as for me," said Sir Lancelot, "I promise you on this book that if I can meet him, by fair means or foul I shall bring him to this court, or else I shall die for it."

And the names of these ten knights who undertook this quest were these: first was Sir Lancelot, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Bors de Ganis, and Bleoberis, and Sir Blamore de Ganis, and Lucan the butler, Sir Uwain, Sir Galihud, Lionel, and Galihodin. So these ten noble knights left the court of King Arthur, and so they rode on their quest together until they came to a cross where four ways parted, and there the company split four ways to look for Sir Tristram.

And as Sir Lancelot rode on by chance, he met Dame Bragwaine, who had been sent into that country to look for Sir Tristram, and she was fleeing as fast as her palfrey could go. So Sir Lancelot met her and asked her why she was fleeing.

"Ah, fair knight," said Dame Bragwaine, "I am fleeing in fear of my life, for Sir Breuse Saunce Pité is following me to kill me."

"Keep close to me," said Sir Lancelot.

Then when Sir Lancelot saw Sir Breuse Saunce Pité, Sir Lancelot shouted at him, and said, "False knight, destroyer of ladies and damsels, your last day has come!"

When Sir Breuse Saunce Pité saw Sir Lancelot's shield he knew it well, for at that time he was not bearing the arms of Cornwall, but his own shield. And then Sir Breuse fled, and Sir Lancelot followed after him. But Sir Breuse was so well mounted that when he wanted to flee he could flee easily, and stand his ground too when he wanted to. And then Sir Lancelot went back to Dame Bragwaine, and she thanked him for his great trouble.

Chapter 37: How Sir Tristram, Sir Palomides, and Sir Dinadan were captured and thrown into prison

Now we will speak of Sir Lucan the butler, who by chance came riding to the same place where Sir Tristram was, and he came in with no other purpose than to ask for lodging. Then the porter asked what his name was.

"Tell your lord that my name is Sir Lucan, the butler, a knight of the Round Table."

So the porter went to Sir Darras, the lord of the place, and told him who was there asking for lodging.

"No, no," said Sir Daname, who was nephew to Sir Darras. "Tell him that he shall not be lodged here. But let him know that I, Sir Daname, will meet him at once, and tell him to make himself ready."

So Sir Daname came out on horseback, and there they met with spears, and Sir Lucan struck Sir Daname down over his horse's crupper, and then he fled into the house, and Sir Lucan rode after him, and asked for him many times.

Then Sir Dinadan said to Sir Tristram, "It is a shame to see the cousin of the lord of this place trampled like that."

"Wait," said Sir Tristram, "and I will put it right."

And meanwhile Sir Dinadan got on horseback, and he jousted with Lucan the butler, and there Sir Lucan ran Dinadan through the thick of the thigh, and so he rode on his way. And Sir Tristram was angry that Sir Dinadan was hurt, and followed after him, meaning to avenge him; and within a while he overtook Sir Lucan, and told him to turn. And so they met, so that Sir Tristram wounded Sir Lucan exceedingly badly and gave him a fall. With that came Sir Uwain, a well-born knight, and when he saw Sir Lucan so hurt he called on Sir Tristram to joust with him.

"Fair knight," said Sir Tristram, "tell me your name, I beg you."

"Sir knight, you may be sure my name is Sir Uwain le Fise de Roy Ureine, that is, the son of King Uriens."

"Ah," said Sir Tristram, "if I had my way I would never fight you, at any time."

"You shall not have your way," said Sir Uwain, "for you shall fight me."

And then Sir Tristram saw no other remedy, but rode against him, and overthrew Sir Uwain and wounded him in the side, and so he went back to his lodging again. And when Sir Dinadan understood that Sir Tristram had wounded Sir Lucan, he would have ridden after Sir Lucan to kill him, but Sir Tristram would not allow it. Then Sir Uwain had a horse-litter made ready, and brought Sir Lucan to the abbey of Ganis; and the castle beside it was called the Castle of Ganis, and Sir Bleoberis was its lord. And at that castle Sir Lancelot had promised all his companions to meet him in the quest for Sir Tristram.

So when Sir Tristram had come to his lodging, a damsel came who told Sir Darras that three of his sons had been killed at that tournament, and two so grievously wounded that they were never likely to help themselves again. And all this was done by a noble knight who carried the black shield, and he was the one who won the prize. Then someone came and told Sir Darras that the same knight, the one who carried the black shield, was in the house. Then Sir Darras went to Sir Tristram's room, and there he found his shield and showed it to the damsel.

"Ah, sir," said the damsel, "that is the very man who killed your three sons."

Then without any delay Sir Darras put Sir Tristram, and Sir Palomides, and Sir Dinadan into a strong prison, and there Sir Tristram came near to dying of a great sickness. And every day Sir Palomides would reproach Sir Tristram over the old hatred between them. And Sir Tristram always spoke courteously and said little. But when Sir Palomides saw Sir Tristram falling sick, then he was downcast for him, and comforted him in the best way he could. And as the French book says, forty knights of Sir Darras's own kin came to him, and they would have killed Sir Tristram and his two companions, but Sir Darras would not allow that, but kept them in prison, and they had food and drink. So Sir Tristram endured great pain there, for sickness had taken hold of him, and that is the greatest pain a prisoner can have. For as long as a prisoner has his bodily health, he can endure, under the mercy of God and in hope of a good release; but when sickness touches a prisoner's body, then a prisoner may say that all his well-being is taken from him, and then he has cause to wail and to weep. And that is just what Sir Tristram did when sickness had taken hold of him, for then he fell into such sorrow that he almost killed himself.

Chapter 38: How King Mark resented Sir Tristram's good name, and how some of King Arthur's knights jousted with knights of Cornwall

Now we will leave Sir Tristram, Sir Palomides and Sir Dinadan in prison, and speak of other knights who searched for Sir Tristram in many different parts of this land. And some went into Cornwall; and by chance Sir Gaheris, King Arthur's nephew, came to King Mark, and there he was well received, and sat at King Mark's own table and ate from his own dish. Then King Mark asked Sir Gaheris what news there was in the realm of Logres.

"Sir," said Sir Gaheris, "the king reigns like a noble knight. And just lately there was as great a jousting and tournament as I ever saw in the realm of Logres, and the noblest knights were at that jousting. But there was one knight who did marvellously for three days, and he carried a black shield, and of all the knights I ever saw, he proved the best."

"Then," said King Mark, "that was Sir Lancelot, or Sir Palomides the pagan."

"Not so," said Sir Gaheris, "for both Sir Lancelot and Sir Palomides were on the opposite side, against the Knight with the Black Shield."

"Then it was Sir Tristram," said the king.

"Yes," said Sir Gaheris.

And with that the king hung his head, and in his heart he was badly afraid that Sir Tristram would win himself such honour in the realm of Logres that he himself would not be able to stand against him. So Sir Gaheris had a fine welcome from King Mark, and from Queen Isolde the Fair, who was glad of Sir Gaheris's words; for she knew well by the deeds and the manner of it that it was Sir Tristram. And then the king held a royal feast, and to that feast came Sir Uwain le Fise de Roy Ureine, whom some called Uwain le Blanchemains. And this Sir Uwain challenged all the knights of Cornwall. Then the king was mad with rage that he had no knights to answer him. Then Sir Andred, King Mark's nephew, leapt up and said, "I will take on Sir Uwain."

Then he went and armed himself and mounted in the best way he could. And there Sir Uwain met Sir Andred, and struck him down so that he lay fainting on the ground. Then King Mark was sorry and angry beyond measure that he had no knight to avenge his nephew Sir Andred.

So the king called Sir Dinas the Seneschal to him, and begged him for his sake to take it on himself to joust with Sir Uwain.

"Sir," said Sir Dinas, "I am very unwilling to fight any knight of the Round Table."

"Even so," said the king, "for my love take on this joust."

So Sir Dinas made himself ready, and at once they met together with great spears, but Sir Dinas was overthrown, horse and man, a great fall. And who was angry but King Mark!

"Alas," he said, "have I no knight who will take on that knight there?"

"Sir," said Sir Gaheris, "for your sake I will joust."

So Sir Gaheris made himself ready, and when he was armed he rode into the field. And when Sir Uwain saw Sir Gaheris's shield he rode up to him and said, "Sir, you are not doing your duty. For, sir, when you were first made a knight of the Round Table you swore that you would never knowingly fight against your own fellowship. And by God, Sir Gaheris, you knew me well enough by my shield, and I know you just as well by yours. And though you would break your oath, I will not break mine. For there is no one here, not even you, who shall think I am afraid of you; I would dare well enough to fight you, and yet we are the sons of two sisters."

Then Sir Gaheris was ashamed, and so with that every knight went his way, and Sir Uwain rode off into the country.

Then King Mark armed himself, and took his horse and his spear, with a squire along with him. And then he rode on ahead of Sir Uwain, and suddenly, at a gap, he ran at him while he was off his guard, and there he struck him almost through the body, and left him there. So within a while Sir Kay came by and found Sir Uwain, and asked him how he had been hurt.

"I don't know why or how," said Sir Uwain, "but I am sure I got this wound by treachery. For a knight came suddenly at me here before I was aware of him, and wounded me without warning."

Then Sir Andred arrived there, looking for King Mark.

"You traitor knight," said Sir Kay, "if I knew it was you who had wounded this noble knight so treacherously, you would never get out of my hands."

"Sir," said Sir Andred, "I never wounded him, and I am willing to let him say so himself."

"Shame on you, false knight," said Sir Kay, "for you men of Cornwall are worth nothing."

So Sir Kay had Sir Uwain carried to the Abbey of the Black Cross, and there he was healed. And then Sir Gaheris took his leave of King Mark, but before he left he said, "Sir king, you brought a foul shame on yourself and your court when you banished Sir Tristram out of this country. For you would have had no need to fear any knight if he had been here."

And so he left.

Chapter 39: Of King Mark's treachery, and how Sir Gaheris struck down both him and his cousin Andred

Then Sir Kay the Seneschal came to King Mark, and there he was given a good welcome, on the outside.

"Now, fair lords," said King Mark, "will you try an adventure in the forest of Morris? I know well it holds as hard an adventure as any I know."

"Sir," said Sir Kay, "I will try it."

And Sir Gaheris said he would think it over, for King Mark was always full of treachery. And with that Sir Gaheris left and rode on his way. And on the same road that Sir Kay was to ride he lay down to rest, ordering his squire to watch for Sir Kay: "And warn me when he comes."

So within a while Sir Kay came riding that way, and then Sir Gaheris took his horse and met him, and said, "Sir Kay, you are not wise to ride at King Mark's request, for everything he does is treachery."

Then Sir Kay said, "I beg you, let us try this adventure."

"I will not fail you," said Sir Gaheris.

And so they rode on until they came to a lake that was called at that time the Perilous Lake, and there they waited in the thicket at the edge of the wood.

Meanwhile King Mark, in the castle of Tintagil, sent away all his barons, and everyone else except those who were in his secrets was sent out of his chamber. And then he had his nephew Sir Andred called, and told him to arm himself and mount quickly; and by that time it was midnight. And so King Mark was armed in black, horse and all; and so they two sallied out at a secret back gate, with their servants with them, and rode until they came to that lake. Then Sir Kay saw them first, and took his spear, and offered to joust. And King Mark rode against him, and they struck each other very hard, for the moon shone as bright as day. And there at that joust Sir Kay's horse fell down, for his horse was not as big as the king's horse, and Sir Kay's horse bruised him very badly. Then Sir Gaheris was angry that Sir Kay had a fall. Then he cried, "Knight, sit fast in your saddle, for I will avenge my companion!"

Then King Mark was afraid of Sir Gaheris, and so, against his will, King Mark rode against him, and Sir Gaheris gave him such a blow that he fell down. So then at once Sir Gaheris ran at Sir Andred and struck him clean off his horse, so that his helmet drove into the earth, and he nearly broke his neck. And with that Sir Gaheris dismounted, and got Sir Kay up. And then they both went on foot to the two of them, and told them to yield and tell their names, or else they would die. Then with great pain Sir Andred spoke first, and said, "It is King Mark of Cornwall, so be careful what you do; and I am Sir Andred, his cousin."

"Shame on you both," said Sir Gaheris, "for a false traitor! You have done false treachery, and he too, under the false welcome you gave us! It would be a pity," said Sir Gaheris, "for you to live any longer."

"Save my life," said King Mark, "and I will make amends; and remember that I am an anointed king."

"It would be all the more shame," said Sir Gaheris, "to save your life. You are a king anointed with the holy oil, and so you ought to stand by all men of honour; and so you deserve to die."

With that he laid into King Mark without saying any more, and King Mark covered himself with his shield and defended himself as well as he could. And then Sir Kay laid into Sir Andred, and with that King Mark yielded to Sir Gaheris. And then he knelt down, and swore his oath on the crossguard of the sword that never while he lived would he be against knights-errant. And he also swore to be a good friend to Sir Tristram, if ever he came into Cornwall.

By then Sir Andred was on the ground, and Sir Kay would have killed him.

"Let him be," said Sir Gaheris. "Don't kill him, I beg you."

"It would be a pity," said Sir Kay, "for him to live any longer. For this man is a close cousin to Sir Tristram, and he has always been a traitor to him, and it was through him that he was exiled out of Cornwall; and so I will kill him," said Sir Kay.

"You shall not," said Sir Gaheris. "Since I have given the king his life, I beg you, give this man his life."

And with that Sir Kay let him go. And so Sir Kay and Sir Gaheris rode on their way to Dinas the Seneschal, because they had heard it said that he loved Sir Tristram well. So they rested there, and soon afterwards they rode to the realm of Logres. And so within a little while they met Sir Lancelot, who always kept Dame Bragwaine with him, thinking that this way he would sooner meet Sir Tristram. And Sir Lancelot asked what news there was in Cornwall, and whether they had heard of Sir Tristram or not. Sir Kay and Sir Gaheris answered that they had heard nothing of him. Then they told Sir Lancelot their adventure, word for word. Then Sir Lancelot smiled and said, "What is bred in the bone is hard to get out of the flesh."

And so they made merry together.

Chapter 40: How Sir Tristram, Sir Palomides, and Sir Dinadan, after a long time in prison, were set free

Now we leave this tale, and speak of Sir Dinas, who had a lady-love in the castle, and she loved another knight better than him. And so when Sir Dinas went out hunting she let herself down from the wall by a towel, and took two of his little hounds with her, and so she went to the knight she loved, and he loved her in return. And when Sir Dinas came home and missed his lady-love and his hounds, he was angrier about his hounds than about the lady. So then he rode after the knight who had his lady-love, and told him to turn and joust. So Sir Dinas struck him down, so that with the fall he broke his leg and his arm. And then his lady and lover begged Sir Dinas's pardon, and said she would love him better than she ever had.

"No," said Sir Dinas, "I will never trust those who have once betrayed me. And so, as you have begun, so end, for I will never have anything to do with you again."

And so Sir Dinas left, and took his hounds with him, and so rode to his castle.

Now we will turn to Sir Lancelot, who was very downcast that he could never hear any news of Sir Tristram, for all this while he was in prison with Sir Darras, with Palomides and Dinadan. Then Dame Bragwaine took her leave to go into Cornwall, and Sir Lancelot, Sir Kay and Sir Gaheris rode to look for Sir Tristram in the country of Surluse.

Now this tale speaks of Sir Tristram and his two companions. For every day Sir Palomides wrangled and spoke out against Sir Tristram.

"I'm amazed at you, Sir Palomides," said Sir Dinadan. "If you had Sir Tristram here, I'm sure you would do him no harm; for if a wolf and a sheep were shut in a prison together, the wolf would leave the sheep in peace. And you may be sure," said Sir Dinadan, "this man here is Sir Tristram, in a word. So now you must do your best with him, and let's see if you can settle it with your hands."

Then Sir Palomides was abashed and said little.

"Sir Palomides," said Sir Tristram then, "I have heard plenty of your ill will against me, but I will not fight you at this time if I can help it, because I fear the lord of this place who has us in his keeping. For if I did not fear him more than I fear you, it would soon be settled."

So they made peace between them. Just then a damsel came in and said, "Knights, take heart, for your lives are safe; I heard my lord Sir Darras say so."

Then all three were glad, for every day they had expected to die.

Then soon after this Sir Tristram fell so sick that he thought he would die. Then Sir Dinadan wept, and so did Sir Palomides, and the two of them grieved greatly. So a damsel came in to them and found them mourning. Then she went to Sir Darras, and told him that the mighty knight who carried the black shield was likely to die.

"That shall not be," said Sir Darras, "for God forbid that, when knights come to me for help, I should let them die in my prison. So," said Sir Darras to the damsel, "fetch that knight and his companions before me."

And then at once Sir Darras saw Sir Tristram brought before him. He said, "Sir knight, I am sorry for your sickness, for you are called a very noble knight, and so you seem to be. And you may be sure it shall never be said that Sir Darras destroyed such a noble knight as you in prison, even though you have killed three of my sons, which grieved me greatly. But now you shall go, and your companions, and your armour and horses have been kept fair and clean, and you shall go wherever you please, on this condition: that you, knight, will promise me to be a good friend to my two sons who are still alive, and also that you tell me your name."

"Sir," he said, "as for me, my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, and I was born in Cornwall, and I am King Mark's nephew. And as for the death of your sons, I could not help it; for if they had been my own nearest kin I could have done no differently. And if I had killed them by treason or treachery, I would have deserved to die."

"I take all this into account," said Sir Darras, "that everything you did was done by the force of knighthood, and that was why I would not put you to death. But since you are Sir Tristram, the good knight, I beg you with all my heart to be a good friend to me and to my sons."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I promise you, on my life, that as long as I live I will do you service, for you have done no more to us than a true-hearted knight ought to do."

Then Sir Tristram rested there until he had recovered from his sickness; and when he was big and strong they took their leave, and every knight took his horse, and so they left and rode together until they came to a crossroads.

"Now, companions," said Sir Tristram, "here we will part, each his own way."

And because Sir Dinadan had the first adventure of them, I will begin with him.

Chapter 41: How Sir Dinadan rescued a lady from Sir Breuse Saunce Pité, and how Sir Tristram received a shield from Morgan le Fay

So as Sir Dinadan rode by a spring he found a lady grieving greatly.

"What is wrong with you?" said Sir Dinadan.

"Sir knight," said the lady, "I am the most wretched lady in the world. For within these five days a knight called Sir Breuse Saunce Pité came here, and he killed my own brother, and ever since he has kept me at his own will, and of all men in the world I hate him most. And so I beg you, by your knighthood, to avenge me, for he will not be long, but will be here at once."

"Let him come," said Sir Dinadan, "and for the honour of all women I will do my part."

With this Sir Breuse came, and when he saw a knight with his lady he was mad with rage. And then he said, "Sir knight, defend yourself against me!"

So they crashed together like thunder, and each struck the other exceedingly hard, but Sir Dinadan put a grievous wound through his shoulder, and before Sir Dinadan could even turn, Sir Breuse was gone and fled. Then the lady begged him to bring her to a castle nearby, only four miles from there; and so Sir Dinadan brought her there, and she was made welcome, for the lord of that castle was her uncle. And so Sir Dinadan rode on his way upon his adventure.

Now we turn this tale to Sir Tristram, who by chance came to a castle to ask for lodging, and Queen Morgan le Fay was in it. And so when Sir Tristram was let into that castle he had a good welcome all that night. And in the morning, when he wanted to leave, the queen said, "You may be sure you shall not leave so easily, for you are here as a prisoner."

"Jesus forbid!" said Sir Tristram. "For I was a prisoner only lately."

"Fair knight," said the queen, "you shall stay with me until I know who you are and where you come from."

And always the queen would seat Sir Tristram on one side of her, and her lover on the other side. And Queen Morgan kept gazing at Sir Tristram, and at that the knight grew jealous, and had a mind to run at Sir Tristram suddenly with a sword, but he held back for shame. Then the queen said to Sir Tristram, "Tell me your name, and I will let you leave when you wish."

"On that condition I will tell you: my name is Sir Tristram de Liones."

"Ah," said Morgan le Fay, "if I had known that, you would not have left as soon as you shall. But since I have made a promise I will keep it, provided that you will promise me to carry a shield that I shall give you to the castle of the Hard Rock, where King Arthur has had a great tournament proclaimed. And I beg you that you will be there, and do as many deeds of arms for me as you can. For at the Castle of Maidens, Sir Tristram, you did deeds of arms as marvellous as any I ever heard of a knight doing."

"Madam," said Sir Tristram, "let me see the shield that I am to carry."

Then the shield was brought out, and its field was gold, with a king and a queen painted on it, and a knight standing above them, one foot on the king's head and the other on the queen's.

"Madam," said Sir Tristram, "this is a fine shield and a mighty one; but what does it mean, this king and this queen, and the knight standing on both their heads?"

"I will tell you," said Morgan le Fay. "It means King Arthur and Queen Guinevere, and a knight who holds them both in bondage and in servitude."

"Who is that knight?" said Sir Tristram.

"That you shall not know at this time," said the queen.

But as the French book says, Queen Morgan loved Sir Lancelot best, and always desired him, and he would never love her nor do anything at her request; and so she kept many knights about her to take him by force. And because she believed that Sir Lancelot loved Queen Guinevere as his lady, and she him in return, Queen Morgan le Fay had that shield made to put Sir Lancelot to shame, so that King Arthur might come to understand the love between them. Then Sir Tristram took that shield and promised her to carry it at the tournament at the Castle of the Hard Rock. But Sir Tristram did not know that the shield was made against Sir Lancelot; but afterwards he knew it.

Chapter 42: How Sir Tristram took the shield with him, and how he slew Morgan le Fay's lover

So then Sir Tristram took his leave of the queen, and took the shield with him. Then came the knight who kept Queen Morgan le Fay as his lover (his name was Sir Hemison), and he made himself ready to follow Sir Tristram.

"Fair friend," said Morgan, "don't ride after that knight, for you will win no honour from him."

"Shame on him, the coward," said Sir Hemison, "for I never knew a good knight to come out of Cornwall, except Sir Tristram de Liones."

"And what if this is he?" she said.

"No, no," he said, "he is with Isolde the Fair, and this is only some foolish knight."

"Alas, my fair friend, you will find him the best knight you ever met, for I know him better than you do."

"For your sake," said Sir Hemison, "I will kill him."

"Ah, fair friend," said the queen, "I am sorry that you will follow that knight, for I am badly afraid for your coming back."

With this the knight rode on his way mad with rage, and he rode after Sir Tristram as fast as if he were being chased by knights. When Sir Tristram heard a knight coming after him so fast, he turned about, and saw a knight coming at him. And when he came near Sir Tristram he cried aloud, "Sir knight, defend yourself against me!"

Then they rushed together as if it were thunder, and Sir Hemison broke his spear on Sir Tristram, but his armour was so good that he could not hurt him. And Sir Tristram struck him harder, and ran him through the body, and he fell over his horse's crupper. Then Sir Tristram turned to do more with his sword, but he saw so much blood running from him that it seemed to him he was likely to die. And so he left him, and came to a fine manor belonging to an old knight, and there Sir Tristram lodged.

Chapter 43: How Morgan le Fay buried her lover, and how Sir Tristram praised Sir Lancelot and his family

Now we stop speaking of Sir Tristram, and speak of the knight who was wounded to the death. Then his servant dismounted, and took off his helmet, and then he asked his lord whether there was any life left in him.

"There is life in me," said the knight, "but it is very little. And so, when you have helped me up, jump up behind me, and hold me tight so that I don't fall, and bring me to Queen Morgan le Fay. For the deep draughts of death are drawing to my heart, so that I cannot live, and I would gladly speak with her before I die; for otherwise my soul will be in great peril if I die."

So at once, with great pain, his servant brought him to the castle, and there Sir Hemison fell down dead. When Morgan le Fay saw him dead she grieved beyond all reason; and then she had him stripped to his shirt, and so she had him put into a tomb. And around the tomb she had these words written: "Here lies Sir Hemison, slain by the hands of Sir Tristram de Liones."

Now we turn to Sir Tristram, who asked the knight his host whether he had seen any knights-errant lately.

"Sir," he said, "last night Ector de Maris lodged here with me, and a damsel with him, and that damsel told me that he was one of the best knights in the world."

"That is not so," said Sir Tristram, "for I know four better knights of his own blood. And the first is Sir Lancelot du Lake, call him the best knight; and Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Bleoberis, Sir Blamore de Ganis, and Sir Gaheris."

"No," said his host, "Sir Gawain is a better knight than he."

"That is not so," said Sir Tristram, "for I have met them both, and I found Sir Gaheris the better knight. And Sir Lamorak I call as good as any of them, except Sir Lancelot."

"Why don't you name Sir Tristram?" said his host. "For I count him as good as any of them."

"I don't know Sir Tristram," said Tristram.

So they talked and joked as long as they cared to, and then went to bed. And in the morning Sir Tristram took his leave of his host and left, and rode toward the Roche Dure, the Hard Rock, and Sir Tristram had no adventure but that one. And so he did not rest until he came to the castle, where he saw five hundred tents.

Chapter 44: How Sir Tristram carried the shield that Morgan le Fay had given him at a tournament

Then the King of Scots and the King of Ireland held the field against King Arthur's knights, and a great fight began there. Then Sir Tristram came in and did marvellous deeds of arms, for there he struck down many knights. And all the while he was in front of King Arthur with that shield. And when King Arthur saw that shield he wondered greatly for what purpose it had been made; but Queen Guinevere guessed it for what it was, and so she was downcast. Now there was a damsel of Queen Morgan's in a chamber near King Arthur, and when she heard King Arthur speak of that shield, she spoke out openly to King Arthur.

"Sir king, you may be sure this shield was made for you, to warn you of your shame and dishonour, and of what concerns you and your queen."

And then at once that damsel stole away secretly, so that no one knew what had become of her. Then King Arthur was grave and angry, and asked where that damsel had come from. There was not one who knew her, or knew what had become of her. Then Queen Guinevere called Sir Ector de Maris to her, and there she made her complaint to him, and said, "I know well this shield was made by Morgan le Fay to insult me and Sir Lancelot, and so I am badly afraid that I may be destroyed."

And all the while the king watched Sir Tristram, who did such marvellous deeds of arms that he wondered hard what knight he could be, and he knew well it was not Sir Lancelot. And he had been told that Sir Tristram was in Brittany with Isolde of the White Hands; for he judged that if he had been in the realm of Logres, Sir Lancelot or some of his companions who were on the quest for Sir Tristram would have found him before that time. So King Arthur wondered what knight he could be. And all the while Sir Arthur's eye was on that shield. The queen saw all that, and it made her badly afraid.

Then all the while Sir Tristram struck down knights, a wonder to see, on the right hand and on the left, so that scarcely any knight could stand against him. And the King of Scots and the King of Ireland began to withdraw. When Arthur saw that, he thought that the knight with the strange shield should not escape him. Then he called Sir Uwain le Blanchemains to him, and told him to arm himself and make ready. So at once King Arthur and Sir Uwain squared up to Sir Tristram, and demanded that he tell them where he had got that shield.

"Sir," he said, "I had it from Queen Morgan le Fay, King Arthur's sister."

So here ends the story of this book, for it is the first book of Sir Tristram de Liones.

Here follows the second book of Sir Tristram.

Book Ten: Sir Tristram, and Other Marvellous Adventures

Chapter 1: How Sir Tristram jousted with King Arthur and struck him down, because he would not tell him why he carried that shield

"And if it turns out that you can describe what you carry," said King Arthur, "then you are worthy to carry the arms."

"As for that," said Sir Tristram, "I will answer you. This shield was given to me, not asked for, by Queen Morgan le Fay. And as for me, I cannot describe these arms, for that is no part of my charge, and yet I trust in God to carry them with honour."

"Truly," said King Arthur, "you ought not to carry any arms unless you knew what you carry. But I beg you, tell me your name."

"To what end?" said Sir Tristram.

"Because I want to know," said Arthur.

"Sir, you shall not know at this time."

"Then you and I shall fight together," said King Arthur.

"Why," said Sir Tristram, "will you fight with me unless I tell you my name? And that is little needed of you, if you were a man of honour, for you have seen me this day at great labour, and so you are an ill-bred knight to ask for a fight with me, considering how hard I have laboured. All the same I will not fail you, and have no doubt that I am not afraid of you. Though you think you have me at a great advantage, yet I shall hold out against you well enough."

And with that King Arthur set his shield and lowered his spear, and Sir Tristram did the same against him, and they came together so eagerly. And there King Arthur broke his spear all to pieces on Sir Tristram's shield. But Sir Tristram hit Arthur in return, so that horse and man fell to the earth. And there King Arthur was wounded in the left side, a great wound and a dangerous one.

Then when Sir Uwain saw his lord Arthur lying on the ground badly wounded, he was exceedingly downcast. And then he set his shield and lowered his spear, and called out loud to Sir Tristram, and said, "Knight, defend yourself."

So they came together like thunder, and Sir Uwain shattered his spear all to pieces on Sir Tristram's shield, and Sir Tristram struck him harder and more heavily, with such force that he carried him clean out of his saddle to the earth. With that Sir Tristram turned about and said, "Fair knights, I had no need to joust with you, for I have had enough to do this day."

Then Arthur got up and went to Sir Uwain, and said to Sir Tristram, "We have got what we deserved, for out of our arrogance we demanded a fight with you, and yet we did not know your name."

"Nevertheless, by the Holy Cross," said Sir Uwain, "in my judgement he is as strong a knight as any now living."

Then Sir Tristram left, and in every place he asked and enquired after Sir Lancelot, but nowhere could he hear of him, whether he was dead or alive; and so Sir Tristram grieved greatly and sorrowed. So Sir Tristram rode by a forest, and then he noticed a fair tower beside a marsh on the one side, and on the other side a fair meadow. And there he saw ten knights fighting together. And the nearer he came, the more he saw that there was only one knight fighting against nine knights, and that one did so marvellously that Sir Tristram wondered greatly that one knight could ever do such great deeds of arms. And then within a little while he had killed half their horses and unhorsed them, and their horses ran loose in the fields and the forest. Then Sir Tristram had such great pity for that one knight who endured so much pain, and all the while he thought, by his shield, that it must be Sir Palomides. And so he rode up to the knights and called out to them, and told them to stop their fighting, for they did themselves great shame, so many knights fighting with one.

Then the master of those knights answered (his name was Breuse Saunce Pité, who was at that time the most dangerous knight living), and said this: "Sir knight, what business do you have meddling with us? And so, if you are wise, go on your way as you came, for this knight shall not escape us."

"That would be a pity," said Sir Tristram, "that so good a knight as he is should be killed so cowardly. And so I warn you, I will help him with all my might."

Chapter 2: How Sir Tristram saved Sir Palomides' life, and how they promised to fight each other within two weeks

So Sir Tristram got down off his horse, because they were on foot, so that they should not kill his horse, and then set his shield, with his sword in his hand, and he struck out on the right hand and on the left exceedingly hard, so that at nearly every stroke he struck down a knight. And when they saw his strokes they all fled with Breuse Saunce Pité to the tower, and Sir Tristram followed hard after them with his sword in his hand, but they escaped into the tower, and shut Sir Tristram outside the gate. And when Sir Tristram saw this he went back to Sir Palomides, and found him sitting under a tree, badly wounded.

"Ah, fair knight," said Sir Tristram, "well met."

"Many thanks," said Sir Palomides, "for your great goodness, for you have rescued my life and saved me from my death."

"What is your name?" said Sir Tristram.

He said, "My name is Sir Palomides."

"O Jesus," said Sir Tristram, "you've had a fine piece of luck from me today, that I should rescue you, and you're the man in the world I hate most. But now get ready, for I will fight you."

"What is your name?" said Sir Palomides.

"My name is Sir Tristram, your mortal enemy."

"That may be so," said Sir Palomides, "but you have done too much for me this day for me to fight with you. For since you have saved my life, it will be no honour to you to fight me, for you are fresh and I am badly wounded. And so, if you must fight me, name me a day, and then I shall meet you without fail."

"You speak well," said Sir Tristram. "Now I name the place: meet me in the meadow by the river of Camelot, where Merlin set up the stone monument."

So they were agreed.

Then Sir Tristram asked Sir Palomides why the ten knights were fighting him.

"For this reason," said Sir Palomides. "As I rode on my adventures in a forest near here, I saw a dead knight lying there, and a lady weeping beside him. And when I saw her grieving so, I asked her who had killed her lord. 'Sir,' she said, 'the falsest knight in the world now living, and he is the vilest wretch that anyone ever heard tell of, and his name is Sir Breuse Saunce Pité.' Then out of pity I had the damsel mount her palfrey, and I promised to be her protection, and to help her bury her lord. And so, suddenly, as I came riding by this tower, out came Sir Breuse Saunce Pité, and suddenly he struck me from my horse. And then, before I could get back to my horse, this Sir Breuse killed the damsel. And so I took my horse again, and I was badly ashamed, and so the fight between us began. And this is the reason why we were fighting."

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "now I understand how your fight came about. But in any case remember the promise you have made me, to fight me two weeks from today."

"I shall not fail you," said Sir Palomides.

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "for now I will not leave you until you are out of danger from your enemies."

So they mounted their horses and rode together into that forest, and there they found a fair spring, with clear water bubbling up.

"Fair sir," said Sir Tristram, "I have a mind to drink of that water."

And then they got down off their horses. And then they noticed, close by them, a great horse tied to a tree, and it kept neighing. And then they noticed a fair knight in armour under a tree, lacking no piece of his armour, except that his helmet lay under his head.

"By the good Lord," said Sir Tristram, "there lies a fine-looking knight. What is best to do?"

"Wake him," said Sir Palomides.

So Sir Tristram woke him with the butt of his spear. And the knight got up in haste and put his helmet on his head, and took a great spear in his hand; and without any more words he charged at Sir Tristram, and struck him clean out of his saddle to the earth, and hurt him in the left side, so that Sir Tristram lay in great danger. Then he galloped on further, and took his distance for the charge, and came crashing down on Sir Palomides, and there he struck him partly through the body, so that he fell from his horse to the earth. And then this strange knight left them there, and went his way through the forest. With this Sir Palomides and Sir Tristram, who were on foot, got their horses back, and each asked the other's advice about what was best to do.

"By my head," said Sir Tristram, "I will follow this strong knight who has shamed us like this."

"Well," said Sir Palomides, "and I will rest near here with a friend of mine."

"Take care," said Sir Tristram to Palomides, "that you don't fail on the day you have set to fight me. For, as I judge it, you will not keep your day, for I am much stronger than you."

"As for that," said Sir Palomides, "let it be as it may, for I am not afraid of you. If I am not sick or a prisoner, I will not fail you. But I have more reason to fear that you will not meet me, for you are riding after that strong knight there. And if you meet him, it will be a hard chance if you ever escape his hands."

Right then Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides parted, and each went his separate way.

Chapter 3: How Sir Tristram went looking for a strong knight who had struck him down, along with many other knights of the Round Table

And so Sir Tristram rode a long way after this strong knight. And at last he saw a lady lying across a dead knight.

"Fair lady," said Sir Tristram, "who has killed your lord?"

"Sir," she said, "a knight came riding here, as my lord and I were resting, and asked him where he was from, and my lord said from Arthur's court. 'Then,' said the strong knight, 'I will joust with you, for I hate all those who are of Arthur's court.' And my lord who lies here dead mounted his horse, and the strong knight and my lord met together, and there he ran my lord clean through with his spear. And so he has brought me into great woe and loss."

"I am sorry for your great grief," said Sir Tristram. "If it please you, tell me your husband's name."

"Sir," she said, "his name was Galardoun, and he would have proved a good knight."

So Sir Tristram left that sorrowful lady, and had very poor lodging. Then on the third day Sir Tristram met Sir Gawain and Sir Bleoberis in a forest, at a lodge, and both of them were badly wounded. Then Sir Tristram asked Sir Gawain and Sir Bleoberis whether they had met such a knight, with such a device, with a covered shield.

"Fair sir," said these knights, "such a knight met us, to our great harm. And first he struck down my companion, Sir Bleoberis, and badly wounded him, because he told me I should not fight with him, since he was too strong for me. That strong knight took his words with scorn, and said he said it in mockery. And then they rode at each other, and so he hurt my companion. And when he had done that, I could not for shame do anything but joust with him. And at the first course he struck me down, and my horse, to the earth. And there he nearly killed me, and he took his horse away from us and left. And it was an evil hour when we met him."

"Fair knights," said Sir Tristram, "he met me the same way, and another knight called Palomides, and he struck us both down with one spear, and hurt us very badly."

"On my faith," said Sir Gawain, "if you take my advice you will let him pass and look for him no further; for at the next feast of the Round Table, on pain of my head, you shall find him there."

"On my faith," said Sir Tristram, "I shall never rest until I find him."

And then Sir Gawain asked him his name. Then he said, "My name is Sir Tristram."

And so each told the other their names, and then Sir Tristram left and rode on his way.

And by chance, in a meadow, Sir Tristram met Sir Kay the Seneschal and Sir Dinadan.

"What news with you," said Sir Tristram, "with you knights?"

"Not good," said these knights.

"Why so?" said Sir Tristram. "Please tell me, for I am riding in search of a knight."

"What device does he carry?" said Sir Kay.

"He carries," said Sir Tristram, "a covered shield, wrapped close in cloth."

"By my head," said Sir Kay, "that is the same knight who met us. For last night we were lodged in a widow's house, and that knight was lodged there too; and when he learned that we were of Arthur's court, he spoke great insults against the king, and especially against Queen Guinevere, and so in the morning a fight was pledged with him for that reason. And at the first encounter," said Sir Kay, "he struck me down from my horse and hurt me exceedingly badly. And when my companion, Sir Dinadan, saw me struck down and hurt, he would not avenge me, but ran away from me. And so he left."

And then Sir Tristram asked them their names, and so each told the other their names. And so Sir Tristram left Sir Kay and Sir Dinadan, and so he passed through a great forest into a plain, until he came upon a priory, and there he rested with a good man six days.

Chapter 4: How Sir Tristram struck down Sir Sagramore le Desirous and Sir Dodinas le Savage

And then he sent his man, who was called Gouvernail, and ordered him to go to a city nearby to fetch him new armour; for it had been a long time since Sir Tristram had been re-equipped, and his armour was battered and broken. And when Gouvernail, his servant, had come back with his gear, he took his leave of the widow, and mounted his horse, and rode on his way early in the morning. And by sudden chance Sir Tristram met Sir Sagramore le Desirous and Sir Dodinas le Savage. And these two knights met Sir Tristram and questioned him, and asked him if he would joust with them.

"Fair knights," said Sir Tristram, "I would joust with you with a good will, but I have promised, on a day set close at hand, to fight a strong knight. And so I am unwilling to fight with you, for if it were my misfortune to be hurt here, I should not be able to fight the fight I promised."

"As for that," said Sagramore, "whether you like it or not, you shall joust with us before you get past us."

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "if you force me to it, I must do what I can."

And then they set their shields, and came running together with great anger. But through Sir Tristram's great strength he struck Sir Sagramore from his horse. Then he spurred his horse on further, and said to Sir Dodinas, "Knight, get ready."

And so by sheer strength Sir Tristram struck Dodinas from his horse. And when he saw them lying on the earth, he took up his bridle and rode on his way, and his man Gouvernail with him.

As soon as Sir Tristram had gone by, Sir Sagramore and Sir Dodinas got their horses back, and mounted nimbly and followed after Sir Tristram. And when Sir Tristram saw them coming so fast after him, he turned his horse back to them, and asked them what they wanted.

"It is not long since I struck you to the earth at your own request and desire. I would have ridden past you, but you would not allow me, and now it seems to me you want to fight me some more."

"That is the truth," said Sir Sagramore and Sir Dodinas, "for we mean to be avenged for the insult you have done us."

"Fair knights," said Sir Tristram, "you have little need of that, for you brought on yourselves all that I did to you. And so I ask you, by your knighthood, to leave me alone for now. For I am sure that if I fight with you I shall not escape without great wounds, and as I suppose, you will not come away without your share either. And this is the reason why I am so unwilling to fight with you: for I must fight within these three days with a good knight, as valiant as any now living, and if I am hurt I shall not be able to fight him."

"What knight is that," said Sir Sagramore, "that you are to fight with?"

"Sirs," he said, "it is a good knight called Sir Palomides."

"By my head," said Sir Sagramore and Sir Dodinas, "you have reason to fear him, for you will find him an exceedingly good knight, and a valiant one. And because you are to fight him, we will spare you for now; otherwise you would not get away from us easily. But, fair knight," said Sir Sagramore, "tell us your name."

"Sir," he said, "my name is Sir Tristram de Liones."

"Ah," said Sagramore and Sir Dodinas, "well met, for we have heard of your great renown."

And then each took leave of the other, and they went on their way.

Chapter 5: How Sir Tristram met Sir Lancelot at the stone monument, and how they fought each other without knowing who the other was

Then Sir Tristram left and rode straight to Camelot, to the stone monument that Merlin had made before, where Sir Lanceor, the king's son of Ireland, was killed by the hands of Balin. And in that same place the fair lady Colombe was killed, who was Sir Lanceor's love; for after he was dead she took his sword and thrust it through her body. And by Merlin's craft this knight Lanceor and his lady Colombe were buried under one stone. And at that time Merlin prophesied that in that same place two of the best knights that ever were in Arthur's days, and the best lovers, would fight. So when Sir Tristram came to the tomb where Lanceor and his lady were buried, he looked about him for Sir Palomides. Then he noticed a handsome knight coming riding towards him, all in white, with a covered shield. When he came near Sir Tristram he called out loud, "You are welcome, sir knight, and well and truly have you kept your promise."

And then they set their shields and lowered their spears, and came together with all the strength of their horses; and they met so fiercely that both horses and knights fell to the earth, and as fast as they could they got clear of their horses, and put their shields before them; and they struck at each other with bright swords, like men of great strength, and each wounded the other wonderfully badly, so that the blood ran out on the grass. And so they fought for the space of four hours, and neither would speak one word to the other, and they had hewn many pieces off each other's armour.

"O Lord Jesus," said Gouvernail, "I marvel greatly at the strokes my master has given your master."

"By my head," said Sir Lancelot's servant, "your master has not given so many but that he has taken as many or more."

"O Jesus," said Gouvernail, "it is too much for Sir Palomides or Sir Lancelot to endure, and yet it would be a pity if either of these good knights should spill the other's blood."

So they both stood and wept, and grieved greatly when they saw the bright swords covered over with the blood of their bodies.

Then at last Sir Lancelot spoke and said, "Knight, you fight wonderfully well, as well as I ever saw a knight fight. So, if it please you, tell me your name."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I am unwilling to tell any man my name."

"Truly," said Sir Lancelot, "if I were asked, I was never unwilling to tell my name."

"That is well said," said Sir Tristram. "Then I ask you to tell me your name."

"Fair knight," he said, "my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"Alas," said Sir Tristram, "what have I done! For you are the man in the world that I love best."

"Fair knight," said Sir Lancelot, "tell me your name."

"Truly," he said, "my name is Sir Tristram de Liones."

"O Jesus," said Sir Lancelot, "what a chance has come to me!"

And with that Sir Lancelot knelt down and surrendered his sword to him. And with that Sir Tristram knelt down and surrendered his sword to him. And so each gave the other the prize. And then they both went straight to the stone, and sat down on it, and took off their helmets to cool themselves, and each kissed the other a hundred times. And then soon after they took off their helmets and rode to Camelot. And there they met Sir Gawain and Sir Gaheris, who had promised Arthur never to come back to the court until they had brought Sir Tristram with them.

Chapter 6: How Sir Lancelot brought Sir Tristram to the court, and of the great joy the king and the others showed at Sir Tristram's coming

"Turn back," said Sir Lancelot, "for your quest is done, for I have met Sir Tristram. Look, here he is in person!"

Then Sir Gawain was glad, and said to Sir Tristram, "You are welcome, for now you have greatly eased me of my labour. For what reason," said Sir Gawain, "did you come to this court?"

"Fair sir," said Sir Tristram, "I came into this country because of Sir Palomides. For he and I had set this day to fight together at the stone monument, and I wonder that I hear nothing of him. And so by chance my lord Sir Lancelot and I met."

With this King Arthur came, and when he learned that Sir Tristram was there, he ran to him and took him by the hand and said, "Sir Tristram, you are as welcome as any knight who ever came to this court."

And when the king had heard how Sir Lancelot and he had fought, and how each had wounded the other wonderfully badly, the king grieved greatly. Then Sir Tristram told the king how he had come there to fight with Sir Palomides. And then he told the king how he had rescued him from the nine knights and Breuse Saunce Pité, "and how I found a knight lying by a spring, and that knight struck down Sir Palomides and me, but his shield was covered with a cloth. So Sir Palomides left me, and I followed after that knight; and in many places I found where he had killed knights, and outjousted many."

"By my head," said Sir Gawain, "that same knight struck me down, and Sir Bleoberis, and hurt us both badly, the one with the covered shield."

"Ah," said Sir Kay, "that knight struck me down and hurt me exceedingly badly, and I would gladly have known who he was, but I could not."

"Jesus have mercy," said Arthur, "what knight was that with the covered shield?"

"I don't know," said Sir Tristram; and so they all said.

"Now," said King Arthur, "then I know, for it is Sir Lancelot."

Then they all looked at Sir Lancelot and said, "You have tricked us with your covered shield."

"It is not the first time," said Arthur, "that he has done so."

"My lord," said Sir Lancelot, "truly, believe me, I was the same knight who carried the covered shield; and because I did not want it known that I was of your court, I spoke no good of your house."

"That is the truth," said Sir Gawain, Sir Kay and Sir Bleoberis.

Then King Arthur took Sir Tristram by the hand and went to the Round Table. Then Queen Guinevere came, and many ladies with her, and all the ladies said with one voice, "Welcome, Sir Tristram!"

"Welcome," said the damsels.

"Welcome," said the knights.

"Welcome," said Arthur, "as one of the best knights, and the noblest in the world, and the man of most honour. For in every kind of hunting you carry off the prize, and of all the measures of the hunting horn you are the first maker, and of all the terms of hunting and hawking you are the founder, and of all instruments of music you are the best. And so, noble knight," said Arthur, "you are welcome to this court. And also, I ask you," said Arthur, "grant me a favour."

"It shall be at your command," said Tristram.

"Well," said Arthur, "what I want of you is that you stay in my court."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I am unwilling to do that, for I have business in many countries."

"Not so," said Arthur. "You have promised it to me; you cannot say no."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I will do as you wish."

Then Arthur went round the seats of the Round Table, and looked at every seat that stood empty for lack of a knight. And then the king saw letters in the seat of Marhaus that said, "This is the seat of the noble knight Sir Tristram." And then Arthur made Sir Tristram a knight of the Round Table, with as much splendour and as great a feast as could be imagined. For Sir Marhaus had been killed earlier by the hands of Sir Tristram on an island; and that was well known at that time in Arthur's court, for this Marhaus was a worthy knight. And Sir Tristram and he fought because of the evil deeds that Marhaus did to the country of Cornwall. And they fought so long, circling and sidestepping, until they fell bleeding to the earth; for they were so badly wounded that they could not stand for bleeding. And Sir Tristram by good fortune recovered, and Sir Marhaus died from the stroke on the head.

So now we leave Sir Tristram and speak of King Mark.

Chapter 7: How King Mark, out of spite against Sir Tristram, came into England with two knights, and how he killed one of the knights

Then King Mark was bitterly resentful of Sir Tristram's renown, and so he drove him out of Cornwall. Yet he was King Mark's nephew; but Mark had great suspicion of Sir Tristram because of his queen, Isolde the Fair, for it seemed to him that there was too much love between the two of them. So when Sir Tristram had left Cornwall for England, King Mark heard of the great feats of prowess that Sir Tristram did there, and it grieved him badly. So he sent men of his own to spy out what deeds he did. And the queen secretly sent spies of her own to learn what deeds he had done, for there was great love between the two of them. So when the messengers had come home, they told the truth as they had heard it, that he surpassed all other knights, unless it was Sir Lancelot. Then King Mark was very downcast at this news, and Isolde the Fair was just as glad. Then, in great spite, he took with him two good knights and two squires, and disguised himself, and set off into England with the intention of killing Sir Tristram. And one of these two knights was called Bersules, and the other knight was called Amant. So as they rode, King Mark asked a knight he met where he would find King Arthur.

He said, "At Camelot."

He also asked that knight about Sir Tristram, whether he had heard of him at King Arthur's court.

"Believe me," said that knight, "you will find Sir Tristram there, a man of as great honour as any now living. For by his prowess he won the tournament of the Castle of Maidens, which stands by the Hard Rock. And since then he has beaten thirty knights with his own hands, men of great honour. And the last fight he ever fought, he fought with Sir Lancelot, and that was a marvellous fight. And it was not by force that Sir Lancelot brought Sir Tristram to the court, and King Arthur rejoiced over him exceedingly, and so made him a knight of the Round Table; and his seat was the one that had been the good knight Sir Marhaus's."

Then King Mark was exceedingly sorry when he heard of the honour done to Sir Tristram; and so they parted.

Then King Mark said to his two knights, "Now I will tell you my plan. You are the men I trust most of anyone alive, and I want you to know that my coming here is for this purpose: to destroy Sir Tristram by trickery or by treason. And it will be hard if he ever escapes our hands."

"Alas," said Sir Bersules, "what do you mean? For you are set on such a course that you are shamefully minded. For Sir Tristram is the most honourable knight we know living, and so I warn you plainly, I will never agree to put him to death. And so I give up my service, and leave you."

When King Mark heard him say so, he suddenly drew his sword and said, "Ah, traitor!" and struck Sir Bersules on the head, so that the sword went down to his teeth.

When Amant the knight saw him do that base deed, he and the squires said it was foully done, and wickedly. "And so we'll serve you no longer. And believe me, we will accuse you of treason before Arthur."

Then King Mark was furiously angry and would have killed Amant; but he and the two squires held together, and cared nothing for his malice. When King Mark saw he could not be avenged on them, he said this to the knight Amant: "Understand this: if you accuse me of treason, I shall defend myself against it before King Arthur. But I demand of you that you do not tell my name, that I am King Mark, whatever becomes of me."

"As for that," said Sir Amant, "I will not give away your name."

And so they parted, and Amant and his companions took the body of Bersules and buried it.

Chapter 8: How King Mark came to a spring where he found Sir Lamorak lamenting for love of King Lot's wife

Then King Mark rode until he came to a spring, and there he rested, and was in doubt whether he would ride to Arthur's court or not, or go back again to his own country. And as he was resting like this by that spring, a well-armed knight on horseback came by him; and he got down, and tied his horse to a tree, and sat down at the edge of the spring; and there he languished and grieved greatly, and made the most sorrowful lament of love that anyone ever heard; and all this while he did not notice King Mark. And this was a great part of his lament. He cried and wept, saying, "O fair Queen of Orkney, King Lot's wife, and mother of Sir Gawain and of Sir Gaheris, and mother of many others, for love of you I am in great pain."

Then King Mark got up and went near him and said, "Fair knight, you have made a pitiful lament."

"Truly," said the knight, "it is a hundred times more pitiful than my heart can put into words."

"I ask you," said King Mark, "tell me your name."

"Sir," he said, "as for my name, I will not hide it from any knight who carries a shield, and my name is Sir Lamorak de Galis."

But when Sir Lamorak heard King Mark speak, he knew well by his speech that he was a Cornish knight.
