"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "I can tell by your tongue that you are from Cornwall, where there lives the most shameful king now living, for he is a great enemy to all good knights. And that is well proved, for he has driven out of that country Sir Tristram, who is the most honourable knight now living, and all knights speak of his honour; and out of jealousy over his queen he has driven him out of his country. It is a pity," said Sir Lamorak, "that any such false coward of a knight as King Mark should ever be matched with so fair and good a lady as Isolde the Fair, for all the world speaks shame of him, and of her all the honour that any queen may have."

"I have no part in this matter," said King Mark, "and I will not speak of it."

"Well said," said Sir Lamorak.

"Sir," said King Mark, "can you tell me any news?"

"I can tell you," said Sir Lamorak, "that there is to be a great tournament soon beside Camelot, at the Castle of Jagent; and the King with the Hundred Knights and the King of Ireland, as I believe, are holding that tournament."

Then a knight came by who was called Sir Dinadan, and greeted them both. And when he learned that King Mark was a knight of Cornwall, he abused him on King Mark's account a thousand times worse than Sir Lamorak had. Then he offered to joust with King Mark. And Mark was very unwilling to do it, but Sir Dinadan egged him on so that he jousted with Sir Lamorak. And Sir Lamorak struck King Mark so hard that he carried him on the end of his spear over his horse's tail. And then King Mark got up again, and followed after Sir Lamorak. But Sir Dinadan would not joust with Sir Lamorak, but he told King Mark that Sir Lamorak was Sir Kay the Seneschal.

"That is not so," said King Mark, "for he is much bigger than Sir Kay."

And so he followed and overtook him, and told him to wait.

"What do you want?" said Sir Lamorak.

"Sir," he said, "I will fight with a sword, for you have shamed me with a spear."

And with that they rushed together with swords, and Sir Lamorak bore with him and held back from him. And King Mark was exceedingly hasty, and struck thick and fast. Sir Lamorak saw he would not stop, and grew somewhat angry, and doubled his strokes, for he was one of the noblest knights in the world; and he beat him so on the helmet that his head hung nearly down on the saddlebow. When Sir Lamorak saw him in such a state, he said, "Sir knight, how are you? It seems to me you have nearly had your fill of fighting. It would be a pity to do you any more harm, for you are only an ordinary knight. And so I give you leave to go where you like."

"Many thanks," said King Mark, "for you and I are no match."

Then Sir Dinadan mocked King Mark and said, "You're not able to match a good knight."

"As for that," said King Mark, "the first time I jousted with this knight, you refused him."

"Do you think that's a shame to me?" said Sir Dinadan. "No, sir. There is always honour for a knight in refusing what he cannot win, and so you would have won much more honour by refusing him as I did. For I warn you plainly, he could beat five like you and me. For you knights of Cornwall are no men of honour, as other knights are. And because you are no men of honour, you hate all men of honour; for there was never bred in your country such a knight as Sir Tristram."

Chapter 9: How King Mark, Sir Lamorak, and Sir Dinadan came to a castle, and how King Mark was recognised there

Then they all rode on together, King Mark, Sir Lamorak and Sir Dinadan, until they came to a bridge, and at the end of it stood a fair tower. Then they saw a well-armed knight on horseback, brandishing a spear, calling out and offering himself to joust.

"Now," said Sir Dinadan to King Mark, "there are two brothers here, one called Alein and the other called Trian, who will joust with anyone who comes through this pass. Now go and offer yourself," said Dinadan to King Mark, "for you're always being laid flat on the ground anyway."

Then King Mark was ashamed, and with that he set his spear in rest and crashed into Sir Trian, and both broke their spears all to pieces, and rode straight past each other. Then Sir Trian sent King Mark another spear to joust again; but on no account would he joust any more. Then all three knights came to the castle, and asked the lord of the castle for lodging.

"You are very welcome," said the knights of the castle, "for the love of the lord of this castle, who is called Sir Tor le Fise Aries."

And then they came into a fair court, well kept, and they had an exceedingly good welcome, until the lieutenant of this castle, who was called Berluse, recognised King Mark of Cornwall.

Then Berluse said, "Sir knight, I know you better than you think, for you are King Mark, who killed my father before my own eyes; and you would have killed me if I had not escaped into a wood. But believe me, for the love of my lord of this castle I will neither hurt you nor harm you, nor anyone of your company. But believe me, when you have left this lodging I shall hurt you if I can, for you killed my father treacherously. But first, for the love of my lord Sir Tor, and for the love of Sir Lamorak, the honourable knight who is lodged here, you shall have no bad lodging; for it is a pity that you should ever be in the company of good knights. For you are the basest knight or king now known alive, for you are a destroyer of good knights, and all that you do is nothing but treason."

Chapter 10: How Sir Berluse met King Mark, and how Sir Dinadan took his side

Then King Mark was badly ashamed, and said little in reply. But when Sir Lamorak and Sir Dinadan knew that he was King Mark, they were sorry to be in his company. So after supper they went to their lodging. So in the morning they rose early, and King Mark and Sir Dinadan rode together; and three miles from their lodging three knights met them, and Sir Berluse was one, and the other two were his cousins. Sir Berluse saw King Mark, and then he shouted aloud, "Traitor, defend yourself, for know this: I am Berluse!"

"Sir knight," said Sir Dinadan, "I advise you to leave off for now, for he is riding to King Arthur; and because I have promised to escort him to my lord King Arthur, I have no choice but to take his side. All the same, I do not love his character, and I would gladly be rid of him."

"Well, Dinadan," said Sir Berluse, "I am sorry that you will take his side, but now do your best."

And then he crashed into King Mark, and struck him so hard on the shield that he carried him clean out of his saddle to the ground. Sir Dinadan saw that, and he set his spear in rest, and ran at one of Berluse's companions, and struck him down out of his saddle. Then Dinadan turned his horse, and struck the third knight to the ground in the same way, for Sir Dinadan was a good knight on horseback; and there a great battle began, for Berluse and his companions held together strongly on foot. And so, through the great strength of Sir Dinadan, King Mark got Berluse to the ground, and his two companions fled; and if it had not been for Sir Dinadan, King Mark would have killed him. And so Sir Dinadan saved his life, for King Mark was nothing but a murderer. And then they took their horses and left, and left Sir Berluse there badly wounded.

Then King Mark and Sir Dinadan rode on some four English leagues, until they came to a bridge where a knight on horseback waited, armed and ready to joust.

"Look," said Sir Dinadan to King Mark, "there waits a knight who will joust, for no one shall pass this bridge without jousting with that knight."

"Good," said King Mark, "for this joust falls to you."

Sir Dinadan knew the knight well, that he was a noble knight, and he would gladly have jousted; but he would rather King Mark had jousted with him. But King Mark would not joust by any means. Then Sir Dinadan could not refuse him in any way. And then each of them made ready his spear and his shield, and they struck together, so that by sheer force Sir Dinadan was struck to the ground; and he rose up swiftly and got his horse, and called on that knight to do battle with swords.

And he answered, "Fair knight, I may not fight with you any more at this time, for such is the custom of this crossing."

Then Sir Dinadan was exceedingly angry that he could not be revenged on that knight; and so he left, and that knight would not tell his name for anything. But all along Sir Dinadan thought he would know him by his shield, that it must be Sir Tor.

Chapter 11: How King Mark mocked Sir Dinadan, and how they met six knights of the Round Table

So as they rode along the way, King Mark began to mock Sir Dinadan, and said, "I thought you knights of the Round Table could never in any way find your match."

"You're right," said Sir Dinadan. "As for you, on my life, I count you none of the best knights. But since you hold me in such scorn, I call on you to joust with me, to test my strength."

"Not so," said King Mark, "for I will not fight with you in any way. But I ask one thing of you: that when you come to Arthur's court, you do not give away my name, for I am so hated there."

"It is a shame to you," said Sir Dinadan, "that you conduct yourself so shamefully. For I can see by you that you are full of cowardice, and you are a murderer, and that is the greatest shame a knight can have. For no knight who is a murderer ever has honour, nor ever shall. For I saw only just now that, through my strength, you would have killed Sir Berluse, a better knight than you are, or ever will be, and of more prowess."

So they rode on, talking, until they came to a fine house, where a knight stood who begged them to take their lodging with him. So at that knight's request they rested there, and made themselves comfortable, and had a warm welcome. For all knights-errant were welcome to him, and especially all those of Arthur's court. Then Sir Dinadan asked his host the name of the knight who kept the bridge.

"Why do you ask?" said the host.

"Because it is not long since he gave me a fall," said Sir Dinadan.

"Ah, fair knight," said his host, "you need not wonder at that, for he is an exceedingly good knight, and his name is Sir Tor, the son of Aries the cowherd."

"Ah," said Sir Dinadan, "was that Sir Tor? Truly, I thought so all along."

Just as they stood talking together like this, they saw six knights of King Arthur's court come riding towards them over a plain, well armed at all points. And Sir Dinadan knew them well there by their shields. The first was the good knight Sir Uwain, the son of King Uriens; the second was the noble knight Sir Brandiles; the third was Ozanna le Cure Hardy; the fourth was Uwain les Avoutres; the fifth was Sir Agravain; the sixth was Sir Mordred, brother to Sir Gawain. When Sir Dinadan had seen these six knights, he thought to himself that he would bring King Mark by some trick to joust with one of them. And at once they took their horses and rode after these knights a good three English miles. Then King Mark saw where all six of them sat around a spring, eating and drinking such food as they had, with their horses walking about and some tied up, and their shields hung in various places around them.

"Look," said Sir Dinadan, "there are knights-errant who will joust with us."

"God forbid," said King Mark, "for they are six and we are only two."

"As for that," said Sir Dinadan, "let's not hold back, for I will take on the foremost." And with that he made himself ready.

When King Mark saw him do so, as fast as Sir Dinadan rode towards them, King Mark rode away from them with all his household servants. So when Sir Dinadan saw that King Mark was gone, he took his spear out of the rest, and threw his shield onto his back, and came riding to the fellowship of the Round Table. And at once Sir Uwain knew Sir Dinadan, and welcomed him, and so did all his fellowship.

Chapter 12: How the six knights sent Sir Dagonet to joust with King Mark, and how King Mark refused him

And then they asked him about his adventures, and whether he had seen Sir Tristram or Sir Lancelot.

"So help me God," said Sir Dinadan, "I have seen neither of them since I left Camelot."

"What knight is that," said Sir Brandiles, "who left you so suddenly and rode over that field?"

"Sir," he said, "it was a knight of Cornwall, and the most horrible coward that ever sat on a horse."

"What is his name?" said all these knights.

"I don't know," said Sir Dinadan.

So when they had rested, and talked together, they took their horses and rode to a castle where an old knight lived who gave all knights-errant a warm welcome. Then, while they were talking, Sir Griflet le Fise de Dieu came into the castle, and he was made welcome there; and they all asked him whether he had seen Sir Lancelot or Sir Tristram.

"Sirs," he answered, "I have not seen him since he left Camelot."

So as Sir Dinadan walked about and looked at the castle, he spotted King Mark in a room nearby, and then he rebuked him, and asked him why he had left like that.

"Sir," he said, "because I did not dare stay, since there were so many of them. But how did you escape?" said King Mark.

"Sir," said Sir Dinadan, "they turned out to be better friends than I had expected."

"Who is captain of that company?" said the king.

Then, to frighten him, Sir Dinadan said that it was Sir Lancelot.

"Oh Jesus," said the king, "could I know Sir Lancelot by his shield?"

"Yes," said Dinadan, "for he carries a silver shield with black bands across it."

He said all this to frighten the king, for Sir Lancelot was not in his company.

"Now I beg you," said King Mark, "to ride in my company."

"I am unwilling to do that," said Sir Dinadan, "because you abandoned my company."

Then Sir Dinadan left King Mark at once, and went to his own fellowship; and so they mounted their horses, and rode on their way, and talked of the Cornish knight, for Dinadan told them that he was in the castle where they had lodged.

"Well said," said Sir Griflet, "for I have brought Sir Dagonet here, King Arthur's fool, who is the best fellow and the merriest in the world."

"Do you want a good plan?" said Sir Dinadan. "I have told the Cornish knight that Sir Lancelot is here, and the Cornish knight asked me what shield he carried. Truly, I told him he carried the same shield that Sir Mordred carries."

"Do you want a good plan?" said Sir Mordred. "I am hurt and cannot well bear my shield or my armour, and so put my shield and my armour on Sir Dagonet, and let him set on the Cornish knight."

"That shall be done," said Sir Dagonet, "by my faith."

Then at once Dagonet was armed in Mordred's armour and his shield, and he was set on a great horse, with a spear in his hand.

"Now," said Dagonet, "show me the knight, and I believe I shall bear him down."

So all these knights rode to the edge of a wood, and waited until King Mark came along the road. Then they sent Sir Dagonet out, and he came on as fast as his horse could run, straight at King Mark. And when he came near King Mark, he shouted as if he were mad, and said, "Defend yourself, knight of Cornwall, for I will kill you!"

As soon as King Mark saw his shield, he said to himself, "That is Sir Lancelot. Alas, now I am done for." And with that he made his horse run as fast as it could, through thick and thin. And all the while Sir Dagonet followed after King Mark, shouting and berating him like a madman, through a great forest. When Sir Uwain and Sir Brandiles saw Dagonet chase King Mark like that, they all laughed as if they were mad. And then they took their horses and rode after them, to see how Sir Dagonet got on; for they would not for anything have had Sir Dagonet come to harm, because King Arthur loved him exceedingly, and had made him a knight with his own hands. And at every tournament he started up something to make King Arthur laugh. Then the knights rode here and there, shouting and chasing after King Mark, so that the whole forest rang with the noise.

Chapter 13: How Sir Palomides by chance met King Mark in flight, and how he overthrew Dagonet and other knights

So by chance King Mark rode past a spring, on the road where a knight-errant stood on horseback, armed at all points, with a great spear in his hand. And when he saw King Mark coming in flight, he said, "Knight, turn back, for shame, and stand with me, and I will be your protection."

"Ah, fair knight," said King Mark, "let me pass, for behind me comes the best knight in the world, with the shield banded in black."

"Shame on you," said the knight. "He is none of the great knights. And if he were Sir Lancelot or Sir Tristram, I would not be afraid to meet the better of the two."

When King Mark heard him say that, he turned his horse and stayed by him. And then that strong knight levelled a spear at Dagonet, and struck him so hard that he carried him over his horse's tail, and nearly broke his neck. And right after him came Sir Brandiles, and when he saw Dagonet take that fall he was exceedingly angry, and shouted, "Defend yourself, knight!" And so they crashed together wondrously hard. But the knight struck Sir Brandiles so hard that he went to the ground, horse and man. Sir Uwain came after and saw all this.

"Jesus," he said, "that is a strong knight."

And then they set their spears in rest, and this knight came on so fiercely that he struck down Sir Uwain. Then came Ozanna with the hardy heart, and he was struck down.

"Now," said Sir Griflet, "if you take my advice, let us send to that knight-errant and find out whether he is of Arthur's court, for I believe it is Sir Lamorak de Galis."

So they sent to him, and begged the strange knight to tell his name, and whether he was of Arthur's court or not.

"As for my name, they shall not know it. But tell them I am a knight-errant as they are, and let them know that I am no knight of King Arthur's court."

And so the squire rode back to them and told them his answer.

"By my head," said Sir Agravain, "he is one of the strongest knights I ever saw, for he has overthrown three noble knights, and we must take him on, for shame."

So Sir Agravain set his spear in rest, and the other was ready, and struck him down over his horse to the ground. And in the same way he struck down Sir Uwain les Avoutres, and Sir Griflet too. Then he had served them all except Sir Dinadan, for he was behind, and Sir Mordred was unarmed, and Dagonet had his armour.

So when this was done, this strong knight rode on his way at a gentle pace, and King Mark rode after him, praising him greatly; but he would answer not a word, but sighed wondrously deeply, hanging his head, and paying no attention to what he said. So they rode a good three English miles, and then this knight called a servant to him, and told him to ride to the fine manor over there: "and commend me to the lady of that castle and place, and ask her to send me refreshment of good food and drink. And if she asks you who I am, tell her that I am the knight who follows the Glatisant Beast," that is to say, in English, the Questing Beast; for wherever that beast went, it gave tongue in its belly with a noise as if it were thirty couple of hounds.

Then the servant went his way and came to the manor, and greeted the lady, and told her where he came from. And when she understood that he came from the knight who followed the Questing Beast, "O sweet Lord Jesus," she said, "when shall I see that noble knight, my dear son Palomides? Alas, will he not stay with me?" And with that she fainted and wept, and grieved exceedingly. And then, as soon as she could, she gave the servant all that he asked. And the servant returned to Sir Palomides, for he was a servant of King Mark's. And as soon as he came, he told them the knight's name was Sir Palomides.

"I am well pleased," said King Mark, "but keep quiet and say nothing."

Then they dismounted and sat down and rested for a while. And with that King Mark at once fell asleep. When Sir Palomides saw him sound asleep, he took his horse and rode his way, and said to them, "I will not be in the company of a sleeping knight." And so he rode off at a great pace.

Chapter 14: How King Mark and Sir Dinadan heard Sir Palomides grieving and mourning for Isolde the Fair

Now we turn to Sir Dinadan, who found these seven knights exceedingly downcast. And when he knew how they had fared, he was just as downcast.

"My lord Uwain," said Dinadan, "I dare bet my head it is Sir Lamorak de Galis. I promise you all I shall find him, if he can be found in this country."

And so Sir Dinadan rode after this knight; and so did King Mark, who looked for him through the forest. So as King Mark rode after Sir Palomides, he heard the sound of a man grieving greatly. Then King Mark rode as near that sound as he could and as he dared. Then he saw a knight who had got down off his horse and had taken off his helmet, and there he was making a pitiful and sorrowful lament, of love.

Now we leave that, and speak of Sir Dinadan, who rode to look for Sir Palomides. And as he came into a forest he met a knight who was hunting a deer.

"Sir," said Sir Dinadan, "have you met a knight with a silver shield with lions' heads on it?"

"Yes, fair knight," said the other, "I met such a knight only a little while ago, and he went straight off that way."

"Many thanks," said Sir Dinadan, "for if I could find the track of his horse, I would not fail to find that knight."

Just then, as Sir Dinadan rode late in the evening, he heard a doleful sound, as if of a man. Then Sir Dinadan rode towards that sound; and when he came near it he got down off his horse and went up close on foot. Then he saw a knight standing under a tree, with his horse tied beside him and the helmet off his head; and all the while that knight made as doleful a lament as ever a knight made. And all the time he lamented for Isolde the Fair, the Queen of Cornwall, and said, "Ah, fair lady, why do I love you? For you are the fairest of all, and yet you never show me love, nor kindness. Alas, and yet I must love you. And I cannot blame you, fair lady, for my own eyes are the cause of this sorrow. And yet I am nothing but a fool to love you, for the best knight in the world loves you, and you love him in return, and that is Sir Tristram de Liones. And the falsest king and knight is your husband, and the greatest coward and the most full of treason is your lord, King Mark. Alas, that ever so fair a lady, peerless above all others, should be matched with the most villainous knight in the world."

King Mark heard all these words, all that Sir Palomides said of him; and so he was afraid, when he saw Sir Dinadan, that if he spotted him he would tell Sir Palomides that he was King Mark. And therefore he drew away, and took his horse and rode to his men, where he had ordered them to wait. And so he rode as fast as he could to Camelot; and that same day he found Amant there, the knight who had earlier accused him of treason before Arthur, ready for him; and so the king at once commanded them to do battle. And by ill luck King Mark struck Amant through the body. And yet Amant had the right on his side. And immediately King Mark took his horse and left the court, for fear of Sir Dinadan, that he would tell Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides who he was. Then there were maidens there, whom Isolde the Fair had sent to Sir Tristram, who knew Sir Amant well.

Chapter 15: How King Mark wrongfully killed Sir Amant in front of King Arthur, and how Sir Lancelot brought King Mark back to King Arthur

Then, with King Arthur's leave, they went to him and spoke with him; for while the broken shaft of the spear was still stuck in his body, he spoke.

"Ah, fair damsels," said Amant, "commend me to Isolde the Fair, and tell her that I am killed for love of her and of Sir Tristram."

And there he told the damsels how cowardly King Mark had killed him, and Sir Bersules his companion: "And for that deed I accused him of treason, and here I am killed in a rightful quarrel; and it was all because Sir Bersules and I would not agree, by treason, to kill the noble knight Sir Tristram."

Then the two maidens cried aloud, so that all the court could hear it, and said, "O sweet Lord Jesus, who knows all hidden things, why do You allow so false a traitor to defeat and kill a true knight who fought in a rightful quarrel?"

Then at once word spread to the king and the queen and to all the lords that it was King Mark who had killed Sir Amant, and Sir Bersules before him; and that was why they had fought their battle. Then King Arthur was angry beyond measure, and so were all the other knights. But when Sir Tristram knew the whole matter he grieved greatly and sorrowed beyond measure, and wept for sorrow at the loss of the noble knights, Sir Bersules and Sir Amant.

When Sir Lancelot saw Sir Tristram weep, he went quickly to King Arthur and said, "Sir, I beg you, give me leave to go back after that false king and knight."

"I beg you," said King Arthur, "fetch him back; but I would not have you kill him, for my honour's sake."

Then Sir Lancelot armed himself in all haste, and mounted a great horse, and took a spear in his hand and rode after King Mark. And three English miles from there Sir Lancelot overtook him, and called out to him, "Turn round, you recreant king and knight! For whether you like it or not, you shall come with me to King Arthur's court."

King Mark turned and looked at Sir Lancelot, and said, "Fair sir, what is your name?"

"Know this," he said, "my name is Sir Lancelot. So defend yourself."

And when King Mark knew that it was Sir Lancelot, coming so fast at him with a spear, he cried out aloud, "I yield to you, Sir Lancelot, honourable knight!"

But Sir Lancelot would not hear him, and came on fast at him. King Mark saw that, and made no defence, but tumbled down out of his saddle to the ground like a sack, and there he lay still, and begged Sir Lancelot for mercy.

"Get up, recreant knight and king!"

"I will not fight," said King Mark, "but wherever you wish, I will go with you."

"Alas, alas," said Sir Lancelot, "that I may not give you one blow, for the love of Sir Tristram and of Isolde the Fair, and for the two knights you have treacherously killed!"

And so he mounted his horse and brought him to King Arthur; and there King Mark dismounted in that same place, and threw his helmet down on the ground away from him, and his sword, and fell flat on the ground at King Arthur's feet, and put himself in his grace and mercy.

"So help me God," said Arthur, "you are welcome in one way, and in another way you are not welcome. In this way you are welcome: that you have come here against your will, as I suppose."

"That is the truth," said King Mark, "or else I would not have been here; for my lord Sir Lancelot brought me here by sheer force, and I have yielded to him as a recreant."

"Well," said Arthur, "you understand that you owe me service, homage and fealty. And you never would do me any, but you have always been against me, and a destroyer of my knights. Now, how will you clear yourself?"

"Sir," said King Mark, "just as your lordship requires of me, to the limit of my power, I will make generous amends." For he was a fair speaker, and false underneath.

Then, to give great pleasure to Sir Tristram, and to make the two of them friends, the king kept King Mark with him for that time, and made a day of reconciliation between them, a broken one.

Chapter 16: How Sir Dinadan told Sir Palomides about the battle between Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram

Now we turn back to Sir Palomides, and how Sir Dinadan comforted him in his great sorrow as best he could.

"What knight are you?" said Sir Palomides.

"Sir, I am a knight-errant as you are, and I have been looking for you a long time by your shield."

"Here is my shield," said Sir Palomides. "Believe me, if you want anything of it, I will defend it."

"No," said Sir Dinadan, "I will not fight with you except in friendship."

"And if you wish otherwise, you will find me ready soon enough," said Palomides.

"Sir," said Sir Dinadan, "which way are you riding?"

"By my head," said Sir Palomides, "I don't know, except as fortune leads me."

"Have you heard or seen anything of Sir Tristram?" said Dinadan.

"So help me God, of Sir Tristram I have both heard and seen. And even though we did not love each other at heart, yet when I was in trouble Sir Tristram saved me from my death. And yet, before he and I parted, by agreement between us both we set a day when we were to meet at the stone grave that Merlin set beside Camelot, and fight a battle there together. But I was hindered," said Sir Palomides, "so that I could not keep my day, and that grieves me badly; but I have a full excuse. For I was a prisoner with a lord, and many others too, and Sir Tristram shall understand perfectly well that I did not break it out of fear or cowardice."

And then Sir Palomides told Sir Dinadan the day on which they were to have met.

"So help me God," said Sir Dinadan, "on that same day Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram met at that same stone grave. And there was the mightiest battle ever seen in this land between two knights, for they fought for more than two hours. And they both bled so much blood there that everyone marvelled that they could ever endure it. And so at last, by agreement between them both, they were made friends and sworn brothers for ever, and no one can judge which is the better knight. And now Sir Tristram has been made a knight of the Round Table, and he sits in the seat of the noble knight Sir Marhaus."

"By my head," said Sir Palomides, "Sir Tristram is far stronger than Sir Lancelot, and the bolder knight."

"Have you tried them both?" said Sir Dinadan.

"I have seen Sir Tristram fight," said Sir Palomides, "but never Sir Lancelot, to my knowledge. But at the spring where Sir Lancelot lay asleep, there with one spear he struck down Sir Tristram and me," said Palomides, "but at that time neither knew the other."

"Fair knight," said Sir Dinadan, "as for Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram, let them be; for the worse of the two will not easily be matched by any knight I know alive."

"No," said Sir Palomides, "God forbid. But if I had a quarrel with the better of the two, I would fight him as willingly as I would you."

"Sir, I beg you, tell me your name, and in good faith I will keep you company until we come to Camelot; and there you shall win great honour now at this great tournament, for Queen Guinevere will be there, and Isolde the Fair of Cornwall."

"Believe me, sir knight, for the love of Isolde the Fair I will be there, and for nothing else; but I will not fight in King Arthur's court."

"Sir," said Dinadan, "I will ride with you and do you service, if you will tell me your name."

"Sir, you shall understand that my name is Sir Palomides, brother to Safere, the good and noble knight. And Sir Segwarides and I are Saracens born, of father and mother."

"Sir," said Sir Dinadan, "I thank you very much for telling me your name. For I am glad that I know your name, and I promise you, on my life, you shall not be harmed by me if I can help it, but rather advanced. And I will help you in that with all my power, I promise you, have no doubt of it. And certainly, on my life, you shall win great honour in King Arthur's court, and be most welcome."

So then they put on their helmets and took up their shields, and mounted their horses, and took the broad road towards Camelot. And then they saw a castle that was fine and rich, and as strong besides as any in this realm.

Chapter 17: How Sir Lamorak jousted with several knights of the castle where Morgan le Fay was

"Sir Palomides," said Dinadan, "here is a castle I know well, and Queen Morgan le Fay, King Arthur's sister, lives in it. And King Arthur gave her this castle, which he has regretted a thousand times since; for ever since then King Arthur and she have been at strife and quarrelling. But he could never get this castle or win it from her by any kind of trickery; and whenever she could, she made war on King Arthur. And she keeps with her all the dangerous knights, to destroy all the knights King Arthur loves. And no knight shall pass this way without jousting with one knight, or with two, or with three. And if it happens that King Arthur's knight is beaten, he shall lose his horse and his armour and everything he has, and if he gets away without being made a prisoner, he will be hard put to it."

"So help me God," said Palomides, "this is a shameful custom, and a villainous practice for a queen to keep, and above all to make such war on her own lord, who is called the Flower of Chivalry, Christian or heathen. And with all my heart I would destroy that shameful custom. And I want all the world to know that she shall have no service from me. And if she sends out any knights to joust, as I suppose she will, they shall have both their hands full."

"And I will not fail you," said Sir Dinadan, "to the limit of my strength, upon my life."

So as they sat on horseback in front of the castle, a knight with a red shield came up, and two squires after him; and he came straight up to Sir Palomides, the good knight, and said to him, "Fair and noble knight-errant, I ask you, for the love you owe to knighthood, not to fight here with these men of this castle." (It was Sir Lamorak who said this.) "For I came here to seek out this deed, and it is my request; and therefore I beg you, knight, leave it to me, and if I am beaten, avenge me."

"In the name of God," said Palomides, "let us see how you get on, and we will watch you."

Then at once a knight of the castle came out and offered to joust with the Knight with the Red Shield. At once they met together, and the one with the red shield struck him so hard that he carried him over to the ground. With that, another knight of the castle came at once, and he was struck so hard that he was thrown from his saddle. And straight after came the third knight, and the Knight with the Red Shield struck him to the ground. Then Sir Palomides came and begged him to let him help in the jousting.

"Fair knight," he said to him, "allow me to have my way this time; for if there were twenty knights, I would not fear them."

And all the while there were many lords and ladies on the walls of the castle, who cried out and said, "Well jousted, Knight with the Red Shield!"

But as soon as the knight had struck them down, his squire took their horses, and took the saddles and bridles off the horses, and turned them loose into the forest, and had the knights held until the jousting was over. Just then the fourth knight came out of the castle, and briskly offered to joust with the Knight with the Red Shield; and he was ready, and he struck him so hard that horse and man fell to the ground, and the knight's back broke with the fall, and his neck too.

"O Jesus," said Sir Palomides, "that is an exceedingly good knight, and the best jouster I ever saw."

"By my head," said Sir Dinadan, "he is as good as Sir Lancelot or Sir Tristram ever were, whatever knight he may be."

Chapter 18: How Sir Palomides wanted to joust with the knights of the castle in Sir Lamorak's place

Then straight away a knight came out of the castle with a shield striped diagonally in black and white. And at once the Knight with the Red Shield and he met so hard that he struck the knight of the castle through the striped shield and through the body, and broke the horse's back.

"Fair knight," said Sir Palomides, "you have too much on your hands, so I beg you, let me joust, for you need a rest."

"Why, sir," said the knight, "do you think I am weak and feeble? Sir, it seems to me you do me wrong, and shame me, when I am doing well enough. I tell you now what I told you before: if there were twenty knights, I would beat them; and if I am beaten or killed, then you may avenge me. And if you think I am weary, and you have an appetite to joust with me, I will find you jousting enough."

"Sir," said Palomides, "I did not say it because I wanted to joust with you, but it seems to me that you have too much on your hands."

"And therefore, if you were well-bred," said the Knight with the Red Shield, "you would not offer me shame. So I call on you to joust with me, and you shall find that I am not weary."

"Since you call on me," said Sir Palomides, "look to yourself."

Then the two knights came together as fast as their horses could run, and the knight struck Sir Palomides so hard on the shield that the spear went into his side, a great wound and a dangerous one. And with that Sir Palomides was thrown from his saddle. And that knight turned to Sir Dinadan; and when Dinadan saw him coming he cried out aloud and said, "Sir, I will not fight with you!" But he did not hold back for that, and came straight at him. So Sir Dinadan, for shame, put out his spear and shattered it all to pieces on the knight. But he struck Sir Dinadan back so hard that he struck him clean out of his saddle; but he would not allow his squires to meddle with their horses, because they were knights-errant.

Then he turned back to the castle, and jousted with seven more knights, and there was not one of them who could withstand him, but he carried each of them to the ground. And of these twelve knights he killed four in fair jousting. And the eight knights he made swear on the crossguard of a sword that they would never keep the evil customs of the castle. And when he had made them swear that oath, he let them go. And all the while the lords and the ladies stood on the castle walls, crying and saying, "Knight with the Red Shield, you have done as marvellously well as any knight we ever saw!"

And with that a knight came out of the castle unarmed, and said, "Knight with the Red Shield, you have done us too much damage today. So go back wherever you like, for there are no more here who will fight with you. We are bitterly sorry that you ever came here, for by you the old custom of this castle is undone."

And with that word he turned back into the castle and shut the gates. Then the Knight with the Red Shield turned and called his squires, and so went on his way, and rode at a great pace.

And when he was gone, Sir Palomides went to Sir Dinadan and said, "I never had such shame from any knight I ever met. And therefore I mean to ride after him and be revenged with my sword, for on horseback I believe I shall win no honour from him."

"Sir Palomides," said Dinadan, "if you take my advice, you will not meddle with him, for you will win no honour from him; and for this reason: you have seen him today with too much to do, and much too worn out."

"By almighty Jesus," said Palomides, "I shall never be at ease until I have fought him."

"Sir," said Dinadan, "then I'll give you my company, as a spectator."

"Well," said Palomides, "then you shall see how we measure our strength."

So they took their horses from their servants, and rode after the Knight with the Red Shield; and down in a valley beside a spring they saw where he had dismounted to rest, and had taken off his helmet to drink at the spring.

Chapter 19: How Sir Lamorak jousted with Sir Palomides and wounded him badly

Then Palomides rode fast until he came near him. And then he said, "Knight, remember the shame you did me just now at the castle. So get ready, for I will fight you."

"Fair knight," he said to Palomides, "you will win no honour from me, for you have seen today that I have been badly worn out."

"As for that," said Palomides, "I will not hold back for it, for believe me, I will be revenged."

"Well," said the knight, "I may manage to hold out against you."

And with that he mounted his horse, and took a great spear in his hand, ready to joust.

"No," said Palomides, "I will not joust, for I am sure I shall win no prize at jousting."

"Fair knight," said that knight, "it would befit a knight to joust and to fight on horseback."

"You shall see what I will do," said Palomides.

And with that he got down on foot, and set his shield in front of him and drew his sword. Then the Knight with the Red Shield got down from his horse, and set his shield in front of him, and so he drew his sword. And then they came together at a gentle pace, and wondrously hard and thick they laid into each other for the space of an hour before they stopped for breath. Then they circled and sidestepped, and grew wondrously angry, and each promised the other death. They hacked so fast with their swords that they cut away half their shields and mail, so that the bare flesh stood out in places beyond their armour. And when Sir Palomides saw his opponent's sword covered with his blood, it grieved him badly. Sometimes they thrust, sometimes they struck like wild men. But at last Sir Palomides grew faint, because of the first wound he had had at the castle with a spear, for that wound grieved him wondrously badly.

"Fair knight," said Palomides, "it seems to me we have tested each other exceedingly hard; and if it may please you, I ask you, by your knighthood, tell me your name."

"Sir," said the knight to Palomides, "I am unwilling to do that, for you have done me wrong, and no knightly deed, to offer me battle, considering how worn out I was. But if you will tell me your name, I will tell you mine."

"Sir," he said, "know this: my name is Palomides."

"Ah, sir, you shall understand that my name is Sir Lamorak de Galis, son and heir of the good knight and king, King Pellinore, and Sir Tor, the good knight, is my half-brother."

When Sir Palomides heard him say so, he knelt down and asked for mercy: "For I have done you an outrage this day; considering the great deeds of arms I have seen you do, I have shamefully and unknightly called on you to do battle."

"Ah, Sir Palomides," said Sir Lamorak, "you have done and said too much to me."

And with that he embraced him with both his arms, and said, "Palomides, worthy knight, in all this land there is none better than you, nor of more prowess, and I am deeply sorry that we fought together."

"I am not," said Sir Palomides, "and yet I am worse wounded than you are; but as for that, I shall soon be healed of it. But truly, I would not have missed our meeting for the fairest castle in this land; for I shall love you all the days of my life above all other knights, except my brother, Sir Safere."

"I say the same," said Sir Lamorak, "except my brother, Sir Tor."

Then Sir Dinadan came up, and he greeted Sir Lamorak with great joy. Then their squires saw to both their shields and their armour, and stopped their wounds. And they rested there for the night at a priory nearby.

Chapter 20: How Sir Lancelot was told that Dagonet had chased King Mark, and how a knight overthrew Dagonet and six other knights

Now we turn back again. When Sir Ganis and Sir Brandiles and their companions came to King Arthur's court, they told the king, Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram how Sir Dagonet, the fool, had chased King Mark through the forest, and how the strong knight had struck them down, all seven, with one spear. There was great laughing and joking at King Mark and at Sir Dagonet. But none of these knights could tell what knight it was who had rescued King Mark. Then they asked King Mark if he knew him, and he answered and said, "He called himself the Knight that Follows the Questing Beast, and by that name he sent one of my servants to a place where his mother was. And when she heard where he came from, she grieved exceedingly, and told my servant his name, and said, 'Oh, my dear son, Sir Palomides, why will you not come to see me?' And therefore, sir," said King Mark, "it is to be understood that his name is Sir Palomides, a noble knight." Then all these seven knights were glad that they knew his name.

Now we turn back again, for in the morning they took their horses, Sir Lamorak, Palomides and Dinadan together, with their squires and servants, and rode until they saw a fair castle that stood on a mountain, well walled in. And they rode there, and there they found a knight called Galahalt, who was lord of that castle, and there they had a warm welcome and were made very comfortable.

"Sir Dinadan," said Sir Lamorak, "what will you do?"

"Oh, sir," said Dinadan, "tomorrow I will go to King Arthur's court."

"By my head," said Sir Palomides, "I will not ride for these three days, for I am badly hurt, and I have bled a great deal, and so I will rest here."

"Truly," said Sir Lamorak, "and I will stay here with you; and when you ride, then I will ride, unless you linger too long, and then I will take my horse. So I beg you, Sir Dinadan, stay and ride with us."

"Upon my faith," said Dinadan, "I will not stay, for I have such a longing to see Sir Tristram that I cannot stay away from him long."

"Ah, Dinadan," said Sir Palomides, "now I understand that you love my mortal enemy, and so how could I trust you?"

"Well," said Dinadan, "I love my lord Sir Tristram above all others, and I will serve him and do him honour."

"So shall I," said Sir Lamorak, "in everything that lies in my power."

So in the morning Sir Dinadan rode to King Arthur's court. And on the way, as he rode, he saw a knight-errant standing there, who made himself ready to joust.

"Not so," said Dinadan, "for I have no wish to joust."

"You shall joust with me," said the knight, "before you pass this way."

"Are you asking for a joust out of love or out of hate?"

The knight answered, "You may be sure I ask it out of love, and not out of hate."

"That may well be so," said Sir Dinadan, "but it's a hard sort of love you offer me, when you want to joust with me with a sharp spear. But, fair knight," said Sir Dinadan, "since you want to joust with me, meet me at King Arthur's court, and there I will joust with you."

"Well," said the knight, "since you will not joust with me, I beg you, tell me your name."

"Sir knight," he said, "my name is Sir Dinadan."

"Ah," said the knight, "I know you very well for a good knight and a noble one, and believe me, I love you with all my heart."

"Then there shall be no jousting between us," said Dinadan.

So they parted. And the same day he came to Camelot, where King Arthur was staying. And there he greeted the king and the queen, Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram; and the whole court was glad of Sir Dinadan, for he was well-bred, wise and courteous, and a good knight. And above all, the valiant knight Sir Tristram loved Sir Dinadan exceedingly, above all other knights except Sir Lancelot.

Then the king asked Sir Dinadan what adventures he had seen.

"Sir," said Dinadan, "I have seen many adventures, and King Mark knows of some of them, but not all."

Then the king listened to Sir Dinadan as he told how Sir Palomides and he had been in front of Morgan le Fay's castle, and how Sir Lamorak had taken the jousts there ahead of them, and how he outjousted twelve knights, and killed four of them, "and how after that he struck down Sir Palomides and me both."

"I cannot believe that," said the king, "for Sir Palomides is an exceedingly good knight."

"That is the very truth," said Sir Dinadan, "but still I saw Sir Lamorak prove the better, hand to hand."

And then he told the king all about that fight, and how Sir Palomides was the weaker, and the more hurt, and had lost more of his blood. "And without a doubt," said Sir Dinadan, "if the fight had lasted longer, Palomides would have been killed."

"O Jesus," said King Arthur, "this is a great marvel to me."

"Sir," said Tristram, "do not marvel at it at all, for in my judgement there is not a more valiant knight living in the world, for I know his strength. And now I will tell you, I was never so worn out by any knight unless it was Sir Lancelot. And there is no knight in the world except Sir Lancelot who did as well as Sir Lamorak."

"So help me God," said the king, "I wish that knight, Sir Lamorak, would come to this court."

"Sir," said Dinadan, "he will be here shortly, and Sir Palomides too, but I am afraid that Palomides cannot travel yet."

Chapter 21: How King Arthur had a joust proclaimed, and how Sir Lamorak came in and overthrew Sir Gawain and many others

Then three days later the king had a joust held at a priory. And many knights of the Round Table made themselves ready there, for Sir Gawain and his brothers made ready to joust; but Tristram, Lancelot and Dinadan would not joust, but let Sir Gawain and his brothers win the prize if they could, for the love of King Arthur. Then in the morning they armed themselves to joust, Sir Gawain and his four brothers, and did great deeds of arms there. And Sir Ector de Maris did marvellously well, but Sir Gawain surpassed all that company; and so King Arthur and all the knights gave Sir Gawain the honour at the beginning.

Just then King Arthur noticed a knight and two squires who came out from the edge of a forest, with a shield covered in leather, and then he came in stealthily and crashed about here and there, and at once with one spear he had struck down two knights of the Round Table. Then with his crashing about he lost the covering of his shield, and then the king and everyone else saw that he carried a red shield.

"O Jesus," said King Arthur, "look, there rides a bold knight, the one with the red shield."

And there was shouting and crying: "Beware the Knight with the Red Shield!"

So within a short while he had overthrown three of Sir Gawain's brothers.

"So help me God," said King Arthur, "it seems to me that is the best jouster I ever saw."

With that he saw him meet Sir Gawain, and he struck him down with such great force that he made him leave his saddle.

"How now," said the king, "Sir Gawain has had a fall. I would be well pleased if I knew what knight he is, the one with the red shield."

"I know him well," said Dinadan, "but you shall not know his name at this time."

"By my head," said Sir Tristram, "he jousted better than Sir Palomides; and if you wish to know his name, believe me, his name is Sir Lamorak de Galis."

As they stood talking like this, Sir Gawain and he met again, and there he struck Sir Gawain from his horse and bruised him badly. And in the sight of King Arthur he struck down twenty knights, besides Sir Gawain and his brothers. And so the prize was given to him outright, as a knight without equal. Then quietly and marvellously Sir Lamorak slipped away from all the company to the edge of the forest. King Arthur saw all this, for his eye never left him. Then the king, Sir Lancelot, Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan took their small riding horses and rode straight after the good knight, Sir Lamorak de Galis, and found him there.

And the king said this: "Ah, fair knight, well met."

When he saw the king he took off his helm and greeted him, and when he saw Sir Tristram he got down off his horse and ran to him to clasp him by the thighs; but Sir Tristram would not allow it, but got down before he reached him, and each took the other in his arms, and they rejoiced greatly over each other. The king was glad, and so was all the fellowship of the Round Table, except Sir Gawain and his brothers. And when they knew that he was Sir Lamorak, they bore him great malice, and were furiously angry with him for having put Sir Gawain to dishonour that day.

Then Gawain called all his brothers together in private council, and said this to them: "Fair brothers, here you can see that the man we hate, King Arthur loves, and the man we love, he hates. And believe me, my fair brothers, this Sir Lamorak will never love us, because we killed his father, King Pellinore, for we believed that he killed our father, the King of Orkney. And to spite us for Pellinore, Sir Lamorak did us a shame with our mother. Therefore I will be revenged."

"Sir," said Sir Gawain's brothers, "let us see how you will or can be revenged, and you will find us ready."

"Well," said Gawain, "keep quiet, and we will watch for our time."

Chapter 22: How King Arthur made King Mark make peace with Sir Tristram, and how they set out for Cornwall

Now we pass over our matter, and leave Sir Gawain, and speak of King Arthur, who one day said to King Mark, "Sir, I beg you, grant me a gift that I will ask of you."

"Sir," said King Mark, "I will give you whatever you desire, if it is in my power."

"Sir, many thanks," said Arthur. "This is what I will ask of you: that you will be a good lord to Sir Tristram, for he is a man of great honour; and that you will take him with you into Cornwall, and let him see his friends, and treat him kindly there for my sake."

"Sir," said King Mark, "I promise you on my life, and by the faith that I owe to God and to you, I will honour him for your sake in everything I can or may."

"Sir," said Arthur, "and I will forgive you all the ill will I ever bore you, provided that you swear that on a book before me."

"With a good will," said King Mark.

And so he swore there on a book before him and all his knights, and with that King Mark and Sir Tristram took each other by the hands, clasped hard together. But for all this King Mark's thoughts were false, as it proved afterwards, for he put Sir Tristram in prison, and like a coward would have killed him.

Then soon afterwards King Mark took his leave to ride into Cornwall, and Sir Tristram made himself ready to ride with him. At this most of the Round Table were angry and downcast, and above all Sir Lancelot, Sir Lamorak and Sir Dinadan were angry beyond measure. For they knew well that King Mark would kill or ruin Sir Tristram.

"Alas," said Dinadan, "that my lord Sir Tristram is going away."

And Sir Tristram felt such sorrow that he was dazed like a fool.

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot to King Arthur, "what have you done? For you will lose the man of greatest honour who ever came into your court."

"It was his own wish," said Arthur, "and so I could do nothing about it, for I have done all that I can and made peace between them."

"Peace!" said Sir Lancelot. "Shame on that peace! For you will hear that he will kill Sir Tristram, or put him in a prison, for he is the most cowardly and the basest king and knight now living."

And with that Sir Lancelot left, and came to King Mark, and spoke to him like this: "Sir king, believe me, the good knight Sir Tristram is going with you. Beware of treason, I warn you. For if you do that knight any harm by any kind of falsehood or treason, by the faith I owe to God and to the order of knighthood, I will kill you with my own hands."

"Sir Lancelot," said the king, "you have said too much to me. I have sworn and spoken at large before King Arthur, in the hearing of all his knights, that I will not kill him or betray him. It would be too great a shame for me to break my promise."

"You speak well," said Sir Lancelot, "but you have such a name for falseness and treason that no one can believe you. Truly, it is well known why you came into this country, and for no other reason than to kill Sir Tristram."

So with great sorrow King Mark and Sir Tristram rode off together, for it was by Sir Tristram's own will and his own doing that he went with King Mark, and it was all so that he could see Isolde the Fair, for without the sight of her Sir Tristram could not live.

Chapter 23: How Sir Percival was knighted by King Arthur, and how a mute maiden spoke and led him to the Round Table

Now we turn back to Sir Lamorak, and speak of his brothers: Sir Tor, who was King Pellinore's first son, fathered on the wife of Aries the cowherd, for he was born out of wedlock; and Sir Aglovale, who was his first son born in wedlock; and Sir Lamorak, Durnore and Percival, who were his sons in wedlock too. So when King Mark and Sir Tristram had left the court, there was great grief and sorrow over Sir Tristram's leaving. Then the king and his knights held no festivities of any kind for eight days afterwards. And at the end of the eight days there came to the court a knight with a young squire. And when this knight had taken off his armour, he went to the king and asked him to make the young squire a knight.

"What lineage does he come of?" said King Arthur.

"Sir," said the knight, "he is the son of King Pellinore, who once did you good service, and he is a brother of Sir Lamorak de Galis, the good knight."

"Well," said the king, "for what reason do you ask me to make him a knight?"

"You may be sure, my lord the king, that this young squire is my brother as well as Sir Lamorak's, and my name is Aglovale."

"Sir Aglovale," said Arthur, "for the love of Sir Lamorak, and for his father's sake, he shall be made a knight tomorrow. Now tell me," said Arthur, "what is his name?"

"Sir," said the knight, "his name is Percival de Galis."

So in the morning the king made him a knight in Camelot. But the king and all the knights thought it would be a long time before he proved a good knight.

Then at dinner, when the king was seated at the table, and every knight according to his prowess, the king commanded that he be seated among the ordinary knights; and so Sir Percival was seated as the king commanded. Now there was a maiden in the queen's court who came of high blood, and she was mute and had never spoken a word. Just then she came straight into the hall, and went to Sir Percival, and took him by the hand, and said aloud, so that the king and all the knights could hear it, "Arise, Sir Percival, the noble knight and God's knight, and come with me."

And so he did. And there she brought him to the right side of the Siege Perilous, and said, "Fair knight, take your seat here, for that seat belongs to you and to no one else."

Then she left at once and asked for a priest. And when she had made her confession and been given communion, she died. Then the king and all the court rejoiced greatly over Sir Percival.

Chapter 24: How Sir Lamorak visited King Lot's wife, and how Sir Gaheris killed her, his own mother

Now we turn to Sir Lamorak, who was greatly praised there. Then, through the doing of Sir Gawain and his brothers, they sent for their mother to come near by, close to a castle beside Camelot; and it was all with the intention of killing Sir Lamorak. The Queen of Orkney was there only a short while, but Sir Lamorak knew she was there, and was very glad; and to bring this matter to its end, he sent word to her, and a night was arranged between them when Sir Lamorak should come to her. Sir Gaheris got wind of this, and he rode there ahead of him that same night, and lay in wait for Sir Lamorak, and then he saw him coming, fully armed. And where Sir Lamorak got down, he tied his horse to a secret back gate, and so he went into a parlour and took off his armour; and then he went to the queen's bed, and she welcomed him with exceedingly great joy, and he her in return, for each loved the other exceedingly. So when the knight, Sir Gaheris, saw his moment, he came to their bedside fully armed, with his sword drawn, and suddenly seized his mother by the hair and struck off her head.

When Sir Lamorak felt the blood dash over him, all hot, the blood of her whom he loved exceedingly, believe me, he was badly shaken and dismayed by that grim knight. And with that Sir Lamorak leapt out of the bed in his shirt, like a knight dismayed, saying this: "Ah, Sir Gaheris, knight of the Round Table, you have done a foul and evil thing, and to your great shame. Alas, why have you killed your mother who bore you? It would have been more right for you to kill me."

"The offence is yours," said Gaheris. "A man is born to offer his service, granted; but still you should beware whom you meddle with, for you have shamed me and my brothers. Your father killed our father; and for you to lie with our mother is more shame than we can stand. And as for your father, King Pellinore, my brother Sir Gawain and I killed him."

"Then you did him the greater wrong," said Sir Lamorak, "for my father did not kill your father; it was Balin le Savage. And my father's death is not avenged yet."

"Drop that talk," said Sir Gaheris, "for if you speak like a traitor I will kill you. But because you are naked I am ashamed to kill you. But believe me, wherever I can catch you, I will kill you. And now my mother is rid of you. Get out, take your armour, and be gone."

Sir Lamorak saw there was no help for it, but armed himself quickly, and took his horse and rode away in great sorrow. But for the shame and grief of it he would not ride to King Arthur's court, but rode another way.

But when it was known that Gaheris had killed his mother, the king was exceedingly angry, and ordered him out of his court. And believe me, Sir Gawain was angry that Gaheris had killed his mother and let Sir Lamorak escape. And the king was exceedingly angry over this matter, and so was Sir Lancelot, and many other knights.

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "here a great wrong has come about through villainy, and through treason plotted beforehand, that your sister has been killed so shamefully. And I dare say that it was done by treason, and I dare say you will lose that good knight Sir Lamorak, which is a great pity. I know well and am sure that if Sir Tristram knew of it, he would never come within your court again, and that would grieve you and all your knights much more."

"God forbid," said the noble King Arthur, "that I should lose Sir Lamorak or Sir Tristram, for then two of my chief knights of the Round Table would be gone."

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "I am sure you will lose Sir Lamorak, for Sir Gawain and his brothers will kill him by one means or another; for they have agreed and sworn among themselves to kill him if ever they see their time."

"That I will prevent," said Arthur.

Chapter 25: How Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred met a knight in flight, and how they were both overthrown, and of Sir Dinadan

Now we leave Sir Lamorak, and speak of Sir Gawain's brothers, and especially of Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred. As they rode on their adventures they met a knight fleeing, badly wounded, and they asked him what news.

"Fair knights," he said, "there is a knight coming after me who will kill me."

With that Sir Dinadan came riding up to them by chance, but he would promise them no help. But Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred promised to rescue him. With that the knight came straight up to them, and at once offered to joust. Sir Mordred saw that and rode at him, but he knocked Mordred over his horse's tail. Sir Agravain saw that, and he rode straight at that knight, and just as he had served Mordred, so he served Agravain, and said to them, "Sirs, you may both be sure that I am Breuse Saunce Pité who has done this to you." And even then he rode over Agravain five or six times.

When Dinadan saw this, he had to joust with him, for shame. And so Dinadan and he met, and by sheer strength Sir Dinadan knocked him over his horse's tail. Then he took his horse and fled, for on foot he was one of the most valiant knights of Arthur's days, and a great destroyer of all good knights.

Then Sir Dinadan rode up to Sir Mordred and Sir Agravain.

"Sir knight," they all said, "you have done well, and you have avenged us well, so we beg you, tell us your name."

"Fair sirs, you ought to know my name: I am called Sir Dinadan."

When they understood that it was Dinadan, they were angrier than they had been before, for they hated him beyond measure because of Sir Lamorak. For Dinadan had this habit: he loved all good knights who were valiant, and he hated all those who were destroyers of good knights. And none hated Dinadan except those who were always called murderers.

Then the hurt knight whom Breuse Saunce Pité had chased spoke up (his name was Dalan), and said, "If you're Dinadan, you killed my father."

"It may well be so," said Dinadan, "but if so, it was in my own defence and at his request."

"By my head," said Dalan, "you'll die for it."

And with that he lowered his spear and set his shield. And to cut a long story short, Sir Dinadan struck him down off his horse, so that his neck was nearly broken. And in the same way he struck down Sir Mordred and Sir Agravain. And later, in the quest of the Holy Grail, they killed Dinadan, like cowards and traitors, which was a great loss, for he was a great jester and an exceedingly good knight.

And so Sir Dinadan rode to a castle called Beale-Valet. And there he found Sir Palomides, who was not yet healed of the wound that Sir Lamorak gave him. And there Dinadan told Palomides all the news he had heard and seen of Sir Tristram, and how he had gone with King Mark, and how with him he has all his will and desire. At that Sir Palomides grew angry, for he loved Isolde the Fair. And then he knew well that Sir Tristram had her for his own.

Chapter 26: How King Arthur, the queen, and Lancelot received letters from Cornwall, and of their reply

Now we leave Sir Palomides and Sir Dinadan in the Castle of Beale-Valet, and turn back to King Arthur. A knight came out of Cornwall, whose name was Fergus, a companion of the Round Table. And there he told the king and Sir Lancelot good news of Sir Tristram, and fine letters were brought, and he told how he had left him in the castle of Tintagil. Then the damsel came who brought fine letters to King Arthur and to Sir Lancelot, and there she was given an exceedingly warm welcome by the king, and by Queen Guinevere, and by Sir Lancelot. Then they wrote fine letters in return. But Sir Lancelot kept warning Sir Tristram to beware of King Mark, for in his letters he always called him King Fox, as much as to say that he goes about everything with tricks and treason. And Sir Tristram thanked Sir Lancelot in his heart for that. Then the damsel went to Isolde the Fair, and brought her letters from the king and from Sir Lancelot, and she was exceedingly glad of them.

"Fair damsel," said Isolde the Fair, "how is my lord Arthur, and Queen Guinevere, and the noble knight Sir Lancelot?"

She answered, to cut a long story short, "All the better that you and Sir Tristram are happy."

"God reward them," said Isolde the Fair, "for Sir Tristram suffers great pain for me, and I for him."

So the damsel left, and brought letters to King Mark. And when he had read them and understood them, he was angry with Sir Tristram, for he believed that Tristram had sent the damsel to King Arthur. For Arthur and Lancelot in a way threatened King Mark. And as King Mark read these letters, he suspected treason from Sir Tristram.

"Damsel," said King Mark, "will you ride back and carry letters from me to King Arthur?"

"Sir," she said, "I am at your command, to ride whenever you wish."

"You speak well," said the king. "Come back tomorrow morning," said the king, "and fetch your letters."

Then she left, and told them how she was to ride back with letters to Arthur.

"Then we beg you," said Isolde the Fair and Sir Tristram, "when you have received your letters, come by us, so that we may see the secrets of your letters."

"Whatever I can do, madam, you know well I must do for Sir Tristram, for I have long been his own maiden."

So in the morning the damsel went to King Mark to collect his letters and leave.

"I am not minded to send my letters at this time," said King Mark.

Then privately and secretly he sent letters to King Arthur, and to Queen Guinevere, and to Sir Lancelot. So the servant set off, and found the king and the queen in Wales, at Caerleon. And as the king and the queen were at Mass, the servant came with the letters. And when Mass was over, the king and the queen opened the letters privately by themselves. And the king's letter began by speaking exceedingly curtly to King Arthur, and told him to look to himself and his own wife and his own knights; for he, Mark, was well able to rule and keep his wife.

Chapter 27: How Sir Lancelot was angry at the letter he received from King Mark, and of Dinadan, who made a song about King Mark

When King Arthur understood the letter, he pondered many things, and thought of what his sister, Queen Morgan le Fay, had said about Queen Guinevere and Sir Lancelot. And he brooded on this thought a long while. Then he reminded himself again that his sister was his own enemy, and that she hated the queen and Sir Lancelot, and so he put all that out of his mind. Then King Arthur read the letter again, and the last clause said that King Mark took Sir Tristram for his mortal enemy; and so he assured Arthur, beyond any doubt, that he would be revenged on Sir Tristram. Then King Arthur was angry with King Mark. And when Queen Guinevere read her letter and understood it, she was angry beyond measure, for the letter spoke shamefully of her and of Sir Lancelot. And so she sent the letter privately to Sir Lancelot. And when he knew what the letter meant, he was so angry that he lay down on his bed to sleep. Sir Dinadan noticed this, for it was his way to be in the confidence of all good knights. And as Sir Lancelot slept, he stole the letter out of his hand and read it word for word. And then he grieved greatly for anger. And then Sir Lancelot woke, and went to a window, and read the letter again, and it made him angry.

"Sir," said Dinadan, "why are you angry? Open your heart to me. Truly, you know well that I wish you well, although I am a poor knight and a servant to you and to all good knights. For though I am not a man of honour myself, I love all those who are men of honour."

"That is true," said Sir Lancelot. "You are a trusty knight, and because I trust you greatly I will tell you my secret."

And when Dinadan understood it all, he said, "This is my advice: think nothing at all of these threats, for King Mark is so base that no man will ever get anything out of him by fair words. But you shall see what I will do. I will make a song about him, and when it is made I will have a harper sing it in front of him."

So at once he went and made it, and taught it to a harper called Eliot. And when he knew it, he taught it to many harpers. And so by the will of Sir Lancelot and of Arthur, the harpers went straight into Wales and into Cornwall, to sing the song that Sir Dinadan had made about King Mark, which was the foulest song that ever a harper sang, with harp or with any other instrument.

Chapter 28: How Sir Tristram was wounded, and of a war made on King Mark, and how Sir Tristram promised to rescue him

Now we turn back to Sir Tristram and to King Mark. As Sir Tristram was at jousts and tournaments, it happened that he was badly hurt, both by a spear and by a sword, but still he always won the prize. And to rest himself he went to a good knight who lived in Cornwall, in a castle, whose name was Sir Dinas the Seneschal. Then by ill fortune a great number of men-at-arms came out of Sessoin, a hideous army, and they came in near the Castle of Tintagil; and their captain's name was Elias, a good fighting man. When King Mark understood that his enemies had come into his land, he grieved and sorrowed greatly, for by his own will King Mark would in no way send for Sir Tristram, for he hated him mortally.

So when his council had gathered, they discussed and weighed many dangers from the strength of their enemies. And then they all agreed at once, and said this to King Mark: "Sir, you may be sure you must send for Sir Tristram, the good knight, or else they will never be overcome. For they must be fought by Sir Tristram, or else we are rowing against the stream."

"Well," said King Mark, "I will do as you advise."

But still he was very unwilling, but need forced him to send for him. Then he was sent for with all the haste that could be, to come to King Mark. And when he understood that King Mark had sent for him, he mounted an easy-paced horse and rode to King Mark.

And when he had come, the king said this: "Fair nephew, Sir Tristram, this is the whole of it. Our enemies from Sessoin have come here, close at hand, and they must be met very soon and without delay, or else they will destroy this country."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "you may be sure that all my strength is at your command. And you may be sure, sir, that for these eight days I can bear no arms, for my wounds are not yet healed. And by that day I will do what I can."

"You speak well," said King Mark. "Then go back and rest and refresh yourself, and I will go and meet the Sessoins with all my strength."

So the king went off to Tintagil, and Sir Tristram went to rest. And the king raised a great army and divided it in three: Sir Dinas the Seneschal led the first part, and Sir Andred led the second part, and Sir Argius led the third part, and he was of King Mark's blood. And the Sessoins had three great divisions, and many good fighting men. And so King Mark, on the advice of his knights, sallied out of the Castle of Tintagil against his enemies. And Dinas, the good knight, rode out in front, and killed two knights with his own hands, and then the battle began. And there was marvellous breaking of spears and striking of swords, and many good knights were cut down. And Sir Dinas the Seneschal was always the best of King Mark's side. And so the battle lasted a long time, with great loss of life. But at last King Mark and Sir Dinas, however unwilling they were, withdrew to the Castle of Tintagil with great slaughter of their people; and the Sessoins followed hard on their heels, so that ten of them got inside the gates and four were killed by the portcullis.

Then King Mark sent for Sir Tristram by a servant, who told him of all the loss of life. Then he sent the servant back, and told him, "Tell King Mark that I will come as soon as I am healed, for before that I can do him no good."

Then King Mark had his answer. With that Elias came and ordered the king to yield up the castle: "For you cannot hold it for any time at all."

"Sir Elias," said the king, "I will yield up the castle if I am not rescued soon."

At once King Mark sent to Sir Tristram again for rescue. By then Sir Tristram was healed, and he had found himself ten good knights of Arthur's; and with them he rode to Tintagil. And when he saw the great army of Sessoins he marvelled very greatly. And then Sir Tristram rode by the woods and by the ditches as secretly as he could, until he came near the gates. And there a knight squared up to him when he saw that Sir Tristram meant to go in; and Sir Tristram struck him down dead, and he served three more the same way. And each of these ten knights killed a man-at-arms. So Sir Tristram went into the Castle of Tintagil. And when King Mark knew that Sir Tristram had come, he was glad of his coming, and so was all the company, and they rejoiced greatly over him.

Chapter 29: How Sir Tristram won the battle, and how Elias asked for a man to fight him in single combat

So in the morning Elias the captain came, and told King Mark, "Come out and do battle. Now that the good knight Sir Tristram has come in, it will be a shame to you," said Elias, "to hide behind your walls."

When King Mark understood this he was angry and said not a word, but went to Sir Tristram and asked him his advice.

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "do you want me to give him his answer?"

"Gladly," said King Mark.

Then Sir Tristram said this to the messenger: "Take your lord word from the king and from me that we will do battle with him tomorrow in the open field."

"What is your name?" said the messenger.

"You may be sure my name is Sir Tristram de Liones."

With that the messenger left and told his lord Elias all that he had heard.

"Sir," said Sir Tristram to King Mark, "I beg you, give me leave to have command of the battle."

"I beg you, take command," said King Mark.

Then Sir Tristram had the battle planned, how it should be fought. He had his army divided into six parts, and appointed Sir Dinas the Seneschal to have the vanguard, and other knights to command the rest. And that same night Sir Tristram burned all the Sessoins' ships down to the cold water. As soon as Elias knew of that, he said it was Sir Tristram's doing: "For he means that not one mother's son of us shall ever escape. So, fair companions, fight boldly tomorrow, and don't lose heart at all; for any one knight, though he were the best knight in the world, cannot fight us all."

Then they drew up their army in four parts, wonderfully well fitted out and equipped with men-at-arms. So those inside sallied out, and those outside fell boldly upon them; and there Sir Dinas did great deeds of arms. Nevertheless, Sir Dinas and his company got the worst of it. With that Sir Tristram came and killed two knights with one spear; then he killed on the right hand and on the left, so that men marvelled that he could ever do such deeds of arms. And then one could see the battle sometimes driven a bowshot from the castle, and sometimes it was at the castle gates. Then Elias the captain came rushing here and there, and hit King Mark so hard on the helm that he made him leave the saddle. And then Sir Dinas got King Mark back on horseback. With that Sir Tristram came in like a lion, and there he met Elias, and he struck him so hard on the helm that he left his saddle. And so they fought until it was night, and because of the great slaughter and the wounded, each side withdrew to rest.

And when King Mark had come inside the Castle of Tintagil, he was a hundred of his knights short, and those outside were two hundred short; and they saw to the wounded men on both sides. And then they went to council; and believe me, each side was unwilling to fight any more, provided that each could come away with its honour. When Elias the captain understood how many of his men were dead, he grieved greatly; and when he knew that they were unwilling to go into battle again, he was angry beyond measure. Then Elias sent word to King Mark, in great scorn, asking whether he could find a knight who would fight for him man to man. And if he could kill King Mark's knight, he was to have the tribute of Cornwall every year. "And if his knight kills mine, I give up my claim entirely, for ever."

Then the messenger went off to King Mark, and told him how his lord Elias had sent him word to find a knight to do battle with him man to man. When King Mark understood the messenger, he told him to wait and he would have his answer. Then he called all his barons together to learn what the best advice was.

They all said at once, "We have no desire to fight in the field, for if it had not been for Sir Tristram's prowess, it is likely that we would never have escaped. And so, sir, as we judge it, it would be well done to find a knight who will do battle with him, since he makes a knightly offer."

Chapter 30: How Sir Elias and Sir Tristram fought each other over the tribute, and how Sir Tristram killed Elias on the field

Nevertheless, when all this was said, they could find no knight who would do battle with him.

"Sir king," they all said, "there is no knight here who dares fight with Elias."

"Alas," said King Mark, "then I am utterly shamed and utterly destroyed, unless my nephew Sir Tristram will take the battle on himself."

"You may be sure," they all said, "he had more than enough on his hands yesterday, and he is weary from his labour, and badly wounded."

"Where is he?" said King Mark.

"Sir," they said, "he is in his bed, resting."

"Alas," said King Mark, "unless I have the help of my nephew Sir Tristram, I am utterly destroyed for ever."

With that someone went to Sir Tristram where he lay, and told him what King Mark had said. And with that Sir Tristram got up quickly, and put on a long gown, and came before the king and all the lords. And when he saw them all so dismayed, he asked the king and the lords what news they had.

"Never worse," said the king. And with that he told him everything, how he had had word from Elias to find a knight to fight for the tribute of Cornwall, "and I can find none."
