"And as for you," said the king and all the lords, "we cannot for shame ask any more of you, for through your boldness yesterday you saved all our lives."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "now that I understand you would have my help, it is only right that I should do everything in my power, saving my honour and my life, even though I am badly bruised and hurt. And since Sir Elias offers so generously, I will fight with him, and either I will be killed on the field, or else I will free Cornwall from the old tribute. And so call his messenger quickly, and he shall be answered, for my wounds are still fresh, and they will be sorer a week from now than they are now; and so he shall have his answer, that I will do battle with him tomorrow."

Then the messenger, who had gone, was brought back before King Mark.

"Listen, fellow," said Sir Tristram. "Go quickly to your lord, and tell him to give true guarantees on his side for the tribute, as the king here shall give on his; and then tell your lord, Sir Elias, that I, Sir Tristram, King Arthur's knight and knight of the Round Table, will meet your lord on horseback tomorrow, to do battle as long as my horse can last, and after that to do battle with him on foot to the uttermost."

The messenger looked Sir Tristram over from top to toe, and with that he left and came to his lord, and told him what answer Sir Tristram had given. And with that hostages were given on both sides, and it was made as sure as it could be that whichever side had the victory, the matter would end there. And then both armies were drawn up on both sides of the field, outside the castle of Tintagil, and no one was armed but Sir Tristram and Sir Elias.

So when the terms were settled, they rode apart, and they came together as fast as their horses could run. And each knight struck the other so hard that both horses and knights went to the ground. Nevertheless they both got up quickly and set their shields on their shoulders, with naked swords in their hands, and they dashed together so that it seemed there was a flaming fire about them. So they circled and sidestepped, and hewed at helms and hauberks, and cut many pieces away from their shields, and each wounded the other exceedingly badly, so that the hot blood fell fresh upon the earth. And by the time they had fought for the space of an hour, Sir Tristram grew faint and weak from loss of blood, and gave ground badly. Sir Elias saw that, and pressed fiercely after him, and wounded him in many places. And all the while Sir Tristram circled and sidestepped, and moved away from him here and there, and covered himself with his shield as well as he could, all weakly, so that everyone said he was beaten; for Sir Elias had given him twenty strokes for one.

Then there was laughing on the Sessoins' side, and great grief on King Mark's side.

"Alas," said the king, "we are shamed and destroyed for ever!" For, as the book says, Sir Tristram was never so matched, unless it was by Sir Lancelot.

So as they stood and watched, both sides, the one side laughing and the other side weeping, Sir Tristram remembered his lady, Isolde the Fair, who was watching him, and how he was likely never to come into her presence again. Then he pulled up his shield, which before had hung very low. And then he set his shield against Elias, and gave him many heavy blows, twenty for one, and broke his shield and his hauberk all to pieces, so that the hot blood ran down to the earth. Then King Mark began to laugh, and all the men of Cornwall, and the other side to weep. And all the while Sir Tristram said to Sir Elias, "Yield!"

Then, when Sir Tristram saw him staggering so on the ground, he said, "Sir Elias, I am truly sorry for you, for you are as exceedingly good a knight as I ever met, except Sir Lancelot."

With that Sir Elias fell to the earth, and there he died.

"What shall I do," said Sir Tristram to King Mark, "now that this battle is at an end?"

Then those of Elias' side left, and King Mark took many prisoners from them, to make good the harm and the damage he had suffered from them; and the rest he sent back into their own country to ransom their companions. Then Sir Tristram's wounds were examined, and he was well healed. Yet for all this King Mark would gladly have killed Sir Tristram. But for all that Sir Tristram ever saw or heard of King Mark, he would never be on his guard against his treachery, but he would always be wherever Isolde the Fair was.

Chapter 31: How at a great feast King Mark held a harper came and sang the song that Dinadan had made

Now we will pass over this matter, and speak of the harpers that Sir Lancelot and Sir Dinadan had sent into Cornwall. And at the great feast that King Mark held for joy that the Sessoins had been driven out of his country, Eliot the harper came with the song that Dinadan had made, and secretly brought it to Sir Tristram, and told him the song that Dinadan had made about King Mark. And when Sir Tristram heard it, he said, "O Lord Jesus, how wonderfully well Dinadan can make a song, and how wonderfully wicked, when the occasion calls for it!"

"Sir," said Eliot, "dare I sing this song before King Mark?"

"Yes, at my own risk," said Sir Tristram, "for I will be your protection."

Then at dinner Eliot the harper came in, and because he was a skilled harper, people listened to him sing that same song that Dinadan had made, which said the vilest things about King Mark and his treason that anyone ever heard.

When the harper had sung his song to the end, King Mark was furiously angry, and said, "You, harper, how dare you be so bold, at the risk of your head, as to sing this song before me?"

"Sir," said Eliot, "you may be sure I am a minstrel, and I must do as I am commanded by these lords whose arms I wear. And sir, believe me, Sir Dinadan, a knight of the Round Table, made this song, and made me sing it before you."

"You speak well," said King Mark, "and because you are a minstrel you shall go free, but I order you to get yourself out of my sight, and fast."

So the harper left and went to Sir Tristram, and told him how he had fared. Then Sir Tristram had letters written, as fine as he could make them, to Lancelot and to Sir Dinadan. And so he had the harper escorted out of the country. But as for King Mark being furiously angry, he certainly was, for he judged that the song that was sung before him had been made on Sir Tristram's advice, and so he thought to kill him and all his well-wishers in that country.

Chapter 32: How King Mark treacherously murdered his brother Boudwin for the good service he had done him

Now we turn to another matter that happened between King Mark and his brother, who was called the good Prince Boudwin, whom all the people of the country loved exceedingly well. So it happened one time that the unbelieving Saracens landed in the country of Cornwall, soon after these Sessoins were gone. And then the good Prince Boudwin, at their landing, raised the country secretly and in haste. And before it was day he had wildfire put in three of his own ships, and suddenly he hoisted the sails, and with the wind he made those ships drive among the fleet of the Saracens. And to cut a long story short, those three ships set fire to all the ships, so that none were saved. And at daybreak the good Prince Boudwin with all his company fell on the unbelievers with shouts and cries, and killed some forty thousand, and left none alive.

When King Mark knew this, he was furiously angry that his brother should win such honour. And because this prince was better loved than he was in all that country, and also because Boudwin loved Sir Tristram well, he therefore thought to kill him. And so, hastily, like a man out of his mind, he sent for Prince Boudwin and Anglides his wife, and told them to bring their young son with them, so that he might see him. All this he did meaning to kill the child as well as his father, for he was the falsest traitor that was ever born. Alas, for his goodness and for his good deeds this noble Prince Boudwin was killed. So when he came with his wife Anglides, the king put on a friendly face to them until they had dined. And when they had dined, King Mark sent for his brother and said this: "Brother, how did you fare when the unbelievers landed near you? It seems to me it was your duty to send me word, so that I could have been at that engagement, for it would have been right that I had the honour and not you."

"Sir," said Prince Boudwin, "it was like this: if I had waited until I had sent for you, those unbelievers would have destroyed my country."

"You lie, you false traitor," said King Mark, "for you are always out to win honour away from me, and to put me to dishonour, and you cherish what I hate."

And with that he stabbed him to the heart with a dagger, so that he never spoke a word after. Then the Lady Anglides grieved greatly, and fainted, for she saw her lord killed before her face. Then there was nothing more to be done, but Prince Boudwin was stripped and brought to burial. But Anglides secretly got hold of her husband's doublet and his shirt, and she kept them hidden.

Then there was much sorrow and weeping, and Sir Tristram, Sir Dinas and Sir Fergus grieved greatly, and so did all the knights who were there; for that prince was exceedingly well loved. So Isolde the Fair sent word to Anglides, Prince Boudwin's wife, and told her to leave quickly, or else her young son, Alisander le Orphelin, would be killed. When she heard this, she took her horse and her child, and rode away with such poor men as dared ride with her.

Chapter 33: How Anglides, Boudwin's wife, escaped with her young son, Alisander le Orphelin, and came to the Castle of Arundel

Even so, when King Mark had done this deed, he still meant to take more vengeance; and with his sword in his hand he went searching from room to room, looking for Anglides and her young son. And when she was found to be missing, he called a good knight who was called Sadok, and ordered him on pain of death to bring Anglides back, and her young son. So Sir Sadok set off and rode after Anglides. And within ten miles he overtook her, and told her to turn back and ride with him to King Mark.

"Alas, fair knight," she said, "what will you gain by my son's death, or by mine? I have had more than enough harm, and too great a loss."

"Madam," said Sadok, "your loss is a grief and a pity. But madam," said Sadok, "if you would leave this country with your son, and keep him until he comes of age, so that he may avenge his father's death, then I would let you go from me, provided you promise me to avenge the death of Prince Boudwin."

"Ah, noble knight, Jesus thank you! And if ever my son, Alisander le Orphelin, lives to be a knight, he shall have his father's doublet and his shirt with the bloody marks, and I will give him such a charge that he will remember it as long as he lives."

And with that Sadok parted from her, and each commended the other to God. And when Sadok came to King Mark, he told him on his faith that he had drowned young Alisander, her son; and King Mark was very glad of it.

Now we turn to Anglides, who rode both night and day wherever chance took her, out of Cornwall, and rested little and in few places; but all the while she made her way south towards the coast, until by fortune she came to a castle that was called Magouns, and is now called Arundel, in Sussex. And the Constable of the castle welcomed her, and said she was welcome to her own castle; and there Anglides was honourably received, for the Constable's wife was her close cousin, and the Constable's name was Bellangere; and that same Constable told Anglides that the castle was hers by right of inheritance. So Anglides lived there through years and winters, until Alisander was big and strong; there was no one so strong in all that country, and there was no one who could match him in any contest of strength.

Chapter 34: How Anglides gave the bloodstained doublet to her son Alisander on the day he was made a knight, and the charge that came with it

Then one day Bellangere the Constable came to Anglides and said, "Madam, it is time my lord Alisander was made a knight, for he is an exceedingly strong young man."

"Sir," she said, "I wish he were made a knight; but then I must give him the heaviest charge that ever a sinful mother gave to her child."

"Do as you please," said Bellangere, "and I will give him notice that he is to be made a knight. Now it would be well done for him to be made a knight on Our Lady's Day in Lent."

"So be it," said Anglides, "and I beg you to make ready for it."

So the Constable came to Alisander, and told him that he was to be made a knight on Our Lady's Day in Lent.

"I thank God," said Alisander. "This is the best news that ever came to me."

Then the Constable chose twenty of the sons of the greatest gentlemen, and the best-born men of the country, who were to be made knights on the same day that Alisander was made a knight. So on that same day, when Alisander and his twenty companions were made knights, at the offering of the mass Anglides came to her son and said this: "O fair sweet son, I charge you on my blessing, and by the high order of chivalry that you take on yourself here this day, that you understand what I am going to say, and the charge I am going to lay on you."

With that she pulled out a bloody doublet and a bloody shirt, all stained with old blood. When Alisander saw this he started back and turned pale, and said, "Fair mother, what can this mean?"

"I will tell you, fair son. This was your own father's doublet and shirt, which he wore on the very day that he was killed."

And there she told him why and for what reason, and how for his goodness King Mark killed him with his dagger before her own eyes. "And so this shall be the charge that I give you."

Chapter 35: How King Mark was told about Sir Alisander, and how he would have killed Sir Sadok for sparing his life

"Now I require you," his mother went on, "and I charge you on my blessing, and by the high order of knighthood, that you take revenge on King Mark for the death of your father."

And with that she fainted. Then Alisander leapt to his mother, and took her up in his arms, and said, "Fair mother, you have given me a great charge, and here I promise you I will be avenged on King Mark when I can; and that I promise to God and to you."

So this feast came to an end, and the Constable, on Anglides' advice, saw to it that Alisander was well horsed and armoured. Then he jousted with his twenty companions who had been made knights with him, and, to cut a long story short, he overthrew all twenty of them, so that not one could stand up to a single blow from him.

Then one of those knights went off to King Mark, and told him everything: how Alisander had been made a knight, and all the charge that his mother gave him, as you have heard before.

"Alas, false treason!" said King Mark. "I thought that young traitor was dead. Alas, whom can I trust?"

And with that King Mark took a sword in his hand, and went looking for Sir Sadok from room to room to kill him. When Sir Sadok saw King Mark coming with his sword in his hand, he said this: "Watch yourself, King Mark, and don't come near me; for know this, I saved Alisander's life, and I have never regretted it, for you falsely and cowardly killed his father Boudwin, like a traitor, for his good deeds; and so I pray Almighty Jesus to send Alisander the might and strength to be revenged on you. And now beware, King Mark, of young Alisander, for he has been made a knight."

"Alas," said King Mark, "that I should ever hear a traitor say such things to my face!"

And with that four of King Mark's knights drew their swords to kill Sir Sadok, but Sir Sadok at once killed them all in King Mark's presence. And then Sir Sadok went on into his room, and took his horse and his armour, and rode on his way at a good pace. For there was neither Sir Tristram, nor Sir Dinas, nor Sir Fergus who bore Sir Sadok any ill will. Then King Mark was angry, and thought to destroy Sir Alisander and Sir Sadok, who had saved him; for King Mark feared and hated Alisander more than any man alive.

When Sir Tristram understood that Alisander had been made a knight, he at once sent him a letter, begging him and charging him to make his way to King Arthur's court, and to put himself under the rule and into the hands of Sir Lancelot. So this letter was sent to Alisander from his cousin, Sir Tristram. And at that time he meant to do as he was told. Then King Mark called the knight who had brought him the news of Alisander, and told him to stay on in that country.

"Sir," said that knight, "so I must, for I dare not go back to my own country."

"No matter," said King Mark. "I will give you twice as much land here as you ever had of your own."

But within a short time Sir Sadok met that false knight, and killed him. Then King Mark was mad with rage beyond measure. Then he sent to Queen Morgan le Fay, and to the Queen of North Wales, begging them in his letters that the two of them, being sorceresses, would set the whole country alight with ladies who were enchantresses, and with such knights as were dangerous, like Malgrin and Breuse Saunce Pité, so that by no means should Alisander le Orphelin escape, but he should be either taken or killed. King Mark made this arrangement in order to destroy Alisander.

Chapter 36: How Sir Alisander won the prize at a tournament, and of Morgan le Fay, and how he fought with Sir Malgrin and slew him

Now we turn again to Sir Alisander, who at his departure took his father's bloody shirt with him from his mother. And he carried it with him always, until the day of his death, as a token to make him remember his father's death. So Alisander meant to ride to London, on Sir Tristram's advice, to Sir Lancelot. And by chance he went along the coast, and took the wrong road. And there he won the prize at a tournament that King Carados held. And there he struck down King Carados and twenty of his knights, and also Sir Safere, a good knight, who was the brother of Sir Palomides, the good knight. A damsel saw all this, and saw the best knight joust that she had ever seen. And each time he struck down a knight, he made him swear to wear no armour for a twelvemonth and a day.

"This is good news," said Morgan le Fay. "This is the knight I would very much like to see."

And so she took her palfrey, and rode a long while, and then she rested in her tent. Then four knights came there, two armed and two unarmed, and they told Morgan le Fay their names: the first was Elias de Gomeret, the second was Cari de Gomeret, and those were armed; the other two were from Cameliard, cousins of Queen Guinevere, and one was called Guy, and the other was called Garaunt, and those were unarmed. There these four knights told Morgan le Fay how a young knight had struck them down before a castle. "For the maiden of that castle said that he had only lately been made a knight, and was young. But as we see it, unless it were Sir Tristram, or Sir Lancelot, or Sir Lamorak, the good knight, there is no one who could stay in the saddle against a single blow of his spear."

"Well," said Morgan le Fay, "I shall meet that knight before long, if he stays in that country."

So we turn to the damsel of the castle, who, when Alisander le Orphelin had outjousted the four knights, called him to her, and said this: "Sir knight, will you, for my sake, joust and fight with a knight of this country who is, and has long been, a bad neighbour to me? His name is Malgrin, and he will not let me be married in any way, for all that I can do, nor will he let any knight have me."

"Damsel," said Alisander, "if he comes while I am here, I will fight with him, and for your sake I will risk my poor body."

And with that she sent for him, for he would come at her command. And when each caught sight of the other, they made ready to joust, and they came together eagerly, and Malgrin broke his spear on Alisander, and Alisander struck him back so hard that he carried him clean out of his saddle to the ground. But this Malgrin got up quickly, and set his shield and drew his sword, and told him to dismount, saying, "Though you have the better of me on horseback, you'll find that I will hold out like a knight on foot."

"Well said," said Alisander; and so he quickly got clear of his horse and handed it to his servant. And then they rushed together like two boars, and laid into each other's helms and shields for a long time, for the space of three hours, so that no one could ever say which was the better knight.

And in the meantime Morgan le Fay came to the damsel of the castle, and they watched the battle. But this Malgrin was a practised old knight, and he was counted one of the most dangerous knights in the world to fight on foot, though on horseback there were many better. And all the while this Malgrin watched for his chance to kill Alisander, and so he wounded him so terribly that it was a marvel he could stand at all, he had bled so much blood; for Alisander fought wildly, and not wisely. And the other was a savage knight, and watched his chance, and struck him hard. And sometimes they rushed together with their shields, like two boars or rams, and both fell flat on their faces on the ground.

"Now, knight," said Malgrin, "hold your hand a while, and tell me who you are."

"I will not," said Alisander, "unless I choose to. But tell me your name, and why you hold this country, or else you shall die at my hands."

"Know this," said Malgrin, "that for the love of this maiden of this castle I have killed ten good knights by mischance; and through my own violence and arrogance I have killed ten other knights."

"So help me God," said Alisander, "this is the foulest confession I ever heard a knight make, nor did I ever hear tell of other men making such a shameful confession; and so it would be a great pity and a great shame to me to let you live any longer. So guard yourself as well as you can, for as I am a true knight, either you shall kill me or else I shall kill you, I promise you faithfully."

Then they laid into each other fiercely, and at last Alisander struck Malgrin to the ground. And then he tore off his helm, and swiftly struck off his head. And when he had done and finished this battle, he at once called his servant to him, who brought him his horse. And then, thinking he was strong enough, he would have mounted. And so she laid Sir Alisander in a horse-litter, and took him into the castle, for he had neither foot nor strength to stand on the ground; for he had sixteen great wounds, and one of them in particular was likely to be his death.

Chapter 37: How Queen Morgan le Fay kept Alisander in her castle, and how she healed his wounds

Then Queen Morgan le Fay examined his wounds, and gave him such an ointment that he was likely to have died of it. And in the morning, when she came to him, he complained bitterly of the pain; and then she put other ointments on him, and then he was out of his pain. Then the damsel of the castle came, and said to Morgan le Fay, "I beg you, help me so that this knight will marry me, for he has won me with his own hands."

"You shall see," said Morgan le Fay, "what I will say."

Then Morgan le Fay went to Alisander, and told him that whatever happened he should refuse this lady "if she asks to marry you, for she is not for you."

So the damsel came and asked him to marry her.

"Damsel," said Orphelin, "I thank you, but as yet I have no mind to marry in this country."

"Sir," she said, "since you will not marry me, I beg you, seeing that you have won me, to give me to a knight of this country who has been my friend, and has loved me for many years."

"With all my heart," said Alisander. "I will agree to that."

Then the knight was sent for; his name was Gerine le Grose. And at once he betrothed them, and married them.

Then Queen Morgan le Fay came to Alisander, and told him to get up, and put him in a horse-litter, and gave him such a drink that for three days and three nights he never woke, but slept; and so she brought him to her own castle, which at that time was called La Beale Regard. Then Morgan le Fay came to Alisander, and asked him if he would like to be well.

"Who would be sick," said Alisander, "if he could be well?"

"Well," said Morgan le Fay, "then you shall promise me by your knighthood that for a twelvemonth and a day from today you will not go beyond the bounds of this castle, and without doubt you shall soon be well."

"I agree," said Sir Alisander.

And there he made her a promise, and then he was soon well. And when Alisander was well, then he regretted his oath, for he could not be revenged on King Mark. Just then there came a damsel who was a cousin of the Earl of Pase, and she was also a cousin of Morgan le Fay. And by right that castle of La Beale Regard should have been hers by true inheritance. So this damsel came into the castle where Alisander lay, and there she found him on his bed, exceedingly downcast and all gloomy.

Chapter 38: How Alisander was freed from Queen Morgan le Fay with the help of a damsel

"Sir knight," said the damsel, "if you would cheer up, I could tell you good news."

"It would be well with me," said Alisander, "if I could hear some good news, for now I stand here a prisoner by my own promise."

"Sir," she said, "you may be sure that you are a prisoner, and worse off than you think; for my lady, my cousin Queen Morgan le Fay, keeps you here for no other purpose than to have her pleasure of you when she feels like it."

"O Jesus defend me," said Alisander, "from such pleasure! For I would rather cut off my own privates than give her pleasure of that kind."

"As Jesus help me," said the damsel, "if you would love me and be guided by me, I will get you free with your honour intact."

"Tell me how," said Alisander, "and you shall have my love."

"Fair knight," she said, "this castle ought by right to be mine, and I have an uncle who is a mighty earl, the Earl of Pase, and of all people he hates Morgan le Fay most; and I will send to him and beg him for my sake to destroy this castle for the evil customs that are kept in it; and then he will come and set wildfire in every part of the castle, and I will get you out by a secret back gate, and there you shall have your horse and your armour."

"Well said, damsel," said Alisander.

And then she said, "You can keep to the ground of this castle for this twelvemonth and a day, and then you will not break your oath."

"Truly, fair damsel," said Alisander, "what you say is true."

And then he kissed her, and gave her pleasure, as it pleased them both, at times and at their leisure.

So at once she sent to her uncle and asked him to come and destroy that castle, for, as the book says, he would have destroyed that castle before, if it had not been for that damsel. When the earl understood her letters, he sent her word back that on such and such a day he would come and destroy that castle. So when that day came, she showed Alisander a back gate through which he was to escape into a garden, and there he would find his armour and his horse. When the appointed day came, the Earl of Pase came there with four hundred knights, and set fire to every part of the castle, so that before they stopped they had not left one stone standing. And all the while the fire was in the castle, he waited in the garden. And when the fire was over, he had it proclaimed that he would hold that piece of ground where the castle of La Beale Regard had stood for a twelvemonth and a day, against all knights who might come.

So it happened that there was a duke called Ansirus, and he was of Sir Lancelot's kin. And this knight was a great pilgrim, for every third year he would be at Jerusalem. And because all his life he made a habit of going on pilgrimage, people called him Duke Ansirus the Pilgrim. And this duke had a daughter called Alice, who was an exceedingly beautiful woman, and because of her father she was called Alice la Beale Pilgrim, the Fair Pilgrim. And as soon as she heard of this proclamation she went to Arthur's court, and said openly, in the hearing of many knights, that whatever knight could overcome the knight who held that piece of ground should have her and all her lands.

When the knights of the Round Table heard her say this, many of them were glad, for she was exceedingly beautiful and had great rents. Then she had it proclaimed in castles and towns on her side, just as fast as Alisander did on his side. Then she pitched her tent right beside the piece of ground that Alisander held. And she was no sooner there than a knight of Arthur's court came, who was called Sagramore le Desirous, and he offered to joust with Alisander; and they met, and Sagramore le Desirous broke his spear on Sir Alisander, but Sir Alisander struck him so hard that he was put out of his saddle. And when the fair Alice saw him joust so well, she thought him an exceedingly handsome knight on horseback. And then she leapt out of her tent, and took Sir Alisander by the bridle, and this is what she said: "Fair knight, I ask you by your knighthood, show me your face."

"I am not afraid," said Alisander, "to show my face."

And then he took off his helm; and when she saw his face, she said, "O sweet Jesus, you I must love, and never any other!"

"Then show me your face," he said.

Chapter 39: How Alisander met Alice la Beale Pilgrim, and how he jousted with two knights, and afterwards of him and Sir Mordred

Then she took the veil from her face. And when he saw her, he said, "Here I have found my love and my lady! Truly, fair lady," he said, "I promise you to be your knight, and no one else's who draws breath."

"Now, noble knight," she said, "tell me your name."

"My name," he said, "is Alisander le Orphelin. Now, damsel, tell me your name," he said.

"My name," she said, "is Alice la Beale Pilgrim. And when we are more at our hearts' ease, both you and I shall tell each other what blood we come from."

So there was great love between them. And as they were talking, there came a knight called Harsouse le Berbuse, and asked to break some of Sir Alisander's spears. Then Sir Alisander met him, and at the first encounter Sir Alisander struck him over his horse's rump. And then there came another knight called Sir Hewgon, and Sir Alisander struck him down as he had the other. Then Sir Hewgon offered to do battle on foot. Sir Alisander overcame him with three strokes, and would have killed him there if he had not yielded. So then Alisander made both those knights swear to wear no armour for a twelvemonth and a day.

Then Sir Alisander dismounted, and went to rest and refresh himself. Then the damsel who had helped Sir Alisander out of the castle, in her merriment, told Alice the whole story, how he had been a prisoner in the castle of La Beale Regard, and there she told her how she got him out of prison.

"Sir," said Alice la Beale Pilgrim, "it seems to me you are much indebted to this maiden."

"That is true," said Sir Alisander.

And there Alice told him what blood she came from. "Sir, you may be sure," she said, "that I am of the blood of King Ban, who was the father of Sir Lancelot."

"Truly, fair lady," said Alisander, "my mother told me that my father was a king's brother, and that I am a close cousin of Sir Tristram."

Then at this point there came three knights, one called Vains, and the second called Harvis de les Marches, and the third called Perin de la Montaine. And with one spear Sir Alisander struck all three of them down, and gave them such falls that they had no wish to fight on foot. So he made them swear to wear no arms for a twelvemonth. So when they had gone, Sir Alisander gazed at his lady Alice on horseback as he stood in her tent. And then he was so enamoured of her that he did not know whether he was on horseback or on foot.

Just then the false knight Sir Mordred came, and saw that Sir Alisander was besotted with his lady; and with that he took his horse by the bridle, and led him here and there, and had planned to lead him out of that place to shame him. When the damsel who had helped him out of that castle saw how shamefully he was being led, she at once had herself armed, and put a shield on her shoulder; and with that she mounted his horse, and took a naked sword in her hand, and she drove at Alisander with all her might, and she gave him such a blow that he thought the fire flew out of his eyes. And when Alisander felt that stroke, he looked around him, and drew his sword. And when she saw that, she fled, and so did Mordred, into the forest, and the damsel fled into the tent. So when Alisander understood for himself how the false knight would have shamed him, if it had not been for the damsel, then he was angry with himself that Sir Mordred had escaped his hands like that. But then Sir Alisander and Alice had a good laugh over the damsel, and how hard she had hit him on the helm.

Then Sir Alisander jousted like this day after day, and on foot he fought many battles with many knights of King Arthur's court, and with many strange knights. So to tell all the battles he fought would be too much to recount, for every day within that twelvemonth he fought with one knight or another, and some days he fought with three or four; and there was never a knight who got the better of him. And at the twelvemonth's end he left with his lady, Alice la Beale Pilgrim. And the damsel would never leave him, and so they went into their own country of Benwick, and lived there in great joy.

Chapter 40: How Sir Galahalt had a joust proclaimed in Surluse, where Queen Guinevere's knights would joust against all comers

But as the book says, King Mark would never stop until he had killed him by treason. And by Alice he had a son who was called Bellangere le Beuse. And by good fortune he came to the court of King Arthur, and proved an exceedingly good knight; and he avenged his father's death, for the false King Mark killed both Sir Tristram and Alisander, falsely and treacherously. And it so happened that Alisander never had the grace or the fortune to come to King Arthur's court. For if he had come to Sir Lancelot, so all the knights who knew him said, he was one of the strongest knights there were in Arthur's days; and great grief was made for him. So we will let him pass, and turn to another tale.

So it happened that Sir Galahalt, the high prince, was lord of the country of Surluse, from which came many good knights. And this noble prince was an exceedingly good man of arms, and he always kept a noble company of knights together. And then he came to Arthur's court and told him his purpose: that it was his wish to have a joust proclaimed in the country of Surluse, which country lay within the lands of King Arthur, and there he asked leave to have the joust proclaimed.

"I give you leave," said King Arthur, "but you may be sure," said King Arthur, "that I cannot be there."

"Sir," said Queen Guinevere, "if it please you, give me leave to be at that joust."

"With right good will," said Arthur, "for Sir Galahalt, the high prince, shall have you in his keeping."

"Sir," said Galahalt, "I will do as you wish."

"Sir," then said the queen, "I will take with me Sir Lancelot, and whatever knights please me best."

"Do as you like," said King Arthur.

So at once she commanded Sir Lancelot to make himself ready, with such knights as he thought best.

So in every good town and castle of this land a proclamation was made, that in the country of Surluse Sir Galahalt would hold a joust that would last eight days, and that the high prince, with the help of Queen Guinevere's knights, would joust against all kinds of men who cared to come. When this proclamation was known, kings and princes, dukes and earls, barons and noble knights made themselves ready to be at that joust. And on the day of the jousting Sir Dinadan came in disguised, and did many great deeds of arms.

Chapter 41: How Sir Lancelot fought in the tournament, and how Sir Palomides fought there for the sake of a damsel

Then, at the request of Queen Guinevere and of King Bagdemagus, Sir Lancelot came into the lists; but he was disguised, and that was why few people knew him. And there Sir Ector de Maris, his own brother, met him, and each broke his spear on the other right down to the hand. And then each of them got another spear. And then Sir Lancelot struck down Sir Ector de Maris, his own brother. Sir Bleoberis saw that, and he gave Sir Lancelot such a blow on the helm that he hardly knew where he was. Then Sir Lancelot was angry, and struck Sir Bleoberis so hard on the helm that his head bowed down backwards. And he struck him another blow, so that he was knocked clean out of his saddle; and so he rode by, and pushed on into the thickest of the fight. When the King of North Wales saw Sir Ector and Bleoberis lying on the ground, he was angry, for they had come in on his side against the men of Surluse. So the King of North Wales charged at Sir Lancelot and broke a spear on him all to pieces. With that Sir Lancelot caught up with the King of North Wales and gave him such a blow on the helm with his sword that he made him get clear of his horse; and at once the king was horsed again. So the party of King Bagdemagus and the party of the King of North Wales crashed into each other, and then a hard fight began; but the men of North Wales were far stronger.

When Sir Lancelot saw his side getting the worst of it, he pushed his way into the thick of the fighting with a sword in his hand; and there he struck down knights on the right hand and on the left, and pulled down knights and tore off their helms, so that everyone wondered that one knight could ever do such deeds of arms. When Sir Meliagaunce, who was the son of King Bagdemagus, saw how Sir Lancelot was faring, he marvelled greatly. And when he understood that it was he, he knew well that he was disguised on his account. Then Sir Meliagaunce asked a knight to kill Sir Lancelot's horse, either with a sword or with a spear. At that time King Bagdemagus met a knight called Sauseise, a good knight, to whom he said, "Now, fair Sauseise, meet my son Meliagaunce and give him a generous payment, for I wish he were well beaten by your hands, so that he might leave this field."

And then Sir Sauseise met Sir Meliagaunce, and each struck the other down. And then they fought on foot, and there Sauseise would have beaten Sir Meliagaunce, if a rescue had not come. So then the high prince sounded the end of the day, and every knight took off his armour and went to the great feast.

Meanwhile a damsel came to the high prince and complained that there was a knight called Goneries who kept all her lands from her. The knight was there present, and he threw down his glove to her, or to anyone who would fight in her name. So the damsel took up the glove very sorrowfully, for want of a champion. Then a young servant came to her and said, "Damsel, will you do as I tell you?"

"Very gladly," said the damsel.

"Then go to a certain knight who is lodging near here in a hermitage, and who follows the Questing Beast, and ask him to take the battle on himself; and I am sure he will grant it to you at once."

So at once she took her palfrey, and within a while she found that knight, and it was Sir Palomides. And when she asked him, he armed himself and rode with her, and made her go to the high prince and ask leave for her knight to do battle.

"Gladly," said the high prince.

Then the knights were ready in the field to joust on horseback; and each got a spear in his hand, and they met so fiercely that their spears shivered all to pieces. Then they snatched out their swords, and Sir Palomides struck Sir Goneries down to the earth. And then he tore off his helm and struck off his head. Then they went to supper, and the damsel loved Palomides as her lover, but the book says she was of his kin. So then Palomides disguised himself in this manner: on his shield he bore the Questing Beast, and on all his trappings too. And when he was ready in this way, he sent to the high prince to give him leave to joust with other knights; but he was afraid of Sir Lancelot. The high prince sent him word back that he would be welcome, and that Sir Lancelot would not joust with him. Then Sir Galahalt, the high prince, had it proclaimed that whatever knight struck down Sir Palomides should have his damsel for himself.

Chapter 42: How Sir Galahalt and Palomides fought each other, and of Sir Dinadan and Sir Galahalt

Here begins the second day. As soon as Sir Palomides came into the field, Sir Galahalt, the high prince, was at the end of the lists, and he met Sir Palomides, and Palomides him, with great spears. And they came together so hard that their spears shivered all to pieces; but Sir Galahalt struck him so hard that he bent him backwards over his horse, and yet he did not lose his stirrups. Then they drew their swords and laid into each other with many heavy blows, so that many honourable knights left what they were doing to watch them. But at last Sir Galahalt, the high prince, struck a mighty stroke at Palomides, hard upon the helm; but the helm was so hard that the sword could not bite, but slipped and struck off the head of Sir Palomides' horse. When the high prince knew and saw the good knight fall to the earth, he was ashamed of that stroke. And with that he got down off his own horse, and begged the good knight Palomides to take that horse as his gift, and to forgive him that deed.

"Sir," said Palomides, "I thank you for your great goodness, for from a man of honour a knight will never have dishonour."

And so he mounted that horse, and the high prince had another at once.

"Now," said the high prince, "I give up that maiden to you, for you have won her."

"Ah," said Palomides, "the damsel and I are both at your command."

So they parted, and Sir Galahalt did great deeds of arms. And just then Dinadan came and met Sir Galahalt, and they came at each other so hard with their spears that their spears broke right down to their hands. But Dinadan had expected the high prince to be more tired than he was. And then he struck many heavy blows at the high prince; but when Dinadan saw that he could not get him to the ground, he said, "My lord, please leave me alone, and take someone else."

The high prince did not know it was Dinadan, and let him go graciously because of his fair words. And so they parted; but soon someone came and told the high prince that it was Dinadan.

"Truly," said the prince, "I am sorry that he has got away from me like that, for now I shall never hear the end of his mocking and his jokes."

And then Galahalt rode fast after him, and called to him, "Stop, Dinadan, for King Arthur's sake!"

"No," said Dinadan, "so God help me, we are not meeting again today."

Then, in that anger, the high prince met Meliagaunce, and he struck him in the throat, so that if he had fallen his neck would have been broken; and with the same spear he struck down another knight. Then the men of North Wales and many strangers came in, and they were close to getting the better of the men of Surluse, for Sir Galahalt, the high prince, always had a great deal on his hands. So then the good knight Semound the Valiant came, with forty knights, and he drove them all back. Then Queen Guinevere and Sir Lancelot had the end of the day sounded, and every knight took off his armour and made ready for the feast.

Chapter 43: How Sir Archade accused Sir Palomides of treason, and how Sir Palomides slew him

When Palomides had taken off his armour, he asked for lodging for himself and the damsel. At once the high prince ordered them to be lodged. And he was hardly in his lodging when a knight came there called Archade, who was the brother of Goneries, whom Palomides had killed before in the damsel's quarrel. And this knight, Archade, called Sir Palomides a traitor, and accused him of his brother's death.

"With the high prince's leave," said Palomides, "I will answer you."

When Sir Galahalt understood their quarrel, he told them to go to dinner: "And as soon as you have dined, see that each knight is ready in the field."

So when they had dined they both armed themselves, and took their horses; and the queen, and the prince, and Sir Lancelot were seated to watch them. And so they let their horses run, and there Sir Palomides carried Archade on his spear over his horse's tail. And then Palomides got down and drew his sword, but Sir Archade could not get up; and there Sir Palomides tore off his helm and struck off his head. Then the high prince and Queen Guinevere went to supper. Then King Bagdemagus sent his son Meliagaunce away, so that Sir Lancelot would not meet him; for he hated Sir Lancelot, and Sir Lancelot did not know it.

Chapter 44: Of the third day, and how Sir Palomides jousted with Sir Lamorak, and other things

Now begins the third day of the jousting; and on that day King Bagdemagus made himself ready; and against him came King Marsil, who held an island as a gift from Sir Galahalt the high prince; and this island was called Pomitain. Then it happened that King Bagdemagus and King Marsil of Pomitain met with spears, and King Marsil took such a blow that he fell over his horse's rump. Then a knight of King Marsil's came in to avenge his lord, and King Bagdemagus struck him down, horse and man, to the earth. So there came an earl who was called Arrouse, and Sir Breuse, and a hundred knights of Pomitain with them, and the King of North Wales was with them; and all these were against the men of Surluse. And then a great battle began, and many knights were thrown under the horses' feet. And King Bagdemagus always did best, for he began first, and he always kept on. Gaheris, Gawain's brother, kept striking at King Bagdemagus' face; and at last King Bagdemagus hurled Gaheris down, horse and man.

Then by chance Sir Palomides, the good knight, met Sir Blamore de Ganis, Sir Bleoberis' brother. And each struck the other with great spears, so that both horses and knights fell to the earth. But Sir Blamore had such a fall that he almost broke his neck, for the blood burst out at his nose, his mouth and his ears; but in the end he recovered well, thanks to good surgeons. Then Duke Chaleins of Clarance came in; and under his command came a knight called Elis la Noire; and King Bagdemagus met him and struck Elis so that he made him leave his saddle. So Duke Chaleins of Clarance did great deeds of arms there, and for all that he came in so late on the third day, no man did as well as he except King Bagdemagus and Sir Palomides; and the prize that day was given to King Bagdemagus. And then they sounded the end of the day, and took off their armour, and went to the feast. Just then Dinadan came, and mocked and joked with King Bagdemagus until all the knights laughed at him; for he was a fine joker, and dearly loved all good knights.

So as soon as they had dined, a young servant came carrying four spears on his back; and he came to Palomides and said this: "There is a knight nearby who has sent you the choice of four spears, and asks you, for your lady's sake, to take one half of these spears and joust with him in the field."

"Tell him," said Palomides, "that I will not fail him."

When Sir Galahalt knew of this, he told Palomides to make himself ready. So Queen Guinevere, the high prince and Sir Lancelot were seated on the stands to judge these two knights. Then Sir Palomides and the strange knight ran at each other so eagerly that their spears broke right down to their hands. At once each of them took a great spear in his hand, and they shivered them all to pieces. And then each took a greater spear, and then the knight struck Sir Palomides down, horse and man, to the earth. And as he was passing over him, the strange knight's horse stumbled and fell down on Palomides. Then they drew their swords and laid into each other wonderfully hard for a long while.

Then the high prince and Sir Lancelot said they had never seen two knights fight better than they did; but the strange knight kept doubling his strokes, and drove Palomides back. With that the high prince cried, "Ho!" and then they went to their lodging. And when they had taken off their armour, they knew it was the noble knight Sir Lamorak. When Sir Lancelot knew it was Sir Lamorak, he made much of him, for above all men on earth he loved him best, except Sir Tristram. Then Queen Guinevere praised him, and so all the other good knights made much of him, except Sir Gawain's brothers. Then Queen Guinevere said to Sir Lancelot, "Sir, I ask you, if you joust any more, that you joust with none of the blood of my lord Arthur."

So he promised he would not, at least for that time.

Chapter 45: Of the fourth day, and of many great feats of arms

Here begins the fourth day. Then the King with the Hundred Knights came into the field, and all the men of North Wales, and Duke Chaleins of Clarance, and King Marsil of Pomitain; and there came Safere, Palomides' brother, and there he told him news of his mother. And his name was called the Earl, and so he accused him before King Arthur: "For he made war on our father and mother, and there I killed him in open battle."

So they went into the field, and the damsel with them; and against them came Sir Bleoberis de Ganis and Sir Ector de Maris. Sir Palomides met Sir Bleoberis, and each struck the other down. And in the same way did Sir Safere and Sir Ector, and the two pairs fought on foot. Then Sir Lamorak came in, and he met the King with the Hundred Knights and struck him clean over his horse's tail. And in the same way he served the King of North Wales, and he also struck down King Marsil. And so, before ever he stopped, he struck down thirty knights with his spear and his sword. When Duke Chaleins saw Lamorak do such great feats, he would not meddle with him, for shame; and then he charged all his knights on pain of death: "None of you touch him; for it would be a shame to all good knights if that knight were shamed."

Then the two kings gathered their men together, and they all set upon Sir Lamorak; and he did not fail them, but rushed here and there, striking on the right hand and on the left, and tore off many helms, so that the high prince and Queen Guinevere said they had never seen a knight do such deeds of arms on horseback.

"Alas," said Lancelot to King Bagdemagus, "I will arm myself and help Sir Lamorak."

"And I will ride with you," said King Bagdemagus.

And when the two of them were mounted they came to Sir Lamorak, who stood among thirty knights; and happy was the man who could reach him with a blow, and he always struck back mightily. Then Sir Lancelot came into the thick of the fighting, and he threw down Sir Mador de la Porte. And with the broken shaft of that spear he threw down many knights. And King Bagdemagus struck on the left hand and on the right marvellously well. And then the three kings fell back. With that Sir Galahalt had the end of the day sounded, and all the heralds gave Sir Lamorak the prize. And all this while Palomides, Sir Bleoberis, Sir Safere and Sir Ector fought on foot; there were never four knights more evenly matched. And then they were parted, and taken to their lodging, and took off their armour, and so they went to the great feast.

But when Sir Lamorak had come into the court, Queen Guinevere took him in her arms and said, "Sir, you have done well this day."

Then the high prince came, and he rejoiced greatly over him, and so did Dinadan, for he wept for joy; but the joy that Sir Lancelot made over Sir Lamorak there no man could tell. Then they went to rest, and in the morning the high prince had the trumpets sound for the field.

Chapter 46: Of the fifth day, and how Sir Lamorak bore himself

Here begins the fifth day. So it happened that Sir Palomides came out in the morning and offered to joust where King Arthur was, in a castle near Surluse; and there an honourable duke met him, and there Sir Palomides struck him over his horse's rump. And this duke was King Arthur's uncle. Then Sir Elise's son rode at Palomides, and Palomides served Elise the same way. When Sir Uwain saw this he was angry. Then he took his horse and met Sir Palomides, and Palomides struck him so hard that he went to the earth, horse and man. And to cut a long story short, he struck down three of Sir Gawain's brothers, that is to say Mordred, Gaheris and Agravain.

"O Jesus," said Arthur, "this is a great insult, that a Saracen should strike down my blood."

And with that King Arthur was mad with rage, and meant to make himself ready to joust. Sir Lamorak saw that, that Arthur and his blood were beaten; and at once he was ready, and asked Palomides if he would joust any more.

"Why shouldn't I?" said Palomides.

Then they crashed together, and broke their spears, and shivered them all to pieces, so that the whole castle rang with their blows. Then each got a greater spear in his hand, and they came together so fiercely; but Sir Palomides' spear burst all to pieces, and Sir Lamorak's held. With that Sir Palomides lost his stirrups and lay stretched out flat on his horse's back. And then Sir Palomides turned back and took his damsel, and Sir Safere went his way.

So, when he had gone, King Arthur came to Sir Lamorak and thanked him for his goodness, and begged him to tell him his name.

"Sir," said Lamorak, "you may be sure I owe you my service, but at this time I will not stay here, for I see many of my enemies about me."

"Alas," said Arthur, "now I know well that it is Sir Lamorak de Galis. O Lamorak, stay with me, and by my crown I shall never fail you; and let Gawain not dare, on his head, nor any of his brothers, to do you any wrong."

"Sir," said Sir Lamorak, "they have done me wrong, and you too."

"That is true," said the king, "for they killed their own mother, my sister, which grieves me sorely. It would have been much fairer and better if you had married her, for you are a king's son as well as they are."

"O Jesus," said the noble knight Sir Lamorak to Arthur, "I shall never forget her death. I promise you, and I swear it to God, I shall avenge her death as soon as I see a fitting time. And if it were not out of reverence for your highness, I would already have been avenged on Sir Gawain and his brothers."

"Truly," said Arthur, "I will make peace between you."

"Sir," said Lamorak, "at this time I cannot stay with you, for I must go to the jousts, where Sir Lancelot is, and the high prince Sir Galahalt."

Now there was a damsel who was the daughter of King Bandes. And there was a Saracen knight called Corsabrin, and he loved the damsel, and he would on no account allow her to be married; for this Corsabrin was always spreading rumours about her, and giving out that she was out of her mind; and in this way he kept her from being married.

Chapter 47: How Sir Palomides fought with Corsabrin over a lady, and how Palomides slew Corsabrin

So by chance this damsel heard tell that Palomides did much for damsels' sake; so she sent him a pennon, a small streamer for his spear, and begged him to fight Sir Corsabrin for her love, and he should have her, and the lands of her father's that would come to her. Then the damsel sent to Corsabrin and told him to go to Sir Palomides, who was a pagan as well as he; and she warned him that she had sent Palomides her pennon, and that if he could overcome Palomides she would marry him. When Corsabrin knew what she had done, he was mad with rage and anger, and rode to Surluse, where the high prince was, and there he found Sir Palomides ready, and he had the pennon. So there they pledged battle with each other before Galahalt.

"Well," said the high prince, "today noble knights must joust, and after dinner we shall see how you can fare."

Then they sounded for the jousts; and in came Dinadan, and met Sir Gerin, a good knight, and he threw him down over his horse's rump; and Sir Dinadan overthrew four more knights; and there he did great deeds of arms, for he was a good knight, but he was a scoffer and a joker, and the merriest knight in company who was living at that time. And he had this way about him, that he loved every good knight, and every good knight loved him back. So then, when the high prince saw Dinadan do so well, he sent to Sir Lancelot and told him to strike down Sir Dinadan: "And when you have done so, bring him before me and the noble Queen Guinevere."

Then Sir Lancelot did as he was asked. Then he and Sir Lamorak struck down many knights, and tore off helms, and drove all the knights before them. And so Sir Lancelot struck down Sir Dinadan, and had his men unarm him, and so brought him to the queen and the high prince, and they laughed at Dinadan so hard that they could not stand.

"Well," said Sir Dinadan, "I'm still not ashamed, for it was that old rascal Sir Lancelot who struck me down."

So they went to dinner, and the whole court had good sport with Dinadan.

Then, when dinner was done, they sounded for the field, to watch Sir Palomides and Corsabrin. Sir Palomides planted his pennon in the middle of the field; and then they crashed together with their spears like thunder, and each struck the other to the earth. And then they pulled out their swords, and set their shields, and laid into each other mightily, as mighty knights, so that there was hardly a piece of armour that would hold on them; for this Corsabrin was an exceedingly cruel knight.

"Corsabrin," said Palomides, "will you give up that damsel over there to me, and the pennon?"

Then Corsabrin was angry beyond measure, and gave Palomides such a blow that he went down on one knee. Then Palomides got up quickly, and struck him on the helm so that he fell flat to the earth. And with that he tore off his helm and said, "Corsabrin, yield, or you will die by my hands."

"Shame on you," said Corsabrin. "Do your worst."

Then he struck off his head. And with that there came such a stink from his body, when the soul left it, that nobody could stand the smell. So the corpse was taken away and buried in a wood, because he was a pagan. Then they sounded the end of the day, and Palomides took off his armour.

Then he went to Queen Guinevere, to the high prince and to Sir Lancelot.

"Sir," said the high prince, "today you have seen a great miracle in Corsabrin, what a smell there was when the soul left the body. So, sir, we would ask you to take baptism upon you, and I promise you all knights will think the more of you, and speak the more of your honour."

"Sir," said Palomides, "I want you all to know that I came into this land to be christened, and in my heart I am christened, and christened I will be. But I have made such a vow that I may not be christened until I have fought seven true battles for Jesus' sake, and then I will be christened; and I trust God will accept my intent, for I mean it truly."

Then Sir Palomides asked Queen Guinevere and the high prince to have supper with him. And so they did, and Sir Lancelot and Sir Lamorak too, and many other good knights. So in the morning they heard their mass, and the trumpets sounded for the field, and then the knights made themselves ready.

Chapter 48: Of the sixth day, and what was done then

Here begins the sixth day. Then Sir Gaheris came in, and Sir Ossaise of Surluse met him there, and Sir Gaheris struck him over his horse's rump. And then each side charged the other, and many spears were broken there, and many knights thrown under the horses' feet. So then Sir Durnore and Sir Aglovale came in, who were brothers of Sir Lamorak, and they met two other knights, and each pair struck each other so hard that all four knights and their horses fell to the earth. When Sir Lamorak saw his two brothers down he was angry beyond measure; and then he got a great spear in his hand, and with it he struck down four good knights, and then his spear broke. Then he pulled out his sword, and struck about him on the right hand and on the left, and tore off helms and pulled down knights, so that everyone marvelled at such deeds of arms as he did; for he carried on so that many knights fled. Then he put his brothers back on their horses, and said, "Brothers, you ought to be ashamed to fall off your horses like that! What is a knight, except when he is on horseback? I think nothing of a knight when he is on foot, for all battles on foot are no better than plunderers' brawls. For no knight should fight on foot unless it is for treason, or else he is driven to it by force; so, brothers, sit tight on your horses, or else never fight again in front of me."

With that Duke Chaleins of Clarance came in, and the Earl Ulbawes of Surluse met him, and each of them struck the other down. Then the knights of both sides put their lords back on their horses; for Sir Ector and Bleoberis were on foot, attending on Duke Chaleins. And the King with the Hundred Knights was with the Earl Ulbawes. With that Gaheris came and laid into the King with the Hundred Knights, and he into him. Then Duke Chaleins came and parted them.

Then they sounded the end of the day, and the knights took off their armour and went to their dinner; and in the middle of their dinner in came Dinadan and began to make fun of everyone. Then he looked at the high prince, who seemed angry over some fault he had found; for it was his way that he loved no fish, and because he had been served fish, which he hated, he was not cheerful. When Sir Dinadan had noticed the high prince, he spotted a fish with a great head, and he got it between two dishes and served the high prince with that fish. And then he said this: "Sir Galahalt, I may well compare you to a wolf, for a wolf will never eat fish, only meat."

Then the high prince laughed at his words.

"Well, well," said Dinadan to Lancelot, "what the devil are you doing in this country? For no ordinary knight can win any honour here because of you."

"Sir Dinadan," said Lancelot, "I promise you I shall never meet you again, nor that great spear of yours, for I can't stay in my saddle when that spear hits me. And if I have any luck, I shall keep well clear of that big rough body you carry around."

"Well," said Dinadan, "keep a good lookout always. God forbid that we ever meet, unless it is over a dish of meat."

Then the queen and the high prince laughed so hard that they could not sit at their table; and so they made great merriment until the morning, and then they heard mass, and the trumpets sounded for the field. And Queen Guinevere and all the great lords were seated, and judges in full armour with their shields, to see fair play.

Chapter 49: Of the seventh battle, and how Sir Lancelot, disguised as a maiden, struck down Sir Dinadan

Now begins the seventh battle. Duke Cambines came in, and Sir Aristance, who was reckoned a good knight, met him there, and they met so hard that each bore the other down, horse and man. Then the Earl of Lambaile came and helped the duke back on his horse. Then Sir Ossaise of Surluse came, and he struck the Earl of Lambaile down from his horse. Then they began to do great deeds of arms, and many spears were broken, and many knights were thrown to the earth. Then the King of North Wales and the Earl Ulbawes struck each other so hard that all the judges thought it was like to be the death of them. Meanwhile Queen Guinevere, and the high prince, and Sir Lancelot made Sir Dinadan get ready to joust there.

"I would ride into the field," said Dinadan, "but then one of you two will meet me."

"By God," said the high prince, "you can see how we sit here as judges with our shields, and you can always look and see whether we are sitting here or not."

So Sir Dinadan left and took his horse, and met many knights, and did exceedingly well. And when he had gone, Sir Lancelot disguised himself, and put a maiden's gown over his armour, freshly dressed up. Then Sir Lancelot had Sir Galihodin lead him through the lists, and everyone wondered what damsel it was. And so, as Sir Dinadan came into the lists, Sir Lancelot, in the damsel's dress, got Galihodin's spear and charged at Sir Dinadan. And all the while Sir Dinadan kept looking up at the place where Sir Lancelot had been, and he saw someone sitting armed in Sir Lancelot's place. But when Dinadan saw a sort of damsel, he was afraid it might be Sir Lancelot in disguise; but Sir Lancelot came at him so fast that he struck him over his horse's rump. And then, with great mockery, they got Sir Dinadan into the forest nearby, and there they stripped him down to his shirt, and put a woman's gown on him, and so brought him into the field; and so they sounded the end of the day. And every knight went and took off his armour. Then Sir Dinadan was brought in among them all. And when Queen Guinevere saw Sir Dinadan brought in among them all like that, she laughed until she fell down, and so did everyone who was there.

"Well," said Dinadan to Lancelot, "you are such a cheat that I can never be on my guard against you."

Then by general agreement they gave Sir Lancelot the prize; the next was Sir Lamorak de Galis, the third was Sir Palomides, the fourth was King Bagdemagus. So these four knights had the prize, and there was great joy, and great splendour in all the court.

And in the morning Queen Guinevere and Sir Lancelot went back to King Arthur; but Sir Lamorak would on no account go with them.

"I will undertake," said Sir Lancelot, "that if you will come with us, King Arthur shall order Sir Gawain and his brothers never to do you harm."

"As for that," said Sir Lamorak, "I will not trust Sir Gawain nor any of his brothers. And you may be sure, Sir Lancelot, that if it were not for my lord King Arthur's sake, I would be a match for Sir Gawain and his brothers well enough. But as for saying that I should trust them, that I never shall; and so I ask you to commend me to my lord Arthur, and to all my lords of the Round Table. And wherever I may come, I shall do you service to the best of my power. And, sir, it was only lately that I avenged that, when my lord Arthur's kin were put to the worse by Sir Palomides."

Then Sir Lamorak parted from Sir Lancelot, and each of them wept at their parting.

Chapter 50: How Sir Tristram was treacherously lured to a tournament to be killed there, and how he was thrown into prison

Now we turn from this matter and speak of Sir Tristram, whom this book is chiefly about, and we leave the king and the queen, Sir Lancelot and Sir Lamorak. And here begins the treason of King Mark, which he plotted against Sir Tristram. A great tournament and jousts were proclaimed along the coasts of Cornwall, and it was all done by Sir Galahalt the high prince and King Bagdemagus, with the intent of killing Lancelot, or else utterly destroying and shaming him; because Sir Lancelot always won the higher prize, this prince and this king held this joust against Sir Lancelot. And so their plan was revealed to King Mark, at which he was very glad.

Then King Mark thought he would have Sir Tristram come to that tournament disguised, so that no man would know him, with the intent that the high prince would think Sir Tristram was Sir Lancelot. So Sir Tristram came in at these jousts. And at that time Sir Lancelot was not there; but when they saw a disguised knight do such deeds of arms, they thought it was Sir Lancelot. And King Mark in particular said plainly that it was Sir Lancelot. Then they set upon him, both King Bagdemagus and the high prince and their knights, so that it was a wonder that Sir Tristram could ever endure that pain. Nevertheless, for all the pain he had, Sir Tristram won the prize at that tournament; and there he hurt many knights and bruised them, and they hurt him and bruised him wonderfully badly. So when the jousts were all over, they knew well that it was Sir Tristram de Liones; and all who were on King Mark's side were glad that Sir Tristram was hurt, and the rest were sorry for his hurt; for Sir Tristram was not so hated within the realm of England as Sir Lancelot was.

Then King Mark came to Sir Tristram and said, "Fair nephew, I am sorry for your hurts."

"Many thanks, my lord," said Sir Tristram.

Then King Mark had Sir Tristram put in a horse-litter, as a great sign of love, and said, "Fair cousin, I will be your doctor myself."

And so he rode off with Sir Tristram, and brought him to a castle while it was still daylight. And then King Mark had Sir Tristram eat. And then afterwards he gave him a drink, and as soon as he had drunk it he fell asleep. And when it was night, he had him carried to another castle, and there he put him in a strong prison, and there he appointed a man and a woman to give him his food and drink. So there he stayed a long while.

Then Sir Tristram was missed, and no one knew what had become of him. When Isolde the Fair heard how he was missing, she went secretly to Sir Sadok and begged him to find out where Sir Tristram was. Then, when Sadok knew how Sir Tristram was missing, he soon found out that he had been put in prison by King Mark and the traitors of Magouns. Then Sadok and two of his cousins lay in ambush, in arms, close by the castle of Tintagil. And as fortune would have it, King Mark came riding by with four of his nephews, and some of the traitors of Magouns. When Sir Sadok saw them, he broke out of the ambush and set upon them there. And when King Mark saw Sir Sadok, he fled as fast as he could; and there Sir Sadok killed all four of King Mark's nephews. But these traitors of Magouns killed one of Sadok's cousins with a great wound in the neck; but Sadok struck the other dead. Then Sir Sadok rode on his way to a castle that was called Liones, and there he found out about the treason and villainy of King Mark. So the men of that castle rode with Sir Sadok until they came to a castle called Arbray; and there in the town they found Sir Dinas the Seneschal, who was a good knight. But when Sir Sadok had told Sir Dinas all about King Mark's treason, he renounced such a king, and said he would give up the lands he held from him. And when he said these words, all the knights there said as Sir Dinas said. Then, on his advice and on Sir Sadok's, he had all the towns and castles in the country of Liones stocked and armed, and gathered all the people they could muster.

Chapter 51: How King Mark had letters forged from the Pope, and how Sir Percival freed Sir Tristram from prison

Now we turn to King Mark. When he had escaped from Sir Sadok he rode to the Castle of Tintagil, and there he raised a great cry and clamour, and called to arms everyone who could bear them. Then they searched and found where four of King Mark's cousins lay dead, and the traitor of Magouns. Then the king had them buried in a chapel. Then the king had it proclaimed through all the country that held of him that they should take up arms, for he understood that he had no choice but to go to war. When King Mark heard and understood how Sir Sadok and Sir Dinas had risen in the country of Liones, he turned his mind to wiles and treason. And this is what he did: he had letters made and forged as if from the Pope, and had a clerk who was a stranger bring them to King Mark; and these letters said that King Mark must make himself ready, on pain of excommunication, to come to the Pope with his army, to help go to Jerusalem and make war on the Saracens.

When this clerk had come, as the king had arranged, King Mark at once sent these letters on to Sir Tristram, and told the clerk to say this: that if he would go to war against the unbelievers, he would be let out of prison and have all his power back. When Sir Tristram understood this letter, he said to the clerk, "Ah, King Mark, you have always been a traitor, and you always will be. But, Clerk," said Sir Tristram, "say this to King Mark: since the Apostolic Pope has sent for him, tell him to go there himself. For tell him, traitor king that he is, I will not go at his command, whether I get out of prison or not, for I can see I am well rewarded for my true service."

Then the clerk went back to King Mark, and told him Sir Tristram's answer.

"Well," said King Mark, "he shall be tricked yet."

So he went into his chamber and forged more letters; and these letters said that the Pope wanted Sir Tristram to come himself, to make war on the unbelievers. When the clerk had come back to Sir Tristram and given him these letters, Sir Tristram looked at them, and saw at once that they were King Mark's forgeries.

"Ah," said Sir Tristram, "you have always been false, King Mark, and false you will end."

Then the clerk left Sir Tristram and went back to King Mark.

By then four wounded knights had come into the Castle of Tintagil, and one of them had his neck nearly broken in two. Another had his arm cut off, the third had been run through with a spear, the fourth had his teeth knocked in two. And when they came before King Mark they cried out, "King, why don't you run? The whole country has risen against you!"

Then King Mark was angry beyond measure.

And in the meantime Sir Percival de Galis came into the country to look for Sir Tristram. And when he heard that Sir Tristram was in prison, Sir Percival freed him outright by his knightly skill. And when Sir Tristram was free he rejoiced greatly over Sir Percival, and so did each of them over the other.

Sir Tristram said to Sir Percival, "If you will stay in these borderlands I will ride with you."

"No," said Percival, "I cannot stay in this country, for I must go into Wales."

So Sir Percival left Sir Tristram, and rode straight to King Mark, and told him how he had freed Sir Tristram. And he also told the king that he had done himself great shame in putting Sir Tristram in prison, "for he is now the most renowned knight living in this world. And believe me, the noblest knights in the world love Sir Tristram, and if he makes war on you, you will not be able to hold out against it."

"That is true," said King Mark, "but I cannot love Sir Tristram, because he loves my queen and my wife, Isolde the Fair."

"Ah, shame on you," said Sir Percival, "never say such a thing again. Aren't you Sir Tristram's uncle, and he your nephew? You should never think that so noble a knight as Sir Tristram would do himself so great a dishonour as to take his uncle's wife. All the same," said Sir Percival, "he may love your queen without sin, because she is said to be one of the most beautiful ladies in the world."

Then Sir Percival left King Mark. And when he had gone, King Mark turned his mind to more treason, even though King Mark had promised Sir Percival never, by any means whatever, to harm Sir Tristram. So at once King Mark sent word to Sir Dinas the Seneschal that he should disband all the people he had raised, for he sent him an oath that he would go himself to the Pope of Rome to make war on the unbelievers, "and this is a fairer war than raising the people against your king like this." When Sir Dinas understood that King Mark would go against the unbelievers, Sir Dinas in all haste disbanded all the people. And when the people had gone off, every man to his home, King Mark found out where Sir Tristram was with Isolde the Fair; and there, by treason, King Mark had him seized and put in prison, against the promise he had made to Sir Percival.

When Queen Isolde understood that Sir Tristram was in prison she grieved as much as ever any lady or gentlewoman grieved. Then Sir Tristram sent a letter to Isolde the Fair, and begged her to be his good lady; and if it pleased her to have a ship made ready for her and for him, he would go with her to the realm of Logres, that is, this land. When Isolde the Fair understood Sir Tristram's letter and what he meant, she sent him another, and told him to take heart, for she would have the ship made ready, and everything that was needed.

Then Isolde the Fair sent to Sir Dinas, and to Sadok, and begged them by all means to seize King Mark and put him in prison until she and Sir Tristram had left for the realm of Logres. When Sir Dinas the Seneschal understood King Mark's treason he gave her his promise in return, and sent her word that King Mark would be put in prison. And as they planned it, so it was done. And then Sir Tristram was freed from prison; and at once, in all haste, Queen Isolde and Sir Tristram went and decided whom they would take with them when they left.

Chapter 52: How Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair came to England, and how Sir Lancelot brought them to Joyous Gard

Then Isolde the Fair and Sir Tristram took their ship, and came by water into this land. And they had not been four days in this land before a jousting and tournament was proclaimed that King Arthur had ordered. When Sir Tristram heard of that tournament he disguised himself, and Isolde the Fair too, and rode to that tournament. And when he came there he saw many knights jousting and tourneying; and so Sir Tristram took his place on the field, and to cut a long story short, he overthrew fourteen knights of the Round Table. When Sir Lancelot saw these knights overthrown like this, Sir Lancelot squared up to Sir Tristram. Isolde the Fair saw that Sir Lancelot had come onto the field. Then Isolde the Fair sent Sir Lancelot a ring, and let him know that it was Sir Tristram de Liones. When Sir Lancelot understood that it was Sir Tristram he was very glad, and would not joust. Then Sir Lancelot watched where Sir Tristram went, and rode after him; and then each of them rejoiced greatly over the other. And so Sir Lancelot brought Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair to Joyous Gard, which was his own castle, that he had won with his own hands. And there Sir Lancelot gave it to them to hold as their own. And believe me, that castle was stocked and furnished for a king and a royal queen to stay in. And Sir Lancelot charged all his people to honour them and love them as they would himself.

So Sir Lancelot went off to King Arthur; and then he told Queen Guinevere that the man who had jousted so well at the last tournament was Sir Tristram. And there he told her how Sir Tristram had Isolde the Fair with him in spite of King Mark, and so Queen Guinevere told all this to King Arthur. When King Arthur knew that Sir Tristram had escaped and come away from King Mark, and had brought Isolde the Fair with him, he was exceedingly glad. So because of Sir Tristram King Arthur had it proclaimed that on May Day there would be a jousting before the castle of Lonazep; and that castle was close by Joyous Gard. And this is how Arthur arranged it: that all the knights of this land, and of Cornwall, and of North Wales, would joust against all these countries, Ireland, Scotland and the rest of Wales, and the country of Gore, and Surluse, and Listinoise, and the men of Northumberland, and all those who held lands of Arthur on this side of the sea. When this proclamation was made many knights were glad and many were not.

"Sir," said Lancelot to Arthur, "by this proclamation you have made, you will put us who are around you in great danger, for there are many knights who are bitterly jealous of us. So when we meet on the day of the jousting there will be hard going among us."

"As for that," said Arthur, "I don't care. There we shall prove who is best with his hands."

So when Sir Lancelot understood why King Arthur was holding this jousting, he made such provision that Isolde the Fair could watch the jousts from a private place that was fitting for her rank.

Now we turn to Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair, and how they took great joy together every day, with every kind of pleasure they could devise.
