And every day Sir Tristram would go riding out hunting, for at that time Sir Tristram was called the best huntsman in the world, and the finest blower of a horn in every kind of measure. For as the books report, from Sir Tristram came all the good terms of venery and hunting, and all the lengths and measures of blowing a horn; and from him we first had all the terms of hawking, and which were beasts of the chase and which were beasts of venery, and which were vermin, and all the horn calls that belong to every kind of game: first the call for the uncoupling of the hounds, then for the seeking, the rechate (the call that brings the hounds back), the call for the flight, for the death, and the strake, and many other calls and terms, so that every gentleman has reason, to the world's end, to praise Sir Tristram and to pray for his soul.

Chapter 53: How Sir Tristram, on the advice of Isolde the Fair, rode out in armour, and how he met Sir Palomides

So one day Isolde the Fair said to Sir Tristram, "I am very surprised," she said, "that you don't keep in mind that you are here in a strange country, and there are many dangerous knights here; and you know well that King Mark is full of treason. If you go riding to chase and hunt unarmed like this, you could be killed."

"My fair lady and my love, I beg your pardon. I will not do it any more."

So from then on Sir Tristram rode hunting every day in armour, with his men carrying his shield and his spear. So one day, a little before the month of May, Sir Tristram was chasing a hart exceedingly eagerly, and the hart ran past a fair spring. And then Sir Tristram got down and took off his helmet to drink of that bubbling water. Just then he heard and saw the Questing Beast come to the spring. When Sir Tristram saw that beast he put on his helmet, for he thought he would hear of Sir Palomides, since that beast was his quest. Just then Sir Tristram saw a knight in armour coming, on a noble warhorse, and he greeted him, and they talked of many things; and this knight's name was Breuse Saunce Pité. And just then the noble knight Sir Palomides came up to them, and each greeted the other, and spoke courteously to the other.

"Fair knights," said Sir Palomides, "I can tell you some news."

"What is that?" said those knights.

"Sirs, believe me, King Mark has been put in prison by his own knights, and it was all for love of Sir Tristram. For King Mark had put Sir Tristram in prison twice, and once Sir Percival freed the noble knight Sir Tristram from prison. And the last time Queen Isolde the Fair freed him, and went clean away with him into this realm; and all this while King Mark, the false traitor, is in prison."

"Is this true?" said Palomides. "Then we shall soon hear of Sir Tristram. And as for saying that I love Isolde the Fair as my lady-love, I dare stand by it that I do, and that she has my service above all other ladies, and will have it for the rest of my life."

And just as they stood talking they saw a knight in full armour coming towards them on a great horse, and one of his men carried his shield, and the other his spear. And as soon as that knight saw them he took his shield and his spear and made ready to joust.

"Fair fellows," said Sir Tristram, "there is a knight over there who will joust with us. Let's see which of us shall meet him, for I can see well that he is of King Arthur's court."

"It won't be long before he is met," said Sir Palomides, "for in my quest of this barking beast I never found a knight who wanted to joust that I refused."

"I could follow that beast as well as you," said Breuse Saunce Pité.

"Then you will fight me," said Palomides.

So Sir Palomides squared up to that other knight, Sir Bleoberis, who was a very noble knight, close kin to Sir Lancelot. And they met so hard that Sir Palomides fell to the ground, horse and all.

Then Sir Bleoberis cried aloud, "Get ready, you false traitor knight, Breuse Saunce Pité! For you may be sure I will fight you to the uttermost, for the noble knights and ladies you have falsely betrayed."

When this false knight and traitor, Breuse Saunce Pité, heard him say so, he took his horse by the bridle and fled as fast as ever his horse could run, for he was badly afraid of him. When Sir Bleoberis saw him flee he followed hard after, through thick and through thin. And by chance, as Sir Breuse fled, he saw just ahead of him three knights of the Round Table, of whom the first was called Sir Ector de Maris, the second Sir Percival de Galis, the third Sir Harry le Fise Lake, a good knight and a bold one. And as for Sir Percival, he was called in his time one of the best knights in the world, and the steadiest. When Breuse saw these knights he rode straight up to them, and cried out to them and begged them to rescue him.

"What do you need?" said Sir Ector.

"Ah, fair knights," said Sir Breuse, "the most treacherous knight there is is following me, the most cowardly and the most villainous; his name is Breuse Saunce Pité, and if he can catch me he will kill me without mercy or pity."

"Stay with us," said Sir Percival, "and we will protect you."

Then they caught sight of Sir Bleoberis, who came riding as fast as he could. Then Sir Ector put himself forward to joust ahead of them all. When Sir Bleoberis saw that they were four knights and he only one, he was in doubt whether to turn back or hold his course.

Then he said to himself, "I am a knight of the Round Table, and rather than shame my oath and my blood I will hold my course, whatever comes of it."

And then Sir Ector lowered his spear, and they struck each other exceedingly hard, but Sir Ector fell to the ground. Sir Percival saw that, and he drove his horse at him as hard as it could go, but Sir Percival took such a stroke that horse and man fell to the ground.

When Sir Harry saw that they were both on the ground, he said to himself, "Breuse was never so strong as this."

So Sir Harry turned his horse, and they met together so strongly that both the horses and the knights fell to the ground, but Sir Bleoberis's horse began to get up again. Breuse saw that, and he came crashing in, and knocked him over and over, and would have killed him as he lay on the ground. Then Sir Harry le Fise Lake got up swiftly, and took the bridle of Sir Breuse's horse, and said, "Shame on you! Never strike a knight when he is on the ground. For this knight cannot be called a shameful knight for his deeds, since, as anyone can see, even lying there on the ground he has fought honourably and got the better of exceedingly good knights."

"I won't stop for that," said Sir Breuse.

"You have no choice," said Sir Harry, "for now."

Then, when Sir Breuse saw that he had no choice and could not have his way, he spoke politely. Then Sir Harry let him go. And then at once he rode his horse over Sir Bleoberis, and dashed him to the ground as if he meant to kill him.

When Sir Harry saw him act so basely he cried, "Traitor knight, stop, for shame!"

And as Sir Harry was getting onto his horse to fight Sir Breuse, Sir Breuse ran at him while he was halfway onto his horse, and struck him down, horse and man, to the ground, and nearly killed Sir Harry, the good knight.

Sir Percival saw that, and then he cried, "Traitor knight, what are you doing?"

And when Sir Percival was on his horse, Sir Breuse turned his horse and fled as fast as ever he could, and Sir Percival and Sir Harry followed hard after him, but the longer they chased the farther behind they were.

Then they turned back and came to Sir Ector de Maris and Sir Bleoberis.

"Ah, fair knights," said Bleoberis, "why have you helped that false knight and traitor?"

"Why," said Sir Harry, "what knight is he? For I know well he is a false knight," said Sir Harry, "and a coward and a wicked knight."

"Sir," said Bleoberis, "he is the most cowardly knight alive, and a devourer of ladies and a destroyer of good knights, and especially of Arthur's."

"What is your name?" said Sir Ector.

"My name is Sir Bleoberis de Ganis."

"Alas, fair cousin," said Ector, "forgive me, for I am Sir Ector de Maris."

Then Sir Percival and Sir Harry rejoiced greatly that they had met Bleoberis, but they were all downcast that Sir Breuse had escaped them, and they grieved greatly over it.

Chapter 54: Of Sir Palomides, and how he met Sir Bleoberis and Sir Ector, and of Sir Percival

Just as they stood there like this, Sir Palomides came up, and when he saw Bleoberis's shield lying on the ground, Palomides said, "Let the man who owns that shield square up to me, for he struck me down near here, by a spring, and so I will fight him on foot."

"I am ready," said Bleoberis, "to answer you here. For you may be sure, sir knight, it was I, and my name is Bleoberis de Ganis."

"Well met," said Palomides, "and you may be sure my name is Palomides the Saracen."

And each of them hated the other to the death.

"Sir Palomides," said Ector, "you may be sure there is neither you nor any knight alive who kills any of our blood but he shall die for it. So if you want to fight, go and find Sir Lancelot or Sir Tristram, and there you will find your match."

"I have met them," said Palomides, "but I never won any honour from them."

"Was there never any other knight," said Sir Ector, "except those two, who was a match for you?"

"Yes," said Palomides, "there was a third, as good a knight as either of them, and for his age he was the best I ever found. For if he had lived until he was a stronger man, there would be no knight alive now like him; and his name was Sir Lamorak de Galis. And when he had jousted at a tournament, he overthrew me there and thirty knights more, and won the prize. And as he was leaving, Sir Gawain and his brothers met him, and with great effort they killed him treacherously, to the great loss of all good knights."

As soon as Sir Percival heard that his brother Sir Lamorak was dead, he fell swooning over his horse's mane, and there he grieved more than any knight ever grieved.

And when Sir Percival got up he said, "Alas, my good and noble brother Sir Lamorak, now we shall never meet again! And I believe a man could not find in all the wide world such a knight as he was for his age. And it is too much to bear, the death of our father King Pellinore, and now the death of our good brother Sir Lamorak."

Then in the meantime a servant came from King Arthur's court, and told them of the great tournament that was to be held at Lonazep, and how these lands, Cornwall and North Wales, would be against all comers.

Chapter 55: How Sir Tristram met Sir Dinadan, and of their talk, and what he said to Sir Gawain's brothers

Now we turn to Sir Tristram. As he rode hunting he met Sir Dinadan, who had come into that country to look for Sir Tristram. Then Sir Dinadan told Sir Tristram his name, but Sir Tristram would not tell him his, and that made Sir Dinadan angry.

"I saw a foolish knight like you just today," said Sir Dinadan, "lying by a spring, and he looked as if he were asleep; and there he lay grinning like a fool, and would not speak, and his shield lay beside him, and his horse stood beside him. And I knew well he was a lover."

"Ah, fair sir," said Sir Tristram, "aren't you a lover?"

"Mary, a curse on that trade!" said Sir Dinadan.

"That is badly said," said Sir Tristram, "for a knight can never be a man of prowess unless he is a lover."

"Well said," said Sir Dinadan. "Now tell me your name, since you're a lover, or else I will fight you."

"As for that," said Sir Tristram, "it is no reason to fight me, that I won't tell you my name. And as for my name, you shall not know it this time."

"Shame on you," said Dinadan. "You call yourself a knight and you don't dare tell me your name? Then I'll fight you."

"As for that," said Sir Tristram, "I will think it over, for I will not fight unless I care to. And if I do fight," said Sir Tristram, "you will not be able to stand against me."

"Shame on you, coward," said Sir Dinadan.

And as they sat their horses there, they saw a knight come riding towards them.

"Look," said Sir Tristram, "here comes a knight riding who will joust with you."

As soon as Sir Dinadan looked at him he said, "That is the same moonstruck knight I saw lying by the spring, neither sleeping nor waking."

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "I know that knight well, with the covered shield of azure. He is the son of the King of Northumberland, his name is Epinogris, and he is as great a lover as any I know, and he loves the daughter of the King of Wales, a very beautiful lady. And now I suppose," said Sir Tristram, "if you ask him he will joust with you, and then you will find out whether a lover is the better knight, or you who will not love any lady."

"Well," said Dinadan, "now you'll see what I can do."

With that Sir Dinadan called out loud, "Sir knight, get ready to joust with me, for it is the custom of knights-errant for one to joust with another."

"Sir," said Epinogris, "is that the rule among you knights-errant, to make a knight joust whether he likes it or not?"

"As for that," said Dinadan, "get ready, for here I come."

And with that they spurred their horses and met together so hard that Epinogris struck Sir Dinadan down.

Then Sir Tristram rode up to Sir Dinadan and said, "Well now! It seems to me the lover has done rather well."

"Shame on you, coward," said Sir Dinadan, "and if you're any good as a knight, avenge me."

"No," said Sir Tristram, "I will not joust this time. But get your horse and let us go from here."

"God keep me from your company," said Sir Dinadan, "for I've never had a scrap of luck since I met you." And so they parted.

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "perhaps I could tell you news of Sir Tristram."

"God keep me from your company," said Dinadan, "for Sir Tristram would be a great deal the worse if he were in your company." And then they parted.

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "it may happen yet that I shall meet you in other places."

So Sir Tristram rode to Joyous Gard, and there he heard a great noise and outcry in that town.

"What is this noise?" said Sir Tristram.

"Sir," they said, "there is a knight of this castle who has been with us a long time, and just now he has been killed by two knights, for no other reason than that our knight said Sir Lancelot was a better knight than Sir Gawain."

"That was a poor reason," said Sir Tristram, "to kill a good knight, for speaking well of his master."

"That is little help to us," said the men of the town. "For if Sir Lancelot had been here, we would soon have been avenged on those false knights."

When Sir Tristram heard them say so he sent for his shield and his spear, and swiftly, within a little while, he had overtaken them, and told them to turn and make amends for the wrong they had done.

"What amends do you want?" said one of the knights.

And with that they took their run, and met each other so hard that Sir Tristram struck that knight down over his horse's tail. Then the other knight squared up to Sir Tristram, and he served that knight the same way. And then they got off their horses as best they could, and set their shields and their swords to fight to the uttermost.

"Knights," said Sir Tristram, "you will tell me where you come from, and what your names are. For you might be such men that you would hardly escape my hands; and you might be men of such a country that, for all your evil deeds, you would go free."

"Know this, sir knight," they said, "we are not afraid to tell you our names. For my name is Sir Agravain, and my name is Gaheris, brothers of the good knight Sir Gawain, and we are King Arthur's nephews."

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "for King Arthur's sake I will let you go this time. But it is a shame," said Sir Tristram, "that Sir Gawain and you, who come of such great blood, you four brothers, should have such a name as you have. For you are called the greatest destroyers and murderers of good knights there are now in this realm; for I have heard it said that Sir Gawain and you killed between you a better knight than any of you ever were, the noble knight Sir Lamorak de Galis. If it had pleased God," said Sir Tristram, "I wish I had been beside Sir Lamorak at his death."

"Then you would have gone the same way," said Sir Gaheris.

"Fair knight," said Sir Tristram, "there would have had to be many more knights than you are."

And with that Sir Tristram left them and rode towards Joyous Gard. And when he had gone they took their horses, and one said to the other, "We'll overtake him and take revenge on him, in spite of Sir Lamorak."

Chapter 56: How Sir Tristram struck down Sir Agravain and Sir Gaheris, and how Sir Dinadan was sent for by Isolde the Fair

So when they had overtaken Sir Tristram, Sir Agravain called to him, "Turn, traitor knight!"

"That is badly said," said Sir Tristram. And with that he drew his sword, and struck Sir Agravain such a blow on the helmet that he tumbled off his horse in a swoon, and he had a grievous wound. And then he turned to Gaheris, and Sir Tristram struck his sword and his helmet together with such force that Gaheris fell out of his saddle. And so Sir Tristram rode to Joyous Gard, and there he got down and took off his armour.

So Sir Tristram told Isolde the Fair all about his adventure, as you have heard before. And when she heard him tell of Sir Dinadan, she said, "Sir, isn't that the man who made the song about King Mark?"

"He is the very man," said Sir Tristram, "for he is the best joker and jester there is, and a noble knight with his hands, and the best companion I know, and all good knights love his company."

"Alas, sir," she said, "why didn't you bring him with you?"

"Don't worry," said Sir Tristram, "for he is riding about this country looking for me, and so he will not leave until he has met me."

And there Sir Tristram told Isolde the Fair how Sir Dinadan held out against all lovers. Just then a servant came in and told Sir Tristram that a knight-errant had come into the town, with such and such colours on his shield.

"That is Sir Dinadan," said Sir Tristram. "Do you know what you should do?" said Sir Tristram. "Send for him, my Lady Isolde, and I will keep out of sight, and you will hear the merriest knight you ever spoke with, and the maddest talker. And I beg you with all my heart to give him a good welcome."

Then at once Isolde the Fair sent into the town, and asked Sir Dinadan to come into the castle and rest there with a lady.

"With all my heart," said Sir Dinadan. And so he mounted his horse and rode into the castle; and there he got down, and his armour was taken off, and he was brought into the castle. At once Isolde the Fair came to him, and each greeted the other; then she asked him where he came from.

"Madam," said Dinadan, "I am of King Arthur's court, and a knight of the Round Table, and my name is Sir Dinadan."

"What are you doing in this country?" said Isolde the Fair.

"Madam," he said, "I am looking for Sir Tristram, the good knight, for I was told that he was in this country."

"That may well be," said Isolde the Fair, "but I know nothing of him."

"Madam," said Dinadan, "I wonder at Sir Tristram and other lovers like him, what is wrong with them that they are so mad and so besotted over women."

"Why," said Isolde the Fair, "are you a knight and not a lover? That's a shame on you. For you cannot be called a good knight unless you take up a quarrel for a lady."

"God keep me from it," said Dinadan, "for the joy of love is too short, and the sorrow of it, and what comes of it, lasts far too long."

"Ah," said Isolde the Fair, "don't say so. For near here was the good knight Sir Bleoberis, who fought three knights at once for a damsel's sake, and won her before the King of Northumberland."

"That's so," said Sir Dinadan, "for I know him well for a good knight and a noble one, and come of noble blood; for they are all noble knights, the family he comes from, that is, Sir Lancelot du Lake's."

"Now tell me, please," said Isolde the Fair, "will you fight for my love against three knights who do me great wrong? And since you are one of King Arthur's knights, I call on you to fight for me."

Then Sir Dinadan said, "I will tell you this: you are as beautiful a lady as I ever saw, and much more beautiful than my lady Queen Guinevere. But believe me, in a word, I will not fight three knights for you, Jesus forbid!"

Then Isolde laughed, and had great fun at his expense. So he had all the welcome she could give him, and he stayed there all that night. And early in the morning Sir Tristram put on his armour, and Isolde the Fair gave him a good helmet; and then he promised her that he would meet Sir Dinadan, and the two of them would ride together to Lonazep, where the tournament was to be. "And there I will make a place ready for you, where you can watch the tournament."

Then Sir Tristram set off with two squires who carried his shield and his spears, which were great and long.

Chapter 57: How Sir Dinadan met Sir Tristram, and how, in jousting with Sir Palomides, Sir Dinadan recognised him

Then after that Sir Dinadan left, and rode on his way at a great pace until he had overtaken Sir Tristram. And when Sir Dinadan had overtaken him he recognised him at once, and he hated his company above all other knights'.

"Ah," said Sir Dinadan, "are you that coward knight I met yesterday? On guard, for you'll joust with me whether you like it or not."

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "I am unwilling to joust."

And so they let their horses run, and Sir Tristram missed him on purpose, and Sir Dinadan broke a spear on Sir Tristram, and with that Sir Dinadan made ready to draw his sword.

"Not so," said Sir Tristram. "Why are you so angry? I will not fight."

"Shame on you, coward," said Dinadan. "You disgrace all knights."

"As for that," said Sir Tristram, "I don't care, for I will ride in your train and be under your protection; for since you are such a good knight, you can keep me safe."

"The devil rid me of you," said Sir Dinadan, "for you are as fine a man of arms, and as fine in your person, as I ever saw, and the biggest coward I ever saw. What are you going to do with those great spears you carry about with you?"

"I will give them," said Sir Tristram, "to some good knight when I come to the tournament; and if I see you do best, I'll give them to you."

So as they rode along talking like this, they saw a knight-errant coming towards them, who made ready to joust.

"Look," said Sir Tristram, "there's one who wants to joust. Now get ready for him."

"Ah, shame on you," said Sir Dinadan.

"No, not so," said Tristram, "for that knight looks like a nasty piece of work."

"Then I'll do it," said Sir Dinadan.

And so they made ready their shields and their spears, and they met together so hard that the other knight struck Sir Dinadan down off his horse.

"There," said Sir Tristram, "it would have been better if you had left it alone."

"Shame on you, coward," said Sir Dinadan.

Then Sir Dinadan jumped up and took his sword in his hand, and offered to fight on foot.

"In friendship or in anger?" said the other knight.

"Let us fight in friendship," said Sir Dinadan.

"What is your name?" said that knight. "Please tell me."

"Know this, my name is Sir Dinadan."

"Ah, Dinadan," said that knight, "and my name is Gareth, the youngest brother of Sir Gawain."

Then each of them gave the other a warm welcome, for this Gareth was the best knight of all the brothers, and he proved a good knight. Then they took their horses, and there they talked about Sir Tristram, and what a coward he was; and Sir Tristram heard every word and laughed them to scorn.

Then they caught sight of a knight coming towards them, well horsed and well armed, and he made himself ready to joust.

"Fair knights," said Sir Tristram, "decide between you who will joust with that knight, for I warn you I will not fight him."

"Then I will," said Sir Gareth.

And so they met, and there that knight struck Sir Gareth down over his horse's rump.

"Well now," said Sir Tristram to Sir Dinadan, "get ready now and avenge the good knight Gareth."

"That I will not," said Sir Dinadan, "for he has struck down a much bigger knight than I am."

"Ah," said Sir Tristram, "now, Sir Dinadan, I can see and feel well that your heart is failing you. So now you'll see what I can do."

And then Sir Tristram crashed into that knight, and knocked him clean off his horse. And when Sir Dinadan saw that, he marvelled greatly; and then he guessed that it was Sir Tristram.

Then this knight who was on foot drew his sword to fight.

"What is your name?" said Sir Tristram.

"Believe me," said that knight, "my name is Sir Palomides."

"Which knight do you hate most?" said Sir Tristram.

"Sir knight," he said, "I hate Sir Tristram to the death, for if I can meet him, one of us will die."

"Well said," said Sir Tristram, "and believe me, I am Sir Tristram de Liones, and now do your worst."

When Sir Palomides heard him say so he was stunned. And then he said this: "I beg you, Sir Tristram, forgive me all my ill will, and if I live I will serve you above all other knights living. And I deeply regret the ill will I have borne you. I don't know what is wrong with me, for it seems to me that you are a good knight, and no other knight who called himself a good knight ought to hate you. So I beg you, Sir Tristram, take no offence at my unkind words."

"Sir Palomides," said Sir Tristram, "you speak well, and I know well that you are a good knight, for I have seen you proved; and you have taken on many great enterprises, and achieved them well. So," said Sir Tristram, "if you have any ill will towards me, now you can settle it, for I am ready for you."

"Not so, my lord Sir Tristram. I will do you knightly service in everything, as you command."

"And on those terms I will take you," said Sir Tristram.

And so they rode on their way talking of many things.

"O my lord Sir Tristram," said Dinadan, "you have made a fool of me, and badly, for God knows I came into this country for your sake, and on the advice of my lord Sir Lancelot; and yet Sir Lancelot would not tell me for certain where I could find you."

"Truly," said Sir Tristram, "Sir Lancelot knew well where I was, for I was staying in his own castle."

Chapter 58: How they approached the Castle of Lonazep, and of their further talk about the death of Sir Lamorak

So they rode on until they came in sight of the Castle of Lonazep. And then they saw four hundred tents and pavilions, and marvellously great preparations.

"God help me," said Sir Tristram, "over there I see the greatest preparations that I ever saw."

"Sir," said Palomides, "it seems to me that there were preparations as great at the Castle of Maidens upon the rock, where you won the prize, for I saw with my own eyes where you outjousted thirty knights."

"Sir," said Dinadan, "and at Surluse, at the tournament that Galahalt of the Long Isles held, which lasted seven days, there was as great a gathering as there is here, for there were many nations."

"Who was the best?" said Sir Tristram.

"Sir, it was Sir Lancelot du Lake and the noble knight Sir Lamorak de Galis, and Sir Lancelot won the prize."

"I don't doubt," said Sir Tristram, "that he won the prize, provided he was not overmatched by many knights. And as for the death of Sir Lamorak," said Sir Tristram, "it was too great a pity, for I dare say he was the cleanest in his strength and the best winded man of his age that was alive. For I knew him to be the strongest knight that I ever met with, unless it was Sir Lancelot. Alas," said Sir Tristram, "I am full of grief for his death. And if they were not the cousins of my lord Arthur who killed him, they should die for it, and all those who consented to his death. And it is for such things," said Sir Tristram, "that I am afraid to go to the court of my lord Arthur. I want you to know that," said Sir Tristram to Gareth.

"Sir, I don't blame you," said Gareth, "for I understand very well the vengefulness of my brothers, Sir Gawain, Agravain, Gaheris and Mordred. But as for me," said Sir Gareth, "I don't meddle in their affairs, and that is why there is none of them who loves me. And because I understand that they are murderers of good knights, I left their company. And I wish to God," said Gareth, "that I had been there when the noble knight Sir Lamorak was killed."

"Now, as Jesus is my help," said Sir Tristram, "that is well said of you, for I would rather have been there than have all the gold between here and Rome."

"Indeed," said Palomides, "and so I wish I had been there. And yet I never won the prize at any jousts or tournament where he was, but he got the better of me, whether on foot or on horseback. And on the day that he was killed he did the greatest deeds of arms that I ever saw a knight do in all the days of my life. And when the prize was given to him by my lord Arthur, Sir Gawain and his three brothers, Agravain, Gaheris and Sir Mordred, set upon Sir Lamorak in a secret place, and there they killed his horse. And so they fought with him on foot for more than three hours, both in front of him and behind him; and Sir Mordred gave him his death wound from behind, in his back, and hacked him all to pieces. One of his squires who saw it told me so."

"Shame on treason!" said Sir Tristram. "For it breaks my heart to hear this tale."

"So it does mine," said Gareth. "Brothers of mine as they are, I shall never love them, nor keep company with them, for that deed."

"Now let us speak of other deeds," said Palomides, "and let him be, for you cannot get his life back."

"That is the greater pity," said Dinadan. "For Sir Gawain and his brothers, except you, Sir Gareth, hate most of the good knights of the Round Table. For I know very well that if they could do it secretly, they hate my lord Sir Lancelot and all his kin, and bear him a great secret spite. And my lord Sir Lancelot is well aware of that, and that is why he keeps the good knights of his kin about him."

Chapter 59: How they came to the bank of the Humber, and how they found a ship there in which lay the body of King Hermance

"Sir," said Palomides, "let us leave this matter, and let us see how we shall do at this tournament. My advice," said Palomides, "is that we four hold together against all who come."

"Not on my advice," said Sir Tristram, "for I can see by their tents that there will be four hundred knights. And have no doubt," said Sir Tristram, "that there will be many good knights among them; and however valiant or strong a man may be, he can still be overmatched. And I have seen that happen to knights many times: when they expected most surely to win honour, they lost it. For valour is worth nothing unless it is mixed with wisdom. And as for me," said Sir Tristram, "it may be that I can keep my own head as well as the next man."

So they rode on until they came to the bank of the Humber, where they heard a cry and a sorrowful sound. Then they saw, coming down the wind, a rich vessel covered over with red silk, and the vessel landed close beside them. With that Sir Tristram dismounted, and his knights too. And so Sir Tristram went ahead and entered the vessel. And when he came inside he saw a fair bed richly covered, and on it lay a dead knight of fine bearing, all armed except for the head, and all bloodied with deadly wounds; and he seemed to have been an exceedingly good knight.

"How can this be," said Sir Tristram, "that this knight has been killed like this?"

Then Sir Tristram noticed a letter in the dead knight's hand.

"Master mariners," said Sir Tristram, "what does that letter mean?"

"Sir," they said, "in that letter you shall hear and learn how he was killed, and for what cause, and what his name was. But, sir," said the mariners, "you may be sure that no man shall take that letter and read it unless he is a good knight, and will faithfully promise to avenge his death. Otherwise no knight shall see that letter opened."

"Believe me," said Sir Tristram, "some of us may avenge his death as well as anyone else; and if it is as you mariners say, his death shall be avenged."

And with that Sir Tristram took the letter out of the knight's hand, and it said this: "I, Hermance, king and lord of the Red City, send my greeting to all knights-errant, commending myself to you noble knights of Arthur's court. I beg them all to find among themselves one knight who will fight for my sake with two brothers whom I raised up from nothing, and who have killed me wickedly and treacherously. And so I beg one good knight to avenge my death. And whoever avenges my death, I will that he shall have my Red City and all my castles."

"Sir," said the mariners, "you may be sure that this king and knight who lies here was a most honourable man and of very great prowess, and he dearly loved all kinds of knights-errant."

"God help me," said Sir Tristram, "this is a pitiful case, and I would very gladly take this enterprise upon myself. But I have made such a promise that I must be at this great tournament, or else I am shamed. For I know well that it was especially for my sake that my lord Arthur had these jousts and this tournament held in this country, and I know well that many honourable people will be at that tournament to see me. And so I am afraid that if I take this enterprise upon myself I shall not come back in time for these jousts."

"Sir," said Palomides, "I beg you, give this enterprise to me, and you shall see me achieve it honourably, or else I shall die in this quarrel."

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "I give you this enterprise, on condition that you are with me at this tournament, which shall be a week from today."

"Sir," said Palomides, "I promise you that I shall be with you by that day, if I am not killed or maimed."

Chapter 60: How Sir Tristram and his companions came and stayed with a host who afterwards fought with Sir Tristram, and other matters

Then Sir Tristram, Gareth and Sir Dinadan left, and left Sir Palomides in the vessel; and so Sir Tristram watched the mariners as they sailed away along the Humber. And when Sir Palomides was out of their sight they took their horses and looked about them. And then they saw a knight who came riding towards them unarmed, with nothing on him but a sword. And when this knight came near them he greeted them, and they greeted him in return.

"Fair knights," said that knight, "since you are knights-errant, I beg you to come and see my castle, and take such hospitality as you find there. I beg you with all my heart."

And so they rode with him to his castle, and there they were brought into the hall, which was finely furnished. And so they were unarmed there, and seated at a table. And when this knight saw Sir Tristram, he knew him at once. And then this knight grew pale, and angry with Sir Tristram. When Sir Tristram saw his host's face change like that, he marvelled, and said, "Sir, my host, what is the matter with you?"

"Know this," said he, "I am the worse for having you here. For I know you, Sir Tristram de Liones. You killed my brother. And so I give you fair warning: I will kill you if I can ever get you in the open."

"Sir knight," said Sir Tristram, "I have no memory of ever killing any brother of yours. And if you say that I did, I will make amends as far as I can."

"I want no amends," said the knight. "Just watch out for me."

So when he had dined Sir Tristram asked for his armour, and left. And so they rode on their way, and after a while Sir Dinadan saw a knight coming, well armed and well mounted, without a shield.

"Sir Tristram," said Sir Dinadan, "look to yourself, for I dare swear that is your host coming over there, who means to fight you."

"Let him come," said Sir Tristram. "I shall face him as well as I can."

At once the knight, when he came near Sir Tristram, shouted to him and told him to stand and defend himself. So they crashed together, but Sir Tristram struck the other knight so hard that he carried him over his horse's rump. That knight got up quickly and took his horse again, and so rode fiercely at Sir Tristram, and struck him twice, hard, on the helm.

"Sir knight," said Sir Tristram, "I beg you to stop and strike me no more, for I would be loath to fight you if I had the choice, for I have your food and your drink inside me."

For all that, he would not stop. And then Sir Tristram gave him such a blow on the helm that he fell headlong from his horse, so that the blood burst out at the breathing holes of his helm, and so he lay still, likely to be dead.

Then Sir Tristram said, "I regret that I struck that blow so hard, for I think he is dead."

And so they left him and rode on their way.

So they had ridden only a little while when they saw two very fine-looking knights riding towards them, well armed and well mounted, with good servants about them. The one was Berrant le Apres, and he was called the King with the Hundred Knights; and the other was Sir Segwarides; and they were two renowned and noble knights. So as they came alongside each other, the king looked at Sir Dinadan, who at that time had Sir Tristram's helm on his shoulder. The king had seen that helm before in the keeping of the Queen of North Wales, and that queen the king loved as his lady-love; and the Queen of North Wales had given that helm to Isolde the Fair, and Queen Isolde the Fair had given it to Sir Tristram.

"Sir knight," said Berrant, "where did you get that helm?"

"What do you want to know for?" said Sir Dinadan.

"Because I will fight you," said the king, "for the love of her who owned that helm. And so defend yourself."

So they parted and came together with all the might of their horses, and there the King with the Hundred Knights struck Sir Dinadan to the ground, horse and all. And then he commanded his servant, "Go and take his helm off, and keep it."

So the servant went to unbuckle his helm.

"What, the helm? What do you think you are doing?" said Sir Tristram. "Leave that helm alone."

"For what purpose, sir knight," said the king, "will you meddle with that helm?"

"Believe me," said Sir Tristram, "that helm shall not part from me until it has been more dearly paid for."

"Then make ready," said Sir Berrant to Sir Tristram.

So they crashed together, and there Sir Tristram struck him down over his horse's tail. And then the king got up quickly, and quickly got back on his horse. And then he struck fiercely at Sir Tristram with many great strokes. And then Sir Tristram gave Sir Berrant such a blow on the helm that he fell down from his horse, badly stunned.

"Look," said Dinadan, "that helm brings bad luck to the two of us. I took a fall for it, and now, sir king, you have taken another."

Then Segwarides asked, "Who will joust with me?"

"I beg you," said Sir Gareth to Dinadan, "let me have this joust."

"Sir," said Dinadan, "I beg you, take it, as far as I'm concerned."

"That isn't fair," said Tristram, "for this joust should be yours."

"In a word," said Dinadan, "I want no part of it."

Then Gareth squared up to Sir Segwarides, and there Sir Segwarides struck Gareth and his horse to the ground.

"Now," said Sir Tristram to Dinadan, "joust with that knight there."

"I want no part of it," said Dinadan.

"Then I will," said Sir Tristram.

And then Sir Tristram rode at him and gave him a fall. And so they left them on foot, and Sir Tristram rode to Joyous Gard. And there Sir Gareth, out of his courtesy, would not have gone into this castle, but Sir Tristram would not allow him to leave. And so they dismounted and unarmed, and were warmly entertained. But when Dinadan came before Isolde the Fair he cursed the time that he ever carried Sir Tristram's helm, and there he told her how Sir Tristram had made a fool of him. Then there was such laughing and joking at Sir Dinadan's expense that they did not know what to do with him.

Chapter 61: How Palomides went to fight two brothers for the death of King Hermance

Now we will leave them merry inside Joyous Gard, and speak of Sir Palomides. Sir Palomides sailed along the Humber to the coast of the sea, where there was a fair castle. And at that time it was early in the morning, before daybreak. Then the mariners went to Sir Palomides, who was fast asleep.

"Sir knight," said the mariners, "you must get up, for here is a castle that you must go into."

"I agree," said Sir Palomides; and with that he went ashore. And then he blew the horn that the mariners had given him. And when the people inside the castle heard that horn they sent out many knights; and there they stood on the walls, and said with one voice, "Welcome to this castle!"

And then it grew full daylight, and Sir Palomides entered the castle. And within a while he was served with many different dishes. Then Sir Palomides heard much weeping and great grief all about him.

"What can this mean?" said Sir Palomides. "I do not like to hear such sorrow, and I would gladly know what it means."

Then there came before him a man whose name was Sir Ebel, who said this: "Believe me, sir knight, this grief and sorrow is made here every day, and for this reason. We had a king who was called Hermance, and he was King of the Red City; and this king who was our lord was a noble knight, generous and free in his spending. And in all the world he loved nothing so much as the knights-errant of King Arthur's court, and all jousting, hunting and every kind of knightly sport. For so kind a king and knight never had the rule of poor people as he was; and because of his goodness and his nobility we mourn for him, and always shall. And all kings and great lords may take warning by our lord, for he was destroyed through his own fault. For if he had cherished those of his own blood he would still be alive, with great riches and in peace. But all great lords may take warning by our king. And alas," said Ebel, "that we must give warning to all others by his death!"

"Tell me," said Palomides, "in what way your lord was killed, and by whom."

"Sir," said Sir Ebel, "our king brought up two men from childhood who are now dangerous knights. And our king held these two knights so dear that he loved no man and trusted no man of his own blood, nor anyone else who was about him. And our king was governed by these two knights, and so they ruled him and his lands without challenge, and they would never allow any of his blood to have any say with our king. And besides, he was so generous and so noble, and they so false and deceitful, that they ruled him without challenge. And the lords of our king's blood saw that, and left him and went to their own estates. Then when these two traitors understood that they had driven all the lords of his blood away from him, they were not content with that rule, but then they meant to have more. For as the old saying has always gone: 'Give a peasant rule, and it will never be enough for him.' For whoever is ruled by a man born a peasant, though the lord of the land is born a gentleman, that same peasant will destroy all the gentlemen about him. And so, all great men and lords, beware whom you take about you. And if you are a knight of King Arthur's court, remember this tale, for this is the end and conclusion of it. My lord and king rode into the forest near here on the advice of these traitors, and there he hunted the red deer, armed at all points, just like a good knight. And so with the exertion he grew thirsty, and then he dismounted and drank at a spring. And when he had dismounted, by the agreement of these two traitors, the one who is called Helius suddenly struck our king through the body with a spear, and so they left him there. And when they had gone, then by chance I came to the spring, and found my lord and king wounded to the death. And when I heard his complaint, I had him brought to the waterside, and I put him in that same ship alive. And when my lord King Hermance was in that vessel, he required me, by the true faith I owed him, to write a letter in this form."

Chapter 62: The text of the letter written asking for vengeance for the king's death, and how Sir Palomides strove to win the right to fight the battle

And the letter, Sir Ebel went on, said this: "Commending myself to King Arthur and to all his knights-errant, I beg them all, since I, King Hermance, King of the Red City, have been killed in this way by wickedness and treason, through two knights of my own, of my own bringing up and of my own making, that some honourable knight will avenge my death, since I have always been, as far as I could, well disposed towards Arthur's court. And whoever will risk his life against these two traitors for my sake in single battle, I, King Hermance, King of the Red City, freely give him all the lands and rents that I ever held in my life."

"This letter," said Ebel, "I wrote at my lord's command, and then he received his Creator in the sacrament. And when he was dead, he had commanded me, before he was cold, to put that letter firmly in his hand. And then he commanded me to send that same vessel off down the Humber, and to give these mariners orders never to stop until they came to Logres, where all the noble knights will gather at this time. 'And there some good knight will have pity on me and avenge my death, for there was never king or lord more falsely or more treacherously killed than I am here, to my death.' That was the complaint of our King Hermance. Now," said Sir Ebel, "you know everything, how our lord was betrayed. We ask you, for God's sake, have pity on his death, and avenge it honourably, and then you may hold all these lands. For we all know well that if you can kill these two traitors, the Red City and all who are in it will take you for their lord."

"Truly," said Sir Palomides, "it grieves my heart to hear you tell this sorrowful tale. And to tell the truth, I saw the very letter that you speak of, and one of the best knights on earth read that letter to me, and at his command I came here to avenge your king's death. And so be done, and let me know where I shall find those traitors, for I shall never be at ease in my heart until I am at grips with them."

"Sir," said Sir Ebel, "then take your ship again, and that ship must bring you to the Delectable Isle, close by the Red City, and we in this castle shall pray for you and wait for your return. For this same castle, if you succeed, must be yours, for our King Hermance had this castle built for love of the two traitors; and so we have held it by strong hand, and so we are hard threatened."

"Do you know what you shall do?" said Sir Palomides. "Whatever becomes of me, see that you keep this castle well. For if I have the misfortune to be killed in this quest, I am sure that one of the best knights in the world will come to avenge my death, and that is Sir Tristram de Liones, or else Sir Lancelot du Lake."

Then Sir Palomides left that castle. And as he came near the city, there came out of a ship a fine-looking knight, armed, to meet him, with his shield on his shoulder and his hand on his sword. And as soon as he came near Sir Palomides he said, "Sir knight, what are you looking for here? Give up this quest, for it is mine, and it was mine before ever it was yours, and so I will have it."

"Sir knight," said Palomides, "it may well be that this quest was yours before it was mine. But when the letter was taken out of the dead king's hand, at that time, by all likelihood, there was no knight who had undertaken to avenge the death of the king. And so at that time I promised to avenge his death, and so I shall, or else I am shamed."

"You speak well," said the knight, "but believe me, then I will fight you, and whichever of us two is the better knight, let him take the battle in hand."

"I agree," said Sir Palomides.

And then they set their shields and pulled out their swords, and laid into each other with many heavy blows, like men of might. And this fighting went on for more than an hour; but at last Sir Palomides grew stronger and had the better wind, so that he struck that knight such a blow that he made him go down on his knees. Then that knight spoke aloud and said, "Noble knight, hold your hand!"

Sir Palomides was courteous, and held back his hand. Then this knight said, "Believe me, knight, you are worthier to have this battle than I am. And I ask you, by your knighthood, tell me your name."

"Sir, my name is Palomides, a knight of King Arthur's and of the Round Table, and I came here to avenge the death of this dead king."

Chapter 63: Of the preparations of Sir Palomides and of the two brothers who were to fight him

"Well met," said the knight to Palomides, "for of all the knights alive, except three, you are the one I would most gladly have. The first is Sir Lancelot du Lake, and Sir Tristram de Liones, and the third is my near cousin, Sir Lamorak de Galis. And I am the brother of King Hermance who is dead, and my name is Sir Herminde."

"You speak well," said Sir Palomides, "and you shall see how I fare. And if I am killed there, go to my lord Sir Lancelot, or else to my lord Sir Tristram, and beg them to avenge my death. For as for Sir Lamorak, you will never see him in this world."

"Alas," said Sir Herminde, "how can that be?"

"He has been killed," said Sir Palomides, "by Sir Gawain and his brothers."

"God help me," said Herminde, "it was not one against one that killed him."

"That is the truth," said Sir Palomides, "for it was four dangerous knights who killed him, that is, Sir Gawain, Sir Agravain, Sir Gaheris and Sir Mordred; but Sir Gareth, the fifth brother, was away, the best knight of them all."

And so Sir Palomides told Herminde the whole story, and how they had killed Sir Lamorak by nothing but treason.

So Sir Palomides took his ship, and landed at the Delectable Isle. And in the meantime Sir Herminde, who was the king's brother, landed at the Red City, and there he told them how a knight of King Arthur's had come to avenge King Hermance's death: "And his name is Sir Palomides, the good knight, who for the most part follows the beast Glatisant, the Questing Beast."

Then the whole city rejoiced greatly, for they had heard much of Sir Palomides and of his noble prowess. So they appointed a messenger, and sent him to the two brothers, and told them to make ready, for a knight had come who would fight them both. So the messenger went to them where they were, at a castle close by, and there he told them how a knight had come from King Arthur's court to fight them both at once.

"He is welcome," they said. "But tell us, we beg you, whether it is Sir Lancelot or any of his blood."

"He is none of that blood," said the messenger.

"Then we care the less," said the two brothers, "for we have no wish to fight with any of the blood of Sir Lancelot."

"Believe me," said the messenger, "his name is Sir Palomides, who is still unchristened, a noble knight."

"Well," they said, "if he is unchristened now, he will never be christened."

So they agreed to be at the city within two days.

And when Sir Palomides came to the city they rejoiced exceedingly over him, and then they looked him over, and saw that he was well made, clean-limbed and big, and sound in all his limbs, and neither too young nor too old. And so all the people praised him. And though he was not christened, yet he believed in the best manner, and was very faithful and true to his promise, and of good character. And he was unchristened because he had made his vow that he would never be christened until he had achieved the beast Glatisant, which was a very wonderful beast, and of great meaning, for Merlin prophesied much about that beast. And Sir Palomides had also vowed never to take full Christianity until he had fought seven battles within the lists.

So on the third day these two brothers came to the city, one called Helius and the other called Helake, who were men of great prowess. For all that they were false and full of treason, and only poor men by birth, yet they were noble knights with their hands. And they brought forty knights with them, so that they would be strong enough for the Red City. So the two brothers came with great boastfulness and pride, for they had put the Red City in fear and done it harm. Then they were brought to the lists, and Sir Palomides came into the place and said this: "Are you the two brothers, Helius and Helake, who killed your king and lord, Sir Hermance, by wickedness and treason, the king for whom I have come here to avenge his death?"

"Know this," said Sir Helius and Sir Helake, "we are the same knights who killed King Hermance. And know this too, Palomides the Saracen: we will handle you so before you leave that you'll wish you'd been christened."

"That may well be," said Sir Palomides, "for I would not wish to die before I was christened. And yet I am not afraid of the two of you, but I trust in God that I shall die a better Christian man than either of you. And have no doubt," said Sir Palomides, "either you or I shall be left dead in this place."

Chapter 64: Of the battle between Sir Palomides and the two brothers, and how the two brothers were slain

Then they drew apart, and the two brothers came against Sir Palomides, and he against them, as fast as their horses could run. And by chance Sir Palomides struck Helake through his shield and through the breast, more than a fathom deep. All this while Sir Helius held his spear upright, and out of pride and arrogance he would not strike Sir Palomides with his spear. But when he saw his brother lying on the ground, and saw that he could not help himself, then he said to Sir Palomides, "Defend yourself!"

And with that he came crashing at Sir Palomides with his spear, and struck him clean out of his saddle. Then Sir Helius rode over Sir Palomides two or three times. And at that Sir Palomides was ashamed, and caught Sir Helius's horse by the bridle; and with that the horse reared, and Sir Palomides heaved after it, and so they both fell to the ground. But Sir Helius leapt up quickly at once, and there he struck Sir Palomides a great blow on the helm, so that he went down on one knee. Then they laid into each other with many heavy blows, and circled and sidestepped, now backward, now sideways, crashing together like two boars, and at that same moment they both fell flat on the ground.

So they went on fighting for two hours without any rest, and never stopped for breath. And then Sir Palomides grew faint and weary, and Sir Helius grew exceedingly strong, and doubled his strokes, and drove Sir Palomides across and along the whole field, so that the people of the city, when they saw Sir Palomides in this state, wept and cried out, and grieved greatly, and the other side rejoiced just as much.

"Alas," said the men of the city, "that this noble knight should be killed like this for our king's sake!"

And as they were weeping and crying out like this, Sir Palomides, who had taken a hundred blows, so that it was a wonder he stood on his feet, at last looked as well as he could at the common people, and saw how they wept for him. And then he said to himself, "Ah, shame on you, Sir Palomides! Why do you hang your head so low?"

And with that he raised his shield, and looked Sir Helius in the face, and he struck him a great blow on the helm, and after that another, and another. And then he struck Sir Helius with such might that he fell flat on the ground. And then he tore his helm off his head, and there he struck him such a blow that he cut his head from his body. And then the people of the city were the most joyful people there could be. So they brought him to his lodging with great ceremony, and there all the people became his men. And then Sir Palomides begged them all to take care of all the lordship of King Hermance: "For, fair sirs, believe me, I cannot stay with you at this time, for I must be with my lord King Arthur in all haste at the Castle of Lonazep, as I have promised."

Then the people were very downcast at his leaving, for the whole city offered Sir Palomides a third part of their goods if he would stay with them; but at that time he would not stay on any account.

And so Sir Palomides left, and so he came to the castle where Sir Ebel was lieutenant. And when the people in the castle knew how Sir Palomides had fared, there was a joyful household. And so Sir Palomides left, and came to the castle of Lonazep. And when he learned that Sir Tristram was not there, he took his way over the Humber, and came to Joyous Gard, where Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair were. Sir Tristram had commanded that whatever knight-errant came within Joyous Gard, that is, into the town, they should warn Sir Tristram. So a man of the town came and told Sir Tristram how there was a knight in the town, an exceedingly fine-looking man.

"What kind of man is he," said Sir Tristram, "and what device does he bear?"

So the man told Sir Tristram all the signs of him.

"That is Palomides," said Dinadan.

"It may well be," said Sir Tristram. "Go to him," said Sir Tristram to Dinadan.

So Dinadan went to Sir Palomides, and there each greeted the other with great joy, and so they lodged together that night. And early in the morning Sir Tristram and Sir Gareth came and caught them in their beds, and so they got up and had breakfast.

Chapter 65: How Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides met Breuse Saunce Pité, and how Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair went to Lonazep

And then Sir Tristram asked Sir Palomides to ride out into the fields and woods. So they agreed to take their ease in the forest. And when they had amused themselves a long while they rode to a fair spring; and at once they saw an armed knight who came riding towards them, and they greeted each other. Then this armed knight spoke to Sir Tristram, and asked who these knights were who were lodged in Joyous Gard.

"I don't know who they are," said Sir Tristram.

"What knights are you?" said that knight. "For it seems to me you are no knights-errant, since you ride unarmed."

"Whether we are knights or not, we don't care to tell you our names."

"You won't tell me your name?" said that knight. "Then defend yourself, for you'll die by my hands."

And with that he took his spear in his hands, and would have run Sir Tristram through. Sir Palomides saw that, and struck his horse slantwise in the middle of the side, so that man and horse fell to the ground. And with that Sir Palomides dismounted and pulled out his sword to kill him.

"Let him be," said Sir Tristram. "Don't kill him. The knight is only a fool, and it would be a shame to kill him. But take away his spear," said Sir Tristram, "and let him take his horse and go where he likes."

So when this knight got up he groaned badly from the fall, and so he took his horse, and when he was mounted he turned his horse, and asked Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides to tell him who they were.

"Now believe me," said Sir Tristram, "my name is Sir Tristram de Liones, and this knight's name is Sir Palomides."

When he knew who they were he put the spurs to his horse, so that they should not ask him his name, and so rode fast away through thick and thin. Then a knight came by them with a shield crossed by a blue band, whose name was Epinogris, and he came towards them at a great gallop.

"Where are you riding?" said Sir Tristram.

"My fair lords," said Epinogris, "I am following the falsest knight alive. And so I beg you to tell me whether you have seen him, for he bears a shield with a red cover over it."

"God help me," said Tristram, "such a knight left us not a quarter of an hour ago. We beg you, tell us his name."

"Alas," said Epinogris, "why did you let him escape from you? He is such a great enemy to all knights-errant. His name is Breuse Saunce Pité."

"Ah, shame on it!" said Sir Palomides. "Alas that he ever escaped my hands, for he is the man in the world I hate most."

Then each knight lamented greatly to the other; and so Epinogris left and followed the chase after him.

Then Sir Tristram and his three companions rode to Joyous Gard; and there Sir Tristram talked with Sir Palomides about his battle, how he had fared at the Red City, and it had ended just as you have heard before.

"Truly," said Sir Tristram, "I am glad you have fared well, for you have done honourably. Well," said Sir Tristram, "we must set out tomorrow."

And then he planned how it should be done; and Sir Tristram arranged to send his two tents to be pitched close by the spring of Lonazep, and in them the queen, Isolde the Fair, would stay.

"That is well said," said Sir Dinadan.

But when Sir Palomides heard of that, his heart was carried away beyond measure; even so he said very little. So when they came to Joyous Gard Sir Palomides would not have gone into the castle, but Sir Tristram took him by the finger and led him into the castle. And when Sir Palomides saw Isolde the Fair he was so carried away that he could scarcely speak. So they went to supper, but Palomides could not eat, and there was all the welcome that could be had. And in the morning they were made ready to ride towards Lonazep.

So Sir Tristram had three squires, and Isolde the Fair had three gentlewomen, and both the queen and they were richly dressed; and they had no other people with them but servants to carry their shields and their spears. And so they rode on. So as they rode they saw a band of knights ahead of them; it was the knight Galihodin, with twenty knights with him.

"Fair companions," said Galihodin, "four knights are coming over there, and a rich and very fair lady. I have a mind to take that lady from them."

"That is not the best advice," said one of Galihodin's men. "But send to them, and find out what they will say."

And so it was done. A squire came to Sir Tristram, and asked them whether they would joust or else lose their lady.

"Not so," said Sir Tristram. "Tell your lord I bid him come, as many of you as there are of us, and win her and take her."

"Sir," said Palomides, "if it please you, let me have this deed, and I will take on all four of them."

"I am willing that you have it," said Sir Tristram, "as you please. Now go and tell your lord Galihodin that this same knight will meet him and his companions."

Chapter 66: How Sir Palomides jousted with Sir Galihodin, and afterwards with Sir Gawain, and struck them down

Then this squire left and told Galihodin; and then Galihodin set his shield and took up a spear, and Sir Palomides another; and there Sir Palomides struck Galihodin so hard that he struck both horse and man to the ground. And he had a terrible fall there. And then another knight came, and he served him the same way; and so he served the third and the fourth, knocking them over their horses' rumps, and all the while Sir Palomides' spear stayed whole. Then six more of Galihodin's knights came, and wanted to be avenged on Sir Palomides.

"Leave it," said Sir Galihodin. "Don't you dare. Not one of you is to meddle with this knight, for he is a man of great goodness and honour, and if he wished it, you would none of you be able to stand against him."

And at that they held still. And Sir Palomides was ready to joust all the while; and when he saw they would joust no more, he rode back to Sir Tristram.

"You have done very well," said Sir Tristram, "and honourably you have done, as a good knight should."

This Galihodin was a near cousin of Galahalt, the high prince; and this Galihodin was a king in the country of Surluse.

So as Sir Tristram, Sir Palomides and Isolde the Fair rode together, they saw four knights ahead of them, and every man had his spear in his hand: the first was Sir Gawain, the second Sir Uwain, the third Sir Sagramore le Desirous, and the fourth was Dodinas le Savage. When Sir Palomides saw that the four knights were ready to joust, he begged Sir Tristram to give him leave to fight them all, for as long as he could keep himself on horseback. "And if I am struck down, I beg you, avenge me."

"Well," said Sir Tristram, "I will do as you wish; and you are not so eager to win honour but that I am just as eager to increase your honour."

And with that Sir Gawain put out his spear, and Sir Palomides another; and they came together so fiercely that Sir Palomides struck Sir Gawain to the ground, horse and all; and in the same way he served Uwain, Sir Dodinas and Sagramore. All four of these knights Sir Palomides struck down, with several spears. And then Sir Tristram went on toward Lonazep.

And when they had gone, Galihodin came up with his ten knights to Sir Gawain, and there he told him all about how he had fared.

"I wonder," said Sir Gawain, "what knights they are, who are dressed like that in green."

"And that knight on the white horse struck me down," said Galihodin, "and my three companions."

"And he did the same to me," said Gawain. "And I know very well," said Sir Gawain, "that the man on the white horse is either Sir Tristram or else Sir Palomides, and that finely dressed lady is Queen Isolde."

So they talked of one thing and another.

And meanwhile Sir Tristram rode on until he came to the spring where his two tents were pitched; and there they dismounted, and there they saw many tents and great splendour. Then Sir Tristram left Sir Palomides and Sir Gareth there with Isolde the Fair, and Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan rode to Lonazep to listen for news; and Sir Tristram rode on Sir Palomides' white horse. And when he came into the castle, Sir Dinadan heard a great horn blow, and many knights gathered to the horn.

Then Sir Tristram asked a knight, "What does the blast of that horn mean?"

"Sir," said that knight, "it is for all those who will hold against King Arthur at this tournament. The first is the King of Ireland, and then the King of Surluse, the King of Listinoise, the King of Northumberland, and the King of the best part of Wales, with many other countries. And they are gathering in council, to decide what order they will keep."

But the King of Ireland, whose name was Marhalt, and who was father to the good knight Sir Marhaus whom Sir Tristram killed, did all the speaking, so that Sir Tristram could hear it. He said, "Lords and companions, let us look to ourselves, for you may be sure King Arthur is certain of many good knights, or else he would not fight us with so few knights. So my advice is this: let every king have a standard and a badge of his own, so that every knight rallies to his own rightful lord, and then every king and captain can help his knights if they have need."

When Sir Tristram had heard all their counsel, he rode to King Arthur to hear his counsel.

Chapter 67: How Sir Tristram and his companions came to the tournament at Lonazep, and of several jousts and matters

But Sir Tristram had no sooner come into the place than Sir Gawain and Sir Galihodin went to King Arthur and told him, "That same green knight in the green armour, with the white horse, struck the two of us down, and six of our companions, this very day."

"Well," said Arthur.

And then he called Sir Tristram and asked him what his name was.

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "you must hold me excused for the present, for you shall not know my name."

And with that Sir Tristram turned back and rode away.

"I am amazed," said Arthur, "that that knight will not tell me his name. But go, Griflet le Fise de Dieu, and ask him to speak with me privately, between the two of us."

Then Sir Griflet rode after him and overtook him, and told him that King Arthur asked him to speak with him secretly, apart.

"On this condition," said Sir Tristram, "I will speak with him: I will turn back if you will guarantee me that he will not ask to hear my name."

"I will undertake," said Sir Griflet, "that he will not press you hard for it."

So they rode together until they came to King Arthur.

"Fair sir," said King Arthur, "why is it you will not tell me your name?"

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "I do not hide my name without a reason."

"Which side will you take?" said King Arthur.

"Truly, my lord," said Sir Tristram, "I do not know yet which side I will be on, until I come to the field; and wherever my heart leads me, there I will hold. But tomorrow you will see and find out which side I come in on."

And with that he turned back and went to his tents.

And in the morning they all armed themselves in green and came into the field; and there young knights began to joust, and did many honourable deeds. Then Gareth spoke to Sir Tristram, and begged him for leave to break his spear, for he thought it a shame to carry his spear back whole. When Sir Tristram heard him say so, he laughed and said, "Please, do your best."

Then Sir Gareth got a spear and offered to joust. A knight saw that who was nephew to the King with the Hundred Knights; his name was Selises, and he was a good man of arms. So this knight Selises squared up to Sir Gareth, and the two of them met so hard that each struck the other down to the ground, horse and all, so that they were both bruised and hurt; and there they lay until the King with the Hundred Knights helped Selises up, and Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides helped Gareth up again. And so they rode with Sir Gareth to their tents, and then they pulled off his helm.

And when Isolde the Fair saw Sir Gareth bruised in the face, she asked him what was wrong with him.

"Madam," said Sir Gareth, "I took a great blow, and I believe I gave one back; but none of my companions, God thank them, would come to my rescue."

"Truly," said Palomides, "it was not the place of any of us to joust today, for no proven knights have jousted today, and you would joust, of your own choosing. And when the other side saw you offer yourself to joust, they sent one against you who is an exceedingly good knight for his age, for I know him well; his name is Selises. And you met him honourably, and neither of you is dishonoured; and so rest yourself, so that you will be ready and sound to joust tomorrow."

"As for that," said Gareth, "I will not fail you, if I can sit astride my horse."

Chapter 68: How Sir Tristram and his companions jousted, and of the noble feats they did in that tournament

"Now which side," said Tristram, "is it best for us to be on tomorrow?"

"Sir," said Palomides, "my advice is that you be against King Arthur tomorrow, for on his side will be Sir Lancelot and many good knights of his blood with him. And the more men of honour there are, the more honour we shall win."

"That is very knightly spoken," said Sir Tristram, "and just as you advise me, so we will do."

"In the name of God," they all said.

So that night they were lodged with the best. And in the morning, when it was day, they were all arrayed in green trappings, shields and spears, and Isolde the Fair in the same colour, and her three damsels. And so these four knights came into the field, from one end to the other. And so they led Isolde the Fair to the place where she was to stand and watch all the jousts, in a bay window; but she was always veiled, so that no one could see her face. And then these three knights rode straight to the side of the King of Scots.

When King Arthur had seen them do all this, he asked Sir Lancelot who these knights and that queen were.

"Sir," said Lancelot, "I cannot tell you for certain; but if Sir Tristram is in this country, or Sir Palomides, you may be sure it is certainly they, and Isolde the Fair."

Then Arthur called Sir Kay to him and said, "Go quickly and find out how many knights of the Round Table are missing here, for you can tell by the seats."

So Sir Kay went, and saw by the names written on the seats that ten knights were missing. And these are the names of those who were not there: Sir Tristram, Sir Palomides, Sir Percival, Sir Gaheris, Sir Epinogris, Sir Mordred, Sir Dinadan, Sir La Cote Male Taile, and Sir Pelleas the noble knight.

"Well," said Arthur, "some of these, I dare say, are here today against us."

Then two brothers came in, cousins of Sir Gawain; the one was called Sir Edward, the other Sir Sadok, and they were two good knights. And they asked King Arthur that they might have the first jousts, because they were of Orkney.

"I am pleased," said King Arthur.

Then Sir Edward met the King of Scots, on whose side were Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides; and Sir Edward struck the King of Scots clean off his horse, and Sir Sadok struck down the King of North Wales and gave him a tremendous fall, so that there was a great cry on King Arthur's side, and that made Sir Palomides exceedingly angry. And so Sir Palomides set his shield and his spear, and with all his might he met Sir Edward of Orkney, and struck him so hard that his horse could not stay on its feet, and so they crashed to the ground; and then with the same spear Sir Palomides struck down Sir Sadok over his horse's rump.

"Oh, Jesus," said Arthur, "what knight is that, dressed all in green? He jousts mightily."

"Believe me," said Sir Gawain, "he is a good knight, and you will see him joust better yet before he goes. And you will see yet," said Sir Gawain, "another, bigger knight in the same colour than he is; for that same knight," said Sir Gawain, "who just now struck down my four cousins, struck me down within these two days, and seven companions besides."

Meanwhile, as they stood there talking, Sir Tristram came into the place on a black horse, and before he stopped he struck down with one spear four good knights of Orkney who were of Sir Gawain's kin; and Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan each struck down a good knight.

"Jesus," said Arthur, "that knight on the black horse is doing mightily and marvellously well."

"Wait," said Sir Gawain. "That knight with the black horse hasn't even begun yet."

Then Sir Tristram put back on their horses the two kings whom Edward and Sadok had unhorsed at the beginning. And then Sir Tristram drew his sword and rode into the thickest of the fighting against the men of Orkney; and there he struck down knights, and tore off helms, and pulled away their shields, and knocked down many knights. He bore himself so that Sir Arthur and all the knights were amazed when they saw one knight do such great deeds of arms. And Sir Palomides did not fail on the other side, but did so marvellously well that everyone wondered at it. For there King Arthur likened Sir Tristram, who was on the black horse, to a mad lion, and likened Sir Palomides on the white horse to a mad leopard, and Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan to eager wolves. But the custom among them was such that none of the kings would help another, but all the company of each standard helped one another as they could. But all the while Sir Tristram did so many deeds of arms that the men of Orkney grew weary of him, and so they withdrew to Lonazep.

Chapter 69: How Sir Tristram was unhorsed and struck down by Sir Lancelot, and how afterwards Sir Tristram struck down King Arthur

Then came the cry of the heralds and of all the common people: "The Green Knight has done marvellously, and beaten all the men of Orkney!"

And there the heralds counted that Sir Tristram, who sat on the black horse, had struck down thirty knights with spear and sword, and Sir Palomides had struck down twenty knights; and most of these fifty knights were of King Arthur's household, and proven knights.

"So help me God," said Arthur to Sir Lancelot, "this is a great shame to us, to see four knights beat so many knights of mine. So make yourself ready, for we will fight them."

"Sir," said Lancelot, "believe me, there are two exceedingly good knights there, and it would be no great honour to us to fight them now, for they have laboured hard today."

"As for that," said Arthur, "I will be avenged. So take with you Sir Bleoberis and Sir Ector, and I will be the fourth," said Arthur.

"Sir," said Lancelot, "you will find me ready, and my brother Sir Ector, and my cousin Sir Bleoberis."

And so when they were ready and on horseback, Sir Arthur said to Sir Lancelot, "Now choose which of them you will meet."

"Sir," said Lancelot, "I will meet the green knight on the black horse" (that was Sir Tristram), "and my cousin Sir Bleoberis shall match the green knight on the white horse" (that was Sir Palomides), "and my brother Sir Ector shall match the green knight on the white horse" (that was Sir Gareth).

"Then I must fight," said Sir Arthur, "the green knight on the grey horse," and that was Sir Dinadan.

"Now let every man take heed of his opponent," said Sir Lancelot.

And so they trotted on together, and there Sir Lancelot met Sir Tristram. So Sir Lancelot struck Sir Tristram so hard on the shield that he bore horse and man to the ground; but Sir Lancelot thought it had been Sir Palomides, and so he rode on. And then Sir Bleoberis met Sir Palomides, and struck him so hard on the shield that Sir Palomides and his white horse went crashing to the ground. Then Sir Ector de Maris struck Sir Gareth so hard that down he fell off his horse. And the noble King Arthur met Sir Dinadan, and struck him clean out of his saddle. And then for a while the talk went round that the green knights had been beaten down.

When the King of North Wales saw that Sir Tristram had had a fall, he remembered what great deeds of arms Sir Tristram had done. Then he made many knights ready, for the custom and the proclamation were such that any knight who was struck down and could not be horsed again by his companions, or by his own strength, should be prisoner for that day to the side that had struck him down. So the King of North Wales came in, and rode straight to Sir Tristram; and when he came near him he quickly dismounted and handed Sir Tristram his horse, and said this: "Noble knight, I do not know you, or what country you are from; but for the noble deeds you have done today, take my horse there, and let me do as well as I can; for, so help me Jesus, you are more worthy to have my horse than I am myself."

"Many thanks," said Sir Tristram, "and if I can, I will repay you. See that you do not go far from us, and I expect I will win you another horse."

And with that Sir Tristram mounted his horse, and there he met King Arthur, and gave him such a blow on the helm with his sword that King Arthur had no power to keep his saddle. And then Sir Tristram gave the King of North Wales King Arthur's horse. Then there was a great crush around King Arthur to horse him again; but Sir Palomides would not let King Arthur be horsed again, but all the while Sir Palomides struck out mightily on the right hand and on the left, like a noble knight. And meanwhile Sir Tristram rode through the thickest of the crowd, and struck down knights on the right hand and on the left, and tore off helms, and so went on out to his tents, and left Sir Palomides on foot; and Sir Tristram changed his horse and disguised himself all in red, horse and armour.

Chapter 70: How Sir Tristram changed his armour and it was all red, and how he bore himself, and how Sir Palomides killed Lancelot's horse

And when the queen, Isolde the Fair, saw that Sir Tristram was unhorsed, and did not know where he was, she wept bitterly. But Sir Tristram, when he was ready, came dashing swiftly into the field, and then Isolde the Fair spotted him. And so he did great deeds of arms; with one spear, and a great one, Sir Tristram struck down five knights before he stopped. Then Sir Lancelot quickly saw that it was Sir Tristram, and then he regretted that he had struck him down; and so Sir Lancelot went out of the thick of the fighting to rest, and soon he came back again. And now when Sir Tristram came into the crowd, by his great strength he put Sir Palomides back on his horse, and Sir Gareth, and Sir Dinadan, and then they began to do marvellously.
