But neither Sir Palomides nor either of his two companions knew who had helped them back on horseback. But all the while Sir Tristram was near them and came to their aid, and they did not know him, because he had changed into red armour; and all this while Sir Lancelot was away.

So when Isolde the Fair recognised Sir Tristram on horseback again, she was exceedingly glad, and then she laughed and looked happy. And as it happened, Sir Palomides looked up toward her where she was in the window, and saw how she laughed; and with that he took such joy in it that he struck down, with spear and with sword, every man he met. For through the sight of her he was so lost in love of her that it seemed to him at that time that if both Sir Tristram and Sir Lancelot had been against him, they would have won no honour from him. And in his heart, as the book says, Sir Palomides wished that he might fight Sir Tristram, with honour, in front of everyone, because of Isolde the Fair. Then Sir Palomides began to double his strength, and he did so marvellously that everyone wondered at him, and all the while he cast his eyes up to Isolde the Fair. And when he saw her look so happy, he bore himself like a lion, so that no man could stand against him.

And then Sir Tristram watched how Sir Palomides was laying about him, and he said to Sir Dinadan, "So help me God, Sir Palomides is an exceedingly good knight, and one who lasts well; but I never saw him do such deeds, nor ever heard tell that he did so much in one day."

"It is his day," said Dinadan; and he would say no more to Sir Tristram. But to himself he said, "If only you knew for whose love he is doing all these deeds of arms! Sir Tristram would soon cut his courage down to size."

"Alas," said Sir Tristram, "that Sir Palomides is not christened."

So said King Arthur, and so said all those who watched him. Then all the people gave him the prize, as the best knight that day, saying he outdid Sir Lancelot or Sir Tristram.

"Well," said Dinadan to himself, "all this honour Sir Palomides has here today he can thank Queen Isolde for; for if she had been away today, Sir Palomides would not have won the prize today."

Just then Sir Lancelot du Lake came into the field, and saw and heard the shouting and the cry, and the great honour Sir Palomides had won. He squared up to Sir Palomides with a great, mighty, long spear, and meant to strike him down. And when Sir Palomides saw Sir Lancelot coming at him so fast, he rode at Sir Lancelot as fast as he could, with his sword; and as Sir Lancelot was about to strike him, he knocked his spear aside and cut it in two with his sword. And Sir Palomides rushed at Sir Lancelot, meaning to put him to shame; and with his sword he struck the neck of the horse Sir Lancelot was riding, and then Sir Lancelot fell to the ground.

Then the cry was huge and loud: "See how Sir Palomides the Saracen has struck down Sir Lancelot's horse!"

At once there were many knights angry with Sir Palomides because he had done that deed; and so many knights there held that it was an unknightly thing to do in a tournament, to kill a horse on purpose, unless it had been done in real battle, life for life.

Chapter 71: What Sir Lancelot said to Sir Palomides, and how the prize for that day was given to Sir Palomides

When Sir Ector de Maris saw his brother Sir Lancelot suffer such an insult, and set on foot like that, he took a spear in a fury and rode against Sir Palomides, and struck him so hard that he bore him clean off his horse. Sir Tristram saw that, who was in red armour, and he struck Sir Ector de Maris clean off his horse.

Then Sir Lancelot set his shield on his shoulder, with his sword naked in his hand, and so came straight at Sir Palomides, fiercely, and said, "Know this: today you have done me the greatest insult that any honourable knight ever did me in tournament or in jousts, and I will be avenged on you for it. So look to yourself."

"Ah, mercy, noble knight," said Palomides, "and forgive me my unworthy deeds, for I have neither the power nor the strength to stand against you; and I have done so much today that I know very well I never did so much before, and never will again in all my days. And so, most noble knight, I beg you, spare me for today, and I promise you I will always be your knight while I live. If you rob me of my honour now, you rob me of the greatest honour I ever had, or ever will have, in all my days."

"Well," said Sir Lancelot, "I see, to tell you the truth, that you have done marvellously well today; and I partly understand for whose love you do it, and I know very well that love is a great mistress. And if my lady were here, as she is not, believe me," said Sir Lancelot, "you would not carry off the honour. But beware that your love is not found out, for if Sir Tristram comes to know it, you will regret it. And since my quarrel is not here, you shall have the honour today, as far as I am concerned; considering the great toil and pain you have had today, it would be no honour to me to take it from you."

And with that Sir Lancelot let Sir Palomides go.

Then Sir Lancelot, by great force and strength, got his own horse back in spite of twenty knights. So when Sir Lancelot was on horseback, he did many marvels, and so did Sir Tristram, and Sir Palomides likewise. Then Sir Lancelot struck down with a spear Sir Dinadan, and the King of Scotland, and the King of Wales, and the King of Northumberland, and the King of Listinoise. So then Sir Lancelot and his companions struck down a good forty knights. Then the King of Ireland and the King of the Straight Marches came to the rescue of Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides. A great fight began there, and many knights were struck down on both sides; and all the while Sir Lancelot spared Sir Tristram, and he spared him. And Sir Palomides would not meddle with Sir Lancelot, and so there was crashing here and there. And then King Arthur sent out many knights of the Round Table; and Sir Palomides was always in the very front, and Sir Tristram did so mightily well that the king and everyone else marvelled.

And then the king had the end of the day sounded; and because Sir Palomides began first, and never once walked or rode out of the field to rest, but was always doing marvellously well, either on foot or on horseback, and lasted longest, King Arthur and all the kings gave Sir Palomides the honour and the prize for that day.

Then Sir Tristram ordered Sir Dinadan to fetch the queen, Isolde the Fair, and bring her to his two tents that stood by the spring. And so Dinadan did as he was ordered. But when Sir Palomides understood and learned that Sir Tristram was the one in the red armour, on a red horse, you may be sure he was glad, and so were Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan, for they had all thought that Sir Tristram had been taken prisoner. And then every knight went off to his lodging.

And then King Arthur and every knight talked of those knights; but above all men they gave Sir Palomides the prize, and all the knights who knew Sir Palomides wondered at his deeds.

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot to Arthur, "as for Sir Palomides, if he is the green knight, I dare say he is the most worthy to have the prize for today, for he never rested, and never changed his gear, and he began first and held on longest. And yet I know very well," said Sir Lancelot, "that there was a better knight than he, and that will be proved before we leave, on my life."

So they talked on both sides; and so Sir Dinadan jeered at Sir Tristram and said, "What the devil has got into you today? For Sir Palomides' strength never flagged once today, but all the while he doubled it."

Chapter 72: How Sir Dinadan goaded Sir Tristram into doing well

"And you, Sir Tristram," Dinadan went on, "have gone about all day as if you were asleep, and so I call you a coward."

"Well, Dinadan," said Sir Tristram, "I was never called a coward before by any knight on earth, in all my life. And know this, sir: I count myself not one bit more a coward because Sir Lancelot gave me a fall, for I except him from all other knights. And make no mistake, Sir Dinadan, if Sir Lancelot has a good quarrel, he is far too good for any knight now living; and still, for his patience, his generosity, his goodness and his courtesy, I call him the knight without a peer."

And so Sir Tristram was more or less angry with Sir Dinadan. But Sir Dinadan said all these words because he wanted to anger Sir Tristram, to make him rouse his spirits and get angry; for Sir Dinadan knew well that if Sir Tristram were thoroughly angry, Sir Palomides would not win the prize in the morning. And it was for this purpose that Sir Dinadan said all this jeering and all these words against Sir Tristram.

"Truly," said Sir Palomides, "as for Sir Lancelot, for noble knighthood, courtesy, prowess and gentleness, I know no one his equal; for today," said Sir Palomides, "I behaved most discourteously toward Sir Lancelot, and most unknightly, and he behaved most knightly and courteously to me in return; for if he had been as ill-bred toward me as I was toward him, I would have won no honour today. And so," said Palomides, "I will be Sir Lancelot's knight as long as my life lasts."

This talk went on in the lodgings of the kings. But all the kings, lords and knights said that for true knighthood, and for sheer strength, for goodness and for courtesy, Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram carried the prize above all the knights who ever were in Arthur's days. And there were never knights in Arthur's days who did half so many deeds as they did; as the book says, ten knights together did not do half the deeds that they did. And there was never a knight in their days who asked Sir Lancelot or Sir Tristram to undertake any quest, so long as it was not to their shame, but they did what he wished.

Chapter 73: How King Arthur and Sir Lancelot came to see Isolde the Fair, and how Palomides struck down King Arthur

So in the morning Sir Lancelot left, and Sir Tristram was ready, and Isolde the Fair with Sir Palomides and Sir Gareth. And so they rode, all in green, very finely dressed, to the forest. And Sir Tristram left Sir Dinadan asleep in his bed. And as they rode, it happened that the king and Lancelot were standing in a window, and saw Sir Tristram and Isolde ride by.

"Sir," said Lancelot, "there rides the most beautiful lady in the world, except your queen, Dame Guinevere."

"Who is that?" said Sir Arthur.

"Sir," he said, "it is Queen Isolde, who, my lady your queen excepted, is without equal."

"Take your horse," said Arthur, "and arm yourself completely, as I will do; and I promise you," said the king, "I will see her."

Then at once they were armed and horsed, and each took a spear and rode to the forest.

"Sir," said Lancelot, "it is not good for you to go too near them, for believe me, there are two knights there as good as any now living; and so, sir, I beg you, do not be too hasty. For perhaps some knights will be displeased if we come upon them suddenly."

"As for that," said Arthur, "I will see her, for I care nothing for whom I offend."

"Sir," said Lancelot, "you are putting yourself in great danger."

"As for that," said the king, "we will take our chance."

So at once the king rode right up to her, and greeted her, and said, "God save you."

"Sir," she said, "you are welcome."

Then the king gazed at her, and liked her wonderfully well.

With that Sir Palomides came up to Arthur and said, "Discourteous knight, what are you looking for here? It is discourteous of you to come upon a lady like this, without warning. So take yourself off."

Sir Arthur paid no attention to Sir Palomides' words, but went on looking at Queen Isolde. Then Sir Palomides grew angry, and with that he took a spear and came crashing down on King Arthur, and struck him down with the spear.

When Sir Lancelot saw that insult from Sir Palomides, he said to himself, "I am loath to fight that knight, and not for his own sake but for Sir Tristram's. And one thing I am sure of: if I strike down Sir Palomides, I must fight Sir Tristram, and that would be too much for me, to match them both, for they are two noble knights. Nevertheless, whether I live or die, I must avenge my lord, and so I will, whatever becomes of me."

And with that Sir Lancelot cried to Sir Palomides, "Guard yourself against me!"

And then Sir Lancelot and Sir Palomides rushed together with two spears, mightily, but Sir Lancelot struck Sir Palomides so hard that he went clean out of his saddle and had a great fall.

When Sir Tristram saw Sir Palomides take that fall, he said to Sir Lancelot, "Sir knight, guard yourself, for I must joust with you."

"As for jousting with me," said Sir Lancelot, "I will not fail you, for I have no fear of you. But I would be loath to fight you if I had the choice, for I want you to know that I must avenge my particular lord, who was unhorsed without warning and in an unknightly way. And so, though I have avenged that fall, take no offence at it, for he is such a friend to me that I cannot see him shamed."

At once Sir Tristram understood, by his bearing and by his knightly words, that it was Sir Lancelot du Lake, and Sir Tristram truly judged that it was King Arthur whom Sir Palomides had struck down. And then Sir Tristram put his spear from him, and put Sir Palomides back on horseback, and Sir Lancelot put King Arthur on horseback, and so they departed.

"So help me God," said Sir Tristram to Palomides, "you did not act honourably when you struck down that knight so suddenly as you did. And believe me, you did yourself great shame, for the knights came here out of their good breeding to see a beautiful lady; and that is every good knight's part, to look upon a beautiful lady; and you had no business showing off such feats of strength in front of my lady. Mark my words, it will turn to anger, for the one you struck down was King Arthur, and the other was the good knight Sir Lancelot. But I will not forget the words of Sir Lancelot when he called him a man of great honour; by that I knew it was King Arthur. And as for Sir Lancelot, if there had been five hundred knights in the meadow, he would not have refused them, and yet he said he would refuse me. By that, again, I knew it was Sir Lancelot, for he always spares me wherever we meet, and shows me great kindness; and of all knights, I except none, let men say what they will, he bears the flower of all chivalry, let anyone tell him so who will. If he is truly angered, and chooses to do his utmost without any favour, I know of no man alive whom Sir Lancelot is not too hard for, be it on horseback or on foot."

"I can never believe," said Palomides, "that King Arthur would ride about so secretly, like a poor knight-errant."

"Ah," said Sir Tristram, "you do not know my lord Arthur, for all knights can learn how to be a knight from him. And so you may well be sorry," said Sir Tristram, "for your unworthy deeds to so noble a king."

"And a thing that is done cannot be undone," said Palomides.

Then Sir Tristram sent Queen Isolde to her lodging in the priory, to watch all the tournament from there.

Chapter 74: How on the second day Palomides deserted Sir Tristram and went over to the opposite side against him

Then a proclamation was made to all the knights that when they heard a horn blow, they should joust as they had done the first day. And just as the brothers Sir Edward and Sir Sadok began the jousts the first day, Sir Uwain, the son of King Uriens, and Sir Lucan the butler began the jousts the second day. And at the first encounter Sir Uwain struck down the King of Scots' son; and Sir Lucan rode against the King of Wales, and they broke their spears all to pieces; and they were both so fierce that they crashed together so that both fell to the ground. Then the men of Orkney horsed Sir Lucan again. And then Sir Tristram de Liones came in; and then Sir Tristram struck down Sir Uwain and Sir Lucan; and Sir Palomides struck down two other knights, and Sir Gareth struck down two other knights.

Then Sir Arthur said to Sir Lancelot, "See how well those three knights are doing, and especially the first who jousted."

"Sir," said Lancelot, "that knight has not even begun yet; but you will see him do marvellously today."

And then the duke's son of Orkney came into the place, and then they began to do many deeds of arms.

When Sir Tristram saw them begin like that, he said to Palomides, "How do you feel? Can you do today as you did yesterday?"

"No," said Palomides, "I feel so weary, and so badly bruised from the deeds of yesterday, that I cannot hold out as I did yesterday."

"I am sorry for that," said Sir Tristram, "for I shall miss you today."

Sir Palomides said, "Do not rely on me, for I cannot do as I did."

All these words Palomides said to deceive Sir Tristram.

"Sir," said Sir Tristram to Sir Gareth, "then I must rely on you; and so I beg you, do not be far from me, so that you can come to my rescue."

"If need be," said Sir Gareth, "I will not fail you in anything I can do."

Then Sir Palomides rode off by himself; and then, to spite Sir Tristram, he put himself in the thickest of the crowd among the men of Orkney, and there he did such marvellous deeds of arms that everyone wondered at him, for no one could stand a single stroke from him.

When Sir Tristram saw Sir Palomides do such deeds, he marvelled, and said to himself, "He is weary of my company."

So Sir Tristram watched him a long while and did little else, for the shouting and the cry were so huge and loud that Sir Tristram wondered where the strength came from that Sir Palomides had there in the field.

"Sir," said Sir Gareth to Sir Tristram, "do you not remember the words Sir Dinadan said to you yesterday, when he called you a coward? Truly, sir, he meant no harm by it, for you are the man he loves most in the world, and all that he said was for your honour. And so," said Sir Gareth to Sir Tristram, "let me see today what you are made of; and do not stand gaping at Sir Palomides like that, for he is straining to win all the glory and honour away from you."

"I can well believe it," said Sir Tristram. "And since I understand his ill will and his envy, you will see, if I exert myself, that the acclaim that is on him now will be gone."

Then Sir Tristram rode into the thickest of the crowd, and then he did so marvellously well, and did such great deeds of arms, that everyone said Sir Tristram did twice as many deeds of arms as Sir Palomides had done before. And then the acclaim passed clean away from Sir Palomides, and all the people cried out for Sir Tristram.

"Oh, Jesus," said the people, "see how Sir Tristram strikes down so many knights with his spear! And see," they all said, "how many knights he strikes down with his sword, and how many knights' helms and shields he has torn off!"

And so he drove all the men of Orkney before him.

"How now?" said Sir Lancelot to King Arthur. "I told you that today a knight would put on a fine show. There rides a knight, you can see, who does knightly, for he has strength and wind."

"So help me God," said Arthur to Lancelot, "you are right, for I never saw a better knight, for he far surpasses Sir Palomides."

"Sir, believe me," said Lancelot, "it must be so, by right, for it is the man himself, that noble knight Sir Tristram."

"I can well believe it," said Arthur.

But when Sir Palomides heard that the shouting and the cry had turned away from him, he rode out to one side and watched Sir Tristram. And when Sir Palomides saw Sir Tristram do so marvellously well, he wept exceedingly bitterly from sheer vexation, for he knew well he would win no honour that day; for Sir Palomides knew well that when Sir Tristram chose to put forth his strength and his manhood, he himself would get but little honour that day.

Chapter 75: How Sir Tristram left the field, and woke Sir Dinadan, and changed into black

Then came King Arthur, and the King of North Wales, and Sir Lancelot du Lake; and Sir Bleoberis, Sir Bors de Ganis and Sir Ector de Maris, these three knights came into the field with Sir Lancelot. And then Sir Lancelot with the three knights of his kin did such great deeds of arms that all the acclaim began to turn to Sir Lancelot. And so they beat the King of Wales and the King of Scots far back, and made them withdraw from the field; but Sir Tristram and Sir Gareth stayed on in the field and withstood everything that came at them, so that all men wondered that any knight could withstand so many blows. But all the while Sir Lancelot, and his three kinsmen at Sir Lancelot's command, held back from Sir Tristram.

Then said Sir Arthur, "Is that Sir Palomides who holds out so well?"

"No," said Sir Lancelot, "believe me, it is the good knight Sir Tristram, for you can see Sir Palomides over there, watching and waiting and doing little or nothing. And sir, you should understand that Sir Tristram expects this day to beat us all out of the field. And as for me," said Sir Lancelot, "I will not beat him, let whoever will beat him. Sir," said Lancelot to Arthur, "you can see how Sir Palomides waits over there as though he were in a dream; believe me, he is very downcast that Tristram does such deeds of arms."

"Then he is nothing but a fool," said Arthur, "for Sir Palomides never was, and never will be, of such prowess as Sir Tristram. And if he has any envy of Sir Tristram, and has come in with him on his side, he is a false knight."

As the king and Sir Lancelot were talking like this, Sir Tristram rode quietly out of the thick of the fighting, so that no one saw him but Isolde the Fair and Sir Palomides, for those two would not take their eyes off Sir Tristram. And when Sir Tristram came to his tents he found Sir Dinadan in his bed asleep.

"Wake up," said Tristram. "You ought to be ashamed to sleep like this when knights are fighting in the field."

Then Sir Dinadan got up quickly and said, "What do you want me to do?"

"Get yourself ready," said Sir Tristram, "to ride with me into the field."

So when Sir Dinadan was armed he looked at Sir Tristram's helmet and at his shield, and when he saw so many dents of blows on his helmet and on his shield he said, "It's a good thing I was asleep, then, for if I had been with you I would have had to follow you out of shame; more out of shame than out of any prowess there is in me. I can see well enough now from those dents that I would have been well and truly beaten, as I was yesterday."

"Stop your joking," said Sir Tristram, "and come on, so that we can get back into the field."

"What," said Sir Dinadan, "is your blood up? Yesterday you went about as though you were dreaming."

So then Sir Tristram was dressed in black armour.

"Oh, Jesus," said Dinadan, "what's got into you today? You seem to me wilder than you were yesterday."

Then Sir Tristram smiled and said to Dinadan, "Keep close to me; if you see me overmatched, make sure you are always behind me, and I will clear the way for you, by God's grace."

So Sir Tristram and Sir Dinadan took their horses. Sir Palomides saw all this, both their going and their coming, and so did Isolde the Fair, for she knew Sir Tristram above all others.

Chapter 76: How Sir Palomides changed his shield and his armour in order to hurt Sir Tristram, and what Sir Lancelot did to Sir Tristram

Then when Sir Palomides saw that Sir Tristram was disguised, he thought he would do him a shameful turn. So Sir Palomides rode to a knight who was badly wounded, who sat by a fair spring away from the field.

"Sir knight," said Sir Palomides, "I beg you to lend me your armour and your shield, for mine is too well known in this field, and that has done me great harm; and you shall have my armour and my shield, which are as sound as yours."

"Gladly," said the knight, "you shall have my armour and my shield, if they can be of any use to you."

So Sir Palomides armed himself hastily in that knight's armour and with his shield, which shone like any crystal or silver, and so he came riding into the field. And then neither Sir Tristram nor anyone of King Arthur's party knew Sir Palomides. And just as Sir Palomides came into the field, Sir Tristram struck down three knights, right in front of Sir Palomides. And then Sir Palomides rode against Sir Tristram, and they met each other with great spears, so that the spears burst in their hands. And then they dashed together eagerly with swords. Then Sir Tristram wondered what knight this was who fought so knightly with him. Then Sir Tristram was angry, for he felt him to be exceedingly strong, so that he judged he would not be able to deal with the rest of the knights, because of the strength of Sir Palomides. So they laid into each other and gave each other many heavy blows, and many knights wondered what knight this could be who matched himself so against the black knight, Sir Tristram. Isolde the Fair knew very well that it was Sir Palomides fighting with Sir Tristram, for she had seen it all from her window where she stood, as Sir Palomides changed armour with the wounded knight. And then she began to weep so bitterly at the malice of Sir Palomides that she fainted where she stood.

Then Sir Lancelot came in with the knights of Orkney. And when the other party saw Sir Lancelot, they cried, "Turn back, turn back, here comes Sir Lancelot du Lake!"

So knights came and said, "Sir Lancelot, you must fight with that knight over there in the black armour" (that was Sir Tristram), "for he has almost overcome that good knight with the silver shield who is fighting with him" (that was Sir Palomides).

Then Sir Lancelot rode between Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides, and Sir Lancelot said to Palomides, "Sir knight, let me have the fight, for you are in need of rest."

Sir Palomides knew Sir Lancelot well, and so did Sir Tristram; but because Sir Lancelot was a far bolder knight than himself, Palomides was glad, and let Sir Lancelot fight with Sir Tristram. For he knew well that Sir Lancelot did not know Sir Tristram, and he hoped that Sir Lancelot would beat or shame Sir Tristram, which would have made Sir Palomides very glad. And so Sir Lancelot gave Sir Tristram many heavy blows, for Sir Lancelot did not know Sir Tristram, but Sir Tristram knew Sir Lancelot well. And so they fought together a long time, so that Isolde the Fair was nearly out of her mind with sorrow.

Then Sir Dinadan told Sir Gareth that the knight in the black armour was Sir Tristram: "And that is Lancelot fighting with him, who is bound to get the better of him, for Sir Tristram has had too much hard work today."

"Then let us strike him down," said Sir Gareth.

"It is better that we do," said Sir Dinadan, "than that Sir Tristram should be shamed, for the strong knight with the silver shield is waiting over there to fall on Sir Tristram if he gets the chance."

Then at once Gareth rushed at Sir Lancelot, and gave him such a great blow on his helmet that he was stunned. And then Sir Dinadan came with a spear, and he struck Sir Lancelot such a blow that horse and all fell to the ground.

"Oh, Jesus," said Sir Tristram to Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan, "shame on you, why did you strike down so good a knight as he is, and above all when I was fighting with him? Now you have done yourselves great shame, and him no dishonour; for I was keeping him reasonably busy, even without your help."

Then Sir Palomides, who was disguised, came and struck Sir Dinadan down from his horse. Then Sir Lancelot, because Sir Dinadan had struck him down before, attacked Sir Dinadan exceedingly hard, and Sir Dinadan defended himself mightily. But Sir Tristram understood well that Sir Dinadan could not hold out against Sir Lancelot, and he was sorry for it. Then Sir Palomides came fresh at Sir Tristram. And when Sir Tristram saw him coming, he thought to be rid of him at once, because he wanted to help Sir Dinadan, who stood in great danger from Sir Lancelot. Then Sir Tristram crashed into Sir Palomides and gave him a great blow, and then Sir Tristram got hold of Sir Palomides and pulled him down underneath him. And so Sir Tristram fell with him; and Sir Tristram leapt up quickly and left Sir Palomides, and went between Sir Lancelot and Dinadan, and then those two began to fight together.

Just then Sir Dinadan got hold of Sir Tristram's horse, and called out loudly so that Sir Lancelot could hear it, "My lord Sir Tristram, take your horse."

And when Sir Lancelot heard him name Sir Tristram, "Oh, Jesus," said Lancelot, "what have I done? I am dishonoured. Ah, my lord Sir Tristram," said Lancelot, "why were you disguised? You have put yourself in great danger today; but I beg you, noble knight, to pardon me, for if I had known you we would never have fought this fight."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "this is not the first kindness you have shown me."

So they were both on horseback again.

Then all the people on the one side gave Sir Lancelot the honour and the prize, and on the other side all the people gave the honour and the prize to the noble knight Sir Tristram. But Lancelot refused it: "For I am not worthy to have this honour, for I appeal to every knight here that Sir Tristram has been longer in the field than I have, and he has struck down many more knights today than I have. And therefore I will give Sir Tristram my voice and my name, and I beg all my lords and companions to do the same."

Then there was the whole voice of dukes and earls, barons and knights, that Sir Tristram had this day proved himself the best knight.

Chapter 77: How Sir Tristram left with Isolde the Fair, and how Palomides followed and made his excuses

Then they sounded the end of the day, and Queen Isolde was led to her tents. But you may be sure she was angry beyond measure with Sir Palomides, for she had seen all his treachery from beginning to end. And all this while neither Sir Tristram, nor Sir Gareth, nor Dinadan knew anything of the treachery of Sir Palomides; but afterwards you will hear how there arose the greatest quarrel between Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides that could be.

So when the tournament was over, Sir Tristram, Gareth and Dinadan rode with Isolde the Fair to those tents. And all the while Sir Palomides rode with them in their company, disguised as he was. But when Sir Tristram had made him out to be the same knight with the silver shield who had pressed him so hard that day, "Sir knight," said Sir Tristram, "believe me, there is no one here who has any need of your company, and therefore I ask you to leave us."

Sir Palomides answered as though he had not known Sir Tristram: "Believe me, sir knight, I will never leave this company, for one of the best knights in the world commanded me to be in this company, and until he releases me from my service I will not be released."

By that Sir Tristram knew that it was Sir Palomides.

"Ah, Sir Palomides," said the noble knight Sir Tristram, "is that the kind of knight you are? You have been wrongly named, for you have long been called a courteous knight, and this day you have shown me great discourtesy, for you nearly brought me to my death. But as for you, I think I would have done well enough; it was Sir Lancelot together with you that was too much for me. For I know no knight living for whom Sir Lancelot is not too good, if he does his utmost."

"Alas," said Sir Palomides, "are you my lord Sir Tristram?"

"Yes, sir, and you know that well enough."

"On my knighthood," said Palomides, "until now I did not know you; I thought you were the King of Ireland, for I know very well you bore his arms."

"His arms I bore," said Sir Tristram, "and I will stand by that, for I won them once in the field from a most noble knight; his name was Sir Marhaus. And with great pain I won against that knight, for there was no other way out; but Sir Marhaus died through bad doctoring, and he never yielded to me."

"Sir," said Palomides, "I thought you had gone over to Sir Lancelot's party, and that is what made me turn."

"Well said," said Sir Tristram, "and I take it so, and I forgive you."

So then they rode to their tents; and when they had dismounted they unarmed, and washed their faces and hands, and so went in to eat, and sat down at their table. But when Isolde saw Sir Palomides her colour changed, and for anger she could not speak. At once Sir Tristram noticed her face and said, "Madam, why do you look at us like that? We have worked hard today."

"My own lord," said Isolde the Fair, "for God's sake do not be displeased with me, for I can do no other; for I saw this day how you were betrayed and nearly brought to your death. Truly, sir, I saw every bit of it, how and in what way, and so, sir, how could I bear such a wicked traitor as Sir Palomides in your presence? For I saw him with my own eyes, how he watched you when you went out of the field. For all the time he waited there on his horse until he saw you coming back in. And then at once I saw him ride to the wounded knight and change armour with him, and then straight away I saw how he rode into the field. And as soon as he had found you he came at you, and so Sir Palomides fought with you on purpose. And as for him, sir, I was not greatly afraid, but I was badly afraid of Lancelot, who did not know you."

"Madam," said Palomides, "you may say whatever you like, I cannot contradict you, but on my knighthood I did not know Sir Tristram."

"Sir Palomides," said Sir Tristram, "I will accept your excuse, but I know well that you spared me very little; but all is pardoned on my side."

Then Isolde the Fair hung her head and said no more at that time.

Chapter 78: How King Arthur and Sir Lancelot came to Sir Tristram's tent while they sat at supper, and of Sir Palomides

And with that two armed knights came to the tent, and there they both dismounted, and came in armed from head to foot.

"Fair knights," said Sir Tristram, "you are to blame to come in on me armed from head to foot like this while we are at our meal; if you wanted anything of us, you could have eased your hearts when we were in the field."

"Not so," said one of those knights. "We have not come with that intent, but believe me, Sir Tristram, we have come here as your friends. And I have come here," said the one, "to see you, and this knight has come to see Isolde the Fair."

Then said Sir Tristram, "I ask you to take off your helmets, so that I can see you."

"We will do that, as you wish," said the knights.

And when their helmets were off, Sir Tristram thought he ought to know them.

Then Sir Dinadan said quietly to Sir Tristram, "Sir, the one who spoke to you first is Sir Lancelot du Lake, and the other is my lord King Arthur."

Then Sir Tristram said to Isolde the Fair, "Madam, get up, for here is my lord, King Arthur."

Then the king and the queen kissed, and Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram embraced each other, and then there was joy beyond measure; and at the request of Isolde the Fair, King Arthur and Lancelot were unarmed, and then there was merry talk.

"Madam," said Sir Arthur, "it is many a day since I first wanted to see you, for you have been praised so far and wide; and now I dare say you are the most beautiful lady I ever saw, and Sir Tristram is as handsome and as good a knight as any I know; so it seems to me you are well matched."

"Sir, God thank you," said the noble knight Sir Tristram, and Isolde with him. "In your great goodness and generosity you have no equal."

So they talked of many things, and of the whole of the jousts.

"But why," said King Arthur, "were you against us, Sir Tristram? You are a knight of the Round Table; by right you should have been with us."

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "Dinadan here, and Sir Gareth your own nephew, made me be against you."

"My lord Arthur," said Gareth, "I can well bear the blame, but it was Sir Tristram's own doing."

"I may well regret it," said Dinadan, "for this ill-starred Sir Tristram brought us to this tournament, and got us a great many hard knocks."

Then the king and Lancelot laughed so hard they could not keep their seats.

"Who was that knight," said Arthur, "who pressed you so hard, the one with the silver shield?"

"Sir," said Sir Tristram, "he is sitting here at this table."

"What," said Arthur, "was it Sir Palomides?"

"Believe me, it was he," said Isolde the Fair.

"God help me," said Arthur, "that was an unknightly thing to do, for so good a knight as you, for I have heard many people call you a courteous knight."

"Sir," said Palomides, "I did not know Sir Tristram, for he was so disguised."

"God help me," said Lancelot, "that may well be, for I did not know Sir Tristram either; but I wonder why you turned to our party."

"That was done for the same reason," said Palomides.

"As for that," said Sir Tristram, "I have pardoned him, and I would be very unwilling to lose his company, for I love his company very well."

So they left that and talked of other things.

And in the evening King Arthur and Sir Lancelot went off to their lodging; but you may be sure Sir Palomides was eaten up with envy, for all that night he never had any rest in his bed, but wailed and wept beyond measure. So in the morning Sir Tristram, Gareth and Dinadan got up early, and then they went to Sir Palomides' room, and there they found him fast asleep, for he had lain awake all night, and it could be seen on his cheeks that he had wept very hard.

"Say nothing," said Sir Tristram, "for I am sure he has taken anger and sorrow from the rebuke that I gave him, and Isolde the Fair with me."

Chapter 79: What Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides did the next day, and how King Arthur was unhorsed

Then Sir Tristram had Sir Palomides called, and told him to make ready, for it was time to go to the field. When they were ready they were armed, and dressed all in red, both Isolde and all of them; and so they led her very briskly through the field to the priory where she was lodged. And then they heard three trumpet blasts, and every king and knight made his way to the field. And the first who were ready to joust were Sir Palomides and Sir Kainus le Strange, a knight of the Round Table. And so the two of them met, but Sir Palomides struck Sir Kainus so hard that he knocked him clean over his horse's rump. And at once Sir Palomides struck down another knight, and then broke his spear, and pulled out his sword and did wonderfully well. And then the acclaim began loudly for Sir Palomides.

"Look," said King Arthur, "Palomides over there is starting to put on his show. God help me," said Arthur, "he is an exceedingly good knight."

And just as they stood talking like this, in came Sir Tristram like thunder, and he met Sir Kay the Seneschal, and there he struck him clean down from his horse; and with that same spear Sir Tristram struck down three more knights, and then he pulled out his sword and did marvellously. Then the acclaim and the cry changed from Sir Palomides and turned to Sir Tristram, and all the people cried, "Oh, Tristram! Oh, Tristram!" And then Sir Palomides was clean forgotten.

"How about that?" said Lancelot to Arthur. "There rides a knight who puts on a show."

"God help me," said Arthur to Lancelot, "you will see today that those two knights will do wonders here today."

"Sir," said Lancelot, "the one knight keeps watching the other, and strives out of envy to outdo the noble knight Sir Tristram, and Tristram knows nothing of the secret envy that Sir Palomides has for him; for all that the noble Sir Tristram does is done out of pure knighthood."

And then Sir Gareth and Dinadan did wonderfully great deeds of arms, as two noble knights, so that King Arthur spoke of them with great honour and praise; and the kings and knights on Sir Tristram's side did exceedingly well, and held together staunchly. Then Sir Arthur and Sir Lancelot took their horses and made ready, and got into the thickest of the crowd. And there Sir Tristram, not knowing him, struck down King Arthur, and then Sir Lancelot would have rescued him, but there were so many on Sir Lancelot that they pulled him down from his horse. And then the King of Ireland and the King of Scots with their knights did their utmost to take King Arthur and Sir Lancelot prisoner. When Sir Lancelot heard them say so, he went at them like a hungry lion, for he fought so that no knight dared come near him.

Then Sir Ector de Maris came, and he rode with a spear against Sir Palomides, and burst it on him all to splinters. And then Sir Ector came back and gave Sir Palomides such a stroke with a sword that he bent down over his saddlebow. And at once Sir Ector pulled Sir Palomides down under his feet; and then Sir Ector de Maris got a horse for Sir Lancelot du Lake, and brought it to him, and told him to mount it; but Sir Palomides leapt in ahead, and got the horse by the bridle, and leapt into the saddle.

"God help me," said Lancelot, "you are more worthy to have that horse than I am."

Then Sir Ector brought Sir Lancelot another horse.

"Many thanks," said Lancelot to his brother.

And so when he was on horseback again, with one spear he struck down four knights. And then Sir Lancelot brought King Arthur one of the best of the four horses. Then Sir Lancelot, with King Arthur and a few knights of Sir Lancelot's kin, did marvellous deeds; for at that time, as the book records, Sir Lancelot struck down and pulled down thirty knights. Even so, the other party held together so firmly that King Arthur and his knights were overmatched. And when Sir Tristram saw that, how hard King Arthur and his knights laboured, and above all the noble deeds that Sir Lancelot did with his own hands, he marvelled greatly.

Chapter 80: How Sir Tristram went over to King Arthur's side, and how Palomides would not

Then Sir Tristram called Sir Palomides, Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan to him, and spoke to them like this: "My good companions, you may be sure that I will go over to King Arthur's party, for I never saw so few men do so well, and it will be a shame to us knights of the Round Table to see our lord King Arthur, and that noble knight Sir Lancelot, dishonoured."

"It will be well done," said Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan.

"Do your best," said Palomides, "for I will not change from the party I came in with."

"That is because of me," said Sir Tristram. "God speed you on your way."

And so Sir Palomides left them. Then Sir Tristram, Gareth and Dinadan turned to join Sir Lancelot. And then Sir Lancelot struck the King of Ireland clean off his horse; and so Sir Lancelot struck down the King of Scots, and the King of Wales; and then Sir Arthur rode at Sir Palomides and struck him clean off his horse; and then Sir Tristram bore down everyone he met. Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan did there as noble knights; then all the other parties began to flee.

"Alas," said Palomides, "that I should ever see this day, for now I have lost all the honour I won."

And then Sir Palomides went his way wailing, and so he took himself off until he came to a spring, and there he turned his horse loose, and took off his armour, and wailed and wept like a madman. Then many knights gave the prize to Sir Tristram, and there were many who gave the prize to Sir Lancelot.

"Fair lords," said Sir Tristram, "I thank you for the honour you would give me, but I beg you with all my heart to give your voice to Sir Lancelot, for by my faith," said Sir Tristram, "I will give Sir Lancelot my voice."

But Sir Lancelot would not have it, and so the prize was divided between the two of them.

Then every man rode to his lodging, and Sir Bleoberis and Sir Ector rode with Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair to their tents. Then, as Sir Palomides was at the spring wailing and weeping, the Kings of Wales and of Scotland came by him in flight, and they saw Sir Palomides in that frenzy.

"Alas," they said, "that so noble a man as you should be in such a state."

And then those kings got Sir Palomides' horse back for him, and made him arm himself and mount his horse, and so he rode with them, grieving greatly. So when Sir Palomides came near the tents where Sir Tristram and Isolde the Fair were, Sir Palomides asked the two kings to wait for him there while he spoke with Sir Tristram. And when he came to the entrance of the tents, Sir Palomides called out loudly, "Where are you, Sir Tristram de Liones?"

"Sir," said Dinadan, "that is Palomides."

"What, Sir Palomides," said Sir Tristram, "won't you come in here among us?"

"Shame on you, traitor," said Palomides, "for believe me, if it were daylight, as it is night, I would kill you with my own hands. And if I can ever get at you," said Palomides, "you'll die for this day's work."

"Sir Palomides," said Sir Tristram, "you blame me wrongly, for if you had done as I did, you would have won honour. But since you give me such fair warning, I will be well on my guard against you."

"Shame on you, traitor," said Palomides, and with that he left.

Then in the morning Sir Tristram, Bleoberis and Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan, partly by water and partly by land, brought Isolde the Fair to Joyous Gard, and there they rested for a week, and made all the merriment and entertainment they could devise. And King Arthur and his knights went back to Camelot, and Sir Palomides rode with the two kings; and all the while he grieved more than any man could imagine, for he was not only grieved to be parted from Isolde the Fair, but he was in part just as sorrowful to be parted from the fellowship of Sir Tristram; for Sir Tristram was so kind and so courteous that whenever Sir Palomides remembered it he could never be merry.

Chapter 81: How Sir Bleoberis and Sir Ector told Queen Guinevere about the beauty of Isolde the Fair

So at the end of the week Sir Bleoberis and Sir Ector took their leave of Sir Tristram and of the queen; and these two good knights were given great gifts; and Sir Gareth and Sir Dinadan stayed with Sir Tristram. And when Sir Bleoberis and Sir Ector came to where Queen Guinevere was lodged, in a castle by the seaside (and by the grace of God the queen had recovered from her illness), she asked the two knights where they had come from. They said that they came from Sir Tristram and from Isolde the Fair.

"How is Sir Tristram," said the queen, "and Isolde the Fair?"

"Truly," said those two knights, "he does as a noble knight should do; and as for Queen Isolde, she has no equal among all ladies; for, to speak of her beauty, her goodness of heart, and her gaiety, and of her virtue, we never saw her match, as far as we have ridden and walked."

"Oh, Jesus have mercy," said Queen Guinevere, "so say all the people who have seen her and spoken with her. I wish to God I had a share of her qualities. And it was my misfortune to be ill while that tournament lasted. And I suppose I shall never see in all my life such a gathering of knights and ladies as you have seen."

Then the knights told her how Palomides won the prize on the first day with great nobility; and on the second day Sir Tristram won the prize; and on the third day Sir Lancelot won the prize.

"Well," said Queen Guinevere, "who did best over all three days?"

"God help us," said these knights, "Sir Lancelot and Sir Tristram had the least dishonour. And believe me, Sir Palomides did exceedingly well and mightily; but he turned against the party he came in with, and that made him lose a great part of his honour, for it seemed that Sir Palomides is exceedingly envious."

"Then he will never win honour," said Queen Guinevere, "for if it happens that an envious man once wins honour, he will be dishonoured twice over for it; and for this reason all men of honour hate an envious man, and will show him no favour; and he who is courteous, and kind, and gracious, finds favour everywhere."

Chapter 82: How Epinogris lamented by a spring, and how Sir Palomides came and found him, and of the sorrows of them both

Now we leave this matter and turn to Sir Palomides, who rode off and lodged with the two kings, which made the kings downcast. Then the King of Ireland sent a man of his to Sir Palomides, and gave him a great warhorse, and the King of Scotland gave him great gifts; and they would gladly have had Sir Palomides stay with them, but he would not stay on any account; and so he left, and rode wherever chance led him, until it was near noon. And then, in a forest, by a spring, Sir Palomides saw a fine knight lying wounded, with his horse tied up beside him; and that knight was grieving more than he had ever heard any man grieve, for he wept without stopping, and sighed as though he would die.

Then Sir Palomides rode up to him and greeted him gently and said, "Fair knight, why are you lamenting like this? Let me lie down and lament with you, for you can be sure I am much more heavy-hearted than you are; for I dare say," said Palomides, "that my sorrow is a hundred times greater than yours, and so let us each pour out our grief to the other."

"First," said the wounded knight, "I ask you to tell me your name, for if you are not one of the noble knights of the Round Table, you will never know my name, whatever becomes of me."

"Fair knight," said Palomides, "such as I am, for better or for worse, you may know that my name is Sir Palomides, son and heir of King Astlabor, and Sir Safere and Sir Segwarides are my two brothers; and know, too, that as for myself I was never christened, but my two brothers are truly christened."

"Oh, noble knight," said that knight, "how glad I am that I have met you; and you may know that my name is Epinogris, son of the King of Northumberland. Now sit down," said Epinogris, "and let us each pour out our grief to the other."

Then Sir Palomides began his lament.

"Now I will tell you," said Palomides, "what pain I suffer. I love the most beautiful queen and lady who was ever alive, and you should know her name is Isolde the Fair, the wife of King Mark of Cornwall."

"It is great folly," said Epinogris, "to love Queen Isolde, for one of the best knights in the world loves her, and that is Sir Tristram de Liones."

"That is true," said Palomides, "for no man knows that better than I do, for I have been in Sir Tristram's company this past month, and with Isolde the Fair as well. And alas," said Palomides, "unlucky man that I am, now I have lost the fellowship of Sir Tristram for ever, and the love of Isolde the Fair for ever, and I am never likely to see her again, and Sir Tristram and I are mortal enemies to each other."

"Well," said Epinogris, "since you loved Isolde the Fair, did she ever love you back, by any sign you could think of or know of? Or did you ever have any pleasure of her?"

"No, on my knighthood," said Palomides, "I never saw any sign that she loved me any more than the rest of the world, and I never had any pleasure of her; but the other day she gave me the worst rebuke I ever had, which will never leave my heart. And yet I fully deserved that rebuke, for I did not act like a knight, and so I have lost her love and Sir Tristram's for ever; and many times I have pushed myself to do many deeds for the sake of Isolde the Fair, and she was the reason I won my honour. Alas," said Sir Palomides, "now I have lost all the honour I ever won, for I will never again have such prowess as I had in the fellowship of Sir Tristram."

Chapter 83: How Sir Palomides brought Sir Epinogris his lady, and how Sir Palomides and Sir Safere were attacked

"No, no," said Epinogris, "your sorrow is a trifle beside my sorrow; for I had my joy of my lady and won her with my own hands, and lost her again: alas that day! This is how I first won her," said Epinogris. "My lady was an earl's daughter, and as the earl and two knights were coming from the tournament of Lonazep, for her sake I set upon this earl and his two knights, with my lady there present; and so by fortune I killed the earl there, and one of the knights, and the other knight fled, and so that night I had my lady. And in the morning, as she and I were resting here beside this well, there came to me a knight-errant, Sir Helior le Preuse by name, a bold knight, and this Sir Helior challenged me to fight for my lady. And then we fought, first on horseback and then on foot, but in the end Sir Helior wounded me so that he left me for dead, and so he took my lady with him. And so my sorrow is greater than yours, for I have had my joy, and you never had yours."

"That is true," said Palomides, "but since I can never recover from mine, I promise you that if I can meet with Sir Helior I will get your lady back for you, or else he will beat me."

Then Sir Palomides made Sir Epinogris take his horse, and so they rode to a hermitage, and there Sir Epinogris rested. And in the meantime Sir Palomides walked quietly out to rest under the trees, and nearby he saw a knight come riding with a shield that he had seen Sir Ector de Maris carry before; and about ten knights came after him, and these ten knights waited under the trees because of the heat. And soon after there came a knight with a green shield bearing a white lion, leading a lady on a palfrey. Then the knight with Sir Ector's shield, who seemed to be the master of the ten knights, rode fiercely after this knight, Sir Helior, for it was he who had wounded Sir Epinogris. And when he came near Sir Helior he told him to defend his lady.

"I will defend her," said Helior, "as well as I can."

And so they charged together so mightily that each of these knights struck the other to the ground, horse and all; and then they got up quickly and drew their swords and took their shields, and laid into each other mightily for more than an hour. Sir Palomides saw and watched all this, but in the end the knight with Sir Ector's shield was the stronger, and at last this knight struck Sir Helior down, and then that knight unlaced his helmet to strike off his head. And then Helior begged for mercy, and begged him to spare his life, and told him to take his lady. Then Sir Palomides got to his feet, because he knew well that this same lady was Epinogris' lady, and he had promised to help him.

Then Sir Palomides went straight to that lady, and took her by the hand, and asked her whether she knew a knight called Epinogris.

"Alas," she said, "that he ever knew me or I him, for for his sake I have lost my honour, and the loss of his life grieves me most of all."

"Not so, lady," said Palomides. "Come with me, for Epinogris is here in this hermitage."

"Ah, how glad I am," said the lady, "if he is alive!"

"Where are you going with that lady?" said the knight with Sir Ector's shield.

"I will do with her whatever I please," said Palomides.

"Believe me," said that knight, "you talk too big, though you think you have the advantage of me, because you have just seen me fight. Do you expect, sir knight, to take that lady away from me so easily? No, never think it; even if you were as good a knight as Sir Lancelot, or Sir Tristram, or Sir Palomides, you'll pay dearer for her than I ever did."

And so they went to battle on foot, and there they gave many heavy blows, and each wounded the other exceedingly badly, and so they fought on for more than an hour. Then Sir Palomides wondered what knight this could be who was so strong and had such good wind to keep it up, and so Palomides said, "Knight, I ask you to tell me your name."

"Believe me," said that knight, "I dare tell you my name, provided you will tell me yours."

"I will," said Palomides.

"Truly," said that knight, "my name is Safere, son of King Astlabor, and Sir Palomides and Sir Segwarides are my brothers."

"Now, believe me, my name is Sir Palomides."

Then Sir Safere knelt down on his knees, and begged his forgiveness; and then they unlaced their helmets and kissed each other, weeping. And in the meantime Sir Epinogris got up out of his bed, and heard them by the sound of the blows, and so he armed himself to help Sir Palomides if there was need.

Chapter 84: How Sir Palomides and Sir Safere escorted Sir Epinogris to his castle, and of other adventures

Then Sir Palomides took the lady by the hand and brought her to Sir Epinogris, and there was great joy between them, for each of them fainted for joy. When they had come together again, "Fair knight and lady," said Sir Safere, "it would be a pity to part you. Jesus send you joy of each other."

"Many thanks, noble knight," said Epinogris, "and many more thanks to my lord Sir Palomides, who has won me back my lady like this by his prowess."

Then Sir Epinogris asked Sir Palomides and Sir Safere, his brother, to ride with them to his castle, for the safety of his person.

"Sir," said Palomides, "we will be ready to escort you, because you are badly wounded."

And so Epinogris and his lady were mounted, and his lady behind him on a soft-paced ambling horse. And then they rode to his castle, where they had a welcome and as great joy as Sir Palomides and Sir Safere had ever had in all the days of their lives.

So in the morning Sir Safere and Sir Palomides left, and rode on all day until after noon. And at last they heard a great weeping and a great noise down in a manor house.

"Sir," said Sir Safere then, "let us find out what this noise is."

"Gladly," said Sir Palomides.

And so they rode on until they came to a fair gate of a manor, and there sat an old man saying his prayers and telling his beads. Then Sir Palomides and Sir Safere dismounted and left their horses, and went in through the gates, and there they saw a great many fine men weeping.

"Fair sirs," said Palomides, "why are you weeping and making this sorrow?"

At once one of the knights of the castle looked at Sir Palomides and knew him, and then he went to his companions and said, "Fair companions, believe me, all of you, we have in this castle the very knight who killed our lord at Lonazep, for I know him well: it is Sir Palomides."

Then they went to arm themselves, all who could bear armour, some on horseback and some on foot, to the number of sixty. And when they were ready they came briskly at Sir Palomides and at Sir Safere with a great noise, and said this: "Defend yourself, Sir Palomides, for you are known, and by right you must die, for you killed our lord. And so, believe us, we will kill you. So defend yourself!"

Then Sir Palomides and Sir Safere set their backs to each other, and gave many great strokes, and took many great strokes; and so they fought against some twenty knights and forty gentlemen and yeomen for nearly two hours. But at last, much against their will, Sir Palomides and Sir Safere were taken and made to yield, and were put in a strong prison. And within three days twelve knights sat in judgement on them, and they found Sir Palomides guilty, and Sir Safere not guilty, of their lord's death. And when Sir Safere was to be set free there was great grief between Sir Palomides and him, and Sir Safere made so many pitiful laments at his parting that no poet could tell the tenth part of them.

"Fair brother," said Palomides, "leave off your grief and your sorrow. And if I am fated to die a shameful death, let it be welcome. But if I had known of this death that I am sentenced to, I would never have yielded."

So Sir Safere parted from his brother with the greatest grief and sorrow that ever a knight showed.

And in the morning the people of the castle appointed twelve knights to ride with Sir Palomides to the father of the same knight that Sir Palomides had killed; and so they bound his legs under an old horse's belly. And then they rode with Sir Palomides towards a castle by the seaside, which was called Pellounes, and there Sir Palomides was to have justice. That was what they had ordained; and so they rode with Sir Palomides close by the castle of Joyous Gard. And as they passed by that castle there came riding out of it past them a knight who knew Sir Palomides. And when that knight saw Sir Palomides bound on a broken-down old warhorse, the knight asked Sir Palomides why he was being led like that.

"Ah, my fair companion and knight," said Palomides, "I am riding towards my death for the killing of a knight at a tournament at Lonazep. And if I had not left my lord Sir Tristram, as I ought not to have done, I might now have been sure of having my life saved. But I beg you, sir knight, commend me to my lord Sir Tristram, and to my lady, Queen Isolde, and tell them that if I ever wronged them, I ask their forgiveness. And I also beg you to commend me to my lord King Arthur, and to all the fellowship of the Round Table, as best I may."

Then that knight wept for pity of Sir Palomides; and with that he rode to Joyous Gard as fast as his horse could run, and the knight quickly got down off his horse and went to Sir Tristram, and there he told him everything, just as you have heard, and all the while the knight wept as if he had gone mad.

Chapter 85: How Sir Tristram made ready to rescue Sir Palomides, but Sir Lancelot rescued him before he arrived

When Sir Tristram heard how Sir Palomides was going to his death, he was grieved to hear it, and said, "Although I am angry with Sir Palomides, all the same I will not allow him to die so shameful a death, for he is a very noble knight."

And then at once Sir Tristram was armed, and took his horse and two squires with him, and rode at a great pace towards the castle of Pellounes, where Sir Palomides was condemned to death. And these twelve knights who were leading Sir Palomides passed by a spring where Sir Lancelot was. He had dismounted there, and had tied his horse to a tree, and taken off his helmet to drink from that spring; and when he saw these knights, Sir Lancelot put on his helmet and let them pass by him. And then he became aware of Sir Palomides, bound, and led shamefully to his death.

"O Jesus," said Lancelot, "what misfortune has befallen him, that he is being led to his death like this? Truly," said Lancelot, "it would be a shame to me to let this noble knight die like this if I could help him. So I will help him, whatever comes of it, or else I shall die for Sir Palomides' sake."

And then Sir Lancelot mounted his horse, and took his spear in his hand, and rode after the twelve knights who were leading Sir Palomides.

"Fair knights," said Sir Lancelot, "where are you taking that knight? It ill becomes him to ride bound."

Then these twelve knights suddenly turned their horses and said to Sir Lancelot, "Sir knight, we advise you not to meddle with this knight, for he has deserved death, and to death he is condemned."

"I am sorry," said Lancelot, "that I cannot have him released by fair means, for he is too good a knight to die such a shameful death. And so, fair knights," said Sir Lancelot, "defend yourselves as well as you can, for I will rescue that knight or die for it."

Then they began to lower their spears, and Sir Lancelot struck the foremost down, horse and man, and he served three more the same way with one spear. And then that spear broke, and with that Sir Lancelot drew his sword, and then he struck out on the right hand and on the left hand. Then within a while he had left none of those twelve knights standing, but he had laid them all on the ground, and most of them were badly wounded. And then Sir Lancelot took the best horse that he found, and untied Sir Palomides and set him on that horse; and so they turned back towards Joyous Gard. And then Sir Palomides saw Sir Tristram, how he came riding. And when Sir Lancelot saw him he knew him well, but Sir Tristram did not know him, because Sir Lancelot had a golden shield on his shoulder. So Sir Lancelot made ready to joust with Sir Tristram, so that Sir Tristram would not guess that he was Sir Lancelot.

Then Sir Palomides cried aloud to Sir Tristram, "O my lord, I beg you, do not joust with this knight, for this good knight has saved me from my death."

When Sir Tristram heard him say so, he came towards them at a gentle trot.

And then Sir Palomides said, "My lord Sir Tristram, I am much beholden to you for your great goodness, that you would offer your noble body to rescue me when I did not deserve it, for I have greatly offended you. Nevertheless," said Sir Palomides, "here we met with this noble knight, who rescued me honourably and like a man from twelve knights, and struck them all down and wounded them badly."

Chapter 86: How Sir Tristram and Lancelot came with Palomides to Joyous Gard, and of Palomides and Sir Tristram

"Fair knight," said Sir Tristram to Sir Lancelot, "where are you from?"

"I am a knight-errant," said Sir Lancelot, "who rides out to seek many adventures."

"What is your name?" said Sir Tristram.

"Sir, at this time I will not tell you."

Then Sir Lancelot said to Sir Tristram and to Palomides, "Now that you two have met, I will leave you."

"Not so," said Sir Tristram. "I beg you, by your knighthood, to ride with me to my castle."

"Believe me," said Sir Lancelot, "I cannot ride with you, for I have many deeds to do in other places, so that at this time I cannot stay with you."

"Ah, Jesus have mercy," said Sir Tristram, "I beg you, as you are a knight true to the order of knighthood, stay and take your ease with me tonight."

Then Sir Tristram had his request granted by Sir Lancelot. And yet even if he had not asked him, Lancelot would have ridden with them, or else have come after them soon; for Sir Lancelot had come into that country for no other reason than to see Sir Tristram. And when they had come into Joyous Gard they dismounted, and their horses were led into a stable; and then they took off their armour. And when Sir Lancelot's helmet was off, Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides knew him. Then Sir Tristram took Sir Lancelot in his arms, and so did Isolde the Fair; and Palomides knelt down on his knees and thanked Sir Lancelot. When Sir Lancelot saw Sir Palomides kneel, he quickly raised him up and said this: "Believe me, Sir Palomides, I, and any knight of honour in this land, ought by every right to help and rescue so noble a knight as you are, proven and renowned throughout all this realm, from end to end and from side to side."

And then there was joy among them; but the more often Sir Palomides saw Isolde the Fair, the more downcast he grew, day by day.

Then within three or four days Sir Lancelot left, and Sir Ector de Maris rode with him; and Dinadan and Sir Palomides were left there with Sir Tristram for two months and more. But all the while Sir Palomides wasted and grieved, so that everyone wondered why he was wasting away like that. So one day, at dawn, Sir Palomides went into the forest by himself alone; and there he found a spring, and then he looked into the spring, and in the water he saw his own face, how it was troubled and faded, nothing like what it used to be.

"What can this mean?" said Sir Palomides, and this is what he said to himself: "Ah, Palomides, Palomides, why are you so faded, you who used to be called one of the handsomest knights in the world? I will lead this life no longer, for I love what I can never get or win."

And with that he lay down by the spring. And then he began to make a song in rhyme about Isolde the Fair and himself.

And meanwhile Sir Tristram had ridden into the forest that same day to hunt the hart in its fat season; but Sir Tristram would never again go hunting unarmed, because of Sir Breuse Saunce Pité. And so as Sir Tristram rode up and down in that forest, he heard someone singing wonderfully loud, and that was Sir Palomides, who lay by the spring. And then Sir Tristram rode quietly towards it, for he thought there was some knight-errant at the spring. And when Sir Tristram came near him he got down from his horse and tied his horse fast to a tree, and then he came near him on foot. And soon he saw where Sir Palomides lay by the spring and sang loudly and merrily; and all the laments were about that noble queen, Isolde the Fair, and they were wonderfully and marvellously well put, and very sorrowfully and pitifully made. And the noble knight Sir Tristram heard the whole song from the beginning to the end, and it grieved and troubled him badly.

But then at last, when Sir Tristram had heard all Sir Palomides' laments, he was angry beyond measure, and thought to kill him where he lay. Then Sir Tristram reminded himself that Sir Palomides was unarmed, and of the noble name that Sir Palomides had, and the noble name that he had himself, and so he held back his anger. And so he went up to Sir Palomides at a slow pace and said, "Sir Palomides, I have heard your lament, and of the treason you have been hiding from me for so long; and know this: for it you shall die. And if it were not for the shame to knighthood, you would not escape my hands, for now I know well that you have been lying in wait for me with treason. Tell me," said Sir Tristram, "how will you clear yourself?"

"Sir," said Palomides, "this is how I will clear myself. As for Queen Isolde the Fair, you may know well that I love her above all other ladies in this world; and I know well it will happen to me, for her love, as it happened to the noble knight Sir Kehydius, who died for the love of Isolde the Fair. And now, Sir Tristram, I want you to know that I have loved Isolde the Fair for many a day, and she has been the cause of my honour, and otherwise I would have been the most worthless knight in the world. For by her, and because of her, I have won the honour that I have; for when I remembered Isolde the Fair I won honour wherever I came, for the most part. And yet I never had reward or kindness from her in all the days of my life, and yet I have been her knight without reward. And so, Sir Tristram, as for death, I do not fear it, for I would as soon die as live. And if I were armed as you are, I would gladly do battle with you."

"You have spoken your treason well enough," said Tristram.

"I have done you no treason," said Palomides, "for love is free for all men; and though I have loved your lady, she is my lady as well as yours. Even so, the wrong is mine, if there is any wrong, for you make her glad, and have your desire of her, and that I never had, and never am likely to have; and yet I shall love her to the last days of my life, as well as you."

Chapter 87: How a day was set for Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides to fight, and how Sir Tristram was wounded

Then Sir Tristram said, "I will fight with you to the uttermost."

"I agree," said Palomides, "for I could never hope to fight in a better quarrel. For if I die at your hands, I could not be killed at the hands of a better knight. And since I understand that I shall never have the joy of Isolde the Fair, I am as willing to die as to live."

"Then set a day," said Sir Tristram, "when we shall do battle."

"A fortnight from today," said Palomides, "I will meet you near here, in the meadow below Joyous Gard."

"Shame on you," said Sir Tristram, "will you set so long a day? Let us fight tomorrow."

"Not so," said Palomides, "for I am thin, and have been long sick for the love of Isolde the Fair, and so I will rest until I have my strength again."

So then Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides promised faithfully to meet at the spring a fortnight from that day.

"I remember," said Sir Tristram to Palomides, "that you broke a promise to me once, when I rescued you from Breuse Saunce Pité and nine knights; and then you promised to meet me at the stone monument by the tomb beside Camelot, and at that time you failed to keep your promise."

"Believe me," said Palomides to Sir Tristram, "I was in prison on that day, so that I could not keep my promise."

"So help me God," said Sir Tristram, "if you had kept your promise, this business would not be here now at this time."

At that Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides parted. And so Sir Palomides took his horse and his armour, and he rode to King Arthur's court; and there Sir Palomides got himself four knights and four sergeants-at-arms, and so he went back again towards Joyous Gard. And meanwhile Sir Tristram chased and hunted at every kind of game; and about three days before the battle was to be, as Sir Tristram chased a hart, an archer shot at the hart, and by mischance he struck Sir Tristram in the thick of the thigh, and the arrow killed Sir Tristram's horse and wounded him. When Sir Tristram was hurt like this he was exceedingly downcast, and you may be sure he bled badly. And then he took another horse, and rode to Joyous Gard with great heaviness of heart, more for the promise he had made to Sir Palomides, to do battle with him within three days after, than for any hurt to his thigh. And so there was neither man nor woman who could cheer him with anything they could do for him, not even Queen Isolde the Fair; for all the while he thought that Sir Palomides had caused him to be struck, so that he would not be able to do battle with him on the day set.

Chapter 88: How Sir Palomides kept his appointment to fight, but Sir Tristram could not come, and other things

But there was no knight at all around Sir Tristram who would believe that Sir Palomides would ever hurt Sir Tristram, either by his own hands or by anyone else's with his consent. Then, when the fifteenth day had come, Sir Palomides came to the spring with four knights of Arthur's court with him, and three sergeants-at-arms. And Sir Palomides brought the knights and the sergeants-at-arms with him for this purpose, that they should bear witness to the battle between Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides. And one sergeant carried in his helmet, the second his spear, the third his sword. So in this way Palomides came into the field, and there he waited nearly two hours; and then he sent a squire to Sir Tristram, and asked him to come into the field to keep his promise.

When the squire had come to Joyous Gard, as soon as Sir Tristram heard of his coming he gave orders that the squire should be brought before him where he lay in his bed.

"My lord Sir Tristram," said Palomides' squire, "believe me, my lord Palomides is waiting for you in the field, and he would like to know whether you will do battle or not."

"Ah, my fair brother," said Sir Tristram, "believe me, I am very sorry for this news. So tell Sir Palomides that if I were well I would not lie here, and he would have no need to send for me if I could either ride or walk. And so that you can say I am no liar..." And Sir Tristram showed him his thigh, and the wound was six inches deep. "And now that you have seen my hurt, tell your lord that this is no pretence, and tell him that I would rather be whole than have all the gold of King Arthur. And tell Palomides that as soon as I am whole I shall seek him the length and breadth of the land, and that I promise you as I am a true knight; and if ever I can meet with him, he shall have his fill of battle from me."

And with this the squire left; and when Palomides knew that Tristram was hurt, he was glad and said, "Now I am sure I shall come to no shame, for I know well I would have had hard handling from him, and in all likelihood I must have had the worse of it, for he is the hardest knight in battle now living, except Sir Lancelot."

And then Sir Palomides went off wherever fortune led him, and within a month Sir Tristram was healed of his hurt. And then he took his horse, and rode from country to country, and he achieved every strange adventure wherever he rode; and he always asked after Sir Palomides, but in all that season of summer Sir Tristram could never meet with Sir Palomides. But as Sir Tristram sought and asked after Sir Palomides in this way, Sir Tristram won many great battles, through which all the fame fell to Sir Tristram, and it faded from Sir Lancelot. And so Sir Lancelot's brothers and his kinsmen would have killed Sir Tristram because of his fame. But when Sir Lancelot knew how his kinsmen were set, he said to them openly, "Believe me, if the envy of any of you is so bold as to lie in wait for my lord Sir Tristram to do him any hurt, shame or wrong, as I am a true knight I shall kill the best of you with my own hands. Alas, shame on you! Would you lie in wait to kill him for his noble deeds? Jesus forbid," said Lancelot, "that any noble knight such as Sir Tristram should ever be destroyed by treason."

The news and fame of this spread into Cornwall, and among the people of Liones, and they were exceedingly glad of it, and rejoiced greatly. And then the people of Liones sent letters of greeting to Sir Tristram, and many great gifts to maintain Sir Tristram's estate; and every so often, in between, Sir Tristram went back to Joyous Gard, where Isolde the Fair was, who loved him as her life.

Here ends the tenth book, which is of Sir Tristram. And here follows the eleventh book, which is of Sir Lancelot.

Book Eleven: Sir Lancelot and Sir Galahad

Chapter 1: How Sir Lancelot rode out on his adventure, and how he helped a sorrowful lady out of her pain, and how he fought with a dragon

Now we leave Sir Tristram de Liones, and speak of Sir Lancelot du Lake, and of Sir Galahad, Sir Lancelot's son, how he was fathered, and in what manner, as the French book tells it. Before the time that Sir Galahad was fathered or born, a hermit came in to King Arthur on Whitsunday, as the knights sat at the Round Table. And when the hermit saw the Siege Perilous, he asked the king and all the knights why that seat was empty.

Sir Arthur and all the knights answered, "No one shall ever sit in that seat but one, unless he is destroyed."

Then the hermit said, "Do you know who he is?"

"No," said Arthur and all the knights, "we do not know who it is that shall sit in it."

"Then I know," said the hermit, "for the man who shall sit there is unborn and not yet fathered, and this same year he shall be fathered who shall sit there in that Siege Perilous, and he shall win the Holy Grail."

When this hermit had said this, he left the court of King Arthur.

And then after this feast Sir Lancelot rode out on his adventure, until one day by chance he crossed over the bridge of Corbin; and there he saw the fairest tower that he had ever seen, and below it was a fair town full of people. And all the people, men and women, cried out at once, "Welcome, Sir Lancelot du Lake, the flower of all knighthood, for by you we shall all be helped out of danger!"

"What do you mean," said Sir Lancelot, "crying out to me like this?"

"Ah, fair knight," they all said, "here in this tower there is a sorrowful lady who has been in pain there for many winters and days, for she is forever boiling in scalding water. And only lately," said all the people, "Sir Gawain was here, and he could not help her, and so he left her in pain."

"Then I may," said Sir Lancelot, "leave her in pain as well as Sir Gawain did."

"No," said the people, "we know well that it is Sir Lancelot who shall free her."

"Well," said Lancelot, "then show me what I must do."

Then they brought Sir Lancelot into the tower; and when he came to the room where this lady was, the iron doors unlocked and unbolted themselves. And so Sir Lancelot went into the room, which was as hot as any steam bath. And there Sir Lancelot took by the hand the fairest lady that he had ever seen, and she was as naked as a needle. By enchantment Queen Morgan le Fay and the Queen of North Wales had put her there in that pain, because she was called the fairest lady of that country; and there she had been five years, and she could never be freed from her great pain until the best knight in the world had taken her by the hand. Then the people brought her clothes. And when she was dressed, Sir Lancelot thought she was the fairest lady in the world, unless it were Queen Guinevere.

Then this lady said to Sir Lancelot, "Sir, if you please, will you go with me to a chapel near here, so that we may give praise and thanks to God?"
