"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "come with me; I will go with you."

So when they came there and gave thanks to God, all the people, both learned and ignorant, gave thanks to God and to him, and said, "Sir knight, since you have freed this lady, you shall free us from a serpent that is here in a tomb."

Then Sir Lancelot took his shield and said, "Take me there, and whatever I can do to please God and you, I will do."

So when Sir Lancelot came there he saw written on the tomb, in letters of gold, these words: "Here shall come a leopard of king's blood, and he shall kill this serpent, and this leopard shall father a lion in this foreign country, and that lion shall surpass all other knights." So then Sir Lancelot lifted up the tomb, and out came a horrible and fiendish dragon, spitting fire from its mouth. Then Sir Lancelot drew his sword and fought with the dragon for a long time, and at last, with great effort, Sir Lancelot killed that dragon. With that King Pelles came, the good and noble knight, and greeted Sir Lancelot, and Lancelot greeted him in return.

"Fair knight," said the king, "what is your name? I ask you, by your knighthood, tell me!"

Chapter 2: How Sir Lancelot came to Pelles, and of the Holy Grail, and of Elaine, King Pelles' daughter

"Sir," said Lancelot, "you may be sure my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"And my name," said the king, "is Pelles, king of the foreign country, and a close kinsman of Joseph of Arimathea."

And then each of them made much of the other, and so they went into the castle to take their meal. And at once a dove came in at a window, and in her mouth there seemed to be a little censer of gold. And with that there was such a fragrance as if all the spices of the world had been there. And immediately there was on the table every kind of food and drink that they could think of. Then in came a damsel, exceedingly fair and young, and she carried a vessel of gold between her hands; and the king knelt to it devoutly, and said his prayers, and so did all who were there.

"O Jesus," said Sir Lancelot, "what can this mean?"

"This is," said the king, "the richest thing that any man living has. And when this thing goes about, the Round Table shall be broken. And believe me," said the king, "this is the Holy Grail that you have seen here."

So the king and Sir Lancelot spent most of that day together. And King Pelles would gladly have found the means to have Sir Lancelot lie with his daughter, the fair Elaine. And this was his purpose: the king knew well that Sir Lancelot would father a child on his daughter, who would be named Sir Galahad the good knight, by whom all the foreign country would be brought out of danger, and by him the Holy Grail would be achieved.

Then a lady called Dame Brisen came forward, and she said to the king, "Sir, believe me, Sir Lancelot loves no lady in the world but Queen Guinevere alone. And so work by my advice, and I shall make him lie with your daughter, and he shall not know but that he is lying with Queen Guinevere."

"O fair lady, Dame Brisen," said the king, "do you hope to bring this about?"

"Sir," she said, "on pain of my life, leave it to me." For this Brisen was one of the greatest enchantresses then living in the world.

Then at once, by Dame Brisen's cunning, she had someone whom Lancelot knew well come to him. And this man brought him a ring from Queen Guinevere, as if it had come from her, and just like the one she usually wore. And when Sir Lancelot saw that token, believe me, he was never so glad.

"Where is my lady?" said Sir Lancelot.

"In the Castle of Case," said the messenger, "only five miles from here."

Then Sir Lancelot meant to be there that same night. And then this Brisen, at the command of King Pelles, had Elaine sent to this castle, with twenty-five knights, to the Castle of Case. Then towards night Sir Lancelot rode to that castle, and there he was at once received honourably by people who seemed to him to be Queen Guinevere's own close household.

So when Sir Lancelot had dismounted, he asked where the queen was. And Dame Brisen said she was in her bed; and then the people were sent away, and Sir Lancelot was led to his room. And then Dame Brisen brought Sir Lancelot a cup full of wine; and as soon as he had drunk that wine he was so besotted and mad that he could make no delay, but without any hindrance he went to bed; and he believed that the maiden Elaine was Queen Guinevere. You may be sure that Sir Lancelot was glad, and so was that lady Elaine, that she had Sir Lancelot in her arms. For she knew well that on that same night Galahad would be fathered on her, who would prove the best knight in the world. And so they lay together until mid-morning; and all the windows and openings of that room were stopped up so that no daylight at all could be seen. And then Sir Lancelot came to himself, and he got up and went to the window.

Chapter 3: How Sir Lancelot was displeased when he learned that he had slept with Dame Elaine, and how she gave birth to Galahad

And as soon as he had opened the window the enchantment was gone; then he knew for himself that he had done wrong.

"Alas," he said, "that I have lived so long! Now I am shamed."

So then he took his sword in his hand and said, "You traitress, who are you that I have lain with all this night? You'll die right here at my hands!"

Then this fair lady Elaine leapt out of her bed, quite naked, and knelt down before Sir Lancelot, and said, "Fair courteous knight, born of king's blood, I beg you to have mercy on me. And as you are renowned as the noblest knight in the world, do not kill me, for I have in my womb a child by you who shall be the noblest knight in the world."

"Ah, false traitress," said Sir Lancelot, "why have you betrayed me? Tell me at once who you are."

"Sir," she said, "I am Elaine, the daughter of King Pelles."

"Well," said Sir Lancelot, "I will forgive you this deed." And with that he took her up in his arms and kissed her, for she was as fair a lady, and as lively and young, and as wise, as any then living. "So help me God," said Sir Lancelot, "I cannot blame you for this. But the woman who worked this enchantment on me, as between you and me, if I can find her, that same Lady Brisen, she shall lose her head for witchcraft, for there was never a knight deceived as I have been this night."

And so Sir Lancelot dressed, and armed himself, and took his leave gently of the young lady Elaine, and so he left.

Then she said, "My lord Sir Lancelot, I beg you, see me as soon as you can, for I have submitted myself to the prophecy that my father told me. And at his command, to fulfil this prophecy, I have given the greatest riches and the fairest flower that I ever had, and that is my maidenhood, which I shall never have again. And so, noble knight, you owe me your good will."

And so Sir Lancelot dressed and was armed, and took his leave gently of the young lady Elaine; and so he left, and rode until he came to the Castle of Corbin, where her father was. And as soon as her time came she gave birth to a fair child, and they christened him Galahad. And you may be sure that child was well cared for and well brought up. And he was named Galahad because Sir Lancelot had been given that name at the font when he was christened; and afterwards the Lady of the Lake confirmed him as Sir Lancelot du Lake.

Then, after this lady had given birth and been churched, as new mothers were, a knight came to her whose name was Sir Bromel la Pleche, who was a great lord. And he had loved that lady for a long time, and he was always wanting to marry her; and she could find no way to put him off, until one day she said to Sir Bromel, "Believe me, sir knight, I will not love you, for my love is set on the best knight in the world."

"Who is he?" said Sir Bromel.

"Sir," she said, "it is Sir Lancelot du Lake that I love and no other, and so woo me no longer."

"Very well," said Sir Bromel, "and since you have told me so much, you shall have little joy of Sir Lancelot, for I shall kill him wherever I meet him."

"Sir," said the Lady Elaine, "do him no treacherous harm."

"You may be sure, my lady," said Bromel, "and I promise you this: for a twelvemonth I shall hold the bridge of Corbin for Sir Lancelot's sake, so that he shall neither come to you nor go from you, but I shall meet with him."

Chapter 4: How Sir Bors came to Dame Elaine and saw Galahad, and how he was fed by the Holy Grail

Then, as it happened by fortune and chance, Sir Bors de Ganis, who was Sir Lancelot's nephew, came over that bridge; and there Sir Bromel and Sir Bors jousted, and Sir Bors struck Sir Bromel such a blow that he carried him over his horse's rump. And then Sir Bromel, as a bold knight, pulled out his sword and set his shield to do battle with Sir Bors. And then Sir Bors dismounted and got clear of his horse, and there they dealt each other many heavy strokes; and they fought like this a long time, until at last Sir Bromel was laid on the ground, and there Sir Bors began to unlace his helmet to kill him. Then Sir Bromel begged Sir Bors for mercy, and yielded to him.

"On this condition you shall have your life," said Sir Bors, "that you go to Sir Lancelot on the next Whitsunday, and yield yourself to him as a recreant knight."

"I will do it," said Sir Bromel, and he swore it on the crossguard of the sword. And so Sir Bors let him go, and rode to King Pelles, who was in Corbin.

And when the king and Elaine his daughter knew that Sir Bors was Sir Lancelot's nephew, they gave him a warm welcome.

Then Dame Elaine said, "We wonder where Sir Lancelot is, for he never came here but once."

"Don't wonder at it," said Sir Bors, "for this half year he has been in prison with Queen Morgan le Fay, King Arthur's sister."

"Alas," said Dame Elaine, "I am sorry for that."

And all the while Sir Bors looked at the child in her arms, and all the while it seemed to him that it was exceedingly like Sir Lancelot.

"Truly," said Elaine, "you may be sure he fathered this child on me."

Then Sir Bors wept for joy, and he prayed to God that it might prove as good a knight as its father was. And then a white dove came in, and she carried a little censer of gold in her mouth, and there was every kind of food and drink; and a maiden carried the Holy Grail, and she said openly, "Believe me, Sir Bors, this child is Galahad, who shall sit in the Siege Perilous and achieve the Holy Grail, and he shall be much better than Sir Lancelot du Lake ever was, who is his own father."

And then they knelt down and made their devotions, and there was such a fragrance as if all the spices in the world had been there. And when the dove took flight, the maiden vanished with the Holy Grail as she had come.

"Sir," said Sir Bors to King Pelles, "this castle may be named the Castle Adventurous, for there are many strange adventures here."

"That is true," said the king, "for this place may well be called the place of adventures, since few knights come here who go away with any honour. However strong he may be, here he may be tested; and only lately Sir Gawain, the good knight, won little honour here. For I tell you," said King Pelles, "no knight shall win any honour here unless he is a man of honour himself and of good living, one who loves God and fears God; otherwise he wins no honour here, however bold he may be."

"That is a marvellous thing," said Sir Bors. "What you mean in this country I don't know, for you have many strange adventures, and so I will lie in this castle tonight."

"You shall not do so," said King Pelles, "if you take my advice, for you will hardly escape without shame."

"I shall take whatever adventure befalls me," said Sir Bors.

"Then I advise you," said the king, "to make a clean confession."

"As for that," said Sir Bors, "I will make my confession gladly."

So Sir Bors was confessed. And as for all women, Sir Bors was a virgin, except for one, who was the daughter of King Brangoris, and on her he fathered a child called Elaine; and except for her Sir Bors was entirely chaste.

And so Sir Bors was led to bed in a fine large room, and many doors were shut around the room. When Sir Bors saw all those doors, he sent all the people away, for he would have nobody with him; but on no account would Sir Bors take off his armour, and so he lay down on the bed just as he was. And just then he saw a light come in, by which he could clearly see a spear, great and long, that came straight at him, aimed at him, and it seemed to Sir Bors that the head of the spear burned like a candle. And at once, before Sir Bors knew it, the spearhead struck him in the shoulder a hand's breadth deep, and that wound pained Sir Bors exceedingly. And then he lay down again for the pain; and immediately after that a knight came in, armed, with his shield on his shoulder and his sword in his hand, and he said to Sir Bors, "Get up, sir knight, and fight with me."

"I am badly hurt," he said, "but all the same I shall not fail you."

And then Sir Bors leapt up and set his shield; and then they laid into each other mightily for a long while. And at last Sir Bors drove him backward until he came to a chamber door, and there that knight went into that chamber and rested a long while. And when he had rested he came out again fresh, and began the fight with Sir Bors anew, mightily and strongly.

Chapter 5: How Sir Bors made Sir Pedivere surrender to him, and of the marvellous adventures he had, and how he achieved them

Then Sir Bors thought that the knight should not go into that chamber to rest again, and so Sir Bors placed himself between the knight and that chamber door, and there Sir Bors struck him down, and then that knight yielded to him.

"What is your name?" said Sir Bors.

"Sir," he said, "my name is Pedivere of the Straight Marches."

So Sir Bors made him swear to be at the court of King Arthur at the next Whitsunday, and to yield himself there as a prisoner, as a knight overcome by the hands of Sir Bors. So Sir Pedivere of the Straight Marches left. And then Sir Bors lay down to rest, and then he heard and felt a great noise in that room. And then Sir Bors saw, coming in (he did not know whether by the doors or the windows), a shower of arrows and crossbow bolts so thick that he marvelled, and many fell on him and wounded him in the places where he was not covered.

And then Sir Bors became aware of a hideous lion coming in; so Sir Bors squared up to the lion, and at once the lion tore his shield from him, and with his sword Sir Bors struck off the lion's head. Just then Sir Bors saw a dragon in the courtyard, exceedingly horrible, and there seemed to be letters of gold written on its forehead; and Sir Bors thought that the letters signified King Arthur. Just then there came a horrible leopard, an old one, and there they fought for a long time, and did great battle together. And at last the dragon spat out of its mouth what seemed to be a hundred dragons; and swiftly all the small dragons killed the old dragon and tore him all to pieces.

Immediately after that an old man came into the hall, and he sat down in a fine chair, and there seemed to be two adders around his neck. And then the old man had a harp, and there he sang an old song of how Joseph of Arimathea came into this land. Then, when he had sung, the old man told Sir Bors to go away from there. "For here you shall have no more adventures; and you have done most honourably, and you shall do better hereafter." And then it seemed to Sir Bors that the whitest dove came in, with a little golden censer in her mouth. And at once the storm, which before had been marvellous to hear, ceased and passed. Then all that court was full of sweet fragrances. Then Sir Bors saw four children carrying four fair candles, and an old man in the middle of the children with a censer in one hand and a spear in his other hand, and that spear was called the Spear of Vengeance.

Chapter 6: How Sir Bors left, and how Sir Lancelot was rebuked by Queen Guinevere, and of his excuse

"Now," said that old man to Sir Bors, "go to your cousin, Sir Lancelot, and tell him of this adventure, which would have been the most fitting for him of all earthly knights. But sin is so foul in him that he cannot achieve such holy deeds; for had it not been for his sin, he would have surpassed all the knights that ever were in his days. And tell Sir Lancelot that in all worldly adventures he surpasses all others in manhood and prowess, but in these spiritual matters he shall have many his betters."

And then Sir Bors saw four gentlewomen come past him, finely dressed; and he saw them go into a room where there was a great light, like a summer's light. And the women knelt down before an altar of silver with four pillars, and something like a bishop knelt down before that table of silver. And as Sir Bors looked above his head he saw a sword like silver, naked, hovering over his head, and the brightness of it struck his eyes so that for that time Sir Bors was blind. And there he heard a voice that said, "Go away from here, Sir Bors, for you are not yet worthy to be in this place."

And then he went back to his bed until the morning. And in the morning King Pelles rejoiced greatly over Sir Bors; and then he left and rode to Camelot, and there he found Sir Lancelot du Lake, and told him of the adventures that he had seen with King Pelles at Corbin.

So the rumour spread through Arthur's court that Lancelot had fathered a child on Elaine, the daughter of King Pelles. At this Queen Guinevere was angry, and gave Sir Lancelot many rebukes, and called him a false knight. And then Sir Lancelot told the queen everything, and how he had been made to lie with Elaine by enchantment, in the likeness of the queen. So the queen held Sir Lancelot excused. And as the book says, King Arthur had been in France, and had made war on the mighty King Claudas, and had won much of his lands. And when the king had come home again, he had a great feast proclaimed, so that all the lords and ladies of all England should be there, except those who were in rebellion against him.

Chapter 7: How Dame Elaine, Galahad's mother, came in great state to Camelot, and how Sir Lancelot behaved there

And when Dame Elaine, the daughter of King Pelles, heard of this feast, she went to her father and asked him to give her leave to ride to that feast.

The king answered, "I am well content that you go there. But whatever you do, as you love me and want my blessing, see that you are dressed and equipped in the richest way; and see that you spare no cost. Ask and you shall have everything you need."

Then, on the advice of Dame Brisen, her maid, everything was made ready for the purpose, so that there was never a lady more richly equipped. So she rode with twenty knights, and ten ladies, and gentlewomen, to the number of a hundred horses. And when she came to Camelot, King Arthur and Queen Guinevere said, and all the knights too, that Dame Elaine was the fairest and the best-arrayed lady that had ever been seen in that court. And as soon as King Arthur knew that she had come, he met her and greeted her, and so did most of the knights of the Round Table, Sir Tristram, Sir Bleoberis, and Sir Gawain, and many more that I will not list. But when Sir Lancelot saw her he was so ashamed, because he had drawn his sword on her the morning after he had lain with her, that he would not greet her or speak to her; and yet Sir Lancelot thought she was the fairest woman he had ever seen in all the days of his life.

But when Dame Elaine saw that Sir Lancelot would not speak to her, she was so downcast that she thought her heart would burst; for you may be sure she loved him beyond measure.

And then Elaine said to her woman, Dame Brisen, "Sir Lancelot's unkindness is all but killing me."

"Ah, hush, madam," said Dame Brisen. "I will undertake that this night he shall lie with you, if you will keep quiet."

"I would rather have that," said Dame Elaine, "than all the gold there is above the earth."

"Leave it to me," said Dame Brisen.

So when Elaine was brought to Queen Guinevere, each gave the other a friendly face, but nothing from the heart. But all the men and women spoke of the beauty of Dame Elaine, and of her great riches.

Then, at night, the queen commanded that Dame Elaine should sleep in a room near her own room, and all under one roof; and so it was done as the queen commanded. Then the queen sent for Sir Lancelot and told him to come to her room that night. "Or else I am sure," said the queen, "that you will go to your lady's bed, Dame Elaine, by whom you fathered Galahad."

"Ah, madam," said Sir Lancelot, "never say so, for what I did was against my will."

"Then," said the queen, "see that you come to me when I send for you."

"Madam," said Lancelot, "I shall not fail you, but I shall be ready at your command."

This bargain was soon struck and made between them, but Dame Brisen knew of it by her arts, and told it to her lady, Dame Elaine.

"Alas," she said, "what shall I do?"

"Leave it to me," said Dame Brisen, "for I shall bring him by the hand right to your bed, and he shall think that I am Queen Guinevere's messenger."

"Now I am happy," said Dame Elaine, "for in all the world I love nothing so much as I do Sir Lancelot."

Chapter 8: How Dame Brisen by enchantment brought Sir Lancelot to Dame Elaine's bed, and how Queen Guinevere rebuked him

So when the time came that everyone was in bed, Dame Brisen came to Sir Lancelot's bedside and said, "Sir Lancelot du Lake, are you asleep? My lady, Queen Guinevere, is lying waiting for you."

"O my fair lady," said Sir Lancelot, "I am ready to go with you wherever you want me."

So Sir Lancelot threw a long gown over himself, with his sword in his hand; and then Dame Brisen took him by the finger and led him to her lady's bed, Dame Elaine's; and then she went away and left them in bed together. You may be sure the lady was glad, and so was Sir Lancelot, for he thought that he had another woman in his arms.

Now we leave them kissing and embracing, as was a natural thing; and now we speak of Queen Guinevere, who sent one of her women to Sir Lancelot's bed; and when she came there she found the bed cold, and he was gone; so she came back to the queen and told her everything.

"Alas," said the queen, "where has that false knight gone?"

Then the queen was nearly out of her wits, and she writhed and tossed like a madwoman, and could not sleep for four or five hours. Now Sir Lancelot had a habit that he had always had: he would chatter in his sleep, and speak often of his lady, Queen Guinevere. So when Sir Lancelot had stayed awake as long as it pleased him, then in the course of nature he slept, and Dame Elaine too. And in his sleep he talked and chattered like a jay, about the love that had been between Queen Guinevere and him. And because he talked so loud, the queen heard him where she lay in her room; and when she heard him chatter like that she was nearly mad and out of her mind, and for anger and pain she did not know what to do. And then she coughed so loud that Sir Lancelot woke, and he knew her way of clearing her throat. And then he knew well that he was not lying beside the queen; and with that he leapt out of his bed like a madman, in his shirt, and the queen met him on the floor, and this is what she said:

"False traitor knight that you are, see that you never stay in my court! Get out of my room, and don't you dare, you false traitor knight that you are, ever come into my sight again!"

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot; and with that he took such a heartfelt sorrow at her words that he fell down on the floor in a faint. And with that Queen Guinevere went away. And when Sir Lancelot came out of his faint, he leapt out of a bay window into a garden, and there the thorns scratched him all over his face and his body; and so he ran off he did not know where, and was as wildly mad as any man ever was; and so he ran for two years, and no man ever had the good fortune to recognise him.

Chapter 9: How Dame Elaine was ordered by Queen Guinevere to leave the court, and how Sir Lancelot went mad

Now we turn to Queen Guinevere and to the fair Lady Elaine. When Dame Elaine heard the queen rebuke Sir Lancelot like that, and saw too how he fainted, and how he leapt out of the bay window, then she said to Queen Guinevere, "Madam, you are greatly to blame for Sir Lancelot, for now you have lost him; for I saw and heard by his face that he is mad for ever. Alas, madam, you commit a great sin, and do yourself great dishonour, for you have a lord of your own, and so it is your part to love him; for there is no queen in this world who has another king such as you have. And if it were not for you, I might have the love of my lord Sir Lancelot; and I have cause to love him, for he took my virginity, and by him I have borne a fair son, and his name is Galahad, and in his time he shall be the best knight in the world."

"Dame Elaine," said the queen, "when it is daylight I charge you and command you to leave my court; and for the love you owe to Sir Lancelot, do not give away his secrets, for if you do, it will be his death."

"As for that," said Dame Elaine, "I dare say he is ruined for ever, and you have done that; for neither you nor I are likely ever to bring him joy again. For he made the most pitiful groans when he leapt out of that bay window that I ever heard a man make."

"Alas," said fair Elaine; and "Alas," said Queen Guinevere, "for now I know well that we have lost him for ever."

So in the morning Dame Elaine took her leave to go, and would stay no longer. Then King Arthur escorted her on her way through a forest with more than a hundred knights. And on the way she told Sir Bors de Ganis everything that had happened that same night, and how Sir Lancelot had leapt out of a window, raging out of his wits.

"Alas," said Sir Bors, "where has my lord, Sir Lancelot, gone?"

"Sir," said Elaine, "I have no idea."

"Alas," said Sir Bors, "between the two of you, you have destroyed that good knight."

"As for me," said Dame Elaine, "I never said or did anything that could displease him in any way. But at the rebuke that Queen Guinevere gave him I saw him faint to the ground; and when he came to, he took his sword in his hand, naked except for his shirt, and leapt out of a window with the most terrible groan that I ever heard a man make."

"Now farewell, Dame Elaine," said Sir Bors, "and keep my lord Arthur talking as long as you can, for I will turn back to Queen Guinevere and give her a piece of my mind. And I beg you, as you ever hope to have my service, keep a good watch and look out in case you ever see my lord Sir Lancelot."

"Truly," said fair Elaine, "I shall do all that I can, for I would be as glad to know where he has gone as you would, or any of his kin, or Queen Guinevere; and I have cause enough for it, as much as anyone else. And believe me," said fair Elaine to Sir Bors, "I would rather lose my life than have him hurt; but alas, I expect never to see him again, and the chief cause of this is Dame Guinevere."

"Madam," said Dame Brisen, who had worked the enchantment between Sir Lancelot and her earlier, "I beg you with all my heart, let Sir Bors go, and let him hurry with all his might as fast as he can to look for Sir Lancelot. For I warn you, he is clean out of his mind; and yet he will be well cured, though only by a miracle."

Then Dame Elaine wept, and so did Sir Bors de Ganis; and so they parted, and Sir Bors rode straight to Queen Guinevere. And when she saw Sir Bors she wept as if she were mad.

"Shame on your weeping," said Sir Bors de Ganis, "for you never weep except when it is too late to help. Alas," said Sir Bors, "that Sir Lancelot's kin ever set eyes on you! For now you have lost the best knight of our blood, the one who was our leader and our support; and I dare say, and will prove it, that no king, Christian or heathen, can find such a knight, for his nobility and courtesy, with his good looks and his gentleness. Alas," said Sir Bors, "what shall we do, we who are of his blood?"

"Alas," said Sir Ector de Maris.

"Alas," said Lionel.

Chapter 10: What sorrow Queen Guinevere felt for Sir Lancelot, and how knights of his kin went looking for him

And when the queen heard them say this she fell to the ground in a dead faint. And then Sir Bors lifted her up and revived her; and when she had come to, she knelt before the three knights, and held up both her hands, and begged them to look for him: "And spare no expense until he is found, for I know he is out of his mind."

And Sir Bors, Sir Ector and Sir Lionel left the queen, for they could not stay any longer for sorrow. And then the queen sent them money enough for their expenses, and so they took their horses and their armour, and set off. And then they rode from country to country, in forests, and in wilderness, and in wastelands; and all the time, as they rode, they kept watch in the forests and among all kinds of people, to listen and ask after him, as a man who was naked, in his shirt, with a sword in his hand. And so they rode for nearly a quarter of a year, up and down and across, in many places, forests and wilderness, and often had poor lodging for his sake; and yet for all their labour and searching they could never hear word of him. And you may be sure these three knights were exceedingly sorry.

Then at last Sir Bors and his companions met a knight called Sir Melion de Tartare.

"Now, fair knight," said Sir Bors, "where are you going?" For they knew each other from before.

"Sir," said Melion, "I am on my way to the court of King Arthur."

"Then we beg you," said Sir Bors, "to tell my lord Arthur, and my lady, Queen Guinevere, and all the fellowship of the Round Table, that we cannot in any way hear tell where Sir Lancelot has gone."

Then Sir Melion left them, and said that he would tell the king, and the queen, and all the fellowship of the Round Table, as they had asked him. So when Sir Melion came to the court of King Arthur he told the king, and the queen, and all the fellowship of the Round Table, what Sir Bors had said about Sir Lancelot. Then Sir Gawain, Sir Uwain, Sir Sagramore le Desirous, Sir Aglovale and Sir Percival de Galis undertook, at the great desire of King Arthur, and above all of the queen, to search throughout all England, Wales and Scotland to find Sir Lancelot; and eighteen more knights rode with them to keep them company. And believe me, they lacked no money for their expenses; and so they were twenty-three knights.

Now we turn to Sir Lancelot, and speak of his trouble and woe, and what pain he endured there; for of cold, hunger and thirst he had plenty. And so, as these noble knights rode together, they agreed to split up, and then they rode in twos, in threes, in fours and in fives, and always they arranged where they should meet. And so Sir Aglovale and Sir Percival rode together to their mother, who was a queen in those days. And when she saw her two sons, she wept tenderly for joy. And then she said, "Ah, my dear sons, when your father was killed he left me four sons, of whom two are now killed. And for the death of my noble son, Sir Lamorak, my heart shall never be glad."

And then she knelt down on her knees before Aglovale and Sir Percival, and begged them to stay at home with her.

"Ah, sweet mother," said Sir Percival, "we cannot, for we come of king's blood on both sides, and so, mother, it is our nature to follow arms and noble deeds."

"Alas, my sweet sons," she said then, "for your sakes I shall lose all my joy and delight, and then I cannot endure wind and weather, what with the death of your father, King Pellinore, who was shamefully killed by the hands of Sir Gawain and his brother, Sir Gaheris: and they did not kill him like men, but by treachery. Ah, my dear sons, this is a pitiful grief for me, your father's death, and the death too of Sir Lamorak, who in knighthood had few equals. Now, my dear sons, keep this in your minds."

Then there was nothing but weeping and sobbing in the court when they were to leave, and she fell into a faint in the middle of the court.

Chapter 11: How a servant of Sir Aglovale's was killed, and what vengeance Sir Aglovale and Sir Percival took for it

And when she had come to, she sent a squire after them with plenty of money for expenses. And so when the squire had caught up with them, they would not let him ride with them, but sent him home again to comfort their mother, asking her humbly for her blessing. And so night overtook this squire, and by misfortune he happened to come to a castle where a baron lived. And so when the squire had come into the castle, the lord asked him where he came from, and whom he served.

"My lord," said the squire, "I serve a good knight who is called Sir Aglovale." The squire said it with good intentions, thinking he would be better treated for Sir Aglovale's sake than if he had said he served the queen, Aglovale's mother.

"Well, fellow," said the lord of that castle, "for Sir Aglovale's sake you'll get a bad lodging. Sir Aglovale killed my brother, and so you'll die, as part payment."

And then that lord commanded his men to take him away and kill him; and so they did, and dragged him out of the castle, and there they killed him without mercy.

Just then, in the morning, Sir Aglovale and Sir Percival came riding by a churchyard, where men and women were busy, and looking at the dead squire, and they meant to bury him.

"What is it there," said Sir Aglovale, "that you are staring at so hard?"

A good man stepped forward and said, "Fair knight, here lies a squire who was shamefully killed last night."

"How was he killed, my good fellow?" said Sir Aglovale.

"My fair sir," said the man, "the lord of this castle lodged this squire last night; and because he said he was the servant of a good knight who is with King Arthur, whose name is Sir Aglovale, the lord ordered him killed, and that is why he is dead."

"Many thanks," said Sir Aglovale, "and you shall see his death avenged swiftly; for I am that same knight for whose sake this squire was killed."

Then Sir Aglovale called Sir Percival to him, and told him to dismount quickly; and so they both dismounted, and handed their horses over to their men, and so they went on foot into the castle. And as soon as they were inside the castle gate, Sir Aglovale told the porter, "Go to your lord and tell him that I am Sir Aglovale, for whose sake this squire was killed last night."

At once the porter told this to his lord, whose name was Goodewin. At once he armed himself, and then he came into the courtyard and said, "Which of you is Sir Aglovale?"

"Here I am," said Aglovale. "Why did you kill my mother's squire last night?"

"I killed him because of you," said Sir Goodewin, "for you killed my brother, Sir Gawdelin."

"As for your brother," said Sir Aglovale, "I admit it, I killed him, for he was a false knight and a betrayer of ladies and of good knights. And for the death of my squire you shall die."

"I defy you," said Sir Goodewin.

Then they laid into each other as fiercely as two lions, and Sir Percival fought with all the rest who would fight. And within a while Sir Percival had killed all who would stand against him; for Sir Percival dealt his strokes so roughly that no man dared face him. And within a while Sir Aglovale had Sir Goodewin on the ground, and there he unlaced his helmet and struck off his head. And then they left and took their horses; and then they had the dead squire carried to a priory, and there they buried him.

Chapter 12: How Sir Percival left his brother in secret, and how he freed a knight bound with a chain, and of other doings

And when this was done they rode into many countries, always asking after Sir Lancelot, but they could never hear of him; and at last they came to a castle called Cardican, and there Sir Percival and Sir Aglovale were lodged together. And secretly, about midnight, Sir Percival came to Aglovale's squire and said, "Get up and make yourself ready, for you and I are going to ride away secretly."

"Sir," said the squire, "I would very gladly ride with you wherever you want me to; but if my lord, your brother, catches me, he will kill me."

"Don't you worry about that, for I shall be your protection."

And so Sir Percival rode until it was past noon, and then he came to a bridge of stone, and there he found a knight who was bound with a chain fast around the waist to a pillar of stone.

"O fair knight," said the bound knight, "I beg you, free me from my bonds."

"What knight are you," said Sir Percival, "and why are you bound like this?"

"Sir, I shall tell you," said the knight. "I am a knight of the Round Table, and my name is Sir Persides; and I came this way by chance, and lodged here in this castle at the foot of the bridge, and in it lives a discourteous lady. And because she offered herself to me as my lover, and I refused her, she set her men on me suddenly, before I could get to my weapon; and so they bound me, and here I know well I shall die, unless some man of honour breaks my bonds."

"Cheer up," said Sir Percival, "and because you are a knight of the Round Table as well as I am, I trust to God to break your bonds."

And with that Sir Percival drew his sword and struck at the chain with such force that he cut the chain in two, and through Sir Persides' hauberk too, and hurt him a little.

"O Jesus," said Sir Persides, "that was as mighty a stroke as I ever felt, for if it had not been for the chain you would have killed me."

And with that Sir Persides saw a knight coming out of a castle as fast as ever he could gallop. "Watch out, sir," said Sir Persides, "here comes a man who wants to fight you."

"Let him come," said Sir Percival.

And so he met that knight in the middle of the bridge; and Sir Percival gave him such a blow that he knocked him clean off his horse and over a section of the bridge, so that if there had not been a little boat under the bridge, that knight would have drowned. And then Sir Percival took the knight's horse and had Sir Persides mount it; and so they rode to the castle, and told the lady to release Sir Persides' servants, or else he would kill every one he found; and so for fear she released them all. Then Sir Percival noticed a lady who stood in that tower.

"Ah, madam," said Sir Percival, "what kind of practice and custom is that for a lady, to destroy good knights unless they will be your lovers? Truly, this is a shameful custom for a lady, and if I did not have a great matter in hand I would put an end to your evil customs."

And so Sir Persides brought Sir Percival to his own castle, and there he gave him a warm welcome all that night. And in the morning, when Sir Percival had heard mass and broken his fast, he told Sir Persides to ride to King Arthur: "And tell the king how you met me; and tell my brother, Sir Aglovale, how I rescued you; and tell him not to look for me, for I am on the quest to find Sir Lancelot du Lake, and though he looks for me he shall not find me; and tell him I will never see him, or the court, until I have found Sir Lancelot. Also tell Sir Kay the Seneschal, and Sir Mordred, that I trust to Jesus to be of as great worth as either of them; for tell them I shall never forget the mockery and scorn they gave me the day that I was made knight. And tell them I will never see that court until men speak more honour of me than they ever did of either of them."

And so Sir Persides left Sir Percival, and then he rode to King Arthur, and told there about Sir Percival. And when Sir Aglovale heard him speak of his brother Sir Percival, he said, "He left me unkindly."

Chapter 13: How Sir Percival met Sir Ector, and how they fought a long time, and each had nearly killed the other

"Sir," said Sir Persides, "on my life, he will prove as noble a knight as any now living."

And when he saw Sir Kay and Sir Mordred, Sir Persides said this: "My fair lords both, Sir Percival greets you both well, and he sent you word by me that he trusts to God, before he ever comes to the court again, to be of as great nobility as ever you both were, and to have more men speak of his nobility than ever did of you."

"That may well be," said Sir Kay and Sir Mordred, "but at the time when he was made knight he looked very unlikely to prove a good knight."

"As for that," said King Arthur, "he is bound to prove a good knight, for his father and his brothers were noble knights."

And now we will turn to Sir Percival, who rode a long way; and in a forest he met a knight with a broken shield and a broken helmet. And as soon as each saw the other they quickly made ready to joust, and so crashed together with all the might of their horses, and met so hard that Sir Percival was struck to the ground. And then Sir Percival got up swiftly, and threw his shield onto his shoulder and drew his sword, and said to the other knight, "Dismount, and let us fight to the uttermost."

"Do you want more?" said that knight.

And with that he dismounted, and sent his horse away from him; and then they came together at an easy pace, and there they laid into each other with noble swords, and sometimes they struck and sometimes they thrust, and each gave the other many great wounds. So they fought for nearly half a day, and never rested except very little, and neither of them had fewer than fifteen wounds, and they bled so much that it was a marvel they could stand on their feet. But this knight who fought with Sir Percival was a proven knight and a skilful fighter, and Sir Percival was young and strong, and not as knowing in fighting as the other was.

Then Sir Percival spoke first, and said, "Sir knight, hold your hand a while, for we have fought too long over a trivial matter and quarrel; and so I beg you, tell me your name, for I was never matched before this time."

"God help me," said that knight, "and never before this time was there any knight who wounded me as badly as you have done, and yet I have fought in many battles. And now you shall know that I am a knight of the Round Table, and my name is Sir Ector de Maris, brother of the good knight Sir Lancelot du Lake."

"Alas," said Sir Percival, "and my name is Sir Percival de Galis, who have taken up my quest to look for Sir Lancelot, and now I am sure that I shall never finish my quest, for you have killed me with your hands."

"It is not so," said Sir Ector, "for I am killed by your hands, and cannot live. So I beg you," said Sir Ector to Sir Percival, "ride from here to a priory near by, and bring me a priest so that I may receive my Saviour, for I cannot live. And when you come to the court of King Arthur, do not tell my brother, Sir Lancelot, how you killed me, for then he would be your mortal enemy; but you may say that I was killed on my quest as I looked for him."

"Alas," said Sir Percival, "you are asking what can never be, for I am so faint from bleeding that I can scarcely stand. How then should I get on my horse?"

Chapter 14: How by a miracle they were both healed when the holy vessel, the Holy Grail, came to them

Then they both grieved beyond measure.

"This will do no good," said Sir Percival.

And then he knelt down and prayed devoutly to Almighty Jesus, for he was one of the best knights in the world at that time, and the one in whom the true faith was strongest. Just then the holy vessel of the Holy Grail came by, with every kind of sweetness and fragrance; but they could not clearly see who carried that vessel, though Sir Percival had a glimpse of the vessel and of the maiden who carried it, for he was a perfectly pure virgin himself. And immediately they were both as whole in skin and limb as they had ever been in their lives. Then they gave thanks to God with great humility.

"O Jesus," said Sir Percival, "what can this mean, that we are healed like this, when just now we were at the point of dying?"

"I know very well," said Sir Ector, "what it is. It is a holy vessel that is carried by a maiden, and in it is part of the holy blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, blessed may he be. But it cannot be seen," said Sir Ector, "except by a perfect man."

"God help me," said Sir Percival, "I saw a damsel, as I thought, all in white, with a vessel in both her hands, and immediately I was whole."

So then they took their horses and their armour, and mended their armour where it was broken as well as they could; and so they mounted their horses, and rode along talking together. And there Sir Ector de Maris told Sir Percival how he had looked for his brother, Sir Lancelot, a long time, and could never hear any news of him: "I have been in many strange adventures on this quest." And so each told the other of their adventures.

Here ends the eleventh book.

Here follows the twelfth book.

Book Twelve: Sir Lancelot and His Madness

Chapter 1: How Sir Lancelot in his madness took a sword and fought with a knight, and leapt into a bed

And now we leave Sir Ector and Sir Percival for a while, and speak of Sir Lancelot, who suffered and endured many hard trials, who ran stark mad from place to place all the while, and lived on fruit and whatever he could get, and drank water, for two years; and he had little other clothing but his shirt and his breeches. So, as Sir Lancelot wandered here and there, he came into a fair meadow where he found a tent; and close by, on a tree, there hung a white shield, and two swords hung beside it, and two spears leaned against a tree there. And when Sir Lancelot saw the swords, at once he leapt to one of them, and took it in his hand, and drew it out. And then he hacked at the shield, so that the whole meadow rang with the blows, and he made as much noise as if ten knights had been fighting together.

Then a dwarf came out, and leapt at Sir Lancelot, and tried to get the sword out of his hand. And then Sir Lancelot took him by both shoulders and threw him to the ground on his neck, so that he nearly broke his neck; and with that the dwarf cried for help. Then out came a fine-looking knight, handsomely dressed in scarlet trimmed with ermine. And as soon as he saw Sir Lancelot he judged that he must be out of his wits. And then he spoke to him kindly: "Good man, put down that sword, for it seems to me you have more need of sleep and of warm clothes than of swinging that sword."

"As for that," said Sir Lancelot, "don't come too near, for if you do, believe me, I will kill you."

And when the knight of the tent saw that, he leapt back inside the tent. And then the dwarf quickly armed him; and so the knight meant to take the sword from Sir Lancelot by force and strength, and so he came stepping out. And when Sir Lancelot saw him coming so, fully armed, with his sword in his hand, then Sir Lancelot flew at him with such force, and hit him such a blow on the helm, that the stroke stunned his brains, and with that the sword broke in three. And the knight fell to the earth as if he were dead, the blood bursting out of his mouth, his nose and his ears. And then Sir Lancelot ran into the tent, and rushed straight into the warm bed; and there was a lady in that bed, and she grabbed her shift and ran out of the tent. And when she saw her lord lying on the ground as if dead, she cried and wept as if she had gone mad. Then with her noise the knight woke out of his faint, and looked up weakly; and then he asked her where that madman was who had given him such a blow: "For I never had such a blow from any man's hand."

"Sir," said the dwarf, "there is no honour in hurting him, for he is a man out of his wits. And have no doubt, he has been a man of great honour, and has gone mad from some sorrow he has taken to heart. And it seems to me," said the dwarf, "he looks very like Sir Lancelot, for I saw him at the great tournament near Lonazep."

"Jesus forbid," said the knight, "that the noble knight Sir Lancelot should ever be in such a state! But whoever he is," said the knight, "I will do him no harm." And this knight's name was Bliant. Then he said to the dwarf, "Ride fast to my brother Sir Selivant, who is at the Castle Blank, and tell him what has happened to me, and tell him to bring a horse-litter with him, and then we will carry this knight to my castle."

Chapter 2: How Sir Lancelot was carried in a horse litter, and how Sir Lancelot rescued Sir Bliant, his host

So the dwarf rode fast, and he came back and brought Sir Selivant with him, and six men with a horse-litter; and so they picked up the feather bed with Sir Lancelot on it, and carried the whole thing away with them to the Castle Blank, and he never woke until he was inside the castle. And then they bound his hands and his feet, and gave him good food and good drink, and brought him back to his strength and his good looks; but they could not bring him back to his wits, nor to knowing himself. So Sir Lancelot was there more than a year and a half, decently clothed and well cared for.

Then one day the lord of that castle, Sir Bliant, took up his arms, on horseback, with a spear, to look for adventures. And as he rode in a forest two knights-errant met him; one was Breuse Saunce Pité, and the other his brother, Sir Bertelot. And these two both charged Sir Bliant at once, and broke their spears on his body. And then they drew their swords and fought a great fight, and fought together for a long time. But at last Sir Bliant was badly wounded, and felt himself growing faint; and then he fled on horseback toward his castle. And as they came rushing under the castle, where Sir Lancelot lay at a window, he saw how two knights were laying into Sir Bliant with their swords. And when Sir Lancelot saw that, mad as he was, he was sorry for his lord, Sir Bliant. And then Sir Lancelot broke the chains off his legs and his arms, and in breaking them he hurt his hands badly. And so Sir Lancelot ran out by a back gate, and there he met the two knights who were chasing Sir Bliant; and there he pulled Sir Bertelot down from his horse with his bare hands, and with that he wrenched his sword out of his hand. And so he leapt at Sir Breuse, and gave him such a blow on the head that he tumbled backward over his horse's rump. And when Sir Bertelot saw his brother take such a fall, he got a spear in his hand, and would have run Sir Lancelot through; Sir Bliant saw that, and struck off Sir Bertelot's hand. And then Sir Breuse and Sir Bertelot got to their horses and fled.

When Sir Selivant came and saw what Sir Lancelot had done for his brother, he thanked God, and so did his brother, that they had ever done him any good. But when Sir Bliant saw that Sir Lancelot was hurt from breaking his irons, he was sorry that he had ever bound him.

"Bind him no more," said Sir Selivant, "for he is lucky to have about, and gracious."

Then they rejoiced greatly over Sir Lancelot, and they bound him no more; and so he stayed there half a year and more. And early one morning Sir Lancelot saw a great boar coming near him with many hounds. But the boar was so big that no hounds could pull him down; and the hunters came after, blowing their horns, some on horseback and some on foot. And then Sir Lancelot saw one of them dismount and tie his horse to a tree, and lean his spear against the tree.

Chapter 3: How Sir Lancelot fought against a boar and slew it, and how he was hurt and brought to a hermitage

So Sir Lancelot came and found the horse tied to a tree, and a spear leaning against a tree, and a sword tied to the saddlebow; and then Sir Lancelot leapt into the saddle and got the spear in his hand, and then he rode after the boar. And then Sir Lancelot saw where the boar had set his rump hard against a tree close by a hermitage. Then Sir Lancelot ran at the boar with his spear, and with that the boar turned nimbly, and ripped out the lungs and the heart of the horse, so that Lancelot fell to the earth; and before Sir Lancelot could get clear of the horse, the boar ripped him through the brawn of the thigh right up to the back of the knee. And then Sir Lancelot was angry, and up he got onto his feet, and drew his sword, and he struck off the boar's head at one stroke. And with that the hermit came out, and saw that he had such a wound. Then the hermit came to Sir Lancelot and pitied him, and wanted to take him home to his hermitage; but when Sir Lancelot heard him speak, he was so angry with his wound that he ran at the hermit to kill him, and the hermit ran away. And when Sir Lancelot could not catch him, he threw his sword after him, for Sir Lancelot could go no further for bleeding. Then the hermit turned back, and asked Sir Lancelot how he had been hurt.

"Fellow," said Sir Lancelot, "this boar has bitten me badly."

"Then come with me," said the hermit, "and I will heal you."

"Go away," said Sir Lancelot, "and leave me alone."

Then the hermit ran off, and there he met a good knight with many men.

"Sir," said the hermit, "close by my place here is the handsomest man I ever saw, and he is badly wounded by a boar, and yet he has killed the boar. But I know well," said the hermit, "that if he is not helped, that fine man will die of that wound, and that would be a great pity."

Then at the hermit's request that knight got a cart, and in that cart the knight put the boar and Sir Lancelot, for Sir Lancelot was so weak that they could handle him very easily. And so Sir Lancelot was brought to the hermitage, and there the hermit healed him of his wound. But the hermit could not provide Sir Lancelot's keep, and so he declined and grew weak, both in body and in mind: for lack of food he grew madder than he had been before.

And then one day Sir Lancelot ran off into the forest; and by chance he came to the city of Corbin, where Dame Elaine was, who bore Galahad, Sir Lancelot's son. And so when he had come into the town he ran through the town to the castle; and then all the young men of that city ran after Sir Lancelot, and there they threw clods of turf at him, and gave him many heavy blows. And whenever Sir Lancelot could reach any of them, he threw them so hard that they never wanted to come into his hands again; for he broke the legs and the arms of some of them. And so he fled into the castle; and then knights and squires came out and rescued Sir Lancelot. And when they looked at him and saw his person, they thought they had never seen so handsome a man. And when they saw so many wounds on him, they all judged that he had been a man of honour. And then they had clothes provided for his body, and straw under him, and a little hut. And then every day they would throw him food, and set drink down for him, but there were few who would bring food to his hands.

Chapter 4: How Sir Lancelot was recognised by Dame Elaine, and was carried into a chamber and afterwards healed by the Holy Grail

So it happened that King Pelles had a nephew, whose name was Castor; and he asked the king to make him a knight, and so at Castor's request the king made him a knight at the feast of Candlemas. And when Sir Castor was made a knight, that same day he gave away many gowns. And then Sir Castor sent for the fool, who was Sir Lancelot. And when he had come before Sir Castor, he gave Sir Lancelot a robe of scarlet and everything that went with it. And when Sir Lancelot was dressed like a knight in this way, he was the handsomest man in all the court, and none was so well made. So when he saw his chance he went into the garden, and there Sir Lancelot lay down by a spring and slept. And so in the afternoon Dame Elaine and her maidens came into the garden to amuse themselves; and as they strolled up and down, one of Dame Elaine's maidens noticed a handsome man lying asleep by the spring, and at once pointed him out to Dame Elaine.

"Hush," said Dame Elaine, "and say not a word."

And then the maiden brought Dame Elaine to where he lay. And when she looked at him, at once she remembered him, and knew him truly for Sir Lancelot; and with that she began weeping so bitterly that she sank right down to the earth. And when she had wept like this for a long while, she got up and called her maidens and said she was sick.

And so she went out of the garden, and she went straight to her father, and there she took him aside by himself; and then she said, "Oh, father, now I need your help, and unless you help me, farewell to my good days for ever."

"What is it, daughter?" said King Pelles.

"Sir," she said, "it is this: I went into your garden to amuse myself, and there, by the spring, I found Sir Lancelot du Lake asleep."

"I can't believe that," said King Pelles.

"Sir," she said, "truly he is there, and it seems to me he must be driven out of his wits."

"Then keep quiet," said the king, "and let me handle it."

Then the king called to him the people he trusted most, four of them, and Dame Elaine, his daughter. And when they came to the spring and looked at Sir Lancelot, at once Dame Brisen recognised him.

"Sir," said Dame Brisen, "we must be careful how we handle him, for this knight is out of his mind, and if we wake him roughly, none of us knows what he will do. But you wait, and I will cast such an enchantment on him that he will not wake for the space of an hour."

And so she did. Then a little while after, the king commanded that everyone should clear away, so that no one would be on the path where the king was coming. And so when this was done, these four men and these ladies laid hands on Sir Lancelot, and so they carried him into a tower, and so into a chamber where the holy vessel of the Holy Grail was; and Sir Lancelot was laid beside that holy vessel by force. And a holy man came and uncovered the vessel, and so by miracle and by the power of that holy vessel Sir Lancelot was healed and recovered. And when he woke he groaned and sighed, and complained greatly that he was in terrible pain.

Chapter 5: How Sir Lancelot, once he was whole and in his right mind, was ashamed, and how Elaine asked for a castle for him

And when Sir Lancelot saw King Pelles and Elaine, he grew ashamed and said this: "O Lord Jesus, how did I come here? For God's sake, my lord, let me know how I came here."

"Sir," said Dame Elaine, "you came into this country like a madman, clean out of your wits, and here you have been kept as a fool; and no one here knew who you were, until by luck a maiden of mine brought me to you where you lay sleeping by a spring, and as soon as I looked at you properly I knew you. And then I told my father, and so you were brought before this holy vessel, and by its power you were healed like this."

"O Jesus have mercy," said Sir Lancelot. "If this is true, how many people there must be who know of my madness!"

"So help me God," said Elaine, "no one but my father, and I, and Dame Brisen."

"Now for the love of Christ," said Sir Lancelot, "keep it secret, and let no one in the world know of it, for I am deeply ashamed that I have gone so far astray; for I am banished out of the country of Logres for ever, that is to say the country of England."

And so Sir Lancelot lay more than a fortnight before he could stir for pain. And then one day he said these words to Dame Elaine: "Lady Elaine, for your sake I have had much hardship, care and anguish; there is no need to go over it again, you know how. All the same, I know well I did you wrong when I drew my sword on you, to kill you, on the morning after I had lain with you. And the whole cause of it was that you and Dame Brisen made me lie with you against my will; and, as you say, that night Galahad your son was conceived."

"That is the truth," said Dame Elaine.

"Now will you, for my love," said Sir Lancelot, "go to your father and get me a place from him where I can live? For I may never come to King Arthur's court."

"Sir," said Dame Elaine, "I will live and die with you, and only for your sake; and if my life could not help you and my death could, believe me, I would die for your sake. And I will go to my father, and I am sure there is nothing I can ask of him that I will not get. And wherever you are, my lord Sir Lancelot, have no doubt that I will be with you, with all the service I can give."

So straight away she went to her father and said, "Sir, my lord Sir Lancelot wishes to be here near you, in some castle of yours."

"Well, daughter," said the king, "since it is his wish to stay in these borderlands, he shall be in the Castle of Bliant, and you shall be there with him, and twenty of the fairest ladies in the country, and they shall all be of high blood, and you shall have ten knights with you; for, daughter, I want you to know that we are all honoured by the blood of Sir Lancelot."

Chapter 6: How Sir Lancelot came to the Joyous Isle, and there named himself Le Chevaler Mal Fet

Then Dame Elaine went to Sir Lancelot, and told him everything her father had arranged for him and her. Then the knight Sir Castor, who was King Pelles's nephew, came to Sir Lancelot, and asked him what his name was.

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "my name is Le Chevaler Mal Fet, that is to say, the knight who has done wrong."

"Sir," said Sir Castor, "that may well be, but all the same it seems to me your name should be Sir Lancelot du Lake, for I have seen you before now."

"Sir," said Lancelot, "you are not behaving like a well-bred knight. Suppose my name were Sir Lancelot, and I did not care to reveal my name: why should it trouble you to keep my secret here, when you are not hurt by it? But mark this: if it is ever in my power, I'll make you pay for it, and that I promise you truly."

Then Sir Castor knelt down and begged Sir Lancelot's pardon: "For I will never tell who you are, as long as you are in these parts." Then Sir Lancelot pardoned him.

And then, after this, King Pelles with ten knights, and Dame Elaine, and twenty ladies, rode to the Castle of Bliant, which stood on an island enclosed in iron, with a fine deep wide water around it. And when they were there Sir Lancelot had it called the Joyous Isle; and there he was called nothing else but Le Chevaler Mal Fet, the knight who has done wrong. Then Sir Lancelot had a shield made for himself, all black, with a crowned queen in the middle of it, all in silver, and a knight in full armour kneeling before her. And every day, whatever merriment all the ladies might make for him, once every day he would look toward the realm of Logres, where King Arthur and Queen Guinevere were. And then he would fall weeping as if his heart would burst.

So it happened at that time that Sir Lancelot heard of a jousting close by his castle, within three leagues. Then he called a dwarf to him, and told him to go to that jousting: "And before the knights leave, see that you make a proclamation there, in the hearing of all the knights, that there is a knight in the Joyous Isle, that is, the Castle of Bliant, and say his name is Le Chevaler Mal Fet, who will joust against any knights who come. And whoever gets the better of that knight shall have a fair maiden and a gerfalcon."

Chapter 7: Of a great tournament on the Joyous Isle, and how Sir Percival and Sir Ector came there, and Sir Percival fought with Sir Lancelot

So when this proclamation was made, knights to the number of five hundred came to the Joyous Isle; and believe me, in Arthur's days there was never seen one knight who did as many deeds of arms as Sir Lancelot did those three days together; for, as the book truly records, he had the better of all five hundred knights, and not one of them was killed. And after that Sir Lancelot gave them all a great feast.

And in the meantime Sir Percival de Galis and Sir Ector de Maris came under that castle that was called the Joyous Isle. And as they looked at that splendid castle they wanted to go to it, but they could not for the broad water, and they could find no bridge. Then they saw on the other side a lady with a sparrowhawk on her hand, and Sir Percival called to her, and asked the lady who was in that castle.

"Fair knights," she said, "here within this castle is the fairest lady in this land, and her name is Elaine. We also have in this castle the fairest knight and the mightiest man, I dare say, who is alive, and he calls himself Le Chevaler Mal Fet."

"How did he come into these borderlands?" said Sir Percival.

"Truly," said the damsel, "he came into this country like a madman, with dogs and boys chasing him through the city of Corbin, and by the holy vessel of the Holy Grail he was brought back to his wits. But he will not fight any knight except between mid-morning and noon. And if you want to come into the castle," said the lady, "you must ride round to the far side of the castle, and there you will find a boat that will carry you and your horse."

Then they left, and came to the boat. And then Sir Percival dismounted, and said to Sir Ector de Maris, "You wait for me here until I find out what kind of knight he is; for it would be a shame to us, since he is only one knight, if we both fought him."

"Do as you like," said Sir Ector, "and I will wait for you here until I hear from you."

Then Sir Percival crossed the water, and when he came to the castle gate he said to the porter, "Go to the good knight within the castle, and tell him a knight-errant has come here to joust with him."

"Sir," said the porter, "ride on into the castle, and there is a common ground for jousting, where lords and ladies can watch you."

So as soon as Sir Lancelot had warning he was quickly ready; and there Sir Percival and Sir Lancelot met with such force, and their spears were so stout, that both the horses and the knights fell to the earth. Then they got clear of their horses, and drew their noble swords, and hewed pieces off their shields, and crashed together with their shields like two boars, and each wounded the other exceedingly badly. At last, when they had fought there more than two hours, Sir Percival spoke first.

"Fair knight," said Sir Percival, "I ask you to tell me your name, for I never met such a knight."

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "my name is Le Chevaler Mal Fet. Now tell me your name," said Sir Lancelot, "I ask you, noble knight."

"Truly," said Sir Percival, "my name is Sir Percival de Galis, and I am brother to the good knight Sir Lamorak de Galis, and King Pellinore was our father, and Sir Aglovale is my brother."

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "what have I done, to fight with you, who are a knight of the Round Table, and whose fellow I once was?"

Chapter 8: How each of them recognised the other, and of their great courtesy, and how Sir Lancelot's brother Sir Ector came to him, and of their joy

And with that Sir Lancelot knelt down on his knees, and threw his shield and his sword away from him. When Sir Percival saw him do this he wondered what he meant. And then he said this: "Sir knight, whoever you are, I charge you by the high order of knighthood, tell me your true name."

Then he said, "So help me God, my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake, son of King Ban of Benwick."

"Alas," said Sir Percival, "what have I done? I was sent by the queen to look for you, and I have been looking for you for nearly two years now, and over there is Sir Ector de Maris, your brother, waiting for me on the far side of that water. Now for God's sake," said Sir Percival, "forgive me the offences I have done you here."

"It is soon forgiven," said Sir Lancelot.

Then Sir Percival sent for Sir Ector de Maris, and when Sir Lancelot caught sight of him, he ran to him and took him in his arms; and then Sir Ector knelt down, and they wept on each other, so that it moved everyone to pity to see them. Then Dame Elaine came, and she gave them as warm a welcome as lay in her power; and there she told Sir Ector and Sir Percival how and in what way Sir Lancelot had come into that country, and how he was healed. And there it came out how long Sir Lancelot had been with Sir Bliant and with Sir Selivant, and how he first met them, and how he left them because of a boar; and how the hermit healed Sir Lancelot of his great wound, and how he came to Corbin.

Chapter 9: How Sir Bors and Sir Lionel came to King Brandegore, and how Sir Bors took his son Helin le Blank, and of Sir Lancelot

Now we leave Sir Lancelot in the Joyous Isle with the Lady Dame Elaine, and Sir Percival and Sir Ector enjoying themselves with them, and turn to Sir Bors de Ganis and Sir Lionel, who had looked for Sir Lancelot for nearly the space of two years, and could never hear of him. And as they rode along like this, by chance they came to the house of Brandegore, and there Sir Bors was well known, for he had fathered a child on the king's daughter fifteen years before, and his name was Helin le Blank. And when Sir Bors saw that child he liked him exceedingly well. And so those knights had a good welcome from King Brandegore. And in the morning Sir Bors came before King Brandegore and said, "Here is my son Helin le Blank, for so it is said he is my son; and since it is so, I want you to know that I will take him with me to the court of King Arthur."

"Sir," said the king, "you may well take him with you, but he is too young."

"As for that," said Sir Bors, "I will have him with me, and bring him to the most honourable house in the world."

So when Sir Bors was to leave there was great sorrow over the departure of Helin le Blank, and there was great weeping. But Sir Bors and Sir Lionel left, and after a while they came to Camelot, where King Arthur was. And when King Arthur understood that Helin le Blank was Sir Bors's son, and King Brandegore's nephew, King Arthur had him made a knight of the Round Table; and so he proved a good knight and a bold one for adventures.

Now we will turn to our matter of Sir Lancelot. It happened one day that Sir Ector and Sir Percival came to Sir Lancelot and asked him what he meant to do, and whether he would go with them to King Arthur or not.

"No," said Sir Lancelot, "that cannot be by any means, for I was so treated at the court that I resolved never to come there again."

"Sir," said Sir Ector, "I am your brother, and you are the man in the world I love most; and if I understood that it would be to your dishonour, you may be sure I would never advise you to it. But King Arthur and all his knights, and Queen Guinevere above all, grieved and sorrowed so much that it was a marvel to hear and see. And you must remember the great honour and renown you have, how you have been more spoken of than any other knight now living; for there is no one who bears the name now but you and Sir Tristram. So, brother," said Sir Ector, "make yourself ready to ride to the court with us, and I dare say there was never a knight more welcome at the court than you. And I know well, and can prove it," said Sir Ector, "that the search for you has cost my lady the queen twenty thousand pounds."

"Well, brother," said Sir Lancelot, "I will do as you advise, and ride with you."

So then they took their horses and made themselves ready, and took their leave of King Pelles and of Dame Elaine. And when Sir Lancelot was to leave, Dame Elaine grieved greatly.

"My lord Sir Lancelot," said Dame Elaine, "at this same feast of Pentecost your son and mine, Galahad, is to be made a knight, for he is now a full fifteen winters old."

"Do as you like," said Sir Lancelot. "God give him grace to prove a good knight."

"As for that," said Dame Elaine, "I have no doubt he will prove the best man of his kin except one."

"Then he will be a good enough man," said Sir Lancelot.

Chapter 10: How Sir Lancelot came to the court with Sir Percival and Sir Ector, and of the great joy over him

Then they left, and within five days' journey they came to Camelot, which in English is Winchester. And when Sir Lancelot had come among them, the king and all the knights rejoiced greatly over him. And there Sir Percival de Galis and Sir Ector de Maris began and told all the adventures: that Sir Lancelot had been out of his mind the whole time of his absence, and how he called himself Le Chevaler Mal Fet, the knight who had done wrong; and how in three days Sir Lancelot struck down five hundred knights. And all the while Sir Ector and Sir Percival told these tales of Sir Lancelot, Queen Guinevere wept as if she would die. Then the queen gave him a joyful welcome.

"O Jesus," said King Arthur, "I wonder what made you, Sir Lancelot, go out of your mind. I and many others think it was for the love of fair Elaine, the daughter of King Pelles, by whom it is rumoured you have had a child, and his name is Galahad, and men say he will do marvels."

"My lord," said Sir Lancelot, "if I did anything foolish, I got what I went looking for."

And with that the king said no more. But all Sir Lancelot's kin knew for whom he had gone out of his mind. And then great feasts were held and there was great joy; and many great lords and ladies, when they heard that Sir Lancelot had come back to the court, rejoiced greatly.

Chapter 11: How Isolde the Fair advised Sir Tristram to go to the court, to the great feast of Pentecost

Now we will leave this matter, and speak of Sir Tristram, and of Sir Palomides, who was the unchristened Saracen. When Sir Tristram had come home to Joyous Gard from his adventures (all this while that Sir Lancelot was missing like this, two years and more, Sir Tristram carried off the renown through all the realm of Logres, and many strange adventures happened to him, and he brought them to an end very well and manfully and honourably), so when he had come home, Isolde the Fair told him of the great feast that was to be held at the Pentecost coming next. And there she told him how Sir Lancelot had been missing two years, and all that while he had been out of his mind, and how he was helped by the holy vessel, the Holy Grail.

"Alas," said Sir Tristram, "that came of some quarrel between him and Queen Guinevere."

"Sir," said Dame Isolde, "I know all about it, for Queen Guinevere sent me a letter in which she wrote me everything that had happened, in order to ask you to look for him. And now, blessed be God," said Isolde the Fair, "he is whole and sound and has come back to the court."

"I am glad of it," said Sir Tristram, "and now you and I will make ready, for both you and I will be at the feast."

"Sir," said Isolde, "if it please you, I will not be there, for because of me you are a marked man to many good knights, and that has given you much more trouble for my sake than you have any need of."

"Then I will not be there," said Sir Tristram, "unless you are there."

"God forbid," said Isolde the Fair, "for then I would be spoken of with shame among all queens and ladies of rank. For you, who are called one of the noblest knights in the world, and a knight of the Round Table, how can you be missing from that feast? What will be said among all the knights? 'See how Sir Tristram hunts, and hawks, and cowers inside a castle with his lady, and forsakes his honour.' 'Alas,' some will say, 'it is a pity he was ever made a knight, or that he should ever have the love of a lady.' And what will queens and ladies say of me? 'It is a pity she is alive, when she will keep so noble a knight as you from his honour.'"

"So help me God," said Sir Tristram to Isolde the Fair, "that is exceedingly well said of you, and nobly advised; and now I well understand that you love me. And as you have advised me, I will do my part accordingly. But no man nor boy shall ride with me, only myself. And so I will ride on Tuesday next, and with no more armour of war than my spear and my sword."

Chapter 12: How Sir Tristram set out unarmed and met Sir Palomides, and how they struck each other, and how Sir Palomides spared him

And so when the day came Sir Tristram took his leave of Isolde the Fair, and she sent four knights with him, and within half a mile he sent them back. And a mile after that Sir Tristram saw ahead of him where Sir Palomides had struck down a knight, and had wounded him almost to death. Then Sir Tristram regretted that he was not armed, and then he halted and waited. With that Sir Palomides recognised Sir Tristram, and cried out loud, "Sir Tristram, now we have met, and before we part we will settle our old scores."

"As for that," said Sir Tristram, "there was never yet a Christian man who could boast that I ever fled from him; and believe me, Sir Palomides, you, a Saracen, will never boast that Sir Tristram de Liones fled from you."

And with that Sir Tristram set his horse running, and with all his might he came straight at Sir Palomides, and burst his spear on him into a hundred pieces. And straight away Sir Tristram drew his sword. And then he turned his horse and struck six great strokes at Palomides on his helm. And then Sir Palomides stood still, and looked at Sir Tristram, and marvelled at his madness and his folly. And then Sir Palomides said to himself, "If Sir Tristram were armed, it would be hard to stop him in this fight; and if I turn back and kill him, I am shamed wherever I go."

Then Sir Tristram spoke and said, "You coward knight, what are you playing at? Why won't you fight me? Have no doubt of it, I'll stand up to all your malice."

"Ah, Sir Tristram," said Palomides, "you know very well I cannot fight you for shame, for you are here without armour and I am armed, and if I kill you, the dishonour will be mine. And you know well," said Sir Palomides to Sir Tristram, "I know your strength and your hardiness to hold out against a good knight."

"That is true," said Sir Tristram. "I understand your valour well."

"You say well," said Sir Palomides. "Now, I ask you, answer me a question that I will put to you."

"Tell me what it is," said Sir Tristram, "and I will answer you truthfully, so help me God."

"Suppose," said Sir Palomides, "that you were armed at all points as well as I am, and I were as unarmoured as you are: what would you do to me now, by your true knighthood?"

"Ah," said Sir Tristram, "now I understand you well, Sir Palomides, for now I must give my own judgement, and, God bless me, what I say will not be said for any fear I have of you. But this is all: understand, Sir Palomides, that at this time you should leave me, for I would not fight you."

"No more will I," said Palomides, "and so ride on your way."

"As for that, I may choose," said Sir Tristram, "whether to ride on or to stay. But, Sir Palomides," said Sir Tristram, "I wonder at one thing: that you, who are so good a knight, will not be christened, when your brother Sir Safere has been christened for many a day."

Chapter 13: How Sir Tristram got himself the armour of a wounded knight, and how he overthrew Sir Palomides

"As for that," said Sir Palomides, "I may not be christened yet, because of a vow I made many years ago; and yet in my heart I believe in Jesus Christ and his gentle mother Mary. But I have only one battle to fight, and when that is done I will be baptised gladly."

"By my head," said Tristram, "as for one battle, you shall not have to look for it any longer. For God forbid," said Sir Tristram, "that through any failing of mine you should live as a Saracen any longer like this. For over there is a knight whom you, Sir Palomides, have hurt and struck down. Now help me to be armed in his armour, and I will soon fulfil your vow."

"As you wish," said Palomides, "so it shall be."

So they both rode to that knight, who was sitting on a bank, and then Sir Tristram greeted him, and he weakly greeted him in return.

"Sir knight," said Sir Tristram, "I ask you to tell me your real name."

"Sir," he said, "my name is Sir Galleron of Galway, a knight of the Round Table."
