"So help me God," said Sir Tristram, "I am very sorry for your wounds. But this is the whole of it: I must beg you to lend me all your armour, every piece, for you see I am unarmed, and I must fight this knight."

"Sir," said the wounded knight, "you shall have it gladly; but you must take care, for I warn you, that knight is strong. Sir," said Galleron, "I beg you, tell me your name, and the name of that knight who has beaten me."

"Sir, as for my name, it is Sir Tristram de Liones; and as for the knight who has hurt you, his name is Sir Palomides, brother to the good knight Sir Safere, and Sir Palomides is still unchristened."

"Alas," said Sir Galleron, "it is a pity that so good a knight and so noble a man of arms should be unchristened."

"So help me God," said Sir Tristram, "either he will kill me or I him, or else he shall be christened before we part."

"My lord Sir Tristram," said Sir Galleron, "your renown and your honour are well known through many realms, and God save you this day from disgrace and shame."

Then Sir Tristram unarmed Galleron, who was a noble knight, and had done many deeds of arms, and he was a big knight, of flesh and bone. And when he was unarmed he stood on his feet, for he was bruised in the back by a spear; and yet, as well as Sir Galleron could, he armed Sir Tristram. And then Sir Tristram mounted his own horse, and took Sir Galleron's spear in his hand; and by then Sir Palomides was ready. And so they came crashing together, and each struck the other in the middle of his shield; and with that Sir Palomides's spear broke, and Sir Tristram struck down the horse. And Sir Palomides, as soon as he could, got clear of his horse, and set his shield, and pulled out his sword. Sir Tristram saw that, and with that he dismounted and tied his horse to a tree.

Chapter 14: How Sir Tristram and Sir Palomides fought a long time, and afterwards made peace, and how Sir Tristram had him christened

And then they came together like two wild boars, laying into each other, circling and sidestepping like noble men who had often been well tested in battle. But all the while Sir Palomides feared the might of Sir Tristram, and so he let him stop for breath. So they fought more than two hours, but often Sir Tristram struck such strokes at Sir Palomides that he brought him to his knees; and Sir Palomides broke and cut away many pieces of Sir Tristram's shield; and then Sir Palomides wounded Sir Tristram, for he was a good fighting man. Then Sir Tristram was mad with rage beyond measure, and rushed at Sir Palomides with such force that Sir Palomides fell flat on his face on the earth; and with that he leapt up nimbly onto his feet, and then Sir Tristram wounded Palomides badly through the shoulder. And all the while Sir Tristram kept fighting just as hard, and Sir Palomides did not hold back, but gave him many heavy strokes. And at last Sir Tristram doubled his strokes, and by luck Sir Tristram struck Sir Palomides's sword out of his hand; and if Sir Palomides had stooped for his sword he would have been killed.

Then Palomides stood still and looked at his sword with a sorrowful heart.

"How now?" said Sir Tristram to Palomides. "Now I have you at a disadvantage, as you had me today. But it shall never be said in any court, nor among good knights, that Sir Tristram would kill any knight who has no weapon. And so take your sword, and let us make an end of this fight."

"As for this fight," said Palomides, "I dare very well finish it, but I have no great wish to fight any more. And this is why," said Palomides: "my offence against you is not so great that we cannot be friends. All the offence I have given is and was for the love of Isolde the Fair. And as for her, I dare say she is peerless above all other ladies, and I never offered her any dishonour; and through her I have won the greater part of my honour. And since I never offended against her own person, and the offence I have done was against your own person, and for that offence you have given me many heavy strokes today, and I have given you some in return; and now I dare say I never felt a man of your might, nor one with so much wind, unless it was Sir Lancelot du Lake: therefore I ask you, my lord, to forgive me all the offence I have given you. And this same day take me to the nearest church, and first let me be fully confessed, and after that see to it that I am truly baptised. And then we will all ride together to Arthur's court, so that we are there for the high feast."

"Now take your horse," said Sir Tristram, "and as you say, so it shall be; and may God forgive you all your ill will, as I do. And within a mile of here is the Suffragan of Carlisle, the assistant bishop, who will give you the sacrament of baptism."

Then they took their horses, and Sir Galleron rode with them. And when they came to the Suffragan, Sir Tristram told him what they wanted. Then the Suffragan had a great vessel filled with water, and when he had blessed it he heard Sir Palomides's full confession, and Sir Tristram and Sir Galleron were his godfathers. And then soon after they left, riding toward Camelot, where King Arthur and Queen Guinevere were, and most of the knights of the Round Table. And so the king and all the court were glad that Sir Palomides was christened. And at that same feast Galahad came in and sat in the Siege Perilous. And so with that all the knights of the Round Table departed and went their separate ways. And Sir Tristram went back to Joyous Gard, and Sir Palomides followed the Questing Beast.

Here ends the second book of Sir Tristram, which was drawn out of French into English. But the third book is not retold here. And here follows the noble tale of the Sangreal, which is called the Holy Vessel, and the meaning of the blessed blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, blessed may it be, which was brought into this land by Joseph of Arimathea. Therefore, blessed Lord, have mercy on all sinful souls.

Here ends the twelfth book.

Here follows the thirteenth book.

Book Thirteen: How Galahad Came to King Arthur's Court, and the Quest of the Holy Grail Began

Chapter 1: How on the eve of the Feast of Pentecost a damsel came into the hall before King Arthur and asked Sir Lancelot to come and dub a knight, and how he went with her

On the eve of Pentecost, when all the fellowship of the Round Table had come to Camelot and had heard their service there, and the tables were set ready for the meal, just then there rode into the hall a very beautiful gentlewoman on horseback, who had ridden very fast, for her horse was all in a sweat. Then she dismounted there, and came before the king and greeted him; and he said, "Damsel, God bless you."

"Sir," she said, "for God's sake tell me where Sir Lancelot is."

"You can see him over there," said the king.

Then she went to Lancelot and said, "Sir Lancelot, I greet you on King Pelles' behalf, and I ask you to come with me to a forest near here."

Then Sir Lancelot asked her whose household she belonged to.

"I live," she said, "with King Pelles."

"What do you want with me?" said Lancelot.

"You shall know," she said, "when you get there."

"Well," he said, "I will gladly go with you."

So Sir Lancelot told his squire to saddle his horse and bring his armour; and the squire did his bidding in all haste.

Then the queen came to Lancelot, and said, "Will you leave us at this high feast?"

"Madam," said the gentlewoman, "believe me, he shall be with you tomorrow by dinner time."

"If I thought," said the queen, "that he would not be with us here tomorrow, he would not go with you with my good will."

At that Sir Lancelot left with the gentlewoman, and rode until he came into a forest and into a great valley, where they saw an abbey of nuns; and there was a squire ready who opened the gates, and so they went in and got down from their horses; and a fair company gathered around Sir Lancelot, and welcomed him, and were exceedingly glad he had come. And then they led him to the Abbess's room and unarmed him; and just then he noticed two of his cousins lying on a bed, Sir Bors and Sir Lionel, and then he woke them; and when they saw him they rejoiced greatly.

"Sir," said Sir Bors to Sir Lancelot, "what chance has brought you here, for we expected to find you at Camelot tomorrow?"

"So help me God," said Sir Lancelot, "a gentlewoman brought me here, but I don't know why."

While they stood talking together like this, in came twelve nuns who brought Galahad with them, who was exceedingly handsome and well made, so that you could scarcely find his match in the world; and all those ladies wept.

"Sir," they all said, "we bring you here this child whom we have brought up, and we ask you to make him a knight, for there is no worthier man's hand from which he could receive the order of knighthood."

Sir Lancelot looked at the young squire and saw that he was comely and modest as a dove, with every kind of good feature, so that he thought he had never seen so finely formed a man of his age.

Then Sir Lancelot said, "Does this wish come from himself?"

He and all of them said yes.

"Then he shall," said Sir Lancelot, "receive the high order of knighthood tomorrow, in honour of the high feast."

That night Sir Lancelot was given an exceedingly warm welcome; and in the morning at the hour of prime, at Galahad's wish, he made him a knight and said, "God make him a good man, for in beauty you fall short of no one alive."

Chapter 2: How letters were found written on the Siege Perilous, and of the marvellous adventure of the sword in a stone

"Now, fair sir," said Sir Lancelot, "will you come with me to the court of King Arthur?"

"No," he said, "I will not go with you at this time."

Then he left them and took his two cousins with him, and so they came to Camelot by mid-morning on Whitsunday. By that time the king and the queen had gone to the great church to hear their service. Then the king and the queen were exceedingly glad to see Sir Bors and Sir Lionel, and so was all the fellowship. So when the king and all the knights had come back from the service, the barons saw, written in golden letters on the seats of the Round Table all around, "Here ought to sit he," and "He ought to sit here." And so they went along until they came to the Siege Perilous, where they found letters newly written in gold which said: "Four hundred and fifty-four winters after the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ have passed, this seat ought to be filled."

Then they all said, "This is a marvellous thing, and a strange adventure."

"In the name of God," said Sir Lancelot; and then he counted up the term of the writing from the birth of our Lord to that day. "It seems to me," said Sir Lancelot, "that this seat ought to be filled this very day, for this is the feast of Pentecost after the four hundred and fifty-fourth year; and if it would please everyone, I would rather none of these letters were seen today, until he has come who is to achieve this adventure."

Then they had a cloth of silk made ready, to cover these letters on the Siege Perilous.

Then the king called for dinner to be served at once.

"Sir," said Sir Kay the Steward, "if you go to your meal now you will break the old custom of your court, for you have never been used to sit down to your meal on this day before you have seen some adventure."

"You are right," said the king, "but I was so glad of Sir Lancelot and of his cousins, who have come to the court safe and sound, that I did not think of my old custom."

So, as they stood talking, in came a squire and said to the king, "Sir, I bring you marvellous news."

"What is it?" said the king.

"Sir, down here at the river there is a great stone which I saw floating on the water, and I saw a sword sticking in it."

The king said, "I will see that marvel."

So all the knights went with him, and when they came to the river they found a stone floating there, as if it were of red marble, and a fine rich sword was stuck in it, and in the pommel were precious stones worked with cunning letters of gold. Then the barons read the letters, which said this: "Never shall any man take me from here, but only he by whose side I ought to hang, and he shall be the best knight in the world."

When the king had seen the letters, he said to Sir Lancelot, "Fair sir, this sword ought to be yours, for I am sure you are the best knight in the world."

Then Sir Lancelot answered very soberly, "Certainly, sir, it is not my sword. Also, sir, believe me, I have no courage to set my hand to it, for it does not belong at my side. Also, whoever tries to take the sword and fails will receive a wound from that sword that will not heal for a long time after. And I want you to know that this same day the adventures of the Sangreal, which is called the Holy Vessel, shall begin."

Chapter 3: How Sir Gawain tried to draw out the sword, and how an old man brought in Galahad

"Now, fair nephew," said the king to Sir Gawain, "you try it, for love of me."

"Sir," he said, "saving your good grace, I will not do that."

"Sir," said the king, "try to take the sword, and do it at my command."

"Sir," said Gawain, "I will obey your command."

And with that he took hold of the sword by the hilt, but he could not stir it.

"I thank you," said the king to Sir Gawain.

"My lord Sir Gawain," said Sir Lancelot, "now believe me, this sword shall touch you so badly that you will wish you had never set your hand to it, not for the best castle in this realm."

"Sir," he said, "I could not refuse my uncle's will and command."

But when the king heard this he regretted it greatly, and told Sir Percival that he should try it, for love of him.

And he said, "Gladly, to keep Sir Gawain company."

And with that he set his hand on the sword and pulled hard, but he could not move it. Then there were no more who dared be so bold as to set their hands to it.

"Now you may go to your dinner," said Sir Kay to the king, "for you have seen a marvellous adventure."

So the king and everyone went back to the court, and every knight knew his own place, and sat down in it, and young men who were knights served them.

So when they had been served, and all the seats were filled except the Siege Perilous alone, at once a marvellous thing happened: all the doors and windows of the palace shut by themselves. And yet the hall was not greatly darkened; and with that they were all dismayed, every one of them.

Then King Arthur spoke first and said, "By God, fair fellows and lords, we have seen marvels today, but before night I think we shall see greater marvels."

Meanwhile there came in a good old man, very aged, dressed all in white, and there was no knight who knew where he came from. And with him he brought a young knight, both of them on foot, the young one in red armour, without sword or shield, except for a scabbard hanging by his side.

And he said these words: "Peace be with you, fair lords." Then the old man said to Arthur, "Sir, I bring here a young knight who is of a king's lineage, and of the kindred of Joseph of Arimathea, through whom the marvels of this court, and of strange realms, shall be fully accomplished."

Chapter 4: How the old man brought Galahad to the Siege Perilous and seated him in it, and how all the knights marvelled

The king was very glad of his words, and said to the good man, "Sir, you are very welcome, and the young knight with you."

Then the old man had the young man take off his armour, and he was in a coat of red silk, and he had a cloak on his shoulder that was furred with ermine, and put that on him. And the old knight said to the young knight, "Sir, follow me."

And at once he led him to the Siege Perilous, beside which Sir Lancelot sat; and the good man lifted up the cloth, and found letters there that said this: "This is the seat of Galahad, the high prince."

"Sir," said the old knight, "believe me, that place is yours."

And then he sat him down firmly in that seat. And then the young knight said to the old man, "Sir, you may go on your way now, for you have done well what you were commanded to do; and commend me to my grandfather, King Pelles, and to my lord Petchere, and tell them on my behalf that I shall come and see them as soon as ever I can."

So the good man left; and twenty noble squires met him, and so they took their horses and went on their way.

Then all the knights of the Round Table marvelled greatly at Sir Galahad, that he dared sit there in that Siege Perilous, and was so young; and they did not know where he came from, except only that he came from God.

And they said, "This is he by whom the Holy Grail shall be achieved, for no one ever sat there but he came to harm."

Then Sir Lancelot looked at his son and rejoiced greatly in him.

Then Bors told his companions, "On my life, this young knight shall come to great honour."

This news spread through all the court, so that it reached the queen. Then she wondered what knight it could be who dared venture to sit in the Siege Perilous. Many told the queen that he looked very like Sir Lancelot.

"I can well believe," said the queen, "that Sir Lancelot fathered him on King Pelles' daughter, by whom he was made to lie, by enchantment, and his name is Galahad. I would gladly see him," said the queen, "for he must surely be a noble man, for so is the father who fathered him, as all the Round Table will bear me out."

So when the meal was over and the king and everyone had risen, the king went to the Siege Perilous and lifted up the cloth, and found the name of Galahad there; and then he showed it to Sir Gawain, and said, "Fair nephew, now we have Sir Galahad among us, the good knight who shall bring honour to us all; and on my life he shall achieve the Holy Grail, just as Sir Lancelot gave us to understand."

Then King Arthur came to Galahad and said, "Sir, you are welcome, for you shall move many good knights to the quest of the Holy Grail, and you shall achieve what no knights could ever bring to an end."

Then the king took him by the hand, and went down from the palace to show Galahad the adventure of the stone.

Chapter 5: How King Arthur showed Galahad the stone floating on the water, and how he drew out the sword

The queen heard of it, and came after them with many ladies, and they showed them the stone where it floated on the water.

"Sir," said the king to Sir Galahad, "here is as great a marvel as I ever saw, and very good knights have tried and failed."

"Sir," said Galahad, "that is no marvel, for this adventure is not theirs but mine; and because I was sure of this sword I brought none with me, for here by my side hangs the scabbard."

And at once he laid his hand on the sword, and easily drew it out of the stone, and put it in the sheath, and said to the king, "Now it goes better than it did before."

"Sir," said the king, "God will send you a shield."

"Now I have that sword," said Galahad, "that once belonged to the good knight Balin le Savage, and he was an exceedingly good fighting man; and with this sword he killed his brother Balan, and that was a great pity, for he was a good knight, and each killed the other because of the Dolorous Stroke that Balin gave to my grandfather King Pelles, which is not yet healed, nor shall it be until I heal him."

With that the king and all the rest saw a lady on a white palfrey come riding down along the river toward them. Then she greeted the king and the queen, and asked whether Sir Lancelot was there.

And then he answered for himself: "I am here, fair lady."

Then she said, weeping all the while, "How your great fortune has changed since this morning!"

"Damsel, why do you say so?" said Lancelot.

"I tell you the truth," said the damsel, "for this morning you were the best knight in the world, but whoever said so now would be a liar, for there is now one better than you, and it is well proved by the adventure of the sword, which you did not dare set your hand to; and that is the change and the loss of your name. And so I give you this to remember: that from now on you must not think that you are the best knight in the world."

"As for that," said Lancelot, "I know well I was never the best."

"Yes," said the damsel, "that you were, and are still, of any sinful man in the world. And, Sir King, Nacien the hermit sends you word that the greatest honour that ever came to a king in Britain shall come to you; and I will tell you why: for this day the Holy Grail shall appear in your house and feed you and all your fellowship of the Round Table."

So she left and went back the same way that she came.

Chapter 6: How King Arthur gathered all the knights to joust in the meadow beside Camelot before they left

"Now," said the king, "I am sure that all of you of the Round Table will depart on this quest of the Holy Grail, and I shall never see you all together again; so I want to see you all together in the meadow of Camelot, to joust and to fight in a tournament, so that after your deaths men may say of it that such good knights were all together on such a day."

They all agreed to that plan, and at the king's request, and put on the armour that belonged to jousting. But the king's whole purpose in all this was to see Galahad put to the test; for the king thought he would not easily come back to the court after he left. So they were assembled in the meadow, rich and poor alike. Then Sir Galahad, at the request of the king and the queen, put on a fine short coat of double mail, and he also put on his helmet, but he would take no shield, for all the king's asking. And then Sir Gawain and other knights begged him to take a spear. He did so; and the queen was in a tower with all her ladies, to watch that tournament. Then Sir Galahad took his place in the middle of the meadow, and began to break spears marvellously, so that everyone wondered at him; for there he outdid all the other knights, for within a short while he had overthrown many good knights of the Round Table, except two, and those were Sir Lancelot and Sir Percival.

Chapter 7: How the queen asked to see Galahad, and how afterwards all the knights were filled by the Holy Grail, and how they vowed to go on its quest

Then the king, at the queen's request, had him dismount and unlace his helmet, so that the queen might see his face.

When she saw him she said, "Truly, I dare say that Sir Lancelot fathered him, for never were two men more alike, and so it is no marvel that he is of great prowess."

Then a lady who stood by the queen said, "Madam, for God's sake, is it right that he should be so good a knight?"

"Yes, truly," said the queen, "for on every side he comes of the best knights in the world and of the highest lineage; for Sir Lancelot is descended in only the eighth degree from our Lord Jesus Christ, and Sir Galahad is in the ninth degree from our Lord Jesus Christ, and so I dare say they are the greatest gentlemen in the world."

And then the king and people of every rank went home to Camelot, and so went to evensong at the great church, and then after that to supper, and every knight sat in his own place as they had before. Then at once they heard a cracking and crying of thunder, so that they thought the place would all be shattered to pieces. In the midst of this blast there came in a sunbeam seven times brighter than any day they had ever seen, and they were all lit by the grace of the Holy Ghost. Then every knight began to look at the others, and each saw the others, as it seemed to them, fairer than they had ever seen them before. And yet there was no knight who could speak a word for a long while, and so they looked at one another as if they had been struck dumb. Then the Holy Grail came into the hall, covered with white samite, but no one could see it, nor who carried it. And all the hall was filled with sweet smells, and every knight had such food and drink as he loved best in this world. And when the Holy Grail had been carried through the hall, the holy vessel suddenly departed, so that they did not know what had become of it; then they all had breath to speak. And then the king gave thanks to God for His good grace that He had sent them.

"Certainly," said the king, "we ought to thank our Lord Jesus greatly for what He has shown us this day, in honour of this high feast of Pentecost."

"Now," said Sir Gawain, "we have been served today with whatever food and drink we thought of; but one thing cheated us: we could not see the Holy Grail, it was so preciously covered. So I will make a vow here, that tomorrow, without waiting any longer, I shall set out on the quest of the Holy Grail, and that I shall keep at it for a year and a day, or more if need be, and I shall never return to the court until I have seen it more openly than it has been seen here; and if I cannot succeed, I shall come back, as one who cannot go against the will of our Lord Jesus Christ."

When the knights of the Round Table heard Sir Gawain say so, most of them rose and made the same vows as Sir Gawain had made. As soon as King Arthur heard this he was greatly displeased, for he knew well that they could not take back their vows.

"Alas," said King Arthur to Sir Gawain, "you have nearly killed me with the vow and promise you have made; for through you I am robbed of the fairest fellowship and the truest in knighthood that was ever seen together in any realm of the world. For when they leave here I am sure they will never all meet again in this world, for many of them will die in the quest. And so I am more than a little sorry, for I have loved them as well as my life, and so it will grieve me very sorely, the breaking of this fellowship; for it has long been my custom to have them in my company."

Chapter 8: How the king and the queen and the ladies mourned greatly at the knights' leaving, and how they set out

And with that the tears came into his eyes. And then he said, "Gawain, Gawain, you have put me in great sorrow, for I greatly fear that my true fellowship will never meet here again."

"Ah," said Sir Lancelot, "comfort yourself; for it shall be a great honour to us, and much more than if we died in any other place, for of death we are sure."

"Ah, Lancelot," said the king, "the great love I have had for you all, all the days of my life, makes me say such sorrowful words; for no Christian king ever had so many worthy men at his table as I have had this day at the Round Table, and that is my great sorrow."

When the queen, the ladies and the gentlewomen knew this news, they had such sorrow and heaviness of heart that no tongue could tell it, for those knights had held them in honour and affection. But above all the others Queen Guinevere grieved greatly.

"I am amazed," she said, "that my lord would allow them to leave him."

So all the court was troubled because of the leaving of those knights. And many of those ladies who loved knights would have gone with their lovers; and so they would have done, had not an old knight in the habit of a religious order come among them; and then he spoke out loud and said, "Fair lords, who have sworn yourselves to the quest of the Holy Grail, Nacien the hermit sends you this word: that no one on this quest is to take a lady or a gentlewoman with him, for it is not fitting in so high a service as the one you labour in; for I warn you plainly, he who is not clean of his sins shall not see the mysteries of our Lord Jesus Christ."

And for this reason they left these ladies and gentlewomen behind.

After this the queen came to Galahad and asked him where he came from, and from what country. He told her where he came from. And she said he was the son of Lancelot. To that he said neither yes nor no.

"So help me God," said the queen, "you need not be ashamed of your father, for he is the handsomest knight, and comes of the best men in the world, and of the stock of kings on every side. And so by right you ought to be, in your deeds, an exceedingly good man; and certainly," she said, "you look very like him."

Then Sir Galahad was a little ashamed and said, "Madam, since you know it for certain, why do you ask me? For he who is my father shall be known openly, and soon enough."

And then they went to their rest. And in honour of Galahad's high rank he was led into King Arthur's own room, and he rested there in the king's own bed.

And as soon as it was day the king got up, for he had had no rest all that night for sorrow. Then he went to Gawain and to Sir Lancelot, who had got up to hear mass.

And then the king said again, "Ah, Gawain, Gawain, you have betrayed me; for my court shall never be the better for you, but you will never be as sorry for me as I am for you."

And with that the tears began to run down his face. And with that the king said, "Ah, knight, Sir Lancelot, I ask you to advise me, for I wish this quest were undone, if it could be."

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "you saw yesterday so many worthy knights who were sworn then that they cannot leave it off in any way at all."

"I know that well," said the king, "but it will weigh so heavily on me at their leaving that I know well no kind of joy will cure me."

And then the king and the queen went to the great church. So at once Lancelot and Gawain ordered their men to bring their armour. And when they were all armed except for their shields and their helmets, they came to their fellowship, who were all ready in the same way, to go to the great church to hear their service.

Then after the service was done the king wanted to know how many had undertaken the quest of the Holy Grail; and he asked them all to be counted. Then they found by the count a hundred and fifty, and all were knights of the Round Table. And then they put on their helmets and set out, and all of them commended themselves wholly to the queen; and there was weeping and great sorrow. Then the queen went off into her room and kept to herself, so that no one should see her great sorrow. When Sir Lancelot missed the queen he went to her room, and when she saw him she cried aloud, "Oh, Lancelot, Lancelot, you have betrayed me and put me to death, to leave my lord like this."

"Ah, madam, I beg you not to be displeased, for I shall come back as soon as I can with honour."

"Alas," she said, "that I ever saw you; but may He who suffered on the cross for all mankind be your good guide and safety, and that of the whole fellowship."

At that Sir Lancelot left, and found his fellowship waiting for him. And so they mounted their horses and rode through the streets of Camelot; and there was weeping from rich and poor, and the king turned away and could not speak for weeping. So within a while they came to a city, and a castle called Vagon. There they went into the castle, and the lord of that castle was an old man called Vagon, and he was a man of good life, and he threw open the gates, and gave them all the welcome he could. And so in the morning they all agreed that they should go their separate ways; and in the morning they set out with weeping faces, and every knight took the way that he liked best.

Chapter 9: How Galahad got himself a shield, and how those fared who dared to take that shield down

Now Sir Galahad rides on still without a shield, and so he rode four days without any adventure. And on the fourth day after evensong he came to a White Abbey, and there he was received with great reverence, and led to a room, and there his armour was taken off; and then he noticed two knights of the Round Table, one was Sir Bagdemagus, and the other was Sir Uwain.

And when they saw him they went to Galahad and made much of him, and so they went to supper.

"Sirs," said Sir Galahad, "what adventure brought you here?"

"Sir," they said, "we have been told that in this place there is a shield that no man may wear hung about his neck without coming to harm, either dead within three days, or maimed for ever."

"Ah, sir," said King Bagdemagus, "I shall wear it tomorrow, to try this adventure."

"In the name of God," said Sir Galahad.

"Sir," said Bagdemagus, "if I cannot achieve the adventure of this shield, you shall take it on yourself, for I am sure you will not fail."

"Sir," said Galahad, "I agree to that very gladly, for I have no shield."

So in the morning they got up and heard mass. Then Bagdemagus asked where the adventurous shield was. At once a monk led him behind an altar where the shield hung, as white as any snow, but in the middle was a red cross.

"Sir," said the monk, "this shield ought not to be hung about any knight's neck unless he is the worthiest knight in the world; so I advise you knights to think carefully."

"Well," said Bagdemagus, "I know well that I am not the best knight in the world, but still I shall try to wear it," and so he carried it out of the church.

And then he said to Galahad, "If you please, wait here until you know how I fare."

"I shall wait for you," said Galahad.

Then King Bagdemagus took a good squire with him, to bring news to Sir Galahad of how he fared.

Then when they had ridden some two miles and came to a fair valley in front of a hermitage, they saw a knight coming from that direction in white armour, horse and all; and he came as fast as his horse could run, with his spear in its rest, and Bagdemagus levelled his spear against him and broke it on the white knight. But the other struck him so hard that he burst the rings of his mail, and thrust him through the right shoulder, for the shield did not cover him at that moment; and so he bore him off his horse. And with that he dismounted and took the white shield from him, saying, "Knight, you have made a great fool of yourself, for this shield ought to be borne by no one but him who shall have no equal among the living."

And then he came to Bagdemagus's squire and said, "Take this shield to the good knight Sir Galahad, whom you left in the abbey, and greet him well from me."

"Sir," said the squire, "what is your name?"

"Never mind my name," said the knight, "for it is not for you to know, nor for any earthly man."

"Now, fair sir," said the squire, "for the reverence of Jesus Christ, tell me why this shield may not be borne unless the one who bears it comes to harm."

"Now since you have begged me in that name," said the knight, "this shield belongs to no man but Galahad."

And the squire went to Bagdemagus and asked whether he was badly wounded or not.

"Yes, truly," he said, "I shall barely escape death."

Then the squire fetched his horse, and brought him with great difficulty to an abbey. Then he was taken down gently and unarmed, and laid in a bed, and his wounds were seen to there. And as the book tells, he lay there a long time, and barely escaped with his life.

Chapter 10: How Galahad left with the shield, and how King Evelake had received the shield from Joseph of Arimathea

"Sir Galahad," said the squire, "the knight who wounded Bagdemagus sends you greeting, and told me that you should bear this shield, through which great adventures shall come about."

"Now blessed be God and fortune," said Galahad.

And then he asked for his armour, and mounted his horse, and hung the white shield about his neck, and commended them to God. And Sir Uwain said he would keep him company if he pleased.

"Sir," said Galahad, "you may not, for I must go alone, except that this squire shall keep me company."

And so Uwain left.

Then within a while Galahad came to where the White Knight was waiting for him by the hermitage, and each greeted the other courteously.

"Sir," said Galahad, "many marvels have come about through this shield."

"Sir," said the knight, "it happened thirty-two years after the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ that Joseph of Arimathea, the noble knight who took our Lord down from the holy Cross, left Jerusalem at that time with a great part of his kindred with him. And so they journeyed on until they came to a city called Sarras. And at the very hour that Joseph came to Sarras there was a king called Evelake, who was at great war with the Saracens, and especially with one Saracen, who was King Evelake's cousin, a rich king and a mighty one, whose lands bordered on this land, and his name was Tolleme la Feintes. So one day these two met to do battle. Then Joseph, the son of Joseph of Arimathea, went to King Evelake and told him he would be defeated and killed unless he left his belief in the old law and believed in the new law. And then and there he showed him the true belief in the Holy Trinity, to which he agreed with all his heart; and there this shield was made for King Evelake, in the name of Him who died on the Cross. And then through his good belief he got the better of King Tolleme. For when Evelake was in the battle there was a cloth set over the shield, and when he was in the greatest danger he had the cloth taken away, and then his enemies saw the figure of a man on the Cross, and because of it they were all defeated. And so it happened that a man of King Evelake's had his hand struck off, and carried that hand in his other hand; and Joseph called that man to him and told him to go and touch the Cross with good devotion. And as soon as that man had touched the Cross with his hand, it was as whole as it had ever been before. Then soon after a great marvel happened: the cross on the shield vanished away all at once, so that no one knew what had become of it. And then King Evelake was baptised, and most of the people of that city with him. So, soon after, Joseph wanted to leave, and King Evelake would go with him, whether he liked it or not. And so by chance they came into this land, which at that time was called Great Britain; and there they found a great wicked pagan, who put Joseph in prison. And so by chance news came to a worthy man called Mondrames, and he gathered all his people because of the great renown he had heard of Joseph; and so he came into the land of Great Britain and stripped this wicked pagan of his lands and destroyed him, and with that freed Joseph from prison. And after that all the people were converted to the Christian faith."

Chapter 11: How Joseph made a cross on the white shield with his blood, and how a monk brought Galahad to a tomb

"Not long after that," the White Knight went on, "Joseph was laid on his deathbed. And when King Evelake saw that, he grieved greatly, and said, 'For love of you I have left my country, and since you must depart out of this world, leave me some token of yours so that I may think of you.'"

"'That I will do most gladly,' said Joseph. 'Now bring me your shield that I gave you when you went into battle against King Tolleme.'"

"Then Joseph bled badly at the nose, so that it could not be stopped by any means. And there on that shield he made a cross of his own blood. 'Now you may see a remembrance that I love you, for you shall never see this shield without thinking of me, and it shall always be as fresh as it is now. And no man shall ever bear this shield about his neck without regretting it, until the time that Galahad, the good knight, bears it; and the last of my line shall have it about his neck, and he shall do many marvellous deeds.'"

"'Now,' said King Evelake, 'where shall I put this shield, so that this worthy knight may have it?'"

"'You shall leave it where Nacien the hermit shall be laid after his death; for that good knight will come there on the fifteenth day after he receives the order of knighthood.' And so the day that they set is this very time, when you have your shield, and in the same abbey lies Nacien the hermit."

And then the White Knight vanished away.

As soon as the squire had heard these words, he got down off his small riding horse and knelt at Galahad's feet, and begged him that he might go with him until Galahad had made him a knight.

"Yes," said Galahad, "I would not refuse you."

"Then will you make me a knight?" said the squire. "And that order, by the grace of God, shall be well placed in me."

So Sir Galahad granted it to him, and turned back to the abbey they had come from; and there people rejoiced greatly over Sir Galahad. And as soon as he had dismounted, a monk took him to a tomb in a churchyard, where there was such a noise that whoever heard it would very nearly go mad or lose his strength.

"And sir," they said, "we think it is a fiend."

Chapter 12: Of the marvel that Sir Galahad saw and heard in the tomb, and how he made Melias a knight

"Now take me there," said Galahad.

And so they did, all armed except for his helmet.

"Now," said the good man, "go to the tomb and lift it up."

So he did, and heard a great noise; and a voice said piteously, so that all men could hear it, "Sir Galahad, servant of Jesus Christ, do not come near me, for you will make me go back again to where I have been so long."

But Galahad was not at all afraid, and lifted up the stone; and out came so foul a smoke, and after it he saw leap out the foulest figure in the likeness of a man that he had ever seen; and then he crossed himself and knew well that it was a fiend. Then he heard a voice say, "Galahad, I see so many angels all around you that my power cannot harm you."

Just then Sir Galahad saw a body lying fully armed in that tomb, and beside him a sword.

"Now, fair brother," said Galahad, "let us remove this body, for it is not worthy to lie in this churchyard, for he was a false Christian."

And with that they all left and went to the abbey. And as soon as he was out of his armour a good man came and sat down beside him and said, "Sir, I will tell you what all that you saw in the tomb signifies. For that covered body signifies the hardship of the world, and the great sin that Our Lord found in the world. For there was such wretchedness that the father did not love the son, nor did the son love the father; and that was one of the reasons that Our Lord took flesh and blood of a pure maiden, for our sins were so great at that time that very nearly everything was wickedness."

"Truly," said Galahad, "I believe you entirely."

So Sir Galahad rested there that night; and in the morning he made the squire a knight, and asked him his name, and what family he came from.

"Sir," he said, "men call me Melias de Lile, and I am the son of the King of Denmark."

"Now, fair sir," said Galahad, "since you are descended from kings and queens, now see that knighthood is well placed in you, for you ought to be a mirror to all chivalry."

"Sir," said Sir Melias, "you speak the truth. But, sir, since you have made me a knight, by rights you must grant me my first wish, if it is reasonable."

"That is true," said Galahad.

"Then," said Melias, "that you will allow me to ride with you in this quest of the Holy Grail, until some adventure parts us."

"I grant it to you, sir."

Then men brought Sir Melias his armour and his spear and his horse, and so Sir Galahad and he rode on all that week before they found any adventure. And then on a Monday morning, as they were leaving an abbey, they came to a cross where two ways parted, and on that cross were letters written that said this: "Now, you knights-errant who go seeking adventurous knights, see here two ways. One way forbids you to go down it, for no man shall come out of it again unless he is a good man and a worthy knight. And if you go on the left hand, you will not easily win prowess there, for on this way you will soon be put to the test."

"Sir," said Melias to Galahad, "if it pleases you to let me take the way on the left hand, tell me, for there I can well prove my strength."

"It would be better," said Galahad, "if you did not ride that way, for I think I would come through that way better than you."

"No, my lord, I beg you, let me have that adventure."

"Take it, in God's name," said Galahad.

Chapter 13: Of the adventure Melias had, and how Galahad avenged him, and how Melias was carried into an abbey

And then Melias rode into an old forest, and he rode in it two days and more. And then he came into a fair meadow, and there was a fair lodge of boughs. And then he saw in that lodge a chair, and in it a crown of gold, finely worked. Also there were cloths spread upon the ground, and many delicious foods set on them. Sir Melias looked at this adventure and thought it marvellous, but he was not hungry; but he took great notice of the crown of gold, and with that he stooped down and picked it up, and rode on his way with it. And at once he saw a knight come riding after him, who said, "Knight, set down that crown, which is not yours, and defend yourself!"

Then Sir Melias crossed himself and said, "Fair Lord of heaven, help and save your new-made knight."

And then they let their horses run as fast as they could, so that the other knight struck Sir Melias through his hauberk and through the left side, so that he fell to the ground near dead. And then he took the crown and went his way; and Sir Melias lay still and had no power to stir.

Meanwhile, by fortune, Sir Galahad came by and found him there in danger of death. And then he said, "Ah, Melias, who has wounded you? It would have been better to have ridden the other way."

And when Sir Melias heard him speak, "Sir," he said, "for the love of God, do not let me die in this forest, but carry me to the abbey near here, so that I may make my confession and have my last rites."

"It shall be done," said Galahad. "But where is the man who has wounded you?"

With that Sir Galahad heard a voice cry out loud among the leaves, "Knight, keep away from me!"

"Ah, sir," said Melias, "beware, for that is the man who has killed me."

Sir Galahad answered, "Sir knight, come on at your peril."

Then each squared up to the other, and they came together as fast as their horses could run, and Galahad struck him so that his spear went through his shoulder, and struck him down off his horse, and in the fall Galahad's spear broke.

With that another knight came out of the leaves and broke a spear on Galahad before he could even turn. Then Galahad drew his sword and struck off the man's left arm, so that it fell to the ground. And then he fled, and Sir Galahad pursued hard after him. And then he turned back to Sir Melias, and there he dismounted and set him gently on his horse in front of him, for the broken shaft of the spear was in his body; and Sir Galahad leapt up behind him, and held him in his arms, and so brought him to the abbey, and there took off his armour and brought him to his room. And then he asked for his Saviour. And when he had received Him, he said to Sir Galahad, "Sir, let death come when it pleases him."

And with that he drew the broken shaft of the spear out of his body, and then he fainted.

Then there came an old monk who had once been a knight, and looked at Sir Melias. And at once he searched his wound; and then he said to Sir Galahad, "I will heal him of his wound, by the grace of God, within the space of seven weeks."

Then Sir Galahad was glad, and took off his armour, and said he would stay there three days. And then he asked Sir Melias how it was with him. Then he said he was on the mend, thank God.

Chapter 14: How Sir Galahad left, and how he was commanded to go to the Castle of Maidens to destroy the wicked custom

"Now I will leave," said Galahad, "for I have much on hand, for many good knights are very busy about it, and this knight and I were in the same quest of the Holy Grail."

"Sir," said a good man, "it was for his sin that he was wounded like this. And I marvel," said the good man to Melias, "how you dared take upon yourself so rich a thing as the high order of knighthood without a clean confession, and that was the reason you were so cruelly wounded. For the way on the right hand signifies the highway of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the way of a good, true, good-living man. And the other way signifies the way of sinners and unbelievers. And when the devil saw your pride and presumption, in taking yourself into the quest of the Holy Grail, that made you be overthrown, for it cannot be achieved except by virtuous living. Also, the writing on the cross was a sign of heavenly deeds, and of knightly deeds in God's works, and not knightly deeds in worldly works. And pride, which is the head of all deadly sins, caused this knight to part from Galahad. And when you took the crown of gold you sinned in covetousness and in theft: none of this was knightly deeds. And as for this Galahad, the holy knight who fought with the two knights: the two knights signify the two deadly sins that were wholly in this knight Melias; and they could not stand against you, Galahad, for you are without deadly sin."

Now Galahad left that place, and commended them all to God.

Sir Melias said, "My lord Galahad, as soon as I can ride I will look for you."

"God send you health," said Galahad, and so took his horse and left, and rode many days' journeys forward and back, wherever adventure would lead him. And at last it happened that he left a place, or a castle, which was called Abblasoure; and he had heard no mass, which he was always used to hearing before he left any castle or place, and he kept that as a custom. Then Sir Galahad came to a mountain where he found an old chapel, and found nobody there, for all, all was desolate; and there he knelt before the altar, and prayed God for wholesome counsel. So as he prayed he heard a voice that said, "Go now, you adventurous knight, to the Castle of Maidens, and there put an end to the wicked customs."

Chapter 15: How Sir Galahad fought with the knights of the castle, and destroyed the wicked custom

When Sir Galahad heard this he thanked God, and took his horse; and he had ridden no more than half a mile when he saw in the valley before him a strong castle with deep moats, and beside it ran a fair river called the Severn; and there he met a man of great age, and they greeted each other, and Galahad asked him the castle's name.

"Fair sir," he said, "it is the Castle of Maidens. That is a cursed castle, and so are all who live in it, for all pity has gone out of it, and all hardness and harm are in it. So I advise you, sir knight, to turn back."

"Sir," said Galahad, "you may be sure I will not turn back."

Then Sir Galahad looked over his arms to see that nothing was missing, and then he put his shield before him; and at once he was met by seven fair maidens, who said to him, "Sir knight, you are riding here in great folly, for you have the water to cross."

"Why should I not cross the water?" said Galahad.

So he rode away from them, and met a squire, who said, "Knight, those knights in the castle defy you, and forbid you to go any further until they know what you want."

"Fair sir," said Galahad, "I have come to destroy the wicked custom of this castle."

"Sir, if you hold to that, you will have enough to do."

"Go now," said Galahad, "and hurry my business along."

Then the squire went into the castle. And soon after, seven knights came out of the castle, and they were all brothers. And when they saw Galahad they cried, "Knight, look to yourself, for we promise you nothing but death!"

"What," said Galahad, "will you all fight me at once?"

"Yes," they said, "you can count on that."

Then Galahad put forward his spear and struck the foremost to the ground, so that he nearly broke his neck. And with that the others struck him great blows on his shield, so that their spears broke. Then Sir Galahad drew his sword, and set upon them so hard that it was a marvel to see, and so by great force he made them leave the field; and Galahad chased them until they went into the castle, and so out through the castle by another gate.

And there Sir Galahad was met by an old man in a religious habit, who said, "Sir, here, take the keys of this castle."

Then Sir Galahad opened the gates, and saw so many people in the streets that he could not count them, and they all said, "Sir, you are welcome, for we have waited here a long time for our deliverance."

Then a gentlewoman came to him and said, "These knights have fled, but they will come back tonight, and begin their evil custom here again."

"What do you want me to do?" said Galahad.

"Sir," said the gentlewoman, "send for all the knights who hold their lands from this castle to come here, and make them swear to keep the customs that were kept here in the old days."

"Gladly," said Galahad.

And she brought him a horn of ivory, richly bound with gold, and said, "Sir, blow this horn, which will be heard two miles around this castle."

When Sir Galahad had blown the horn he sat down on a bed.

Then a priest came to Galahad and said, "Sir, it is more than seven years now since these seven brothers came into this castle and lodged with the lord of this castle, who was called Duke Lianour, and he was lord of all this country. And when they saw the duke's daughter, who was a very beautiful woman, then by their false deceit they started a quarrel among themselves, and the duke in his goodness tried to part them, and there they killed him and his eldest son. And then they took the maiden and the treasure of the castle. And then by great force they held all the knights of this castle under their rule against their will, in great servitude and tribute, robbing and plundering the poor common people of all they had. So it happened one day that the duke's daughter said, 'You have done me great wrong in killing my own father and my brother, and in holding our lands like this. Nevertheless,' she said, 'you shall not hold this castle for many years, for you will be overcome by one knight.' This she prophesied seven years ago. 'Well,' said the seven knights, 'since you say so, no lady or knight shall ever pass this castle without being made to stay, whether they like it or not, or die for it, until that knight comes by whom we shall lose this castle.' And that is why it is called the Maidens' Castle, for they have devoured many maidens."

"Now," said Galahad, "is she here, the one through whom this castle was lost?"

"No, sir," said the priest, "she was dead within three nights after she was forced like this; and since then they have kept her younger sister, who suffers great pains, with many other ladies."

By this time the knights of the country had come, and then he made them do homage and swear fealty to the king's daughter, and set their hearts much at ease. And in the morning someone came to Galahad and told him that Gawain, Gareth and Uwain had killed the seven brothers.

"I can well believe it," said Sir Galahad, and took his armour and his horse, and commended them to God.

Chapter 16: How Sir Gawain came to the abbey to follow Galahad, and how he made his confession to a hermit

Now, the tale says, after Sir Gawain left, he rode many days' journeys, both this way and that. And at last he came to the abbey where Sir Galahad had the white shield, and there Sir Gawain learned the way to follow Sir Galahad; and so he rode to the abbey where Melias lay sick, and there Sir Melias told Sir Gawain of the marvellous adventures that Sir Galahad had done.

"Certainly," said Sir Gawain, "I am sorry that I did not take the way he went, for if I can meet him I will not lightly part from him, for Sir Galahad achieves all marvellous adventures."

"Sir," said one of the monks, "he will not have your company."

"Why?" said Sir Gawain.

"Sir," he said, "because you are wicked and sinful, and he is truly blessed."

Just as they stood talking like this, Sir Gareth came riding in. And then they rejoiced over each other. And in the morning they heard mass, and so left. And on the way they met Sir Uwain les Avoutres, and there Sir Uwain told Sir Gawain that he had met with no adventure since he left the court.

"Nor have we," said Sir Gawain.

And the three knights each promised the others not to part while they were in that quest, unless fortune caused it.

So they set off and rode where fortune took them, until they came by the Castle of Maidens; and there the seven brothers saw the three knights, and said, "Since we have been driven out of this castle by one knight, we will destroy all of King Arthur's knights that we can overcome, for the love of Sir Galahad."

And with that the seven knights set upon the three knights, and by fortune Sir Gawain killed one of the brothers, and each one of his companions killed another, and so they killed the rest. And then they took the way under the castle, and there they lost the way that Sir Galahad had ridden, and there each of them parted from the others; and Sir Gawain rode until he came to a hermitage, and there he found the good man saying his evensong of Our Lady; and there Sir Gawain asked for lodging for charity, and the good man granted it to him gladly.

Then the good man asked him who he was.

"Sir," he said, "I am a knight of King Arthur's who is in the quest of the Holy Grail, and my name is Sir Gawain."

"Sir," said the good man, "I would like to know how things stand between God and you."

"Sir," said Sir Gawain, "I will willingly show you my life, if it pleases you." And there he told the hermit how a monk of an abbey had called him a wicked knight.

"He might well say it," said the hermit, "for when you were first made a knight you should have given yourself to knightly deeds and virtuous living, and you have done the opposite, for you have lived wickedly for many winters; and Sir Galahad is a virgin and never sinned, and that is the reason that wherever he goes he shall achieve what neither you nor any like you shall attain, nor anyone in your company, for you have led the most faithless life that I ever heard of a knight living. For certainly, if you had not been as wicked as you are, the seven brothers would never have been killed by you and your two companions. For Sir Galahad by himself alone beat all seven of them the day before, but his way of life is such that he will not lightly kill any man. Also I can tell you that the Castle of Maidens signifies the good souls that were in prison before the Incarnation of Jesus Christ. And the seven knights signify the seven deadly sins that reigned in the world at that time; and I may liken the good Galahad to the Son of the High Father, who came down within a maiden and bought all the souls out of bondage: so did Sir Galahad free all the maidens out of the woeful castle."

"Now, Sir Gawain," said the good man, "you must do penance for your sin."

"Sir, what penance shall I do?"

"Such as I will give," said the good man.

"No," said Sir Gawain, "I can do no penance; for we knights-errant often suffer great woe and pain."

"Well," said the good man, and then he held his peace.

And in the morning Sir Gawain left the hermit, and commended him to God. And by chance he met Sir Aglovale and Sir Griflet, two knights of the Round Table. And they rode four days without finding any adventure, and on the fifth day they parted. And each went as chance befell him. Here the tale leaves Sir Gawain and his companions, and we speak of Sir Galahad.

Chapter 17: How Sir Galahad met Sir Lancelot and Sir Percival, and struck them down, and rode away from them

So when Sir Galahad had left the Castle of Maidens he rode until he came to a wild forest, and there he met Sir Lancelot and Sir Percival, but they did not know him, for he was newly disguised. Just then Sir Lancelot, his father, lowered his spear and broke it on Sir Galahad, and Galahad struck him back so hard that he struck down horse and man. And then he drew his sword, and turned on Sir Percival, and struck him so hard on the helmet that it split down to the steel cap beneath; and if the sword had not swerved Sir Percival would have been killed, and with the stroke he fell out of his saddle. This joust was done in front of the hermitage where a recluse lived. And when she saw Sir Galahad ride, she said, "God be with you, best knight in the world." "Ah, certainly," she said, out loud, so that Lancelot and Percival could hear it, "if those two knights had known you as well as I do, they would not have taken you on."

When Sir Galahad heard her say this he was afraid of being recognised, and with that he struck his horse with his spurs and rode away from them at a great pace. Then they both realised that he was Galahad; and up they got on their horses, and rode hard after him, but in a little while he was out of their sight. And then they turned back, downcast.

"Let us ask that recluse over there for some news," said Percival.

"Do as you like," said Sir Lancelot.

When Sir Percival came to the recluse she knew him well enough, and Sir Lancelot too. But Sir Lancelot rode across and along a wild forest, and kept to no path but where wild adventure led him. And at last he came to a stone cross where two ways parted in waste land; and by the cross was a stone that was of marble, but it was so dark that Sir Lancelot could not tell what it was. Then Sir Lancelot looked about him, and saw an old chapel, and there he expected to have found people; and Sir Lancelot tied his horse to a tree, and there he took off his shield and hung it on a tree, and then went to the chapel door, and found it deserted and broken. And inside he found a fair altar, very richly adorned with cloth of pure silk, and there stood a fair bright candlestick, which held six great candles, and the candlestick was of silver. And when Sir Lancelot saw this light he had a great wish to go into the chapel, but he could find no place where he might enter; then he was exceedingly downcast and dismayed. Then he went back to his horse and took off his saddle and bridle, and let him graze, and unlaced his helmet, and took off his sword belt, and lay down to sleep on his shield in front of the cross.

Chapter 18: How Sir Lancelot, half asleep and half awake, saw a sick man carried in a litter, and how he was healed by the Holy Grail

And so he fell asleep; and half awake and half asleep he saw two palfreys come by him, all fair and white, which carried a litter, and in it lay a sick knight. And when he was near the cross he stopped there and stayed still. All this Sir Lancelot saw and watched, for he was not truly asleep; and he heard him say, "O sweet Lord, when will this sorrow leave me? And when will the holy vessel come by me, through which I shall be blessed? For I have endured like this for a long time, for a little sin."

For a long while the knight lamented like this, and all the while Sir Lancelot heard it. With that Sir Lancelot saw the candlestick with the six candles come before the cross, and he saw nobody bringing it. Also there came a table of silver, and the holy vessel of the Holy Grail, which Lancelot had seen before in the house of King Pescheour, the Fisher King. And with that the sick knight sat up, and held up both his hands, and said, "Fair sweet Lord, who are here within this holy vessel, take heed of me, so that I may be made whole of this sickness."

And with that he went on his hands and knees so near that he touched the holy vessel and kissed it, and at once he was whole; and then he said, "Lord God, I thank You, for I am healed of this sickness."

So when the holy vessel had been there a long while, it went into the chapel with the candlestick and the light, so that Lancelot did not know where it had gone; for he was so weighed down by sin that he had no power to rise up before the holy vessel. And for that, many men spoke shame of him afterwards, but he repented after that. Then the sick knight got up and kissed the cross; at once his squire brought him his arms, and asked his lord how he was.

"Certainly," he said, "I thank God, very well; I am healed through the holy vessel. But I marvel at this sleeping knight, who had no power to wake when this holy vessel was brought here."

"I dare well say," said the squire, "that he is living in some deadly sin that he has never confessed."

"On my faith," said the knight, "whoever he is, he is unfortunate, for as I judge he is of the fellowship of the Round Table, which has entered into the quest of the Holy Grail."

"Sir," said the squire, "I have brought you all your arms here except your helmet and your sword, and so, with my agreement, you may take this knight's helmet and his sword now."

And so he did. And when he was fully armed he took Sir Lancelot's horse, for it was better than his own; and so they left the cross.

Chapter 19: How a voice spoke to Sir Lancelot, and how he found his horse and his helmet taken away, and afterwards went on foot

Then at once Sir Lancelot woke, and sat up, and thought over what he had seen there, and whether it was dreams or not. Just then he heard a voice that said, "Sir Lancelot, harder than the stone, and more bitter than the wood, and more naked and barer than the leaf of the fig tree: go away from here, and take yourself out of this holy place."

And when Sir Lancelot heard this he was exceedingly downcast and did not know what to do, and so he left, weeping bitterly, and cursed the time that he was born. For then he believed he would never have honour again. For those words went to his heart, until he knew why he was called so. Then Sir Lancelot went to the cross and found his helmet, his sword and his horse taken away. And then he called himself a true wretch, and the most unhappy of all knights; and there he said, "My sin and my wickedness have brought me to great dishonour. For when I sought worldly adventures for worldly desires, I always achieved them and had the better of it in every place, and I was never beaten in any quarrel, whether it was right or wrong. And now I take upon me the adventures of holy things, and now I see and understand that my old sin hinders me and shames me, so that I had no power to stir or speak when the holy blood appeared before me."

So he grieved like this until it was day, and heard the birds sing: then he was somewhat comforted. But when Sir Lancelot found his horse and his armour gone, then he knew well that God was displeased with him.

Then he left the cross on foot and went into a forest; and so by six in the morning he came to a high hill, and found a hermitage, and a hermit in it who was going to mass. And then Lancelot knelt down and cried to Our Lord for mercy for his wicked works. So when mass was done Lancelot called to him, and begged him for charity to hear his life.

"Willingly," said the good man. "Sir," he said, "are you of King Arthur's court and of the fellowship of the Round Table?"

"Yes, truly, and my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake, who has been very well spoken of, and now my good fortune is changed, for I am the greatest wretch in the world."

The hermit looked at him and marvelled at how humbled he was.

"Sir," said the hermit, "you ought to thank God more than any knight living, for He has caused you to have more worldly honour than any knight now alive. And it was your presumption, in taking it upon yourself to be in His presence in deadly sin, where His flesh and His blood were, that caused you not to be able to see it with worldly eyes; for He will not appear where such sinners are, unless it is to their great harm and their great shame. And there is no knight living now who ought to give God such great thanks as you, for He has given you beauty, comeliness, and great strength above all other knights; and so you are more beholden to God than any other man, to love Him and fear Him, for your strength and manhood will be of little use to you if God is against you."

Chapter 20: How Sir Lancelot made his confession, and what sorrow he felt, and of the good examples that were shown him

Then Sir Lancelot wept, with a heavy face, and said, "Now I know well that you are telling me the truth."

"Sir," said the good man, "hide no old sin from me."

"Truly," said Sir Lancelot, "I am very loath to reveal it. For these fourteen years I have never revealed one thing that I have done, and for that I may now blame my shame and my misfortune."

And then he told that good man all his life, and how he had loved a queen beyond measure, and for a very long time. "And all my great deeds of arms that I have done, I did for the most part for the queen's sake, and for her sake I would fight, whether it was right or wrong, and I never fought only for God's sake, but to win honour and to make myself the better loved, and I thanked God for it little or not at all."

Then Sir Lancelot said, "I beg you, counsel me."

"I will counsel you," said the hermit, "if you will promise me that you will never come into that queen's company, as far as you can avoid it."

And then Sir Lancelot promised him that he would not, on his life.

"See that your heart and your mouth agree," said the good man, "and I promise you that you will have more honour than you ever had."

"Holy father," said Sir Lancelot, "I marvel at the voice that said such marvellous words to me, as you have heard already."

"Do not marvel at it," said the good man, "for it seems clear that God loves you. For men may understand that a stone is hard by nature, and one more than another especially; and that is to be understood of you, Sir Lancelot, for you will not leave your sin for any goodness that God has sent you. So you are harder than any stone, and you would never be made soft, neither by water nor by fire; and that is to say, the heat of the Holy Ghost cannot enter into you. Now take heed: in all the world men will not find one knight to whom Our Lord has given so much grace as He has given you. For He has given you beauty with comeliness, He has given you understanding, and discretion to know good from evil, He has given you prowess and boldness, and has given you to do such great deeds that you have always had the better of it, wherever you came; and now Our Lord will bear with you no longer, but you shall know Him, whether you will or not. And as to why the voice called you more bitter than wood: where too much sin lives, there can be only a little sweetness, and so you are likened to an old rotten tree."

"Now I have shown you why you are harder than the stone and more bitter than the tree. Now I will show you why you are more naked and barer than the fig tree. It happened that Our Lord preached in Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, and there He found that all hardness was lodged in the people, and in the whole town He found not one who would give Him lodging. And then He went outside the town, and found in the middle of the road a fig tree, which was very fair and well furnished with leaves, but it had no fruit. Then Our Lord cursed the tree that bore no fruit; the fig tree signifies Jerusalem, which had leaves and no fruit. So you, Sir Lancelot, when the Holy Grail was brought before you, He found no fruit in you, neither good thought nor good will, and found you defiled with lechery."

"Certainly," said Sir Lancelot, "all that you have said is true, and from now on I intend, by the grace of God, never to be as wicked as I have been, but to follow knighthood and to do feats of arms."

Then the good man gave Sir Lancelot such penance as he could do, and told him to pursue knighthood, and so absolved him, and begged Sir Lancelot to stay with him all that day.

"Gladly," said Sir Lancelot, "for I have neither helmet, nor horse, nor sword."

"As for that," said the good man, "I will help you to a horse before tomorrow evening, and to everything that belonged to you."

And then Sir Lancelot repented greatly.

Here ends the history of Sir Lancelot.

And here follows the story of Sir Percival de Galis, which is the fourteenth book.

Book Fourteen: The Quest of the Holy Grail

Chapter 1: How Sir Percival came to a recluse and asked her advice, and how she told him that she was his aunt

Now the tale says that when Sir Lancelot had ridden off after Sir Galahad, who had had all these adventures told above, Sir Percival turned back to the recluse, where he thought he would get news of the knight that Lancelot was following. And so he knelt at her window, and the recluse opened it and asked Sir Percival what he wanted.

"Madam," he said, "I am a knight of King Arthur's court, and my name is Sir Percival de Galis."

When the recluse heard his name she was overjoyed to see him, for she had loved him much more than any other knight, as she ought to have done, for she was his aunt. And then she ordered the gates to be opened, and there she gave him all the welcome she could, and everything in her power was at his command.

So in the morning Sir Percival went to the recluse and asked her if she knew that knight with the white shield.

"Sir," she said, "why do you want to know?"

"Truly, madam," said Sir Percival, "I shall never be at ease until I know that knight's company, and can fight with him, for I cannot let him go so easily, since the shame is still on me."

"Ah, Percival," she said, "would you fight with him? I can see very well that you are eager to be killed as your father was, through recklessness."

"Madam," said Sir Percival, "it seems by your words that you know me."

"Yes," she said, "I ought to know you well, for I am your aunt, although I am in a priory now. For some people once called me the Queen of the Waste Lands, and I was called the richest queen in the world; and my riches never pleased me as much as my poverty does."

Then Sir Percival wept out of pure pity when he knew that she was his aunt.

"Ah, fair nephew," she said, "when did you last hear news of your mother?"

"Truly," he said, "I have heard none of her, but I dream of her often in my sleep; and so I do not know whether she is dead or alive."

"Certainly, fair nephew," she said, "your mother is dead, for after you left her she fell into such grief that, soon after she had made her confession, she died."

"Now God have mercy on her soul," said Sir Percival. "I am deeply sorry for it; but we must all leave this life. Now, fair aunt, tell me, who is the knight? I think it is the one who bore the red arms on Whitsunday."

"Believe me," she said, "this is he, for he ought not to do otherwise than go in red arms; and that same knight has no equal, for he does everything by miracle, and he shall never be overcome by any earthly man's hand."

Chapter 2: How Merlin likened the Round Table to the world, and how the knights who would achieve the Holy Grail would be known

"Also," she said, "Merlin made the Round Table as a sign of the roundness of the world, for by the Round Table the world is rightly signified. For all the world, Christian and heathen, comes to the Round Table; and when they are chosen to be of the fellowship of the Round Table they think themselves more blessed and more honoured than if they had won half the world. And you have seen that they have left their fathers and their mothers, and all their kin, and their wives and their children, to be of your fellowship. It is plain to see in you; for since you left your mother you would never go to see her, such fellowship did you find at the Round Table."

"When Merlin had founded the Round Table he said that through those who would be fellows of the Round Table the truth of the Holy Grail would be well known. And people asked him how they might know the ones who would do best and achieve the Holy Grail. Then he said there would be three white bulls who would achieve it, and two of them would be virgins, and the third would be chaste. And one of the three would surpass his father as much as the lion surpasses the leopard, both in strength and in daring."

"Those who heard Merlin say this said to Merlin, 'Since there is to be such a knight, you should make, by your arts, a seat in which no man may sit but he alone who will surpass all other knights.' Then Merlin answered that he would do so. And then he made the Siege Perilous, in which Galahad sat at his meal last Whitsunday."

"Now, madam," said Sir Percival, "I have heard so much from you that by my own good will I will never fight Sir Galahad except in the way of friendship. And for God's love, fair aunt, can you show me some way to find him? For I would dearly love his company."

"Fair nephew," she said, "you must ride to a castle called Goothe, where he has a first cousin, and there you may be lodged tonight. And as he directs you, follow after as fast as you can; and if he can tell you no news of him, ride straight to the Castle of Carbonek, where the Maimed King lies, for there you will hear true news of him."

Chapter 3: How Sir Percival came to a monastery, where he found King Evelake, who was an old man

Then Sir Percival left his aunt, and each of them grieved greatly. And so he rode until the time of evensong. And then he heard a clock strike; and then he noticed a house well enclosed with walls and deep ditches, and there he knocked at the gate and was let in, and he dismounted and was led to a room, and soon he was out of his armour. And there he had a very good welcome all that night; and in the morning he heard his mass, and in the monastery he found a priest ready at the altar. And on the right side he saw a pew closed in with iron, and behind the altar he saw a bed, rich and fair, as if of cloth of silk and gold.

Then Sir Percival noticed that there was a man or a woman in it, for the face was covered; then he stopped looking and listened to the service. And when it came to the consecration, the one who lay within that partition raised himself up and uncovered his head; and then he seemed to Sir Percival an exceedingly old man, and he had a crown of gold on his head, and his shoulders were bare and uncovered down to his navel. And then Sir Percival saw that his body was full of great wounds, on the shoulders, the arms and the face. And all the while he held up his hands toward Our Lord's body, and cried, "Fair, sweet Father, Jesus Christ, do not forget me." And so he lay down, but he was always at his prayers and devotions; and he seemed to be three hundred years old. And when the mass was done the priest took Our Lord's body and carried it to the sick king. And when he had received it he took off his crown, and commanded the crown to be set on the altar.

Then Sir Percival asked one of the brothers who he was.

"Sir," said the good man, "you have heard much of Joseph of Arimathea, how he was sent by Jesus Christ into this land to teach and preach the holy Christian faith; and for that he suffered many persecutions that the enemies of Christ did to him. And in the city of Sarras he converted a king whose name was Evelake. And so this king came with Joseph into this land, and he was always eager to be where the Holy Grail was; and once he came so near it that Our Lord was displeased with him, but still he followed it more and more, until God struck him almost blind. Then this king begged for mercy, and said, 'Fair Lord, let me never die until the good knight of my blood in the ninth generation has come, so that I may see him plainly, the one who shall achieve the Holy Grail, and so that I may kiss him.'"

Chapter 4: How Sir Percival saw many men-at-arms carrying a dead knight, and how he fought against them

"When the king had made his prayers in this way, he heard a voice that said, 'Your prayers are heard, for you shall not die until he has kissed you. And when that knight comes, the clearness of your eyes will come back, and you will see plainly, and your wounds will be healed, and before then they shall never close.' And this happened to King Evelake, and this same king has lived this holy life these three hundred years, and men say the knight who will heal him is at the court. Sir," said the good man, "I beg you, tell me what knight you are, and whether you are of King Arthur's court and of the Round Table."

"Yes, truly," he said, "and my name is Sir Percival de Galis."

And when the good man understood his name he rejoiced greatly over him.
