And then Sir Percival left and rode until the hour of noon. And in a valley he met some twenty men-at-arms, who were carrying on a bier a knight who had been killed. And when they saw Sir Percival they asked him where he came from.

And he answered, "From the court of King Arthur."

Then they all cried out at once, "Kill him!"

Then Sir Percival struck the first to the ground, with his horse on top of him. And then seven of the knights struck on his shield all at once, and the rest killed his horse so that he fell to the ground. So they would have killed him or taken him, if the good knight Sir Galahad, with the red arms, had not come into those parts by chance. And when he saw all those knights against one knight he cried, "Spare me that knight's life!" And then he turned toward the twenty men-at-arms as fast as his horse could carry him, with his spear in rest, and struck the foremost to the ground, horse and man. And when his spear was broken he set his hand to his sword, and struck on the right hand and on the left so that it was a marvel to see, and at every stroke he struck one down or put him to shame, so that they would fight no more but fled into a thick forest, and Sir Galahad followed them.

And when Sir Percival saw him chase them like that, he grieved greatly that his horse was gone. And then he knew well that it was Sir Galahad.

And then he cried aloud, "Ah, fair knight, wait, and let me give you thanks, for you have done a great deal for me."

But Sir Galahad rode on so fast that at last he passed out of his sight. And Sir Percival went after him on foot as fast as he could, crying out. And then he met a yeoman riding on a small riding horse, who led in his hand a great steed blacker than any bear.

"Ah, fair friend," said Sir Percival, "as surely as I will ever do anything for you, and be your true knight at the first need you ask of me, lend me that black steed, so that I may overtake a knight who is riding ahead of me."

"Sir knight," said the yeoman, "I beg you to excuse me from that, for I cannot do it. For believe me, the horse belongs to such a man that if I lent it to you or to any man, he would kill me."

"Alas," said Sir Percival, "I never had so great a sorrow as I have had at losing that knight."

"Sir," said the yeoman, "I am very sorry for you, for a good horse would suit you well; but I dare not give you this horse unless you take him from me."

"That I will not do," said Sir Percival.

And so they parted; and Sir Percival sat down under a tree, and grieved beyond measure. And as he sat there, a knight came riding on the horse that the yeoman had been leading, and he was fully armed.

Chapter 5: How a yeoman asked him to win back a horse, and how Sir Percival's own horse was killed, and how he got a horse

And at once the yeoman came spurring after as fast as he could, and asked Sir Percival if he had seen any knight riding on his black steed.

"Yes, sir, truly," he said. "Why, sir, do you ask me that?"

"Ah, sir, he has taken that steed from me by force; and so my lord will kill me wherever he finds me."

"Well," said Sir Percival, "what do you want me to do? You can see well that I am on foot, but if I had a good horse I would soon bring him back."

"Sir," said the yeoman, "take my small riding horse and do the best you can, and I will follow you on foot to learn how you get on."

Then Sir Percival mounted that small horse, and rode as fast as he could, and at last he saw that knight.

And then he cried, "Knight, turn back!"

And he turned and set his spear against Sir Percival, and he struck the small horse in the middle of the breast so that it fell down dead to the ground, and Sir Percival had a great fall there, and the other rode on his way.

And then Sir Percival was mad with rage, and cried, "Wait, you wicked knight! Coward, false-hearted knight, turn back and fight me on foot!"

But he did not answer, but went on his way. When Sir Percival saw that he would not turn, he threw away his helmet and sword, and said, "Now I am a true wretch, cursed and the most unlucky of all knights."

So in this sorrow he stayed there all that day until it was night; and then he was faint, and lay down and slept until midnight; and then he woke and saw before him a woman, who said to him very fiercely, "Sir Percival, what are you doing here?"

He answered, "I am doing neither good nor great harm."

"If you will promise me," she said, "that you will do my will when I summon you, I will lend you my own horse, which will carry you wherever you wish."

Sir Percival was glad of her offer, and promised her to fulfil all her desire.

"Then wait for me here, and I will go and fetch you a horse."

And so she soon came back and brought a horse with her that was utterly black. When Percival looked at that horse he marvelled that it was so big and so well equipped; and even so he was bold enough, and he leapt onto him, and took no thought for himself. And as soon as he was on him he thrust his spurs into him, and so he rode along beside a forest, and the moon shone clear. And within an hour or less the horse carried him four days' journey from there, until he came to a rough water that roared, and his horse would have carried him into it.

Chapter 6: Of the great danger Sir Percival was in because of his horse, and how he saw a serpent and a lion fight

And when Sir Percival came near the brink, and saw the water so rough, he was afraid to cross it. And then he made the sign of the cross on his forehead. When the fiend felt himself burdened with that, he shook Sir Percival off, and he went into the water crying and roaring and making great lament, and it seemed to Sir Percival that the water burned. Then Sir Percival understood that it was a fiend, which would have brought him to his damnation. Then he commended himself to God, and prayed Our Lord to keep him from all such temptations; and so he prayed all that night until morning, when it was day. Then he saw that he was on a wild mountain that was almost entirely surrounded by the sea, so that he could see no land around him that might bring him help, but only wild beasts.

And then he went into a valley, and there he saw a young serpent carrying a young lion by the neck, and so it came past Sir Percival. With that a great lion came crying and roaring after the serpent. And as soon as Sir Percival saw this he marvelled, and hurried there, but at once the lion had overtaken the serpent and began to fight him. And then Sir Percival thought he would help the lion, for he was the more natural beast of the two; and with that he drew his sword, and set his shield before him, and there he gave the serpent such a blow that he had a deadly wound. When the lion saw that, he made no sign of fighting him, but gave him all the welcome a beast can give a man. Then Percival saw that, and threw down his shield, which was broken; and then he took off his helmet to get his breath, for he was greatly heated from fighting the serpent. And the lion kept going round him, fawning like a spaniel. And then he stroked him on the neck and on the shoulders. And then he thanked God for the company of that beast. And about noon the lion took up his little cub and bundled him up and carried him back to where he came from.

Then Sir Percival was alone. And as the tale tells, he was one of the men in the world at that time who believed most in Our Lord Jesus Christ, for in those days there were only a few people who believed in God perfectly. For in those days the son spared his father no more than a stranger. And so Sir Percival took comfort in our Lord Jesus, and begged God that no temptation should bring him out of God's service, but that he might endure as his true champion. So when Sir Percival had prayed, he saw the lion come toward him, and then he lay down at his feet. And so all that night the lion and he slept together; and while Sir Percival slept he dreamed a marvellous dream: that two ladies met him there, and that one sat on a lion, and the other sat on a serpent, and that one of them was young, and the other was old. And he thought that the younger one said, "Sir Percival, my lord greets you, and sends you word to prepare yourself and make ready, for tomorrow you must fight the strongest champion in the world. And if you are overcome, you will not get off with the loss of any of your limbs, but you will be shamed for ever, to the world's end."

And then he asked her who her lord was. And she said the greatest lord in all the world. And so she left so suddenly that he did not know where she had gone.

Chapter 7: Of the vision Sir Percival saw, and how his vision was explained, and of his lion

Then the other lady, who rode on the serpent, came forward, and she said, "Sir Percival, I have a complaint against you for what you have done to me, when I have not wronged you."

"Certainly, madam," he said, "I never wronged you nor any lady."

"Yes," she said, "I will tell you why. I have kept a serpent in this place for a long while, which served me a long while, and yesterday you killed him as he was taking his prey. Tell me for what reason you killed him, for the lion was not yours."

"Madam," said Sir Percival, "I know well the lion was not mine, but I did it because the lion is of a nobler nature than the serpent, and so I killed him. It seems to me I did you no wrong. Madam," he said, "what do you want me to do?"

"I want you," she said, "to become my man, in amends for my beast."

And then he answered, "That I will not grant you."

"No?" she said. "Truly, you were never anything but my servant until you received the homage of Our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore I warn you, wherever I find you unguarded I will take you, as one who was once my man."

And so she left Sir Percival and left him sleeping, and he was badly troubled by his vision. And in the morning he got up and crossed himself, and he was exceedingly weak.

Then Sir Percival looked out to sea, and saw a ship come sailing toward him; and Sir Percival went to the ship and found it covered inside and out with white samite. And at the side stood an old man dressed in a surplice, in the likeness of a priest.

"Sir," said Sir Percival, "you are welcome."

"God keep you," said the good man. "Sir," said the old man, "where are you from?"

"Sir," said Sir Percival, "I am of King Arthur's court, and a knight of the Round Table, and I am on the quest of the Holy Grail; and here I am in great hardship, and never likely to escape out of this wilderness."

"Do not fear," said the good man. "If you are as true a knight as the order of chivalry requires, and of such heart as you ought to be, you need not fear that any enemy will kill you."

"Who are you?" said Sir Percival.

"Sir," said the old man, "I am from a strange country, and I have come here to comfort you."

"Sir," said Sir Percival, "what does the dream that I dreamed last night mean?"

And there he told him all of it.

"She who rode on the lion stands for the new law of holy church, that is to say, faith, good hope, belief and baptism. There is good reason why she seemed younger than the other, for she was born in the resurrection and the passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ. And out of great love she came to you to warn you of the great battle that is coming to you."

"Whom shall I fight?" said Sir Percival.

"The greatest champion in the world," said the old man. "For as the lady said, unless you acquit yourself well you will not get off with the loss of one limb, but you will be shamed to the world's end. And she who rode on the serpent stands for the old law, and that serpent stands for a fiend. And as for her blaming you for killing her servant, that means nothing; the serpent that you killed stands for the devil that you rode on to the rock. And when you made the sign of the cross, there you killed him, and put away his power. And when she asked you for amends, and to become her man, and you said you would not, that was to make you believe in her and leave your baptism."

So he commanded Sir Percival to go, and so he leapt over the side, and the ship and all went away he did not know where. Then he went up onto the rock and found the lion, which always kept him company, and he stroked him on the back and rejoiced greatly in him.

Chapter 8: How Sir Percival saw a ship coming towards him, and how the lady of the ship told him how she had been disinherited

When Sir Percival had stayed there until midday, he saw a ship come rowing over the sea as if all the wind in the world were driving it. And so it drove in under that rock. And when Sir Percival saw this he hurried there, and found the ship covered with silk blacker than any bear, and in it was a gentlewoman of great beauty, and she was dressed so richly that no one could be better.

And when she saw Sir Percival she said, "Who brought you into this wilderness, where you are never likely to get away from here? For you will die here of hunger and distress."

"Damsel," said Sir Percival, "I serve the best man in the world, and in his service he will not let me die. For whoever knocks shall enter, and whoever asks shall have, and whoever seeks him, he does not hide from him."

But then she said, "Sir Percival, do you know who I am?"

"Yes," he said.

"Now who taught you my name?" she said.

"Now," said Sir Percival, "I know you better than you think."

"And I have come out of the waste forest, where I found the Red Knight with the white shield," said the damsel.

"Ah, damsel," he said, "I would very gladly meet that knight."

"Sir knight," she said, "if you will promise me, by the faith that you owe to knighthood, that you will do my will whenever I summon you, then I will bring you to that knight."

"Yes," he said, "I promise to fulfil your desire."

"Well," she said, "now I will tell you. I saw him in the forest chasing two knights to a water called Mortaise; and he drove them into the water for fear of death, and the two knights crossed over, and the Red Knight went over after them, and there his horse was drowned, and he, through great strength, escaped to the land."

So she told him, and Sir Percival was exceedingly glad of it. Then she asked him if he had eaten any food lately.

"No, madam, truly, I have eaten no food these three days, but just now I spoke here with a good man who fed me with his good and holy words, and refreshed me greatly."

"Ah, sir knight," she said, "that same man is an enchanter and a spinner of words. For if you believe him you will certainly be shamed, and die on this rock of sheer hunger, and be eaten by wild beasts; and you are a young man and a handsome knight, and I will help you if you will let me."

"Who are you," said Sir Percival, "who offer me such great kindness?"

"I am," she said, "a gentlewoman who has been disinherited, who was once the richest woman in the world."

"Damsel," said Sir Percival, "who has disinherited you? For I feel great pity for you."

"Sir," she said, "I lived with the greatest man in the world, and he made me so fair and bright that there was none like me; and because of that great beauty I had a little more pride than I ought to have had. Also I said a word that did not please him. And then he would not let me stay any longer in his company, and so he drove me out of my inheritance, and so disinherited me, and he never had pity on me, nor on any of my followers, nor on my court. And since then, sir knight, since this happened to me, I and my people have taken many of his men from him, and made them become my men. For they never ask anything of me that I do not give them, that and much more. So I and all my servants have been against him night and day. Therefore I know of no good knight, nor any good man, whom I do not try to get on my side if I can. And since I know that you are a good knight, I beg you to help me; and since you are a fellow of the Round Table, you ought not to fail any gentlewoman who has been disinherited, if she asks you for help."

Chapter 9: How Sir Percival promised her help, and how he asked for her love, and how he was saved from the fiend

Then Sir Percival promised her all the help he could give; and then she thanked him. And at that time the weather was hot. Then she called a gentlewoman to her and told her to bring out a tent; and so she did, and pitched it on the gravel.

"Sir," she said, "now you may rest in this heat of the day."

Then he thanked her, and she took off his helmet and his shield, and there he slept a long while. And then he woke and asked her if she had any food.

And she said, "Yes, and you shall have plenty."

And so plenty was set on the table, and so much on it that he marvelled, for there was every kind of food he could think of. He also drank there the strongest wine he had ever drunk, as he thought, and with that he grew a little more heated than he ought to have been. With that he looked at the gentlewoman, and he thought she was the most beautiful creature he had ever seen. And then Sir Percival offered her his love, and begged her to be his. Then she refused him, after a fashion, when he asked her, so that he would be the more ardent for her, and he never stopped begging her for her love.

And when she saw him well heated, then she said, "Sir Percival, believe me, I will not do your will unless you swear that from now on you will be my true servant, and do nothing but what I command you. Will you promise me this, as you are a true knight?"

"Yes," he said, "fair lady, on my life."

"Well," she said, "now you shall do with me whatever you please; and now, believe me, you are the knight in the world I most desire."

And then two squires were ordered to make a bed in the middle of the tent. And at once she was undressed and laid in it. And then Sir Percival lay down beside her naked. And by chance and by grace he saw his sword lying on the ground, out of its sheath, and in its pommel was a red cross and the sign of the crucifix, and he thought of his knighthood and of the promise he had made earlier to the good man. Then he made the sign of the cross on his forehead, and with that the tent turned upside down, and then it changed into a smoke and a black cloud, and then he was afraid and cried aloud:

Chapter 10: How Sir Percival for penance stabbed himself through the thigh, and how she was revealed to be the devil

"Fair sweet Father, Jesus Christ, do not let me be shamed, who would have been lost if not for your good grace!"

And then he looked into a ship, and saw her go into it, and she said, "Sir Percival, you have betrayed me."

And so she went away with the wind, roaring and yelling, so that it seemed all the water burned behind her. Then Sir Percival grieved greatly, and drew his sword to him, saying, "Since my flesh would be my master, I will punish it." And with that he drove the sword through his thigh, so that the blood spurted out around him, and he said, "O good Lord, take this in recompense for what I have done against you, my Lord."

So then he dressed himself and armed himself, and called himself a wretch, saying, "How near I was to being lost, and to losing what I could never have got back, which was my virginity, for that can never be recovered once it is lost."

And then he stopped his bleeding wound with a piece of his shirt. So, as he was lamenting, he saw the same ship come from the East that the good man had been in the day before, and the noble knight was ashamed of himself, and with that he fell into a faint. And when he came to, he went to him weakly, and there he greeted this good man.

And then he asked Sir Percival, "How have you done since I left?"

"Sir," he said, "a gentlewoman was here, and she led me into deadly sin."

And there he told him all of it.

"Did you not know the maiden?" said the good man.

"Sir," he said, "no, but I know well that the fiend sent her here to shame me."

"O good knight," he said, "you are a fool, for that gentlewoman was the master fiend of hell, who has power over all devils, and she was the old lady you saw in your vision riding on the serpent."

Then he told Sir Percival how our Lord Jesus Christ drove him out of heaven for his sin, he who was the brightest angel of heaven, and so he lost his inheritance.

"And that was the champion you fought with, who would have overcome you if not for the grace of God. Now beware, Sir Percival, and take this as an example."

And then the good man vanished. Then Sir Percival took up his arms, and went into the ship, and so departed from there.

Here ends the fourteenth book, which is of Sir Percival.

And here follows the tale of Sir Lancelot, which is the fifteenth book.

Book Fifteen: Sir Lancelot

Chapter 1: How Sir Lancelot came to a chapel, where he found a man of religion a hundred years old lying dead in a white shirt

When the hermit had kept Sir Lancelot three days, the hermit got him a horse, a helmet and a sword. And then he left at about the hour of noon. And then he saw a little house. And when he came near he saw a chapel, and beside it he saw an old man who was dressed all in white, very richly.

And then Sir Lancelot said, "God save you."

"God keep you," said the good man, "and make you a good knight."

Then Sir Lancelot dismounted and went into the chapel, and there he saw an old man lying dead, in a white shirt of exceedingly fine cloth.

"Sir," said the good man, "this man who is dead ought not to be in such clothing as you see him in, for in that he broke the oath of his order; for he has been a man of religion more than a hundred years."

And then the good man and Sir Lancelot went into the chapel; and the good man put a stole around his neck, and took a book, and then he conjured on that book; and with that they saw a figure so hideous and horrible that there was no man so hard-hearted or so hardy but he would have been afraid.

Then the fiend said, "You have troubled me greatly. Now tell me what you want with me."

"I want you," said the good man, "to tell me how my brother came to be dead, and whether he is saved or damned."

Then he said in a horrible voice, "He is not lost but saved."

"How can that be?" said the good man. "It seemed to me that he did not live well, for he broke his order by wearing a shirt where he ought to wear none, and whoever offends against our order does not do well."

"Not so," said the fiend. "This man who lies here dead came of a great lineage. And there was a lord called the Earl de Vale, who made great war on this man's nephew, who was called Aguarus. And so this Aguarus saw that the earl was stronger than he was. Then he went to take the advice of his uncle, who lies here dead, as you can see. And then this man asked leave, and went out of his hermitage to support his nephew against the mighty earl; and so it happened that this man who lies here dead did so much by his wisdom and his daring that the earl was taken, and three of his lords, by the strength of this dead man."

Chapter 2: Of a dead man, how men tried to hack at him and could not, and how Sir Lancelot took the dead man's hair shirt

"Then," said the fiend, "there was peace between the earl and this Aguarus, and a firm guarantee that the earl would never make war on him again. Then this dead man who lies here came back to this hermitage; and then the earl set two of his nephews to take revenge on this man. So one day they came, and found this dead man at the consecration in his mass, and they waited for him until he had said mass. And then they set on him and drew their swords to kill him; but no sword would bite on him any more than on a spike of steel, for the high Lord whom he served preserved him. Then they made a great fire, and took off all his clothes, and the hair shirt off his back. And then this dead man, the hermit, said to them, 'Do you think you will burn me? It will not be in your power to harm so much as a thread on me, if there were any on my body.' 'No?' said one of them. 'We shall try it.' And then they stripped him, and put this shirt on him, and threw him in a fire, and there he lay all that night in that fire until it was day, and was not dead. And so in the morning I came and found him dead; but I found neither thread nor skin harmed, and so I took him out of the fire with great fear, and laid him here as you can see. And now you may let me go on my way, for I have told you the truth."

And then he left in a great storm. Then the good man and Sir Lancelot were gladder than they had been before. And then Sir Lancelot stayed with that good man that night.

"Sir," said the good man, "are you not Sir Lancelot du Lake?"

"Yes, sir," he said.

"What are you seeking in this country?"

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "I am going to seek the adventures of the Holy Grail."

"Well," he said, "you may well seek it, but even if it were here you would have no more power to see it than a blind man would have to see a bright sword. And that is because of your sin, or else you would be more able than any man living."

And then Sir Lancelot began to weep.

Then the good man said, "Have you made your confession since you entered on the quest of the Holy Grail?"

"Yes, sir," said Sir Lancelot.

Then in the morning, when the good man had sung his mass, they buried the dead man.

Then Sir Lancelot said, "Father, what shall I do?"

"Now," said the good man, "I ask you to take this hair shirt that belonged to this holy man and put it next to your skin, and it will do you great good."

"Sir, I will do it," said Sir Lancelot.

"Also I charge you to eat no meat as long as you are on the quest of the Holy Grail, and to drink no wine, and to hear mass every day if you can."

So he took the hair shirt and put it on, and so left at evensong time. And so he rode into a forest, and there he met a gentlewoman riding on a white palfrey.

And then she asked him, "Sir knight, where are you riding?"

"Certainly, damsel," said Lancelot, "I do not know where I am riding, except as fortune leads me."

"Ah, Sir Lancelot," she said, "I know what adventure you are seeking, for you were nearer to it once than you are now, and yet you shall see it more plainly than you ever did, and you will understand that in a short time."

Then Sir Lancelot asked her where he might find lodging that night.

"You will not find any this day or night, but tomorrow you will find good lodging, and relief from what you are anxious about."

And then he commended her to God. Then he rode until he came to a Cross, and took that for his host for that night.

Chapter 3: Of a vision Sir Lancelot had, and how he told it to a hermit and asked his advice

And so he put his horse out to graze, and took off his helmet and his shield, and prayed to the Cross that he might never fall into deadly sin again. And so he lay down to sleep. And as soon as he was asleep a vision came to him there: that a man came before him all surrounded by stars, and that man had a crown of gold on his head, and that man led in his company seven kings and two knights. And all these worshipped the Cross, kneeling on their knees and holding up their hands toward heaven.

And they all said, "Fair sweet Father of heaven, come and visit us, and give each of us what we have deserved."

Then Lancelot looked up to heaven, and it seemed to him that the clouds opened, and an old man came down with a company of angels, and alighted among them, and gave each of them his blessing, and called them his servants, and good and true knights. And when this old man had said this he came to one of those knights, and said, "I have lost all that I put into you, for you have conducted yourself against me like a warrior, and fought wrongful wars out of vainglory, more for the pleasure of the world than to please me. Therefore you will be destroyed unless you give me back my treasure."

All this vision Sir Lancelot saw at the Cross. And in the morning he took his horse and rode until midday; and there by chance he met the same knight who had taken his horse, his helmet and his sword while he slept, when the Holy Grail appeared before the Cross. When Sir Lancelot saw him he did not greet him kindly, but cried aloud, "Knight, defend yourself! You have done me a great wrong."

And then they set their spears before them, and Sir Lancelot came at him so fiercely that he struck him and his horse down to the ground, so that he nearly broke his neck. Then Sir Lancelot took the knight's horse, which had been his own before, and got down from the horse he was sitting on, and mounted his own horse, and tied the knight's own horse to a tree, so that he might find that horse when he got up. Then Sir Lancelot rode until night, and by chance he met a hermit, and each of them greeted the other; and there he rested with that good man all night, and gave his horse what feed he could get.

Then the good man said to Lancelot, "Where are you from?"

"Sir," he said, "I am of Arthur's court, and my name is Sir Lancelot du Lake, and I am on the quest of the Holy Grail; and so I beg you to advise me about a vision that I had at the Cross."

And so he told him all of it.

Chapter 4: How the hermit explained Sir Lancelot's vision to him, and told him that Sir Galahad was his son

"Look, Sir Lancelot," said the good man, "there you may understand the high lineage you come from, and what your vision means. Forty years after the passion of Jesus Christ, Joseph of Arimathea preached the victory of King Evelake, so that he got the better of his enemies in his battles. And as for the seven kings and the two knights: the first of them is called Nappus, a holy man; and the second was called Nacien, in memory of his grandfather, and in him dwelt our Lord Jesus Christ; and the third was called Helias le Grose; and the fourth was called Lisais; and the fifth was called Jonas. He left his own country and went into Wales, and took there the daughter of Manuel as his wife, by whom he had the land of Gaul, and he came to live in this country. And from him came King Lancelot, your grandfather, who married the King of Ireland's daughter there, and he was as worthy a man as you are; and from him came King Ban, your father, who was the last of the seven kings. And as for you, Sir Lancelot, it means that the angels said you were none of the seven fellowships. And the last was the ninth knight; he was signified by a lion, for he would surpass every kind of earthly knight, and that is Sir Galahad, whom you fathered on King Pelles's daughter. And you ought to thank God more than any other man living, for among earthly sinners you have no equal in knighthood, nor ever will have. But you have given God little thanks for all the great virtues that God has lent you."

"Sir," said Lancelot, "you say that that good knight is my son."

"You ought to know that, and no man better," said the good man, "for you knew King Pelles's daughter in the flesh, and on her you fathered Galahad, and he was the one who sat in the Siege Perilous at the feast of Pentecost. And so make it openly known that he is your son, fathered on King Pelles's daughter, for that will be to your honour and credit, and to all your kindred's. And I advise you never, anywhere, to press him to fight with you."

"Well," said Lancelot, "it seems to me that good knight should pray for me to the High Father, that I do not fall into sin again."

"You may be sure," said the good man, "that you fare much the better for his prayer; but the son shall not bear the wickedness of the father, nor shall the father bear the wickedness of the son, but each shall bear his own burden. And so beseech God alone, and He will help you in all your needs."

And then Sir Lancelot and he went to supper, and so Lancelot lay down to rest, and the hair shirt pricked Sir Lancelot's skin so much that it hurt him very badly, but he took it meekly, and endured the pain. And so in the morning he heard his mass and took his arms, and so took his leave.

Chapter 5: How Sir Lancelot jousted with many knights, and how he was taken prisoner

And then he mounted his horse, and rode into a forest, and kept to no highway. And as he looked ahead of him he saw a fair plain, and beside it a fair castle, and before the castle were many tents of silk, of various colours. And it seemed to him that he saw five hundred knights riding there on horseback; and there were two sides. Those who were of the castle were all on black horses, with black trappings, and those who were outside were all on white horses with white trappings, and they all crashed into each other so that Sir Lancelot marvelled at it. And at last he thought that the side of the castle was getting the worst of it.

Then Sir Lancelot thought he would help the weaker side there, to increase his own renown in arms. And so Sir Lancelot thrust in on the side of the castle, and struck down a knight, horse and man, to the ground. And then he rushed here and there, and did marvellous deeds of arms. And then he drew his sword, and struck many knights to the ground, so that all who saw him marvelled that any one knight could do such great deeds of arms.

But all the while the white knights kept close around Sir Lancelot, to tire him and wear out his wind. But at last, since no man can endure for ever, Sir Lancelot grew so faint from fighting and toiling, and was so weary from his great deeds, that he could not lift up his arms to give a single stroke, so that he thought he would never bear arms again. And then they all took him and led him away into a forest, and there made him dismount and rest.

And then all the company of the castle was overcome for lack of him.

Then they all said to Sir Lancelot, "Blessed be God that you are now of our company, for we will hold you in our prison."

And so they left him with few words. And then Sir Lancelot grieved greatly. "For never before now was I at a tournament or jousts but I had the best of it, and now I am shamed." And then he said, "Now I am sure that I am more sinful than I ever was."

So he rode on grieving, and for half a day he was close to despair, until he came into a deep valley. And when Sir Lancelot saw that he could not ride up the mountain, he dismounted there under an apple tree, and there he left his helmet and his shield, and put his horse out to graze. And then he lay down to sleep.

And then it seemed to him that an old man came before him, who said, "Ah, Lancelot, man of evil faith and poor belief, why is your will turned so easily toward your deadly sin?"

And when he had said this he vanished, and Lancelot did not know where he had gone. Then he took his horse, and armed himself; and as he rode along he saw a chapel where there was a recluse, who had a window through which she could see up to the altar. And she called aloud to Lancelot, because he looked like a knight-errant. And then he came, and she asked him who he was, and from what place, and what he was going about to seek.

Chapter 6: How Sir Lancelot told his vision to a woman, and how she explained it to him

And then he told her all of it, word for word, and the truth of how it went with him at the tournament. And after that he told her the vision he had had that night in his sleep, and begged her to tell him what it might mean, for he was not at all easy about it.

"Ah, Lancelot," she said, "as long as you were a knight of earthly knighthood you were the most marvellous man in the world, and the most adventurous. Now," said the lady, "since you have been set among the knights of heavenly adventures, do not wonder if things went against you at that tournament, for that tournament yesterday was nothing but a sign from Our Lord. And even so there was no enchantment in it, for those at the tournament were earthly knights. The tournament was a sign to see who would have the most knights, Eliazar, the son of King Pelles, or Argustus, the son of King Harlon. But Eliazar was all clothed in white, and Argustus was covered in black, and they were the ones who were overcome."

"I will tell you all that this means," she said. "On the day of Pentecost, when King Arthur held his court, it happened that earthly kings and knights began a tournament together, that is to say, the quest of the Holy Grail. The earthly knights were the ones who were clothed all in black, and the covering stands for the sins they have not confessed. And those with the covering of white stand for virginity, and for those who chose chastity. And so the quest was begun in them. Then you saw the sinners and the good men, and when you saw the sinners being overcome, you leaned to that side out of boastfulness and worldly pride, and all that must be left behind in that quest; for in this quest you will have many companions who are your betters. For you are so feeble, so full of bad trust and so short of good belief, that this is what happened when you were there, where they took you and led you into the forest. And at once the Holy Grail appeared to the white knights, but you were so feeble in good belief and faith that you could not bear it, for all the teaching of the good man, but at once you turned to the sinners. And that caused your mishap, so that you should know good from evil, and the vainglory of the world, which is not worth a pear. And out of great pride you grieved greatly that you had not overcome all the white knights with the covering of white, by whom virginity and chastity were signified; and so God was angry with you, for God loves no such deeds in this quest. And this vision means that you were of evil faith and of poor belief, which will make you fall into the deep pit of hell if you do not take care. Now I have warned you of your vainglory and of your pride, by which you have many times offended against your Maker. Beware of everlasting pain, for of all earthly knights I have the most pity for you, for I know well that you have no equal among earthly sinful men."

And so she invited Sir Lancelot to dinner. And after dinner he took his horse and commended her to God, and so rode into a deep valley, and there he saw a river and a high mountain. And he had to cross the water, which was hideous; and then, in the name of God, he went into it with a good heart. And when he came over he saw an armed knight, horse and man as black as any bear. Without a word he struck Sir Lancelot's horse to the ground; and so he went on, and Lancelot did not know where he had gone. And then he took his helmet and his shield, and thanked God for his adventure.

Here the story of Sir Lancelot leaves off, and we speak of Sir Gawain, which is the sixteenth book.

Book Sixteen: Sir Bors and His Brother Sir Lionel

Chapter 1: How Sir Gawain grew nearly weary of the quest of the Holy Grail, and of his marvellous dream

When Sir Gawain had left his companions he rode a long time without any adventure. For he did not find a tenth part of the adventures he was used to finding. Sir Gawain rode from Whitsun until Michaelmas, the end of September, and found no adventure that pleased him. So one day it happened that Gawain met Sir Ector de Maris, and each of them rejoiced so greatly in the other that it was a marvel to tell. And so they told each other their news, and complained bitterly that they could find no adventure.

"Truly," said Sir Gawain to Sir Ector, "I am nearly weary of this quest, and I am loath to follow it any further in strange countries."

"One thing makes me wonder," said Sir Ector. "I have met twenty knights, companions of mine, and they all complain as I do."

"I wonder," said Sir Gawain, "where Sir Lancelot, your brother, is."

"Truly," said Sir Ector, "I can hear no news of him, nor of Sir Galahad, Percival, nor Sir Bors."

"Let them be," said Sir Gawain, "for those four have no equals. And if it were not for one thing in Sir Lancelot, he would have no equal among earthly men; but he is as we are, except that he took more pains. And if these four meet together, any man will be loath to meet with them; for if they fail of the Holy Grail, it is wasted labour for all the rest of us to try to win it."

So Ector and Gawain rode for more than eight days, and on a Saturday they found an old chapel, which was so ruined that it seemed no one ever came there. And there they dismounted, and set their spears by the door, and went into the chapel, and said their prayers there a long while, and sat down in the seats of the chapel. And as they talked of one thing and another, they fell asleep for heaviness of heart, and marvellous adventures came to them both. It seemed to Sir Gawain that he came into a meadow full of grasses and flowers, and there he saw a hayrack with bulls feeding at it, a hundred and fifty of them, proud and black, except that three of them were all white, and one of those had a black spot, and the other two were so fair and so white that they could be no whiter. And these three bulls that were so fair were tied with two strong cords. And the rest of the bulls said among themselves, "Let us go away from here to look for better pasture." And so some went, and some came back, but they were so lean that they could not stand upright; and of the bulls that were so white, one came back and no more. But when this white bull had come back among the others, a great cry rose up for lack of the breath that failed them; and so they scattered, one here and another there. This was the vision that came to Gawain that night.

Chapter 2: Of Sir Ector's vision, and how he jousted with Sir Uwain les Avoutres, his sworn brother

But to Ector de Maris came another vision, the opposite of it. For it seemed to him that his brother, Sir Lancelot, and he got down out of a chariot and leapt onto two horses, and the one said to the other, "Let us go and seek what we shall not find." And he thought that a man beat Sir Lancelot, and stripped him, and dressed him in other clothes, which were all full of knots, and set him on a donkey, and so he rode until he came to the fairest spring he had ever seen; and Sir Lancelot got down and wanted to drink from that spring. And when he stooped to drink the water, the water sank away from him. And when Sir Lancelot saw that, he turned and went back toward the place he had come from. And in the meantime he thought that he himself and Sir Ector rode until they came to a rich man's house where there was a wedding. And there he saw a king, who said, "Sir knight, there is no place here for you." And then he turned back to the chariot that he had come from.

So after a while both Gawain and Ector woke up, and each told the other his vision, and they marvelled greatly at them.

"Truly," said Ector, "I shall never be merry until I hear news of my brother Lancelot."

Now as they sat talking like this, they saw a hand showing to the elbow, and it was covered with red samite, and from it hung a bridle that was not very rich, and in its fist it held a great candle which burned very bright; and so it passed before them, and went into the chapel, and then vanished, and they did not know where. And at once a voice came down, which said, "Knights of very evil faith and of poor belief, these two things have failed you, and therefore you may not come to the adventures of the Holy Grail."

Then Gawain spoke first and said, "Ector, did you hear those words?"

"Yes, truly," said Sir Ector, "I heard everything. Now let us go," said Sir Ector, "to some hermit who will tell us the meaning of our visions, for it seems to me that all our labour is in vain."

And so they left and rode into a valley, and there they met a squire riding on a small riding horse, and they greeted him courteously.

"Sir," said Gawain, "can you direct us to a hermit?"

"There is one on a little mountain here, but it is so rough that no horse can go up there, and so you must go on foot. There you will find a poor house, and in it is Nacien the hermit, who is the holiest man in this country."

And so they parted from each other.

And then in a valley they met a knight in full armour, who challenged them to joust as soon as he saw them.

"In the name of God," said Sir Gawain, "since I left Camelot no one has challenged me to joust except once."

"And now, sir," said Ector, "let me joust with him."

"No," said Gawain, "you shall not, unless I am beaten; I shall not mind then if you go after me."

And then each of them took up position against the other to joust, and they came together as fast as their horses could run, and burst their shields and their mail, the one more than the other. And Gawain was wounded in the left side, but the other knight was struck through the breast, and the spear came out at the other side, and so they both fell out of their saddles, and in falling they both broke their spears.

Gawain got up at once and put his hand to his sword, and cast his shield before him. But it was all for nothing, for the knight had no strength to get up against him.

Then Gawain said, "You must yield as a beaten man, or else I may kill you."

"Ah, sir knight," he said, "I am as good as dead. For God's sake and of your nobility, take me to an abbey here, so that I may receive my Creator."

"Sir," said Gawain, "I know of no religious house near here."

"Sir," said the knight, "set me on a horse in front of you, and I will show you the way."

Gawain set him up in the saddle, and leapt up behind him to hold him up, and so they came to an abbey where they were well received; and at once his armour was taken off, and he received his Creator. Then he begged Gawain to draw the broken spear shaft out of his body. Then Gawain asked him who he was, for he did not know him.

"I am," he said, "of King Arthur's court, and I was a companion of the Round Table, and we were sworn brothers together. And now, Sir Gawain, you have killed me, and my name is Uwain les Avoutres, who was once the son of King Uriens, and I was on the quest of the Holy Grail. And now may God forgive you for it, for it will always be said that one sworn brother killed the other."

Chapter 3: How Sir Gawain and Sir Ector came to a hermitage to be confessed, and how they told the hermit their visions

"Alas," said Gawain, "that this mischance ever happened to me."

"No matter," said Uwain. "Since I must die this death, I could not die by the hand of a more honourable man. But when you come to the court, commend me to my lord King Arthur, and to all those who are left alive, and for old brotherhood think of me."

Then Gawain began to weep, and Ector too. And then Uwain himself and Sir Gawain drew out the broken spear shaft, and at once the soul left the body. Then Sir Gawain and Sir Ector buried him as men ought to bury a king's son, and had his name written on the tomb, and by whom he was killed.

Then Gawain and Ector left, as downcast as they could be over their mischance, and so they rode until they came to the rough mountain, and there they tied up their horses and went on foot to the hermitage. And when they had come up they saw a poor house, and beside the chapel a little garden, where Nacien the hermit gathered roots and herbs, for he had tasted no other food for a long while. And when he saw the knights-errant he came toward them and greeted them, and they greeted him in return.

"Fair lords," he said, "what adventure brought you here?"

"Sir," said Gawain, "we have come to speak with you, to be confessed."

"Sir," said the hermit, "I am ready."

Then they told him so much that he knew well who they were. And then he thought he would counsel them if he could.

Then Gawain began first and told him of the vision he had had in the chapel, and Ector told him everything as it is told above.

"Sir," said the hermit to Sir Gawain, "by the fair meadow and the hayrack in it you ought to understand the Round Table, and by the meadow you ought to understand humility and patience; those are the things which are always green and alive. For no one can ever overcome humility and patience; that is why the Round Table was founded, and its knighthood has always been such, through the brotherhood that was there, that it could not be overcome; for men said it was founded in patience and in humility. At the hayrack a hundred and fifty bulls were feeding; but they did not feed in the meadow, though their hearts should have been set in humility and patience; and the bulls were proud and black, all but three. By the bulls you are to understand the fellowship of the Round Table, who for their sin and their wickedness are black. Blackness means being without good or virtuous works. And the three bulls which were white, except only one that was spotted: the two white ones stand for Sir Galahad and Sir Percival, for they are virgins, pure and without spot; and the third, which had a spot, signifies Sir Bors de Ganis, who sinned only once against his virginity, but since then he has kept himself so well in chastity that all is forgiven him, and his misdeeds too. And as for why those three were tied by the necks: they are three knights in virginity and chastity, and there is no pride rooted in them. And the black bulls which said, 'Let us go away from here,' were those who at Pentecost, at the high feast, took it on themselves to go on the quest of the Holy Grail without confession: they could not enter the meadow of humility and patience. And so they went back into waste countries, which signifies death, for many of them will die there: each of them will kill another for sin, and those who escape will be so lean that it will be a marvel to see them. And of the three bulls without spot, one will come back, and the other two never."

Chapter 4: How the hermit explained their visions

Then Nacien spoke to Ector: "It is true that Lancelot and you came down out of one chariot: the chariot signifies the mastery and lordship which you came down from. But you two knights," said the hermit, "you go to seek what you shall never find, that is, the Holy Grail; for it is the secret thing of our Lord Jesus Christ. What does it mean that Sir Lancelot fell down off his horse? He has left pride and taken himself to humility, for he has cried loudly for mercy for his sin, and bitterly repented, and our Lord has clothed him in His clothing, which is full of knots: that is the hair shirt that he wears every day. And the donkey that he rode on is a beast of humility, for God would not ride on any warhorse, nor on any palfrey; so it was as a sign that a donkey signifies meekness that you saw Sir Lancelot ride on one in your sleep. And as for the spring, where the water sank away from him when he went to drink from it, and when he saw he could not have it he went back to where he came from: the spring signifies the high grace of God, and the more men desire to take it, the more their desire will be. So when he came near the Holy Grail, he humbled himself so that he did not hold himself a man worthy to be so near the Holy Vessel, for he had been so defiled by deadly sin for so many years; yet when he knelt to drink from the spring, there he saw great providence of the Holy Grail. And because he served the devil so long, he shall suffer punishment for twenty-four days, because he has been the devil's servant for twenty-four years. And then soon after he will return out of this country to Camelot, and he will tell part of the things that he has found."

"Now," said the hermit, "I will tell you what the hand with the candle and the bridle means. You are to understand by it the Holy Ghost, in whom charity always is; and the bridle signifies abstinence. For when abstinence is bridled in a Christian man's heart, she holds him so tight that he does not fall into deadly sin. And the candle, which gives brightness and sight, signifies the right way of Jesus Christ. And when he went and said, 'Knights of poor faith and of wicked belief,' these three things had failed, charity, abstinence and truth; therefore you may not achieve that high adventure of the Holy Grail."

Chapter 5: Of the good advice that the hermit gave them

"Certainly," said Gawain, "what you have said is true, for I see it plainly. Now, I beg you, good man and holy father, tell me why we have not met with as many adventures as we used to, when we commonly had the better of them."

"I will tell you gladly," said the good man. "The adventure of the Holy Grail, which you and many others have undertaken the quest of and do not find: the reason is that it does not appear to sinners. So do not marvel if you fail of it, and many others with you. For you are a faithless knight and a great murderer, and to good men it signifies other things than murder. For I dare say that, sinful as Sir Lancelot has been, since he went on the quest of the Holy Grail he has never killed a man, nor shall he, until he comes back to Camelot; for he has taken it on himself to forsake sin. And were it not that he is unsteady, and in his thoughts is likely to turn back, he would be the next to achieve it, after Galahad his son. But God knows his thoughts and his unsteadiness, and yet he will die a very holy man, and without doubt he has no equal among earthly sinful men."

"Sir," said Gawain, "it seems to me from your words that because of our sins it will do us no good to toil in this quest."

"Truly," said the good man, "there are a hundred like you who will never succeed in it, except to have shame."

And when they had heard these words they commended him to God.

Then the good man called Gawain, and said, "It is a long time since you were made a knight, and never since then have you served your Maker, and now you are so old a tree that there is neither life nor fruit in you. So take thought that you yield to Our Lord the bare bark, since the Fiend has the leaves and the fruit."

"Sir," said Gawain, "if I had the time I would speak with you, but my companion here, Sir Ector, has gone, and is waiting for me down there below the hill."

"Well," said the good man, "you would do better to take counsel."

Then Gawain left and came to Ector, and so they took their horses and rode until they came to a forester's house, who gave them very good lodging. And in the morning they left their host, and rode a long time before they could find any adventure.

Chapter 6: How Sir Bors met a hermit, and how he made his confession to him, and of the penance laid on him

When Bors had left Camelot he met a man of religion riding on a donkey, and Sir Bors greeted him. At once the good man knew that he was one of the knights-errant who were on the quest of the Holy Grail.

"Who are you?" said the good man.

"Sir," he said, "I am a knight who would gladly have counsel in the quest of the Holy Grail, for whoever can bring it to an end will have great earthly honour."

"Certainly," said the good man, "that is true, for he will be the best knight in the world, and the fairest of all the fellowship. But believe me, no one shall achieve it except by cleanness, that is, by pure confession."

So they rode together until they came to a hermitage. And there he begged Bors to stay all that night with him. And so Bors dismounted and put off his armour, and begged him that he might be confessed; and so they went into the chapel, and there he made a clean confession, and they ate bread and drank water together.

"Now," said the good man, "I beg you to eat nothing else until you sit at the table where the Holy Grail will be."

"Sir," he said, "I agree to that. But how do you know that I shall sit there?"

"Yes," said the good man, "I know that; but there will be only a few of your companions with you."

"All is welcome," said Sir Bors, "that God sends me."

"Also," said the good man, "instead of a shirt, and as a sign of chastisement, you shall wear a garment. So I beg you, take off all your clothes and your shirt."

And so he did. And then he gave him a scarlet coat, which was to serve instead of his shirt until he had fulfilled the quest of the Holy Grail. And the good man found in him so marvellous a life, and so steadfast, that he marvelled, and perceived that he had never been corrupted by the lusts of the flesh except at the one time when he fathered Helin le Blank.

Then he armed himself, and took his leave, and so departed. And a little way from there he looked up into a tree, and there he saw an exceedingly great bird on an old tree, and the tree was exceedingly dry, without leaves; and the bird sat at the top, and had young ones, which were dead of hunger. So he struck himself with his beak, which was great and sharp. And so the great bird bled until he died among his young. And the young birds took life from the blood of the great bird. When Bors saw this he knew well that it was a great sign; and when he saw that the great bird did not rise again, he took his horse and went on his way. So by evensong, by chance, he came to a strong, high tower, and there he was gladly given lodging.

Chapter 7: How Sir Bors lodged with a lady, and how he took it on himself to fight against a champion for her land

And when his armour had been taken off they led him into a high tower where there was a lady, young, lively and fair. And she received him with great joy, and had him sit down beside her, and so he was set to supper with meat and many delicacies. And when Sir Bors saw that, he remembered his penance, and told a squire to bring him water. And so he brought it to him, and he soaked bread in it and ate it.

"Ah," said the lady, "I think you do not like my food."

"Yes, truly," said Sir Bors, "God thank you, madam, but I may eat no other food today."

Then she said no more for that time, for she was loath to displease him. Then after supper they talked of one thing and another.

With that a squire came and said, "Madam, you must provide yourself with a champion for tomorrow, or else your sister will have this castle and your lands too, unless you can find a knight who will fight tomorrow in your quarrel against Pridam le Noire."

Then she grieved and said, "Ah, Lord God, why did You grant me to hold my land, if I am now to be robbed of it without reason and right?"

And when Sir Bors had heard her speak like this, he said, "I will comfort you."

"Sir," she said, "I will tell you. There was a king here called Aniause, who held all this land in his keeping. So it happened by ill luck that he loved a gentlewoman a good deal older than I am. So he gave all this land into her keeping, and all his men to govern; and she brought in many evil customs, by which she put to death a great part of his kinsmen. And when he saw that, he had her driven out of this land, and handed it over to me, with all this land as my own domain. But as soon as that worthy king was dead, this other lady began to make war on me, and has destroyed many of my men, and turned them against me, so that I have hardly a man left; and I have nothing else but this high tower that she has left me. And even so she has promised that she will have this tower, unless I can find a knight to fight with her champion."

"Now tell me," said Sir Bors, "who is this Pridam le Noire?"

"Sir," she said, "he is the most feared man in this land."

"Now you may send her word that you have found a knight who will fight with that Pridam le Noire in God's quarrel and yours."

Then that lady was not a little glad, and sent word that she had found her champion, and that night Bors was well entertained. But he would not get into any bed, but lay on the floor, and he would never do otherwise until he had accomplished the quest of the Holy Grail.

Chapter 8: Of a vision Sir Bors had that night, and how he fought and overcame his opponent

And as soon as he was asleep a vision came to him: two birds came to him, the one as white as a swan, and the other marvellously black; but it was not as big as the other, but in the likeness of a raven. Then the white bird came to him and said, "If you would give me food and serve me, I would give you all the riches of the world, and I will make you as fair and as white as I am."

So the white bird went away, and the black bird came to him and said, "If you will, serve me tomorrow, and do not hold me in contempt because I am black, for believe me, my blackness is worth more than the other's whiteness."

And then he went away.

And he had another vision. It seemed to him that he came to a great place which looked like a chapel, and there he found a chair set on the left side, which was worm-eaten and feeble. And on the right hand were two flowers like lilies, and the one would have taken away the other's whiteness, but a good man parted them, so that the one did not touch the other; and then out of each flower came many flowers, and fruit in great plenty. Then it seemed to him that the good man said, "Would not a man do great folly who let these two flowers perish to save the rotten tree, so that it did not fall to the earth?"

"Sir," he said, "it seems to me that this wood could be of no use."

"Then take care," said the good man, "that you never see such an adventure happen to you."

Then he woke and made the sign of the cross in the middle of his forehead, and so got up and dressed. And the lady of the place came, and she greeted him, and he her in return, and so they went to a chapel and heard their service. And there came a company of knights, whom the lady had sent for, to lead Sir Bors to the battle. Then he asked for his arms. And when he was armed she begged him to take a little morsel to eat.

"No, madam," he said, "that I will not do until I have fought my battle, by the grace of God."

And so he leapt onto his horse and departed, with all the knights and men. And as soon as these two ladies met, the one whom Bors was to fight for made her complaint, and said, "Madam, you have done me wrong in robbing me of my lands that King Aniause gave me, and I am very loath that there should be any battle."

"You have no choice," said the other lady, "unless your knight withdraws."

Then the proclamation was made that whichever of the two knights had the better, his lady should have all the land. Now the one knight went off to one side, and the other to the other. Then they came together with such a great charge that they pierced their shields and their hauberks, and the spears flew in pieces, and they wounded each other badly. Then they crashed together, so that they both fell to the earth, with their horses between their legs; and at once they got up, and set hand to their swords, and struck each other on the head, so that they made great, deep wounds, and the blood ran out of their bodies. For Sir Bors found more defence in that knight than he had expected. For this Pridam was an exceedingly good knight, and he wounded Sir Bors very badly, and Bors him in return; but this Pridam kept up the fight just as hard all the while. Sir Bors saw that, and let him go on until he was nearly spent. And then he pressed on him more and more, and the other gave ground for fear of death. So as he drew back he fell flat on his back, and Sir Bors pulled at his helm so hard that he tore it from his head, and gave him great strokes in the face with the flat of his sword, and told him to yield or he would kill him.

Then he begged for mercy and said, "Fair knight, for the love of God do not kill me, and I will give you my word never to make war against your lady, but always to be on her side."

Then Bors let him be; then the old lady fled with all her knights.

Chapter 9: How the lady won back her lands through the battle Sir Bors fought, and of his leaving, and how he met Sir Lionel taken prisoner and beaten with thorns, and also of a maiden who was about to be dishonoured

So then Bors came to all those who held lands from his lady, and said he would destroy them unless they did her such service as belonged to their lands. So they did their homage, and those who would not were driven out of their lands. So it came about that the young lady came into her estate again, through the mighty prowess of Sir Bors de Ganis. So when all the country was well settled in peace, Sir Bors took his leave and departed; and she thanked him greatly, and would have given him great riches, but he refused them.

Then he rode all that day until night, and came to lodge with a lady who knew him well enough, and gave him a great welcome. In the morning, as soon as day appeared, Bors left there, and so rode into a forest until the hour of midday, and there a marvellous adventure befell him. At the parting of two ways he met two knights who were leading Lionel, his brother, stark naked, bound onto a strong small riding horse, with his hands bound in front of his chest. And each of them held thorns in his hands, with which they went on beating him so hard that the blood ran down in more than a hundred places on his body, so that he was all blood in front and behind. But he never said a word; like the great-hearted man he was, he endured everything they did to him as if he felt no pain.

At once Sir Bors made ready to rescue him, since he was his brother. And then he looked to the other side of him, and saw a knight who was carrying off a fair gentlewoman, and meant to take her into the thickest part of the forest, to be the more safely out of the way of those who were looking for him. And she, who felt anything but safe, cried out in a loud voice, "Saint Mary, help your maiden!"

And at once she saw Sir Bors come riding. And when she came near him she judged him to be a knight of the Round Table, and from that she hoped for some comfort; and then she implored him, by the faith that he owed to Him in whose service he had entered, "and for the faith you owe to the high order of knighthood, and for the sake of the noble King Arthur, who I suppose made you a knight, that you help me, and do not let me be shamed by this knight."

When Bors heard her speak like this he was so full of sorrow that he did not know what to do. "For if I leave my brother in danger he must be killed, and I would not have that for all the earth. And if I do not help the maiden she is shamed for ever, and she will also lose her virginity, which she can never get back."

Then he lifted up his eyes and said, weeping, "Fair sweet Lord Jesus Christ, whose liege man I am, keep Lionel my brother, so that these knights do not kill him; and for pity of you, and for Mary's sake, I will help this maiden."

Chapter 10: How Sir Bors left off rescuing his brother and rescued the damsel, and how he was told that Lionel was dead

Then he turned towards the knight who had the gentlewoman, and he cried, "Sir knight, take your hand off that maiden, or you are a dead man!"

And then the knight set the maiden down. He was armed at every point, except that he had no spear. Then he set his shield and drew his sword, and Bors struck him so hard that the spear went through his shield and his hauberk at the left shoulder. And by great strength he beat him down to the ground, and as Bors pulled his spear out, the knight fainted. Then Bors came to the maiden and said, "How does it seem to you now? You are free of this knight for the present."

"Now, sir," she said, "I beg you, take me back to the place where this knight took me."

"I will do that gladly," he said; and he took the wounded knight's horse, and set the gentlewoman on it, and so brought her where she wished.

"Sir knight," she said, "you have done better than you expected, for if I had lost my maidenhood, five hundred men would have died for it."

"What knight was he who had you in the forest?"

"On my faith," she said, "he is my cousin. And I never knew by what trickery the devil inflamed him, for yesterday he took me secretly from my father; for neither I nor any of my father's men suspected him at all. And if he had had my maidenhood he would have died for the sin, and his body would have been shamed and dishonoured for ever."

As she stood there talking with him, twelve knights came looking for her, and at once she told them all how Bors had rescued her. Then they rejoiced greatly, and begged him to come to her father, a great lord, where he would be most welcome.

"Truly," said Bors, "that cannot be at this time, for I have a great adventure to carry out in this country." So he commended them to God and left.

Then Sir Bors rode after Lionel his brother by the tracks of their horses, and so he rode searching for a long while. Then he overtook a man in the clothes of a religious order, riding a strong black horse, blacker than a berry, and the man said, "Sir knight, what are you looking for?"

"Sir," he said, "I am looking for my brother, whom I saw a little while ago being beaten by two knights."

"Ah, Bors, do not be dismayed, and do not fall into despair; for I will tell you the news such as it is, and truly, he is dead."

Then he showed him a newly killed body lying in a bush, and it seemed to him plainly that it was the body of Lionel. And then he grieved so much that he fell to the ground in a faint, and lay there a long while. And when he came to himself he said, "Fair brother, since the fellowship of you and me is broken, I shall never have joy in my heart. And now may He whom I have taken for my master be my help."

And when he had said this he lifted the body lightly in his arms and laid it across the saddlebow. And then he said to the man, "Can you direct me to some chapel where I may bury this body?"

"Come on," he said, "there is one close by."

And so they rode until they saw a fine tower, and in front of it there seemed to be an old, decaying chapel. And then they both dismounted, and laid him in a marble tomb.

Chapter 11: How Sir Bors told a priest the dream he had dreamed, and of the advice the priest gave him

"Now let us leave him here," said the good man, "and go to our lodging until tomorrow. We will come back here to do him service."

"Sir," said Bors, "are you a priest?"

"Yes, truly," he said.

"Then I beg you, explain to me a dream that came to me last night."

"Go on," he said.

Then he began, and told him all about the great bird in the forest, and after that about his birds, one white and the other black, and about the rotten tree, and the white flowers.

"Sir, I will tell you part of it now, and the rest tomorrow. The white bird stands for a gentlewoman, fair and rich, who loves you as a lover and has loved you long; and if you refuse her love she will go and die at once, if you have no pity on her. That is what the great bird means, which will make you refuse her. Now it is not out of any fear you have, nor any dread of God, that you will refuse her; you would do it only to be thought chaste, to win the praise of the vain glory of the world. For this will happen to you now if you refuse her: Lancelot, the good knight, your cousin, will die. And then men will say that you are a killer, both of your brother, Sir Lionel, and of your cousin, Sir Lancelot du Lake, whom you could easily have saved and rescued; but you chose to rescue a maiden who is nothing to you. Now consider whether it would have been the greater harm, your brother's death, or to have let her lose her maidenhood."

Then he asked him, "Have you heard the meaning of your dream that I have told you?"

"Yes, truly," said Sir Bors, "I have heard and well understood all your explanation and interpretation of my dream."

Then said the man in the black clothes, "Then it will be your fault if Sir Lancelot, your cousin, dies."

"Sir," said Bors, "I would hate that; for believe me, there is nothing in the world I would not rather do than see my lord Sir Lancelot du Lake die through my fault."

"Choose now, the one or the other," said the good man.

And then he led Sir Bors into a high tower, and there he found knights and ladies. The ladies said he was welcome, and so they took off his armour. And when he was in his doublet they brought him a cloak trimmed with ermine and put it around him; and then they gave him such a welcome that he forgot all his sorrow and anguish, and set his heart only on these delights and luxuries, and gave no more thought to his brother Sir Lionel, nor to Sir Lancelot du Lake his cousin. And at once there came out of a chamber to him the fairest lady he had ever seen, and more richly dressed than he had ever seen Queen Guinevere or any other lady of rank.

"Look, Sir Bors," they said, "here is the lady to whom we owe all our service, and I believe she is the richest lady and the fairest in all the world, and the one who loves you best above all other knights, for she will have no knight but you."

And when he heard that speech he was dismayed. Nevertheless she greeted him, and he her; and then they sat down together and spoke of many things, until she begged him to be her love, for she had loved him above all earthly men, and she would make him richer than any man of his age had ever been. When Bors understood her words he was very ill at ease, for he would on no account break his chastity, and so he did not know how to answer her.

Chapter 12: How the devil in a woman's likeness tried to get Sir Bors to sleep with her, and how by God's grace he escaped

"Alas, Bors," she said, "will you not do my will?"

"Madam," said Bors, "there is no lady in the world whose will I would do in this matter, for my brother lies dead, who was killed only just now."

"Ah, Bors," she said, "I have loved you long, for the great beauty I have seen in you and the great boldness I have heard of in you, so that you must lie with me this night; and so I beg you to grant it to me."

"Truly," he said, "I will not do it in any way."

Then she made such a show of grief before him as though she would have died. "Well, Bors," she said, "you have brought me to this, close to my end." And with that she took him by the hand and told him to look at her. "And you shall see how I will die for your love."

"Ah," he said then, "that I shall never see."

Then she left and went up onto a high battlement, and took twelve gentlewomen with her; and when they were up there, one of the gentlewomen cried out and said, "Ah, Sir Bors, noble knight, have mercy on us all, and let my lady have her will! And if you do not, we must all die with our lady, by falling from this high tower. And if you let us die like this for so small a thing, all ladies and gentlewomen will speak of you with dishonour."

Then he looked up, and they all seemed to be ladies of high rank, and richly and finely dressed. Then he had great pity on them; nevertheless he was settled in his own mind that he would rather they all lost their souls than he lost his. And with that they all fell down at once to the ground. And when he saw that, he was utterly dismayed, and marvelled greatly at it. With that he crossed himself, body and face. And at once he heard a great noise and a great cry, as though all the fiends of hell were about him; and with that he saw neither tower, nor lady, nor gentlewoman, nor the chapel where he had brought his brother. Then he held up both his hands to heaven and said, "Fair Father God, I have had a narrow escape!" And then he took his arms and his horse and rode on his way.

Then he heard a clock strike on his right hand; and he went that way and came to an abbey on his right hand, enclosed with high walls, and there he was let in. They supposed that he was one of the quest of the Holy Grail, so they led him into a chamber and took off his armour.

"Sirs," said Sir Bors, "if there is any holy man in this house, I beg you, let me speak with him."

Then one of them led him to the Abbot, who was in a chapel. And then Sir Bors greeted him, and he greeted him in return.

"Sir," said Bors, "I am a knight-errant." And he told him all the adventure that he had seen.

"Sir knight," said the Abbot, "I do not know who you are, for I never thought that a knight of your age could be so strong in the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, you shall go to your rest, for I will not advise you today; it is too late. And tomorrow I will advise you as well as I can."

Chapter 13: Of the holy conversation of an abbot with Sir Bors, and how the abbot advised him

And that night Sir Bors was richly served; and early in the morning he heard mass, and the Abbot came to him and bade him good morning, and Bors returned it. And then he told him that he was a companion of the quest of the Holy Grail, and how the holy man had charged him to eat only bread and water.

Then the Abbot said, "Our Lord Jesus Christ showed Himself to you in the likeness of a soul that suffered great anguish for us, since He was put upon the cross and bled His heart's blood for mankind. There was the sign and the likeness of the Holy Grail that appeared before you, for the blood that the great bird bled brought the chicks back from death to life. And the bare tree signifies the world, which is naked and without fruit unless the fruit comes from Our Lord. Also the lady you fought for, and King Aniause who was lord there before, signify Jesus Christ, who is the King of the world. And your fighting the champion for the lady signifies this: when you took up the battle for the lady, by her you are to understand the new law of Jesus Christ and Holy Church; and by the other lady you are to understand the old law and the devil, who wars against Holy Church all day long; and so your battle was a just one. For you are Jesus Christ's knights, and so you ought to be defenders of Holy Church. And by the black bird you may understand Holy Church, which says, 'I am black, but I am fair.' And by the white bird men may understand the devil, and I will tell you how: the swan is white outside and black within. It is hypocrisy, which is sallow or pale on the outside and looks from without like the servants of Jesus Christ, but within they are so horrible with filth and sin, and they deceive the world wickedly. Also, when the devil appeared to you in the likeness of a man of religion, and blamed you for leaving your brother for a lady, he led you to where it seemed to you your brother had been killed; but he is still alive. And all this was done to lead you into error, and bring you to despair and lechery, for he knew you were tender-hearted; and all of it was so that you should not find the blessed adventure of the Holy Grail. And the third bird signifies the hard battle against the fair ladies, who were all devils. Also the dry tree and the white lily: the dry tree signifies your brother Lionel, who is dry and without virtue, and so many men ought to call him the rotten tree and the worm-eaten tree, for he is a murderer and acts against the order of knighthood. And the two white flowers signify two virgins: the one is a knight who was wounded the other day, and the other is the gentlewoman you rescued. And as for why the one flower drew close to the other, that was the knight who would have defiled her and himself both. And, Sir Bors, you would have been a great fool, and in great danger, to have watched those two flowers perish in order to help the rotten tree; for if they had sinned together they would have been damned. And because you rescued them both, men may call you a true knight and servant of Jesus Christ."

Chapter 14: How Sir Bors met his brother Sir Lionel, and how Sir Lionel meant to kill Sir Bors

Then Sir Bors went on from there and commended the Abbot to God. And then he rode all that day, and lodged with an old lady. And in the morning he rode to a castle in a valley, and there he met a yeoman going at a great pace towards a forest.

"Tell me," said Sir Bors, "can you tell me of any adventure?"

"Sir," he said, "here below this castle there is to be a great and marvellous tournament."

"What people will be in it?" said Sir Bors.

"The Earl of Plains will be on the one side, and the lady's nephew of Hervin on the other."
