Then Bors thought he would be there, in case he might meet his brother Sir Lionel, or any others of his fellowship who were in the quest of the Holy Grail. And then he turned aside to a hermitage that stood at the edge of the forest.

And when he got there he found Sir Lionel his brother, who sat fully armed at the entrance of the chapel door, to lodge there until the morning when the tournament was to be. And when Sir Bors saw him he was so glad of him that his joy was a marvel to tell. And then he dismounted from his horse and said, "Fair sweet brother, when did you come here?"

As soon as Lionel saw him he said, "Ah, Bors, you have nothing to boast of, for as far as you were concerned I might have been killed. When you saw two knights leading me away and beating me, you left me to go and help a gentlewoman, and left me in danger of death; for never before did any brother do another so great a betrayal. And for that misdeed I promise you nothing now but death, for you have well deserved it. So look out for yourself from now on, and you'll find out as soon as I am armed."

When Sir Bors understood his brother's anger he knelt down on the ground and begged his pardon, holding up both his hands, and begged him to forgive him his ill will.

"No," said Lionel, "that will never be, if I can get the upper hand. I swear it to God: you will die for it, for it would be a pity for you to live any longer."

Then and there he went in and took his armour, and mounted his horse, and came before him and said, "Bors, keep away from me, for I will treat you as I would a felon or a traitor; for you are the most faithless knight that ever came out of so worthy a house as that of King Bors de Ganis, who was our father. So get up on your horse, and that way you will be at your best advantage. And if you won't, I'll ride at you where you stand on foot, and so the shame will be mine and the harm yours; but I care nothing for that shame."

When Sir Bors saw that he must fight his brother or else die, he did not know what to do. His heart advised him against it, since Lionel was born before him, and so he owed him reverence. Yet he knelt down before the feet of Lionel's horse and said, "Fair sweet brother, have mercy on me and do not kill me, and remember the great love that ought to be between the two of us."

Lionel cared nothing for what Sir Bors said to him, for the devil had brought him to such a will that he meant to kill him. Then, when Lionel saw that he would do nothing else, and would not get up to give him battle, he charged right over him, so that he struck Bors down to the ground with his horse, feet upward, and hurt him so badly that he fainted from the distress he felt at the thought of dying without confession. So when Lionel saw this, he dismounted from his horse to strike off his head. And so he took him by the helm, and would have torn it from his head. Then the hermit came running to him, who was a good man and of great age, and had heard all the words that passed between them, and so he threw himself down upon Sir Bors.

Chapter 15: How Sir Colgrevance fought against Sir Lionel to save Sir Bors, and how the hermit was killed

Then he said to Lionel, "Ah, noble knight, have mercy on me and on your brother, for if you kill him you will die in sin, and that would be a sorrowful thing, for he is one of the worthiest knights in the world, and of the best character."

"So help me God," said Lionel, "sir priest, unless you get away from him I will kill you, and he will be none the sooner spared for it."

"Certainly," said the good man, "I would rather you killed me than him, for my death will be no great harm, not half so much as his."

"Very well," said Lionel, "I'm content." And he set his hand to his sword and struck him so hard that his head flew backward. Even so, he did not hold back from his wicked purpose, but took his brother by the helm and unlaced it to strike off his head, and he would have killed him without fail. But so it happened that Colgrevance, a fellow of the Round Table, came there at that moment, as Our Lord willed. And when he saw the good man killed he wondered greatly what it could be. And then he saw that Lionel was about to kill his brother, and he recognised Sir Bors, whom he loved very much. Then he leapt down and took Lionel by the shoulders, and pulled him hard back from Bors, and said, "Lionel, will you kill your brother, one of the worthiest knights in the world? No good man should allow that."

"What," said Lionel, "will you stop me? Then if you meddle in this I'll kill you, and him after."

"What," said Colgrevance, "is it true that you will kill him?"

"Kill him I will," he said, "whoever says otherwise, for he has done so much against me that he has well deserved it."

And so he ran at him, and would have struck him through the head; and Sir Colgrevance ran between them and said, "If you are so bold as to do that again, the two of us will fight it out together."

When Lionel heard his words he took his shield before him and asked him who he was. And he told him: Colgrevance, one of his fellows. Then Lionel defied him, and gave him a great stroke through the helm. Then he drew his sword, for he was an exceedingly good knight, and defended himself most manfully. The battle lasted so long that Bors got up, in great pain, and saw Colgrevance, the good knight, fighting with his brother for his sake. Then he was very sorry and downcast, and thought that if Colgrevance killed his brother he would never have joy; and if his brother killed Colgrevance, "the shame would be mine for ever." Then he would have got up to part them, but he did not have the strength to stand on his feet; so he waited there until Colgrevance had the worst of it, for Lionel was a knight of great prowess and very bold, and he had pierced Colgrevance's hauberk and helm, so that he expected nothing but death; for he had lost so much blood that it was a marvel he could stand upright. Then he looked at Sir Bors, who was sitting up, trying to raise himself, and said, "Ah, Bors, why don't you come and get me out of danger of death, which I put myself into to help you, when you were close to death just now?"

"Certainly," said Lionel, "that won't do you any good, for neither of you will be able to protect the other: you will both die by my hand."

When Bors heard that, he made such an effort that he got up and put on his helm. Then for the first time he saw the hermit-priest who had been killed, and he grieved over him marvellously.

Chapter 16: How Sir Lionel slew Sir Colgrevance, and how afterwards he meant to slay Sir Bors

Then Colgrevance called out again and again to Sir Bors, "Why will you let me die here for your sake? If it pleases you that I die for you, it will please me all the better, to save a worthy man."

At that word Sir Lionel struck the helm off his head. Then Colgrevance saw that he could not escape; then he said, "Fair sweet Jesus, have mercy on my soul for what I have done wrong; and may the sorrow my heart suffers for doing good, and the charity I would have done here, be a relief of penance to me for my soul's health."

At these words Lionel struck him so hard that he bore him to the ground. Having killed Colgrevance, he ran at his brother like a fiend, and gave him such a stroke that he made him stagger. And Bors, who was full of humility, begged him for God's love to leave off this battle, "For if it happened, fair brother, that I killed you or you me, we would both die in that sin."

"May God never help me if I have any mercy on you, if I can get the upper hand."

Then Bors drew his sword, weeping, and said, "Fair brother, God knows my intent. Ah, fair brother, you have done great evil this day to kill such a holy priest, who never did any wrong. You have also killed a noble knight, and one of our fellows. And you know well that I am not much afraid of you, but I fear the wrath of God; and this is an unnatural war, so may God show a miracle upon us both. Now God have mercy on me, though I defend my life against my brother."

With that Bors lifted his hand and would have struck his brother.

Chapter 17: How a voice came that commanded Sir Bors not to touch him, and of a cloud that came between them

And then he heard a voice that said, "Flee, Bors, and do not touch him, or else you will kill him."

At that moment a cloud came down between them, in the likeness of a fire and a marvellous flame, so that both their shields burned. Then they were so badly frightened that they both fell to the ground, and lay there a long while in a faint. And when they came to themselves, Bors saw that his brother had come to no harm; then he held up both his hands, for he feared God had taken vengeance on him. With that he heard a voice say, "Bors, go from here, and keep your brother company no longer, but take your way straight to the sea, for Sir Percival is waiting for you there."

Then he said to his brother, "Fair sweet brother, for God's love forgive me all the wrong I have done you."

Then he answered, "May God forgive you, and I do, gladly."

So Sir Bors left him and rode the shortest way to the sea. And at last, by fortune, he came to an abbey which was near the sea. That night Bors rested there; and in his sleep a voice came to him and told him to go to the sea. Then he leapt up and made the sign of the cross in the middle of his forehead, and took his armour, and made his horse ready, and mounted; and he rode out through a gap in a broken wall, and rode on until he came to the sea. And on the shore he found a ship covered all in white samite, and he dismounted and commended himself to Jesus Christ. And as soon as he went aboard the ship, it set off out to sea, and went so fast that it seemed to him the ship was flying. But it was soon dark, so that he could recognise no one, and so he slept until it was day. Then he woke, and saw in the middle of the ship a knight lying fully armed except for his helm. Then he knew that it was Sir Percival of Wales, and he was overjoyed to see him. But Sir Percival was taken aback at the sight of him, and asked him who he was.

"Ah, fair sir," said Bors, "don't you know me?"

"Certainly," he said, "I wonder how you came here, unless Our Lord brought you here Himself."

Then Sir Bors smiled and took off his helm. Then Percival knew him, and each rejoiced so greatly in the other that it was a marvel to hear. Then Bors told him how he had come into the ship, and at whose bidding; and each told the other of their temptations, as you have heard before. So they went down the sea, sometimes backward, sometimes forward, and each comforted the other, and they were often at their prayers.

Then said Sir Percival, "We lack nothing but Galahad, the good knight."

Thus ends the sixteenth book, which is of Sir Gawain, Ector de Maris, Sir Bors de Ganis and Sir Percival.

Here follows the seventeenth book, which is of the noble knight Sir Galahad.

Book Seventeen: The Holy Grail

Chapter 1: How Sir Galahad fought at a tournament, and how he was recognised by Sir Gawain and Sir Ector de Maris

Now this story says that when Galahad had rescued Percival from the twenty knights, he went then into a waste forest, in which he rode for many days; and he met with many adventures, which he brought to an end, and of which the story makes no mention here. Then one day he took his way to the sea, and it happened as he passed by a castle that there was a marvellous tournament going on there; but those outside had done so much that those inside were getting the worst of it, and yet those inside were good enough knights. When Galahad saw that those inside were in such great distress that men were killing them at the gate of the castle, he decided to help them, and he set his spear forward and struck the first man so that he fell to the earth, and the spear broke to pieces. Then he drew his sword and struck where they were thickest, and he did such wonderful deeds of arms that they all marvelled. Then it happened that Gawain and Sir Ector de Maris were with the knights outside. But when they saw the white shield with the red cross, the one said to the other, "There is the good knight, Sir Galahad, the high prince. Now a man would be a great fool to meet him in a fight." So by chance Galahad came upon Sir Gawain, and he struck him so hard that he split his helm and the iron cap under it to the head, so that Gawain fell to the earth; but the stroke was so great that it slanted down to the ground and carved his horse's shoulder in two.

When Ector saw Gawain down he drew aside, and thought it no wisdom to stand against him, and also out of natural love, because he was Galahad's uncle. So through his great boldness Galahad beat back all the knights outside. And then those inside came out and chased them all about. But when Galahad saw that none of them would turn back to fight, he slipped away secretly, so that no one knew what had become of him.

"Now by my head," said Gawain to Ector, "now the marvels are true that were said by Lancelot du Lake, that the sword which stuck in the stone would give me such a blow that I would not have it for the best castle in this world; and truly, now it is proved true, for I never had such a stroke from a man's hand before."

"Sir," said Ector, "it seems to me your quest is done."

"And yours is not done," said Gawain, "but mine is done. I shall seek no further."

Then Gawain was carried into a castle, and they took off his armour and laid him in a rich bed, and a doctor found that he would live, and be healed within a month. So Gawain and Ector stayed together, for Sir Ector would not leave until Gawain was healed.

And the good knight Galahad rode on so long that he came that night to the Castle of Carbonek; and it so happened that night overtook him at a hermitage. And the good man was glad when he saw that he was a knight-errant. Then, when they were at rest, there came a gentlewoman knocking at the door, and called for Galahad, and so the good man came to the door to find out what she wanted. Then she called to the hermit, "Sir Ulfin, I am a gentlewoman who would speak with the knight who is with you."

Then the good man woke Galahad, and said to him, "Get up, and speak with a gentlewoman who seems to have great need of you."

Then Galahad went to her and asked her what she wanted.

"Galahad," she said, "I want you to arm yourself, and mount your horse and follow me, for within these three days I will show you the highest adventure that any knight ever saw."

At once Galahad armed himself, and took his horse, and commended himself to God, and told the gentlewoman to go ahead, and he would follow wherever she pleased.

Chapter 2: How Sir Galahad rode with a damsel, and came to the ship where Sir Bors and Sir Percival were

So she rode as fast as her palfrey could carry her, until she came to the sea, which was called Collibe. And at nightfall they came to a castle in a valley, enclosed by running water and by strong, high walls; and so she went into the castle with Galahad, and there he was given a warm welcome, for the lady of that castle was the damsel's mistress. So when he had taken off his armour, the damsel said, "Madam, shall we stay here all this day?"

"No," she said, "only until he has dined and slept a little."

So he ate and slept a while, until the maiden called him, and he armed himself by torchlight. And when the maiden and he were both on horseback, the lady gave Galahad a fair page, richly dressed; and so they left the castle and rode until they came to the seaside. And there they found the ship that Bors and Percival were in, and they called from the ship's side, "Sir Galahad, you are welcome! We have waited for you a long time."

And when he heard them he asked them who they were.

"Sir," she said, "leave your horse here, and I will leave mine." And they took their saddles and their bridles with them, and made the sign of the cross over them, and so went aboard the ship. And the two knights received them both with great joy, and each knew the other; and so the wind rose, and drove them through the sea at a marvellous pace. And within a while it was dawn.

Then Galahad took off his helm and his sword, and asked his companions where that fair ship had come from.

"Truly," they said, "you know as well as we do, except by God's grace."

And then each told the other of all their hard adventures, and of their great temptations.

"Truly," said Galahad, "you are much bound to God, for you have come safely through great adventures; and if it had not been for the gentlewoman I would not have come here; for as for you, I never expected to find you in these strange countries."

"Ah, Galahad," said Bors, "if Lancelot your father were here, then we would be well content, for then it would seem to us that we lacked nothing."

"That cannot be," said Galahad, "unless it pleased Our Lord."

By then the ship had gone from the land of Logres, and by chance it came in between two rocks, exceedingly great and marvellous; but there they could not land, for there was a whirlpool of the sea there; except that there was another ship, and onto it they could go without danger.

"Let us go there," said the gentlewoman, "and there we shall see adventures, for such is Our Lord's will."

And when they came there they found the ship rich enough, but they found neither man nor woman in it. But at the end of the ship they found two fair inscriptions, which spoke a dreadful and a marvellous word: "You who shall enter this ship, take care that you be steadfast in faith, for I am Faith, and so take care how you enter, for if you fail I shall not help you."

Then the gentlewoman said, "Percival, do you know who I am?"

"Certainly not," he said, "to my knowledge."

"Know this," she said, "that I am your sister, the daughter of King Pellinore, and so believe me, you are the man in the world I love most; and if you are not perfect in your belief in Jesus Christ, do not enter in any way at all, for then you would perish in the ship, for it is so perfect that it will suffer no sinner in it."

When Percival understood that she was truly his sister, he was glad at heart, and said, "Fair sister, I will go in, for if I am an unbeliever or an untrue knight, there I shall perish."

Chapter 3: How Sir Galahad went aboard the ship, and of a fine bed in it, with other marvellous things, and of a sword

In the meantime Galahad crossed himself and went aboard; and then after him the gentlewoman, and then Sir Bors and Sir Percival. And when they were in, it was so marvellously fair and rich that they marvelled; and in the middle of the ship was a fair bed, and Galahad went to it, and found a crown of silk there. And at its foot was a sword, rich and fair, and it was drawn out of the sheath half a foot and more. And the sword was of many fashions: the pommel was of stone, and there were in it all the colours that any man could find, and each of the colours had its own powers; and the grip plates of the hilt were made of the ribs of two different beasts. The one beast was a serpent that lived in Calidone, and is called the Serpent of the Fiend; and its bone has such a power that no hand that holds it shall ever be weary or hurt. And the other beast is a fish, not very large, that lives in the river Euphrates; and that fish is called Ertanax, and its bones are of such a nature that whoever holds them shall have so much will that he shall never be weary, and he shall not think of any joy or sorrow that he has had, but only of the thing that he sees before him. And as for this sword, no man shall ever grasp it by the hilt but one; but he shall surpass all others.

"In the name of God," said Percival, "I will try to hold it."

So he set his hand to the sword, but he could not grasp it.

"By my faith," he said, "now I have failed."

Bors set his hand to it and failed.

Then Galahad looked at the sword and saw letters like blood that said: "Let no one try to draw me out of my sheath unless he is bolder than any other; and whoever draws me, believe me, he shall never escape being shamed in his body, or wounded to the death."

"By my faith," said Galahad, "I would draw this sword out of the sheath, but the forbidding is so great that I will not set my hand to it."

"Now, sirs," said the gentlewoman, "know this, that the drawing of this sword is forbidden to all men except only to you. Also, this ship came to land in the realm of Logres; and at that time there was deadly war between King Labor, who was father to the Maimed King, and King Hurlame, who was a Saracen. But then he was newly christened, so that men held him afterwards one of the cleverest men in the world. And so one day it happened that King Labor and King Hurlame had gathered their people by the sea, where this ship had come to land; and there King Hurlame was defeated, and his men killed; and he was afraid of being killed, and fled to his ship, and there found this sword and drew it, and came out and found King Labor, the man in all Christendom in whom there was then the greatest faith. And when King Hurlame saw King Labor he raised this sword, and struck him on the helm so hard that he split him and his horse to the ground with the first stroke of his sword. And this was in the realm of Logres; and so great plague and great harm fell on both realms. For after that neither corn nor grass grew, nor hardly any fruit, nor were there any fish in the water; and that is why men call it the lands of the two borders, the Waste Land, because of that dolorous stroke. And when King Hurlame saw that this sword cut so well, he turned back to fetch the scabbard, and so came into this ship and went aboard, and put the sword back in its sheath. And as soon as he had done it he fell down dead before the bed. So the sword was proved, that no one ever drew it without being killed or maimed. So he lay there until a maiden came into the ship and threw him out, for there was no man in the world bold enough to go into that ship because of the prohibition."

Chapter 4: Of the marvels of the sword and of the scabbard

And then they looked at the scabbard. It seemed to be made of a serpent's skin, and on it were letters of gold and silver. And the girdle was a poor thing to look at, and not fit to hold so rich a sword. And the letters said: "He who shall wield me ought to be bolder than any other, if he bears me as truly as I ought to be borne. For the body of him by whom I ought to hang shall not be shamed in any place while he is girded with this girdle, and let no one ever be so bold as to take this girdle away; for it ought not to be taken away except by the hands of a maiden, and she must be a king's daughter and a queen's, and she must be a maiden all the days of her life, both in will and in deed. And if she breaks her virginity she shall die the most shameful death that any woman ever died."

"Sir," said Percival, "turn this sword over, so that we may see what is on the other side."

And it was red as blood, with letters as black as any coal, which said: "He who shall praise me most shall find me most to blame at a time of great need; and to the one to whom I should be most courteous I shall be most cruel, and that shall be at one time."

"Fair brother," she said to Percival, "it happened some forty years after the Passion of Jesus Christ that Nacien, the brother-in-law of King Mordrains, was carried, by the commandment of Our Lord, to a town more than fourteen days' journey from his country, onto an island in the parts of the West that men called the Isle of Turnance. So it happened that he found this ship at the entrance of a rock, and he found the bed and this sword just as we have heard now. Even so, he did not have the boldness to draw it; and he stayed there some eight days, and on the ninth day a great wind blew up which carried him away from the island, and brought him to another island by a rock, and there he found the greatest giant that any man ever saw. With that this horrible giant came to kill him; and he looked about him and could not flee, and he had nothing to defend himself with. So he ran to the sword, and when he saw it naked he praised it highly, and then he shook it, and with that he broke it in the middle. 'Ah,' said Nacien, 'the thing that I most praised I ought now most to blame.' And with that he threw the pieces of his sword over the bed. And afterwards he leapt over the side to fight with the giant, and killed him."

"And at once he went aboard the ship again, and the wind rose and drove him through the sea, so that by chance he came to another ship where King Mordrains was, who had been sorely tempted by a fiend at the Port of Perilous Rock. And when the one saw the other they rejoiced greatly over each other, and each told the other of his adventure, and how the sword had failed him in his greatest need. When Mordrains saw the sword he praised it highly. 'But,' he said, 'the breaking was not to be done except by your own wickedness, for you are in some sin.' And there he took the sword and set the pieces together, and they joined as fair as they ever were before; and he put the sword in the sheath, and laid it down on the bed. Then they heard a voice that said, 'Get out of this ship for a little while, and go into the other, for fear you fall into deadly sin; for if you are found in deadly sin you cannot escape, but will perish.' And so they went into the other ship. And as Nacien went over the side he was struck by a sword on the right foot, so that he fell flat on his face on the ship's deck; and with that he said, 'O God, how I am hurt!' And then a voice came and said, 'Take that for the offence you committed in drawing this sword. That is why you receive a wound, for you were never worthy to handle it, as the writing says.'"

"In the name of God," said Galahad, "you are very wise in these matters."

Chapter 5: How King Pelles was struck through both thighs because he drew the sword, and other marvellous stories

"Sir," she said, "there was a king called Pelles, the Maimed King. And while he could still ride he did much to uphold Christendom and Holy Church. So one day he was hunting in a wood of his that ran down to the sea; and at last he lost his hounds and all his knights except only one. And there he and his knight went on until they came toward Ireland, and there he found the ship. And when he saw the letters and understood them, he went in all the same, for he was very perfect in his life, but his knight had no courage to go in; and there he found this sword, and drew it out as far as you can see. So with that a spear came in, with which he was struck through both thighs, and he could never be healed after that, nor shall he be until we come to him. So," she said, "was not King Pelles, your grandfather, maimed for his boldness?"

"In the name of God, damsel," said Galahad.

So they went toward the bed to look all about it, and above its head there hung two swords. Also there were two spindles which were as white as any snow, and others that were as red as blood, and others above them as green as any emerald: these were the three colours of the spindles, and they were the natural colour of the wood within, without any painting.

"These spindles," said the damsel, "came from the time when sinful Eve went to gather the fruit for which Adam and she were put out of paradise: she took with her the bough on which the apple hung. Then she saw that the branch was fair and green, and she remembered the loss that came from the tree. Then she decided to keep the branch as long as she could. And because she had no chest to keep it in, she put it in the earth. So by the will of Our Lord the branch grew into a great tree within a little while, and it was as white as any snow, branches, boughs and leaves: that was a sign that a maiden had planted it. But afterwards God came to Adam, and told him to know his wife in the flesh, as nature required. So Adam lay with his wife under the same tree; and at once the tree that had been white turned as green as any grass, and everything that came out of it; and at the same time that they lay together, Abel was conceived. So the tree was green in colour for a long time. And so it happened many days after that, under the same tree, Cain killed Abel, from which came a great marvel. For as soon as Abel had received his death under the green tree, it lost its green colour and became red; and that was a sign of the blood. And at once all the plants that had grown from it died, but the tree grew and flourished marvellously, and it was the fairest tree and the most delightful that any man could behold and see; and so the plants that had grown out of it before Abel was killed under it all died."

So the tree lasted until Solomon, King David's son, reigned and held the land after his father. This Solomon was wise, and knew all the powers of stones and trees, and he knew the course of the stars, and many other different things. This Solomon had a wicked wife, because of whom he thought that there had never been a good woman, and so he scorned women in his books. So a voice once answered him: "Solomon, if sorrow comes to a man through a woman, never mind it; for yet there shall come a woman from whom shall come a hundred times more joy to men than this sorrow gives grief; and that woman shall be born of your line."

Then when Solomon heard these words he thought himself nothing but a fool, and he found the truth of it in old books. Also the Holy Ghost showed him the coming of the glorious Virgin Mary. Then he asked the voice whether it would be in the branch of his line.

"No," said the voice, "but there shall come a man who shall be a virgin, and the last of your blood, and he shall be as good a knight as Duke Josua, your brother-in-law."

Chapter 6: How Solomon took David's sword on the advice of his wife, and of other marvellous matters

"Now I have made certain for you the thing you were in doubt of."

Then Solomon was glad that any such man should come of his line; but all the while he wondered and pondered who that should be, and what his name might be. His wife saw that he was pondering, and thought she would find it out at some time; and so she waited her chance, and asked him the reason for his pondering, and he told her all of it, how the voice had spoken to him.

"Well," she said, "I will have a ship made of the best and most lasting wood that men can find."

So Solomon sent for all the carpenters of the land, and the best ones. And when they had made the ship the lady said to Solomon, "Sir," she said, "since it is so that this knight is to surpass all the knights of chivalry who have been before him and who shall come after him, I will tell you something more," she said. "You shall go into Our Lord's temple, where King David's sword is, your father's, which is the most marvellous and the sharpest that was ever taken in any knight's hand. So take that, and take off the pommel, and make a pommel of precious stones for it, so cunningly made that no one can see but that it is all one piece; and after that, have a hilt made for it so marvellously and wonderfully that no one may recognise it; and after that, have a marvellous sheath made. And when you have done all this, I will have a girdle made for it, such as shall please me."

King Solomon had all this made as she planned it, both the ship and all the rest. And when the ship was ready in the sea to sail, the lady had a great bed made, marvellously rich, and set it at the head of the bed, covered with silk, and laid the sword at its foot; and the girdles were of hemp, and at that the king was angry.

"Sir, believe me," she said, "I have nothing so high that it would be worthy to hold up so high a sword; and a maiden shall bring other girdles to it, but I do not know when it shall be, nor at what time."

And then she had a covering made for the ship, of silk cloth that would never rot in any kind of weather. Then that lady went and had a carpenter come to the tree under which Abel was killed.

"Now," she said, "carve me out of this tree as much wood as will make me a spindle."

"Ah, madam," he said, "this is the tree that our first mother planted."

"Do it," she said, "or I will destroy you."

As soon as he began to work, drops of blood came out; and then he would have stopped, but she would not allow him to, and so he took away as much wood as would make a spindle; and so she made him take as much from the green tree and from the white tree. And when these three spindles were shaped she had them fastened to the canopy of the bed.

When Solomon saw this, he said to his wife, "You have done marvellously; for though all the world were here right now, no one could work out why all this was made, except Our Lord Himself; and you who have done it do not know what it will mean."

"Let it be, now," she said, "for you will hear news of it sooner than you think."

Now you shall hear a wonderful tale of King Solomon and his wife.

Chapter 7: A wonderful tale of King Solomon and his wife

That night Solomon lay in front of the ship with only a few companions. And when he was asleep it seemed to him that a great company of angels came from heaven, and came down into the ship, and took water which was brought by an angel in a vessel of silver, and sprinkled all the ship with it. And afterwards he came to the sword and drew letters on the hilt. And afterwards he went to the ship's side, and wrote other letters there, which said: "You who would come into me, take care that you are full in the faith, for I am nothing but Faith and Belief."

When Solomon saw these letters he was dismayed, so that he did not dare go in, and so he drew back; and at once the ship was pushed out into the sea, and it went so fast that he lost sight of it within a little while. And then a small voice said, "Solomon, the last knight of your line shall rest in this bed."

Then Solomon went and woke his wife, and told her of the adventures of the ship.

Now the story says that the three companions looked at the bed and the three spindles for a long while. Then they were certain that they were of natural colours, without painting. Then they lifted a cloth which lay above the floor, and found there what seemed to be a rich purse. And Percival took it, and found a written paper in it, and so he read it, and it told of the making of the spindles and of the ship, where it came from, and by whom it was made.

"Now," said Galahad, "where shall we find the gentlewoman who is to make new girdles for the sword?"

"Fair sir," said Percival's sister, "do not be dismayed, for by God's leave I will make a girdle for the sword, such as shall belong to it."

And then she opened a box and took out girdles which were finely worked with golden threads, and on them were set very precious stones, and a rich buckle of gold.

"Look, lords," she said, "here is a girdle that ought to be set about the sword. And believe me, the greatest part of this girdle was made of my hair, which I loved well while I was a woman of the world. But as soon as I knew that this adventure was ordained for me, I cut off my hair, and made this girdle in the name of God."

"You are well met," said Sir Bors, "for certainly you have saved us from a great deal of trouble, which we would have gone into if it had not been for your news."

Then the gentlewoman went and set it on the sword as its girdle.

"Now," said the fellowship, "what is the name of the sword, and what shall we call it?"

"Truly," she said, "the name of the sword is the Sword with the Strange Girdles; and the sheath is Mover of Blood; for no man who has blood in him shall ever see the one part of the sheath, which was made of the Tree of Life."

Then they said to Galahad, "In the name of Jesus Christ, we beg you to gird yourself with this sword, which has been so much longed for in the realm of Logres."

"Now let me begin to grip this sword," said Galahad, "to give you courage; but believe me, it belongs no more to me than it does to you."

And then he closed his fingers round it a good way; and then she girded the sword about his waist.

"Now I do not care if I die," she said, "for now I count myself one of the blessed maidens of the world, who has made the worthiest knight in the world."

"Damsel," said Galahad, "you have done so much that I will be your knight all the days of my life."

Then they left that ship and went to the other. And at once the wind drove them out to sea at a great pace, but they had no food. But it happened that in the morning they came to a castle that men call Carteloise, which was in the borders of Scotland. And when they had passed the harbour, the gentlewoman said, "Lords, there are men here who, if they knew that you were of King Arthur's court, would attack you at once."

"Damsel," said Galahad, "He who brought us out of the rock shall deliver us from them."

Chapter 8: How Galahad and his companions came to a castle, and how they were attacked there, and how they slew their enemies, and other matters

So it happened, as they were speaking like this, that a squire came by them and asked who they were; and they said they were of King Arthur's household.

"Is that true?" he said. "Now by my head," he said, "you are in a bad way." And then he turned back to the cliff fortress.

And within a while they heard a horn blow. Then a gentlewoman came to them and asked them where they were from; and they told her.

"Fair lords," she said, "for the love of God turn back if you can, for you have come to your death."

"No," they said, "we will not turn back, for He in whose service we have set out shall help us."

Then, as they stood talking, knights came up well armed, and told them to yield or else die.

"That yielding," they said, "will do you harm."

And with that they let their horses run at them, and Sir Percival struck the foremost to the earth, and took his horse and mounted it, and Galahad did the same. Bors served another the same way too, for they had no horses in that country, for they had left their horses behind when they took ship in other countries. And so when they were mounted they began to set upon them; and the men of the castle fled into the strong fortress, and the three knights after them into the castle, and there they dismounted, and with their swords they cut them down, and got into the hall.

Then, when they saw the great multitude of people they had killed, they counted themselves great sinners.

"Certainly," said Bors, "I think that if God had loved them, we would not have had the power to kill them like this. But they have done so much against Our Lord that He would not allow them to reign any longer."

"Do not say so," said Galahad, "for if they did wrong against God, the vengeance is not ours, but His who has power over it."

Then there came out of a chamber a good man who was a priest, and he carried the Body of Our Lord in a cup. And when he saw the men lying dead in the hall he was utterly dismayed; and Galahad took off his helm and knelt down, and so did his two companions.

"Sir," they said, "have no fear of us, for we are of King Arthur's court."

Then the good man asked how they had been killed so suddenly, and they told him.

"Truly," said the good man, "if you could live as long as the world lasts, you could never have done so great a work of charity as this."

"Sir," said Galahad, "I am very sorry for it, since they were christened men."

"No, do not be sorry," he said, "for they were not christened, and I will tell you what I know of this castle. Not more than a year ago, the lord here was Earl Hernox, and he had three sons, good knights of arms, and a daughter, the fairest gentlewoman that men knew. And those three knights loved their sister so badly that they burned with desire for her, and so they lay with her against her will. And because she cried out to her father, they killed her, and took their father and put him in prison, and wounded him almost to death, but a cousin of hers rescued him. And then they did great wickedness: they killed clerks and priests, and had chapels torn down, so that Our Lord's service could not be served or said. And this very day her father sent for me to hear his confession and give him communion; but no man ever had such shame as I had this day from the three brothers. But the earl told me to bear it, for he said they would not last long, for three servants of Our Lord would destroy them; and now it is brought to an end. And by this you may know that Our Lord is not displeased with your deeds."

"Certainly," said Galahad, "if it had not pleased Our Lord, we would never have killed so many men in so short a while."

And then they brought the Earl Hernox out of prison into the middle of the hall, and he knew Galahad at once, and yet he had never seen him before except by a revelation of Our Lord.

Chapter 9: How the three knights, with Percival's sister, came to the same forest, and of a hart and four lions, and other things

Then he began to weep very tenderly, and said, "I have waited a long time for you to come. But for God's love, hold me in your arms, so that my soul may leave my body in the arms of as good a man as you are."

"Gladly," said Galahad.

And then a voice spoke on high, so that all heard it: "Galahad, you have avenged me well on God's enemies. Now you must go to the Maimed King as soon as you can, for through you he shall receive the health he has waited for so long."

And with that the soul left the body, and Galahad had him buried as was fitting.

Then the three knights left at once, and Percival's sister with them. And so they came into a desolate forest, and there they saw in front of them a white hart, which four lions were leading. Then they agreed among themselves to follow it to find out where it was going; and so they rode after it at a great pace until they came to a valley, and near it was a hermitage where a holy man lived, and the hart and the lions went in there too. So when they saw all this they turned to the chapel, and saw the holy man in a religious habit and in the armour of Our Lord, the vestments of the mass, for he was going to sing the mass of the Holy Ghost; and so they went in and heard mass. And at the silent prayers of the mass the three of them saw the hart become a man, which amazed them, and he was set upon the altar in a rich seat; and they saw that the four lions were changed, the one into the form of a man, the next into the form of a lion, the third into an eagle, and the fourth was changed into an ox. Then they took up their seat where the hart sat, and went out through a glass window, and nothing was damaged or broken; and the knights heard a voice say, "In just this way the Son of God entered the womb of the maiden Mary, whose virginity was neither damaged nor harmed." And when they heard these words they fell down to the earth and were stunned; and with that there was a great brightness.

And when they had come to themselves again they went to the holy man and begged him to tell them the truth.

"What have you seen?" he said.

And they told him all that they had seen.

"Ah, lords," he said, "you are welcome. Now I know well that you are the good knights who shall bring the Holy Grail to its end; for you are the ones to whom Our Lord shall show great secrets. And it is right that Our Lord should be signified by a hart, for when the hart is old he grows young again in his white skin. Just so Our Lord comes again from death to life, for He lost His earthly flesh, the mortal flesh which He had taken in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary; and for that reason Our Lord appeared as a white hart without a spot. And the four that were with Him are to be understood as the Four Evangelists, who set down in writing a part of the deeds of Jesus Christ that He did once when He was among you as an earthly man. For believe me, never before could any knight know the truth of this; for often before now Our Lord has shown Himself to good men and to good knights in the likeness of a hart, but I believe that from now on you will see it no more."

And then they rejoiced greatly, and stayed there all that day. And the next morning, when they had heard mass, they left and commended the holy man to God; and so they came to a castle and passed it by. Then a knight in armour came after them and said, "Lords, listen to what I have to say to you."

Chapter 10: How they were asked to keep a strange custom, which they would not obey, and so they fought and slew many knights

"This gentlewoman you are leading with you, is she a maiden?"

"Sir," she said, "a maiden I am."

Then he took her horse by the bridle and said, "By the Holy Cross, you shall not get away from me before you have paid the custom of this castle."

"Let her go," said Percival. "You are not wise, for a maiden is free wherever she comes."

Meanwhile some ten or twelve knights in armour came out of the castle, and with them came gentlewomen holding a dish of silver.

And then they said, "This gentlewoman must pay us the custom of this castle."

"Sir," said one knight, "every maiden who passes by here must give this dish full of blood from her right arm."

"Shame on you who brought in such customs," said Galahad. "And so God save me, I promise you this: you shall not have it from this gentlewoman while I live."

"So help me God," said Percival, "I would rather be killed."

"And so would I," said Sir Bors.

"By my faith," said the knight, "then you shall die, for you cannot hold out against us, even if you were the best knights in the world."

Then they charged at each other, and the three companions beat the ten knights, and then set their hands to their swords and beat them down and killed them. Then some sixty knights in armour came out of the castle.

"Fair lords," said the three companions, "have mercy on yourselves and do not fight with us."

"No, fair lords," said the knights of the castle, "we advise you to withdraw, for you are the best knights in the world, and so do no more, for you have done enough. We will let you go with the harm you have done, but we must have the custom."

"Truly," said Galahad, "you are wasting your words."

"Well," they said, "do you want to die?"

"We have not come to that yet," said Galahad.

Then they began to fight together, and Galahad drew his sword, the one with the strange girdles, and struck on the right hand and on the left, and killed whoever stood up to him, and did such marvels that no one who saw him thought he was an earthly man, but some unearthly prodigy. And his two companions helped him exceedingly well, and so they each kept up the engagement equally hard until it was night: then they had to break off.

Then a good knight came out and said to the three companions, "If you will come in tonight and take such lodging as there is here, you shall be very welcome. And we promise you on our lives, and as we are true knights, to leave you tomorrow in the same state as we find you, without any treachery. And as soon as you know about the custom, we dare say you will agree to it."

"For God's love," said the gentlewoman, "go in there, and do not hold back for my sake."

"Let us go," said Galahad; and so they went into the chapel. And when they had dismounted, the people there made them very welcome. Then after a while the three knights asked about the custom of the castle, and the reason for it.

"What it is," they said, "we will tell you truly."

Chapter 11: How Sir Percival's sister bled a dish full of blood to heal a lady, and so died, and how her body was put in a ship

"There is a gentlewoman in this castle to whom we belong, and this castle is hers, and many others too. Many years ago it happened that a sickness came upon her; and when she had lain sick a long time she fell into a leprosy, and no doctor could give her any remedy. But at last an old man said that if she could have a dish full of the blood of a maiden who was a pure virgin in will and in deed, and a king's daughter, that blood would be her health, if she were anointed with it; and that is why this custom was made."

"Now, fair knights," said Percival's sister, "I can see well that this gentlewoman is as good as dead."

"Truly," said Galahad, "if you bleed so much you may die."

"Truly," she said, "if I die to heal her I shall win great honour and my soul's health, and honour for my family; and one harm is better than two. And so there shall be no more fighting, but tomorrow I shall pay you the custom of this castle."

And then there was great joy, more than there had been before, for otherwise there would have been mortal war in the morning; and she would have it no other way, whether they liked it or not.

That night the three companions were given the best of everything; and in the morning they heard mass, and Sir Percival's sister told them to bring out the sick lady. So she was brought, and she was very ill.

Then Percival's sister said, "Who will let my blood?"

So someone came forward and opened her vein, and she bled so much that the dish was full. Then she lifted up her hand and crossed herself; and then she said to the lady, "Madam, I have come to my death to make you whole. For God's love, pray for me."

With that she fell into a faint. Then Galahad and his two companions leapt up to her, and lifted her up and stopped the bleeding, but she had bled so much that she could not live.

Then she said, when she had come to, "Fair brother Percival, I am dying for the healing of this lady, so I ask you not to bury me in this country, but as soon as I am dead put me in a boat at the nearest harbour, and let me go wherever chance will take me. And as soon as you three come to the City of Sarras, to achieve the Holy Grail there, you shall find me arrived beneath a tower, and bury me there in the holy place; for I tell you this much, Galahad shall be buried there, and you too, in the same place."

Then Percival understood these words, and promised it to her, weeping.

And then a voice said, "Lords and companions, tomorrow at the hour of prime you three shall part, each from the others, until the adventure brings you to the Maimed King."

Then she asked for her Saviour in the sacrament; and as soon as she had received it the soul left the body. And that same day the lady was healed, when she was anointed with the blood. Then Sir Percival wrote a letter telling all the ways she had helped them in strange adventures, and put it in her right hand, and so laid her in a barge, and covered it with black silk; and so the wind rose, and drove the barge away from the land, and all the knights watched it until it was out of their sight. Then they all went back towards the castle, and at once there came a sudden storm, with thunder, lightning and rain, as if the whole earth would have broken apart. And half the castle was turned upside down. It was past evensong before the storm stopped.

Then they saw in front of them a knight in armour, badly wounded in the body and in the head, who said, "O God, help me, for now is my need!"

After this knight came another knight and a dwarf, who shouted to him from far off, "Stand! You can't escape!"

Then the wounded knight held up his hands to God, praying that he should not die in such distress.

"Truly," said Galahad, "I will help him, for the sake of Him he is calling on."

"Sir," said Bors, "I will do it, for it is not a task for you, since he is only one knight."

"Sir," said Galahad, "I grant it."

So Sir Bors took his horse, and commended himself to God, and rode after them to rescue the wounded knight. Now we turn to the two companions.

Chapter 12: How Galahad and Percival found in a castle many tombs of maidens who had bled to death

Now the story says that all night Galahad and Percival were in a chapel at their prayers, praying for Sir Bors to be kept safe. Then in the morning they put on their armour and went towards the castle, to find out what had happened to the people in it. And when they came there they found that there was neither man nor woman who was not dead, by the vengeance of Our Lord.

With that they heard a voice that said, "This vengeance is for the shedding of maidens' blood."

They also found, at the end of the chapel, a churchyard, and in it they could see some sixty fair tombs. And that place was so fair and so delightful that it seemed to them there had been no storm there; for there lay the bodies of all the good maidens who had been martyred for the sick lady's sake. They also found the names of each of them, and what blood they came from, and all were of kings' blood, and twelve of them were kings' daughters. Then they left and went into a forest.

"Now," said Percival to Galahad, "we must part. So let us pray Our Lord that we may meet again soon."

Then they took off their helmets and kissed each other, and wept at their parting.

Chapter 13: How Sir Lancelot boarded the ship where Sir Percival's sister lay dead, and how he met Sir Galahad, his son

Now the story says that when Lancelot had come to the water of Mortoise, as was told before, he was in great peril, and so he lay down and slept, and accepted whatever adventure God would send him. So when he was asleep a vision came to him and said, "Lancelot, get up and take your armour, and go aboard the first ship you find."

And when he heard these words he leapt up and saw a great brightness all around him. And then he lifted up his hand and crossed himself, and so took his arms and made himself ready; and so by chance he came to a shore, and found a ship that had neither sail nor oar. And as soon as he was inside the ship he felt the greatest sweetness he had ever felt, and he was filled with everything he could think of or desire.

Then he said, "Fair sweet Father, Jesus Christ, I do not know what joy I am in, for this joy surpasses all the earthly joys I was ever in."

And so in this joy he lay down on the deck of the ship, and slept until day. And when he woke he found there a fair bed, and lying in it a gentlewoman, dead, who was Sir Percival's sister. And as Lancelot looked her over carefully, he noticed a letter in her right hand, which he read, and which told him all the adventures that you have heard before, and what family she came from. So Sir Lancelot stayed with this gentlewoman a month and more. If you ask how he lived: He who fed the people of Israel with manna in the desert, so was he fed; for every day, when he had said his prayers, he was sustained by the grace of the Holy Ghost.

So one night he went to amuse himself by the waterside, for he was somewhat weary of the ship. And then he listened and heard a horse coming, and someone riding on it. And when it came near, it seemed to be a knight. And so Lancelot let him pass, and the knight went to where the ship was; and there he dismounted, and took off the saddle and the bridle and sent the horse away, and went into the ship.

And then Lancelot turned to him and said, "You are welcome."

And he answered and greeted him in return, and asked him, "What is your name? For my heart goes out to you greatly."

"Truly," he said, "my name is Lancelot du Lake."

"Sir," said he, "then you are welcome, for you were the one who began me in this world."

"Ah," said Lancelot, "are you Galahad?"

"Yes, truly," he said; and so he knelt down and asked for his blessing, and afterwards took off his helmet and kissed him.

And there was great joy between them, for no tongue can tell the joy they had in each other, and many a loving word was spoken between them, as is natural between kin, which there is no need to repeat here. And there each told the other of the adventures and marvels that had befallen them on their many journeys since they left the court.

As soon as Galahad saw the gentlewoman dead in the bed, he knew her well enough, and spoke of her with great honour, saying she was the best maiden living, and that her death was a great pity. But when Lancelot heard how the marvellous sword had been won, and who made it, and all the marvels told before, he begged Galahad, his son, to show him the sword, and so he did; and at once Lancelot kissed the pommel, and the hilt, and the scabbard.

"Truly," said Lancelot, "never before did I know of such high adventures, so marvellous and strange."

So Lancelot and Galahad stayed in that ship half a year, and served God day and night with all their strength; and often they landed on islands far from people, where nothing came but wild beasts, and there they found many strange and perilous adventures, which they brought to an end. But because those adventures were with wild beasts, and not in the quest of the Holy Grail, the tale makes no mention of them here, for it would take too long to tell of all the adventures that befell them.

Chapter 14: How a knight brought Sir Galahad a horse, and told him to come away from his father, Sir Lancelot

So afterwards, on a Monday, it happened that they landed at the edge of a forest, in front of a cross. And then they saw a knight armed all in white, richly mounted, leading a white horse in his right hand. And so he came to the ship, and greeted the two knights in the name of the High Lord, and said, "Galahad, sir, you have been with your father long enough. Come out of the ship, and leap up on this horse, and go where the adventures shall lead you in the quest of the Holy Grail."

Then Galahad went to his father and kissed him tenderly, and said, "Fair sweet father, I do not know when I shall see you again, until I see the body of Jesus Christ."

"I beg you," said Lancelot, "pray to the High Father that He keep me in His service."

And so Galahad took his horse, and then they heard a voice that said, "Take care to do well, for the one of you shall never see the other again before the dreadful Day of Judgement."

"Now, son Galahad," said Lancelot, "since we must part and never see each other again, I pray to the High Father to preserve both you and me."

"Sir," said Galahad, "no prayer avails as much as yours."

And with that Galahad rode into the forest.

And the wind rose, and drove Lancelot for more than a month across the sea, and he slept but little, but prayed to God that he might see some sign of the Holy Grail. So it happened one night, at midnight, that he arrived in front of a castle, on its back side, a rich and fair one, and there was a back gate open towards the sea. It stood open without any guard, except that two lions guarded the entrance; and the moon shone clear.

At once Sir Lancelot heard a voice that said, "Lancelot, go out of this ship and enter the castle, where you shall see a great part of your desire."

Then he ran to his arms, and armed himself, and so went to the gate and saw the lions. Then he set his hand to his sword and drew it. Then suddenly a dwarf came and struck him on the arm so hard that the sword fell out of his hand.

Then he heard a voice say, "O man of evil faith and poor belief, why do you trust more in your armour than in your Maker? For He could help you more than your armour, He in whose service you are set."

Then Lancelot said, "Fair Father Jesus Christ, I thank You for Your great mercy, that You rebuke me for my misdeed. Now I see well that You hold me for Your servant."

Then he took up his sword again and put it back in its sheath, and made the sign of the cross on his forehead, and came to the lions, and they made as if to do him harm. Nevertheless he passed by them without hurt, and went into the castle, to the keep, and there everyone was asleep. Then Lancelot went in, armed as he was, for he found no gate or door that was not open. And at last he found a room whose door was shut, and he set his hand to it to open it, but he could not.

Chapter 15: How Sir Lancelot stood before the door of the chamber where the Holy Grail was

Then he strained hard to open the door. Then he listened and heard a voice singing so sweetly that it seemed no earthly thing; and he thought the voice said, "Joy and honour be to the Father of Heaven."

Then Lancelot knelt down before the room, for he knew well that the Holy Grail was inside that room.

Then he said, "Fair sweet Father, Jesus Christ, if ever I did anything that pleased You, Lord, for Your pity do not scorn me for the sins I have done in the past, and show me something of what I am seeking."

And with that he saw the door of the room open, and out of it came a great brightness, so that the house was as bright as if all the torches in the world had been there.

So he came to the door of the room, and would have gone in. And at once a voice said to him, "Flee, Lancelot, and do not go in, for you ought not to do it; and if you go in, you shall regret it."

Then he drew back, very downcast. Then he looked up into the middle of the room, and saw a table of silver, and the Holy Vessel, covered with red samite, and many angels around it, of whom one held a burning candle of wax, and another held a cross and the ornaments of an altar. And before the Holy Vessel he saw a holy man dressed as a priest. And it seemed that he was at the consecration of the mass. And it seemed to Lancelot that above the priest's hands there were three men, of whom two put the youngest, in likeness, between the priest's hands; and so the priest lifted it up very high, and it seemed that he was showing it to the people. And then Lancelot marvelled not a little, for he thought the priest was so heavily weighed down by the figure that it seemed to him he would fall to the earth.

And when he saw no one near who would help him, then he came to the door at a great pace, and said, "Fair Father Jesus Christ, do not count it as a sin if I help the good man, who has great need of help."

At once he went into the room, and came towards the table of silver; and when he came near he felt a breath which he thought was mingled with fire, and it struck him so hard in the face that he thought it burned his face. And with that he fell to the earth, and had no power to get up, like a man so overcome that he had lost the power of his body, and his hearing, and his sight. Then he felt many hands around him, which picked him up and carried him out of the door of the room, without his coming out of his faint at all, and left him there, seeming dead to everyone.

So the next morning, when it was broad day, the people within got up, and found Lancelot lying before the door of the room. They all marvelled at how he had got in, and so they looked him over, and felt his pulse to find out whether there was any life in him; and so they found life in him, but he could not stand or stir any limb he had. And so they took him by every part of his body, and carried him into a room, and laid him in a rich bed, far from everyone; and so he lay four days.

Then one said he was alive, and another said no.

"In the name of God," said an old man, "I tell you truly, he is not dead, but as full of life as the mightiest of you all. And so I advise you that he be well cared for until God sends him life again."

Chapter 16: How Sir Lancelot lay like a dead man for twenty-four days and as many nights, and several other matters

In this way they cared for Lancelot twenty-four days and as many nights, and all that time he lay still as a dead man; and on the twenty-fifth day, after midday, it happened that he opened his eyes. And when he saw people he grieved greatly, and said, "Why have you woken me? For I was more at ease than I am now. O Jesus Christ, who could be so blessed as to see openly Your great marvels of secrecy, there where no sinner may be!"

"What have you seen?" said those around him.

"I have seen," he said, "marvels so great that no tongue can tell them, and more than any heart can think. And if my son had not been here before me, I would have seen much more."

Then they told him how he had lain there twenty-four days and nights. Then he thought it was punishment for the twenty-four years he had been a sinner, and that for this Our Lord had put him to penance for twenty-four days and nights. Then Sir Lancelot looked in front of him, and saw the hair shirt he had worn for nearly a year, and he was very sorry that he had broken the promise he had vowed to the hermit.

Then they asked how it was with him.

"Truly," he said, "I am whole in body, thanks be to Our Lord. And so, sirs, for God's love tell me where I am."

Then they all said that he was in the castle of Carbonek.

With that a gentlewoman came and brought him a shirt of fine linen cloth, but he did not change into it there, but took the hair shirt back to him again.

"Sir," they said, "the quest of the Holy Grail is achieved now, for you; you shall never see any more of the Holy Grail than you have seen."

"Now I thank God," said Lancelot, "for His great mercy in what I have seen, for it is enough for me. For as I believe, no man in this world has lived better than I have done, to achieve what I have achieved."

And with that he took the hair shirt and put it on, and over it he put a linen shirt, and after that a robe of scarlet, fresh and new. And when he was dressed like this they all marvelled, for they knew him, that he was Lancelot, the good knight.

And then they all said, "O my lord Sir Lancelot, is it you?"

And he said, "Truly, I am he."

Then word came to King Pelles that the knight who had lain so long as if dead was Sir Lancelot. Then the king was very glad, and went to see him. And when Lancelot saw him coming he went to meet him, and there the king made him very welcome. And there the king told him the news that his fair daughter was dead.

Then Lancelot was very sad about it, and said, "Sir, I am sorry for the death of your daughter, for she was a very fair lady, fresh and young. And I know well that she bore the best knight who is now on the earth, or who ever was since God was born."

So the king kept him there four days, and on the next day he took his leave of King Pelles and of all the company, and thanked them for their great trouble.

Just as they sat at their dinner in the great hall, it so happened that the Holy Grail had filled the table with every kind of food that any heart could think of. And as they sat there they saw all the doors and the windows of the place shut without anyone's hand, at which they were all dismayed, and no one knew what to do.

And then it happened suddenly that a knight came to the main door and knocked, and shouted, "Open the door!"

But they would not. And still he shouted, "Open!" But they would not. And at last it annoyed them so much that the king himself got up and came to a window, there where the knight was calling.

Then he said, "Sir knight, you shall not come in at this time, while the Holy Grail is here, and so go elsewhere. For truly you are none of the knights of the quest, but one of those who have served the Fiend and left the service of Our Lord."

And the knight was exceedingly angry at the king's words.

"Sir knight," said the king, "since you are so eager to come in, tell me what country you are from."

"Sir," he said, "I am from the realm of Logres, and my name is Ector de Maris, and I am brother to my lord, Sir Lancelot."

"In the name of God," said the king, "I am sorry for what I have said, for your brother is here inside."

And when Ector de Maris understood that his brother was there, for he was the man in the world he most feared and loved, he said, "Ah God, now my sorrow and shame are doubled. The holy man on the hill spoke very truly to Gawain and to me about our dreams."

Then he rode out of the court as fast as his horse could go, and so on through the castle.

Chapter 17: How Sir Lancelot returned towards Logres, and of other adventures he saw on the way

Then King Pelles came to Sir Lancelot and told him news of his brother, at which he was so sorry that he did not know what to do. So Sir Lancelot departed, and took his arms, and said he would go and see the realm of Logres, "which I have not seen in twelve months." And with that he commended the king to God, and so rode through many realms. And at last he came to a white abbey, and there they gave him a warm welcome that night; and in the morning he rose and heard mass. And before an altar he found a rich tomb, which was newly made; and then he looked closely, and saw that the sides were written in gold, which said: "Here lies King Bagdemagus of Gore, whom King Arthur's nephew killed"; and it named him, Sir Gawain. Then he was not a little sorry, for Lancelot loved him much more than any other, and if it had been anyone other than Gawain, he would not have escaped from death to life; and he said to himself, "Ah, Lord God, this is a great blow to King Arthur's court, the loss of such a man." And then he departed and came to the abbey where Galahad did the adventure of the tombs, and won the white shield with the red cross; and there he was given a warm welcome all that night.

And in the morning he turned towards Camelot, where he found King Arthur and the queen. But many of the knights of the Round Table were killed and destroyed, more than half. And so three had come home, Ector, Gawain and Lionel, and many others that need not be listed. And all the court was exceedingly glad of Sir Lancelot, and the king asked him much news of his son Galahad. And there Lancelot told the king of the adventures that had befallen him since he departed. And he also told him of the adventures of Galahad, Percival and Bors, which he knew from the letter of the dead damsel, and as Galahad had told him.

"Now would to God," said the king, "that they were all three here."

"That shall never be," said Lancelot, "for two of them you shall never see again, but one of them shall come back."

Now we leave this story and speak of Galahad.

Chapter 18: How Galahad came to King Mordrains, and of other matters and adventures

Now, the story says, Galahad rode many days' journeys in vain. And at last he came to the abbey where King Mordrains was, and when he heard that, he thought he would stay to see him. And in the morning, when he had heard mass, Galahad came to King Mordrains, and at once the king saw him, who had lain blind for a long time. And then he turned towards him, and said, "Galahad, servant of Jesus Christ, whose coming I have waited for so long, now embrace me and let me rest on your breast, so that I may rest between your arms. For you are a pure virgin above all knights, like the flower of the lily, in which virginity is signified, and you are the rose, which is the flower of all good virtues, and in colour like fire. For the fire of the Holy Ghost has taken such hold in you that my flesh, which was all dead with old age, has become young again."

When Galahad heard his words, he embraced him, all his body. Then the king said, "Fair Lord Jesus Christ, now I have my wish. Now I ask You, at this point where I am, to come and visit me." And at once Our Lord heard his prayer: with that the soul departed from the body.

And then Galahad buried him as a king ought to be buried, and so departed, and so came into a perilous forest where he found the spring that boils with great waves, as the tale told before. And as soon as Galahad set his hand to it, it stopped, so that it burned no more, and the heat went away. For its burning was a sign of lechery, which was much practised at that time. But that heat could not withstand his pure virginity. And this was taken in that country for a miracle. And so ever after it was called Galahad's spring.

Then by chance he came into the country of Gore, and into the abbey where Lancelot had been before, and found the tomb of King Bagdemagus, but he was the founder of it, Joseph of Arimathea's son; and the tomb of Simeon, where Lancelot had failed. Then he looked into a vault under the church, and there he saw a tomb that burned most marvellously. Then he asked the brothers what it was.

"Sir," they said, "a marvellous adventure that can never be brought to an end except by him who surpasses in goodness and in knighthood all those of the Round Table."

"I wish," said Galahad, "that you would lead me to it."

"Gladly," they said, and so they led him to a cave. And he went down the steps, and came near the tomb. And then the flames died, and the fire stopped, which for many a day had been great. Then a voice came that said, "You owe great thanks to Our Lord, who has given you a good hour, so that you may draw souls out of earthly pain, and put them into the joys of paradise. I am of your kindred, and I have dwelt in this heat for three hundred and fifty-four years to be purged of the sin that I committed against Joseph of Arimathea."

Then Galahad took the body in his arms and carried it into the church. And that night Galahad lay in the abbey; and in the morning he had a service said for him, and buried him before the high altar.

Chapter 19: How Sir Percival and Sir Bors met Sir Galahad, and how they came to the castle of Carbonek, and other matters

So he departed from there, and commended the brothers to God; and so he rode for five days until he came to the Maimed King. And all those five days Percival followed him, asking where he had been; and so someone told him how the adventures of Logres had been achieved. So one day it happened that they came out of a great forest, and there they came across Sir Bors, who was riding alone. There is no need to tell whether they were glad; and he greeted them, and they wished him honour and good fortune, and each told the other his news.

Then Bors said, "For more than a year and a half I have not slept ten nights where men live, but only in wild forests and in mountains; but God was always my comfort."

Then they rode a long while until they came to the castle of Carbonek. And when they had entered the castle, King Pelles knew them; then there was great joy, for they knew well by their coming that they had fulfilled the quest of the Holy Grail. Then Eliazar, King Pelles' son, brought before them the broken sword with which Joseph was stabbed through the thigh. Then Bors set his hand to it, to see whether he could join it together again; but it would not be. Then he handed it to Percival, but he had no more power over it than Bors.

"Now you have it," said Percival to Galahad, "for if it is ever achieved by any man of flesh and blood, you must do it."

And then he took the pieces and set them together, and it seemed that they had never been broken, and it was as sound as when it was first forged. And when those in the castle saw that the adventure of the sword was achieved, they gave the sword to Bors, for it could not be better placed; for he was a good knight and a worthy man.

And a little before evening the sword rose up, great and marvellous, and was full of such great heat that many men fell down for fear. And at once a voice came down among them, and said, "Let those who ought not to sit at the table of Jesus Christ rise, for now true knights shall be fed."

So they went away from there, all except King Pelles and Eliazar his son, who were holy men, and a maid who was his niece; and so these three companions and those three were there, and no more. At once they saw knights come in at the hall door, all armed, and they took off their helmets and their armour, and said to Galahad, "Sir, we have hurried hard to be with you at this table, where the holy food shall be shared out."

Then he said, "You are welcome, but where are you from?"

So three of them said they were from Gaul, and another three said they were from Ireland, and the other three said they were from Denmark. And as they sat there, a wooden bed came out of a chamber, carried by four gentlewomen; and in the bed lay a good man, sick, with a crown of gold on his head; and there in the middle of the room they set him down, and went their way again. Then he lifted up his head, and said, "Galahad, knight, you are welcome, for I have greatly longed for your coming, for I have been a long time in such pain and in such anguish. But now I trust in God that the time has come when my pain shall be eased, so that I shall pass out of this world, as was promised me long ago."

With that a voice said, "There are two among you who are not in the quest of the Holy Grail, and therefore leave."

Chapter 20: How Galahad and his companions were fed by the Holy Grail, and how Our Lord appeared to them, and other things

Then King Pelles and his son departed. And with that it seemed to them that there came a man, and four angels from heaven, a man dressed like a bishop, with a cross in his hand; and these four angels carried him in a chair, and set him down before the table of silver on which the Holy Grail stood. And it seemed that he had letters in the middle of his forehead, which said: "See here Joseph, the first bishop of Christendom, the same whom Our Lord succoured in the city of Sarras in the spiritual place." Then the knights marvelled, for that bishop had been dead more than three hundred years before.

"O knights," he said, "do not marvel, for I was once an earthly man."

With that they heard the chamber door open, and there they saw angels; and two carried candles of wax, and the third a towel, and the fourth a spear which bled marvellously, so that three drops fell into a box which he held in his other hand. And they set the candles on the table, and the third set the towel on the vessel, and the fourth set the holy spear straight upright on the vessel. And then the bishop made as though he were going to the consecration of the mass. And then he took a wafer which was made in the likeness of bread. And at the lifting up there came a figure in the likeness of a child, and the face was as red and as bright as any fire, and he struck himself into the bread, so that they all saw that the bread was formed of a man of flesh; and then he put it into the Holy Vessel again, and then he did all that belonged to a priest to do at a mass. And then he went to Galahad and kissed him, and told him to go and kiss his companions: and so he did at once.

"Now," he said, "servants of Jesus Christ, you shall be fed before this table with sweet food that knights never tasted."

And when he had spoken, he vanished away. And they sat down at the table in great fear, and said their prayers.

Then they looked and saw a man come out of the Holy Vessel, who had all the signs of the Passion of Jesus Christ, bleeding openly, and he said, "My knights, and my servants, and my true children, who have come out of mortal life into spiritual life, I will no longer hide myself from you, but you shall now see a part of my secrets and of my hidden things. Now hold and receive the high food that you have so much desired."

Then he himself took the Holy Vessel and came to Galahad; and he knelt down, and there he received his Saviour, and after him all his companions received it; and they thought it so sweet that it was marvellous to tell. Then he said to Galahad, "Son, do you know what I hold between my hands?"

"No," said Galahad, "unless you will tell me."

"This is," he said, "the holy dish in which I ate the lamb on Maundy Thursday. And now you have seen what you most desired to see, but you have not yet seen it as openly as you shall see it in the city of Sarras in the spiritual place. Therefore you must go from here and carry this Holy Vessel with you; for this night it shall depart from the realm of Logres, so that it shall never be seen here again. And do you know why? Because he is not served nor worshipped as is his due by the people of this land, for they have turned to evil living; therefore I shall strip them of the honour that I have done them.
