And therefore you three go tomorrow to the sea, where you shall find your ship ready, and take with you the sword with the strange girdles, and no one more with you but Sir Percival and Sir Bors. Also I wish you to take with you some of the blood of this spear, to anoint the Maimed King, both his legs and all his body, and he shall have his health."

"Sir," said Galahad, "why shall these other companions not go with us?"

"For this reason: just as I sent my apostles apart, one here and another there, so I wish you to go apart; and two of you shall die in my service, but one of you shall come back and tell the news."

Then he gave them his blessing and vanished away.

Chapter 21: How Galahad anointed the Maimed King with the blood of the spear, and of other adventures

And Galahad went at once to the spear which lay on the table, and touched the blood with his fingers, and came afterwards to the Maimed King and anointed his legs.

And with that he dressed himself at once, and leapt to his feet out of his bed a whole man, and thanked Our Lord that He had healed him. And that was not for the world's sake, for he at once gave himself to a house of religion of white monks, and was a most holy man.

That same night, about midnight, a voice came among them which said, "My sons and not my chief sons, my friends and not my warriors, go from here to where you hope to do best, and as I told you."

"Ah, thanks be to You, Lord, that You deign to call us, Your sinners. Now we may well prove that we have not lost our labour."

And at once, in all haste, they took their armour and departed.

But as for the three knights of Gaul, one of them was called Claudine, King Claudas' son, and the other two were men of high birth. Then Galahad asked each of them, if they came to King Arthur's court, to "greet my lord Sir Lancelot, my father, and all the fellowship of the Round Table"; and he asked them, if they came to those parts, not to forget it.

Right so Galahad departed, and Percival and Bors with him; and so they rode three days, and then they came to a shore, and found the ship that the tale spoke of before. And when they came on board, they found in the middle of it the table of silver which they had left with the Maimed King, and the Holy Grail, which was covered with red samite.

Then they were glad to have such things in their company; and so they entered and made great reverence to it; and Galahad prayed a long time to Our Lord that, at whatever time he asked, he should pass out of this world.

He prayed so much that at last a voice said to him, "Galahad, you shall have your request; and when you ask for the death of your body you shall have it, and then you shall find the life of the soul."

Percival heard this, and begged him, by the fellowship that was between them, to tell him why he asked for such things.

"That I will tell you," said Galahad. "The other day, when we saw a part of the adventures of the Holy Grail, I was in such joy of heart that I believe no earthly man was ever so joyful. And therefore I know well that when my body is dead, my soul shall be in great joy, to see the blessed Trinity every day, and the majesty of Our Lord Jesus Christ."

They were in the ship so long that they said to Galahad, "Sir, you ought to lie in this bed, for so the inscription says." And so he lay down and slept a long while; and when he woke he looked before him and saw the city of Sarras. And as they were about to land, they saw the ship in which Percival had put his sister.

"Truly," said Percival, "in the name of God, my sister has kept her promise to us well."

Then they took the table of silver out of the ship, and Galahad gave it to Percival and to Bors to go in front, and Galahad came behind. And right so they went to the city, and at the gate of the city they saw a crooked old man. Then Galahad called him and told him to help carry this heavy thing.

"Truly," said the old man, "it is ten years since I could walk without crutches."

"Never mind that," said Galahad, "but get up and show your good will."

And so he tried, and found himself as whole as he ever was. Then he ran to the table, and took one end of it opposite Galahad. And at once a great stir arose in the city, that a cripple had been made whole by marvellous knights who had entered the city.

Then soon after, the three knights went to the water, and brought Percival's sister up into the palace, and buried her as richly as a king's daughter ought to be buried. And when the king of the city, who was called Estorause, saw the companions, he asked them where they were from, and what it was that they had brought on the table of silver. And they told him the truth of the Holy Grail, and the power which God had sent there. Then the king, who was a tyrant, and came of a line of pagans, took them and put them in prison in a deep pit.

Chapter 22: How they were fed by the Holy Grail while they were in prison, and how Galahad was made king

But as soon as they were there, Our Lord sent them the Holy Grail, by whose grace they were always filled while they were in prison.

So at the year's end it happened that this King Estorause lay sick, and felt that he would die. Then he sent for the three knights, and they came before him; and he begged their pardon for what he had done to them, and they forgave him graciously; and he died at once. When the king was dead, all the city was dismayed, and did not know who should be their king. Right as they were in council, a voice came among them, and told them to choose the youngest of those three knights to be their king: "For he shall maintain you and all yours well." So they made Galahad king with the full assent of the holy city, and otherwise they would have killed him. And when he had come to look over the land, he had a chest of gold and of precious stones made above the table of silver, which covered the Holy Vessel. And every day, early, the three companions would come before it and say their prayers.

Now at the year's end, on the very same day that Galahad had first worn the crown of gold, he rose early, and his companions with him, and came to the palace, and saw before them the Holy Vessel, and a man kneeling on his knees in the likeness of a bishop, who had about him a great fellowship of angels, as if it had been Jesus Christ himself; and then he rose and began a mass of Our Lady. And when he came to the sacrament of the mass, and had done, he at once called Galahad, and said to him, "Come forward, servant of Jesus Christ, and you shall see what you have so much desired to see."

And then Galahad began to tremble very hard, as his mortal flesh began to behold the spiritual things. Then he held up his hands towards heaven and said, "Lord, I thank You, for now I see what has been my desire for many a day. Now, blessed Lord, I would not live any longer, if it might please You, Lord."

And with that the good man took Our Lord's body between his hands, and offered it to Galahad, and he received it most gladly and meekly.

"Now do you know who I am?" said the good man.

"No," said Galahad.

"I am Joseph of Arimathea, whom Our Lord has sent here to you to keep you company. And do you know why He has sent me rather than any other? Because you have resembled me in two things: in that you have seen the marvels of the Holy Grail, and in that you have been a pure virgin, as I have been and am."

And when he had said these words, Galahad went to Percival and kissed him, and commended him to God; and so he went to Sir Bors and kissed him, and commended him to God, and said, "Fair lord, greet my lord Sir Lancelot, my father, for me, and as soon as you see him, tell him to remember this unstable world."

And with that he knelt down before the table and said his prayers, and then suddenly his soul departed to Jesus Christ, and a great multitude of angels carried his soul up to heaven, so that the two companions could plainly see it. The two companions also saw a hand come from heaven, but they did not see the body. And then it came straight to the Vessel, and took it and the spear, and so carried it up to heaven. Since then there was never any man so bold as to say that he had seen the Holy Grail.

Chapter 23: Of the sorrow Percival and Bors felt when Galahad was dead, and of how Percival died, and other matters

When Percival and Bors saw Galahad dead, they grieved as much as ever two men did. And if they had not been good men, they might easily have fallen into despair. And the people of the country and of the city were deeply downcast. And then he was buried; and as soon as he was buried, Sir Percival gave himself to a hermitage outside the city, and took the habit of religion. And Bors was always with him, but he never changed out of his secular clothes, because he intended to go back to the realm of Logres. So Sir Percival lived a year and two months in the hermitage, a most holy life, and then passed out of this world; and Bors had him buried beside his sister and beside Galahad in the spiritual place.

When Bors saw that he was in countries as far away as the parts of Babylon, he departed from Sarras, and armed himself and came to the sea, and went on board a ship; and so by good fortune he came into the realm of Logres; and he rode so fast that he came to Camelot, where the king was. And then great joy was made of him in the court, for they had all thought he was dead, since he had been out of the country so long. And when they had eaten, the king had great scholars come before him, so that they could write a chronicle of the high adventures of the good knights. When Bors had told him of the adventures of the Holy Grail, such as had befallen him and his three companions, that is, Lancelot, Percival, Galahad and himself, then Lancelot told the adventures of the Holy Grail that he had seen. All this was written in great books, and stored away in chests at Salisbury.

And at once Sir Bors said to Sir Lancelot, "Galahad, your own son, sent you his greetings by me, and after you King Arthur and all the court, and so did Sir Percival; for I buried them with my own hands in the city of Sarras. Also, Sir Lancelot, Galahad begged you to remember this unstable world, as you promised him when you were together for more than half a year."

"This is true," said Lancelot. "Now I trust to God that his prayer shall help me."

Then Lancelot took Sir Bors in his arms, and said, "Noble cousin, you are most welcome to me, and in all that I can ever do for you and for yours, you shall find my poor body ready at all times, while the spirit is in it; and that I promise you faithfully, and never to fail. And believe me, noble cousin, Sir Bors, you and I will never part from each other while our lives last."

"Sir," he said, "I will do as you will."

Thus ends the history of the Holy Grail, which was briefly drawn out of French into English, and which is a story chronicled as one of the truest and the holiest that is in this world, and which is the seventeenth book.

And here follows the eighteenth book.

Book Eighteen: Sir Lancelot and the Queen

Chapter 1: Of the joy King Arthur and the queen had at the achieving of the Holy Grail, and how Lancelot fell back into his old love

So after the quest of the Holy Grail was fulfilled, and all the knights who were left alive had come back to the Round Table, as the book of the Holy Grail tells, then there was great joy in the court. And above all King Arthur and Queen Guinevere rejoiced greatly over the remnant who had come home, and the king and the queen were exceedingly glad of Sir Lancelot and of Sir Bors, for they had been away an exceedingly long time on the quest of the Holy Grail.

Then, as the book says, Sir Lancelot began to go to Queen Guinevere again, and forgot the promise and the perfection that he had made on the quest. For, as the book says, if Sir Lancelot had not been so set inwardly on the queen, in his private thoughts and in his mind, as he seemed outwardly to be set on God, no knight would have surpassed him in the quest of the Holy Grail. But his thoughts were always secretly on the queen, and so they loved each other more hotly than they had done before, and had so many secret meetings together that many in the court spoke of it, and above all Sir Agravain, Sir Gawain's brother, for he was always loose-tongued.

So it happened that Sir Lancelot had many ladies and damsels coming to him daily, begging him to be their champion, and in all such matters of right Sir Lancelot applied himself daily to do the work for the pleasure of Our Lord Jesus Christ. And as much as ever he could he kept himself away from the company and fellowship of Queen Guinevere, to avoid scandal and rumour; and because of that the queen grew angry with Sir Lancelot. And one day she called Sir Lancelot to her chamber, and said this: "Sir Lancelot, I see and feel every day that your love is beginning to cool, for you take no joy in being in my presence, but you are always away from this court, and you take up quarrels and causes for ladies and gentlewomen nowadays more than you ever used to before."

"Ah, madam," said Lancelot, "in this you must hold me excused, for several reasons. One is that I have only lately come from the quest of the Holy Grail; and I thank God for His great mercy, and never for my own deserving, that on that quest of mine I saw as much as any sinful man ever saw, and so I was told. And if I had not had my private thoughts of returning to your love again, as I do, I would have seen as great mysteries as ever my son Galahad saw, or Percival, or Sir Bors; and so, madam, I have only lately come from that quest. Believe me, madam, the high service in which I did my diligent labour cannot yet be lightly forgotten. Also, madam, believe me, there are many men who speak of our love in this court, and watch you and me closely, such as Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred. And madam, believe me, I fear them more for your sake than for any fear I have of them for myself, for I may manage to escape and get myself clear in a great need, where you must stay and bear everything that will be said to you. And then if you fall into any distress through wilful folly, there is no other remedy or help but through me and my kin. And believe me, madam, the boldness of you and me will bring us to great shame and scandal, and I would be loath to see you dishonoured. And that is the reason I take it upon myself to do more for damsels and maidens than I ever did before: so that men should understand that my joy and my delight and my pleasure is to fight for damsels and maidens."

Chapter 2: How the queen commanded Sir Lancelot to leave the court, and of the sorrow Lancelot felt

All this while the queen stood still and let Sir Lancelot say what he wished. And when he had said it all she burst into tears, and so she sobbed and wept a long while. And when she could speak she said, "Lancelot, now I understand very well that you are a false, faithless knight and a common lecher, and that you love and keep other ladies, and have nothing but disdain and scorn for me. For believe me," she said, "now I understand your falseness, and so I shall never love you again. And don't you ever dare come into my sight. And here and now I banish you from this court, so that you never come within it; and I forbid you my company, and on pain of your head, see me no more."

At that Sir Lancelot left in great heaviness of heart, so that he could scarcely hold himself up for the grief he made.

Then he called Sir Bors, Sir Ector de Maris and Sir Lionel, and told them how the queen had forbidden him the court, and so he meant to go away into his own country.

"Fair sir," said Sir Bors de Ganis, "you shall not leave this land, if you take my advice. You must remember in what honour you are renowned, and called the noblest knight in the world; and you have many great matters in hand. And women in their haste will often do what they bitterly regret. And so, by my advice, you shall take your horse and ride to the good hermit near here beside Windsor, who was once a good knight, his name is Sir Brasias, and there you shall stay until I send you word of better news."

"Brother," said Sir Lancelot, "believe me, I am very loath to leave this realm, but the queen has forbidden me so sternly that it seems to me she will never be my good lady again as she has been."

"Never say so," said Sir Bors, "for many times before this she has been angry with you, and afterwards she was the first to regret it."

"You speak well," said Lancelot, "for now I will do as you advise, and take my horse and my armour, and ride to the hermit Sir Brasias, and there I will rest until I hear some kind of news from you. But, fair brother, I beg you, win me back the love of my lady Queen Guinevere, if you can."

"Sir," said Sir Bors, "you need not urge me in such matters, for you know well I will do what I can to please you."

And then the noble knight Sir Lancelot left suddenly, with a very heavy heart, so that no living creature knew of him, or where he had gone, except Sir Bors. So when Sir Lancelot had gone, the queen outwardly showed no sort of sorrow to any of his kin or to anyone else. But believe me, inwardly, as the book says, she grieved deeply; but she carried it off with a proud face, as though she felt nothing and feared nothing.

Chapter 3: How at a dinner the queen gave a knight was poisoned, and Sir Mador laid the blame on the queen

And then the queen had a private dinner made in London for the knights of the Round Table. And it was all to show outwardly that she took as great joy in all the other knights of the Round Table as she did in Sir Lancelot. At that dinner she had only Sir Gawain and his brothers, that is to say Sir Agravain, Sir Gaheris, Sir Gareth and Sir Mordred. Also there were Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Blamore de Ganis, Sir Bleoberis de Ganis, Sir Galihud, Sir Galihodin, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Lionel, Sir Palomides, Safere his brother, Sir La Cote Male Taile, Sir Persant, Sir Ironside, Sir Brandiles, Sir Kay the Seneschal, Sir Mador de la Porte, Sir Patrise, a knight of Ireland, Aliduk, Sir Astamore, and Sir Pinel le Savage, who was cousin to Sir Lamorak de Galis, the good knight whom Sir Gawain and his brothers killed by treachery. And so these twenty-four knights were to dine with the queen in a private place by themselves, and a great feast was made of all kinds of delicacies.

But Sir Gawain had a custom that he kept daily at dinner and at supper: he loved all kinds of fruit, and above all apples and pears. And so whoever dined or feasted Sir Gawain would usually provide good fruit for him, and so did the queen, to please Sir Gawain; she had all kinds of fruit provided for him, for Sir Gawain was an exceedingly hot-blooded knight by nature. And this Pinel hated Sir Gawain because of his kinsman Sir Lamorak de Galis; and so, out of pure envy and hate, Sir Pinel poisoned certain apples, to poison Sir Gawain. And so all went well until the end of the meal; and then by misfortune it happened that a good knight named Patrise, cousin to Sir Mador de la Porte, took a poisoned apple. And when he had eaten it he swelled up until he burst, and there Sir Patrise fell down suddenly dead among them.

Then every knight leapt up from the table, ashamed and raging with anger, nearly out of their wits. For they did not know what to say; seeing that Queen Guinevere had made the feast and dinner, they all had suspicion of her.

"My lady the queen," said Gawain, "believe me, madam, this dinner was made for me, for everyone who knows my habits knows that I love fruit, and now I see well that I came near to being killed. And so, madam, I fear you will be put to shame."

Then the queen stood still and was so badly dismayed that she did not know what to say.

"This shall not end like this," said Sir Mador de la Porte, "for here I have lost a very noble knight of my blood; and so for this shame and insult I will be avenged to the uttermost."

And there, openly, Sir Mador accused the queen of the death of his cousin Sir Patrise. Then they all stood still, so that no one would say a word against him, for they all had great suspicion of the queen, because she had had that dinner made. And the queen was so dismayed that she could do nothing else but weep so bitterly that she fell in a faint. At this noise and outcry King Arthur came to them, and when he learned of that trouble he was an exceedingly sorrowful man.

Chapter 4: How Sir Mador accused the queen of treason, and at first no knight would fight for her

And all the while Sir Mador stood still before the king, and all the while he accused the queen of treason; for the custom at that time was that every kind of shameful killing was called treason.

"Fair lords," said King Arthur, "I am sorry for this trouble, but the case is such that I may not take part in this matter, for I must be a rightful judge; and I am sorry that I may not do battle for my wife, for as I judge it this deed never came from her. And so I suppose she shall not be wholly dishonoured, but that some good knight will put his body in danger for my queen rather than see her burned in a wrongful cause. And so, Sir Mador, do not be so hasty, for it may be that she will not be entirely without friends. And so ask for your day of battle, and she shall provide herself with some good knight who will answer you, or else it would be a great shame to me and to all my court."

"My gracious lord," said Sir Mador, "you must hold me excused, for though you are our king in that rank, you are only a knight as we are, and you are sworn to knighthood just as we are. And so I beg you not to be displeased, for there is not one of the twenty-four knights who were invited to this dinner who does not have great suspicion of the queen. What do you all say, my lords?" said Sir Mador.

Then they answered at once that they could not clear the queen; for she had made the dinner, and either it must have come from her or from her servants.

"Alas," said the queen, "I made this dinner with good intent, and never for any evil, so help me Almighty God in my right, for I never intended to do such evil deeds; and I appeal to God on that."

"My lord the king," said Sir Mador, "I ask you, as you are a righteous king, to give me a day on which I may have justice."

"Well," said the king, "I set the day fifteen days from today, when you are to be ready, armed, on horseback, in the meadow beside Westminster. And if it happens that there is any knight to meet you, then do your best, and God defend the right. And if it happens that there is no knight on that day, then my queen must be burned, and she shall be there, ready to receive her judgement."

"I am answered," said Sir Mador.

And every knight went where he pleased.

So when the king and the queen were together the king asked the queen how this had come about.

The queen answered, "So help me God, I do not know how, or in what way."

"Where is Sir Lancelot?" said King Arthur. "If he were here he would not hesitate to do battle for you."

"Sir," said the queen, "I do not know where he is, but his brother and his kinsmen think that he is not in this realm."

"I am sorry for that," said King Arthur, "for if he were here he would soon stop this strife. Then I will advise you," said the king, "to go to Sir Bors and ask him to do battle for you for Sir Lancelot's sake, and on my life he will not refuse you. For I see well," said the king, "that none of these twenty-four knights who were with you at your dinner, where Sir Patrise was killed, will do battle for you, and not one of them will speak well of you, and that will be a great scandal for you in this court."

"Alas," said the queen, "I cannot help it, but now I miss Sir Lancelot, for if he were here he would soon set my heart at ease."

"What is the matter with you," said the king, "that you cannot keep Sir Lancelot on your side? For believe me," said the king, "whoever has Sir Lancelot on his side has the man of greatest honour in the world on his side. Now go your way," said the king to the queen, "and ask Sir Bors to do battle for you for Sir Lancelot's sake."

Chapter 5: How the queen asked Sir Bors to fight for her, and how he agreed on a condition, and how he warned Sir Lancelot of it

So the queen left the king, and sent for Sir Bors to come to her chamber. And when he had come she begged him for help.

"Madam," he said, "what would you have me do? For I may not, with my honour, take part in this matter, because I was at the same dinner, for fear that any of those knights would suspect me. Also, madam," said Sir Bors, "now you miss Sir Lancelot, for he would not have failed you either in right or in wrong, as you have well proved when you have been in danger; and now you have driven him out of this country, the man by whom you and all of us were daily honoured. And so, madam, I marvel how you dare for shame ask me to do anything for you, seeing that you have chased him out of your country, the man by whom we were upheld and honoured."

"Alas, fair knight," said the queen, "I put myself wholly in your grace, and all that has been done amiss I will put right as you advise me."

And with that she knelt down on both her knees, and begged Sir Bors to have mercy on her: "Or else I shall have a shameful death, and I never did anything to deserve it."

Just then King Arthur came, and found the queen kneeling before Sir Bors. Then Sir Bors pulled her up, and said, "Madam, you do me great dishonour."

"Ah, noble knight," said the king, "have mercy on my queen, courteous knight, for I am now certain that she is falsely accused. And so, courteous knight," said the king, "promise her to do battle for her, I beg you, for the love of Sir Lancelot."

"My lord," said Sir Bors, "you ask of me the greatest thing that any man could ask of me; and believe me, if I agree to do battle for the queen I shall anger many of my fellowship of the Round Table. But as for that," said Bors, "I will grant it, my lord: for my lord Sir Lancelot's sake, and for your sake, I will be the queen's champion on that day, unless by chance a better knight than I am comes to do battle for her."

"Will you promise me this," said the king, "on your faith?"

"Yes, sir," said Sir Bors, "in that I will not fail you, nor her either, unless a better knight than I am comes, and then he shall have the battle."

Then the king and the queen were exceedingly glad, and so they left, and thanked him heartily.

So then Sir Bors set off secretly one day, and rode to Sir Lancelot where he was with the hermit Sir Brasias, and told him all that had happened.

"Ah, Jesus," said Sir Lancelot, "this has turned out happily, just as I would have it. And so I beg you, make yourself ready to do battle, but see that you wait until you see me come, as long as you can. For I am sure Mador is a hot-tempered knight when he is inflamed, for the longer you hold him off the hastier he will be for the battle."

"Sir," said Bors, "leave him to me. Don't doubt it, you shall have all your will."

Then Sir Bors left him and came back to the court. Then it was rumoured all over the court that Sir Bors was to do battle for the queen; and because of that many knights were displeased with him, that he would take it on himself to do battle in the queen's cause; for there were only a few knights in all the court who did not think the queen was in the wrong, and that she had committed that treason.

So Sir Bors answered his fellows of the Round Table like this: "Believe me, my fair lords, it would be a shame to us all if we stood by and saw the most noble queen in the world shamed openly, considering that her lord and our lord is the man of greatest honour in the world, and the most Christian, and he has always honoured us all in all places."

Many answered him back: "As for our most noble King Arthur, we love him and honour him as well as you do, but as for Queen Guinevere, we do not love her, because she is a destroyer of good knights."

"Fair lords," said Sir Bors, "it seems to me you do not speak as you should. For never yet in all my days have I known, or heard it said, that she was ever a destroyer of any good knight. But at all times, as far as ever I could tell, she was an upholder of good knights; and she has always been generous and open-handed with her goods to all good knights, and the most bountiful lady with her gifts and her good grace that I ever saw or heard tell of. And so it would be a shame," said Sir Bors, "to all of us, toward our most noble king's wife, if we allowed her to be shamefully put to death. And believe me," said Sir Bors, "I will not allow it, for I dare say this much: the queen is not guilty of Sir Patrise's death, for she never bore him any ill will, nor any of the twenty-four knights who were at that dinner. For I dare say she invited us to dinner out of good love, and not out of any evil design, and I have no doubt that will be proved hereafter; for however the game goes, there was treason among us."

Then some said to Sir Bors, "We can well believe what you say."

And so some of them were well pleased, and some were not.

Chapter 6: How on the day Sir Bors made ready to fight for the queen, and how, as he was about to fight, another knight took his place

The day came on fast, until it was the evening before the battle was to be. Then the queen sent for Sir Bors and asked him what he intended.

"Truly, madam," he said, "I intend just what I promised you, that is to say, I shall not fail you, unless by chance a better knight than I am comes to do battle for you; then, madam, I am released from my promise."

"Do you wish," said the queen, "that I tell my lord Arthur this?"

"Do as you please, madam."

Then the queen went to the king and told him Sir Bors's answer.

"Have no doubt about Sir Bors," said the king, "for I call him now one of the best knights in the world, and the most dependable man."

And so things went on until the morning, and the king and the queen and all the knights who were there at that time made their way to the meadow beside Westminster where the battle was to be. And so when the king had come with the queen and many knights of the Round Table, then the queen was put there in the Constable's custody, and a great fire was made around an iron stake, so that if Sir Mador de la Porte had the better of it, she would be burned. Such was the custom in those days: that neither for favour, nor for love, nor for kinship, should there be anything but righteous judgement, as much upon a king as upon a knight, and as much upon a queen as upon any other poor lady.

So in the meantime Sir Mador de la Porte came in, and swore his oath before the king that the queen had done this treason to his cousin Sir Patrise, and that he would prove his oath with his body, hand to hand, against anyone who said the contrary.

Just then Sir Bors de Ganis came in, and said that as for Queen Guinevere, she was in the right, "and I will make it good with my hands that she is not guilty of this treason that is laid on her."

"Then get ready," said Sir Mador, "and we shall prove whether you are in the right or I am."

"Sir Mador," said Sir Bors, "believe me, I know you for a good knight. Nevertheless I shall not fear you so greatly, but I trust to God I shall be able to withstand your malice. But this much I have promised my lord Arthur and my lady the queen: that I shall do battle for her in this cause to the uttermost, unless a better knight than I am comes and releases me."

"Is that all?" said Sir Mador. "Either come out and do battle with me, or else say no."

"Take your horse," said Sir Bors, "and, as I suppose, you shall not wait long before you are answered."

Then each of them went to his tent and made ready for horseback as he thought best. And at once Sir Mador came into the field with his shield on his shoulder and his spear in his hand; and so he rode around the place, calling out to Arthur, "Tell your champion to come out, if he dares."

Then Sir Bors was ashamed, and took his horse and came to the end of the lists. And then he saw, coming from a wood close by, a knight all armed, on a white horse, with a strange shield bearing strange arms. And he came riding as fast as his horse could run, and so he came to Sir Bors, and said this: "Fair knight, I beg you not to be displeased, for here a better knight than you must have this battle; and so I beg you to withdraw. For believe me, I have made a very long journey today, and this battle ought to be mine, and so I promised you when I last spoke with you; and with all my heart I thank you for your good will."

Then Sir Bors rode to King Arthur and told him how a knight had come who wanted to have the battle, to fight for the queen.

"What knight is he?" said the king.

"I do not know," said Sir Bors, "but he made an agreement with me to be here this day. Now, my lord," said Sir Bors, "here I am released."

Chapter 7: How Sir Lancelot fought against Sir Mador for the queen, and how he overcame Sir Mador and cleared the queen

Then the king called to that knight, and asked him if he would fight for the queen.

Then he answered the king, "That is why I came here. And so, sir king," he said, "do not delay me any longer, for I may not stay. For as soon as I have finished this battle I must leave here, for I have many matters to deal with elsewhere. For believe me," said that knight, "it is a dishonour to all you knights of the Round Table, to see and know so noble a lady and so courteous a queen as Queen Guinevere is, rebuked and shamed like this among you."

Then they all marvelled what knight that might be who took the battle on himself like that. For there was not one who knew him, unless it was Sir Bors.

Then Sir Mador de la Porte said to the king, "Now let me know who it is I am to fight with."

And then they rode to the ends of the lists, and there they levelled their spears, and ran together with all their might. And Sir Mador's spear broke all to pieces, but the other's spear held, and bore Sir Mador's horse and all over backward to the earth, a great fall. But strongly and swiftly he got clear of his horse and put his shield before him, and then drew his sword, and told the other knight to dismount and do battle with him on foot. Then that knight got down from his horse nimbly, like a valiant man, and put his shield before him and drew his sword. And so they came eagerly to battle, and each gave the other many great strokes, circling and sidestepping, slashing and thrusting, and crashing together with their swords as if they were wild boars. So they fought for nearly an hour, for this Sir Mador was a strong knight, and well proved in many hard battles. But at last this knight struck Sir Mador face down upon the earth, and the knight stepped close to him to have pulled Sir Mador flat on the ground; and with that Sir Mador suddenly got up, and as he rose he struck that knight through the thick of the thighs, so that the blood ran out fiercely. And when the knight felt himself so wounded, and saw his blood, he let him get up on his feet. And then he gave him such a blow on the helm that he fell flat to the earth, and with that he strode to him to pull his helm off his head. And then Sir Mador begged that knight to spare his life, and so he yielded himself as beaten, and released the queen from his accusation.

"I will not grant you your life," said that knight, "except on condition that you freely release the queen for ever, and that no mention be made upon Sir Patrise's tomb that Queen Guinevere ever consented to that treason."

"All this shall be done," said Sir Mador. "I give up my accusation entirely, for ever."

Then the knights who were the marshals of the lists took up Sir Mador and led him to his tent, and the other knight went straight to the foot of the stairs where King Arthur sat. And by that time the queen had come to the king, and they kissed each other heartily. And when the king saw that knight, he stooped down to him and thanked him, and so did the queen; and the king begged him to take off his helmet, and to rest, and to take some bread soaked in wine. And then he took off his helm to drink, and then every knight knew that it was Sir Lancelot du Lake. As soon as the king knew that, he took the queen by the hand, and went to Sir Lancelot, and said, "Sir, many thanks for the great labour you have had this day for me and for my queen."

"My lord," said Sir Lancelot, "believe me, by right I ought always to do battle in your cause, and in my lady the queen's cause. For you are the man who gave me the high order of knighthood, and that day my lady your queen did me great honour, or else I would have been shamed. For that same day that you made me a knight, through my haste I lost my sword, and my lady your queen found it, and wrapped it in her train, and gave me my sword when I needed it; or else I would have been shamed among all knights. And so, my lord Arthur, I promised her that day to be her knight for ever, in right or in wrong."

"Many thanks," said the king, "for this day's work. And believe me," said the king, "I shall repay your goodness."

And all the while the queen gazed at Sir Lancelot, and wept so tenderly that she almost sank to the ground, for sorrow that he had done her such great goodness when she had shown him great unkindness. Then the knights of his kin gathered around him, and there they all rejoiced greatly over one another. And so all the knights of the Round Table who were there at that time came and welcomed him. And then Sir Mador was taken to be cared for by the doctors, and Sir Lancelot was healed of his wound. And then there was great joy and merriment in that court.

Chapter 8: How the truth was made known by the Damsel of the Lake, and of several other matters

And so it happened that the Damsel of the Lake, whose name was Nimue, who had married the good knight Sir Pelleas, came to the court; for she always did great good to King Arthur and to all his knights through her sorcery and enchantments. And so when she heard how the queen was in trouble over the death of Sir Patrise, then she said openly that the queen was never guilty; and there she revealed by whom it was done, and named him, Sir Pinel; and why he did it was openly revealed there too. And so the queen was cleared, and the knight Pinel fled into his own country. Then it was openly known that Sir Pinel had poisoned the apples at the feast with the intention of killing Sir Gawain, because Sir Gawain and his brothers had killed Sir Lamorak de Galis, to whom Sir Pinel was cousin. Then Sir Patrise was buried in a tomb in the church of Westminster, and on it was written: "Here lies Sir Patrise of Ireland, killed by Sir Pinel le Savage, who poisoned apples to kill Sir Gawain; and by misfortune Sir Patrise ate one of those apples, and then suddenly he burst." Also it was written upon the tomb that Queen Guinevere was accused of treason over the death of Sir Patrise by Sir Mador de la Porte; and an account was given there of how Sir Lancelot fought with him for Queen Guinevere, and overcame him in open battle. All this was written upon the tomb of Sir Patrise to clear the queen. And then Sir Mador sued daily and for a long time to have the queen's good grace; and so, through Sir Lancelot, he was brought back into the queen's good grace, and all was forgiven.

So things went on until the feast of Our Lady's Assumption. Within fifteen days of that feast the king had a great jousting and a tournament proclaimed, to be held on that day at Camelot, that is, Winchester; and the king had it proclaimed that he and the King of Scots would joust against all who would come against them. And when this proclamation was made, many knights came there. So there came the King of North Wales, and King Anguish of Ireland, and the King with the Hundred Knights, and Galahalt, the high prince, and the King of Northumberland, and many other noble dukes and earls of various countries. So King Arthur made ready to leave for these jousts, and would have had the queen with him, but at that time she would not go, she said, for she was sick and could not ride at that time.

"I am sorry for that," said the king, "for in these seven years you have not seen such a noble company together, except at Whitsun when Galahad left the court."

"Truly," said the queen to the king, "you must hold me excused. I cannot be there, and I am sorry for it."

And many thought the queen would not be there because of Sir Lancelot du Lake; for Sir Lancelot would not ride with the king, for he said that he was not healed of the wound that Sir Mador had given him. Because of that the king was downcast and exceedingly angry. And so he set off toward Winchester with his company; and so on the way the king lodged in a town called Astolat, which in English is now called Guildford, and there the king stayed in the castle.

So when the king had gone, the queen called Sir Lancelot to her, and said this: "Sir Lancelot, you are greatly to blame for staying behind my lord like this. What do you suppose your enemies and mine will say and think? Nothing else but, 'See how Sir Lancelot always stays behind the king, and so does the queen, so that they can have their pleasure together.' And that is what they will say," said the queen to Sir Lancelot, "have no doubt of it."

Chapter 9: How Sir Lancelot rode to Astolat, and took a sleeve to wear on his helmet at a maiden's request

"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "I praise your good sense; it has come to you only lately that you are so wise. And therefore, madam, this time I will be ruled by your advice, and tonight I will take my rest, and tomorrow early I will take my way toward Winchester. But you may be sure," said Sir Lancelot to the queen, "that at those jousts I will be against the king, and against all his fellowship."

"You may do there as you please," said the queen, "but by my advice you will not be against your king and your fellowship. For among them are very many hardy knights of your own blood, as you know well enough; there is no need to name them over."

"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "I beg you not to be displeased with me, for I will take whatever chance God sends me."

And so early the next morning Sir Lancelot heard mass and broke his fast, and so took his leave of the queen and departed. And then he rode on and on until he came to Astolat, that is Guildford; and there it happened that in the evening he came to the house of an old baron who was called Sir Bernard of Astolat. And as Sir Lancelot went into his lodging, King Arthur saw him as he was walking in a garden beside the castle, saw how he took his lodging, and knew him very well.

"Well, now," said King Arthur to the knights who were with him in that garden beside the castle, "I have just seen a knight who will play his part at the jousts we are going to. I promise you he will do marvels."

"Who is that? Tell us, we beg you," said many knights who were there at that time.

"You won't learn it from me," said the king, "not at this time."

And so the king smiled, and went to his lodging.

So when Sir Lancelot was in his lodging, and had taken off his armour in his chamber, the old baron came to him, bowing respectfully, and welcomed him in the best manner; but the old knight did not know Sir Lancelot.

"Fair sir," said Sir Lancelot to his host, "I would ask you to lend me a shield that is not commonly known, for mine is well known."

"Sir," said his host, "you shall have your wish, for it seems to me you are one of the likeliest knights in the world, and therefore I will show you friendship. Sir, you may be sure I have two sons who were made knights only lately, and the elder is called Sir Tirre, and he was hurt the very day he was made a knight, so that he cannot ride; and you shall have his shield, for that is not known, I dare say, anywhere but here. And my younger son is called Lavaine, and if it pleases you, he shall ride with you to those jousts; and he is strong and vigorous for his age. For my heart tells me strongly that you must be a noble knight, and therefore I beg you, tell me your name," said Sir Bernard.

"As for that," said Sir Lancelot, "you must hold me excused for now; and if God gives me grace to do well at the jousts, I will come back and tell you. But I beg you," said Sir Lancelot, "by all means let me have your son, Sir Lavaine, with me, and let me have his brother's shield."

"All this shall be done," said Sir Bernard.

This old baron had a daughter who in those days was called the Fair Maiden of Astolat. And all the while she gazed at Sir Lancelot in wonder; and as the book says, she set such a love upon Sir Lancelot that she could never take her love back, and of it she died; and her name was Elaine le Blank. So as she came and went she was so hot in her love that she begged Sir Lancelot to wear a token of hers at the jousts.

"Fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "if I grant you that, you may say I do more for love of you than I ever did for lady or damsel."

Then he remembered that he meant to go to the jousts in disguise. And because he had never before that time worn any kind of token of any damsel, he thought that he would wear one of hers, so that none of his own blood would know him by it; and then he said, "Fair maiden, I will grant you that, to wear a token of yours on my helmet; and so whatever it is, show it to me."

"Sir," she said, "it is a red sleeve of mine, of scarlet, finely embroidered with great pearls." And so she brought it to him.

So Sir Lancelot took it, and said, "Never before did I do so much for any damsel."

And then Sir Lancelot gave his shield into the fair maiden's keeping, and asked her to keep it until he came back; and so that night he had a merry rest and a warm welcome, for the damsel Elaine was always about Sir Lancelot for as long as she was allowed to be.

Chapter 10: How the tournament began at Winchester, and what knights were at the jousts, and other things

So one day, in the morning, King Arthur and all his knights departed, for their king had waited there three days for his noble knights. And so when the king had ridden off, Sir Lancelot and Sir Lavaine made themselves ready to ride, and each of them had a white shield, and Sir Lancelot had the red sleeve carried with him. And so they took their leave of Sir Bernard, the old baron, and of his daughter, the Fair Maiden of Astolat. And then they rode on until they came to Camelot, which at that time was called Winchester; and there was a great crowd of kings, dukes, earls and barons, and many noble knights. But there Sir Lancelot was lodged in secret, through Sir Lavaine's arranging, with a rich townsman, so that no one in that town knew who they were. And so they rested there until Our Lady's Day of the Assumption, when the great feast was to be held. So then the trumpets blew to call them to the field, and King Arthur was seated high up on a stand to watch who did best. But as the French book says, the king would not allow Sir Gawain to leave his side, for Sir Gawain never got the better of things if Sir Lancelot was in the field; and many times Sir Gawain had been put to shame when Lancelot came into any jousts in disguise.

Then some of the kings, such as King Anguish of Ireland and the King of Scots, had at that time come over to King Arthur's side. And then on the other side were the King of North Wales, and the King with the Hundred Knights, and the King of Northumberland, and Sir Galahalt, the high prince. But these three kings and this duke were far too weak to hold out against King Arthur's side, for with him were the noblest knights in the world. So then each side drew back from the other, and every man made himself ready in his best manner to do what he could.

Then Sir Lancelot made himself ready, and put the red sleeve on his head, and fastened it tight; and so Sir Lancelot and Sir Lavaine left Winchester in secret, and rode to a little leafy wood behind the side that held against King Arthur's side, and there they kept still until the two sides crashed together. And then the King of Scots and the King of Ireland came in on Arthur's side, and against them came the King of Northumberland; and the King with the Hundred Knights struck down the King of Northumberland, and the King with the Hundred Knights struck down King Anguish of Ireland. Then Sir Palomides, who was on Arthur's side, met Sir Galahalt, and each of them struck the other down, and each side helped its lords back on horseback. So a hard attack began on both sides. And then in came Sir Brandiles, Sir Sagramore le Desirous, Sir Dodinas le Savage, Sir Kay the Seneschal, Sir Griflet le Fise de Dieu, Sir Mordred, Sir Meliot de Logres, Sir Ozanna le Cure Hardy, Sir Safere, Sir Epinogris and Sir Galleron of Galway. All these fifteen knights were knights of the Round Table. So these, with others besides, came in together, and beat back the King of Northumberland and the King of North Wales. When Sir Lancelot saw this, as he waited in the little leafy wood, he said to Sir Lavaine, "Look over there, at that company of good knights; they hold together like boars that are worried by dogs."

"That is true," said Sir Lavaine.

Chapter 11: How Sir Lancelot and Sir Lavaine entered the field against the knights of King Arthur's court, and how Lancelot was wounded

"Now," said Sir Lancelot, "if you will help me a little, you shall see that company over there, which is now chasing these men on our side, go back as fast as they came forward."

"Sir, don't hold back," said Sir Lavaine, "for I will do what I can."

Then Sir Lancelot and Sir Lavaine came in at the thickest of the fighting, and there Sir Lancelot struck down Sir Brandiles, Sir Sagramore, Sir Dodinas, Sir Kay and Sir Griflet, and all this he did with one spear; and Sir Lavaine struck down Sir Lucan the butler and Sir Bedivere. And then Sir Lancelot got another spear, and there he struck down Sir Agravain, Sir Gaheris, and Sir Mordred, and Sir Meliot de Logres; and Sir Lavaine struck down Ozanna le Cure Hardy. And then Sir Lancelot drew his sword, and there he struck on the right hand and on the left, and by great force he unhorsed Sir Safere, Sir Epinogris and Sir Galleron; and then the knights of the Round Table drew back, after they had got their horses again as best they could.

"Oh, Jesus have mercy," said Sir Gawain, "what knight is that over there, who does such marvellous deeds of arms in that field?"

"I know well who he is," said King Arthur, "but at this time I will not name him."

"Sir," said Sir Gawain, "I would say it was Sir Lancelot, by his riding and by the blows I see him deal, but still it seems to me it cannot be he, because he wears the red sleeve on his head; for I never knew him wear a token at any jousts, of lady or gentlewoman."

"Let him be," said King Arthur. "He will be better known, and do more, before he leaves."

Then the side that was against King Arthur took heart, and then those who before had been badly beaten held together. Then Sir Bors, Sir Ector de Maris and Sir Lionel called to them the knights of their blood, such as Sir Blamore de Ganis, Sir Bleoberis, Sir Aliduke, Sir Galihud, Sir Galihodin and Sir Bellangere le Beuse. So these nine knights of Sir Lancelot's kin thrust in mightily, for they were all noble knights; and out of the great hatred and resentment they had toward him, they meant to put that noble knight Sir Lancelot to shame, and Sir Lavaine too, for they did not know them; and so they came crashing in together, and struck down many knights of North Wales and of Northumberland. And when Sir Lancelot saw them doing so, he got a spear in his hand; and there Sir Bors, Sir Ector and Sir Lionel all met him at once, and all three of them struck him at once with their spears. And with the force of themselves they struck Sir Lancelot's horse to the ground; and by misfortune Sir Bors struck Sir Lancelot through the shield into the side, and the spear broke, and the head was left in his side.

When Sir Lavaine saw his master lying on the ground, he ran at the King of Scots and struck him to the ground; and by great force he took his horse, and brought it to Sir Lancelot, and in spite of them all he got him to mount that horse. And then Lancelot got a spear in his hand, and there he struck Sir Bors, horse and man, to the ground. In the same way he served Sir Ector and Sir Lionel; and Sir Lavaine struck down Sir Blamore de Ganis. And then Sir Lancelot drew his sword, for he felt himself so badly hurt that he expected to have his death there. And then he gave Sir Bleoberis such a blow on the helmet that he fell down to the ground in a faint. And in the same way he served Sir Aliduke and Sir Galihud. And Sir Lavaine struck down Sir Bellangere, who was the son of Alisander le Orphelin.

And by this time Sir Bors was on horseback again, and then he came with Sir Ector and Sir Lionel, and all three of them struck with their swords on Sir Lancelot's helmet. And when he felt their blows, and his wound, which was so grievous, then he resolved to do what he could while he could last. And then he gave Sir Bors such a blow that he made him bow his head exceedingly low; and with that he tore off his helmet, and might have killed him; and so he pulled him down, and in the same way he served Sir Ector and Sir Lionel. For as the book says, he might have killed them, but when he saw their faces his heart would not let him do it, and he left them there. And then afterwards he crashed into the thickest of the crowd of them all, and did there the most marvellous deeds of arms that any man ever saw or heard tell of, and Sir Lavaine, the good knight, was with him all the while. And there Sir Lancelot with his sword struck down and pulled down, as the French book tells, more than thirty knights, and most of them were of the Round Table; and Sir Lavaine did very well that day, for he struck down ten knights of the Round Table.

Chapter 12: How Sir Lancelot and Sir Lavaine left the field, and what danger Lancelot was in

"Jesus have mercy," said Sir Gawain to Arthur, "I wonder what knight he is, the one with the red sleeve."

"Sir," said King Arthur, "he will be known before he leaves."

And then the king had the horns blown to send them to their lodgings, and the heralds gave the prize to the knight with the white shield who wore the red sleeve. Then the King with the Hundred Knights, the King of North Wales, the King of Northumberland, and Sir Galahalt, the high prince, came and said to Sir Lancelot, "Fair knight, God bless you, for you have done much for us this day; and so we beg you to come with us, so that you may receive the honour and the prize, as you have honourably deserved."

"My fair lords," said Sir Lancelot, "believe me, if I have earned thanks I have paid dearly for them, and I regret it, for I am not likely ever to escape with my life. And so, fair lords, I beg you to allow me to go where I please, for I am badly hurt. I care nothing for any honour, for I would rather rest than be lord of all the world."

And with that he groaned pitifully, and rode off from them at a great gallop until he came under the edge of a wood.

And when he saw that he was nearly a mile from the field, so that he was sure he could not be seen, then he said in a loud voice, "Oh, noble knight, Sir Lavaine, help me get this broken spear shaft out of my side, for it sticks in so hard that it is nearly killing me."

"Oh, my own lord," said Sir Lavaine, "I would gladly do whatever would please you, but I am badly afraid that if I pull out the broken shaft you will be in danger of death."

"I charge you," said Sir Lancelot, "as you love me, draw it out."

And with that he got down from his horse, and so did Sir Lavaine; and at once Sir Lavaine drew the broken shaft out of his side, and he gave a great shriek and a terrible, ghastly groan, and the blood burst out, nearly a pint at once, so that at last he sank down on his buttocks, and so fainted, pale as death.

"Alas," said Sir Lavaine, "what shall I do?"

And then he turned Sir Lancelot into the wind; but even so he lay there nearly half an hour as if he were dead.

And so at last Sir Lancelot opened his eyes, and said, "Oh, Lavaine, help me get on my horse, for close by here, within two miles, there is a good hermit who was once a very noble knight and a great lord of estates. And out of great goodness he has taken himself to voluntary poverty, and given up many lands; and his name is Sir Baudwin of Brittany, and he is a very fine surgeon and a good doctor. Now let us see; help me up so that I can get there, for my heart always tells me that I shall never die at my first cousin's hands."

And then with great pain Sir Lavaine helped him onto his horse. And then they rode together at a great gallop, and all the while Sir Lancelot bled so that it ran down to the ground; and so by good fortune they came to that hermitage, which stood under a wood, with a great cliff on the other side, and a fair stream running below it. And then Sir Lavaine beat on the gate with the butt of his spear, and cried out hard, "Let us in, for Jesus' sake!"

And a handsome boy came to them, and asked them what they wanted.

"Fair son," said Sir Lavaine, "go and beg your lord, the hermit, for God's sake to let in a knight here who is very badly wounded; and tell your lord that this day I saw him do more deeds of arms than I ever heard tell that any man did."

So the boy went in quickly, and then he brought the hermit, who was an exceedingly good man. When Sir Lavaine saw him he begged him for God's sake for help.

"What knight is he?" said the hermit. "Is he of King Arthur's household, or not?"

"I don't know," said Sir Lavaine, "who he is, or what his name is, but I know well that I saw him do marvellously this day in deeds of arms."

"On whose side was he?" said the hermit.

"Sir," said Sir Lavaine, "he was against King Arthur this day, and there he won the prize over all the knights of the Round Table."

"I have seen the day," said the hermit, "when I would have loved him the less for being against my lord, King Arthur, for once I was one of the fellowship of the Round Table; but I thank God that now I am of another mind. But where is he? Let me see him."

Then Sir Lavaine brought the hermit to him.

Chapter 13: How Lancelot was brought to a hermit to be healed of his wound, and of other matters

And when the hermit looked at him, as he sat leaning on his saddlebow, bleeding pitifully all the while, the knight-hermit kept thinking that he ought to know him, but he could not place him, because he was so pale from bleeding.

"What knight are you," said the hermit, "and where were you born?"

"My fair lord," said Sir Lancelot, "I am a stranger and a knight-errant, who travels through many realms to win honour."

Then the hermit looked at him more carefully, and saw by a wound on his cheek that he was Sir Lancelot.

"Alas," said the hermit, "my own lord, why do you hide your name from me? Truly, I ought by rights to know you, for you are the noblest knight in the world, for I know you well for Sir Lancelot."

"Sir," he said, "since you know me, help me if you can, for God's sake, for I would be out of this pain at once, one way or the other, to death or to life."

"Have no fear," said the hermit, "you shall live and do very well."

And so the hermit called two of his servants to him, and so he and his servants carried him into the hermitage, and quickly took off his armour, and laid him in his bed. And then at once the hermit stopped his bleeding, and made him drink good wine, so that Sir Lancelot was well refreshed and came to himself. For in those days it was not the custom of hermits as it is nowadays, for there were no hermits in those days who had not been men of honour and of prowess; and those hermits kept great households, and gave relief to people who were in distress.

Now we turn to King Arthur, and leave Sir Lancelot in the hermitage. So when the kings of both sides had come together, and the great feast was to be held, King Arthur asked the King of North Wales and his fellowship where that knight was who had worn the red sleeve. "Bring him before me, so that he may have his praise, and honour, and the prize, as is right."

Then Sir Galahalt, the high prince, and the King with the Hundred Knights spoke: "We think that knight has come to harm, and that he is never likely to see you or any of us again, and that is the greatest pity we ever knew of any knight."

"Alas," said Arthur, "how can this be? Is he so badly hurt? What is his name?" said King Arthur.

"Truly," they all said, "we do not know his name, or where he came from, or where he was going."

"Alas," said the king, "this is the worst news that has come to me in these seven years, for I would not for all the lands I rule have it known to me that that noble knight was dead."

"Do you know him?" they all said.

"As for that," said Arthur, "whether I know him or not, you shall not learn from me what man he is; but may Almighty Jesus send me good news of him."

And so said they all.

"By my head," said Sir Gawain, "if the good knight is so badly hurt, it is a great loss and a pity to all this land, for he is one of the noblest knights I ever saw handle a spear or a sword in the field; and if he can be found, I will find him, for I am sure he is not far from this town."

"You will have done well," said King Arthur, "if you can find him, unless he is in such a state that he cannot help himself."

"Jesus forbid," said Sir Gawain, "but I will know who he is, if I can find him."

At once Sir Gawain took a squire with him, on small riding horses, and rode all around Camelot for six or seven miles; but he came back again and could hear no word of him. Then within two days King Arthur and all the fellowship returned to London again. And so as they rode along the way it happened that Sir Gawain lodged at Astolat with Sir Bernard, where Sir Lancelot had lodged. And so as Sir Gawain was in his chamber resting, Sir Bernard, the old baron, came to him, and his daughter Elaine, to entertain him and to ask him what news there was, and who did best at that tournament of Winchester.

"So help me God," said Sir Gawain, "there were two knights who carried two white shields, but one of them wore a red sleeve on his head, and certainly he was one of the best knights I ever saw joust in the field. For I dare say," said Sir Gawain, "that that one knight with the red sleeve struck down forty knights of the Round Table, and his companion did very well and honourably."

"Now blessed be God," said the Fair Maiden of Astolat, "that that knight did so well, for he is the first man in the world I ever loved, and truly he will be the last that I ever love."

"Now, fair maid," said Sir Gawain, "is that good knight your love?"

"Certainly, sir," she said, "you may be sure he is my love."

"Then do you know his name?" said Sir Gawain.

"No, truly," said the damsel, "I don't know his name, or where he comes from; but as for saying that I love him, I promise you, and God, that I love him."

"How did you first come to know him?" said Sir Gawain.

Chapter 14: How Sir Gawain lodged with the lord of Astolat, and there learned that it was Sir Lancelot who wore the red sleeve

Then she told him all that you have heard before, and how her father gave him her brother to serve him, and how her father lent him her brother Sir Tirre's shield. "And he left his own shield here with me."

"For what reason did he do that?" said Sir Gawain.

"For this reason," said the damsel: "his shield was too well known among many noble knights."

"Ah, fair damsel," said Sir Gawain, "if you please, let me have a sight of that shield."

"Sir," she said, "it is in my chamber, in a cover, and if you will come with me you shall see it."

"No," said Sir Bernard to his daughter, "have it sent for."

So when the shield had come, Sir Gawain took off the cover, and when he looked at that shield he knew at once that it was Sir Lancelot's shield, and his own coat of arms.

"Ah, Jesus have mercy," said Sir Gawain, "now my heart is heavier than it ever was before."

"Why?" said Elaine.

"Because I have good cause," said Sir Gawain. "Is the knight who owns this shield your love?"

"Yes, truly," she said, "he is my love. I wish to God I were his."

"So God help me," said Sir Gawain, "fair damsel, you have chosen well, for if he is your love, you love the most honourable knight in the world, and the man of most renown."

"So I always thought," said the damsel, "for never before that time did I love any knight, of all the knights I ever saw."

"God grant," said Sir Gawain, "that each of you may have joy of the other, but that is a great hazard. But truly," said Sir Gawain to the damsel, "you may count yourself very fortunate, for I have known that noble knight these twenty-four years, and never before that day did I, or any other knight, I will swear to it, see or hear tell that he ever wore a token or sign of any lady, gentlewoman or maiden, at any jousts or tournament. And therefore, fair maiden," said Sir Gawain, "you are much obliged to him and owe him thanks. But I fear," said Sir Gawain, "that you will never see him in this world, and that is the greatest pity there ever was for any earthly knight."

"Alas," she said, "how can this be? Is he dead?"

"I don't say so," said Sir Gawain, "but you may be sure he is grievously wounded, by every kind of sign, and by the look of things more likely to be dead than alive; and you may be sure he is the noble knight Sir Lancelot, for I know him by this shield."

"Alas," said the Fair Maiden of Astolat, "how can this be, and what was his wound?"

"Truly," said Sir Gawain, "the man in the world who loved him best wounded him so; and I dare say," said Sir Gawain, "that if the knight who wounded him knew for certain that he had wounded Sir Lancelot, it would be the greatest sorrow that ever came to his heart."

"Now, dear father," said Elaine then, "I beg you to give me leave to ride and look for him, or else I know well I shall go out of my mind; for I will never stop until I find him and my brother, Sir Lavaine."

"Do as you please," said her father, "for I am deeply sorry for the hurt of that noble knight."

At once the maiden made herself ready, grieving greatly in front of Sir Gawain.

Then in the morning Sir Gawain came to King Arthur, and told him how he had found Sir Lancelot's shield in the keeping of the Fair Maiden of Astolat.

"I knew all that beforehand," said King Arthur, "and that was why I would not let you fight in the great jousts; for I saw him," said King Arthur, "when he came to his lodging in Astolat very late in the evening. But I do marvel," said Arthur, "that he would ever wear the token of any damsel, for before now I never heard or knew that he ever wore a token of any earthly woman."

"By my head," said Sir Gawain, "the Fair Maiden of Astolat loves him marvellously well; what it means I cannot say; and she has ridden after him to look for him."

So the king and all of them came to London, and there Sir Gawain told the whole court openly that it was Sir Lancelot who had jousted best.

Chapter 15: Of the sorrow Sir Bors felt at Lancelot's wound, and of the anger the queen felt because Lancelot wore the sleeve

And when Sir Bors heard that, you may be sure he was a downcast man, and so were all his kinsmen. But when Queen Guinevere learned that Sir Lancelot had worn the red sleeve of the Fair Maiden of Astolat, she was nearly out of her mind with anger. And then she sent for Sir Bors de Ganis in all the haste there could be. So when Sir Bors had come before the queen, she said, "Ah, Sir Bors, have you heard how falsely Sir Lancelot has betrayed me?"

"Alas, madam," said Sir Bors, "I am afraid he has betrayed himself, and all of us."

"No matter," said the queen, "even if he is destroyed, for he is a false traitor of a knight."

"Madam," said Sir Bors, "I beg you, do not say so, for believe me, I cannot hear such language about him."

"Why, Sir Bors," she said, "should I not call him a traitor, when he wore the red sleeve on his head at Winchester, at the great jousts?"

"Madam," said Sir Bors, "I bitterly regret that sleeve-wearing, but I dare say he did it with no evil intent; he wore the red sleeve for this reason, so that none of his blood would know him. For before then, neither we nor any of us ever knew him to wear a token or sign of maiden, lady or gentlewoman."

"Shame on him," said the queen. "Yet for all his pride and boastfulness, there you proved yourself his better."

"No, madam, never say so again, for he beat me and my fellows, and could have killed us if he had wanted to."

"Shame on him," said the queen, "for I heard Sir Gawain say in front of my lord Arthur that it would be a marvel to tell of the great love there is between the Fair Maiden of Astolat and him."

"Madam," said Sir Bors, "I cannot stop Sir Gawain from saying what he pleases; but I dare say, as for my lord Sir Lancelot, that he loves no lady, gentlewoman or maiden, but loves them all alike. And therefore, madam," said Sir Bors, "you may say what you will, but believe me, I will hurry to look for him, and find him wherever he is, and God send me good news of him."

And so we leave them there, and speak of Sir Lancelot, who lay in great danger.

So when fair Elaine came to Winchester she searched all about there, and by good fortune Sir Lavaine had ridden out for exercise, to warm up his horse. And as soon as Elaine saw him she knew him, and then she called out loudly to him. And when he heard her he came to her at once, and then she asked her brother how my lord Sir Lancelot was.

"Who told you, sister, that my lord's name was Sir Lancelot?"

Then she told him how Sir Gawain had known him by his shield. So they rode together until they came to the hermitage, and at once she dismounted.

So Sir Lavaine brought her in to Sir Lancelot; and when she saw him lying so sick and pale in his bed she could not speak, but suddenly fell down to the ground in a faint, and there she lay a long while. And when she had recovered, she shrieked and said, "My lord Sir Lancelot, alas, why are you in this state?" And then she fainted again.

And then Sir Lancelot asked Sir Lavaine to lift her up: "And bring her to me."

And when she came to herself Sir Lancelot kissed her, and said, "Fair maiden, why do you carry on like this? You put me to pain; and so make no more such a show of grief, for if you have come to comfort me, you are very welcome; and from this little hurt that I have, I shall be well again very quickly, by the grace of God. But I wonder," said Sir Lancelot, "who told you my name?"

Then the fair maiden told him all about how Sir Gawain had lodged with her father. "And there he found out your name by your shield."

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "I regret that my name is known, for I am sure it will turn to anger."

And then Sir Lancelot turned it over in his mind that Sir Gawain would tell Queen Guinevere how he had worn the red sleeve, and for whom; and he knew well that would turn to great anger.

So this maiden Elaine never left Sir Lancelot, but watched over him day and night, and tended him so well that the French book says there was never a woman who did more kindly for a man than she. Then Sir Lancelot asked Sir Lavaine to set watchers in Winchester for Sir Bors, in case he came there, and told him the signs he would know him by: a wound in his forehead.

"For I am quite sure," said Sir Lancelot, "that Sir Bors will look for me, for he is the same good knight who wounded me."

Chapter 16: How Sir Bors searched for Lancelot and found him in the hermitage, and of their lamenting together

Now we turn to Sir Bors de Ganis, who came to Winchester to look for his cousin Sir Lancelot. And so when he came to Winchester, there were men there whom Sir Lavaine had set to lie in wait for such a man, and at once Sir Lavaine had word of it; and then Sir Lavaine came to Winchester and found Sir Bors, and there he told him who he was, and whom he was with, and what that man's name was.

"Now, fair knight," said Sir Bors, "I beg you to bring me to my lord, Sir Lancelot."

"Sir," said Sir Lavaine, "take your horse, and within this hour you shall see him."

And so they set off, and came to the hermitage.

And when Sir Bors saw Sir Lancelot lying in his bed, pale and drained of colour, at once Sir Bors lost his composure, and out of the love of kin and out of pity he could not speak, but wept tenderly for a long while. And then, when he could speak, he said this: "Oh, my lord Sir Lancelot, God bless you, and send you a quick recovery. And very heavy-hearted I am at my misfortune and my ill luck, for now I may call myself ill-fated. And I fear that God is greatly displeased with me, that He would allow me such a shame as to wound you, who are the leader of us all, and all our honour; and therefore I call myself ill-fated. Alas that ever such a wretched knight as I am should have the power, by ill luck, to wound the noblest knight in the world! When I so shamefully set upon you and overpowered you, and when you might have killed me, you spared me; and I did not do the same, for I and your own blood did our uttermost against you. I marvel," said Sir Bors, "that my heart or my blood would let me do it. And so, my lord Sir Lancelot, I ask your forgiveness."

"Fair cousin," said Sir Lancelot, "you are very welcome; and believe me, you say too much in order to please me, and it does not please me, for I got just what I was asking for. For I meant in my pride to overcome you all, and there in my pride I was nearly killed, and that was through my own fault, for I might have given you warning that I was there. And then I would have had no hurt; for it is an old saying that there is hard battle where kin and friends fight against each other: there can be no mercy, only war to the death. Therefore, fair cousin," said Sir Lancelot, "let this talk pass, and all that God sends shall be welcome; and let us leave this matter and speak of something cheerful, for what is done cannot be undone; and let us find a remedy, so that I may be well as soon as possible."

Then Sir Bors leaned on his bedside, and told Sir Lancelot how the queen was exceedingly angry with him because he had worn the red sleeve at the great jousts; and there Sir Bors told him all about how Sir Gawain had found it out: "By your shield, which you left with the Fair Maiden of Astolat."

"Then the queen is angry," said Sir Lancelot, "and so I am very heavy-hearted, for I deserved no anger; all that I did was so that I would not be known."

"That is just how I excused you," said Sir Bors, "but it was all in vain, for she said a great deal more to me than I am telling you now. But is this she," said Sir Bors, "who is so busy about you, the one they call the Fair Maiden of Astolat?"

"That is she," said Sir Lancelot, "and I can find no way to put her from me."

"Why should you put her from you?" said Sir Bors. "She is an exceedingly beautiful damsel, and fine-looking, and well brought up; and I wish to God, fair cousin," said Sir Bors, "that you could love her; but as to that, I cannot and dare not advise you. But I see well," said Sir Bors, "by her care for you, that she loves you with her whole heart."

"I am sorry for that," said Sir Lancelot.

"Sir," said Sir Bors, "she is not the first who has wasted her pains on you, and that is the more pity."

And so they talked of many more things. And so within three or four days Sir Lancelot was big and strong again.

Chapter 17: How Sir Lancelot put on his armour to test whether he could bear arms, and how his wounds burst open again

Then Sir Bors told Sir Lancelot how a great tournament and jousts had been sworn between King Arthur and the King of North Wales, to be held on All Hallows' Day, near Winchester.

"Is that true?" said Sir Lancelot. "Then you shall stay with me a little while longer, until I am well, for I feel myself very big and strong."

"God be blessed," said Sir Bors.

Then they were there together nearly a month, and all the while this maiden Elaine worked diligently for Sir Lancelot night and day, so that there was never a child or a wife more meek to her father or her husband than that Fair Maiden of Astolat was; and so Sir Bors was greatly pleased with her.

So one day, by the agreement of Sir Lancelot, Sir Bors and Sir Lavaine, they had the hermit go into the woods to look for various herbs, and so Sir Lancelot had fair Elaine gather herbs for him to make him a bath. Meanwhile Sir Lancelot had himself armed in every piece; and there he meant to test his armour and his spear, to see whether his wound would let him or not. And so when he was on his horse he spurred him fiercely, and the horse was exceedingly lively and fresh, because he had not been worked for a month before. And then Sir Lancelot levelled that spear in the rest. That warhorse leapt mightily when he felt the spurs; and the man on him (and it was the noblest horse in the world) held him in mightily and steadily, and kept the spear still in the rest; and with that Sir Lancelot strained himself so hard, with such great force, to get the horse forward, that the seal of his wound burst open both inside and out; and with that the blood came out so fiercely that he felt himself so weak that he could not sit on his horse. And then Sir Lancelot cried out to Sir Bors, "Ah, Sir Bors and Sir Lavaine, help, for I have come to my end!" And with that he fell down on one side to the earth like a dead body. And then Sir Bors and Sir Lavaine came to him, grieving beyond measure. And so by chance the maiden Elaine heard their mourning, and then she came there; and when she found Sir Lancelot there in that place in his armour, she cried and wept as if she had gone mad; and then she kissed him, and did what she could to wake him. And then she rebuked her brother and Sir Bors, and called them false traitors, and asked why they would take him out of his bed; and there she cried, and said she would accuse them of his death.

With this the holy hermit came, Sir Baudwin of Brittany, and when he found Sir Lancelot in that state he said little, but you may be sure he was angry; and then he told them, "Let us get him inside." And so they all carried him to the hermitage, and took off his armour, and laid him in his bed; and all the while his wound bled pitifully, but he did not stir a limb. Then the knight-hermit put something in his nose and a little water in his mouth. And then Sir Lancelot woke from his faint, and then the hermit stopped his bleeding. And when he could speak, the hermit asked Sir Lancelot why he had put his life in danger.

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "because I thought I was strong, and also Sir Bors told me that there would be great jousts at All Hallows between King Arthur and the King of North Wales, and so I thought I would test for myself whether I could be there or not."

"Ah, Sir Lancelot," said the hermit, "your heart and your spirit will never be done until your last day, but now you shall do as I advise. Let Sir Bors leave you, and let him do what he can at that tournament. And by the grace of God," said the knight-hermit, "by the time the tournament is over and you come back here," he said to Sir Bors, "Sir Lancelot shall be as whole as you are, provided he will be ruled by me."

Chapter 18: How Sir Bors returned and brought news of Sir Lancelot, and of the tournament, and to whom the prize was given
