Then Sir Bors made ready to leave Sir Lancelot; and then Sir Lancelot said, "Fair cousin, Sir Bors, commend me to all those I ought to be commended to. And I beg you, exert yourself at those jousts so that you may be the best, for love of me; and I shall wait for you here, at the mercy of God, until you come again."

And so Sir Bors left and came to the court of King Arthur, and told them where he had left Sir Lancelot.

"I am sorry for that," said the king, "but since he will live, we may all thank God."

And there Sir Bors told the queen what danger Sir Lancelot had been in when he tried to test his horse. "And all that he did, madam, was for love of you, because he wanted to be at this tournament."

"Shame on him, the recreant knight," said the queen, "for believe me, I am very sorry that he will live."

"He will live," said Sir Bors, "and anyone who wished otherwise, except you, madam, we who are of his blood would help to cut their lives short. But madam," said Sir Bors, "you have often been displeased with my lord Sir Lancelot, but every time, in the end, you find him a true knight." And so he left.

And then every knight of the Round Table who was there at that time made ready to be at those jousts at All Hallows, and many knights of various countries made their way there. And as All Hallows drew near, the King of North Wales came there, and the King with the Hundred Knights, and Sir Galahalt, the high prince, of Surluse; and King Anguish of Ireland came there, and the King of Scots. So these three kings came on King Arthur's side. And so that day Sir Gawain did great deeds of arms, and began first. And the heralds counted that Sir Gawain struck down twenty knights. Then Sir Bors de Ganis came in at the same time, and he was counted as striking down twenty knights; and so the prize was shared between them both, for they began first and lasted longest. Also Sir Gareth, as the book says, did great deeds of arms that day, for he struck down and pulled down thirty knights. But when he had done these deeds he did not stay, but left at once, and so he lost his prize. And Sir Palomides did great deeds of arms that day, for he struck down twenty knights, but he left suddenly, and men thought that Sir Gareth and he had ridden off together after some adventure or other.

So when this tournament was over Sir Bors left and rode until he came to Sir Lancelot, his cousin; and then he found him walking on his feet, and there each rejoiced greatly in the other; and so Sir Bors told Sir Lancelot all about the jousts, just as you have heard.

"I wonder," said Sir Lancelot, "that Sir Gareth would not stay, when he had done such deeds of arms."

"We all wondered at it," said Sir Bors, "for unless it were you, or Sir Tristram, or Sir Lamorak de Galis, I never saw a knight bear down so many in so little a while as Sir Gareth did; and at once he was gone, we did not know where."

"By my head," said Sir Lancelot, "he is a noble knight, and a mighty man, and has great staying power; and if he were well tested," said Sir Lancelot, "I would judge he was a match for any knight alive. And he is a well-bred knight, courteous, true and generous, meek and mild, and in him there is no kind of malice or deceit, but he is plain, faithful and true."

So then they made ready to leave the hermit. And so one morning they took their horses, and Elaine le Blank with them; and when they came to Astolat they were well lodged there, and had a warm welcome from Sir Bernard, the old baron, and from Sir Tirre, his son. And so in the morning, when Sir Lancelot was to leave, fair Elaine brought her father with her, and Sir Lavaine, and Sir Tirre, and this is what she said:

Chapter 19: Of the great lament of the Fair Maid of Astolat when Lancelot was to leave, and how she died for love of him

"My lord, Sir Lancelot," said fair Elaine, "now I see you are going to leave; now, fair knight and courteous knight, have mercy on me, and do not let me die for love of you."

"What would you have me do?" said Sir Lancelot.

"I would have you for my husband," said Elaine.

"Fair damsel, I thank you," said Sir Lancelot, "but truly," he said, "I have resolved never to be a married man."

"Then, fair knight," she said, "will you be my lover?"

"God forbid," said Sir Lancelot, "for then I would repay your father and your brother very badly for their great goodness."

"Alas," she said, "then I must die for love of you."

"You shall not," said Sir Lancelot, "for believe me, fair maiden, I could have been married if I had wished, but I have never set myself to marry yet. But because, fair damsel, you love me as you say you do, I will show you some kindness for your good will and kindness, and it is this: wherever you choose to set your heart on some good knight who will marry you, I shall give you, the two of you together, a thousand pounds a year, to you and to your heirs. This much I will give you, fair madam, for your kindness, and always, while I live, I will be your own knight."

"I will have none of all this," said the maiden, "for unless you will marry me, or else be my lover at the least, believe me, Sir Lancelot, my good days are done."

"Fair damsel," said Sir Lancelot, "you must forgive me these two things."

Then she shrieked shrilly, and fell down in a faint; and then women carried her into her room, and there she grieved beyond all bounds. And then Sir Lancelot wanted to leave, and there he asked Sir Lavaine what he would do.

"What should I do," said Sir Lavaine, "but follow you, unless you drive me away, or order me to go from you?"

Then Sir Bernard came to Sir Lancelot and said to him, "I can see nothing else but that my daughter Elaine will die for your sake."

"I cannot help it," said Sir Lancelot, "for I am deeply sorry for it, for I appeal to you yourself that my offer is fair; and I regret," said Sir Lancelot, "that she loves me as she does. I was never the cause of it, for I appeal to your son that early or late I never offered her favours or fair promises; and as for me," said Sir Lancelot, "I dare do all that a knight should do to prove that she is a pure maiden as far as I am concerned, both in deed and in will. And I am very grieved at her distress, for she is a very fair maiden, good and well-bred, and well brought up."

"Father," said Sir Lavaine, "I dare swear she is a pure maiden as far as my lord Sir Lancelot is concerned; but she is doing as I do, for since I first saw my lord Sir Lancelot I could never leave him, and I never will, if I can follow him."

Then Sir Lancelot took his leave, and so they left, and came to Winchester. And when Arthur knew that Sir Lancelot had come safe and sound, the king rejoiced greatly over him, and so did Sir Gawain and all the knights of the Round Table except Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred. But Queen Guinevere was mad with anger at Sir Lancelot, and would by no means speak with him, but kept herself away from him; and Sir Lancelot tried every way he could to speak with the queen, but it could not be.

Now we speak of the Fair Maiden of Astolat, who grieved so day and night that she never slept, ate or drank, and all the while she made her lament for Sir Lancelot. So when she had gone on like this for ten days, and grew so weak that she must surely pass out of this world, then she made a full confession, and received her Creator. And still she went on lamenting for Sir Lancelot. Then her confessor told her to leave such thoughts.

Then she said, "Why should I leave such thoughts? Am I not an earthly woman? And as long as the breath is in my body I may lament, for I believe I do no wrong though I love an earthly man; and I take God as my witness that I never loved anyone but Sir Lancelot du Lake, and never shall, and I am a pure maiden, for him and for all others. And since it is God's will that I shall die for the love of so noble a knight, I beseech the High Father of Heaven to have mercy on my soul, and that my countless pains that I suffered may be a lightening of part of my sins. For, sweet Lord Jesus," said the fair maiden, "I take You as my witness, I was never a great offender against Your laws, except that I loved this noble knight, Sir Lancelot, beyond measure, and of myself, good Lord, I could not withstand the burning love from which I have my death."

And then she called her father, Sir Bernard, and her brother, Sir Tirre, and earnestly begged her father that her brother might write a letter just as she would dictate it; and so her father granted it. And when the letter had been written word for word as she composed it, then she begged her father that she might be watched over until she was dead. "And while my body is still warm, let this letter be put in my right hand, and my hand tied fast around the letter until I am cold; and let me be put in a fine bed with all the richest clothes I have around me, and so let my bed and all my richest clothes be carried with me in a cart to the nearest place on the Thames; and there let me be put in a barge, with only one man with me, someone you trust to steer me there, and let my barge be covered all over with black samite. Father, I beg you, let this be done."

So her father faithfully promised her that everything would be done just as she had planned. Then her father and her brother grieved greatly, for when this was done she died at once. And so when she was dead, the body and the bed and all were taken the nearest way to the Thames, and there the man, and the body, and everything were put on the Thames; and so the man steered the barge to Westminster, and there he rowed to and fro a long while before anyone noticed it.

Chapter 20: How the body of the Maid of Astolat arrived before King Arthur, and of the burial, and how Sir Lancelot made the offering at her Mass

So by chance King Arthur and Queen Guinevere were talking together at a window, and so as they looked out on the Thames they saw this black barge, and wondered what it meant. Then the king called Sir Kay, and showed it to him.

"Sir," said Sir Kay, "you may be sure there is some news here."

"Go there," said the king to Sir Kay, "and take Sir Brandiles and Agravain with you, and bring me back word quickly of what is there."

Then these four knights left and came to the barge and went aboard; and there they found the fairest body lying in a rich bed, and a poor man sitting in the end of the barge, and he would not speak a word. So these four knights went back to the king, and told him what they had found.

"I will see that fair body," said the king. And so then the king took the queen by the hand, and went there.

Then the king had the barge held fast, and then the king and the queen went aboard, with certain knights with them; and there he saw the fairest woman lying in a rich bed, covered to her waist with many rich cloths, and all of them were cloth of gold, and she lay as though she were smiling. Then the queen noticed a letter in her right hand, and told the king. Then the king took it and said, "Now I am sure this letter will tell who she was, and why she has come here." So then the king and the queen left the barge, and ordered a certain man to keep watch over it.

And so when the king had come into his chamber, he called many knights around him, and said that he wanted to know openly what was written in that letter. Then the king broke the seal, and had a clerk read it, and this was what the letter said: "Most noble knight, Sir Lancelot, now death has set us two at odds over my love for you. I was your lover, the one men called the Fair Maiden of Astolat; so to all ladies I make my lament. Yet pray for my soul, and at least bury me, and make the offering at my Mass: this is my last request. And I died a pure maiden, I take God as my witness. Pray for my soul, Sir Lancelot, as you are peerless." This was all the substance of the letter. And when it had been read, the king, the queen and all the knights wept for pity at its sorrowful lament. Then Sir Lancelot was sent for; and when he had come, King Arthur had the letter read to him.

And when Sir Lancelot had heard it word for word, he said, "My lord Arthur, believe me, I am very grieved at the death of this fair damsel. God knows I was never the cause of her death by my will, and I appeal to her own brother on that: here he is, Sir Lavaine. I will not deny," said Sir Lancelot, "that she was both fair and good, and I was much beholden to her, but she loved me beyond measure."

"You might have shown her," said the queen, "some kindness and courtesy that might have saved her life."

"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "she would take no other answer but that she would be my wife, or else my lover; and of these two I would grant her neither. But for the good love she showed me I offered her a thousand pounds a year, to her and to her heirs, and to marry whatever knight she could find that she loved best in her heart. For, madam," said Sir Lancelot, "I do not like to be forced to love; for love must rise from the heart, and not by any force."

"That is the truth," said the king, "and many a knight's love is free in itself, and will never be bound, for where he is bound he loses himself."

Then the king said to Sir Lancelot, "It will be to your honour to see that she is buried honourably."

"Sir," said Sir Lancelot, "that shall be done as best I can arrange it."

And so many knights went there to look at that fair maiden. And so in the morning she was buried richly, and Sir Lancelot made the offering at her Mass; and all the knights of the Round Table who were there at that time made their offering with Sir Lancelot. And then the poor man went away again with the barge. Then the queen sent for Sir Lancelot, and begged his pardon, because she had been angry with him without cause.

"This is not the first time," said Sir Lancelot, "that you have been displeased with me without cause. But, madam, I must always bear with you, and whatever sorrow I endure, I care nothing for it."

So this went on all that winter, with all kinds of hunting and hawking, and there were many jousts and tournaments between many great lords; and everywhere Sir Lavaine won great honour, so that he was nobly renowned among many knights of the Round Table.

Chapter 21: Of great jousts held all through Christmas, and of great jousting and a tournament proclaimed by King Arthur, and of Sir Lancelot

So it went on until Christmas, and then every day there were jousts held for a diamond, so that whoever jousted best should have a diamond. But Sir Lancelot would not joust unless it was at great jousts that had been proclaimed. But Sir Lavaine jousted there all that Christmas exceedingly well, and was praised as the best, for there were only a few who did so well. And so knights of every kind judged that Sir Lavaine should be made a knight of the Round Table at the next feast of Pentecost. So after Christmas King Arthur called many knights to him, and there they planned together to set up sides and a great tournament and jousts. And the King of North Wales said to Arthur that he would have on his side King Anguish of Ireland, and the King with the Hundred Knights, and the King of Northumberland, and Sir Galahalt, the high prince. And so these four kings and this mighty duke took sides against King Arthur and the knights of the Round Table. And it was proclaimed that the day of the jousts should be near Westminster, on Candlemas Day, and many knights were glad of it, and made ready to be at those jousts in the finest fashion.

Then Queen Guinevere sent for Sir Lancelot, and said this: "I warn you not to ride any more in any jousts or tournaments unless your kinsmen can know you. And at these jousts that are coming you shall have a sleeve of gold from me; and I beg you, for my sake, exert yourself there, so that men may speak of your honour. But I charge you, as you want my love, to warn your kinsmen that you will wear that sleeve of gold on your helmet that day."

"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "it shall be done."

And so each rejoiced greatly in the other. And when Sir Lancelot saw his moment, he told Sir Bors that he would leave, and take no one with him but Sir Lavaine, to the good hermit who lived in that forest of Windsor; his name was Sir Brasias; and there he meant to rest, and take all the rest he could, because he wanted to be fresh on that day of the jousts.

So Sir Lancelot and Sir Lavaine left, so that no living creature knew what had become of him, except the noblemen of his blood. And when he had come to the hermitage, you may be sure he had a good welcome. And so every day Sir Lancelot would go to a spring close by the hermitage, and there he would lie down, and watch the spring well up and bubble, and sometimes he slept there. Now at that time there was a lady living in that forest, and she was a great huntress, and she hunted every day, and always carried her bow with her; and no men ever went with her, but always women, and they were archers, and could kill a deer well, both by stalking it and by lying in wait for it; and every day they carried bows and arrows, horns and hunting knives, and they had many good dogs, both for tracking on the leash and for running down the game. So it happened that this lady the huntress had loosed her dog for the bow at a barren hind, and so this barren hind took flight over hedges and woods. And all the while this lady and some of her women kept up with the hind, and followed it by the noise of the hounds, meaning to meet the hind at some water; and so it happened that the hind came to the spring where Sir Lancelot was sleeping and dozing. And so when the hind came to the spring, she went into the water because of the heat, and there she lay a long while; and the dog came after, and cast about, for she had lost the true scent of the hind. Just then the lady huntress came, who knew by the dog she had that the hind had taken to the water at that spring; and she came up boldly and found the hind, and she put a broad arrow to her bow, and shot at the hind, and overshot the hind; and so by mischance the arrow struck Sir Lancelot in the thick of the buttock, in past the barbs. When Sir Lancelot felt himself so hurt, he leapt up wildly, and saw the lady who had shot him. And when he saw she was a woman, he said this: "Lady or damsel, whatever you are, it was an evil hour you took up a bow. The devil made you an archer!"

Chapter 22: How Lancelot, after he was wounded by a lady, came to a hermit, and of other matters

"Now, mercy, fair sir," said the lady. "I am a gentlewoman who hunts here in this forest, and God knows I did not see you; but there was a barren hind here in the water at this spring, and I thought I was doing well, but my hand swerved."

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "you have done me harm."

And so the lady left, and Sir Lancelot pulled out the arrow as best he could, and left the head still in his buttock, and so he went weakly to the hermitage, bleeding all the way as he went. And when Sir Lavaine and the hermit saw that Sir Lancelot was hurt, you may be sure they were exceedingly downcast, but Sir Lavaine did not know how he had been hurt or by whom. And then they were angry beyond measure.

Then with great difficulty the hermit got the arrowhead out of Sir Lancelot's buttock, and he lost much of his blood, and the wound was exceedingly painful, and unluckily struck, for it was in such a place that he could not sit in any saddle.

"Jesus have mercy," said Sir Lancelot. "I may call myself the unluckiest man alive, for always, when I most want to win honour, some unlucky thing befalls me. Now, so help me Jesus," said Sir Lancelot, "even if no one but God were willing, I shall be in the field at the jousts on Candlemas Day, whatever comes of it." So everything that could be got to heal Sir Lancelot was got.

So when the day came, Sir Lancelot had himself arrayed, and Sir Lavaine, and their horses, as though they were Saracens; and so they left and came near the field. The King of North Wales came with a hundred knights, and the King of Northumberland brought a hundred good knights with him, and King Anguish of Ireland brought a hundred good knights with him ready to joust, and Sir Galahalt, the high prince, brought a hundred good knights with him, and the King with the Hundred Knights brought as many with him, and all these were proven good knights. Then King Arthur's side came in; and the King of Scots came in with a hundred knights, and King Uriens of Gore brought a hundred knights with him, and King Howell of Brittany brought a hundred knights with him, and Chaleins of Clarance brought a hundred knights with him, and King Arthur himself came into the field with two hundred knights, and most of them were knights of the Round Table, who were proven noble knights; and old knights were set in the stands with the queen, to judge who did best.

Chapter 23: How Sir Lancelot bore himself at the jousts, and other men too

Then they sounded the trumpets for the field; and there the King of North Wales met the King of Scots, and there the King of Scots took a fall; and the King of Ireland struck down King Uriens; and the King of Northumberland struck down King Howell of Brittany; and Sir Galahalt, the high prince, struck down Chaleins of Clarance. And then King Arthur was mad with anger, and charged at the King with the Hundred Knights, and there King Arthur struck him down; and afterwards, with that same spear, King Arthur struck down three other knights. And then, when his spear was broken, King Arthur did exceedingly well; and so with that Sir Gawain and Sir Gaheris came in, and Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred, and there each of them struck down a knight, and Sir Gawain struck down four knights. And then a fierce fight began, for then the knights of Lancelot's blood came in, and Sir Gareth and Sir Palomides with them, and many knights of the Round Table, and they began to press the four kings and the mighty duke so hard that they were routed. But this Duke Galahalt, the high prince, was a noble knight, and by his mighty prowess in arms he held the knights of the Round Table hard pressed.

Sir Lancelot saw all this, and then he came into the field with Sir Lavaine like thunder. And then at once Sir Bors and the knights of his blood saw Sir Lancelot, and Sir Bors said to them all, "I warn you, beware of the man with the sleeve of gold on his head, for he is Sir Lancelot du Lake himself." And out of great goodness Sir Bors warned Sir Gareth.

"I am well pleased," said Sir Gareth, "that I know him."

"But who is he," they all said, "who rides with him in the same array?"

"That is the good and well-bred knight Sir Lavaine," said Sir Bors.

So Sir Lancelot met Sir Gawain, and there by force Sir Lancelot struck down Sir Gawain and his horse to the earth; and so he struck down Sir Agravain and Sir Gaheris, and he also struck down Sir Mordred, and all this with one spear. Then Sir Lavaine met Sir Palomides, and they met each other so hard and so fiercely that both their horses fell to the earth. And then they were horsed again, and then Sir Lancelot met Sir Palomides, and there Sir Palomides took a fall; and so Sir Lancelot, before he ever stopped, as fast as he could get spears, struck down thirty knights, and most of them were knights of the Round Table. And all the while the knights of his blood drew off, and found their fighting in other places where Sir Lancelot did not come.

And then King Arthur was angry when he saw Sir Lancelot do such deeds; and then the king called to him Sir Gawain, Sir Mordred, Sir Kay, Sir Griflet, Sir Lucan the butler, Sir Bedivere, Sir Palomides, and Sir Safere, his brother; and so the king, with these nine knights, made ready to set upon Sir Lancelot, and upon Sir Lavaine. Sir Bors and Sir Gareth saw all this.

"Now I am very much afraid," said Sir Bors, "that my lord Sir Lancelot will be hard matched."

"By my head," said Sir Gareth, "I will ride to my lord Sir Lancelot to help him, come what may to me, for he is the man who made me a knight."

"You shall not," said Sir Bors, "if you take my advice, unless you were disguised."

"You shall see me disguised," said Sir Gareth. And with that he saw a Welsh knight where he had gone to rest, and he had been badly hurt earlier by Sir Gawain; and Sir Gareth rode to him, and begged him, by his knighthood, to lend him his shield in exchange for his own.

"Gladly," said the Welsh knight.

And when Sir Gareth had his shield, the book says it was green, with a maiden painted in it. Then Sir Gareth came driving at Sir Lancelot as hard as he could, and said, "Knight, look to yourself, for there comes King Arthur with nine noble knights with him to put you to shame; and so I have come to keep you company, for the old love you have shown me."

"Many thanks," said Sir Lancelot.

"Sir," said Sir Gareth, "you take on Sir Gawain, and I shall take on Sir Palomides; and let Sir Lavaine match himself with the noble King Arthur. And when we have dealt with them, let us three hold steadfastly together."

Then King Arthur came with his nine knights, and Sir Lancelot met Sir Gawain, and gave him such a blow that the saddlebow of his saddle burst, and Sir Gawain fell to the earth. Then Sir Gareth met the good knight Sir Palomides, and he gave him such a blow that both his horse and he crashed to the earth. Then King Arthur met Sir Lavaine, and there each of them struck the other to the earth, horse and all, so that they lay there a long while. Then Sir Lancelot struck down Sir Agravain, and Sir Gaheris, and Sir Mordred; and Sir Gareth struck down Sir Kay, and Sir Safere, and Sir Griflet. And then Sir Lavaine was horsed again, and he struck down Sir Lucan the butler and Sir Bedivere; and then a great throng of good knights began.

Then Sir Lancelot crashed here and there, and tore off helmets and pulled them away, so that at that time no one could stand a blow from him, with spear or with sword. And Sir Gareth did such deeds of arms that all men wondered what knight he was with the green shield, for that day he struck down and pulled down more than thirty knights. And, as the French book says, Sir Lancelot wondered, when he saw Sir Gareth do such deeds, what knight he could be; and Sir Lavaine pulled down and struck down twenty knights. Sir Lancelot did not know Sir Gareth, either; for if Sir Tristram de Liones or Sir Lamorak de Galis had been alive, Sir Lancelot would have thought he was one of those two. So all the while Sir Lancelot, Sir Gareth and Sir Lavaine fought, and on the one side Sir Bors, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Lionel, Sir Lamorak de Galis, Sir Bleoberis, Sir Galihud, Sir Galihodin, Sir Pelleas, and more of King Ban's blood with them fought on another side of the field, and held the King with the Hundred Knights and the King of Northumberland hard pressed.

Chapter 24: How King Arthur marvelled at the jousting in the field, and how he rode out and found Sir Lancelot

So this tournament and these jousts lasted a long time, until it was nearly night, for the knights of the Round Table kept rallying to King Arthur; for the king was angry beyond measure that he and his knights could not prevail that day.

Then Sir Gawain said to the king, "I wonder where Sir Bors de Ganis and his company of Sir Lancelot's blood have been all this day; I wonder that all this day they have not been around you. It is for some reason," said Sir Gawain.

"By my head," said Sir Kay, "Sir Bors has been over there on the right-hand side of this field all day, and there he and his kin are doing more honourably than we are."

"That may well be," said Sir Gawain, "but I am always afraid of trickery; for on pain of my life," said Sir Gawain, "this knight with the red sleeve of gold is Sir Lancelot himself, I can see it well by his riding and by his great strokes; and the other knight in the same colours is the good young knight Sir Lavaine. Also, that knight with the green shield is my brother Sir Gareth, and he has disguised himself, for no one will ever make him go against Sir Lancelot, because Sir Lancelot made him a knight."

"By my head," said Arthur, "nephew, I believe you; so tell me now what your best advice is."

"Sir," said Sir Gawain, "you shall have my advice: have the trumpets sound the retreat to quarters. For if he is Sir Lancelot du Lake, with my brother Sir Gareth beside him, and with the help of that good young knight Sir Lavaine, believe me truly, it will be no use to fight with them, unless we were to fall on one knight ten or twelve at a time, and that would be no honour, but shame."

"You speak the truth," said the king; "and to tell the truth," said the king, "it would be a shame to us, as many as we are, to set upon them any more. For believe me," said King Arthur, "they are three good knights, and especially that knight with the sleeve of gold."

So then they sounded the retreat to quarters; but straight away King Arthur sent word to the four kings and to the mighty duke, and asked them not to let the knight with the sleeve of gold leave them, so that the king might speak with him. Then straight away King Arthur dismounted and took off his armour, and took a little riding horse and rode after Sir Lancelot, for all the while he had kept a watch on him. And so he found him among the four kings and the duke; and there the king invited them all to supper, and they said they would come gladly. And when they had taken off their armour, then King Arthur knew Sir Lancelot, Sir Lavaine and Sir Gareth.

"Ah, Sir Lancelot," said King Arthur, "you have given me and my knights hot work today."

So they all went to Arthur's lodging together, and there was a great feast and great revelry, and the prize was given to Sir Lancelot; and the heralds declared that he had struck down fifty knights, and Sir Gareth thirty-five, and Sir Lavaine twenty-four knights. Then Sir Lancelot told the king and the queen how the lady huntress had shot him in the forest of Windsor, in the buttock, with a broad arrow, and how the wound from it had at that time been six inches deep, and as long. Also Arthur blamed Sir Gareth because he had left his company and held with Sir Lancelot.

"My lord," said Sir Gareth, "he made me a knight, and when I saw him so hard pressed, I thought it was to my honour to help him; for I saw him do so much, and so many noble knights against him. And when I understood that he was Sir Lancelot du Lake, I was ashamed to see so many knights against him alone."

"Truly," said King Arthur to Sir Gareth, "you speak well, and you have done honourably, and won great honour for yourself; and all the days of my life," said King Arthur to Sir Gareth, "you may be sure I shall love you and trust you all the better. For always," said Arthur, "it is an honourable knight's deed to help another honourable knight when he sees him in great danger; for an honourable man will always be loath to see an honourable man shamed. And the man who has no honour, and goes about with cowardice, will never show courtesy, nor any kind of goodness, where he sees a man in any danger, for a coward will never show mercy; and a good man will always do to another man as he would have done to himself."

So then there were great feasts for kings and dukes, and revelry, games and sport, and every kind of nobility was practised; and whoever was courteous, true and faithful to his friend was cherished in that time.

Chapter 25: How true love is likened to summer

And so it went on from Candlemas until after Easter, until the month of May had come, when every lively heart begins to blossom and to bring forth fruit. For just as herbs and trees bring forth fruit and flourish in May, in the same way every joyful heart that is in any way a lover springs up and flourishes in vigorous deeds. For that joyful month of May gives all lovers heart, in something to drive him to some kind of thing more in that month than in any other month, for various reasons. For then all herbs and trees renew a man and woman, and in the same way lovers call back to mind old courtesy and old service, and many kind deeds that were forgotten through neglect. For just as the wasting of winter always wipes out and defaces green summer, so it goes with unstable love in man and woman. For in many people there is no steadfastness; for we may see every day that, at a little blast of winter's wasting, at once we deface and put aside true love, which cost so much, for little or nothing. This is no wisdom or steadfastness, but it is weakness of nature and great dishonour, whoever does it. And so, just as the month of May flowers and flourishes in many gardens, in the same way let every man of honour make his heart flourish in this world, first towards God, and next towards the joy of the one he promised his faith to. For there was never an honourable man or an honourable woman but they loved one better than another; and honour in arms may never be put to shame, but first keep the honour for God, and secondly the quarrel must come from your lady. And such love I call virtuous love.

But nowadays men cannot love for a week without having all their desires. That love cannot last by reason; for where they are quickly agreed, and the heat is hasty, it soon cools. Just so it goes with love nowadays, soon hot, soon cold: this is no steadfastness. But the old love was not like that. Men and women could love each other seven years, and there was no lecherous lust between them, and then there was love, truth and faithfulness. And look, in the same way love was practised in King Arthur's days. And so I liken love nowadays to summer and winter; for just as the one is hot and the other cold, so it goes with love nowadays. So all you who are lovers, call to your remembrance the month of May, like Queen Guinevere, of whom I make a little mention here, because while she lived she was a true lover, and therefore she had a good end.

Here ends the eighteenth book.

And here follows the nineteenth book.

Book Nineteen: Queen Guinevere and Sir Lancelot

Chapter 1: How Queen Guinevere rode out Maying with certain knights of the Round Table, all dressed in green

So it happened in the month of May that Queen Guinevere called her knights of the Round Table to her, and she gave them notice that early the next morning she would ride out Maying, to gather the May greenery in the woods and fields near Westminster.

"And I warn you that there must be none of you who is not well horsed, and that you must all be dressed in green, either in silk or in cloth. And I will bring ten ladies with me, and every knight shall have a lady riding behind him, and every knight shall have a squire and two yeomen. And I want you all to be well horsed," she said.

So they made themselves ready in the brightest and freshest way. And these were the names of the knights: Sir Kay le Seneschal, Sir Agravain, Sir Brandiles, Sir Sagramore le Desirous, Sir Dodinas le Savage, Sir Ozanna le Cure Hardy, Sir Ladinas of the Forest Savage, Sir Persant of Inde, Sir Ironside, who was called the Knight of the Red Launds, and Sir Pelleas, the lover. And these ten knights made themselves ready in the brightest and freshest way to ride with the queen. And so in the morning they mounted their horses with the queen, and rode Maying in the woods and meadows as it pleased them, in great joy and delight. For the queen had planned to be back with King Arthur by ten o'clock at the latest, and that was her intention at the time.

Now there was a knight called Meliagaunce, and he was the son of King Bagdemagus, and at that time this knight held a castle, the gift of King Arthur, within seven miles of Westminster. And this knight, Sir Meliagaunce, loved Queen Guinevere exceedingly well, and so he had done for many long years. And the book says he had been lying in wait to carry off the queen, but he always held back because of Sir Lancelot; for he would on no account meddle with the queen if Sir Lancelot was in her company, or anywhere near her. And at that time it was the custom that the queen never rode out without a great company of men-at-arms about her, and many of them were good knights, and most of them were young men who wanted to win honour. And they were called the Queen's Knights. And in no battle, tournament or joust did any of them ever bear any sign of their own coats of arms, but only plain white shields, and that was why they were called the Queen's Knights. And then, when any of them happened to win great honour by his noble deeds, at the next Feast of Pentecost, if any had been killed or had died (and there was never a year that passed without some dying), the man of greatest honour among those called the Queen's Knights was chosen in the dead man's place. And this was how they all first rose, before they were famous men of honour, both Sir Lancelot and all the rest of them.

But this knight, Sir Meliagaunce, had watched the queen closely and learned her plans, and that Sir Lancelot was not with her, and that she had no men-at-arms with her, only the ten noble knights all dressed in green for Maying. Then he provided himself with some twenty men-at-arms and a hundred archers to destroy the queen and her knights, for he thought that this was the best time to take the queen.

Chapter 2: How Sir Meliagaunce captured the queen and her knights, who were badly wounded in the fighting

So when the queen and all her knights had gone Maying, and all of them were decked with herbs, mosses and flowers in the best and freshest way, just then Sir Meliagaunce came out of a wood with some eight score men, a hundred and sixty, well armed, as if they were going to fight a pitched battle. And he ordered the queen and her knights to stay where they were, for they would stay whether they liked it or not.

"Traitor knight," said Queen Guinevere, "what do you mean to do? Will you shame yourself? Remember that you are a king's son, and a knight of the Round Table, and here you are about to dishonour the noble king who made you a knight. You shame all knighthood and yourself. And me, let me tell you, you shall never shame, for I would rather cut my own throat in two than let you dishonour me."

"As for all this talk," said Sir Meliagaunce, "let it be as it may. For believe me, madam, I have loved you for many a year, and never before now could I get you at such an advantage as I have you now, and so I will take you as I find you."

Then all ten of the noble knights spoke at once, and said, "Sir Meliagaunce, you may be sure that you are about to put your honour in danger of disgrace, and you also mean to put our lives in danger, though we are unarmed. You have us at a great advantage, for it seems you have been lying in wait for us. But rather than let you bring shame on the queen and on us all, we would just as soon lose our lives, for if we did otherwise, we would be shamed for ever."

Then Sir Meliagaunce said, "Defend yourselves as well as you can, and keep the queen."

Then the ten knights of the Round Table drew their swords, and the others charged at them with their spears, and the ten knights stood up to them manfully, and struck their spears aside so that no spear did them any harm. Then they laid into each other with swords, and very soon Sir Kay, Sir Sagramore, Sir Agravain, Sir Dodinas, Sir Ladinas and Sir Ozanna were struck to the ground with terrible wounds. Then Sir Brandiles, and Sir Persant, Sir Ironside and Sir Pelleas fought long, and they were badly wounded. For these ten knights, before ever they were laid on the ground, killed forty men of the boldest and best of them.

So when the queen saw her knights so grievously wounded, and that they must be killed in the end, then out of pity and sorrow she cried out to Sir Meliagaunce, "Don't kill my noble knights, and I will go with you on this condition: that you spare them, and let them be hurt no more, and that they are taken with me wherever you take me. For I will kill myself rather than go with you, unless these noble knights of mine may stay in my presence."

"Madam," said Meliagaunce, "for your sake they shall be taken with you into my own castle, provided that you do as you are told, and ride with me."

Then the queen begged the four knights to stop fighting, and said that she and they would not be parted.

"Madam," said Sir Pelleas, "we will do as you do, for as for me, I care nothing for my life or death."

For, as the French book says, Sir Pelleas dealt such blows there that no armour could withstand him.

Chapter 3: How Sir Lancelot got word that the queen had been captured, and how Sir Meliagaunce laid an ambush for Lancelot

Then at the queen's command they left off fighting, and set the wounded knights on horseback, some sitting up, some slung across their horses, so that it was pitiful to see them. And then Sir Meliagaunce ordered the queen and all her knights that none of her company should leave her; for he was badly afraid of Sir Lancelot du Lake, in case he should get any word of it. The queen saw all this, and secretly she called to her a page of her chamber who had a swift horse.

"Go," she said to him, "when you see your chance, and take this ring to Sir Lancelot du Lake, and beg him, as he loves me, to come to me and rescue me, if he ever wants to have joy of me. And don't spare your horse," said the queen, "for water or for land."

So the boy watched for his chance, and swiftly he put the spurs to his horse, and rode away as fast as he could. And when Sir Meliagaunce saw him flee like that, he understood that it was by the queen's command, to warn Sir Lancelot. Then the best mounted of them chased him and shot at him, but the boy got clear of them all in no time.

And then Sir Meliagaunce said to the queen, "Madam, you mean to betray me, but I will make arrangements for Sir Lancelot, so that he shall not get to you easily."

And then he rode with her, and all of them, to his castle, in all the haste they could. And on the way Sir Meliagaunce set the best archers he could find in his country in an ambush, thirty of them, to lie in wait for Sir Lancelot, ordering them that if they saw a knight of that kind come along the road on a white horse, they must on no account fail to kill his horse, but on no account fight him hand to hand, "for he is too bold to be overcome."

So this was done, and they came to his castle. But the queen would on no account let any of the ten knights or her ladies out of her sight, but they were always in her presence. For the book says that Sir Meliagaunce did not dare to use force, for fear of Sir Lancelot, since he believed that Lancelot had been warned.

So when the boy had got away from Sir Meliagaunce's company, within a while he came to Westminster, and at once he found Sir Lancelot. And when he had given his message, and handed him the queen's ring, "Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "now I am shamed for ever, unless I can rescue that noble lady from dishonour."

Then he eagerly called for his armour. And all the while the boy told Sir Lancelot how the ten knights had fought marvellously, and how Sir Pelleas, and Sir Ironside, and Sir Brandiles, and Sir Persant of Inde had fought strongly, but above all Sir Pelleas, whom no one could withstand; and how they had all fought until at last they were laid on the ground; and how then the queen had made terms to save their lives, and had gone with Sir Meliagaunce.

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "that most noble lady, that she should be so ruined! I would rather," said Sir Lancelot, "than have all France, that I had been there well armed."

So when Sir Lancelot was armed and on his horse, he asked the page of the queen's chamber to tell Sir Lavaine how suddenly he had left, and for what reason. "And beg him, as he loves me, to hurry after me, and not to stop until he comes to the castle where Sir Meliagaunce stays, or lives. For there," said Sir Lancelot, "he shall hear of me, if I am a living man, and I will rescue the queen and the ten knights whom he has treacherously taken, and I will prove that on his head, and on all who side with him."

Chapter 4: How Sir Lancelot's horse was killed, and how Sir Lancelot rode in a cart to rescue the queen

Then Sir Lancelot rode as fast as he could, and the book says he took to the water at Westminster Bridge, and made his horse swim over the Thames to Lambeth. And then within a while he came to the very place where the ten noble knights had fought with Sir Meliagaunce. And then Sir Lancelot followed the track until he came to a wood, and there was a narrow way, and there the thirty archers ordered Sir Lancelot to turn back, and follow that track no further.

"What authority do you have," said Sir Lancelot, "to make me, a knight of the Round Table, leave my rightful way?"

"You'll leave this way, or else you'll go it on foot, for be sure of this, your horse will be killed."

"That's no great feat," said Sir Lancelot, "to kill my horse. But as for myself, when my horse is killed, I don't give a straw for you, not if you were five hundred more."

So then they shot Sir Lancelot's horse, and struck him with many arrows. And then Sir Lancelot got clear of his horse, and went on foot. But there were so many ditches and hedges between them and him that he could not get at any of them.

"Alas, for shame," said Lancelot, "that ever one knight should betray another knight! But it is an old saying: a good man is never in danger except when he is in the power of a coward."

Then Sir Lancelot walked a while, and then he was badly weighed down by his armour, his shield, and his spear, and all that belonged to him. Believe me, he was sorely troubled, and he was very unwilling to leave behind anything that belonged to him, for he greatly feared the treachery of Sir Meliagaunce.

Then by chance a cart came by him, which had come there to fetch wood.

"Tell me, carter," said Sir Lancelot, "what shall I give you to let me jump into your cart, and for you to take me to a castle two miles from here?"

"You're not getting into my cart," said the carter, "for I've been sent to fetch wood for my lord, Sir Meliagaunce."

"He is the one I want to speak with," said Sir Lancelot.

"You're not coming with me," said the carter.

Then Sir Lancelot leapt at him, and gave him such a blow that he fell to the ground stone dead. Then the other carter, his companion, was afraid, and expected to go the same way. And then he cried, "Fair lord, save my life, and I will take you wherever you like."

"Then I order you," said Sir Lancelot, "to drive me and this cart straight to Sir Meliagaunce's gate."

"Jump up into the cart," said the carter, "and you'll be there in no time."

So the carter drove on at a great gallop, and Sir Lancelot's horse followed the cart, with more than forty arrows in him, broad-headed and rough.

And for more than an hour and a half Dame Guinevere had been waiting in a bay window with her ladies, and she saw an armed knight standing in a cart.

"Look, madam," said a lady, "there's a fine armed knight riding in a cart. I suppose he's riding to his hanging."

"Where?" said the queen.

Then she saw by his shield that it was he himself, Sir Lancelot du Lake. And then she saw his horse coming along behind that cart, all the way, and all the way it trod its own guts and its belly under its feet.

"Alas," said the queen, "now I see and know well that happy is the man who has a trusty friend. Ah, most noble knight," said Queen Guinevere, "I see you are in a hard spot, when you ride in a cart."

Then she rebuked the lady who had likened Sir Lancelot riding in a cart to riding to his hanging. "It was foul-mouthed," said the queen, "and an evil comparison, to liken the most noble knight in the world to such a shameful death. O Jesus defend him and keep him," said the queen, "from any harmful end."

By this time Sir Lancelot had come to the gates of that castle, and there he got down, and shouted, so that the whole castle rang with it, "Where are you, false traitor, Sir Meliagaunce, and knight of the Round Table? Come out here now, you traitor knight, you and your company with you; for here I am, Sir Lancelot du Lake, who will fight with you."

And with that he flung the gate wide open on the porter, and struck him under the ear with his gauntlet, so that his neck broke in two.

Chapter 5: How Sir Meliagaunce begged the queen's forgiveness, and how she calmed Sir Lancelot, and other matters

When Sir Meliagaunce heard that Sir Lancelot was there, he ran to Queen Guinevere, and fell on his knee, and said, "Mercy, madam! Now I put myself wholly at your mercy."

"What's the matter with you now?" said Queen Guinevere. "Truly, I might well have known that some good knight would avenge me, even if my lord Arthur knew nothing of this work of yours."

"Madam," said Sir Meliagaunce, "all that is amiss on my part shall be put right exactly as you yourself decide, and I put myself wholly at your mercy."

"What would you have me do?" said the queen.

"I would ask no more," said Meliagaunce, "than that you take it all into your own hands, and that you govern my lord Sir Lancelot. And whatever welcome can be given him in this poor castle, you and he shall have until tomorrow, and then you and all of them may go back to Westminster. And my body and all that I have I will put at your command."

"You speak well," said the queen, "and peace is always better than war, and the less talk there is, the greater my honour."

Then the queen and her ladies went down to the knight, Sir Lancelot, who stood in the inner court, angry beyond measure, waiting for battle. And all the while he kept calling, "You traitor knight, come out!"

Then the queen came to him and said, "Sir Lancelot, why are you so worked up?"

"Ah, madam," said Sir Lancelot, "why do you ask me that? It seems to me," said Sir Lancelot, "that you ought to be angrier than I am, for you have suffered the harm and the dishonour. For believe me, madam, my harm is only small, the killing of a mare's son, a mere horse; but the insult grieves me far more than all my harm."

"Truly," said the queen, "you speak the truth. But I thank you with all my heart," said the queen, "but you must come in with me peaceably, for everything has been put in my hands, and all that is evil shall turn out for the best. For the knight bitterly repents of the misdeed that he has fallen into."

"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "since it is so that you have come to terms with him, as for me I cannot go against it, even though Sir Meliagaunce has acted very shamefully towards me, and like a coward. Ah, madam," said Sir Lancelot, "if I had known you would come to terms with him so soon, I would not have made such haste to you."

"Why do you say that?" said the queen. "Do you regret your good deeds? Believe me," said the queen, "I never came to terms with him for any favour or love I had for him, but to put a stop to every shameful rumour."

"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "you know very well that I was never willing or glad to have shameful slander or rumour. And there is neither king, queen nor knight alive, except my lord King Arthur, and you, madam, who could stop me from making Sir Meliagaunce's heart go very cold before ever I left this place."

"That I know well," said the queen, "but what more do you want? You shall have everything arranged just as you wish to have it."

"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "so long as you are pleased, I don't mind. As for me, you will soon please me."

Just then the queen took Sir Lancelot by his bare hand, for he had taken off his gauntlet, and so she went with him to her chamber; and then she ordered him to be unarmed. And then Sir Lancelot asked where the ten knights were who had been badly wounded. So she showed them to Sir Lancelot, and there they rejoiced greatly at his coming, and Sir Lancelot grieved greatly over their wounds, and lamented them deeply. And there Sir Lancelot told them how in his cowardice and treachery Meliagaunce had set archers to kill his horse, and how he had been forced to put himself in a cart. So they all complained to each other; and they would very gladly have been avenged, but they held their peace because of the queen. Then, as the French book says, Sir Lancelot was called for many a day afterwards le Chevaler du Chariot, the Knight of the Cart, and did many deeds, and had great adventures. And so we leave this tale of le Chevaler du Chariot, and turn to this tale.

So Sir Lancelot had a warm welcome from the queen, and then Sir Lancelot made a promise with the queen that the same night Sir Lancelot would come to a window that faced out onto a garden. And that window was barred with iron, and there Sir Lancelot promised to meet her when everyone was asleep.

So then Sir Lavaine came riding hard to the gates, shouting, "Where is my lord, Sir Lancelot du Lake?"

Then he was sent for, and when Sir Lavaine saw Sir Lancelot, he said, "My lord, I could see well you were in a hard spot, for I found your horse that was killed with arrows."

"As for that," said Sir Lancelot, "I beg you, Sir Lavaine, speak of other things, and let this pass, and we will put it right another time when we best can."

Chapter 6: How Sir Lancelot came to the queen in the night and lay with her, and how Sir Meliagaunce accused the queen of treason

Then the knights who were hurt had their wounds probed, and soft salves were laid on their wounds. And so the time passed until supper, and all the welcome that could be given them there was given to the queen and all her knights. Then, when it was time, they went to their rooms. But the queen would on no account allow the wounded knights to be away from her, so they were laid in alcoves beside her chamber, on beds and pillows, so that she could see to them herself, and see that they lacked nothing.

So when Sir Lancelot was in the room that had been assigned to him, he called Sir Lavaine to him, and told him that he must go that night to speak with his lady, Dame Guinevere.

"Sir," said Sir Lavaine, "let me go with you, if you please, for I am badly afraid of the treachery of Sir Meliagaunce."

"No," said Sir Lancelot, "I thank you, but I will have nobody with me."

Then Sir Lancelot took his sword in his hand, and went secretly to a place where he had noticed a ladder beforehand, and he took it under his arm, and carried it through the garden, and set it up against the window. And there the queen was ready at once to meet him. And then they made their complaints to each other about many different things, and then Sir Lancelot wished that he could come in to her.

"Believe me," said the queen, "I would like it as much as you, that you could come in to me."

"Would you, madam," said Sir Lancelot, "with all your heart, that I were with you?"

"Yes, truly," said the queen.

"Now I will prove my strength," said Sir Lancelot, "for your love."

And then he set his hands on the bars of iron, and he pulled at them with such strength that he burst them clean out of the stone walls, and with that one of the iron bars cut through the flesh of his hand to the bone. And then he leapt into the chamber to the queen.

"Make no noise," said the queen, "for my wounded knights are lying here close by me."

So, to pass on with this tale, Sir Lancelot went to bed with the queen, and he paid no attention to his hurt hand, but took his pleasure and his delight until the dawning of the day. And believe me, he did not sleep but kept watch, and when he saw that the time had come when he could stay no longer, he took his leave and left by the window, and put it back together as well as he could, and so went off to his own room. And there he told Sir Lavaine how he was hurt. Then Sir Lavaine dressed his hand and stopped the bleeding, and put a glove on it, so that it would not be noticed. And so the queen lay long in her bed, until nine o'clock.

Then Sir Meliagaunce went to the queen's chamber, and found her ladies there already dressed.

"Jesus have mercy," said Sir Meliagaunce, "what is the matter with you, madam, that you sleep so long?"

And with that he opened the bed-curtain to look at her. And then he saw where she lay, and all the sheet and pillow were bloodied with the blood of Sir Lancelot and his hurt hand. When Sir Meliagaunce saw that blood, he judged that she had been false to the king, and that one of the wounded knights had lain with her all that night.

"Ah, madam," said Sir Meliagaunce, "now I have found you a false traitress to my lord Arthur. For now I can prove well that it was not for nothing that you had these wounded knights laid within the bounds of your chamber. And so I will accuse you of treason before my lord, King Arthur. And now I have caught you, madam, in a shameful deed; and that they are all false, or some of them, I will make good by combat, for a wounded knight has lain with you this night."

"That is false," said the queen, "and I appeal to them all as witnesses."

Then, when the ten knights heard Sir Meliagaunce's words, they all spoke with one voice and said to Sir Meliagaunce, "You lie, and you wrongly accuse us of such a deed, and any one of us will make that good by combat. Choose whichever of us you like, when we are healed of our wounds."

"You will not," said Sir Meliagaunce. "Away with your proud talk, for here you can all see," said Sir Meliagaunce, "that a wounded knight has lain with the queen this night."

Then they were all ashamed when they saw that blood. And believe me, Sir Meliagaunce was exceedingly glad that he had the queen at such an advantage, for he thought that by this he could cover up his own treason. So, in the middle of this uproar, Sir Lancelot came in, and found them all in a great commotion.

Chapter 7: How Sir Lancelot answered for the queen and pledged to fight Sir Meliagaunce, and how Sir Lancelot was caught in a trap

"What is all this?" said Sir Lancelot.

Then Sir Meliagaunce told them what he had found, and showed them the queen's bed.

"Truly," said Sir Lancelot, "you did not act rightly, or like a knight, in touching a queen's bed while its curtains were drawn and she was lying in it. For I dare say my lord Arthur himself would not have drawn back her curtains while she was in her bed, unless it had pleased him to lie down beside her. And so you have acted dishonourably and shamefully, to your own disgrace."

"I don't know what you mean," said Sir Meliagaunce, "but I am quite sure that one of her wounded knights has lain with her this night, and so I will prove with my hands that she is a traitress to my lord Arthur."

"Be careful what you do," said Lancelot, "for if you say so, and will prove it, your challenge will be taken up."

"My lord, Sir Lancelot," said Sir Meliagaunce, "I advise you to be careful what you do. For though you are as good a knight as any, and you know well that you are renowned as the best knight in the world, still you should think twice before doing battle in a wrong quarrel, for God will have a stroke in every battle."

"As for that," said Sir Lancelot, "God is to be feared. But to that I say no, plainly: that this night none of these ten wounded knights lay with my lady Queen Guinevere, and I will prove with my hands that what you say is untrue."

"Take it," said Sir Meliagaunce, "here is my glove, as pledge that she is a traitress to my lord, King Arthur, and that this night one of the wounded knights lay with her."

"And I accept your glove," said Sir Lancelot.

And so the pledges were sealed with their seal rings, and handed over to the ten knights.

"On what day shall we do battle together?" said Sir Lancelot.

"A week from today," said Sir Meliagaunce, "in the field beside Westminster."

"I agree," said Sir Lancelot.

"But now," said Sir Meliagaunce, "since it is so that we must fight together, I beg you, as you are a noble knight, to plan no treachery against me, and no foul play, in the meantime, and to let no one do so on your behalf."

"So help me God," said Sir Lancelot, "you shall know very well that I was never a man of that character. For I appeal to all knights who have ever known me: I never dealt in treachery, nor did I ever love the company of any man who dealt in treachery."

"Then let us go to dinner," said Meliagaunce, "and after dinner you and the queen and all of you may ride to Westminster."

"Gladly," said Sir Lancelot.

Then Sir Meliagaunce said to Sir Lancelot, "Would you like to see the passages of this castle?"

"With pleasure," said Sir Lancelot.

And then they went together from room to room, for Sir Lancelot feared no dangers. For a man of honour and of prowess always fears dangers least, because he thinks every man is as he is himself; but the man who deals in treachery often puts another man in great danger. So it happened to Sir Lancelot, who feared no danger, that as he went with Sir Meliagaunce he stepped on a trapdoor and the board tipped over, and Sir Lancelot fell down more than ten fathoms into a cave full of straw. And then Sir Meliagaunce went away, and made no fuss, as if he did not know where he was.

And when Sir Lancelot was missed like this, they wondered what had become of him. And then the queen and many of them thought that he had left, as he often used to do, suddenly. For Sir Meliagaunce quickly had Sir Lavaine's horse taken away and put aside, so that they would all believe Sir Lancelot had left suddenly. So the time passed until after dinner. And then Sir Lavaine would not rest until he had arranged litters for the wounded knights, so that they could be laid in them; and so, with the queen and all of them, both ladies and gentlewomen and others, they went to Westminster. And there the knights told King Arthur how Meliagaunce had accused the queen of high treason, and how Sir Lancelot had accepted his glove, "and a week from today they will do battle before you."

"By my head," said King Arthur, "I fear Sir Meliagaunce has taken a heavy task upon himself. But where is Sir Lancelot?" said the king.

"Sir," they all said, "we don't know where he is, but we think he has ridden off to some adventure, as he very often does, for he has Sir Lavaine's horse."

"Let him be," said the king. "He will turn up, unless he has been trapped by some treachery."

Chapter 8: How Sir Lancelot was freed from prison by a lady, and took a white warhorse and came to keep his appointed day

So we leave Sir Lancelot lying in that cave in great pain. And every day a lady came and brought him his food and his drink, and wooed him, wanting to lie with him; and always the noble knight, Sir Lancelot, told her no.

"Sir Lancelot," she said, "you are not wise, for you can never get out of this prison unless you have my help. And besides, your lady, Queen Guinevere, will be burned through your failing, unless you are there on the day of the battle."

"God forbid," said Sir Lancelot, "that she should be burned through my failing. And if it turns out," said Sir Lancelot, "that I cannot be there, it will be well understood, by the king and by the queen and by all men of honour, that I am dead, sick, or in prison. For all men who know me will say for me that I am in some bad trouble if I am not there that day. And I know well there is some good knight, either of my blood or some other who loves me, who will take up my quarrel. And therefore," said Sir Lancelot, "you may be sure you will not frighten me; and if there were no other woman in all this land but you, I would not lie with you."

"Then you're shamed," said the lady, "and ruined for ever."

"As for the world's shame, Jesus defend me from it; and as for my distress, it is welcome, whatever it is that God sends me."

So she came to him on the same day that the battle was to be, and said, "Sir Lancelot, I think you are too hard-hearted. But if you would only kiss me once, I would set you free, and give you your armour, and the best horse in Sir Meliagaunce's stable."

"As for kissing you," said Sir Lancelot, "I may do that and lose no honour. And believe me, if I thought there were any dishonour in kissing you, I would not do it."

Then he kissed her, and then she got him out, and brought him to his armour. And when he was armed, she took him to a stable where twelve good warhorses stood, and told him to choose the best. Then Sir Lancelot looked at a white warhorse that pleased him best; and at once he ordered the grooms to saddle him quickly with the best war saddle there was; and it was done as he ordered. Then he took his spear in his hand, and his sword by his side, and commended the lady to God, and said, "Lady, for this good deed I will do you service, if it is ever in my power."

Chapter 9: How Sir Lancelot arrived just as Sir Meliagaunce was waiting for him in the field, and made ready for battle

Now we leave Sir Lancelot galloping as fast as he could, and speak of Queen Guinevere, who was brought to a fire to be burned. For Sir Meliagaunce was sure, so he thought, that Sir Lancelot would not be at that battle; and so he kept crying out to King Arthur to do him justice, or else bring out Sir Lancelot du Lake. Then the king and all the court were sorely dismayed and ashamed that the queen should be burned through Sir Lancelot's failing.

"My lord Arthur," said Sir Lavaine, "you may understand that all is not well with my lord Sir Lancelot. For if he were alive, and not sick or in prison, believe me, he would be here; for you never heard that he ever failed in his part for anyone he was to do battle for. And therefore," said Sir Lavaine, "my lord King Arthur, I beg you to give me leave to do battle here this day for my lord and master, and to save my lady the queen."

"Many thanks, noble Sir Lavaine," said King Arthur, "for I dare say that everything Sir Meliagaunce charges against my lady the queen is false. For I have spoken with all ten of the wounded knights, and there is not one of them, if he were whole and able to do battle, who would not prove on Sir Meliagaunce's body that what he charges against my queen is false."

"So will I," said Sir Lavaine, "in the defence of my lord Sir Lancelot, if you will give me leave."

"Now I give you leave," said King Arthur, "and do your best, for I dare well say there has been some treason done to Sir Lancelot."

Then Sir Lavaine was armed and horsed, and quickly he rode to the end of the lists to carry out this battle. And just as the heralds were about to cry, "Lesses les aler!", which is to say, "Let them go!", at that very moment in came Sir Lancelot, driving with all the force of his horse. And then Arthur cried, "Ho!" and "Hold!" Then Sir Lancelot was called on horseback before King Arthur, and there he told openly before the king and everyone how Sir Meliagaunce had treated him from first to last. And when the king and the queen and all the lords knew of the treason of Sir Meliagaunce, they were all ashamed on his behalf. Then Queen Guinevere was sent for, and set beside the king, in great trust in her champion. And then there was nothing more to say, but Sir Lancelot and Sir Meliagaunce squared up to each other for battle, and took their spears. And so they came together like thunder, and there Sir Lancelot bore him down clean over his horse's rump. And then Sir Lancelot dismounted and set his shield on his shoulder, with his sword in his hand, and Sir Meliagaunce in the same way squared up to him. And there they struck many great strokes at each other; and at last Sir Lancelot struck him such a blow on the helmet that he fell sideways to the ground. And then he cried out to him aloud, "Most noble knight, Sir Lancelot du Lake, save my life, for I yield myself to you. And I beg you, as you are a knight and a fellow of the Round Table, do not kill me, for I yield myself as beaten; and whether I live or die, I put myself in the king's hands and yours."

Then Sir Lancelot did not know what to do, for he would rather have had his revenge on Sir Meliagaunce than all the riches of the world. And Sir Lancelot looked up at Queen Guinevere, to see if he could tell by any sign or look what she would have done. And then the queen nodded at Sir Lancelot, as though she would say, "Kill him." Sir Lancelot knew full well by the nod of her head that she wanted him dead. Then Sir Lancelot told him to get up, for shame, and fight that battle to the uttermost.

"No," said Sir Meliagaunce, "I will never get up until you accept me as yielded and recreant."

"I will make you a generous offer," said Sir Lancelot. "That is to say, I will take the armour off my head and off the left quarter of my body, all that can be unarmed, and have my left hand tied behind me, so that it cannot help me; and just so I will do battle with you."

Then Sir Meliagaunce sprang to his feet, and said aloud, "My lord Arthur, take note of this offer, for I will take it. And let him be unarmed and bound according to his offer."

"What do you say?" said King Arthur to Sir Lancelot. "Will you stand by your offer?"

"Yes, my lord," said Sir Lancelot, "I will never go back on what I have once said."

Then the marshals of the field took the armour off Sir Lancelot, first from his head, and then from his left arm and his left side, and they bound his left arm behind his back, without a shield or anything, and then they were set against each other. Believe me, many a lady and knight marvelled that Sir Lancelot would put himself in danger like that. Then Sir Meliagaunce came with his sword raised high, and Sir Lancelot showed him openly his bare head and his bare left side. And when he thought he would strike him on the bare head, then swiftly Sir Lancelot drew back his left leg and his left side, and put his right hand and his sword to meet that stroke, and so turned it aside with great skill. And then, with great force, Sir Lancelot struck him such a blow on the helmet that the stroke split the head in two. Then there was no more to do, but he was dragged out of the field. And at the earnest request of the knights of the Round Table, the king allowed him to be buried, with an inscription over him telling who killed him and for what cause he was killed. And then the king and the queen made more of Sir Lancelot du Lake, and he was more cherished, than ever he had been before.

Chapter 10: How Sir Urre came to Arthur's court to be healed of his wounds, and how King Arthur would be the first to handle him

Then, as the French book tells, there was a good knight in the land of Hungary, and his name was Sir Urre. And he was a knight-errant, and wherever he could hear of any deeds of honour, there he would be. So it happened that in Spain there was an earl's son whose name was Alphegus; and at a great tournament in Spain this Sir Urre, the knight of Hungary, and Sir Alphegus of Spain met each other out of sheer envy, and each took on the other to the uttermost. And by chance Sir Urre killed Sir Alphegus, the earl's son of Spain. But this knight who was killed had given Sir Urre, before ever he was killed, seven great wounds, three on the head, and four on his body and on his left hand. And this Sir Alphegus had a mother, who was a great sorceress; and she, in spite for her son's death, worked by her subtle arts so that Sir Urre should never be whole, but his wounds should always fester at one time and bleed at another, so that he should never be whole until the best knight in the world had probed his wounds. And so she boasted of it, and through that it became known that Sir Urre would never be whole.

Then his mother had a horse-litter made, and put him in it between two palfreys. And then she took Sir Urre's sister with him, a very beautiful damsel, whose name was Felelolie; and then she took a page with them to look after their horses; and so they led Sir Urre through many countries. For, as the French book says, she led him like this for seven years through all the Christian lands, and she could never find a knight who could ease her son. So she came into Scotland and into the lands of England, and by chance she came, near the feast of Pentecost, to King Arthur's court, which at that time was held at Carlisle. And when she came there, she made it openly known that she had come into that land to heal her son.

Then King Arthur had that lady called, and asked her the reason why she had brought that wounded knight into that land.

"My most noble king," said that lady, "believe me, I brought him here to be healed of his wounds, which for all these seven years could not be made whole."

And then she told the king where he was wounded, and by whom, and how the dead knight's mother had revealed in her pride how she had brought it about by enchantment, so that he should never be whole until the best knight in the world had probed his wounds. "And so I have passed through all the Christian lands to have him healed, except this land. And if I fail to heal him here in this land, I will never take any more trouble over it; and that is a pity, for he was a good knight, and of great nobility."

"What is his name?" said Arthur.

"My good and gracious lord," she said, "his name is Sir Urre of the Mount."

"In good time," said the king, "and since you have come into this land, you are very welcome. And believe me, here your son shall be healed, if ever any Christian man can heal him. And to give all other men of honour heart, I myself will try to handle your son, and so shall all the kings, dukes and earls who are here with me at this time. I will command them to it, and I know well they will obey and do as I command. And believe me," said King Arthur to Urre's sister, "I will begin to handle him, and probe his wounds as well as I can, not presuming that I am worthy enough to heal your son by my deeds; but I will encourage other men of honour to do as I do."

And then the king commanded all the kings, dukes and earls, and all the noble knights of the Round Table who were there at that time, to come into the meadow of Carlisle. And at that time there were only a hundred and ten of the Round Table there, for forty knights were away. And so here we must begin with King Arthur, as it is natural to begin with him who was the man of greatest honour of any christened man at that time.

Chapter 11: How King Arthur handled Sir Urre, and after him many other knights of the Round Table

Then King Arthur looked at Sir Urre, and the king thought he would be a very fine man when he was whole. And then King Arthur had him taken down off the litter and laid him on the ground, and a cushion of gold was laid there for him to kneel on.

And then noble Arthur said, "Fair knight, I am sorry for your hurt, and to encourage all the other noble knights I will ask you gently to allow me to handle your wounds."

"Most noble Christian king," said Urre, "do as you wish, for I am at the mercy of God, and at your command."

So then Arthur gently handled him, and then some of his wounds began to bleed again. Then King Clarence of Northumberland probed them, and it would not be. And then Sir Barant le Apres, who was called the King with the Hundred Knights, tried and failed; and so did King Uriens of the land of Gore; so did King Anguish of Ireland; so did King Nentres of Garlot; so did King Carados of Scotland; so did the Duke Galahalt, the high prince; so did Constantine, who was Sir Cador's son of Cornwall; so did Duke Chaleins of Clarance; so did the Earl Ulbause; so did the Earl Lambaile; so did the Earl Aristause.

Then in came Sir Gawain with his three sons, Sir Gingalin, Sir Florence and Sir Lovel (these two were begotten on Sir Brandiles' sister); and they all failed. Then in came Sir Agravain, Sir Gaheris, Sir Mordred, and the good knight Sir Gareth, who in true knighthood was worth all his brothers. So came the knights of Lancelot's kin; but Sir Lancelot was not at court at that time, for he was away then on his adventures. Then came Sir Lionel, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Blamore de Ganis, Sir Bleoberis de Ganis, Sir Gahalantine, Sir Galihodin, Sir Menaduke, Sir Villiers the Valiant, Sir Hebes le Renoumes. All these were of Sir Lancelot's kin, and they all failed. Then in came Sir Sagramore le Desirous, Sir Dodinas le Savage, Sir Dinadan, Sir Bruin le Noire, whom Sir Kay named La Cote Male Taile, and Sir Kay the seneschal, Sir Kay de Stranges, Sir Meliot de Logres, Sir Petipase of Winchelsea, Sir Galleron of Galway, Sir Melion of the Mountain, Sir Cardok, Sir Uwain les Avoutres, and Sir Ozanna le Cure Hardy.

Then in came Sir Astamor, and Sir Gromere, Grummor's son, Sir Crosselm, and Sir Servause le Breuse, who was said to be an exceedingly strong knight. For, as the book says, the chief Lady of the Lake feasted Sir Lancelot and Servause le Breuse, and when she had feasted them both, at different times, she asked each of them to grant her a favour. And they granted it her. And then she asked Sir Servause to promise her never to do battle against Sir Lancelot du Lake, and in the same way she asked Sir Lancelot never to do battle against Sir Servause; and so each of them promised her. For the French book says that Sir Servause never had the heart or the desire to do battle against any man, except against giants, and against dragons and wild beasts. So we pass on to those who, at the king's request, all made ready, all who were there at that high feast of the knights of the Round Table, to probe Sir Urre's wounds; and the king did it with this intent, to learn which was the noblest knight among them.

Then came Sir Aglovale, Sir Durnore, and Sir Tor, who was begotten on the wife of Aries the cowherd, though he was begotten before Aries married her; and King Pellinore fathered them all: first Sir Tor, Sir Aglovale, Sir Durnore, Sir Lamorak, one of the noblest knights that ever was in Arthur's days as a knight of this world, and Sir Percival, who was peerless, except for Sir Galahad, in holy deeds; but they died in the quest of the Holy Grail. Then came Sir Griflet le Fise de Dieu, Sir Lucan the butler, Sir Bedivere his brother, Sir Brandiles, Sir Constantine, Sir Cador's son of Cornwall, who was king after Arthur's days, and Sir Clegis, Sir Sadok, Sir Dinas the seneschal of Cornwall, Sir Fergus, Sir Driant, Sir Lambegus, Sir Clarrus of Clermont, Sir Cloddrus, Sir Hectimere, Sir Edward of Caernarvon, Sir Dinas, Sir Priamus, who was christened by Sir Tristram, the noble knight, and these three were brothers; Sir Helin le Blank, who was Sir Bors's son, whom he fathered on King Brandegore's daughter, and Sir Brian de Listinoise; Sir Gaunter, Sir Raynold and Sir Gilmere, three brothers whom Sir Lancelot overcame on a bridge when he wore Sir Kay's armour. Sir Guyart le Petite, Sir Bellangere le Beuse, who was the son of the good knight Sir Alisander le Orphelin, who was killed by the treason of King Mark. That same traitor king also killed the noble knight Sir Tristram, with a sharp sword, as he sat harping before his lady Isolde the Fair; and his death was mourned by every knight there ever was in Arthur's days. There were never any so mourned as Sir Tristram and Sir Lamorak, for they were treacherously killed, Sir Tristram by King Mark, and Sir Lamorak by Sir Gawain and his brothers. And this Sir Bellangere avenged the death of his father Alisander, and of Sir Tristram, for he killed King Mark; and Isolde the Fair died swooning on the body of Sir Tristram, and that was a great pity. And all who were with King Mark and had agreed to the death of Sir Tristram were killed, such as Sir Andred and many others.
