Then came Sir Hebes, Sir Morganore, Sir Sentraile, Sir Suppinabilis, Sir Bellangere le Orgulous, whom the good knight Sir Lamorak overcame in open battle; Sir Neroveus and Sir Plenorius, two good knights whom Sir Lancelot overcame; Sir Darras, Sir Harry le Fise Lake, Sir Erminide, brother to King Hermaunce, for whom Sir Palomides fought at the Red City against two brothers; and Sir Selises of the Dolorous Tower, Sir Edward of Orkney, Sir Ironside, who was called the noble Knight of the Red Launds, whom Sir Gareth overcame for the love of Dame Lionesse, Sir Arrok de Grevaunt, Sir Degrane Saunce Velany, who fought with the giant of the Black Hill, and Sir Epinogris, who was the son of the King of Northumberland. Sir Pelleas, who loved the lady Ettard, and he would have died for love of her had it not been for one of the Ladies of the Lake, whose name was Dame Nimue; and she married Sir Pelleas, and she kept him safe so that he was never killed; and he was a very noble knight. And Sir Lamiel of Cardiff, who was a great lover. Sir Plaine de Fors, Sir Melias de Lile, Sir Bohart le Cure Hardy, who was King Arthur's son, Sir Mador de la Porte, Sir Colgrevance, Sir Hervise de la Forest Savage, Sir Marrok, the good knight who was betrayed by his wife, for she made him a werewolf, a man turned into a wolf by magic, for seven years; Sir Persant, Sir Pertolepe, his brother, who was called the Green Knight, and Sir Perimones, brother to them both, who was called the Red Knight, whom Sir Gareth overcame when he was called Beaumains. All these hundred and ten knights probed Sir Urre's wounds by the command of King Arthur.

Chapter 12: How Sir Lancelot was commanded by Arthur to handle his wounds, and at once he was completely whole, and how they thanked God

"Jesus have mercy," said King Arthur, "where is Sir Lancelot du Lake, that he is not here at this time?"

And as they stood and talked of many things, someone spotted Sir Lancelot riding towards them, and told the king.

"Quiet," said the king. "Let nothing at all be said until he has come to us."

So when Sir Lancelot saw King Arthur, he dismounted from his horse and came to the king, and greeted him and all of them. As soon as the maiden, Sir Urre's sister, saw Sir Lancelot, she ran to her brother where he lay in his litter, and said, "Brother, a knight has come here to whom my heart goes out greatly."

"Fair sister," said Sir Urre, "my heart too grows light towards him, and I truly hope now to be healed; for my heart goes out to him more than to all these who have probed my wounds."

Then Arthur said to Sir Lancelot, "You must do as we have done," and told Sir Lancelot what they had done, and showed him all of them who had probed his wounds.

"Jesus defend me," said Sir Lancelot, "that I should presume, when so many kings and knights have tried and failed, to achieve what all of you, my lords, could not achieve."

"You have no choice," said King Arthur, "for I will command you to do as we have all done."

"My most renowned lord," said Sir Lancelot, "you know well I dare not, and cannot, disobey your command. But if I could or dared, believe me, I would not take it upon myself to touch that wounded knight with the intent of surpassing all other knights. Jesus defend me from that shame."

"You take it wrongly," said King Arthur. "You shall not do it out of any presumption, but to keep us company, since you are a fellow of the Round Table. And believe me," said King Arthur, "if you do not prevail and heal him, I dare say there is no knight in this land who can heal him. And therefore I beg you, do as we have done."

And then all the kings and knights, for the most part, begged Sir Lancelot to probe his wounds. And then the wounded knight, Sir Urre, sat himself up weakly, and begged Sir Lancelot with all his heart, saying, "Courteous knight, I beg you for God's sake heal my wounds; for it seems to me that ever since you came here my wounds do not pain me."

"Ah, my fair lord," said Sir Lancelot, "would to Jesus that I could help you. I am sorely ashamed that I should be put to this, for I was never worthy enough to do so high a thing."

Then Sir Lancelot knelt down by the wounded knight, saying, "My lord Arthur, I must do your command, which is much against my heart."

And then he held up his hands, and looked to the east, saying secretly to himself, "Blessed Father, Son and Holy Ghost, I beseech You of Your mercy that my simple honour and good name be kept safe; and You, blessed Trinity, may give power to heal this sick knight by Your great power and grace, but, good Lord, never of myself."

And then Sir Lancelot asked Sir Urre to let him see his head. And then, kneeling devoutly, he probed the three wounds, so that they bled a little; and at once all the wounds healed cleanly, and looked as if they had been whole for seven years. And in the same way he probed the other three wounds on his body, and they healed in the same way. And then, last of all, he probed the one that was in his hand, and at once it healed cleanly.

Then King Arthur and all the kings and knights knelt down and gave thanks and praise to God and to His Blessed Mother. And all the while Sir Lancelot wept like a child that has been beaten. Then King Arthur had priests and clergy arrayed in the most devout manner, to bring Sir Urre into Carlisle with singing and praise to God. And when this was done, the king had him dressed in the richest clothes that could be imagined; and then there were few better built knights in all the court, for he was exceedingly well made and strongly built. And Arthur asked Sir Urre how he felt.

"My good lord," he said, "I never felt so vigorous."

"Will you joust and do deeds of arms?" said King Arthur.

"Sir," said Urre, "if I had all that belongs to jousting, I would soon be ready."

Chapter 13: How a match was made of a hundred knights against a hundred knights, and of other matters

Then Arthur set up a side of a hundred knights to be against another hundred knights. And so the next morning they jousted for a diamond; but none of the haughty knights jousted there. And so, to cut the tale short, Sir Urre and Sir Lavaine jousted best that day, for there was not one of them who did not overthrow and pull down thirty knights. And then, by the assent of all the kings and lords, Sir Urre and Sir Lavaine were made knights of the Round Table. And Sir Lavaine set his love on Dame Felelolie, Sir Urre's sister, and then they were married with great joy, and King Arthur gave each of them a barony of lands. And this Sir Urre would never leave Sir Lancelot, but he and Sir Lavaine always attended on him; and in all the court they were counted good knights, and very eager in arms; and they did many noble deeds, for they would have no rest, but always sought adventures.

So they lived at that court in great nobility and joy for a long time. But every night and day Sir Agravain, Sir Gawain's brother, kept watch on Queen Guinevere and Sir Lancelot du Lake, to bring them to rebuke and shame. And so I leave this tale here, and pass over great books of Sir Lancelot du Lake, of the great adventures he did when he was called Le Chevaler du Chariot. For, as the French book says, because of the scorn of knights and ladies who called him the knight who rode in the cart, as if he were being taken to the gallows, he rode in a cart for a twelvemonth, in scorn of all those who called him so; for, a little after he had killed Sir Meliagaunce in the queen's quarrel, he never came on horseback for a twelvemonth. And, as the French book says, in that twelvemonth he fought more than forty battles. And because I have lost the true story of Le Chevaler du Chariot, I depart from the tale of Sir Lancelot, and here I go on to the death of King Arthur; and Sir Agravain was the cause of that.

Here ends the nineteenth book.

And here follows the most piteous history of the death of King Arthur, which is the twentieth book.

Book Twenty: The Piteous Death of King Arthur

Chapter 1: How Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred kept pressing Sir Gawain to expose the love between Sir Lancelot and Queen Guinevere

In May, when every vigorous heart flourishes and buds (for as the season is joyful to look on, and comforting, so men and women rejoice and are glad that summer is coming with its fresh flowers, while winter, with its rough winds and blasts, makes a vigorous man and woman cower and sit close by the fire), so in this season, in the month of May, there came about a great anger and misfortune that did not stop until the flower of chivalry of all the world was destroyed and slain. And it was all because of two ill-fated knights, who were called Agravain and Sir Mordred, and who were brothers of Sir Gawain. For this Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred had always had a secret hatred of the queen, Dame Guinevere, and of Sir Lancelot, and day and night they were always watching Sir Lancelot.

So it happened, by ill luck, that Sir Gawain and all his brothers were in King Arthur's chamber. And then Sir Agravain said this openly, and not in any private counsel, so that many knights might hear it: "I wonder that we are not all ashamed both to see and to know how Sir Lancelot lies with the queen day and night, and we all know it is so; and it is shameful of us all that we allow so noble a king as King Arthur is to be shamed like this."

Then Sir Gawain spoke, and said, "Brother Sir Agravain, I beg you and order you, raise no such matters in front of me any more, for believe me," said Sir Gawain, "I will have no part in your plans."

"God help me," said Sir Gaheris and Sir Gareth, "we will have nothing to do with your doings, brother Agravain."

"Then I will," said Sir Mordred.

"I can well believe that," said Sir Gawain, "for you will always agree to any mischief, brother Sir Mordred. And I wish you would leave all this, and not make yourself so busy, for I know," said Sir Gawain, "what will come of it."

"Let come of it what may," said Sir Agravain, "I will reveal it to the king."

"Not with my consent," said Sir Gawain, "for if war and ruin rise between Sir Lancelot and us, believe me, brother, many kings and great lords will hold with Sir Lancelot. Also, brother Sir Agravain," said Sir Gawain, "you must remember how many times Sir Lancelot has rescued the king and the queen; and the best of us all would have been stone cold at the heart's root if Sir Lancelot had not been a better man than we are, and he has proved that many a time. And as for my part," said Sir Gawain, "I will never be against Sir Lancelot, for one day's deed: when he rescued me from King Carados of the Dolorous Tower, and killed him, and saved my life. Also, brother Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred, in the same way Sir Lancelot rescued you both, and sixty-two others, from Sir Turquine. It seems to me, brother, that such kind deeds and kindness should be remembered."

"Do as you please," said Sir Agravain, "for I will hide it no longer."

With these words King Arthur came up to them.

"Now, brother, stop your noise," said Sir Gawain.

"We will not," said Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred.

"Is that so?" said Sir Gawain. "Then God speed you, for I will not listen to your tales or have any part in your plans."

"Nor will I," said Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris, "for we will never speak evil of that man. Because," said Sir Gareth, "Sir Lancelot made me a knight, I ought in no way to speak ill of him."

And with that the three of them left, grieving greatly.

"Alas," said Sir Gawain and Sir Gareth, "now this realm is wholly brought to ruin, and the noble fellowship of the Round Table will be scattered."

And so they left.

Chapter 2: How Sir Agravain revealed their love to King Arthur, and how King Arthur gave them leave to take Sir Lancelot

And then Sir Arthur asked them what the noise was about.

"My lord," said Agravain, "I will tell you what I can keep in no longer. Here I am, and my brother Sir Mordred, and we told my brothers Sir Gawain, Sir Gaheris and Sir Gareth this, which we all know: that Sir Lancelot is keeping your queen, and has done for a long time. And we are your sister's sons, and we can put up with it no longer. And we all know that you ought to be above Sir Lancelot, and you are the king who made him a knight; and so we will prove it, that he is a traitor to your person."

"If it is so," said Sir Arthur, "believe me, he is nothing else. But I would be loath to begin such a thing unless I had proof of it. For Sir Lancelot is a bold knight, and you all know he is the best knight among us all; and unless he is taken in the act, he will fight with whoever brings up the accusation, and I know no knight who is able to match him. So if it is true, as you say, I would want him taken in the act."

For, as the French book says, the king was very loath that any rumour should touch Sir Lancelot and his queen. For the king had a suspicion, but he would not hear of it, for Sir Lancelot had done so much for him and for the queen so many times that, believe me, the king loved him exceedingly.

"My lord," said Sir Agravain, "tomorrow you will ride out hunting, and you need not doubt that Sir Lancelot will not go with you. Then, when it draws towards night, you can send the queen word that you will stay out all that night, and so you can send for your cooks. And then, on pain of death, we will take him that night with the queen, and either we will bring him to you dead or alive."

"Very well," said the king. "Then I advise you," said the king, "to take a trusty company with you."

"Sir," said Agravain, "my brother Sir Mordred and I will take twelve knights of the Round Table with us."

"Be careful," said King Arthur, "for I warn you, you will find him strong."

"Leave it to us," said Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred.

So in the morning King Arthur rode out hunting, and sent word to the queen that he would be out all that night. Then Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred got twelve knights together, and hid themselves in a chamber in the Castle of Carlisle, and these were their names: Sir Colgrevance, Sir Mador de la Porte, Sir Gingaline, Sir Meliot de Logres, Sir Petipase of Winchelsea, Sir Galleron of Galway, Sir Melion of the Mountain, Sir Astamore, Sir Gromore Somir Joure, Sir Curselaine, Sir Florence, Sir Lovel. So these twelve knights were with Sir Mordred and Sir Agravain, and all of them were from Scotland, either of Sir Gawain's kin or well-wishers to his brothers.

So when the night came, Sir Lancelot told Sir Bors that he was going that night to speak with the queen.

"Sir," said Sir Bors, "if you take my advice, you will not go tonight."

"Why?" said Sir Lancelot.

"Sir," said Sir Bors, "I am always afraid of Sir Agravain, who watches you day by day to bring shame on you and on all of us. And never yet has my heart been set against any going of yours, any time you went to the queen, as much as now. For I suspect that the king is away from the queen tonight because perhaps he has set some watch for you and the queen, and so I badly fear treason."

"Have no fear," said Sir Lancelot, "for I will go and come back, and make no delay."

"Sir," said Sir Bors, "I am sorry for it, for I badly fear that your going out tonight will bring grief on us all."

"Fair nephew," said Sir Lancelot, "I wonder very much why you say this, since the queen has sent for me. And believe me, I will not be such a coward that she should not know I will come to her at her good pleasure."

"God speed you well," said Sir Bors, "and send you back safe and sound."

Chapter 3: How Sir Lancelot was spied in the queen's chamber, and how Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred came with twelve knights to kill him

So Sir Lancelot left, and took his sword under his arm, and so, in his cloak, that noble knight put himself in great danger. And so he went on until he came to the queen's chamber, and then Sir Lancelot was quickly let into the chamber. And then, as the French book says, the queen and Lancelot were together. And whether they were in bed or at other kinds of pastime, I don't care to make any mention of it here, for love in those days was not as it is nowadays. But as they were together like this, Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred came, with twelve knights of the Round Table with them, and they shouted, "Traitor knight, Sir Lancelot du Lake, now you're caught!"

And they shouted this so loudly that all the court might hear it; and all fourteen of them were armed at every point as if they were to fight in a battle.

"Alas," said Queen Guinevere, "now we are both ruined."

"Madam," said Sir Lancelot, "is there any armour here in your chamber that I could cover my poor body with? If there is any, give it to me, and I will soon put a stop to their malice, by the grace of God."

"Truly," said the queen, "I have no armour, shield, sword or spear. And so I badly fear our long love has come to a disastrous end, for I can hear by their noise that there are many noble knights, and I know very well they are fully armed, and against them you can put up no resistance. So you are likely to be killed, and then I shall be burned. For if you could escape them," said the queen, "I would have no doubt that you would rescue me from whatever danger I stood in."

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "never in all my life was I in such a hard spot as this, that I should be killed so shamefully for lack of my armour."

But all the while Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred kept shouting, "Traitor knight, come out of the queen's chamber! For you can be sure you're so surrounded that you will not escape."

"Oh, Jesus have mercy," said Sir Lancelot, "I cannot bear this shameful cry and noise, for death at once would be better than to endure this pain."

Then he took the queen in his arms, and kissed her, and said, "Most noble Christian queen, I beg you, as you have always been my special good lady, and I at all times your true poor knight as far as I was able, and as I never failed you in right or in wrong since the first day King Arthur made me a knight, that you will pray for my soul if I am killed here. For I am quite sure that Sir Bors, my nephew, and all the rest of my kin, with Sir Lavaine and Sir Urre, will not fail to rescue you from the fire. And so, my own lady, take comfort, whatever becomes of me, and go with Sir Bors, my nephew, and Sir Urre, and they will all do everything they can or may to please you, so that you shall live like a queen upon my lands."

"No, Lancelot," said the queen, "believe me, I will never live after your days. But if you are killed I will take my death as meekly, for Jesus Christ's sake, as ever any Christian queen did."

"Well, madam," said Lancelot, "since the day has come that our love must part, believe me, I will sell my life as dearly as I can. And I am a thousand times more grieved," said Sir Lancelot, "for you than for myself. And now I would rather have good armour on me, so that men might speak of my deeds before ever I am killed, than be lord of all Christendom."

"Truly," said the queen, "I wish it might please God that they would take me and kill me, and let you escape."

"That shall never be," said Sir Lancelot. "God keep me from such a shame! But Jesus, be You my shield and my armour!"

Chapter 4: How Sir Lancelot slew Sir Colgrevance and put on his armour, and afterwards slew Sir Agravain and twelve of his companions

And with that Sir Lancelot wrapped his cloak around his arm well and securely. And by then they had brought a great bench out of the hall, and with it they battered at the door.

"Fair lords," said Sir Lancelot, "stop your noise and your battering, and I will open this door, and then you can do with me whatever you please."

"Come on, then," they all said, "and do it, for it does you no good to fight against us all. So let us into this chamber, and we will spare your life until you come to King Arthur."

Then Lancelot unbarred the door, and with his left hand he held it open a little, so that only one man could come in at a time. And so there came striding in a good knight, a big man and a large one, and his name was Colgrevance of Gore, and he struck at Sir Lancelot mightily with a sword. And Sir Lancelot turned the stroke aside, and gave him such a blow on the helmet that he fell flat on his face, dead, inside the chamber door. And then Sir Lancelot with great strength dragged that dead knight inside the chamber door; and with the help of the queen and her ladies Sir Lancelot was quickly armed in Sir Colgrevance's armour.

And all the while Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred stood there shouting, "Traitor knight, come out of the queen's chamber!"

"Stop your noise," said Sir Lancelot to Sir Agravain, "for believe me, Sir Agravain, you will not take me prisoner tonight. And so, if you take my advice, all of you go away from this chamber door, and stop making such shouting and such slander as you are doing. For I promise you on my knighthood, if you will go away and make no more noise, I will appear before you all tomorrow in front of the king, and then let it be seen which of you, or all of you together, will accuse me of treason. And there I will answer you as a knight should: that I came here to the queen with no kind of evil intent, and I will prove that and make it good on you with my own hands."

"Shame on you, traitor," said Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred. "We'll have you whether you like it or not, and kill you if we please. For we'll have you know we have King Arthur's leave to spare you or to kill you."

"Ah, sirs," said Sir Lancelot, "is there no other mercy to be had from you? Then look to yourselves."

So then Sir Lancelot threw the chamber door wide open, and mightily and knightly he strode in among them; and at once, at the first blow, he killed Sir Agravain. And twelve of his companions after him, within a little while, he laid cold on the ground, for there was none of the twelve who could withstand one blow from Sir Lancelot. Sir Lancelot also wounded Sir Mordred, and he fled with all his might.

And then Sir Lancelot went back to the queen, and said, "Madam, now you may be sure all our true love is brought to an end, for from now on King Arthur will always be my enemy. And so, madam, if it pleases you to let me take you with me, I will save you from every kind of danger."

"That is not the best course," said the queen. "It seems to me that now you have done so much harm, it will be best for you to hold still for now. And if you see that tomorrow they mean to put me to death, then you can rescue me as you think best."

"Gladly," said Sir Lancelot, "for have no doubt, while I am alive I will rescue you."

And then he kissed her, and each gave the other a ring; and so he left the queen there, and went to his lodging.

Chapter 5: How Sir Lancelot came to Sir Bors, and told him how he had fared, and what danger he had been in, and how he had escaped

When Sir Bors saw Sir Lancelot, he was never so glad of his homecoming as he was then.

"Jesus have mercy," said Sir Lancelot, "why are you all armed? What does this mean?"

"Sir," said Sir Bors, "after you had left us, all of us who are of your blood and who wish you well were so troubled that some of us leapt out of our beds naked, and some in their dreams caught naked swords in their hands. So," said Sir Bors, "we judge there is some great strife at hand. And then we all judged that you had been trapped by some treason, and so we made ourselves ready like this, whatever need you might be in."

"My fair nephew," said Sir Lancelot to Sir Bors, "now you shall know everything: that tonight I was in a harder spot than ever I was in my life, and yet I escaped."

And so he told them all how, and in what manner, as you have heard before.

"And so, my companions," said Sir Lancelot, "I beg you all to be of good heart in whatever need I stand, for now war has come to us all."

"Sir," said Bors, "all is welcome that God sends us. We have had much good fortune with you, and much honour, and so we will take the bad with you as we have taken the good."

"And so," they all said (there were many good knights there), "see that you take no discouragement, for there are no bands of knights under heaven but we shall be able to hurt them as much as they can hurt us. And so don't lose heart in any way, and we will gather together those we love and who love us, and whatever you want done shall be done. And so, Sir Lancelot," they said, "we will take the bad with the good."

"Many thanks," said Sir Lancelot, "for your good comfort, for in my great distress, my fair nephew, you comfort me greatly, and I am much beholden to you. But this, my fair nephew, I would like you to do, in all the haste you can, before it is broad day: look in the lodgings of those who are lodged here near the king, and see which will hold with me and which will not. For now I want to know my friends from my foes."

"Sir," said Sir Bors, "I will do my best, and before seven o'clock I will know, of those you have spoken of, who will hold with you."

Then Sir Bors called to him Sir Lionel, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Blamore de Ganis, Sir Bleoberis de Ganis, Sir Gahalantine, Sir Galihodin, Sir Galihud, Sir Menadeuke, Sir Villiers the Valiant, Sir Hebes le Renoumes, Sir Lavaine, Sir Urre of Hungary, Sir Nerounes, Sir Plenorius. These two knights Sir Lancelot had made, and one of them he had won on a bridge, and so they would never be against him. And Harry le Fise du Lake, and Sir Selises of the Dolorous Tower, and Sir Melias de Lile, and Sir Bellangere le Beuse, who was the son of Sir Alisander le Orphelin; and because his mother, Alice la Beale Pilgrim, was kin to Sir Lancelot, he held with him. So there came Sir Palomides and Sir Safere, his brother, to hold with Sir Lancelot, and Sir Clegis of Sadok, and Sir Dinas, and Sir Clarrus of Clermont. So these twenty-two knights drew together, and by then they were armed and on horseback, and promised Sir Lancelot to do whatever he wanted. Then there joined them, from North Wales and from Cornwall together, for Sir Lamorak's sake and for Sir Tristram's sake, as many as eighty knights.

"My lords," said Sir Lancelot, "believe me, ever since I came into this country I have wished my lord King Arthur well, and my lady Queen Guinevere, as far as I was able. And tonight, because my lady the queen sent for me to speak with her, I think it was arranged by treason (though I dare fully clear her of it herself), for I was there nearly killed by a plot laid beforehand. But as Jesus provided for me, I escaped all their malice and treason."

And then that noble knight Sir Lancelot told them all how he had been in a hard spot in the queen's chamber, and how and in what manner he escaped from them.

"And so," said Sir Lancelot, "believe me, my fair lords, I am sure there is nothing but war for me and mine. And because I have killed these knights tonight, I know very well (Sir Agravain, Sir Gawain's brother, among them, and at least twelve of his companions), for this reason I am now sure of mortal war, for these knights were sent and appointed by King Arthur to betray me. And so the king, in his heat and malice, will condemn the queen to the fire, and I cannot allow that, that she should be burned for my sake. For if I may be heard and allowed and taken at my word, I will fight for the queen, that she is a true lady to her lord. But I fear the king, in his heat, will not take me as I ought to be taken."

Chapter 6: Of the counsel and advice taken by Sir Lancelot and his friends to save the queen

"My lord Sir Lancelot," said Sir Bors, "my advice is that you take the bad with the good, and take it with patience, and thank God for it. And since it has turned out as it has, I advise you to look after yourself, for if you will stand up for yourself, there is no company of Christian knights that shall do you wrong. Also I will advise you, my lord Sir Lancelot, that if my lady Queen Guinevere is in distress, seeing that she is in trouble for your sake, you rescue her like a knight. If you did otherwise, all the world would speak shame of you to the world's end. Since you were taken with her, whether you did right or wrong, it is now your part to hold with the queen, so that she is not killed and put to a disastrous death; for if she dies like that, the shame will be yours."

"Jesus keep me from shame," said Sir Lancelot, "and keep and save my lady the queen from dishonour and a shameful death, and may she never be destroyed through my failing. So, my fair lords, my kin and my friends," said Sir Lancelot, "what will you do?"

Then they all said, "We will do as you do."

"I put this to you," said Sir Lancelot, "that if my lord Arthur, through evil counsel, tomorrow in his heat puts my lady the queen to the fire, to be burned there, now I beg you, advise me what is best to do."

Then they all said at once, with one voice, "Sir, we think it best that you rescue the queen like a knight, seeing that if she is burned it is for your sake. And it is to be supposed that if you could be laid hands on, you would have the same death, or a more shameful one. And, sir, we all say that you have many times rescued her from death in other men's quarrels; it seems to us all the more to your honour that you rescue the queen from this peril, since she has it for your sake."

Then Sir Lancelot stood still, and said, "My fair lords, believe me, I would be loath to do anything that would dishonour you or my blood; and believe me, I would be loath that my lady the queen should die a shameful death. But if it is so that you advise me to rescue her, I must do a great deal of harm before I rescue her. And perhaps I shall destroy some of my best friends there, which I would much regret. And perhaps there are some who, if they could well bring it about, or dared disobey my lord King Arthur, would soon come over to me, and I would be loath to hurt them. And if it turns out that I rescue her, where shall I keep her?"

"That will be the least of our cares," said Sir Bors. "How did the noble knight Sir Tristram manage, with your good will? Did he not keep Isolde the Fair with him for nearly three years in Joyous Gard? That was done by the advice of you all, and that same place is your own. And in the same way you can do so, if you please, and carry the queen off quickly, if it turns out that the king condemns her to be burned. And in Joyous Gard you can keep her long enough until the king's heat is past. And then you shall bring the queen back to the king with great honour; and then perhaps you will have thanks for bringing her home, and love and thanks where others will have ill will."

"That is hard to do," said Sir Lancelot, "for I can take a warning from Sir Tristram. For when, by means of negotiations, Sir Tristram brought Isolde the Fair back from Joyous Gard to King Mark, look what happened in the end: how shamefully that false traitor King Mark killed him as he sat harping before his lady Isolde the Fair. With a sharpened blade he thrust him from behind, to the heart. It grieves me," said Sir Lancelot, "to speak of his death, for all the world cannot find such a knight."

"All this is true," said Sir Bors, "but there is one thing that ought to hearten you and all of us. You know well that King Arthur and King Mark were never alike in character, for there was never yet a man who could prove King Arthur false to his promise."

So, to cut a long story short, they all agreed that, for better or for worse, if it turned out that the queen was brought to the fire that morning, they would all rescue her at once. And so, on Sir Lancelot's advice, they all set themselves in ambush in a wood, as near Carlisle as they could, and there they waited quietly, to learn what the king would do.

Chapter 7: How Sir Mordred rode in haste to the king, to tell him of the fight and the death of Sir Agravain and the other knights

Now we turn back to Sir Mordred, who, when he had escaped from the noble knight Sir Lancelot, at once got his horse and mounted it, and rode to King Arthur, badly wounded and beaten, and bled all over; and there he told the king everything, how it had gone, and how they had all been killed except himself alone.

"Jesus have mercy, how can this be?" said the king. "Did you take him in the queen's chamber?"

"Yes, God help me," said Sir Mordred. "There we found him unarmed, and there he killed Colgrevance, and armed himself in his armour."

And he told the king all this from the beginning to the end.

"Jesus have mercy," said the king, "he is a marvellous knight of prowess. Alas, I bitterly regret," said the king, "that Sir Lancelot should ever be against me. Now I am sure the noble fellowship of the Round Table is broken for ever, for many a noble knight will hold with him. And now it has turned out so," said the king, "that I cannot, with my honour, do otherwise: the queen must suffer death."

So then, in this heat, great preparation was made for the queen to be condemned to death. And the law was such in those days that whoever they were, of whatever rank or degree, if they were found guilty of treason there should be no other remedy but death; and either witnesses or being taken in the act was to be the cause of their swift judgment. And just so was it ordained for Queen Guinevere, because Sir Mordred had escaped badly wounded, and because of the death of thirteen knights of the Round Table. These proofs and evidences caused King Arthur to command the queen to the fire, to be burned there.

Then Sir Gawain spoke, and said, "My lord Arthur, I would advise you not to be over-hasty, but to put off this judgment of my lady the queen, for many reasons. One is that, though it is true that Sir Lancelot was found in the queen's chamber, yet it may be that he came there for no evil. For you know, my lord," said Sir Gawain, "that the queen is much beholden to Sir Lancelot, more than to any other knight, for many times he has saved her life, and fought for her when all the court refused the queen. And perhaps she sent for him for good, and for no evil, to reward him for the good deeds he had done for her in times past. And perhaps my lady the queen sent for him with the intention that Sir Lancelot should come to her privately and secretly, thinking it was best to do so in order to avoid and guard against slander. For often we do many things that we think are for the best, and yet perhaps they turn out for the worst. For I dare say," said Sir Gawain, "my lady your queen is both good and true to you. And as for Sir Lancelot," said Sir Gawain, "I dare say he will make it good on any knight living who will lay dishonour or shame on him, and in the same way he will make it good for my lady Dame Guinevere."

"That I well believe," said King Arthur, "but I will not go that way with Sir Lancelot, for he trusts so much in his hands and his strength that he fears no man. And so he shall never fight for my queen again, for she shall have the law. And if I can get Sir Lancelot, believe me, he shall have a shameful death."

"Jesus forbid," said Sir Gawain, "that I should ever see it."

"Why do you say that?" said King Arthur. "Truly, you have no reason to love Sir Lancelot, for this very night just past he killed your brother Sir Agravain, a very good knight, and he almost killed your other brother Sir Mordred, and he also killed thirteen noble knights there. And also, Sir Gawain, remember he killed two sons of yours, Sir Florence and Sir Lovel."

"My lord," said Sir Gawain, "I know of all this, and I bitterly regret their deaths. But since I gave them warning, and told my brothers and my sons beforehand what would come of it in the end, and since they would not take my advice, I will not meddle in it, nor take any revenge for their deaths; for I told them it was no use fighting with Sir Lancelot. All the same, I am sorry for the death of my brothers and of my sons, for they are the cause of their own deaths. For many times I warned my brother Sir Agravain, and I told him of the perils that have now come about."

Chapter 8: How Sir Lancelot and his kinsmen rescued the queen from the fire, and how he slew many knights

Then the noble King Arthur said to Sir Gawain, "Dear nephew, I ask you to make yourself ready in your best armour, with your brothers Sir Gaheris and Sir Gareth, to bring my queen to the fire, there to have her judgment and receive her death."

"No, my most noble lord," said Sir Gawain, "that I will never do. For believe me, I will never be in that place where so noble a queen as my lady Dame Guinevere comes to a shameful end. For believe me," said Sir Gawain, "my heart will never let me see her die; and it shall never be said that I was ever of your counsel in her death."

Then the king said to Sir Gawain, "Allow your brothers Sir Gaheris and Sir Gareth to be there."

"My lord," said Sir Gawain, "believe me, they will be unwilling to be there, because of the many things that are likely to happen there; but they are young, and hardly able to say no to you."

Then Sir Gaheris and the good knight Sir Gareth spoke to Arthur. "Sir, you may well command us to be there, but believe me, it will be sorely against our will. But if we are there by your strict command, you must plainly hold us excused: we will be there peaceably, and wear no armour of war."

"In the name of God," said the king, "then make yourselves ready, for she shall have her judgment very soon."

"Alas," said Sir Gawain, "that I should ever live to see this woeful day."

So Sir Gawain turned away and wept bitterly, and so he went into his room. And then the queen was led out of Carlisle, and there she was stripped to her shift. And so then her confessor was brought to her, so that she could confess her misdeeds and be absolved. Then there was weeping and wailing and wringing of hands among many lords and ladies; but there were only a few, by comparison, who would wear any armour to uphold the queen's death.

Then there was a man whom Sir Lancelot had sent to that place to watch for the time when the queen should go to her death. And as soon as he saw the queen stripped to her shift, and confessed, he gave Sir Lancelot warning. Then there was nothing but spurring and snatching up of horses, and at once they came to the fire. And whoever stood against them was killed there; no one could withstand Sir Lancelot, and so all who bore arms and stood against them were killed there, a great many noble knights. For there were killed Sir Belliance le Orgulous, Sir Segwarides, Sir Griflet, Sir Brandiles, Sir Aglovale, Sir Tor; Sir Gaunter, Sir Gilmere and Sir Raynold, three brothers; Sir Damas, Sir Priamus, Sir Kay the Stranger, Sir Driant, Sir Lambegus, Sir Herminde; Sir Pertolepe and Sir Perimones, two brothers who were called the Green Knight and the Red Knight. And so in this rushing and crashing, as Sir Lancelot pushed his way here and there, it was his misfortune to kill Sir Gaheris and Sir Gareth, the noble knight, for they were unarmed and off their guard. For, as the French book says, Sir Lancelot struck Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris on the skull, so that they were killed in the field; though in very truth Sir Lancelot did not see them, and so they were found dead in the thickest of the press.

Then, when Sir Lancelot had done this, and had killed or put to flight all who would stand against him, he rode straight to Dame Guinevere, and had a coat and a gown thrown over her; and then he had her set up behind him, and begged her to take heart. Believe me, the queen was glad that she had escaped death. And then she thanked God and Sir Lancelot; and so he rode away with the queen, as the French book says, to Joyous Gard, and there he kept her as a noble knight should. And many great lords and some kings sent Sir Lancelot many good knights, and many noble knights came over to Sir Lancelot. When it was known openly that King Arthur and Sir Lancelot were at strife, many knights were glad of their strife, and many were very sorrowful at it.

Chapter 9: Of the sorrow and lament of King Arthur for the death of his nephews and other good knights, and also for the queen, his wife

So we turn back to King Arthur. When he was told how, and in what manner, the queen had been taken away from the fire, and when he heard of the death of his noble knights, and above all of the deaths of Sir Gaheris and Sir Gareth, the king fainted from pure sorrow. And when he came out of his faint, he said, "Alas that I ever wore a crown upon my head! For now I have lost the fairest fellowship of noble knights that ever a Christian king held together. Alas, my good knights are killed and taken from me: within these two days I have lost forty knights, and also the noble fellowship of Sir Lancelot and his kin, for now I can never hold them together again with my honour. Alas that this war ever began!"

"Now, good companions," said the king, "I order you that no man tell Sir Gawain of the death of his two brothers. For I am sure," said the king, "when Sir Gawain hears that Sir Gareth is dead, he will go nearly out of his mind. Jesus have mercy," said the king, "why did he kill Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris? For I dare say that Sir Gareth loved Sir Lancelot above all men on earth."

"That is true," said some knights, "but they were killed in the crush, as Sir Lancelot pushed his way into the thick of the press; and since they were unarmed, he struck them and did not know whom he struck, and so they were killed by ill luck."

"Their deaths," said Arthur, "will cause the greatest deadly war there ever was. I am sure that if Sir Gawain knew Sir Gareth had been killed, I would never have any peace from him until I had destroyed Sir Lancelot's kin and himself too, or else he destroyed me. And therefore," said the king, "believe me, my heart was never so heavy as it is now. And I am much sorrier for the loss of my good knights than for the loss of my fair queen; for I could have queens enough, but such a fellowship of good knights will never be together in any company again. And now I dare say," said King Arthur, "there was never a Christian king who held such a fellowship together. And alas that Sir Lancelot and I should ever be at strife. Ah, Agravain, Agravain," said the king, "Jesus forgive your soul for it, for the ill will that you and your brother Sir Mordred had towards Sir Lancelot has caused all this sorrow."

And all the while, among these laments, the king wept and fainted.

Then a man came to Sir Gawain and told him how the queen had been led away by Sir Lancelot, and nearly twenty-four knights killed.

"Jesus protect my brothers!" said Sir Gawain. "For I knew very well that Sir Lancelot would rescue her, or else die in that field. And to tell the truth, he would not have been a man of honour if he had not rescued the queen that day, since she was to have been burned for his sake. And in that," said Sir Gawain, "he has done only what a knight should, and what I would have done myself if I had stood in his place. But where are my brothers?" said Sir Gawain. "I am surprised I hear nothing of them."

"Truly," said the man, "Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris are killed."

"Jesus forbid!" said Sir Gawain. "Not for the whole world would I want them killed, and above all my good brother Sir Gareth."

"Sir," said the man, "he is killed, and that is a great pity."

"Who killed him?" said Sir Gawain.

"Sir," said the man, "Lancelot killed them both."

"That I cannot believe," said Sir Gawain, "that he ever killed my brother Sir Gareth. For I dare say my brother Gareth loved him better than me, and all his brothers, and the king too. And I dare say too that if Sir Lancelot had asked my brother Sir Gareth, he would have been on his side against the king and all of us. And so I can never believe that Sir Lancelot killed my brother."

"Sir," said the man, "it is reported that he killed him."

Chapter 10: How King Arthur, at Sir Gawain's request, decided to make war on Sir Lancelot, and laid siege to his castle called Joyous Gard

"Alas," said Sir Gawain, "now my joy is gone."

And then he fell down in a faint, and he lay there a long time as if he were dead. And then, when he came out of his faint, he cried out sorrowfully, "Alas!" And at once Sir Gawain ran to the king, crying and weeping. "O King Arthur, my uncle, my good brother Sir Gareth is killed, and so is my brother Sir Gaheris, who were two noble knights."

Then the king wept, and Gawain too; and so they fainted. And when they had revived, Sir Gawain spoke. "Sir, I will go and see my brother Sir Gareth."

"You may not see him," said the king, "for I had him buried, and Sir Gaheris too. For I well understood that you would grieve beyond all bounds, and the sight of Sir Gareth would have doubled your sorrow."

"Alas, my lord," said Sir Gawain, "how did he kill my brother Sir Gareth? My own good lord, I beg you, tell me."

"Truly," said the king, "I will tell you as it was told to me. Sir Lancelot killed him, and Sir Gaheris too."

"Alas," said Sir Gawain, "neither of them bore any arms against him, not either of them."

"I do not know how it was," said the king, "but as it is said, Sir Lancelot killed them both in the thickest of the press and did not know them. And therefore let us work out a remedy to avenge their deaths."

"My king, my lord, and my uncle," said Sir Gawain, "believe me, now I will make you a promise that I will keep by my knighthood: from this day on I will never let Sir Lancelot be, until one of us has killed the other. And therefore I ask you, my lord and king, prepare yourself for war, for believe me, I will be avenged on Sir Lancelot. And therefore, as you want my service and my love, hurry to it now, and call on your friends. For I promise to God," said Sir Gawain, "that for the death of my brother Sir Gareth I will seek Sir Lancelot through seven kings' realms, until I kill him or else he kills me."

"You will not need to seek him so far," said the king, "for, as I hear, Sir Lancelot will wait for me and you in Joyous Gard; and many people are flocking to him, as I hear."

"That I can believe," said Sir Gawain. "But, my lord," he said, "call on your friends, and I will call on mine."

"It shall be done," said the king, "and I expect I shall be strong enough to drag him out of the biggest tower of his castle."

So then the king sent letters and writs throughout all England, through its length and its breadth, to summon all his knights. And so many knights, dukes and earls came to Arthur, so that he had a great army. And when they were assembled, the king told them how Sir Lancelot had robbed him of his queen. Then the king and all his army made ready to lay siege to Sir Lancelot, where he lay inside Joyous Gard. Sir Lancelot heard of it, and provided himself with many good knights, for many knights held with him, some for his own sake and some for the queen's sake. So both sides were well stocked and armed with every kind of thing that belonged to war. But King Arthur's army was so big that Sir Lancelot would not wait for him in the open field, for he was very unwilling to do battle against the king. But Sir Lancelot withdrew to his strong castle with every kind of provision, and as many noble men as he could keep within the town and the castle. Then King Arthur came with Sir Gawain and a huge army, and laid siege all around Joyous Gard, both to the town and to the castle, and there they made fierce war on both sides. But for a long time Sir Lancelot would on no account ride out or go out of his castle; nor would he let any of his good knights sally out, nor any of the town or of the castle, until fifteen weeks had passed.

Chapter 11: Of the talk between King Arthur and Sir Lancelot, and how King Arthur reproached him

Then it happened one day at harvest time that Sir Lancelot looked over the walls, and called down aloud to King Arthur and Sir Gawain. "My lords both, believe me, all that you do at this siege is in vain, for here you win no honour, only blame and dishonour. For if I cared to come out myself, with my good knights, I would very soon make an end of this war."

"Come out," said Arthur to Lancelot, "if you dare, and I promise you I will meet you in the middle of the field."

"God forbid," said Sir Lancelot, "that I should ever fight with the most noble king who made me a knight."

"To hell with your fair talk," said the king. "For believe me, and trust it, I am your mortal enemy, and always will be until the day I die. For you have killed my good knights, and very noble men of my blood, whom I can never get back again. And you have lain with my queen, and kept her for many winters, and then, like a traitor, taken her from me by force."

"My most noble lord and king," said Sir Lancelot, "you may say what you like, for you know well that I will not quarrel with you yourself. But where you say I have killed your good knights, I know well that I have done so, and I bitterly regret it; but I was forced to fight them to save my life, or else I would have had to let them kill me. And as for my lady Queen Guinevere: except for your own royal person, and my lord Sir Gawain, there is no knight under heaven who dares to prove on my body that I was ever a traitor to your person. And where it pleases you to say that I have kept my lady your queen for years and winters, to that I will always give a full answer, and prove it on any knight alive, except your person and Sir Gawain, that my lady Queen Guinevere is as true a lady to your person as any lady living is to her lord; and that I will make good with my hands. And yet it has pleased her good grace to hold me in affection, and to cherish me more than any other knight. And to the best of my power I have deserved her love in return. For many times, my lord, you have agreed in your anger that she should be burned and destroyed, and then it was my fortune to fight for her; and before I left her adversary, they confessed their falsehood, and she was cleared with all honour. And at such times, my lord Arthur," said Sir Lancelot, "you loved me, and thanked me when I saved your queen from the fire; and then you promised to be my good lord for ever; and now I think you reward me very badly for my good service. And, my good lord, it seems to me I would have lost a great part of my honour as a knight if I had let my lady your queen be burned, and all the more since she was to have been burned for my sake. For since I have fought battles for your queen in other quarrels than my own, it seems to me I had all the more right to fight for her now in a rightful quarrel. And therefore, my good and gracious lord," said Sir Lancelot, "take your queen back into your good grace, for she is fair, and true, and good."

"Shame on you, false recreant knight!" said Sir Gawain. "I tell you, my lord my uncle King Arthur shall have his queen, and you too, whether you like it or not, and kill you both if it pleases him."

"That may well be," said Sir Lancelot. "But believe me, my lord Sir Gawain, if I cared to come out of this castle, you would find me and the queen harder to win than any hard battle you ever won."

"Shame on your proud words!" said Sir Gawain. "As for my lady the queen, I will never speak shame of her. But you, false recreant knight," said Sir Gawain, "what cause did you have to kill my good brother Sir Gareth, who loved you more than all my kin? Alas, you made him a knight with your own hands. Why did you kill him, when he loved you so well?"

"Making excuses does me no good," said Sir Lancelot, "but by Jesus, and by the faith that I owe to the high order of knighthood, I would as willingly have killed my nephew Sir Bors de Ganis at that moment. But alas that I was so unlucky," said Lancelot, "that I did not see Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris."

"You lie, recreant knight!" said Sir Gawain. "You killed him to spite me. And therefore, know this: I will make war on you, all the while that I live."

"I am sorry for that," said Sir Lancelot, "for I well understand it does no good to look for any agreement while you, Sir Gawain, are so bitterly set against me. And if you were not, I would have no doubt of winning back the good grace of my lord Arthur."

"I can well believe it, false recreant knight," said Sir Gawain, "for you have domineered over me and all of us for many long days, and destroyed many of our good knights."

"You say what pleases you," said Sir Lancelot. "And yet it can never be said of me, and openly proved, that I ever killed any good knight by treason planned beforehand, as you have done, my lord Sir Gawain. And I never did, except in my own defence, when I was driven to it to save my life."

"Ah, false knight," said Sir Gawain, "you mean Sir Lamorak. Know this, I killed him."

"You did not kill him yourself," said Sir Lancelot. "It would have been too much for you to have killed him, for he was one of the best knights of his time in all Christendom, and his death was a great pity."

Chapter 12: How Sir Lancelot's cousins and kinsmen urged him to go out to battle, and how they made ready

"Well, well," said Sir Gawain to Lancelot, "since you reproach me with Sir Lamorak, know this: I will never leave you alone until I have you at such a disadvantage that you cannot escape my hands."

"I can well believe it," said Sir Lancelot. "If you can get hold of me, I will get little mercy."

But, as the French book says, the noble King Arthur would have taken his queen back, and been reconciled with Sir Lancelot, but Sir Gawain would not allow him to by any means. And then Sir Gawain had many men cry out against Sir Lancelot; and all together they called him a false recreant knight.

Then, when Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Ector de Maris and Sir Lionel heard this outcry, they called to them Sir Palomides, Sir Safere's brother, and Sir Lavaine, with many more of their kin, and they all went to Sir Lancelot and said this: "My lord Sir Lancelot, believe me, we are filled with scorn at the great insults we heard Gawain say to you. And so we beg you, and charge you, as you want our service, keep us no longer within these walls. For believe us plainly, we will ride out into the field and do battle with them. For you behave like a man who is afraid, and for all your fair speech it will do you no good. For believe us, Sir Gawain will not let you be reconciled with King Arthur; and therefore fight for your life and your right, if you dare."

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "I am very unwilling to ride out of this castle and do battle."

Then Sir Lancelot called down aloud to Arthur and Sir Gawain. "My lords, I ask you and beg you, since I am pressed and called upon like this to ride out into the field, that neither you, my lord King Arthur, nor you, Sir Gawain, come into the field."

"What shall we do then?" said Sir Gawain. "Is this not the king's quarrel with you, to fight it out? And it is my quarrel to fight with you, Sir Lancelot, because of the death of my brother Sir Gareth."

"Then I must go to battle," said Sir Lancelot. "Now believe me, my lord Arthur and Sir Gawain, you will regret it whenever I do battle with you."

And so then they parted from each other; and then each side made ready to do battle in the morning, and great preparations were made on both sides. And Sir Gawain had many knights set to lie in wait for Sir Lancelot, to overthrow him and kill him. And in the morning, at mid-morning, Arthur was ready in the field with three great armies. And then Sir Lancelot's fellowship came out at three gates, in very good order; and Sir Lionel came in the front division, and Sir Lancelot came in the middle, and Sir Bors came out at the third gate. So they came out in order and discipline, like the very noble knights they were. And all the while Sir Lancelot ordered all his knights, whatever happened, to spare King Arthur and Sir Gawain.

Chapter 13: How Sir Gawain jousted and struck down Sir Lionel, and how Sir Lancelot put King Arthur back on his horse

Then Sir Gawain came out from the king's army, and he rode out in front and offered to joust. And Sir Lionel was a fierce knight, and he quickly rode against Sir Gawain; and there Sir Gawain struck Sir Lionel right through the body, so that he crashed to the ground as if he were dead. And then Sir Ector de Maris and others carried him into the castle. Then a great fight began, and many people were killed. And all the while Sir Lancelot did what he could to save the people on King Arthur's side; for Sir Palomides, and Sir Bors, and Sir Safere overthrew many knights, for they were deadly knights. And Sir Blamore de Ganis, and Sir Bleoberis de Ganis, with Sir Bellangere le Beuse, these six knights did much harm. And all the while King Arthur kept close to Sir Lancelot, to kill him, and Sir Lancelot let him be, and would not strike back.

So Sir Bors rode against King Arthur, and there Sir Bors struck him down with a spear. And so he dismounted and drew his sword, and said to Sir Lancelot, "Shall I make an end of this war?" And he meant that he would kill King Arthur.

"Don't you dare," said Sir Lancelot, "on pain of your head, touch him again. For I will never see that most noble king who made me a knight either killed or shamed."

And with that Sir Lancelot got down from his horse, and took up the king and put him back on his horse, and said this: "My lord Arthur, for the love of God, stop this strife, for you win no honour here. I could do my uttermost, but all the time I hold back from you, and neither you nor any of yours holds back from me. My lord, remember what I have done in many places, and now I am badly rewarded."

Then, when King Arthur was on horseback, he looked at Sir Lancelot, and then the tears burst from his eyes, as he thought of the great courtesy that was in Sir Lancelot, more than in any other man. And with that the king rode away, and could look at him no longer, and said, "Alas that this war ever began!"

And then both sides drew back from the battle to rest, and buried the dead, and laid soothing salves on the wounded men; and so they held out that night until the morning. And in the morning, by mid-morning, they made ready to do battle. And then Sir Bors led the vanguard.

So in the morning Sir Gawain came, as fierce as any boar, with a great spear in his hand. And when Sir Bors saw him, he meant to avenge his brother Sir Lionel for the injury that Sir Gawain had done him the day before. And so, as they knew each other, they set their spears in rest, and with all the might of their horses and of themselves they met together so fiercely that each ran the other through, and so they both fell to the ground. And then the armies joined, and there was great slaughter on both sides. Then Sir Lancelot rescued Sir Bors, and sent him into the castle; but neither Sir Gawain nor Sir Bors died of their wounds, for they were all healed.

Then Sir Lavaine and Sir Urre begged Sir Lancelot to exert himself, and fight as they had done. "For we see you hold back and spare them, and that does much harm. So we beg you, spare your enemies no more than they spare you."

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "I have no heart to fight against my lord Arthur, for it always seems to me that I am not doing as I ought."

"My lord," said Sir Palomides, "though you spare them all this day, they will never thank you for it; and if they can get you at a disadvantage, you are as good as dead."

So then Sir Lancelot understood that they told him the truth; and then he exerted himself more than he had done before, and all the more because his nephew Sir Bors was badly wounded. And then within a little while, by the time of evensong, Sir Lancelot and his side had the upper hand, for their horses waded in blood above the fetlocks, so many people were killed. And then, out of pity, Sir Lancelot held back his knights, and let King Arthur's side draw off to one side. And then Sir Lancelot's side withdrew into his castle, and both sides buried the dead and put salve on the wounded men.

So when Sir Gawain was hurt, those on King Arthur's side were not so proud to do battle as they had been before. This war was talked of through all Christendom, and at last it was reported before the Pope. And he, considering the great goodness of King Arthur and of Sir Lancelot, who were called the noblest knights in the world, called to him a noble churchman who was there at that time (the French book says it was the Bishop of Rochester). And the Pope gave him papal bulls sealed with lead to take to King Arthur of England, charging him, on pain of laying all England under interdict, with every church in it shut, to take his queen Dame Guinevere back to him again, and be reconciled with Sir Lancelot.

Chapter 14: How the Pope sent his papal bulls to make peace, and how Sir Lancelot brought the queen to King Arthur

So when this Bishop had come to Carlisle, he showed the king these bulls. And when the king understood these bulls, he did not know what to do. He would very gladly have been reconciled with Sir Lancelot, but Sir Gawain would not allow him; but as for having the queen back, to that he agreed. But on no account would Sir Gawain allow the king to be reconciled with Sir Lancelot; but as for the queen, he consented. And then the Bishop had from the king his great seal, and his guarantee, as he was a true anointed king, that Sir Lancelot should come safely and go safely, and that the queen should not be reproached by the king, nor by anyone else, for anything done in times past. And of all these terms the Bishop brought with him sure guarantees and writings, to show Sir Lancelot.

So when the Bishop had come to Joyous Gard, he showed Sir Lancelot there how the Pope had written to Arthur and to him, and there he told him the dangers if he kept the queen from the king.

"It was never in my thoughts," said Lancelot, "to keep the queen from my lord Arthur. But since she was to have died for my sake, it seemed to me it was my part to save her life, and put her out of that danger until a better remedy might come. And now I thank God," said Sir Lancelot, "that the Pope has made her peace. For God knows," said Sir Lancelot, "I will be a thousand times gladder to bring her back than I ever was to take her away; provided that I can be sure to come safely and go safely, and that the queen shall have her freedom as she had before, and that never, for anything that has been alleged before this time, shall she stand in any danger from this day on. For otherwise," said Sir Lancelot, "I dare risk myself to keep her from a harder attack than any I ever kept her from."

"You will not need to fear so much," said the Bishop. "For believe me, the Pope must be obeyed, and it would not be to the Pope's honour, nor to my poor good name, to let you be wronged, nor the queen either, neither put in danger nor shamed."

And then he showed Sir Lancelot all his writings, both from the Pope and from King Arthur.

"This is sure enough," said Sir Lancelot, "for I dare trust my lord's own writing and his seal completely, for he was never shamed in his promise. Therefore," said Sir Lancelot to the Bishop, "you shall ride ahead to the king, and commend me to his good grace, and let him know that eight days from today, by the grace of God, I myself will bring my lady Queen Guinevere to him. And then say to my most dread king that I will speak out boldly for the queen, and that I will make no exception, for dread or fear, except the king himself and my lord Sir Gawain; and that is more for the king's love than for Gawain's own."

So the Bishop left, and came to the king at Carlisle, and told him everything, how Sir Lancelot had answered him; and then the tears burst from the king's eyes. Then Sir Lancelot provided himself with a hundred knights, and all were dressed in green velvet, and their horses were draped in trappings to their heels; and every knight held an olive branch in his hand, as a token of peace. And the queen had twenty-four gentlewomen following her in the same way; and Sir Lancelot had twelve warhorses following him, and on every warhorse sat a young man of good birth, and they were all dressed in green velvet, with girdles of gold about their waists, and the horses draped in the same way down to the heels, with many jewelled clasps, set with stones and pearls in gold, a thousand of them. And the queen and Sir Lancelot were dressed in white cloth of gold tissue. And just as you have heard, as the French book tells, he rode with the queen from Joyous Gard to Carlisle. And so Sir Lancelot rode through Carlisle, and so into the castle, so that everyone could see; and believe me, there was many a weeping eye. And then Sir Lancelot himself dismounted and got clear of his horse, and took the queen, and so led her to where King Arthur sat on his throne; and Sir Gawain sat in front of him, and many other great lords. So when Sir Lancelot saw the king and Sir Gawain, he led the queen by the arm, and then he knelt down, and the queen too. Believe me, there were many bold knights there with King Arthur who wept as tenderly as if they had seen all their kin before them. So the king sat still and said no word. And when Sir Lancelot saw his face, he rose and raised the queen with him, and then he spoke, like a true knight.

Chapter 15: Of the handing over of the queen to the king by Sir Lancelot, and what words Sir Gawain had for Sir Lancelot

"My most revered king," said Sir Lancelot, "you are to understand that, by the Pope's command and yours, I have brought my lady the queen to you, as right requires. And if there is any knight, of whatever rank he may be, except your own person, who will say or dares say that she is anything but true and pure to you, I, Sir Lancelot du Lake, here and now will make it good upon his body that she is a true lady to you. But you have listened to liars, and that has caused the strife between you and me. For there was a time, my lord Arthur, when you were greatly pleased with me when I did battle for my lady, your queen. And you know full well, my most noble king, that she has been put to great wrong before this time. And since it pleased you many times that I should fight for her, it seems to me, my good lord, that I had all the more cause to rescue her from the fire, seeing that she was to have been burned for my sake. For those who told you those tales were liars, and so it fell out against them. For in all likelihood, if the might of God had not been with me, I could never have held out against fourteen knights, and they armed and ready by plan, and I unarmed and with no plan at all. For I was sent for to come to my lady your queen, I do not know for what reason; but I was no sooner inside the chamber door than at once Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred called me traitor and recreant knight."

"They called you right," said Sir Gawain.

"My lord Sir Gawain," said Sir Lancelot, "in their quarrel they did not prove themselves in the right."

"Well, well, Sir Lancelot," said the king, "I have given you no cause to do to me as you have done, for I have honoured you and yours more than any of all my knights."

"My good lord," said Sir Lancelot, "if you will not be displeased, you are to understand that I and mine have often done you better service than any other knights have done, in many different places. And where you have been in a very hard spot at various times, I have myself rescued you from many dangers. And always, to the best of my power, I was glad to please you, and my lord Sir Gawain. Both in jousts and tournaments, and in pitched battles, both on horseback and on foot, I have often rescued you, and my lord Sir Gawain, and many more of your knights, in many different places. For now I will boast," said Sir Lancelot. "I want you all to know that I never yet found any kind of knight but that I was too hard for him, if I did my uttermost, thanks be to God. Though I have been matched with good knights, such as Sir Tristram and Sir Lamorak, I always had a goodwill toward them and a judgement of what they were. And I take God to witness," said Sir Lancelot, "I was never angry, nor greatly downcast, with any good knight if I saw him busy about winning honour. And I was always glad when I found any knight who could stand against me on horseback and on foot. Yet Sir Carados of the Dolorous Tower was a very noble knight and an exceedingly strong man, and you know that, my lord Sir Gawain. For he might well be called a noble knight when by sheer force he pulled you out of your saddle and bound you across his saddlebow in front of him; and there, my lord Sir Gawain, I rescued you, and killed him before your eyes. Also I found his brother, Sir Turquine, in the same way leading Sir Gaheris, your brother, bound in front of him; and there I rescued your brother and killed that Turquine, and freed sixty-four of my lord Arthur's knights from his prison. And now I dare say," said Sir Lancelot, "I never met with knights so strong, nor so good at fighting, as Sir Carados and Sir Turquine were, for I fought with them to the uttermost. And therefore," said Sir Lancelot to Sir Gawain, "it seems to me that you ought by rights to remember this. For if I could have your goodwill, I would trust to God to have my lord Arthur's good grace."

Chapter 16: Of the talk between Sir Gawain and Sir Lancelot, with much other speech

"The king may do as he likes," said Sir Gawain, "but you may be sure, Sir Lancelot, you and I will never be reconciled while we live, for you have killed three of my brothers. And two of them you killed treacherously and pitilessly, for they wore no armour against you, nor would they wear any."

"I wish to God they had been armed," said Sir Lancelot, "for then they would be alive. And believe me, Sir Gawain, as for Sir Gareth, I love none of my own kinsmen as much as I loved him. And as long as I live," said Sir Lancelot, "I will mourn Sir Gareth's death, and not only for the great fear I have of you, but many causes make me sorrowful. One is that I made him a knight. Another is that I know well he loved me above all other knights. And the third is that he was exceedingly noble, true, courteous and well-bred, and of good character. The fourth is that I knew well, as soon as I heard that Sir Gareth was dead, I would never again have your love, but everlasting war between us; and I knew well too that you would make my noble lord Arthur my mortal enemy for ever. And as Jesus is my help," said Sir Lancelot, "I never killed Sir Gareth or Sir Gaheris by my will; but alas that they were ever unarmed on that ill-fated day. But this much I will offer," said Sir Lancelot, "if it may please the king's good grace, and you, my lord Sir Gawain. I will begin first at Sandwich, and there I will go in my shirt, barefoot; and at the end of every ten miles I will found and have built a house of religion, of whatever order you will assign me, with a whole community of monks, to sing and read day and night, especially for the sake of Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris. And this I will carry out from Sandwich to Carlisle, and every house shall have enough income to live on. And this I will carry out while I have any income in Christendom; and there shall not be one of all these religious houses but it shall be completed, furnished and fitted out in everything as a holy place ought to be, I promise you faithfully. And this, Sir Gawain, seems to me fairer and holier, and far better for their souls, than that you, my most noble king, and you, Sir Gawain, should make war on me, for you will gain nothing by it."

Then all the knights and ladies who were there wept as if they were mad, and the tears fell on King Arthur's cheeks.

"Sir Lancelot," said Sir Gawain, "I have heard your speech very well, and your great offers. But you may be sure, let the king do as he pleases, I will never forgive my brothers' deaths, and above all the death of my brother Sir Gareth. And if my uncle, King Arthur, makes peace with you, he will lose my service. For you may be sure you are false both to the king and to me."

"Sir," said Lancelot, "there is no man alive who can prove that. And if you, Sir Gawain, will charge me with so grave a thing, you must pardon me, for then I have no choice but to answer you."

"No," said Sir Gawain, "we are past that for now, and the Pope is the cause of it. For he has charged my uncle the king that he must take his queen back and make peace with you, Sir Lancelot, for this time; and therefore you shall go safe as you came. But you shall not stay in this land more than fifteen days; that is the summons I give you. So the king and we had agreed and settled it before you came. Otherwise," said Sir Gawain, "you may be sure you would not have come here, except against your will. And if it were not for the Pope's command," said Sir Gawain, "I would do battle with my own body against your body, and prove it upon you, that you have been false both to my uncle King Arthur and to me; and that I will prove upon your body once you have gone from here, wherever I find you."

Chapter 17: How Sir Lancelot left the king and Joyous Gard for the sea, and what knights went with him

Then Sir Lancelot sighed, and with that the tears fell on his cheeks, and then he said this: "Alas, most noble Christian realm, which I have loved above all other realms, and in you I have won a great part of my honour, and now I must leave in this way. Truly I regret that I ever came into this realm, to be so shamefully banished, undeserved and without cause. But fortune is so changeable, and her wheel so moveable, that there is no constant staying, and that may be proved by many old chronicles, of noble Hector, and Troilus, and Alexander the mighty conqueror, and many more besides: when they were highest in their royalty, they came down lowest. And so it goes with me," said Sir Lancelot, "for in this realm I had honour, and through me and mine the whole Round Table has been increased in honour, through me and my blood, more than through any other. And therefore you may be sure, Sir Gawain, I can live on my own lands as well as any knight who is here. And if you, my most revered king, come upon my lands with Sir Gawain to make war on me, I must bear with you as well as I can. But as for you, Sir Gawain, if you come there, I beg you not to charge me with treason or felony, for if you do, I must answer you."

"Do your best," said Sir Gawain, "and so hurry up and be gone. And you may be sure we will soon come after you, and break the strongest castle you have upon your head."

"There will be no need for that," said Sir Lancelot, "for if I were as proud as you are, believe me, I would meet you in the middle of the field."

"Make no more talk," said Sir Gawain, "but hand over the queen, and take yourself quickly out of this court."

"Well," said Sir Lancelot, "if I had known of this short welcome, I would have thought twice before I came here. For if the queen were as dear to me as you make out, I would have dared to keep her from the fellowship of the best knights under heaven."

And then Sir Lancelot said to Guinevere, in the hearing of the king and all of them, "Madam, now I must leave you and this noble fellowship for ever. And since it is so, I beg you to pray for me, and speak well of me. And if you are in a hard spot because of any false tongues, my lady, send me word quickly; and if any knight's hands can free you by battle, I will free you."

And with that Sir Lancelot kissed the queen; and then he said openly before them all, "Now let us see who in this place dares say the queen is not true to my lord Arthur. Let us see who will speak, if he dares to speak."

And with that he brought the queen to the king, and then Sir Lancelot took his leave and left. And there was neither king, duke nor earl, baron nor knight, lady nor gentlewoman, but they all wept like people out of their minds, except Sir Gawain. And when the noble Sir Lancelot mounted his horse to ride out of Carlisle, there was sobbing and weeping out of pure grief at his leaving. And so he took his way to Joyous Gard, and from then on he called it the Dolorous Gard. And so Sir Lancelot left the court for ever.

And so when he came to Joyous Gard he called his company to him, and asked them what they would do. Then they all answered together with one voice that they would do as he would do.

"My fair companions," said Sir Lancelot, "I must leave this most noble realm, and now that I must leave it, it grieves me badly, for I shall leave with no honour. For a man driven out never left a realm with any honour; and that is my sorrow, for I fear always that after my days men will write in their chronicles of me that I was driven out of this land. And otherwise, my fair lords, be sure of this: if I had not feared shame, my lady Queen Guinevere and I would never have parted."

Then many noble knights spoke, such as Sir Palomides, Sir Safere his brother, and Sir Bellangere le Beuse, and Sir Urre, with Sir Lavaine, and many others: "Sir, if you are minded to stay in this land, we will never fail you. And if you do not care to stay in this land, there is not one of the good knights here who will fail you, for many reasons. One is that all of us who are not of your blood will never be welcome at the court. And since it pleased us to take your part in your distress and sorrow in this realm, believe me, it will please us just as well to go into other countries with you, and to take whatever part you take there."

"My fair lords," said Sir Lancelot, "I understand you well, and I thank you as best I can. And you are to understand that I will share out with you, in this manner, such inheritance as I was born to: that is to say, I will divide all my income and all my lands freely among you, and I myself will have as little as any of you. For if I have enough for my own person, I will ask for no other rich array. And I trust to God to maintain you on my lands as well as any knights were ever maintained."

Then all the knights spoke at once: "Shame on any man who leaves you! For we all understand that in this realm there will be no peace now, but always strife and quarrelling, now that the fellowship of the Round Table is broken. For by the noble fellowship of the Round Table King Arthur was held up, and by their nobility the king and all his realm were at peace and rest; and a great part of that," they said, "was all because of your nobility."

Chapter 18: How Sir Lancelot crossed the sea, and how he made great lords of the knights who went with him

"Truly," said Sir Lancelot, "I thank you all for your kind words. And yet I know well that the whole stability of this realm did not lie in me; but as far as I could, I did my duty. And I am quite sure I knew of many rebellions in my day that were put down by me, and I believe we shall all hear of them in a short while, and that I deeply regret. For I always fear," said Sir Lancelot, "that Sir Mordred will make trouble, for he is exceedingly envious and sets himself to make trouble."

So they agreed to go with Sir Lancelot to his lands. And to cut a long story short, they packed up, and paid everyone who asked for payment; and a full hundred knights left with Sir Lancelot at once, and made their vows that they would never leave him, for better or for worse.

And so they took ship at Cardiff, and sailed to Benwick. Some men call it Bayonne, and some men call it Beaune, where the wine of Beaune comes from. But to tell the truth, Sir Lancelot and his nephews were lords of all France, and of all the lands that belonged to France; he and his kindred enjoyed it all through Sir Lancelot's noble prowess. And then Sir Lancelot stocked and furnished and armed all his noble towns and castles. Then all the people of those lands came to Sir Lancelot on foot and did him homage.
