And so when he had settled all these countries, he called a parliament without delay; and there he crowned Sir Lionel King of France; and Sir Bors he crowned king of all King Claudas's lands; and Sir Ector de Maris, who was Sir Lancelot's youngest brother, he crowned King of Benwick, and king of all Guienne, which was Sir Lancelot's own land. And he made Sir Ector prince over them all, and so he shared it out.

Then Sir Lancelot raised up all his noble knights, and first he raised up those of his own blood. That was Sir Blamore: he made him Duke of the Limousin in Guienne. And Sir Bleoberis he made Duke of Poitiers, and Sir Gahalantine he made Duke of Querne, and Sir Galihodin he made Duke of Saintonge, and Sir Galihud he made Earl of Perigord, and Sir Menadeuke he made Earl of Rouergue, and Sir Villiers the Valiant he made Earl of Bearn, and Sir Hebes le Renoumes he made Earl of Comminges, and Sir Lavaine he made Earl of Armagnac, and Sir Urre he made Earl of Astarac, and Sir Neroneus he made Earl of Pardiac, and Sir Plenorius he made Earl of Foix, and Sir Selises of the Dolorous Tower he made Earl of Masauke, and Sir Melias de Lile he made Earl of Tursauk, and Sir Bellangere le Beuse he made Earl of the Landes, and Sir Palomides he made Duke of Provence, and Sir Safere he made Duke of Languedoc, and to Sir Clegis he gave the Earldom of Agen, and to Sir Sadok he gave the Earldom of Sarlat, and Sir Dinas the Seneschal he made Duke of Anjou, and Sir Clarrus he made Duke of Normandy. So Sir Lancelot rewarded his noble knights, and many more, whom it would take too long, it seems to me, to list.

Chapter 19: How King Arthur and Sir Gawain made a great army ready to cross the sea and make war on Sir Lancelot

So we leave Sir Lancelot in his lands, and his noble knights with him, and return again to King Arthur and to Sir Gawain, who made a great army ready, to the number of sixty thousand. And everything was made ready for their shipping to cross the sea, and so they took ship at Cardiff. And there King Arthur made Sir Mordred chief ruler of all England, and he also put Queen Guinevere in his keeping. Because Sir Mordred was King Arthur's son, he gave him the rule of his land and of his wife. And so the king crossed the sea and landed on Sir Lancelot's lands, and there, through the vengeance of Sir Gawain, he burned and laid waste all that they could overrun.

When word of this came to Sir Lancelot, that King Arthur and Sir Gawain had landed on his lands and were making a very great destruction and waste, then Sir Bors spoke, and said, "My lord Sir Lancelot, it is a shame that we allow them to ride over our lands like this. For believe me, put up with them as long as you like, they will show you no favour if they can get their hands on you."

Then Sir Lionel, who was wary and wise, said, "My lord Sir Lancelot, I will give this advice. Let us hold our strong walled towns until they suffer hunger and cold and blow on their nails; and then let us set on them fresh, and cut them down like sheep in a field, so that foreigners may take warning for ever how they land on our lands."

Then King Bagdemagus spoke to Sir Lancelot: "Sir, your courtesy will be the ruin of us all, and your courtesy has woken all this sorrow. For if they ride over our lands like this, they will in time bring us all to nothing while we hide in holes like this."

Then Sir Galihud said to Sir Lancelot, "Sir, here are knights come of kings' blood, who will not hang their heads for long, and they are within these walls. So give us leave, as we are knights, to meet them in the field, and we will kill them, so that they will curse the time they ever came into this country."

Then seven brothers of North Wales spoke, and they were seven noble knights; a man might search seven kings' lands before he could find seven such knights. Then they all said at once, "Sir Lancelot, for Christ's sake let us ride out with Sir Galihud, for we were never used to cowering in castles or in noble towns."

Then Sir Lancelot, who was master and governor of them all, spoke: "My fair lords, believe me, I am very unwilling to ride out with my knights and shed Christian blood. And besides, I understand that my lands are very bare for supporting any army for long, because of the mighty wars that King Claudas once made upon this country, upon my father King Ban, and on my uncle King Bors. However, for this time we will keep to our strong walls, and I will send a messenger to my lord Arthur to make a treaty; for peace is better than war for ever."

So Sir Lancelot sent out a damsel, and a dwarf with her, asking King Arthur to leave off his warring on his lands. And so she leapt onto a palfrey, and the dwarf ran by her side. And when she came to King Arthur's tent, she dismounted there; and there a well-bred knight met her, Sir Lucan the butler, and said, "Fair damsel, do you come from Sir Lancelot du Lake?"

"Yes, sir," she said, "and that is why I have come here, to speak with my lord the king."

"Alas," said Sir Lucan, "my lord Arthur would love Lancelot, but Sir Gawain will not let him." And then he said, "I pray to God, damsel, that you may succeed, for all of us who are about the king wish that Sir Lancelot fared the best of any knight living."

And so with this Lucan led the damsel to the king where he sat with Sir Gawain, to hear what she would say. So when she had told her tale, the tears ran out of the king's eyes, and all the lords were very glad to advise the king to make peace with Sir Lancelot, all except Sir Gawain. And he said, "My lord my uncle, what will you do? Will you turn back now, now that you have come this far on this campaign? All the world will speak of your disgrace."

"No," said Arthur, "believe me, Sir Gawain, I will do as you advise me. And yet it seems to me," said Arthur, "his fair offers were not to be refused. But since I have come so far on this campaign, I want you to give the damsel her answer, for I cannot speak to her for pity, her offers are so generous."

Chapter 20: What message Sir Gawain sent to Sir Lancelot, and how King Arthur laid siege to Benwick, and other matters

Then Sir Gawain said this to the damsel: "Damsel, tell Sir Lancelot that it is wasted effort now to plead with my uncle. For tell him that if he had wanted to make any effort for peace, he should have made it before this; for tell him now it is too late. And say that I, Sir Gawain, send him this word: that I promise him, by the faith I owe to God and to knighthood, I will never leave him until he has killed me or I him."

So the damsel wept and left, and there were many weeping eyes. And so Sir Lucan brought the damsel to her palfrey, and so she came to Sir Lancelot where he was among all his knights. And when Sir Lancelot had heard this answer, the tears ran down his cheeks. And then his noble knights strode up around him, and said, "Sir Lancelot, why do you look like this? Think what you are, and what men we are, and let us noble knights match them in the middle of the field."

"That could easily be done," said Sir Lancelot, "but I was never so unwilling to do battle. And therefore I beg you, fair sirs, as you love me, be ruled as I would have you. For I will always flee from that noble king who made me a knight. And when I can go no further, I must defend myself, and that will be more honour for me and for us all than to set ourselves against that noble king whom we have all served."

Then they held their tongues, and that night they took their rest.

And in the morning early, at the dawning of the day, as knights looked out, they saw the city of Benwick besieged all round. And quickly the besiegers began to set up ladders, and then those in the town fought them off and beat them from the walls stoutly. Then Sir Gawain came out, well armed, on a strong steed, and he came before the main gate with his spear in his hand, crying, "Sir Lancelot, where are you? Is there not one of you proud knights who dares break a spear with me?"

Then Sir Bors made himself ready, and came out of the town, and there Sir Gawain met Sir Bors. And at that time he struck Sir Bors down from his horse, and almost killed him; and so Sir Bors was rescued and carried into the town. Then Sir Lionel came out, Sir Bors's brother, and meant to avenge him; and each set his spear in rest, and they charged together. And there they met fiercely, but Sir Gawain had such grace that he struck Sir Lionel down, and wounded him there exceedingly badly; and then Sir Lionel was rescued and carried into the town. And this Sir Gawain came every day, and he never failed to strike down one knight or another.

So they went on like this for half a year, and there was much slaughter of people on both sides. Then it happened one day that Sir Gawain came before the gates, armed at all points, on a noble horse, with a great spear in his hand; and then he cried in a loud voice, "Where are you now, you false traitor, Sir Lancelot? Why do you hide inside holes and walls like a coward? Look out now, you false traitor knight, and here I will take revenge on your body for the death of my three brothers!"

Sir Lancelot heard every bit of all this talk; and his kin and his knights drew around him, and they all said at once to Sir Lancelot, "Sir Lancelot, now you must defend yourself like a knight, or else you will be shamed for ever. For now that you are accused of treason, it is time for you to stir, for you have slept too long and put up with too much."

"So God help me," said Sir Lancelot, "I am very downcast at Sir Gawain's words, for now he has charged me with a grave charge. And therefore I know as well as you do that I must defend myself, or else be shamed as a recreant."

Then Sir Lancelot ordered his strongest horse to be saddled, and had his arms fetched, and all brought to the gate of the tower. And then Sir Lancelot spoke out from on high to King Arthur, and said, "My lord Arthur, noble king who made me a knight, believe me, I am very sorrowful for your sake that you pursue me like this. And I always held back from you; for if I had wanted to be vengeful, I might have met you in the middle of the field, and there made your boldest knights very tame. And now I have held back for half a year, and allowed you and Sir Gawain to do whatever you would do; and now I can bear it no longer, for now I must defend myself, since Sir Gawain has accused me of treason. And that is greatly against my will, that I should ever fight against any of your blood; but now I cannot refuse it, for I am driven to it like a beast brought to bay."

Then Sir Gawain said, "Sir Lancelot, if you dare do battle, stop your babbling and come out, and let us ease our hearts."

Then Sir Lancelot armed himself swiftly, and mounted his horse, and each of the knights took great spears in their hands. And the army outside stood still, all apart, and the noble knights came out of the city in great numbers, so many that when Arthur saw the number of men and knights, he marvelled, and said to himself, "Alas that Sir Lancelot was ever against me, for now I see he has held back from me."

And so the agreement was made that no man should come near them, or have anything to do with them, until the one was dead or had yielded.

Chapter 21: How Sir Lancelot and Sir Gawain fought together, and how Sir Gawain was overthrown and wounded

Then Sir Gawain and Sir Lancelot drew a great way apart, and then they came together with all their horses' might, as fast as they could run, and each struck the other in the middle of his shield. But the knights were so strong, and their spears so big, that their horses could not withstand their blows, and so their horses fell to the earth. And then they got clear of their horses, and set their shields in front of them. Then they stood together and gave many heavy blows on various places of their bodies, so that the blood burst out on many sides and places.

Then Sir Gawain had a grace and gift that a holy man had given him: every day of the year, from mid-morning until high noon, his might increased threefold in those three hours, and that made Sir Gawain win great honour. And for his sake King Arthur made an ordinance that all battles, for whatever quarrel, that were to be fought before King Arthur should begin at mid-morning. And all this was done out of love for Sir Gawain, so that in all likelihood, if Sir Gawain were on the one side, he would have the better of the battle while his strength lasted those three hours. But there were very few knights living at that time who knew of this advantage that Sir Gawain had, except King Arthur alone.

So Sir Lancelot fought with Sir Gawain, and when Sir Lancelot felt his might increase more and more, Sir Lancelot wondered, and greatly feared to be shamed. For, as the French book says, when Sir Lancelot felt Sir Gawain double his strength, he thought he was a fiend and no earthly man. And so Sir Lancelot circled and sidestepped, and covered himself with his shield, and saved his strength and his quickness for three hours. And all that while Sir Gawain gave him many heavy charges and many heavy blows, so that all the knights who watched Sir Lancelot marvelled how he could hold out against him; but they little understood the labour Sir Lancelot had to hold out against him. And then, when it was past noon, Sir Gawain had nothing more than his own might. When Sir Lancelot felt him come down like this, then he drew himself up and stood close to Sir Gawain, and said this: "My lord Sir Gawain, now I feel that you are done. Now, my lord Sir Gawain, I must do my part, for I have borne many great and grievous blows from you this day with great pain."

Then Sir Lancelot doubled his blows, and gave Sir Gawain such a blow on the helmet that he fell down on his side, and Sir Lancelot drew back from him.

"Why are you drawing back?" said Sir Gawain. "Now turn back, false traitor knight, and kill me! For if you leave me like this, when I am healed I will do battle with you again."

"I will stand up to you, sir, by God's grace," said Sir Lancelot, "but you may be sure, Sir Gawain, I will never strike a fallen knight."

And so Sir Lancelot went into the city; and Sir Gawain was carried into King Arthur's tent, and doctors were brought to him, and they probed his wounds and dressed them with soft ointments.

And then Sir Lancelot said, "Now good day to you, my lord the king, for believe me, you will win no honour at these walls. And if I were to bring my knights out, many a man would die. Therefore, my lord Arthur, remember old kindness; and however it goes with me, may Jesus be your guide in all places."

Chapter 22: Of the sorrow King Arthur felt for the war, and of another battle where Sir Gawain again got the worst of it

"Alas," said the king, "that this ill-fated war was ever begun! For Sir Lancelot always holds back from me everywhere, and from my kin in the same way, and that was plain to see this day with my nephew Sir Gawain."

Then King Arthur fell sick with sorrow for Sir Gawain, because he was so badly hurt, and because of the war between him and Sir Lancelot. So then those on King Arthur's side kept up the siege, with little fighting on the outside; and those inside kept to their walls, and defended them when there was need. So Sir Gawain lay sick three weeks in his tents, with every kind of doctoring that could be had. And as soon as Sir Gawain could walk and ride, he armed himself at all points, and leapt onto a warhorse, and took a spear in his hand, and so he came riding before the main gate of Benwick. And there he cried aloud, "Where are you, Sir Lancelot? Come out, you false traitor knight and recreant, for I am here, Sir Gawain, who will prove what I say on you!"

Sir Lancelot heard all this talk, and then he said this: "Sir Gawain, I am sorry for your foul words, that you will not stop your talk. For you know well, Sir Gawain, I know your might and all that you can do; and you know well, Sir Gawain, you cannot do me much harm."

"Come down, traitor knight," said he, "and prove the contrary with your hands! For it was my bad luck in the last battle to be hurt by your hands; so you may be sure I have come this day to make up for it, for I mean this day to lay you as low as you laid me."

"Jesus forbid," said Sir Lancelot, "that I should ever be so far in your power as you have been in mine, for then my days would be done. But Sir Gawain," said Sir Lancelot, "you shall not think that I will hang back long; but since you call me a traitor so unknightly, you shall have both your hands full of me."

And then Sir Lancelot armed himself at all points, and mounted his horse, and took a great spear in his hand, and rode out at the gate. And both the armies were assembled, those outside and those inside, and stood in array very manfully. And both sides were ordered to hold themselves still, to see and watch the battle of these two noble knights. And then they laid their spears in their rests, and they came together like thunder, and Sir Gawain broke his spear upon Sir Lancelot into a hundred pieces right up to his hand. And Sir Lancelot struck him with a greater might, so that the feet of Sir Gawain's horse rose up, and so the horse and he fell to the earth. Then Sir Gawain nimbly got clear of his horse, and put his shield in front of him, and eagerly drew his sword, and said to Sir Lancelot, "Get down, traitor knight! For if this mare's son has failed me, you may be sure a king's son and a queen's son will not fail you."

Then Sir Lancelot got clear of his horse, and set his shield in front of him, and drew his sword; and so they stood together and gave many heavy blows, so that all men on both sides were exceedingly amazed at it. But when Sir Lancelot felt Sir Gawain's might increase so marvellously, he held back his courage and his breath, and kept his might wonderfully hidden; and under his shield he circled and sidestepped here and there, to break Sir Gawain's blows and his spirit. And Sir Gawain strained himself with all his might and power to destroy Sir Lancelot; for, as the French book says, always as Sir Gawain's might increased, just so increased his breath and his ill will. So Sir Gawain gave Sir Lancelot great trouble for three hours, so that he had very great pains to defend himself.

And when the three hours were past, and Sir Lancelot felt that Sir Gawain had come back to his own proper strength, then Sir Lancelot said to Sir Gawain, "Now I have tested you twice, and found that you are a very dangerous knight and a wonderful man for your might. And you have done many wonderful deeds in your day, for by your increasing might you have deceived many a very noble and valiant knight. And now that I feel you have done your mighty deeds, now believe me, I must do my deeds."

And then Sir Lancelot stood close to Sir Gawain, and then Sir Lancelot doubled his blows. And Sir Gawain defended himself mightily, but nevertheless Sir Lancelot struck such a blow on Sir Gawain's helmet, and on the old wound, that Sir Gawain sank down on one side in a faint. And as soon as he came to, he waved and thrust at Sir Lancelot as he lay, and said, "Traitor knight, you may be sure I am not dead yet. Come near me and finish this battle to the uttermost!"

"I will do no more than I have done," said Sir Lancelot. "For when I see you on your feet, I will do battle with you all the while I see you stand on your feet; but as for striking a wounded man who cannot stand, God keep me from such a shame!"

And then he turned and went his way toward the city. And Sir Gawain kept calling him traitor knight all the while, and said, "You may be sure, Sir Lancelot, when I am healed I will do battle with you again, for I will never leave you until one of us is killed."

So the siege went on, and Sir Gawain lay sick for nearly a month; and when he was well recovered, and would have been ready within three days to do battle again with Sir Lancelot, just then news came to Arthur from England that made King Arthur and all his army move.

Here follows the twenty-first book.

Book Twenty-One: King Arthur's Last Departing, and How Sir Lancelot Came to Avenge His Death

Chapter 1: How Sir Mordred presumed to make himself King of England, and tried to marry the queen, his father's wife

While Sir Mordred was ruler of all England, he had letters made as though they came from over the sea, and the letters said that King Arthur had been killed in battle with Sir Lancelot. So Sir Mordred called a parliament, and summoned the lords together, and there he made them choose him king; and so he was crowned at Canterbury, and held a feast there for fifteen days. And afterwards he went to Winchester, and there he took Queen Guinevere, and said plainly that he would marry her, who was his uncle's wife and his father's wife. And so he made ready for the feast, and a day was set for them to be married; at which Queen Guinevere was exceedingly downcast. But she did not dare show what was in her heart, but spoke him fair, and agreed to Sir Mordred's will. Then she asked Sir Mordred's leave to go to London, to buy all the things that belonged to the wedding. And because of her fair words Sir Mordred trusted her well enough, and gave her leave to go. And so when she came to London she took the Tower of London, and suddenly, in all the haste she could, she stocked it with all kinds of provisions, and manned it well, and so held it.

Then when Sir Mordred knew and understood how he had been tricked, he was angry beyond measure. And to cut a long story short, he went and laid a mighty siege around the Tower of London, and made many great assaults on it, and hurled many great stones at them from his siege engines, and fired great guns. But none of it could do Sir Mordred any good, for Queen Guinevere would never, for fair words or foul, trust herself to come into his hands again.

Then came the Bishop of Canterbury, who was a noble scholar and a holy man, and this is what he said to Sir Mordred: "Sir, what are you going to do? Will you first offend God and then shame yourself, and all knighthood? Is King Arthur not your uncle, no further off than your mother's brother? And on her, his own sister, King Arthur himself fathered you. So how can you marry your father's wife? Sir," said the noble scholar, "give up this idea, or I will curse you with book and bell and candle."

"Do your worst," said Sir Mordred. "And you can be sure I'll defy you."

"Sir," said the Bishop, "and you may be sure I will not be afraid to do what I ought to do. And you spread it about that my lord Arthur is killed, and that is not so, and so you will make foul work in this land."

"Quiet, you lying priest," said Sir Mordred, "for if you provoke me any more I'll have your head struck off."

So the Bishop left and pronounced the curse in the haughtiest way that it could be done. And then Sir Mordred went looking for the Bishop of Canterbury, to have him killed. Then the Bishop fled, and took part of his goods with him, and went to a place near Glastonbury; and there he lived as a priest and hermit in a chapel, in poverty and in holy prayer, for he understood well that a disastrous war was at hand.

Then Sir Mordred pressed Queen Guinevere with letters and messengers, and by fair means and foul, to make her come out of the Tower of London; but none of it did any good, for she answered him curtly, openly and in private, that she would rather kill herself than be married to him. Then word came to Sir Mordred that King Arthur had raised the siege against Sir Lancelot and was coming home with a great army, to take vengeance on Sir Mordred. So Sir Mordred had writs written and sent to all the barons of this land, and many people flocked to him. For the common talk among them then was that with Arthur there was no other life but war and strife, and with Sir Mordred there was great joy and happiness. So Sir Arthur was slandered and spoken ill of. And there were many whom King Arthur had raised up from nothing, and given lands, who could not then say a good word for him. Look, all you Englishmen, do you not see what a wretched thing this was? For he who was the greatest king and knight in the world, and loved the fellowship of noble knights the most, and by whom they were all upheld, even with him these Englishmen could not be content. Look, this was the old custom and habit of this land; and men say too that we of this land have not yet lost or forgotten that custom and habit. Alas, this is a great failing of ours, we Englishmen, for nothing pleases us for long. And that was how the people behaved at that time: they were better pleased with Sir Mordred than they were with King Arthur. And many people flocked to Sir Mordred, and said they would stand by him for better and for worse. And so Sir Mordred went with a great army to Dover, for he had heard that Sir Arthur would land there, and so he meant to drive his own father from his lands; and most of England held with Sir Mordred, the people were so fickle and so fond of anything new.

Chapter 2: How King Arthur, when he had the news, came back to Dover, where Sir Mordred met him to stop his landing, and of the death of Sir Gawain

And so, while Sir Mordred was at Dover with his army, King Arthur came with a great navy of ships, and galleys, and carracks. And there was Sir Mordred, ready and waiting for his landing, to stop his own father from landing on the land that he was king over. Then there was launching of boats great and small, full of noble men-at-arms; and there was great slaughter of well-born knights, and many a bold baron was laid low, on both sides. But King Arthur was so courageous that no knights of any kind could stop him landing, and his knights followed him fiercely; and so they landed in spite of Sir Mordred and all his army, and drove Sir Mordred back, so that he fled, and all his people.

So when this battle was over, King Arthur had his people who were dead buried. And then the noble Sir Gawain was found in a great boat, lying more than half dead. When Sir Arthur knew that Sir Gawain was laid so low, he went to him; and there the king grieved beyond measure, and took Sir Gawain in his arms, and three times he fainted there. And then when he came to himself, he said, "Alas, Sir Gawain, my sister's son, here you lie now, the man in the world that I loved most; and now my joy is gone. For now, my nephew Sir Gawain, I will open my heart to you: in Sir Lancelot and you I had my greatest joy, and my trust, and now I have lost my joy in you both; and so all my earthly joy is gone from me."

"My uncle King Arthur," said Sir Gawain, "believe me, my death-day has come, and all through my own rashness and wilfulness; for I have been struck on the old wound that Sir Lancelot gave me, and I feel well that I must die of it. And if Sir Lancelot had been with you as he used to be, this ill-fated war would never have begun; and I am the cause of all of it, for Sir Lancelot and his kin, through their prowess, held all your inveterate enemies in subjection and in their power. And now," said Sir Gawain, "you will miss Sir Lancelot. But alas, I would not make peace with him. And so," said Sir Gawain, "I beg you, fair uncle, let me have paper, pen and ink, so that I may write a letter to Sir Lancelot with my own hands."

And then when paper and ink were brought, Gawain was propped up, weakly, by King Arthur, for he had made his confession a little before; and then he wrote this, as the French book tells: "To Sir Lancelot, flower of all the noble knights that ever I heard of or saw in my days, I, Sir Gawain, King Lot's son of Orkney, sister's son to the noble King Arthur, send you greeting, and let you know that on the tenth day of May I was struck on the old wound that you gave me before the city of Benwick, and through that same wound that you gave me I have come to my death-day. And I want all the world to know that I, Sir Gawain, knight of the Round Table, sought my own death, and not through any fault of yours, but it was my own seeking; and so I beg you, Sir Lancelot, to come back to this realm, and see my tomb, and say some prayer, more or less, for my soul. And this same day that I wrote this letter, I was hurt to the death in the same wound that I had from your hand, Sir Lancelot; for by no nobler man could I have been killed. Also, Sir Lancelot, for all the love that ever was between us, make no delay, but come over the sea in all haste, so that you and your noble knights may rescue that noble king who made you knight, that is my lord Arthur; for he is hard beset by a false traitor, who is my half-brother, Sir Mordred. And he has had himself crowned king, and would have married my lady Queen Guinevere, and so he would have done if she had not shut herself in the Tower of London. And so on the tenth day of May just past, my lord Arthur and all of us landed against them at Dover; and there we put that false traitor, Sir Mordred, to flight, and there it was my misfortune to be struck on the wound of your stroke. And at the date of this letter, it was written only two and a half hours before my death, written with my own hand, and so signed with part of my heart's blood. And I beg you, most famous knight in the world, to come and see my tomb."

And then Sir Gawain wept, and King Arthur wept; and then they both fainted. And when they both came to themselves, the king had Sir Gawain receive his Saviour in communion. And then Sir Gawain begged the king to send for Sir Lancelot, and to cherish him above all other knights.

And so at the hour of noon Sir Gawain gave up the ghost; and then the king had him buried in a chapel inside Dover Castle; and there all men may still see his skull, and the same wound can be seen that Sir Lancelot gave him in battle. Then the king was told that Sir Mordred had pitched a new camp on Barham Down. And in the morning the king rode there to meet him, and there was a great battle between them, and many people were killed on both sides; but in the end Sir Arthur's side came off best, and Sir Mordred and his side fled to Canterbury.

Chapter 3: How afterwards Sir Gawain's ghost appeared to King Arthur, and warned him not to fight that day

And then the king had all the towns searched for his knights who had been killed, and buried them; and those who were badly wounded he had treated with soothing salves. Then many people flocked to King Arthur. And then they said that Sir Mordred was making war on King Arthur wrongfully. And then King Arthur moved with his army down by the seaside, westward towards Salisbury; and a day was appointed between King Arthur and Sir Mordred, that they should meet on a down beside Salisbury, not far from the seaside. And this day was appointed for the Monday after Trinity Sunday, at which King Arthur was exceedingly glad, that he might be avenged on Sir Mordred. Then Sir Mordred raised many people around London, for the men of Kent, Sussex and Surrey, Essex, and Suffolk and Norfolk held for the most part with Sir Mordred; and many a noble knight went over to Sir Mordred and to the king: but those who loved Sir Lancelot went over to Sir Mordred.

So on the night of Trinity Sunday, King Arthur dreamed a marvellous dream, and it was this: it seemed to him that he sat on a platform in a chair, and the chair was fastened to a wheel, and King Arthur sat on it in the richest cloth of gold that could be made. And the king thought there was beneath him, far below him, a hideous deep black water, and in it were all kinds of serpents, and dragons, and wild beasts, foul and horrible. And suddenly the king thought the wheel turned upside down, and he fell among the serpents, and every beast took him by a limb. And then the king cried out as he lay asleep in his bed, "Help!"

And then knights, squires and yeomen woke the king; and then he was so bewildered that he did not know where he was. And then he fell into a doze again, neither sleeping nor fully awake. And it truly seemed to the king that Sir Gawain came to him, with a number of fair ladies with him. And when King Arthur saw him, he said, "Welcome, my sister's son. I thought you were dead, and now I see you alive, and I owe great thanks to Almighty Jesus. O fair nephew and my sister's son, who are these ladies who have come here with you?"

"Sir," said Sir Gawain, "these are all ladies for whom I fought when I was a living man, and these are all the ones I did battle for in a righteous quarrel; and at their great prayer God has given them the grace, because I did battle for them, to bring me here to you. God has given me leave to do this much, to warn you of your death. For if you fight tomorrow with Sir Mordred, as you have both agreed, have no doubt that you will be killed, and most of your people on both sides. And for the great grace and goodness that Almighty Jesus has for you, and out of pity for you and for many other good men who would be killed there, God has sent me to you by His special grace, to warn you that on no account are you to do battle tomorrow, but to make a truce for a month; and offer generous terms, so that tomorrow is put off. For within a month Sir Lancelot will come with all his noble knights, and rescue you with honour, and kill Sir Mordred, and every one who will hold with him."

Then Sir Gawain and all the ladies vanished.

And at once the king called for his knights, squires and yeomen, and ordered them to fetch his noble lords and wise bishops to him quickly. And when they had come, the king told them his vision, what Sir Gawain had told him, and how he had warned him that if he fought in the morning he would be killed. Then the king commanded Sir Lucan the butler, and his brother Sir Bedivere, with two bishops with them, and charged them by any means they could to "make a truce for a month with Sir Mordred, and do not hold back: offer him lands and goods, as much as you think best."

So then they left, and came to Sir Mordred, where he had a grim army of a hundred thousand men. And there they pleaded with Sir Mordred for a long time; and at last Sir Mordred agreed to have Cornwall and Kent in Arthur's lifetime, and after that all England, after the days of King Arthur.

Chapter 4: How by the mischance of an adder the battle began, in which Mordred was slain and Arthur mortally wounded

Then they agreed that King Arthur and Sir Mordred should meet between their two armies, and each of them should bring fourteen men; and they came back to Arthur with this word. Then he said, "I am glad that this is done." And so he went into the field. And when Arthur was about to set out, he warned all his army that if they saw any sword drawn, "see that you come on fiercely, and kill that traitor, Sir Mordred, for I do not trust him in any way."

In the same way Sir Mordred warned his army: "If you see any sword drawn, see that you come on fiercely, and so kill everyone who stands before you; for I will not trust this treaty in any way, for I know well my father will be avenged on me."

And so they met as they had arranged, and so they were agreed and fully reconciled; and wine was fetched, and they drank. Very soon an adder came out of a little heath bush, and it stung a knight on the foot. And when the knight felt himself stung, he looked down and saw the adder, and then he drew his sword to kill the adder, and thought of no other harm. And when the armies on both sides saw that sword drawn, they blew bugles, trumpets and horns, and shouted grimly. And so both armies made for each other. And King Arthur mounted his horse, and said, "Alas, this unlucky day!" and so rode to his side. And Sir Mordred did the same. And never was there seen a more sorrowful battle in any Christian land; for there was nothing but rushing and riding, thrusting and striking, and many a grim word was spoken by each to the other, and many a deadly stroke struck. But all the while King Arthur rode through Sir Mordred's ranks many times, and did very nobly, as a noble king should, and never at any time did he flag; and Sir Mordred that day did his duty, and put himself in great peril. And so they fought all the long day, and never stopped until the noble knights were laid on the cold earth; and still they fought on till it was near night, and by that time a hundred thousand lay dead on the down. Then Arthur was mad with rage beyond measure, when he saw his people killed around him like that.

Then the king looked about him, and then he saw that of all his army and all his good knights, no more were left alive but two knights: one was Sir Lucan the butler, and the other his brother Sir Bedivere, and they were very badly wounded.

"Jesus have mercy," said the king, "what has become of all my noble knights? Alas, that ever I should see this sorrowful day, for now," said Arthur, "I have come to my end. But I wish to God I knew where that traitor Sir Mordred is, who has caused all this misery."

Then King Arthur saw where Sir Mordred was leaning on his sword among a great heap of dead men.

"Now give me my spear," said Arthur to Sir Lucan, "for over there I have spotted the traitor who has brought about all this woe."

"Sir, let him be," said Sir Lucan, "for he is ill-fated; and if you live through this ill-fated day you will be very well revenged on him. Good lord, remember your dream last night, and what the spirit of Sir Gawain told you this night; and still God in His great goodness has kept you safe till now. So, for God's sake, my lord, leave it at this. For, blessed be God, you have won the field: here there are three of us alive, and with Sir Mordred there is no one alive. And if you leave off now, this wicked day of destiny is past."

"Come death to me, come life," said the king, "now that I see him over there alone he shall never escape my hands, for I shall never have him at a better advantage."

"God speed you well," said Sir Bedivere.

Then the king took his spear in both his hands, and ran towards Sir Mordred, crying, "Traitor, now your death-day has come!"

And when Sir Mordred heard Sir Arthur, he ran at him with his sword drawn in his hand. And there King Arthur struck Sir Mordred under the shield, with a thrust of his spear, right through the body, more than a fathom. And when Sir Mordred felt that he had his death wound, he thrust himself with all the strength he had up to the hand-guard of King Arthur's spear. And even so he struck his father Arthur, with his sword held in both his hands, on the side of the head, so that the sword pierced the helmet and the skull; and with that Sir Mordred fell stark dead to the earth. And the noble Arthur fell to the earth in a faint, and there he fainted again and again. And Sir Lucan the butler and Sir Bedivere lifted him up again and again. And so, weakly, the two of them led him between them to a little chapel not far from the seaside. And when the king was there he felt himself somewhat eased.

Then they heard people crying out in the field.

"Now go, Sir Lucan," said the king, "and let me know what that noise in the field means."

So Sir Lucan left, though he was grievously wounded in many places. And as he went, he saw and heard by the moonlight how plunderers and robbers had come into the field, to plunder and to rob many a noble knight of brooches and rosaries, of many a good ring, and of many a rich jewel; and any who were not quite dead, they killed there for their armour and their riches. When Sir Lucan understood what was going on, he came back to the king as soon as he could, and told him all that he had heard and seen.

"So, by my advice," said Sir Lucan, "it is best that we bring you to some town."

"I wish it could be so," said the king.

Chapter 5: How King Arthur ordered his sword Excalibur thrown into the water, and how he was given over to ladies in a barge

"But I cannot stand, my head is reeling so," the king went on.

"Ah, Sir Lancelot," said King Arthur, "this day I have sorely missed you. Alas, that ever I was against you, for now I have my death, as Sir Gawain warned me in my dream."

Then Sir Lucan lifted the king on one side, and Sir Bedivere on the other, and in the lifting the king fainted; and with the lift Sir Lucan fell in a faint, so that part of his guts fell out of his body, and with that the noble knight's heart burst. And when the king came to, he saw Sir Lucan, how he lay foaming at the mouth, and part of his guts lay at his feet.

"Alas," said the king, "this is a very heavy sight to me, to see this noble duke die like this for my sake, for he wanted to help me, when he had more need of help than I did. Alas, he would not complain, his heart was so set on helping me. Now Jesus have mercy on his soul!"

Then Sir Bedivere wept for the death of his brother.

"Stop this mourning and weeping," said the king, "for none of it will do me any good. For believe me, if I could live myself, the death of Sir Lucan would grieve me for ever; but my time is running out fast," said the king. "So," said Arthur to Sir Bedivere, "take Excalibur, my good sword, and go with it to the water's edge over there, and when you get there I charge you to throw my sword into that water, and come back and tell me what you see there."

"My lord," said Bedivere, "your command will be done, and I will quickly bring you word again."

So Sir Bedivere left, and on the way he looked at that noble sword, and saw that the pommel and the hilt were all of precious stones; and then he said to himself, "If I throw this rich sword into the water, no good will ever come of it, only harm and loss."

And then Sir Bedivere hid Excalibur under a tree. And so, as soon as he could, he came back to the king, and said he had been to the water and had thrown the sword into the water.

"What did you see there?" said the king.

"Sir," he said, "I saw nothing but waves and winds."

"That is not the truth," said the king. "So go back quickly, and do my command; as you are dear and beloved to me, do not spare it, but throw it in."

Then Sir Bedivere went back again, and took the sword in his hand; and then it seemed to him a sin and a shame to throw away that noble sword, and so he hid the sword a second time, and went back again, and told the king that he had been to the water and done his command.

"What did you see there?" said the king.

"Sir," he said, "I saw nothing but the water rippling and the waves running dark."

"Ah, traitor, faithless," said King Arthur, "now you have betrayed me twice. Who would have thought it, of you, who have been so dear and beloved to me? And you are called a noble knight, and you would betray me for the richness of the sword. But now go again quickly, for your long delay is putting my life in great danger, for I have taken cold. And unless you do as I tell you now, if ever I set eyes on you again I will kill you with my own hands; for you would see me dead for the sake of my rich sword."

Then Sir Bedivere left, and went to the sword, and quickly took it up, and went to the water's edge; and there he wound the belt around the hilt, and then he threw the sword as far into the water as he could; and there came an arm and a hand above the water, and met it, and caught it, and so shook it three times and brandished it, and then the hand vanished with the sword into the water. So Sir Bedivere came back to the king, and told him what he had seen.

"Alas," said the king, "help me away from here, for I am afraid I have waited too long."

Then Sir Bedivere took the king on his back, and so went with him to that water's edge. And when they were at the water's edge, close by the bank a little barge was floating with many fair ladies in it, and among them all was a queen, and they all had black hoods, and they all wept and shrieked when they saw King Arthur.

"Now put me into the barge," said the king.

And so he did, gently; and there three queens received him with great mourning; and so they sat down, and King Arthur laid his head in the lap of one of them. And then that queen said, "Ah, dear brother, why have you stayed away from me so long? Alas, this wound on your head has caught too much cold."

And so then they rowed away from the land, and Sir Bedivere watched all those ladies go from him. Then Sir Bedivere cried out, "Ah, my lord Arthur, what will become of me, now that you go from me and leave me here alone among my enemies?"

"Comfort yourself," said the king, "and do as well as you can, for there is no trust left in me to trust in. For I will go into the vale of Avalon to be healed of my grievous wound. And if you never hear of me again, pray for my soul."

But all the while the queens and ladies wept and shrieked, so that it was pitiful to hear. And as soon as Sir Bedivere had lost sight of the barge, he wept and wailed, and so he took to the forest; and so he walked all that night, and in the morning he saw, between two grey old woods, a chapel and a hermitage.

Chapter 6: How Sir Bedivere found King Arthur dead the next morning in a hermitage, and how he stayed there with the hermit

Then Sir Bedivere was glad, and went there; and when he came into the chapel, he saw a hermit lying face down, stretched out on the ground, close beside a tomb that was newly dug. When the hermit saw Sir Bedivere he knew him well, for only a little before he had been the Bishop of Canterbury whom Sir Mordred had driven out.

"Sir," said Bedivere, "what man is buried there, that you pray so hard for?"

"Fair son," said the hermit, "I do not know for certain, only by guessing. But this night, at midnight, a number of ladies came here, and brought a dead body here, and begged me to bury him; and here they offered a hundred tapers, and they gave me a hundred gold coins."

"Alas," said Sir Bedivere, "that was my lord King Arthur, who lies buried here in this chapel."

Then Sir Bedivere fainted; and when he came to, he begged the hermit to let him stay there with him from then on, to live with fasting and prayer. "For I will never go from here of my own will," said Sir Bedivere, "but stay here all the days of my life to pray for my lord Arthur."

"You are welcome to me," said the hermit, "for I know you better than you think I do. You are the bold Bedivere, and the very noble duke, Sir Lucan the butler, was your brother."

Then Sir Bedivere told the hermit everything, as you have heard it before. So Sir Bedivere stayed there with the hermit who had once been Bishop of Canterbury, and there Sir Bedivere put on poor clothes, and served the hermit very humbly in fasting and in prayer.

So of Arthur I never find anything more written in books that are authoritative, nor did I ever hear or read anything more of the real certainty of his death, except that he was led away in a ship in which there were three queens: one was King Arthur's sister, Queen Morgan le Fay; the second was the Queen of North Wales; the third was the Queen of the Waste Lands. Also there was Nimue, the chief Lady of the Lake, who had married Pelleas the good knight; and this lady had done much for King Arthur, for she would never let Sir Pelleas be in any place where he would be in danger of his life; and so he lived out his days to the very end with her, in great peace. More of the death of King Arthur I could never find, except that ladies brought him to his burial; and such a one was buried there, as the hermit bore witness, who had once been Bishop of Canterbury. But even so the hermit did not know for certain that it was truly the body of King Arthur: for Sir Bedivere, knight of the Round Table, had this tale written down.

Chapter 7: Of what some men believe about the death of King Arthur, and how Queen Guinevere became a nun at Almesbury

Yet some men say in many parts of England that King Arthur is not dead, but was taken by the will of our Lord Jesus into another place; and men say that he will come again, and he will win the Holy Cross. I will not say that it shall be so, but rather I will say: here in this world he changed his life. But many men say that there is written upon his tomb this verse: Hic jacet Arthurus, rex quondam, rexque futurus. Here lies Arthur, the once and future king.

So I leave Sir Bedivere here with the hermit, who lived at that time in a chapel beside Glastonbury, and there was his hermitage. And so they lived in their prayers, and fastings, and great abstinence. And when Queen Guinevere understood that King Arthur was killed, and all the noble knights, Sir Mordred and all the rest, then the queen stole away, with five ladies, and so she went to Almesbury; and there she had herself made a nun, and wore white clothes and black, and she took on as great a penance as ever any sinful lady did in this land, and no one could ever make her merry; but she lived in fasting, prayer and works of charity, so that all kinds of people marvelled at how virtuously she was changed. Now we leave Queen Guinevere in Almesbury, a nun in white clothes and black, and there she was abbess and ruler, as was only right; and we turn from her, and speak of Sir Lancelot du Lake.

Chapter 8: How Sir Lancelot, when he heard of the death of King Arthur and of Sir Gawain, and other matters, came to England

And when he heard in his own country that Sir Mordred was crowned king in England, and had made war against King Arthur, his own father, and would hinder him from landing in his own land; and when it was also told Sir Lancelot how Sir Mordred had laid siege to the Tower of London, because the queen would not marry him; then Sir Lancelot was angry beyond measure, and said to his kinsmen, "Alas, that double traitor Sir Mordred! Now I regret that he ever escaped my hands, for he has done great shame to my lord Arthur. For I can tell from the sorrowful letter that my lord Sir Gawain sent me, on whose soul Jesus have mercy, that my lord Arthur is in a very hard spot. Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "that I should ever live to hear that the most noble king, who made me a knight, is overthrown like this by his own subject in his own kingdom! And this sorrowful letter that my lord Sir Gawain sent me before his death, begging me to come and see his tomb: believe me, his sorrowful words shall never leave my heart, for he was as noble a knight as ever was born. And in an ill-fated hour was I born, that I should ever have the ill luck to kill, first Sir Gawain, Sir Gaheris the good knight, and my own friend Sir Gareth, that most noble knight. Alas, I may well say I am ill-fated," said Sir Lancelot, "that I should ever do things so ill-fatedly. And alas, and yet I never had the luck to kill that traitor, Sir Mordred!"

"Leave your laments," said Sir Bors, "and first avenge the death of Sir Gawain. And it will be well done for you to see Sir Gawain's tomb; and secondly, avenge my lord Arthur, and my lady Queen Guinevere."

"I thank you," said Sir Lancelot, "for you always look to my honour."

Then they made themselves ready with all the haste they could, with ships and galleys, for Sir Lancelot and his army to cross into England. And so he crossed the sea until he came to Dover, and there he landed with seven kings, and their numbers were fearsome to behold. Then Sir Lancelot asked the men of Dover what had become of King Arthur. Then the people told him how he was killed, and Sir Mordred, and a hundred thousand died in one day; and how Sir Mordred had given King Arthur the first battle there at his landing, and there the good Sir Gawain was killed; and how the next morning Sir Mordred fought with the king on Barham Down, and there the king got the better of Sir Mordred.

"Alas," said Sir Lancelot, "this is the heaviest news that ever came to me. Now, fair sirs," said Sir Lancelot, "show me the tomb of Sir Gawain."

And then certain people of the town brought him into the castle of Dover, and showed him the tomb. Then Sir Lancelot knelt down and wept, and prayed with all his heart for his soul. And that night he gave out alms, and all who would come had as much meat, fish, wine and ale as they wanted, and every man and woman had twelve pence, whoever came. He dealt out this money with his own hand, in a mourning gown; and all the while he wept, and begged them to pray for the soul of Sir Gawain. And the next morning all the priests and clerks who could be found in the country were there, and sang the Requiem mass. And there Sir Lancelot made the first offering, and he offered a hundred pounds; and then the seven kings offered forty pounds apiece; and there were also a thousand knights, and each of them offered a pound; and the offering lasted from morning till night. And Sir Lancelot lay two nights on his tomb, praying and weeping.

Then on the third day Sir Lancelot called the kings, dukes, earls, barons and knights together, and spoke like this: "My fair lords, I thank you all for coming into this country with me. But we came too late, and I shall regret it as long as I live; but against death no man may rebel. But since it is so," said Sir Lancelot, "I will ride myself and look for my lady Queen Guinevere, for I hear she has had great pain and much distress; and I have heard that she has fled into the west. Therefore you shall all wait for me here, and unless I come back within fifteen days, then take your ships and your company, and go home to your own country, for I will do as I tell you."

Chapter 9: How Sir Lancelot set out to find Queen Guinevere, and how he found her at Almesbury

Then Sir Bors de Ganis came, and said, "My lord Sir Lancelot, what do you mean to do, riding now through this kingdom? Believe me, you will find few friends."

"Be that as it may," said Sir Lancelot, "you stay here, for I will go on my journey, and no man or boy shall go with me."

So it was no use arguing, and he left and rode westward, and there he searched for seven or eight days. And at last he came to a nunnery, and then Queen Guinevere caught sight of Sir Lancelot as he walked in the cloister. And when she saw him there she fainted three times, so that all the ladies and gentlewomen had their hands full holding the queen up. So when she could speak, she called ladies and gentlewomen to her, and said, "You wonder, fair ladies, why I carry on like this. Truly," she said, "it is at the sight of that knight who is standing over there. So I beg you all, call him to me."

When Sir Lancelot was brought to her, she said to all the ladies, "Through this man and me all this war has been brought about, and the death of the noblest knights in the world; for through the love that we have loved together my most noble lord is killed. Therefore, Sir Lancelot, know this: I have set myself on this course to win the salvation of my soul. And yet I trust, through God's grace, that after my death I shall have a sight of the blessed face of Christ, and at Doomsday sit on His right side; for there are saints in heaven as sinful as ever I was. Therefore, Sir Lancelot, I ask you and beg you with all my heart, for all the love that ever was between us, never to look me in the face again. And I command you, in God's name, to leave my company, and go back to your kingdom, and keep your realm well from war and ruin. For as much as I have loved you, my heart will not let me see you, for through you and me the flower of kings and knights is destroyed. Therefore, Sir Lancelot, go to your kingdom, and there take a wife, and live with her in joy and happiness. And I beg you with all my heart, pray for me to our Lord, that I may make amends for my sinful life."

"Now, sweet madam," said Sir Lancelot, "do you want me to go back now to my own country, and marry a lady there? No, madam, believe me, that I will never do, for I will never be so false to you in what I have promised. But the same life that you have taken up, I will take up too, to please Jesus, and above all I mean to pray for you."

"If you will do that," said the queen, "keep your promise. But I can never believe that you will not turn back to the world again."

"Well, madam," he said, "you may say what you please, but you never yet knew me to break my promise; and God forbid that I should not forsake the world as you have done. For in the quest of the Holy Grail I would have forsaken the vanities of the world, had it not been for your love. And if I had done so at that time, with my heart, will and thought, I would have surpassed all the knights who were on the quest of the Grail, except Sir Galahad, my son. And therefore, lady, since you have given yourself to the perfect life, I must by right give myself to it too. For I call God to witness, in you I have had all my earthly joy; and if I had found you of another mind now, I had meant to take you away to my own kingdom."

Chapter 10: How Sir Lancelot came to the hermitage where the Archbishop of Canterbury was, and how he put on a monk's habit

"But since I find you of this mind," Sir Lancelot went on, "I assure you faithfully, I will give myself to penance for ever, and pray while my life lasts, if I can find any hermit, of the grey order or the white, who will take me in. And so, madam, I beg you, kiss me, and never again."

"No," said the queen, "that I will never do. Keep yourself from such things now."

And they parted. But there was never a man so hard-hearted that he would not have wept to see the grief they made; for they lamented as if they had been stung with spears, and many times they fainted, and the ladies carried the queen to her room.

And Sir Lancelot came to himself, and went and took his horse, and rode all that day and all night in a forest, weeping. And at last he saw a hermitage, and a chapel standing between two cliffs; and then he heard a little bell ringing for mass, and he rode there and dismounted, and tied his horse to the gate, and heard mass. And the one who sang the mass was the Bishop of Canterbury. Both the Bishop and Sir Bedivere knew Sir Lancelot, and they talked together after mass. But when Sir Bedivere had told his whole tale, Sir Lancelot's heart almost burst for sorrow, and Sir Lancelot threw his arms wide, and said, "Alas, who can trust this world?" And then he knelt down on his knee, and begged the Bishop to hear his confession and absolve him. And then he begged the Bishop to let him be his brother. Then the Bishop said, "Gladly." And there he put a habit on Sir Lancelot, and there he served God day and night with prayers and fasting.

So the great army waited at Dover. And then Sir Lionel took fifteen lords with him, and rode to London to look for Sir Lancelot; and there Sir Lionel was killed, and many of his lords. Then Sir Bors de Ganis had the great army go home again; and Sir Bors, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Blamore, Sir Bleoberis, with others of Sir Lancelot's kin, took it on themselves to ride all over England, across and lengthwise, to look for Sir Lancelot. So Sir Bors by chance rode on until he came to the same chapel where Sir Lancelot was; and so Sir Bors heard a little bell tolling, ringing for mass; and there he dismounted and heard mass. And when mass was done, the Bishop, Sir Lancelot and Sir Bedivere came to Sir Bors. And when Sir Bors saw Sir Lancelot dressed in that manner, he begged the Bishop that he might wear the same. And so a habit was put on him, and there he lived in prayer and fasting. And within half a year there had come Sir Galihud, Sir Galihodin, Sir Blamore, Sir Bleoberis, Sir Villiars, Sir Clarrus and Sir Gahalantine. So all these seven noble knights stayed on there. And when they saw that Sir Lancelot had given himself to such a perfect life, they had no wish to leave, but took the same habit as he had.

So they lived in great penance for six years; and then Sir Lancelot was ordained a priest by the Bishop, and for a year he sang mass. And there was not one of these other knights who did not read in books, and help to sing mass, and ring bells, and do all kinds of service with their own hands. And so their horses went wherever they liked, for they paid no attention to any worldly riches. For when they saw Sir Lancelot endure such penance, in prayers and fasting, they cared nothing what hardship they endured, seeing the noblest knight in the world keep such abstinence that he grew very thin. And so one night a vision came to Sir Lancelot, and charged him, in remission of his sins, to hurry to Almesbury: "And by the time you get there, you will find Queen Guinevere dead. And therefore take your companions with you, and get them a horse bier, and fetch her body, and bury her by her husband, the noble King Arthur." So this vision came to Sir Lancelot three times in one night.

Chapter 11: How Sir Lancelot went with his seven companions to Almesbury, and found Queen Guinevere dead there, and how they carried her to Glastonbury

Then Sir Lancelot got up before daybreak, and told the hermit.

"It would be well done," said the hermit, "for you to make yourself ready, and not disobey the vision."

Then Sir Lancelot took his eight companions with him, and they went on foot from Glastonbury to Almesbury, which is little more than thirty miles. And they got there within two days, for they were weak and feeble at walking. And when Sir Lancelot had come into the nunnery at Almesbury, Queen Guinevere had died only half an hour before. And the ladies told Sir Lancelot that Queen Guinevere had told them all, before she died, that Sir Lancelot had been a priest for nearly a year: "And he is coming here as fast as he can to fetch my body; and he shall bury me beside my lord, King Arthur." And so the queen said in the hearing of them all, "I beseech Almighty God that I may never have the power to see Sir Lancelot with my worldly eyes." "And this," said all the ladies, "was her prayer all the time for these two days, until she was dead."

Then Sir Lancelot looked on her face, but he did not weep much, but sighed. And so he performed all the rites of the service himself, both the dirge and, the next morning, the mass he sang. And a horse bier was made ready; and so, with a hundred torches always burning around the queen's body, and with Sir Lancelot and his eight companions always walking around the horse bier, singing and reading many a holy prayer, and burning frankincense over the body, Sir Lancelot and his eight companions went on foot from Almesbury to Glastonbury.

And when they had come to the chapel and the hermitage, she had a dirge there, with great devotion. And the next morning the hermit who had once been Bishop of Canterbury sang the Requiem mass with great devotion. And Sir Lancelot was the first to make an offering, and then his eight companions too. And then she was wrapped in waxed cloth of Rennes, from head to toe, thirty times over, and after that she was put in a sheet of lead, and then in a coffin of marble. And when she was put in the earth, Sir Lancelot fainted, and lay still a long time, until the hermit came and woke him, and said, "You are to blame, for you displease God with such a show of grief."

"Truly," said Sir Lancelot, "I trust I do not displease God, for He knows what is in my heart. For my sorrow was not, and is not, for any delight in sin; but my sorrow can never have an end. For when I remember her beauty, and her nobility, that was in her king as well as in her, then when I saw his body and her body lying together like this, truly my heart would not hold up my sorrowful body. And also when I remember how, through my failing, my arrogance and my pride, they were both laid so low, who were the peerless of all Christian people who ever lived, believe me," said Sir Lancelot, "this remembrance of their kindness and my unkindness sank so deep into my heart that I could not hold myself up."

So the French book tells it.

Chapter 12: How Sir Lancelot fell sick and afterwards died, and how his body was carried to Joyous Gard to be buried

Then Sir Lancelot never afterwards ate more than a little food, nor drank, until he was dead. For then he sickened more and more, and dried up, and wasted away. For neither the Bishop nor any of his companions could make him eat, and he drank little, so that he had become a cubit shorter than he had been, and people could not recognise him. For always, day and night, he prayed, though sometimes he slept a broken sleep; and he was always lying face down on the tomb of King Arthur and Queen Guinevere. And there was no comfort that the Bishop, or Sir Bors, or any of his companions could give him that did any good. So within six weeks after, Sir Lancelot fell sick, and lay in his bed; and then he sent for the Bishop who was a hermit there, and all his true companions. Then Sir Lancelot said in a sorrowful voice, "Sir Bishop, I beg you, give me all the rites that belong to a Christian man."

"You won't need them," said the hermit and all his companions. "It is only melancholy in your blood. You will be well mended by the grace of God tomorrow."

"My fair lords," said Sir Lancelot, "believe me, my sorrowful body is bound for the earth. I have had warning of it, more than I will tell you now. Therefore give me my rites."

So when he had been given communion and anointed, and had all that a Christian man ought to have, he begged the Bishop that his companions might carry his body to Joyous Gard. (Some men say it was Alnwick, and some men say it was Bamburgh.)

"Even so," said Sir Lancelot, "I am deeply sorry for it, but I once made a vow that I would be buried in Joyous Gard. And so as not to break my vow, I beg you all, take me there."

Then there was weeping and wringing of hands among his companions.

So at a certain hour of the night they all went to their beds, for they all lay in one room. And so after midnight, towards day, the Bishop who was then a hermit, as he lay asleep in his bed, burst into great laughter. And with that the whole company woke up, and came to the Bishop, and asked him what was the matter.

"Ah, Jesus have mercy," said the Bishop, "why did you wake me? I was never in all my life so happy and so much at ease."

"Why is that?" said Sir Bors.

"Truly," said the Bishop, "Sir Lancelot was here with me, with more angels than I ever saw men in one day. And I saw the angels lift Sir Lancelot up to heaven, and the gates of heaven opened to receive him."

"That is only the troubling of dreams," said Sir Bors, "for I don't doubt that there is nothing wrong with Sir Lancelot but good."

"That may well be," said the Bishop. "Go to his bed, and then you will find out the truth."

So when Sir Bors and his companions came to his bed they found him stone dead, and he lay as if he had smiled, and the sweetest scent around him that they had ever smelled.

Then there was weeping and wringing of hands, and the greatest grief that ever men made. And in the morning the Bishop said his Requiem mass, and afterwards the Bishop and all the nine knights put Sir Lancelot in the same horse bier that Queen Guinevere had been laid in before she was buried. And so the Bishop and all of them together went with the body of Sir Lancelot day after day, until they came to Joyous Gard; and all the way they had a hundred torches burning around him. And so within fifteen days they came to Joyous Gard. And there they laid his body in the middle of the choir, and sang and read many psalms and prayers over him and around him.

And all the while his face was left uncovered and bare, so that all people might look on him. For such was the custom in those days, that all men of honour should lie like that with their faces uncovered until they were buried. And just as they were at their service, there came Sir Ector de Maris, who for seven years had searched all England, Scotland and Wales, looking for his brother, Sir Lancelot.

Chapter 13: How Sir Ector found his brother Sir Lancelot dead, and how Constantine reigned after Arthur, and of the end of this book

And when Sir Ector heard such sound and saw such light in the choir of Joyous Gard, he dismounted and let his horse go, and came into the choir, and there he saw men singing and weeping. And they all knew Sir Ector, but he did not know them. Then Sir Bors went to Sir Ector, and told him how his brother, Sir Lancelot, lay there dead; and then Sir Ector threw his shield, sword and helmet from him. And when he looked on Sir Lancelot's face, he fell down in a faint. And when he came to, it would be hard for any tongue to tell the sorrowful laments he made for his brother.

"Ah, Lancelot," he said, "you were the head of all Christian knights! And now I dare say," said Sir Ector, "you, Sir Lancelot, lying there, that you were never matched by any earthly knight's hand. And you were the most courteous knight that ever bore shield. And you were the truest friend to your lover that ever bestrode horse. And you were the truest lover, of a sinful man, that ever loved woman. And you were the kindest man that ever struck with sword. And you were the goodliest person that ever came among the press of knights. And you were the meekest man and the gentlest that ever ate in hall among ladies. And you were the sternest knight to your mortal foe that ever put spear in the rest."

Then there was weeping and grief beyond measure.

So they kept Sir Lancelot's body above ground for fifteen days, and then they buried it with great devotion. And then, at their leisure, they all went with the Bishop of Canterbury to his hermitage, and there they were together for more than a month. Then Sir Constantine, who was the son of Sir Cador of Cornwall, was chosen king of England. And he was a most noble knight, and he ruled this realm with honour. And then this King Constantine sent for the Bishop of Canterbury, for he had heard where he was. And so he was restored to his bishopric, and left that hermitage. And Sir Bedivere stayed on there as a hermit to the end of his life. Then Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Gahalantine, Sir Galihud, Sir Galihodin, Sir Blamore, Sir Bleoberis, Sir Villiers the Valiant and Sir Clarrus of Clermont, all these knights went back to their own countries. King Constantine would have kept them with him, but they would not stay in this realm. And there they all lived in their countries as holy men. And some English books say that they never went out of England after the death of Sir Lancelot, but that was only the partiality of the authors. For the French book says, and it is a book of authority, that Sir Bors, Sir Ector, Sir Blamore and Sir Bleoberis went into the Holy Land, where Jesus Christ lived and died, as soon as they had settled their lands. For the book says that Sir Lancelot commanded them to do so before he passed out of this world. And these four knights fought many battles against the unbelievers, the Turks. And there they died upon a Good Friday, for God's sake.

Here is the end of the book of King Arthur and of his noble knights of the Round Table, who, when they were all together, were always a hundred and forty. And here is the end of the death of Arthur. I pray you all, gentlemen and gentlewomen who read this book of Arthur and his knights from the beginning to the end, pray for me while I am alive, that God send me good deliverance, and when I am dead, I pray you all, pray for my soul. For this book was finished in the ninth year of the reign of King Edward the Fourth, by Sir Thomas Malory, knight, as Jesus help him by his great might, as he is the servant of Jesus both day and night.

Thus ends this noble and joyous book entitled Le Morte d'Arthur, which, for all its title, tells of the birth, life and deeds of the said King Arthur, and of his noble knights of the Round Table, their marvellous quests and adventures, the achieving of the Holy Grail, and in the end the sorrowful death and departing out of this world of them all. This book was translated into English by Sir Thomas Malory, knight, as is said before, and by me divided into twenty-one books, set into chapters and printed, and finished in the abbey at Westminster, the last day of July, in the year of our Lord 1485.
